This game is chocked full of blood, fun, hectic choices, running, VERMIN, atmosphere, and an unforgiving difficulty. It really is L4D set in the Warhammer Old World but that's only a good thing. Where L4D perfectly captured the atmosphere and ambience of a zombie apocalypse, Warhammer: Vermintide has the atmosphere and vibe of the Warhammer World in general - and the Empire and Skavens in particular - nailed!
It's not an easy game but it's a good game that gives you a challenge, makes you fight through it and then have a real sense of achievement once you're done. The game will ofcourse be easier with three friends, but my brother and I managed to do the first few missions with just the two of us and 2 avatars controlled by the AI. The AI will get confused from time to time but only once did it really pose a problem (the two NPCs insisted we killed a Ratling gunner that was standing on the top of a house very far off).
The five classes are each great in their own way and feels/plays reasonably differently (although Dwarf with Axe/Shield and Empire Soldier with Sword/Shield does look alike). Most will find a favourite or two and start playing them primarily to get more skilled with them. This really pays off as it helps you in identifying strengths/weaknesses.
If you liked L4D or L4D2 you should get this game.
If you like action-packed FPS games you should get this game.
If you like the Warhammer World you should get this game.

I don't frequently review games, but I feel like this deserves some mention. I don't know what concerns me more about this game: the fact that the voice acting is so horrible, or that people actually gave this game positive reviews.
I was mildly annoyed with how poor the voice acting was until I reached the character that everyone else seems to be mentioning, "The Rat." I'm wondering how this made it through a team of people who are smart enough to render these wonderful enviornments and all of the beautiful set pieces that are strewn throughout.  Most of the games shortcomings are pretty easily tolerable until you get to the point where the game starts throwing deliberate insta-death at you.
That platforming isn't really all that well established earlier on and then suddenly you are forced to utilize skills that you don't have in some Super Meatboy nonsense maze. Out of nowhere instadeath can be fun for a bit but building the entire middle point of your game around it really concerns me.
Additionally I'm confused as to what on earth is going on with the story. I assume that at the deaths of some of the characters the player is supposed to feel "sad." I don't even know the names of the people that are dying or why I'm chasing after them. Additionally there are a few completely nonsensical flashbacks that don't really add to the plot. If I'm supposed to be getting backstory from the "lost journal" bits that I keep finding, I'm not. I don't care enough about the main character to bother with more exposition.
Anyway, this review is just a reiteration of what everyone else was saying. I posted it because I'm deeply concerned that so many other people enjoyed this game.
Grab it if it's on sale. Or hell, just close your hand in a door and get the same amount of enjoyment out of it.

This reminds me of Limbo in a couple of ways. First, obviously, the silhouette art style. Second, the gameplay feels like Limbo, it's a 2.5D platformer that demands repetition. Walk forward, get killed by trap, restart, walk forward avoiding trap, walk forward again die by another trap, repeat. Doesn't sound like loads of fun putting it this way but can be satisfying. the similarities with Limbo end there, as Deadlight lacks most of what made Limbo shine, its originality. In fact these games lie in complete opposite sides of the originality spectrum! Deadlight is a zombie apocalipse game, for christ sake. They call zombies "shadows", and everytime they do that I roll my eyes. I rolled my eyes a lot during this game.
My biggest complaint with the gameplay is how finicky it seems to interact with the environment. These are not a big issue during normal platforming, but when the game shoves a time constraint in there is incredibly frustrating. There was this part where I had to run from zombies, I'm sorry, 'shadows' and block the door behind you. You have to stop, turn around, take a step forward, not so much! back up a little, there, now turn around again, good! NOW you can interact with that thing to block the door. I mean, if you weren't eaten by zombies now. Stuff like that sucks.
Don't tell me to relax! I'm ALREADY RELAXED !!!1 :E

A short platformer with a zombie-related story. Actually, it's pretty much The Walking Dead for pre-schoolers, but without any of the good parts.
OVERALL - 4 / 10
PROS
+ good visuals / art
+ controls aren't completely terrible
CONS
- combat doesn't feel like it was well thought out (it just kind of... exists, and only seems to act as a barrier for puzzles)
- story and dialogue are cringe-worthy (the worst voice acting since Sang-Froid)
- "secrets" aren't secret (also, why the hell are the main character's diary pages EVERYWHERE?!)
- seriously, the dialogue is horrid, and the choices people make are absurd
- why can we only move on a 2D plane when there are quite obviously better paths in the 3D environment?
DETAILS
I have absolutely no idea why this game has such good reviews, it is terrible. You can play 80-90% of the game just by using WASD and space, and eve most of that is spent just moving right on the screen and jumping. Every once in a while a zombie will get in your way and you'll have to use your other hand to swat at it and kill it.
There aren't any real puzzles in the game, you just end up running and climbing things almost the entire time. The items you get along the way are mostly pointless. You get a slingshot that is only used for a couple of puzzles in the middle of the game, and also get 2 weapons (shotgun and a pistol) which are about is useful.
The ending of this game just made me laugh at how absurd and terrible the "AI" is: [extremely minor spoiler] somehow you're fighting human soldiers that have rifles, yet instead of killing you they really like to run up to you and point their guns at you and then let you draw your weapon and kill them. I'm entirely convinced the people who made this game have no idea what a real gunfight looks like.
Anyways, this game was really not even worth the time of writing this review, so I'm just going to end here and hopefully you will, too.

Melody's Escape is exactly what it markets itself as. It's a rythym/runner game that analyzes audio files that you select from your computer and creates a course based on the tempo and intensity of the song. While initially I was not exactly happy with the visuals straining my eyes while I played my first couple of songs, I realized this was only because I had neglected to change some visual settings to fit my computer well. Now that I have my settings down the game runs incredibly smoothly at about 150 to 200fps. But let's get down to what this review is really about.
I've only played the game for about two hours at the time of writing and I can already say I'm hooked and even passionate enough about the game to have already earned the badge. The gameplay is largely dependant on the type of song that you chose for the level, as when the intensity of the song changes so does your game. The first song I played was a tribute song for Lapis Lazuli (Steven Universe) that my girlfriend showed me just minutes before I bought the game. I was so astonished at how fun the game was (even though I was terrible at the game at first). It's just brilliant, how Melody's Escape turns your music into a track that fits so well. It was like someone had spent hours designing the level just for that song, but it had only taken roughly ten seconds. Now mind you, the tracks aren't always so perfect as it depends largely on the audio file you use.
Before you purchase this game you should know that there are no pre-installed songs in this game, so you'll need to hunt down the mp3 file of the songs that you'd like to play. I suggest one of the many free sites that converts youtube videos into an mp3 to start building a collection of tracks to play in this game.

So, over a year since I reviewed this, and I'm reviewing my review. This game is better, but not quite what it used to be.
As a slightly OCD person who loves exploration, crafting and survival but hates zombies and multiplayer, this game is great... to a point.
I still haven't bothered figured out the colony building stuff yet, because it isn't explained very well and there is almost endless fun to be had wandering around the beautiful landscapes collecting plants, hunting the wildlife, mining for materials, building crazy hideouts and dodging angry aliens.
Sure there is a basic storyline there to sort of help you learn the systems, but you can choose to ignore it and it just seems to be kept on indefinite pause. Unfortunately you don't start with many crafting recipies and it takes a long time to collect them.
Adventure mode dispenses with the story altogether and lets you go totally nuts. This WAS much better because you used to start with all the crafting recipies you needed, now there is some sort of story thing added into Adventure mode, and you don't start with everything.
Feel like carving a secret base into one of those giant rock pillars? Sure!
Build a ridiculous treehouse mansion? Sure!
Dig a giant pitfall trap to help you kill those tough critters? Sure!
(Just remember the gravity differences!)
And then there is the item creation system... where the creative fun begins all over again with the ability to custom design weapons, vehicles and objects... almost anything you can think of, and a few things you hadn't. Just be careful with the vehicles, as there are some balance issues if you don't know what you're doing.
Unless you need to drag an NPC on a follow mission, I find running and the jetpack are the best ways to get around anyway.
There are a few problems:
-Waiting for repairs. Earlier on, you could repair your tools instantly at a machine as long as you had the right materials. This was brilliant. Now you need the right materials and a minute. 60 seconds realtime. WHY? I don't want to twiddle my thumbs for a minute, I want to repair my stuff so I can get on with playing your game! That is why I bought your game. Sadly it is now easier to continually make new stuff and sell worn out crap to the NPCs.
-The supercritters. At one point you could build a gun with 4 barrels to help you hunt those tough critters the quest occasionally asks for, but someone thought that made the game too easy. Now you need to dig yourself a defensible hole and pray the critter lines up in the right place so you can spend 5 minutes realtime shooting it.
-Having to begin all over again after any major update. I was okay with this at first, but it keeps  happening every now and then. Hopefully this will be over now it is officially released.
-The Workshop. I don't know why they bothered, because subscribing to anything doesn't work.
This was the first Early Access game I bought, but it didn't feel like one. Everything that I wanted was extremely well done, and the bits I didn't really care about were the dodgy bits they seemed to be working on. Which was great, as I didn't use them ayway. It felt like they released a good game, and were still working away to make it truly epic. And they're still going.
As long as you can ignore the Workshop and the repair wait, this game is brilliant.
Calling this game an alpha release is generous at best. You will not play this game, you will test it for bugs, and there will be many.

It's a 2D Sidescroller/Platformer (like the original "Prince of Persia" or "Flashback").
The game is *alright* but I couldn't get myself motivated to play it a second time because wrestling with the clunky controls makes it a very frustrating experience (even on a xbox controller).
The graphics are great for the genre, the concept is good, the atmosphere is alright, but a platformer with crappy controls will fall flat everytime. I don't mind the linearity so much in this genre but the game is too slow and tutorialized to help make a case for replayability (and considering it took me about 2h on my only run, that kinds of seals the matter).

This game is a mixed bag. The idea is decent but the execution is lacking. This is best described as prince of persia with guns where you would rather flight than fight. It's fairly short (about 6h for everything game has to offer - nightmare mode), but that's not really it's biggest gripe.
The controls are slugish and nonresponsive. This is especially true when you need to draw a weapon after say having just jumped. There were also at least 3-4 times when I bugged the game out (no way forward other than to reset to last checkpoint). Since I played this on a keyboard I imagine the experience would be better on a controller (since this was clearly ported from Xbox).
During the middle part of the game, you will be going through a trap maze. While the traps themselves are not difficult, it _is_ difficult sometimes to figure out what can be interacted with in the scene to work around the problem. Given sensitive timing this will lead to you dying quite a bit until you figure out the strategy. Checkpoints are not too far out, but exiting the game and coming back in will set you back much further (in my experience).
On the good side, graphics are very decent, voice acting feels somewhat forced but its ok. I find the slideshow scenes between levels to be a joke (sorry guys we had a tight budget), but did not detract from the game. Music improves the experience a bit. Controls and lack of hints aside, the challenge is set just right, provided you can ignore the frustration from sluggish controls at times.
Verdict? Get it only if you love platformers and only if its on steep discount (75%).

When it comes to “use your own music” games, Steam’s been noticeably lacking something a bit more like a traditional rhythm game, especially since Rhythm Zone got pulled and Stepmania isn’t on Steam. Melody’s Escape fills this void.
It’s a visually impressive game, I’ll give it that; but it’s Early Access, and it’s just very, very barebones at the moment. What you see in the trailer is all you’re getting: you’re an iPod model running across silhouetted terrain and hitting notes in time to the music. You get teleported to one of four psychedelic environments depending on the music’s level of intensity. If you crank up the difficulty, you’ll need to use twin-stick controls to hit different types of notes separately: one stick to navigate terrain, and the other to collect colored orbs. The harder modes can be quite frustrating if you’re not the ambidextrous type, and personally I opted to stay on a lower skill level that didn’t make me have to keep stopping to think about which stick I needed to use. You’re scored based on how many notes you hit, how well you hit each individual note, and how long you held streaks for multipliers.
(Note: if you’re impressed with the part in the trailer where she flies, you should know that they cut out that mechanic and replaced it with something else).
There are some interesting customization features. You can customize the skin of your character, or search Steam Workshop for player-created skins. You can also customize your own difficulty level with a surprising number of options.
And that’s basically it. There are no leaderboards yet, and not a lot of variety to the levels. There are no unlockables, no powerups, and no level progression. But what’s there is very solid and bug-free, the beat detection and level generation is suitably forgiving and works well enough, not to mention that it all just looks so awesome. Seeing as though it’s an Early Access game, I’m giving it a tentative thumbs-up; if you want a classic DDR / Guitar Hero experience generated by your own music, this is for you. If you like what you see, at least give it a follow so you can see if anything becomes of this project.

Almost as good as the original. The soundtrack is excellent again, and the gameplay remains similar. However, the level design has taken a turn for the worse.
Specifically, the game uses extremely long hallways in several levels, to the point where it becomes frustrating. Enemies can and will shoot you from a distance and you'll have no chance to respond. Your only hope is to memorize their approximate locations and shoot blindly off-screen. This is most noticeable in the Hawaii segments, which seem like a different person made them.
There's a reason cs_office isn't a realistic depiction of an office in Counter-Strike: the long, regular hallways make for dull gameplay. So it is in HM2's Hawaii sections, combined with some seriously psychic AI.
Finally, the very beginning of the game has a "sexual violence or not" prompt. As far as I can tell, it applies to one scene and is never used again. I'm not sure if they were going for Super Edgy Themes but they failed.
The core gameplay is mostly excellent. If you liked HM1, you'll like this one. If you haven't played HM1, play that first. This is more difficult, less polished, and lengthier.

Wouldn't recommend it.  Huge fan of the first game, absolutely loved it, but this game did away with a lot of the best parts.  You play as characters using masks maybe 15% of the total game, the narrative jumps around Tarantino-style (not a bad thing in and of itself, but done here in a way that seems to force the story down your throat while also being conceitedly full of itself for having a story that's told anachronically).  Levels are ridiculously big, which just amounts to a lot of lost work when one guy with a pistol snipes you from off screen setting you back ten minutes of carefully orchestrated kills. "Cheap deaths" are the order of the day, with enemies sniping you from across the room off-screen (even when you are fully extended in their direction in look mode).  Way more gun-toting enemies is going to me way more often you will find yourself up against insurmountable odds.  Not only that, but if you're going melee from personal choice or a mask choice, you will spend an inordinate amount of time waiting for one guy to isolate himself so you can alert him and pull him over to you, kill him, and repeat with the next ten guys. All the while trying to not get shot through four sets of windows that line up just perfectly so the dude in the exact opposite corner of the building from you happens to patrol by at the just the right second and kills you flawlessly. Start over.
The game I loved can be seen in how it inspired this game, but they really just ruined it.  It's full of itself, it's way too hard to be worth it (I beat it, but at that point, it was more about spite and pride than anything even resembling enjoyment), and the best things that made HM1 great are either removed entirely, ignored, or in way too small of quantity here.
Pay money for the SOUNDTRACK.  THAT is still incredible.  Don't pay money for the game.

After about 60+ Hours, I LOVE this game, but, I won't recommend this game to other people. There are quite a few reasons that this game is not recommended. Some small reasons and many big reasons why I cannot recommend this game. After being on VETERAN status, which you have to pay for real money, I've put approximately 30+ hours of gameplay on one of my characters and I'm still no where near the point where I can even command an Assault Team. The Grind in this game, even with Veteran status is LONG and Unending.
Weapons; the difference in weapons available to a new player and a player who either paid for, or have played the game for quite awhile is as different as night and day. The beginner weapons available are nowhere near as potent as weapons that are unlockable later. It's strange how people have so many issues with this game, commenting that their AMD cards can't handle the game and such. I've got an R9 Series card, a 280 if I recall correctly and only around 3 gigs of Ram and plethora of cores. I have no issues running this game at all on medium high settings at all. The game IS CPU heavy, I will have to say my CPU is almost always at 80% or higher while playing but the developers have already stated they know this is an issue and they're working to fix it, specifically the FX for weapons and lighting being the main culprit for this.  That's a good selling point for me by the way, the developpers speaking with the fans.
The connectivity issues I've actually only had issues with /once/ during the beta, when the game exploded in popularity and people started trying to hack into their servers for whatever reason. The developpers kept in contact with the fans, and worked on it through the night as they do live in Sweden mind you. After that, there were no connection issues. The aspect of host migration is kind of disappointing but like I've mentioned prior, the developpers are working on fixing that. I also haven't had any of the sync errors people seem to have with the skaven hitting through walls, and at unimaginable distances.
The loot system is sometimes a letdown, but also sometimes it's a damn great thing. It's based off of dice, 7 in total with 5 variants of dice to use. Bone dice, with 2/6 sides being counted as a success, Loot Dice, 3/6, Chaos 5/6, and Skaven which are a gaurenteed boost to your loot with 6/6. The game has ways of allowing players to increase their chance at better loot through gathering tomes and grimoires, the tomes awarding Chaos die, andthe Grimoires awarding the Skaven die. There is /no/ trading in the game, but as always when the fanbase asked about it on Reddit the devs said they'd be making tweaks and adding things to the loot system if the fanbase asks for it. Something people seemingly don't quite understand about the Dev team.
As for actual gameplay, it's quite addicting. The ranged combat is satisfying, especially with something as lackluster as a bow. The guns in the game feel, and hit heavy and you can tell when it hits the skaven fur that it's done damage. The enemies are rather textbook, with your horde based rats, armored tanks who are hard to take down for some and also travel in randomized patrols, Globadiers who throw toxin that disorients and damages, Gutter Runners who are copy pasted hunters from L4D, Mangrabbers who drag you away and lynch you, mind you they're also REALLY squishy, a single longbow shot takes them down and they have to get close. OP as♥♥♥♥♥♥at first, but easy to deal with. Then the Rat Ogre, a team wiper or sometimes a total push over based on equipment. It's basically a tank, and functions nearly the same without throwing concrete. Melee feels great, being fluid and lethal for some classes and for others hard and absolutely thrashing to anything caught in the path. I.E. Waywatcher and Imperial Soldier respectivelly.
Overall the games a solid 9/10 in my book, and will easily raise up towards a ten as the devs release more content, more characters, and more loot through paid and free DLC.  Just for a quick reference for those who do read this, this is the Reddit Ask us anything that Fatshark(The Company behind Vermintide) held during the beta.
You'll see quickly that some of the concerns and questions the negative reviews have on this game are addressed mostly in the Reddit post.

Some incidents make him seperate with the group and now he is on his own until he finds them. In my opinion, this is the only first person game that truly captures the tension of surviving a zombie apocalypse.   You have limited resources in terms of ammo, weapons, and supplies and everyone needs to stick together to have a greater chance of survival.  Since ammo is limited you need to headshot zombies unless you want to risk infection and fight hand to hand. The maps are dark and foreboding.  The weapons look great and the sounds are crisp and accurate.  The zombie models and sounds are also good too.
On the downside, there aren’t a lot of maps to play right now.  There also isn’t much interactivity with the map objects either.  The developers said they will be releasing more downloadable content with two more maps (which I believe brings it to three more from the original build), and a few more weapons.
There are also some technical problems as well. The zombie spawning is bugged.   For example, on the prison map you are spawned as a zombie and cannot get to the survivors because you’ve spawned in a portion of the map the survivors don’t have access to.   Other times you are spawned into a place on the map as a zombie almost on the complete opposite side of the map where the survivors are.  There’s no waypoints as a zombie to the survivors, so unless you know the map really well you will be out of the action for a long, long time.
There is some occasional, inexplicable in game lag.  Not sure if it’s a limitation of the engine they used but as a survivor trying to headshot zombies, the lag will cause you to miss and you could become lunch and then turned.
There are only a few game modes right now.  One is a way point mode where you find things to aid in an escape, and another mode where you escort survivors to an extraction zone.  The developers have said that more modes are coming.
The development cycle on this game has been really slow.  Sometimes no updates are released for a month or more.  The developers say they are bringing more people into the team so hopefully when that happens updates will pick up.
I would recommend this game if you can handle the above problems.
Update 02/23/16
I no longer recommend this game.  It appears the company has abandoned it, as evidenced by the regular price drops into the bargain basement and no more updates.  All the company spokesperson on Steam talks about are free giveaways and playing other people's games.  The game is still littered with bugs which will likely never be fixed.
I wish I had never bought this game. It is essentially the same as the free game zombie panic source  but with game breaking bugs and no support.

Almost as good as the original. The soundtrack is excellent again, and the gameplay remains similar. However, the level design has taken a turn for the worse.
Specifically, the game uses extremely long hallways in several levels, to the point where it becomes frustrating. Enemies can and will shoot you from a distance and you'll have no chance to respond. Your only hope is to memorize their approximate locations and shoot blindly off-screen. This is most noticeable in the Hawaii segments, which seem like a different person made them.
There's a reason cs_office isn't a realistic depiction of an office in Counter-Strike: the long, regular hallways make for dull gameplay. So it is in HM2's Hawaii sections, combined with some seriously psychic AI.
Finally, the very beginning of the game has a "sexual violence or not" prompt. As far as I can tell, it applies to one scene and is never used again. I'm not sure if they were going for Super Edgy Themes but they failed.
The core gameplay is mostly excellent. If you liked HM1, you'll like this one. If you haven't played HM1, play that first. This is more difficult, less polished, and lengthier.

Wouldn't recommend it.  Huge fan of the first game, absolutely loved it, but this game did away with a lot of the best parts.  You play as characters using masks maybe 15% of the total game, the narrative jumps around Tarantino-style (not a bad thing in and of itself, but done here in a way that seems to force the story down your throat while also being conceitedly full of itself for having a story that's told anachronically).  Levels are ridiculously big, which just amounts to a lot of lost work when one guy with a pistol snipes you from off screen setting you back ten minutes of carefully orchestrated kills. "Cheap deaths" are the order of the day, with enemies sniping you from across the room off-screen (even when you are fully extended in their direction in look mode).  Way more gun-toting enemies is going to me way more often you will find yourself up against insurmountable odds.  Not only that, but if you're going melee from personal choice or a mask choice, you will spend an inordinate amount of time waiting for one guy to isolate himself so you can alert him and pull him over to you, kill him, and repeat with the next ten guys. All the while trying to not get shot through four sets of windows that line up just perfectly so the dude in the exact opposite corner of the building from you happens to patrol by at the just the right second and kills you flawlessly. Start over.
The game I loved can be seen in how it inspired this game, but they really just ruined it.  It's full of itself, it's way too hard to be worth it (I beat it, but at that point, it was more about spite and pride than anything even resembling enjoyment), and the best things that made HM1 great are either removed entirely, ignored, or in way too small of quantity here.
Pay money for the SOUNDTRACK.  THAT is still incredible.  Don't pay money for the game.

Fun melee combat, decent variety so far of level atmospheres. Pretty great level design and sound assets. Plenty of great warhammer lore, with more room for expasion campaigns etc. The heros play differently and there is more than enough content (about 13 levels with hidden loot rooms and explorable areas). Similar to L4D but the larger melee focus is more enjoyable, just needs some more Skaven enemy types. Totally worth 30 in my book. Keep in mind I love Warhammer Fantasy.

It's strange how people have so many issues with this game, commenting that their AMD cards can't handle the game and such. I've got an R9 Series card, a 280 if I recall correctly and only around 3 gigs of Ram and plethora of cores. I have no issues running this game at all on medium high settings at all. The game IS CPU heavy, I will have to say my CPU is almost always at 80% or higher while playing but the developers have already stated they know this is an issue and they're working to fix it, specifically the FX for weapons and lighting being the main culprit for this.  That's a good selling point for me by the way, the developpers speaking with the fans.
The connectivity issues I've actually only had issues with /once/ during the beta, when the game exploded in popularity and people started trying to hack into their servers for whatever reason. The developpers kept in contact with the fans, and worked on it through the night as they do live in Sweden mind you. After that, there were no connection issues. The aspect of host migration is kind of disappointing but like I've mentioned prior, the developpers are working on fixing that. I also haven't had any of the sync errors people seem to have with the skaven hitting through walls, and at unimaginable distances.
The loot system is sometimes a letdown, but also sometimes it's a damn great thing. It's based off of dice, 7 in total with 5 variants of dice to use. Bone dice, with 2/6 sides being counted as a success, Loot Dice, 3/6, Chaos 5/6, and Skaven which are a gaurenteed boost to your loot with 6/6. The game has ways of allowing players to increase their chance at better loot through gathering tomes and grimoires, the tomes awarding Chaos die, andthe Grimoires awarding the Skaven die. There is /no/ trading in the game, but as always when the fanbase asked about it on Reddit the devs said they'd be making tweaks and adding things to the loot system if the fanbase asks for it. Something people seemingly don't quite understand about the Dev team.
As for actual gameplay, it's quite addicting. The ranged combat is satisfying, especially with something as lackluster as a bow. The guns in the game feel, and hit heavy and you can tell when it hits the skaven fur that it's done damage. The enemies are rather textbook, with your horde based rats, armored tanks who are hard to take down for some and also travel in randomized patrols, Globadiers who throw toxin that disorients and damages, Gutter Runners who are copy pasted hunters from L4D, Mangrabbers who drag you away and lynch you, mind you they're also REALLY squishy, a single longbow shot takes them down and they have to get close. OP as♥♥♥♥♥♥at first, but easy to deal with. Then the Rat Ogre, a team wiper or sometimes a total push over based on equipment. It's basically a tank, and functions nearly the same without throwing concrete. Melee feels great, being fluid and lethal for some classes and for others hard and absolutely thrashing to anything caught in the path. I.E. Waywatcher and Imperial Soldier respectivelly.
Overall the games a solid 9/10 in my book, and will easily raise up towards a ten as the devs release more content, more characters, and more loot through paid and free DLC.  Just for a quick reference for those who do read this, this is the Reddit Ask us anything that Fatshark(The Company behind Vermintide) held during the beta.
You'll see quickly that some of the concerns and questions the negative reviews have on this game are addressed mostly in the Reddit post.

Deadlight is, for me, a perfect palate cleanser. It doesn't do anything "perfectly" other than setting, but it does everything well. 2d platformer zombie narrative driven quasi puzzle adventure game. whew!. It NAILS its atmosphere. Everything is saturated in darkness. The zombies are almost never fully detailed but are shadows with glowing eyes. The world is a dulled and muted place and although my explanation of it is lacking, all I can say is that graphically they nailed the world and atmosphere. It's linear, no open world here and pretty short. My stats say a total of 4.5 hours for my one run through and I think that I spent 30 minutes on pause.
However, I tend to run two games at the same time and after completing a big one I feel somewhat drained? No, maybe just reluctant to start a new big endeavor....
That is where I found myself starting Deadlight. I had just completed a big open world shooter spending a ton of enjoyed time there and I'm still playing another large RPG and I needed some light fare before I started another big time investment or I knew I'd start something for an hour and never come back.
Deadlight was perfect. Challenging once in a while but never roadblocked. Always moving forward. The story, told in part through roughly drawn comic style cutscenes and partly through the diary of the main character was enough to make me  question his sanity and the ulitmate conclusion.
Admittedly, I got this game through a humble bundle so I didn't pay full price but knowing my experience $15/3.5 hours=less than $5 an hour= same price as an itunes rental.....I can totally justify that purchase.
If its sitting in your library and you haven't played it I would totally remcommend it. If you see it on sale, I would totally recomend it. If you need a break from your more intense games, but are still looking to play a game....I would totally recomend it. It's a good experience. A burner. Use, enjoy, dispose.

This game plays very much like Left 4 Dead, but with less arcade elements. Combat is actually challenging and mostly melee based, though there are ranged abilities and bows.
There are common enemies and special enemies, just like in Left 4 Dead. The special enemies work in similar fashion: there is an agile 'hunter' which will pounce and immobilize his target. There is a 'smoker' which will drag you away from the group rendering its target helpless. There is also a special enemy that employs gas area of effect attacks, and a 'tank'. The specials are an exact copy of how L4D players will know them.
The maps are fairly large and very well detailed. A match can take around 10 minutes at times. Once a match is finished, everyone rolls dices which determine the loot reward quality you'll get. You can increase the odds by searching the map actively for tomes and extra loot dices.

Issue with being banned:
Believe me or not, I've never hacked this game.
I had this game installed as part of a secondary steam library installed on a 60GB SSD I had in my computer. This game and PoE were the only ones on the drive, so that they'd load faster.
After that hard drive started to fail regularly, and windows recommended I replaced it. I tried backing up that game and some other files. I failed to realize that the transfer failed partly through. I restarted my computer with the 60GB SSD missing and I launched H&G from the new drive. Upon automatically logging in with steam, I was immediately permabanned for hacking.
When I sent in a support ticket, explaining my situation and asking what happened, I didn't receive a reply for over 10 days. When I finally did receive a reply, I was told they were not obligated to tell me how I was caught, and my account would remain permanently banned.
Upon logging into another steam account and logging in, I found that account wasn't banned and I didn't get banned for hacking (I still wasn't hacking.)
After a few days, when trying to play from my new account and repeatedly got "Error code: 34" upong googling this I found out I was hardware ID banned. (They didn't even say I was banned, or why I was banned.)

Okay, I've been mulling over what kind of rating to give Hotline Miami 2 and how it compares to Hotline Miami. Here are some things that notably stand out to me;
1. The disjointed narrative really doesn't make sense in the beginning unless you pay a lot of attention to what is going on and who you are playing as. There are very, very subtle details that you should pay attention to.
2. This game follows an alternate reality rather than modern day, where Russia attacks and takes control of part of Hawaii. It was something I really wasn't expecting due to the first game's focus on Jacket rather than what was going on around him.
3. The controls seem a lot looser than the first, which really makes things a bit of a cluster and a half, but it is manageable. However, since HLM2 relies more on gun play than melee, why wouldn't you tighten down your aiming? I prefer free aiming than locking on.
4. The level design really could use some work; levels are often too large with a lot of gun wielding baddies that would like nothing better than to end your day with a bullet. Believe me, almost clearing out an entire level only to be killed by the last enemy is an incredibly frustrating experience you will come to know time and time again. Either zoom out the camera so we can see more, or make the levels smaller.
5. The music, like always, is incredible. I'd rather not compare it to the first because the two really stand up on their own.  HLM has more of a lively, ecstatic feel while HLM2 is more gloomy and hollow, tying well to the theme of both games.
6. HLM is more about reactive gameplay and reacting to your surroundings while the sequel is more about planning your route through the sections and using each character's mechanic correctly. I will say Evan's mechanic of not killing enemies and unloading weapons was refreshing and cool.
7. HLM2 is about two to two and a half times longer than the original, which is both good and bad. Good for more gameplay, bad because it may overstay its welcome.
8. HLM2 is noticably harder than the original. The difficulty spikes rather early on, but you will eventually be able to handle what it throws at you.
9. I did notice that sometimes you can get hit with a bullet and not die instantly, but there will be blood on the ground where you were shot. I don't know what determines this or what causes it, I just know its a thing.
At the end of the day, I have to give Hotline Miami 2 a 7/10 because of its story and music. The gameplay surprisingly didn't get repetitive, but having to replay floors over and over again just got incredibly frustrating. I saw a good comparison of HLM2 to Super Mario Brothers 2 Japan (SMB: The Lost Levels); take the most difficult and satisfying parts of the game out and expand upon them to where it is ball-bustingly hard, but you eventually earn the title of defeating it.
Also, it's quite dirty to exclude the soundtrack from the special edition, but that's just my opinion.

You release a game and charge people real money for it, then something basic like loading a saved game fails... leaves a pretty sour taste. (See Update below for possible fix)

Pros:

Cons:
- Save game issues mentioned (ranted about) above
- fairly sparse world - needs more living things
- camera needs some work
- AI pathfinding needs some improving
- Creatures will chase you FOREVER until you kill them or die
- Fighting is a little rudimentary
- Quest / story bugs...losing track of NPCs etc
- MANY random crashes seemingly for no reason
Verdict:
Buy it on special and wait until its a bit more ironed out before playing it.  Once the problems are fixed Ill probably change this to a "Yes" reccomendation :)
Update:  Turns out the work-around for the save / load issue is to *only* save very far away from where you dig (particularly around the crater), and *not* to dig below sea level... so basically go back to a camp and save there.  Seems to work so far.
Note: I am updating this review as I play more...

What can I say about this game? Paradox created a true sandbox game. That being said, it's just that, a sandbox game. It's not for people who want clear cut objectives or endgame missions and the such. You are basically thrusted into a world with little to no information on the world and it doesn't hold your hand either. The point is to immerse yourself into a world that has castles and a war torn land. You make your own story and that's what makes this game one of my favorites. You can be a ruthless bandit or a noble knight or a king ruling over your domain. The possiblities are seemingly endless. This game demands, I mean DEMANDS, your time and effort to get the full playablity out of this. The combat is a little shotty, but it does the job well enough. The graphics are subpar, but in this massive world, it does a decent job holding up. The only story that's handed to you is that you are a foriegner to this land and you have to carve your own existance in this land of opportunity. The beginning is nothing but a grind. However, after you get past the beginning, you will see a living world that feels real with the politics and war games. Finally, there are literally hundreds of mods out there that only enhance this game, adding great features to it. I would recommend the Dipolmacy mod, giving more depth to the political spectrum that is Calradia. The Floris mod is a combination of some of the more game enhancing mods that make the world more realisitc. This game is great and a lot of fun if you put your mind to it. If you love immersion, then this is the game for you.

I honestly have no idea why this game gets such great reviews. It's an Early Access game, but the last time I saw it was a year ago. To say it's improved would be a gross overstatement.
First off, optimization sucks. I have a rig that can run most AAA games with ease on full. I've tried all of the rendering options, and no matter what I do, the game absolutely slows to a 10 fps crawl even when I'm the only living thing on a small, barren island. It's not like the game looks good or anything, it's pretty basic.
The world generation is terrible and very frequently I've seen trees and boulders sticking out of the sides of islands. Along with that I've fallen out of the game world twice in 20 minutes.
The UI is clunky and the controls are terrible. It gives you the illusion of having two control schemes only for one to just flat out not work and you're forced to work with its default awful WoW-type interface that tries to be both an MMO and Minecraft, but is bad at both. The animations are buggy and I've frequently been moonwalking underwater. Chatting with other players is difficult and a huge pain. Some hotkeys, like holstering your item, just flat out don't work. Also, the HUD is useless in informing you if you've taken any damage or are undergoing any effects.
Honestly, I haven't gotten far into the game, only an hour or so with half in SP and half in MP, but I feel like I've played all I need to know that this game's not worth it, at least not right now.
Say all you want about how it's an Early Access game, but the truth of the matter is, at the time of this writing, from what I've played, this game barely passes as an alpha. It's riddled with bugs, is unpolished as hell, and has quality worse than most free games out there. I came in expecting a 3D Starbound sandbox and got just another stagnant, buggy as hell Early Access game. Don't buy it.

Melody's Escape, a brilliant rhythm game which can be a nice into into the rhythm game catagory.
A fairly simple control scheme involving only 4 inputs on the easier difficulties which increases to eight once you move into the harder of the four (excluding the custom difficulty which you are capable of making even harder). Each input has a distinctive colour on the default theme making you able to correspond the colours to the inputs rather than identifying each note individually making long streams not as fearsome as they initially looked.
If you have a large library of music then you are going to have a good time on this game, however for people with mass amounts of songs in a single genre, you might want to be careful about the purchase of this game.
I jumped right into this game with my love of rhythm games and enjoyed it very much until the audio detection was incapable of finding stable tempos in my songs. In my library of 166 songs (This is all from a single genre) I am capable of playing around 25% of them due to the beat detection being unable to find a stable 4/4. The result of the game being unable to find a stable tempo causes it to engage a detection mode which is labeled "Energy Peaks". This detection would be a great work around, provided that it worked consistently throughout an entire song which I have never found to be the case.
When the detection is in "Energy Peaks" mode, it will detect any spike in activity on a song and then place a beat there, for songs with a loud singer; all hell breaks loose on the song making you unable to correctly time your inputs unless you use visual ques rather than audatory cues which is not what you should really have to do in a rhythm game.
Energy Peaks works wonders for instumental songs though so if you are playing songs without singing then you should be able to play them all and not have to deal with bad sync.
The only thing that I feel is missing from this game is a song editor or at least some way you are able to influence how the song is generated. I have found too many songs which will change from sprinting to flying after a chorus rather than during the chorus only to return right back to sprinting after the next verse starts following the bridge from chorus to verse.
So if you have a wide variety of songs then buy this game if you are a fan of rhythm games or if you want to get into them. Although if you have a single genre which you love make sure that your songs have a prominent and stable BPM to prevent Energy Peaks from not properally syncing.

As much as it pains me to say so, I really can't recommend Deadlight. It's a nice 2D zombie survival game with fantastic graphics and a somewhat decent, if slightly jumbled, storyline, though.
The biggest pitfall this game has is the fact that it's a platformer, and while the zombie melee fighting is annoying (if there's more than 1 zombie you're basically dead), the platforming sections of the game are truly, truly atrocious, mainly owing to the fact that the controls are way too imprecise for a platforming aspect that demands precision. Super Meat Boy, this is not!
And the chase sequences... oh, the chase sequences... do you remember the Charles Lee chase at the end of Assassin's Creed III? Do you remember the amount of times you died having no clue what went wrong or what you were supposed to do? How many times you wanted to throw your controller out the window? Several of the chase sequences in Deadlight gave me exactly that feeling, again owing to wonky controls as well as slow (but fluid) animations that'll completely ruin any platforming potential this game might have had.
And it's such a shame, though, because Deadlight has TONS of potential! The environments are beautiful and feel alive (or rather: undead), the cutscenes have really nice artwork, there are even fun little secrets... But it's all for naught when the gameplay at the core of your game is abysmal, which, I'm sorry to say, is the case of the platforming here. Such a shame...

In the wake of what seems to be endless hordes of zombie games I saw what seemed like a cool little platformer called Deadlight. There aren't many platform zombie games (that I know of) so this is already unique in it's own right but what captured me from the start about this game is it's gritty visual style.
I'm not a big fan of the platform genre but the zombie apocalypse setting convinced me to give this a try. There are a few interesting features about this game that I particularly enjoyed. I liked how Randall, the main character, was always in one dimension while at the same time the game gave the impression of depth through such devices as the zombies coming out of the background. A lot of the stark atmosphere of the game came from the relatively spartan graphics and the simple interactions with the environment. It was easy to learn new actions and distinguish Randal from the enemies or other things in the game except during the few times where the visual background cues were way too subtle making it hard to see where you were supposed to jump and it took a few tries to figure out where to go next.
The complaints that I have about this game boil down to mainly the voice acting which destroyed the illusion somewhat, buggy interaction glitches and the simplistic story. In the cut scenes it always felt like the characters, other than Randall, were talking in a void. Perhaps the voice actors were given a script to read without knowing what was actually happening in the current scene but it felt terribly overacted. In particular the Rat's voice was so much lower than Randall's that it was nearly impossible to hear and understand what he was saying half of the time. All this made the game feel unpolished.
As for bugs I would say that at times the character wouldn't respond to the commands that you issued him. I'm not sure if that had to do with my timing or the lag between the controller and game but it was incredibly frustrating. At one point it got so bad that I began questioning my sanity. Having to redo a scene multiple times in a row and subsequently dying in the same way over and over again caused me to swear and argue with my computer to prove to it that I did indeed press the correct button at the correct time. I started to wonder if this is what people mean when they say that videogames cause violence. I certainly felt the rising of a murderous rage within me.
Can't say I am a big fan of the axe combat either. It felt extremely inexact and was very difficult to get Randall to finish off the zombie enemies on the ground. He just wouldn't respond to finish them off and continue hacking at the air space above their bodies. The controls could have been made much better and in return the game would have been that much more enjoyable.
Overall I would give this game a 60/100. The story is rather simplistic even though it had a couple of original elements. Many things in the game made absolutely no sense like the Rat and his nonsensical motivations, for example. It's still playable but just barely.
On a side note: I tried to get all the achievements (except Nightmare Mode) in the game and found out that the game doesn't record one particular secret until I found all the other secrets first. I had to redo that scene 3 times before it recognized my achievement in the end unlocking 3 achievements in a row.

Some men are Dead to Rights. Others are Dead to Lights. And then a few still, who lack the proper character limits, are Deadlight. This is a story of a man who is Deadlight.
In Deadlight, you play as a man with a beard who is looking for his family. He talks to other survivors, and then zombies kill them and he kills the zombies. There are flashback scenes, and grittily stylized 2D motion comic cutscenes. Eventually the zombies are replaced with the worst kind of men--mad men. They are even worse than the underground platforming dungeons of the rat men who literally call themselves The Rat in an epic blunder clearly lacking any degree of subtlety or self-awareness. There is no subtlety in this world. Only death. Memento mori. RIP.
But during all of this thrilling and very thoughtful storytelling, there is something... wrong. There is something off about this whole experience. Maybe you don't realize it yet, but the main character does, slowly. As the story progresses and things reach their ultimate conclusion, all is suddenly brought to light and the darkest innermost secret of the world is revealed.

There was a recurring Monty Python sketch where a group of middle-aged women would announce that they were going to reenact some famous historical event, but every single event was represented by a hilarious speeded-up handbag fight in a muddy field. I find myself reminded of it with the Call of Duty series; every time I think it's gonna do something else for once, it blows a whistle and everything descends into squeals and handbag-slapping.
Case in point, CoD: Ghosts. Not only is it not a game about the vengeful spirits hanging around English chip shops, but it's also not the game it purports to be in its own intro sequence. The Ghosts, as the name might imply, are ostensibly a legendary stealth unit that specializes in taking down larger forces through sneaky guerrilla tactics. So obviously, one of the first things you do in the game is ram-raid an enemy base in a burning truck and start gunning down every living thing from the dandelions on upwards. Yeah, that's some good ghostin' there, lads! Truly, thou art akin to the flicker of a candlelight shadow as you waddle around an open field being shot at from nineteen different directions.
The other thing I gathered ahead of time was that the plot would be about a weakened U.S. fighting a superior foe, which would make a nice change from the usual case wherein the heroes jump all over vastly inferior foes for floating the idea that maybe the U.S. could stop eating all the pancakes for five minutes. So here's the sitch: the U.S. has been invaded by all of South America. OK, gonna have to stop you there, Call of Duty: Ghosts; I get that all of your plots are birthed from the fantasies crossing the mind of a paranoid, xenophobic ♥♥♥♥wit as he has violent grunting sex with a pile of damp moss, but at least you used to stick to foreigners who potentially are enemies of the U.S., and South America has better things to do with its time than sit around shaking its fist at your freedoms all day, at least as long as association football exists!
Anyway, they attack America by hijacking America's orbital missile weapon. OK, gonna stop you there again, Ghosts! Firstly, so much for the enemy being "superior" if they can't make their own superweapons and gotta pinch 'em like safari park baboons nicking the windscreen wipers. And secondly, orbital ♥♥♥♥ing missile weapon!? This invasion is sounding more justifiable by the second! 'Cause not only is the U.S. outsourcing their weapons development to ♥♥♥♥ing Megatron, but they also appear to have exterminated every single member of their population who isn't a burly white dude.
Just for fun I kept a running tally of all the characters in the story campaign who aren't burly white dudes and you are under no obligation to shoot. The final total was three: a female astronaut right at the start who immediately dies, a helicopter that spoke with a woman's voice, and a black member of the Ghosts unit who immediately dies. And, frankly, when that happens, the main characters displayed less emotion than when their dog got shot. "Dammit, the black guy died!", they seemed to say, "Now we can't claim to have tons of black friends while arguing on the internet!"
You are one of two burly white brothers whose burly white dad has been secretly testing them over the years to make them worthy of joining the Ghosts, it never having occurred to him that they might prefer to become pastry chefs or something. The main baddie turns out to be a burly white friend of the burly white dad who was captured by the enemy and turned to their side.  Damn South Americans! It's not enough for them to steal our orbital doomsday satellites, they have to start harnessing the power of our burly white dudes as well!
Also, there's a dog. A German Shepherd, the burliest and whitest of all the dogs, who was a bit of unique selling point in the lead-up: he'll run out and savage South Americans at your command because he's been fed on an exclusive diet of neck-shaped burritos. And there are missions where you play as the dog, and finally get to do some ♥♥♥♥ing ghosting as you sneak around the long grass internally debating the choices at the throat buffet. I was gonna bring up Ghost Dog: Way of the Samurai, but that might be too cosmopolitan a reference for this game.
All of which would have had more of an impact if the dog got to be in more than two levels before the game goes "Right, hope you got your money's worth!" and sends him to the time-out kennel forever. Not that I was expecting him to tag along for the scuba diving bit, ♥♥♥♥ing amazing as that would've been, but the fact is his role in the game is just another momentary gameplay gimmick. It would've been nice if he'd had some kind of personality besides being just another piece of military hardware for the armchair generals to masturbate over. Although, the same could be said of the human characters!
Speaking of hardware, there are the standard apocalyptic coffee break sequences, where you pull out a remote from the♥♥♥♥♥♥dimension and rain predator drone death down on an enemy unable to in any way defend themselves or fight back. And d'you know what? I don't see how I'm supposed to have any grasp of the relative enemy threat when we may or may not be packing armfuls of superweapons we forgot to mention. Like after the enemy base ram-raid, I'm told to pick off the stragglers with the robot sniper. Hold on a second, when did we set up a ♥♥♥♥ing robot sniper? What did we bring it here in? How did we set it up without the enemy noticing; did we disguise it as a badger-watching station?
Incidentally, the Ghosts are well-♥♥♥♥ing-equipped for a guerrilla unit. "Oh, no, America has been attacked and is weakened and there's no defenses except an inexhaustible supply of tank battalions and an army of killer robots. And we would've had a doomsday satellite if the rest of the world hadn't gotten all weird about it!" Which they were entirely right to be because when the player wrestles control of the satellite back at the end, they immediately use it to wipe hundreds of thinking, feeling blips off the map as casually as one were to use a windscreen wiper on a rainy day!
Yet again, it seems like they cut out every moment in the story that could've built context but didn't have any explosions in it. And if they hadn't added voiced plot-dumps to the loading screens, the experience would've been as coherent as scrambled porn intercut with the fantasies of Tea Party members. And "fantasy" really is the word; the vehicles all handle like turbo-boosted magic carpets, lest anything requiring actual skill get in the way of your unpleasant paranoid battle-glory daydream, so divorced from reality it might as well be taking place in ♥♥♥♥ing Narnia!
So however you might have expected a game called Ghosts to differ from the modern shooter routine of meaningless violence and empty spectacle, you were wrong, ya idiot! But somehow it's only getting worse! Black Ops II actually came across as at least slightly self-aware, and Modern Warfare (One) went so far as being profound, such as in that bit where you die slowly and horribly in a nuclear blast. If that happened in CoD: Ghosts, you'd probably just fart all the radiation out in one big heroic guff, pull the broken glass out of your eyeballs and then use it to shiv the Ayatollah. - Yahtzee

Hotline Miami was a game with a lot to say, but it spoke with actions. The actions of Jacket in the first game, and its presentation through the perspective of a limited set of characters, are the inspiration for everything in this game. It's interesting to see reviews of the game tack fairly negative in regard to the methods of storytelling applied to Hotline Miami 2, particularly in regard to the multiple characters with constricting move sets.
A good way to think about Hotline Miami 2 and Hotline Miami is to think about them like Metal Gear Solid and Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty. There's so roughness to the comparison, but I believe it fits.
Hotline Miami is a sandbox. In many ways the plot and pace of the game are dictated by the idea of creating a simple repetitive formula that could be enjoyable to endure for several hours for the reward at the end. THIS WORKED. It worked very, very well. But to repeat it in Hotline Miami 2 would severely damage the world created and the tone set by the original. In Hotline Miami you play as a couple (primarily one) very skilled killer, with nothing to lose. In Hotline Miami 2, you play as many scared, lonely, VERY DIFFERENT people all with various things holding them back or compelling them forward.
This is where I fail to see the argument than any of the characters move sets are restricting. Maybe on the surface yes, because all of them aren't jacket. Mark is bad at making human shields, Tony has heavy hands but he doesn't know how to shoot a gun. What presents as limitations creates a richness in a game that at this time has barely been broken in by the players.
In terms of having something to say, Hotline Miami 2 won't shut up compared to the silent protagonist of the previous outing. I don't think this is a bad thing. The dialogue that feels forced usually feels that way because it is, but this isn't a bad thing. Stylistically, it gels well with the pretext set up by Hotline Miami 2's sporadic structure. These are vhs tapes, b-movies, slasher flicks, gangster pulp stories, but does that really keep them from being "real"- It begs the question over and over, "what is real anyway?" Where the movies real? Was it all a dream? Were the killings the movie was inspired by real or because jacket is in the movie does that mean hotline miami is midnight animal part 1? If you murder someone in a dream, or you kill a hallucination, what's different from killing someone in real life, to you anyway?
It mostly doesn't matter right? What's real and what's not. What matters is who you are and what you do: The fans are bored and they decide to play vigilante. Evan is losing his mind, and his family writing a book (his bonus mission is worth unlocking). The ghost wolves all break different ways.
But where do we all end up? Where does it all lead? The fighting and the violence? What are we left with in the final moments of each of these people? These games have asked the question, “You like hurting people, don't you?” A leading question that we've all, finding ourselves here now one way or another, have said yes to. What are we to do, sitting on the edge of that violence culminating in fireballs all over the world, with that information then?
There's a deep story here spanning these two games that is worth unraveling, whether they challenge you, offend you, or make you question yourself and the people around them, put yourself through it now before you're left to you ignorance in the years to come.

The story mode has the feel of classic sci fi novels such as Dragons Dawn, the prequel for The Dragon Riders of Pern with a story of surviving on a new alien world while trying to develop a colony, yet there are large threats looming that will threaten all you work to build.
Honestly I really do love this game perhaps more in its possbility then in practice. It sadly ended up rushed out of EA status, and then has been price dropped within only a few months of official release slapping every EA player/tester/bug reporter in the face.
You see one of the original selling points to buy into EA was that they said the price would only go up after release. We who supported them during the rough times and offered input and acted as beta testers that used our game time on a rough, buggy, often crashing and losing all save data with every update while giving them the data to track down and smooth out those rough spots ended up being taken advantage of.
It is official now that the game is only going to have a minimal staff working on some minor final polish. Many of the EA features hung out as future implimentations are so much dust in the wind and leaves the taste of hope now bitter bile.
The price only a few months after release is being dropped below what any EA player bought in at, and new comers will be treated to a cheaper, cleaner, smoother game at the expense of we who came before.
Id even bought a 2nd copy for a friend who found the EA game so buggy he never got that into it while I poured more then 80 hours into around 4 or 5 different play throughs in story mode during different updates.
I dont know what else to say except sure its a fun enough game, and certainly worth the new lower price point and if it goes on sale for 50% off or more it will be silly cheap for so much potential game time.
Yet I cant help but feel it has ended up another one of those early access titles that an indie company used to bring in cash and before the game was really done turn to another project. Now I feel any money spent on this title only benefits a future game I have no real interest in.
Buy it if it looks fun to you, but only knowing that its not half the game it could of and should  become. That it still has plenty of rough spots, still feels like it should be listed as early access, and that we who came before you got used both our time and money with many a hinted at feature never coming to pass.
Sorry pathea but you broke my heart.

Melody's Escape is a deceptively simple yet challenging obstacle-based rhythm game with a lot of potential versatility in playstyle. While still in Early Access, it has almost no technical errors and the developer is extremely active, so I would recommend it to people who enjoy rhythm games, especially people who are looking for a different type of procedurally-generated music gameplay. I am terrible at obstacle running games, but I have never ever found the platforming element of this game to be obtrusive or overwhelming because it integrates so well with the beat and feels so smooth on a sensory level.
The visuals are quite polished and clear, with a striking and elegant aesthetic; they are also easily modded and customised. The colours are rich without being distracting and can be altered both ingame and via a modding interface, and provide lovely implicit feedback for passing obstacles. The gameplay is rewarding immersively with the flow of the music and quite addictive. Melody's Escape primarily syncs to tempo and tests rhythm, beat awareness, and precision in timing, so it works less efficiently with noisy tracks, but its level generation otherwise handles most genres I have thrown at it quite well and has a good fallback method for dealing with offtempo songs.
Low BPM songs are as pleasing to play as high BPM songs, although they generally have fewer obstacles and the running pace is slower, and there are difficulty settings which treat songs with <150 BPM as if they had double their actual BPM for the purposes of level generation if that annoys you. Instrumentals and vocal songs work equally well.
While the strength of Melody's Escape generally lies in its concept and its simplicity, the game is easy to recommend because of its many difficulty settings. There are four preset difficulty modes with different input and then a custom mode which can be used to alter obstacle density, running speed, input timing window, and input methods, which gives the player the opportunity to emphasise the challenges they would like the most.
The four input methods in order of difficulty are one colour (the track is divided into segments of different running speed based on intensity of the song, and to pass an obstacle you must press or hold the associated colour key), all colours (all obstacles have their own individual colour assigned to them regardless of segment), colour or direction (solid obstacles -- jumping, sliding, diving -- require direction key input, either from the gamepad or using the arrow buttons, while colour orbs require their individual colour key input), and tandem colour and direction (passing an obstacle requires both the correct colour and direction key).
Monochrome play is relaxing and purely a test of precision, while tandem colour and direction play is a frenetic test of reaction timing and mechanics.
The sync with the track is quite good and failing to pass certain obstacles results in stumbling or respawning, so there is no way to actually fail a song as in other rhythm games which involve shooting elements, etc. The only real ingame objective that exists is to pass every obstacle (a perfect chain), but the game assigns ratings based on score and keeps track of your high score, so you can play as you wish on the mode that suits you best. This is why I have accrued so much playtime so quickly, because I found exploring the full potential of the game challenging and enjoyable.
Essentially, you get out of Melody's Escape what you put into it, which is hopefully a huge and diverse music collection. It is absolutely worth its current price and even more so on sale. It is an easy pick-up-and-play game with almost no set-up overhead and a low skill floor, but possesses depth, complexity, and replay value as you attempt to master it.
I disagree with some of the other reviewers on one thing; I am a keyboard-only player and really enjoy this game. I have no doubt the game is more intuitive with a Microsoft controller, but do not feel as if anything is lacking from keyboard play.
Technically, the game can be played with either keyboard or gamepad quite well, and no clicking is necessary. There is a slight learning curve for the colour input scheme for keyboard players because the colours are by default designed to match Microsoft controllers, but it translates fine to WASD/SZXC/etc. keyboard schemes. The visual processing can be demanding but there is an FPS counter ingame and many options to increase performance at the expense of graphical intensity (mostly bloom), which is also a matter of subjective preference anyway. Input windows etc. are all smooth assuming consistent 60 FPS.
The game has very good file handling options and does not require pre-indexing directories. You can save tracks as favourites and generate favourite folders. From experience it supports a wide variety of formats (mp3, m4a, ogg, wav, flac, aac, aiff, mpeg, wmv, and more) and also playlists (.m3u files), which sets it apart in endurance play from other rhythm games. Handles large and long tracks fine.
It does lack support for kanji, hangul, some unusual Latin characters with diacritics, etc. which can make track selection a difficulty for songs with names entirely in those characters. (Katakana and hiragana are supported, for the record). This appears to be unlikely to change in the near future and is the only potential sticking point I see for rhythm game fans.
As I have stated, this game is very much alive and being worked on, and developer support is extremely prompt. However, were the developer to suddenly disappear, I would still recommend this game as is. The primary focuses of development now are perfecting visuals (which are already on par with  the available rhythm games on Steam) and fixing some very uncommon errors. For almost every player this game should be in a well-functional state and require minimal or no tweaking to maximise performance.
Overall I completely recommend Melody's Escape to any fan of rhythm games or procedurally generated music games such as Audiosurf, Osu, etc. It is well-made, performs smoothly, has active developer support, and copes well with virtually all music types. The tracks are varied enough for such a simple set of obstacles to keep you entertained for quite some time. There are few technical issues, the levels are graceful, and the aesthetics of the game are beautiful in a way that only enhances the music. Nothing ingame detracts from the music itself but the gameplay itself is still rewarding and intense, which is to me a perfect and mesmerising balance.

Where to start?
The physics engine is awful, infantry apparently wipe butter on their boots before every game, you cannot stop without sliding, and moving indoors feels like you are magnetically attracted to the walls. Planes are insanely sloppy, They are unbalanced by nation, flying is clunky (Dogfighting success is moving your mouse upwards as fast as possible,) and they're both a pain to play as and against. Tanks are pretty simple too, there is no kind of module-damage whatsoever, and the tanks depend on a health system. Just like everything else, they move terribly. It's as if the devs had a desire to implement gears for the tanks but didn't have enough time. Once you reach the speed limit of the tank, it feels like an RC car.
Lastly, the gold shop. I know some people claim the game is or is not pay to win. Well... It's not. The better word would be pay to progress, but this game does it so, so wrong. At the current patch, MOST people would probably hit rank 5 or something slightly lower/higher without using gold and then give up. The grind becomes untolerable after these levels. A single game won't even give you a single percent of the xp required to level up on higher ranks. What's the alternative? Pay $$$ to just instantly buy a character at a higher level. No grind required. If you have enough gold, there is absolutely no grind in the game. Literally everything in the game except the medals can be bought with gold. Guns, vehicles, ammo, mods, you name it. Like I said, it's not exactly pay to win because you don't pay to get overpowered stuff, as you can still unlock these things normally, but with an excruciating amount of playtime for the more advanced things. There's a fine line between paying to save some time and sanity, and then paying to instantly and effortlessly get your way to the top.
There's plenty more things to talk about, but I would fry my fingers typing so much, and most of which is already in other reviews. It's a shame, because there are few real "combined arms" type WWII games out there, but this just isn't the one. It's getting worse by each update. Just save yourself the time and effort. Right now, it's not even worth that.

One of the first things I noticed about Hotline Miami 2 was that its soundtrack felt slower to me, more cinematic and larger in scope. I think that best encapsulates HLM2: larger in scope. A lot about this game won't make sense on your first play through, you will curse frequently and the playstyle you were used to is no longer effective in this game. Still, this game builds on what made the first one great and offers a ton more replayability for those who want it.
Moving on to level design, because this is a controversial talking point for this game, I am ambivalent. Hotline 1 feels claustrophobic compared to this game. There is a lot more space to run and maneuver, which becomes important the more that gunplay gets involved. Because practically every enemy has guns, levels are no longer small hallways. There is a lot more happening in the background now too. You'll notice it most in the second scene, but it's present all over the game. Set pieces that tip over or rotate as you move past them. You'll also notice A TON OF WINDOWS have now been added to the game. I personally found some levels to be extremely frustrating, but I also learned more about how the game works (like using windows to my advantage). As someone who appreciates a game that teaches players, I ultimately enjoyed this aspect.
They've stopped that annoying camera bobbing thing that made 1 feel like it was floating in a pool of water, but they didn't pull the camera back. Because so many enemies with guns appear off screen, you will frequently die from bullets shot by guns you can't see. That means mastering, or becoming familiar with, shift looking is crucial. Failure to shift look will extend your play time by several excruciating hours. Stop resisting shift look because you can snipe with pistols from across the map.
This is a game built for perfectionists and speedrunners. That unforgiving difficulty is why NES games like Ninja Gaiden live on in our hearts. It's not about finishing the level, anyone can do that with a simple game of peek-a-boo as has been pointed out on these forums. It's about discovering methods to lure and murder in groups. Combos are so much more effective (and harder to get) in this game, and boldness and flexibility scores actually matter. This game, when played at a high level, is all about speed and flexibility. You can dodge bullets now, something that was virtually impossible in part one.
I have come to the realization that the story is like an homage to Drive. If you've ever seen that movie, it's easy to find yourself left with a lot of questions about the characters you just met. Much like in HLM1, where the world is not quite what it seems. For instance, the community has yet to come to a consensus on how much of HLM1 happened in Jacket's real life and how much was a coma dream. There are two stories happening here: what you actually see and how it fits into the scope of the Hotline Miami timeline. The latter is what makes the story rewarding, because the former is quite jumbled and in some cases very abrupt.
Those who want to replay a game and learn it will find the experience of Hotline Miami 2 to be a frustrating climb to a satisfying top. Those expecting a fun and twitchy murder simulator that lasts for a few hours might find themselves disappointed by this experience.
Ask yourself which of these gamers you are before you buy this game.
[[*Edit: A note on hard mode. I thought it was too hard, like suck the fun out of the game hard. I'll probably finish it because I'm kind of a super fan of this game, but I am not enjoying that part at all.]]

You love top down shooters. You enjoy mashing buttons over and over until you get that perfect combo, until you pass the level like a lightning, following the most efficient pattern and sweeping everything in you path. You want to listen to music so great that it makes you wonder: "How... how do you extract sounds so sweet out of a synthesizer?"
Finally, YOU LIKE HURTING OTHER PEOPLE.
Hotline Miami 2 might be just a choice for you.
Order your copy today at 1-800-GITGOOD.
