Let's get this out of the way first: Hotline Miami 2 is hard.  Like really hard.  Like I got the achievement for dying 1000 times when I was maybe 3/4 done with the story hard.  But it's also a fun and stylish experience with a variety of characters coupled with a once again outstanding soundtrack.  This time around there is a more coherent story, and rather than choosing from an assortment of masks at the start of each level you generally start as a different character that has his own gameplay style.  My favorite of the new styles is probably a set of twins where one carries a chainsaw that your left click will swing, while the other twin starts with a pistol that you can shoot with a right click: they're difficult to control at first but once you get the hang of it there's lots of fun to be had.  Other notable characters are the soldiers, who get a choice of a gun to start (ammo can be found in crates found in their levels) while a right click has them pull out a knife, and also a reporter who won't use guns (he will pick them up, but just unloads them and drops them immediately) and prefers to knockout his enemies rather than kill them.
Hotline 2 is a challenging game that will punish your smallest mistakes, but you will figure out the levels and be satisfied when you clear them.  The story took me around 7 hours to finish the first time through, but this is the type of game that begs to be perfected, and I can see myself coming back to it in the future.

First, I highly recommend that you play the first Hotline Miami before playing this one. It'll make a little more sense, but no promises.
Wrong Number is set after the events of the first, with the arrest of Jacket after his murder spree through the Russian mafia. You play as a group of vigilantes, known as the Fans, who emulate Jacket's actions in hopes of receiving the mysterious phone calls to give them direction, murdering hoodlums in the signature gory manner of the series.
Wrong Number is set before the events of the first, during a war against Soviet Russia, who have invaded Hawaii. You play as a member of the "Ghost Wolves", constantly being sent on dangerous missions by command to remove the Russian menace, while pining for home.
Wrong Number is set during the trial of Jacket, which is hotly debated thanks to anti-Russian factions decrying him as a American hero. You play as a reporter, who fights his way to the truth behind the group that is manipulating these murderers and what conspiracy it may be hiding.
Wrong Number is set after the events of the first, on the set of the slasher flick "Midnight Animal" obviously aping Jacket's murders. You play as a troubled actor, casted as Pig-Man, who acts out the urgings of the Director but soon begins to lose the difference between the movie and reality.
Wrong Number is set during an investigation of the Miami Mutilator, who has been brutally murdering his victims while claiming his innocence in their spilled blood. You play as a loose cannon cop, who's fighting his way through the criminal underworld while chasing this illusive killer.
All these plotlines, and more, weave through the narrative on another psychedelic spree of colorful visuals, detailed sprite work and interesting level design. While much more dialogue heavy than the first, the game still offers the lightning fast dance of mutilation, gunfire and brutality that the first one did with an emphasis on smooth action, varied style and combos to get the best ranks (don't worry, it's easy to replay specific levels, all intros and dialogue being skippable). Although, depending on your character, you won't be able to pick from a large variety of masks, most characters have either a few choices or gameplay quirk to keep every level fresh, yet give you something to master (each Fan is represented by a mask while the Reporter favors melee and can extend combos by dismantling firearms he goes, while the Soldier has a few guns to choose from before each assault).
Gameplay remains the same, with quick death and quicker restarts, melee being silent and guns attracting attention and the ability to throw weapons and stun enemies. Doors remain a fearful nether-realm to the police officers, mobsters and dogs that populate each level, but smarter AI would probably make the game impossible. Blood still splatters, executions are still brutal and weapons are varied and fun to experiment with.
Wrong Number is perhaps a perfect sequel. It keeps the razor-sharp gameplay that fans of the original will know and love, while improves the roster of options and gives you a deeper, yet still utterly bizarre narrative to feast on, if you can keep up with who's where at what time.

Melody's Escape is a deceptively simple yet challenging obstacle-based rhythm game with a lot of potential versatility in playstyle. While still in Early Access, it has almost no technical errors and the developer is extremely active, so I would recommend it to people who enjoy rhythm games, especially people who are looking for a different type of procedurally-generated music gameplay. I am terrible at obstacle running games, but I have never ever found the platforming element of this game to be obtrusive or overwhelming because it integrates so well with the beat and feels so smooth on a sensory level.
The visuals are quite polished and clear, with a striking and elegant aesthetic; they are also easily modded and customised. The colours are rich without being distracting and can be altered both ingame and via a modding interface, and provide lovely implicit feedback for passing obstacles. The gameplay is rewarding immersively with the flow of the music and quite addictive. Melody's Escape primarily syncs to tempo and tests rhythm, beat awareness, and precision in timing, so it works less efficiently with noisy tracks, but its level generation otherwise handles most genres I have thrown at it quite well and has a good fallback method for dealing with offtempo songs.
Low BPM songs are as pleasing to play as high BPM songs, although they generally have fewer obstacles and the running pace is slower, and there are difficulty settings which treat songs with <150 BPM as if they had double their actual BPM for the purposes of level generation if that annoys you. Instrumentals and vocal songs work equally well.
While the strength of Melody's Escape generally lies in its concept and its simplicity, the game is easy to recommend because of its many difficulty settings. There are four preset difficulty modes with different input and then a custom mode which can be used to alter obstacle density, running speed, input timing window, and input methods, which gives the player the opportunity to emphasise the challenges they would like the most.
The four input methods in order of difficulty are one colour (the track is divided into segments of different running speed based on intensity of the song, and to pass an obstacle you must press or hold the associated colour key), all colours (all obstacles have their own individual colour assigned to them regardless of segment), colour or direction (solid obstacles -- jumping, sliding, diving -- require direction key input, either from the gamepad or using the arrow buttons, while colour orbs require their individual colour key input), and tandem colour and direction (passing an obstacle requires both the correct colour and direction key).
Monochrome play is relaxing and purely a test of precision, while tandem colour and direction play is a frenetic test of reaction timing and mechanics.
The sync with the track is quite good and failing to pass certain obstacles results in stumbling or respawning, so there is no way to actually fail a song as in other rhythm games which involve shooting elements, etc. The only real ingame objective that exists is to pass every obstacle (a perfect chain), but the game assigns ratings based on score and keeps track of your high score, so you can play as you wish on the mode that suits you best. This is why I have accrued so much playtime so quickly, because I found exploring the full potential of the game challenging and enjoyable.
Essentially, you get out of Melody's Escape what you put into it, which is hopefully a huge and diverse music collection. It is absolutely worth its current price and even more so on sale. It is an easy pick-up-and-play game with almost no set-up overhead and a low skill floor, but possesses depth, complexity, and replay value as you attempt to master it.
I disagree with some of the other reviewers on one thing; I am a keyboard-only player and really enjoy this game. I have no doubt the game is more intuitive with a Microsoft controller, but do not feel as if anything is lacking from keyboard play.
Technically, the game can be played with either keyboard or gamepad quite well, and no clicking is necessary. There is a slight learning curve for the colour input scheme for keyboard players because the colours are by default designed to match Microsoft controllers, but it translates fine to WASD/SZXC/etc. keyboard schemes. The visual processing can be demanding but there is an FPS counter ingame and many options to increase performance at the expense of graphical intensity (mostly bloom), which is also a matter of subjective preference anyway. Input windows etc. are all smooth assuming consistent 60 FPS.
The game has very good file handling options and does not require pre-indexing directories. You can save tracks as favourites and generate favourite folders. From experience it supports a wide variety of formats (mp3, m4a, ogg, wav, flac, aac, aiff, mpeg, wmv, and more) and also playlists (.m3u files), which sets it apart in endurance play from other rhythm games. Handles large and long tracks fine.
It does lack support for kanji, hangul, some unusual Latin characters with diacritics, etc. which can make track selection a difficulty for songs with names entirely in those characters. (Katakana and hiragana are supported, for the record). This appears to be unlikely to change in the near future and is the only potential sticking point I see for rhythm game fans.
As I have stated, this game is very much alive and being worked on, and developer support is extremely prompt. However, were the developer to suddenly disappear, I would still recommend this game as is. The primary focuses of development now are perfecting visuals (which are already on par with  the available rhythm games on Steam) and fixing some very uncommon errors. For almost every player this game should be in a well-functional state and require minimal or no tweaking to maximise performance.
Overall I completely recommend Melody's Escape to any fan of rhythm games or procedurally generated music games such as Audiosurf, Osu, etc. It is well-made, performs smoothly, has active developer support, and copes well with virtually all music types. The tracks are varied enough for such a simple set of obstacles to keep you entertained for quite some time. There are few technical issues, the levels are graceful, and the aesthetics of the game are beautiful in a way that only enhances the music. Nothing ingame detracts from the music itself but the gameplay itself is still rewarding and intense, which is to me a perfect and mesmerising balance.

I really wanted to like this game. I sat for a couple 5 hour sessions to really get into the game. I thought the leveling up of the 3 characters to level 3 was slow, but reasonable. Grinding is grinding after all. But as soon as I passed to the level 3 threshold, the whole experience changed. Suddenly I was a guy with a simple rifle going against snipers and tanks. There was no way for me to do any damage to the tanks, and of course I could never even find the snipers. It went from a competitive enjoyment I was willing to spend some cash on to me deciding to go elsewhere.
Really dissapointed.
UPDATE: So, I read some of the other reviews and continued playing to give it a shot. The game has grown on me since then. I have not put a dime of money into the game, so I am not one of the "pay to play" guys. I have to say, my experience has significantly improved since my original review. I think it is a combination of factors which lead to this. First, obviously having a higher ranked character gives you more access to equipment upgrades and just time grinding in the system makes you better at the game overall. I have gotten better with my headshots and learned the maps to know where I should go to get the best angles.
For the most part, I feel like the developers have done a good job fixing the balance in new matches. I am not the most advanced player in any of the games I played, nor am I the weakest. I am just a solid middle of the pack guy and I have a lot of fun. Sure, I get spawn sniped every once in a while, or a game may get one sided that its like 4 guys against 8 tanks. But those are very rare, and happen just as often to put you at the advantage, as they do put you at a disadvantage.
The game play overall is really fun, and I think most of the major bugs have been worked out of the system. I appreciate that the developers are still investing time and effort into upgrading the platform. I have been playing about 2 months now and I have seen at least 3 major upgrades in that time, and the developers indicate they aren't slowing down.
One of the few complaints I do have is with the airplanes in the game. They are very clunky to maneuver and there is no training for them. I do hope the developers spend some time with that. But I thoroughly enjoy the tanks, and you can see a marked difference between driving a lower tier tank vs a higher tier tank. And I absolutely recommend getting a paratrooper. That is a ton of fun.
Ultimately, I am changing my recommendation to YES for this game. There is definitely a learning curve, but you can't beat free for this game.

It was alright.  Terribly short, very linear.  I wish it had more substance to it.  In many areas success was largely trial and error, and the blending of the background and non-interactive elements with the interactive ones occasionally made it confusing how to solve certain puzzles.
Probably the most frustrating part was the helicoptor.  Anyone who has played this section probably knows what I'm talking about.  When you get to this point, make absolutely sure your framerate is good, or you will die, a lot. Even if it's good, you'll still probably die a lot, but slightly less.
I'm giving it a recommendation because in retrospect, it was a decent game, fairly compelling story, just terribly frustrating.  I would like to see more games like it, better fleshed out, more open ended, less linear.  And no "perfect or die" helicoptor sections.  Maybe streamline the climbing up-and-over mechanism.
Buy it if you like atmospheric story driven zombie puzzle/platformers.  But I'd recommend waiting for a sale, and not paying more than $5.

I've purchased and played a handful of Early Access games... Planet Explorers is an AMAZING game.  I've been playing the story mode... the writing itself and dialogue is nothing spectacular - but the game mechanics and concepts are really enjoyable for anyone that likes the ability to create, and build within a game (I love the colony aspect of the game as well as the crafting - crafting is actually practical... I think there may need to be some balancing tweaks with regards to resource costs etc., but the overall concepts are extremely ambitious and this game actually looks like it is going to pull it off.  As an Early Access game - it already is very much playable - and I'm really happy with this purchase.  I can't wait to see what the final product looks like - and the devs seem to be making regular updates, so it is a win-win for everyone (they get some funding and I get to enjoy an awesome game NOW - and LATER).
Update - ~10 months later.... the dev team seems to have spent the past 10 months migrating to Unity 5 (to imrpove graphics etc) - but the gameplay hasn't really evolved (in fact it seems to have introduced more bugs and actual gameplay seems to be around the same place as 10 months ago). I had been enthusiastically checking for new updates/progress on a weekly - then monthly basis - but it's been very disappointing overall.
It's unfortunate since this game really did seem to hold a lot of promise.  It may still turn out to be a great game in the end, but at the current pace it will likely be some time...
I'd definitely suggest that you read through some recent reviews and recent forum posts before purchasing - whereas previously I wouldn't have hestitated to recommend.

This was not the game I thought it would be. The first time I saw it was on sales, less than 5 bucks so I bought it after watching the official gameplay and some reviews. But then, after 10 minutes of playing it, I knew it would be♥♥♥♥♥♥ Why?
Story - 4/10 - The story starts as♥♥♥♥♥♥ The main character is the badass tough zombie apocalypse survivor with a voice like Snake's from MGS. But he has a family: wife and daughter. Those things don't seem to get along together that well. And, if you read his journal entries, you'll find out some things about his past and that he was kind of a open-minded person and a 'phylosopher'. Again, those things do not get along very well. And the game is so short, only based on the main character's search for his family. You don't feel any connection with anyone of your group. The ending is also so bad (kinda predictable). You can enjoy the story, if you imagine the main character as Rick from The Walking Dead and not Snake!
Gameplay - 6/10 - The gameplay seemed cool on the gameplay trailer. But only because I had no clue that's what I had to do the entire game. It's extremely repetitive! The combat is also too poor. You think you'll need all those bullets, but the game is so short that you actually wonder how can this cost more than 10 bucks! This is not a game for 2D style. The zombies and obstacles are only there to slow you down. The Rat's Labyrinth is the biggest slow down sequence ever. Why did that old man make you go throw that maze?! No idea! It's just there to bore you to death and prolongue the game. After you finish the game you can have some fun doing an one take playthrough of the game using Nightmare Mode and gather all the collectibles.
Graphics and atmosphere - 6/10 - The best thing this game has is the cutscenes' artwork. But that is also a problem. If the gameplay was like the cutscenes (in terms of graphics) it would be a bit more enjoyable. The atmosphere is good in a way (the colourless apocalyptic world) but it makes it difficult for you to know where can you jump towards and grab on to.

I still have high hopes for this game, it really is pretty fun once you settle in. But the biggest downfall has to be the blurry graphics. I have a fairly decent rig, but no matter what I do, i cant get rid of the blurry graphics on the player (and some of the terrain). It almost looks like the player is having a fit, even though standing still (constantly shaking). I bought this game early on, and to this date have not seen a graphical improvement, which is sad because, artistically, the game is beautiful. Without resolving the blurry graphics, the game simply becomes too difficult on the eyes to really enjoy. I am running a resolution of 2560 x 1440, and it honestly looks pretty poor. I cannot recommend this game in its current state. If they resolve this issue at some point in the future then I would say grab it at that point, but until then your better off saving your money.
P.S = For those of you who own this game, i found a way that helps stop the choppy gameplay (even though i own a decent rig). On your launch menu, set OpenCl Calculation to cpu. I am not an expert, but it seems when setting this option to your graphics card it simply pushes it too hard and so you end up with choppy gameplay. With cpu selected, you can select the highest resolution and graphics quality (also off the launch menu) and see a drastic speed improvement in game.
Furthermore, launch the game and enter the settings menu. Set grass density to dense, and disable antialiasing and anisotropic filtering. Also disable shadows and set terrain distance to 1km. See how this works for your performance and then try playing around with the AA, AF and Shadows to see what options work for you.
I hope this helps you enjoy the game a bit more. I still cannot figure out how to limit the blurry graphics and the Players (and NPC characters for that matter) caffeince induced "shakes". If anyone knows how to solve this please let me know. I dont think offering the characters a chamomile tea would help :)

WAIT TO BUY THIS GAME.
P.E. still needs a lot of polishing, but I think the game is, even for Early Access, at a point that it can be very fun and is playable, which compared to other Early Access games is saying something. The downsides start to pile up when you look at multiplayer, which honestly is pretty damn lackluster, as well as a HORRIBLE mess for server admins, and personally I bought this game to play with friends, not by myself.
The creation and sharing system is by and far the strongest plus for this game, it's fairly easy to make things that look and perform well, and even better that you can spend more time and effort to make something that mimics something from real-life, another game, book, anything. Single-player and the story-mode are fantastic, and paced well, it allows you to learn the game at a fairly brisk pace without swamping you with all the extras and nuances to the game and others like it. However, multiplayer is a bit of a different beast, and the main reason I can't reccommend the title.
My first issue with multiplayer is that a large chunk of the game is inaccessable. All the stuff is still THERE, buildable, and the like, but it doesn't actually DO anything, because a few other bits and pieces are not buildable, so essentially you waste a lot of resources getting to what would have normally been considered the mid-game from a single player standpoint, which is establishing a colony. Essentially, multiplayer in its current state is adventuring and roaming around in whatever vehicle you may whip up, fighting the bosses and building houses that house nothing but yourself. Which, if this is your cup-of-tea, you would love multiplayer as it is now.
From an admin perspective, you may as well just be another player. Your UI is not changed save the ability to kick and ban players from the server - but only if they are online at the same time as you - there is no server log of players actions, any way to report bad players or similar functions. You need to rely on a 3rd party resource such as a forum to get this across and *hope* an admin is online at the same time as the offender. Not to mention, there is not console for admins. If the server bugs out, as it frequently does due to being Early Access and people lose things, well, tough♥♥♥♥♥♥ The developers at Pathea don't agree that admins should have the power to spawn anything, it exists, just not for anyone who isn't a game dev:
IMO: that's the stupidest excuse I've ever seen. as it boils down to something akin to 'We can't trust you with the console' which is silly. If players don't like how an admin operates their server, they'll look for a different one.
At this stage in the Alpha, I DO enjoy the game as a single player experience, as the game is decently polished in that regard, but if you are looking to buy this more for a multiplayer focus, wait until it is further polished.
EDIT: It is worth noting that the main site, where the developers post updates has been hacked several times in the past month, so the forum link may be inaccessable. Not entirely the developers fault, but a show that Pathea is a bit rough-on-the-rails and slow in development in part due to their attention being elsewhere. Prior to the hacking, development was still pretty slow, but they maintain contact with early-adopters, which I see as a plus.

Sad to report that it doesn't live up to the expectations of what many fans including me might have had about it.
Hotline Miami is considered a classic. Addictive and gory gameplay, arcade like feel, and a great soundtrack to boot made the violent acid fest warrant the cult following that it had earnt. So I feel bad saying that the sequel in one word is just 'okay'.
It feels like they tried to up the ante with this one, building upon the ideas of the first game and mixing it with new ideas. Sadly, the new ideas aren't that good. For example, you play several characters instead of just one, each with their own playstyle. For example, one character gains more points for non-lethal takedowns and for disarming firearms, and another has switches between his rifle and his combat knife. While this is an interesting concept, it unfortunately betrays itself in the fact that you don't get the same freedom as you did in the first game, where before a level you can pick between 20~ masks that each have their own perks to it, allowing you to adapt your own playstyle. Here, it forcibly sets rules upon you that you may or may not like.
It's also not as polished as the last game. There are technical glitches where my swings don't connect with an enemy, causing them to return the favour with a 12-Gauge to the torso, they get perpetually stuck in walls, or that they don't hear the guy next door being mown down with an UZI. If you're reading this before buying this game, let me tell you two things I wish I knew before playing this game and the first:
1) For storyline and gameplay purposes playing the first game is required. On top of that try your best to remember what the top-down view of the characters look like because more than once you will see some characters standing some place and being able to tell it's them will help greatly in trying to decipher this somewhat vauge story.
2) No matter what the game tells you, do NOT be afraid to die or use guns! I found myself more cautious in the first game, which made the progression a LOT slower. Being loud and alerting enemies is not always a bad thing.
Now for a little pre-review backstory (not part of the review, skipable):
I only finished the original Hotline Miami a few days before the release of Hotline Miami 2. I had bought it back around christmas of 2013 but I soon gave up and moved on to other things (as I said earlier I was going through this seemingly-easy game REALLY slowly and I had started to get bored). Soon though I began craving the game again but, to my surprise, it didn't work. I tried everything I could think of at the time to get it to work (which didn't include consulting the internet) but it was still broken. Fast forward about a year later and we're a week before Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number's release. I decided to try again at Hotline Miami. I opened it up and still no luck. I went though the normal stuff but then I happened to notice and 'updated' or 'original' setting on the launcher. I set it to original to see if that would work and it did! I went into the game and beat it rather quickly. Looking back at it now I'm actually happy that I played it just a few days before the relese of HM2 because that gave me the knowlage and ability to be able to beat HM2 that I wouldn't have had otherwise.
Now for the review:
Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is by FAR one of my favorite games. Although I did find some stuff annoying, for the most part HM2 is WAY more polished than the first game. To anyone saying that HM2 is buggier than HM1 please go replay the first game then come back. The storyline is just vauge, intriguing and has lots of little hints here and there that you won't notice unless you pay attention. (Spoiler, sorta) Although the ending is a bit disappointing, I can see why the devs did it that way and I respect that.
Pros:
*More playable characters (this is debatable but I think it's a pro).
*New, more varying weapons.
*Better, more polished mechanics (with a few exeptions).
*More AMAZING music.
*Extremely Gorey (again, this is debatable if this is actually a pro or not).
Cons:
*Levels can sometimes be TOO large.
*Windows can be a ♥♥♥♥♥ and can REALLY screw you over on a good run.
*Dog and npc AI can be a bit weird sometimes.
Opinions:
(Spoilers)
*The fans are my favorite characters in this game, specifically Alex & Ash. Just the idea of a brother-sister combo going on a murder spree seems cool to me.
*I would have liked to have seen Biker In a better state. Meeting him at a bar only to find out he had just left after the first game and went crazy was really disapointing because he was my favorite character in the first game.
*At first I was sad that I didn't get to play as Jacket but now I'm glad. It makes sense from a story perspective and I'm glad they didn't include him as a playable character.
*I liked seeing Jacket and Beard(aka Soldier)'s backstory in the war. It was really cool once I realized that the silent guy with the team was jacket.
*Some levels in hard mode seemed a little TOO hard and required too much accuracy and precision.
Overall I do think this game is better than it's predecessor because of the more levels and more characters. I'm glad that this is an official ending to the saga and they're not pulling a valve and leaving us wondering where the third game is. I'm happy with this ending but I still have so many un-answered questions that I'm sure I will find the answers to later. Thank you Dennation for making such an amazing series.

[EARLY ACCESS REVIEW]
Last date played: 4/17/2016
There are definitely some things to like about Melody's Escape, and maybe with some more tweaking and pruning it could carve out a comfy niche for itself in this genre, but its current form still feels like an idea that is not yet fully realized. The game pairs the rhythm platforming of Bit.Trip Runner with the 4x4 split button configuration of Before The Echo (formerly known as "Sequence").
Here is a breakdown of the good/bad as I currently see it:
It's still in Early Access and it seems promising. There is a kernel of something here that I definitely like. It just doesn't quite feel fully realized yet. I hope to update this review at a later date with a "recommended". I'll keep my eye on it and my fingers crossed.
indie, early access

For an early access game, it runs and plays fluidly, like REALLY good, and is definitely an interesting and varied change of pace from the typical rhythm game, The controls are very responsive, the music, whatever your musical tastes are catered to almost a whim in this game, and with workshop support opens up another realm of customization towards the game. The learning curve is on the medium-hard side, easy to pick up , but fairly hard to master.
PROS
-Extremely fun to play your music to
-Responsive and intuitive controls
-Freedom to use whatever control scheme fits your playstyle (analog sticks, D-Pad, ABXY, Keyboard)
-Workshop opens up the potential to tailor the game to however one wants to see it (for the time being limited to just character models)
-Music detection system is nearly flawless on generation of most music tracks
-Sharp graphics
CONS
-Needs player generated tracks
-Track/Level editor to make custom levels and sequences rather than use the automated system to generate tracks (Not saying the detection is always bad, but sometimes certain tracks lack sync with specific moments in tune with the music)
-Player made level browsers (If above is implemented)
-Animation needs variety, maybe different variations of jumps, ducks and flying? It gets a tad bit boring to see Melody perform the same jumps, kicks and ducks. Stylize the game and spice it up, or hopefully add workshop support for this (Was really, really impressed with the slo-mo jumps in tune with the music, and definitely want to see more moments like this in context with the music being played)
-Level design is minimal and alright, but could use a touch of custom backgrounds, obstacles and environments, it does become a bit bland after a while
-Could use a customizable interface and music map (optionally or in tandem with the track time left)
If implemented, please make it optional, as not everyone would like this, so everyone has freedom of choice for how they want their interface to be.
With a little bit more polish, this game is well worth the price tag it's advertised for and I highly recommend anyone skeptical of trying out this rhythm game to give it a shot, because it's definitely one of the best rhythm games I've seen in a long time. I will update this review as the development of this game progresses. 9/10

As expected, Planet Explorers is a work in progress, and aside from the bugs, what's there could easily be a stand-alone game.  The number of hours of playtime I have enjoyed is staggering when compared to most AAA titles, so I consider it money well spent.
That said, the game is very rough around the edges, so if you are the type to get frustrated easily by bugs, glitches, and terrible ally pathfinding, you might want to give the game some time to mature.  I lost count of how many times I arrived at a quest destination after a long journey, only to realize that the quest NPC(s) was nowhere to be found.  Most of the time, retracing my steps would lead me to said NPC(s) running mindlessly into a tree or rock, which I would have to destroy to snap them out of their strange trance.  Occasionally, they would get stuck on nothing.  Occasionally, I would get stuck on nothing, too.  This is just the tip of the iceberg.
But if you can tolerate typical early access issues during early access, I think you will find the story is quite atypical--in a good way--for this sort of game, and the city building is shaping up to be something special.  It isn't quite there yet, but Planet Explorers has tons of quests, tons of dialog, and tons of ways to utilize and/or manage your colony.  The voxel system itself is pretty flexible, and once you get used to it (which does take some time) the in-game editor is surprisingly easy to use.  You can make decorations, equipments, and even vehicles.
UPDATE 4/29/2016
Quite some time has passed, and that time has not been kind to this title.  It is nearly as clumsy as it ever was, and other Early Access games have since been released in a worse state only to progress leaps and bounds beyond Planet Explorers.  I am not yet ready to change my recommendation to a "No", but I am close.  I suspect I will have to, at some point.  For now, if this is your niche, I still cautiously recommend it.

Edit: 1 year later: The tutorial is a pain, they've updated a bunch  of the graphics, sounds, etc. The theme song has words now (I liked it when it didn't :( ). I get a car really soon so I don't have to walk 500 miles earlly in the game. Yay! It stutters a lot now, but that might just be because of all the stuff I have running in the background. Apparently the story's grown since I last played, so I'll try to see what's new.

A prime example of not following its own rules is the first tool you pick up, a fireman's axe... with it, you are supposed to be able to knock down zombies and finish them off (stamina permitting), and break through boarded-up doors and the like.  Well, knocking down zombies works great, but finishing them off rarely if ever works, especially after the first attempt.  Likewise, in at least one instance, I came across a boarded-up doorway that the axe just bounced off... because the developers' intent was for you to wall-jump off that doorway to reach a ledge.
So, if you like spending your playtime trying to guess what a game's developer was thinking (either on a specific puzzle or a broader design choice), go ahead and snag this game... otherwise, steer clear.

Contagion is a great playing multiplayer game that’s updated rather constantly. It has a lot of replay ability due to its difficult maps and randomly generated level paths, zombie placement and item drop. It’s very good at luring you into a false sense of security and then dumping a massive hoard of zombies on you at the worst possible moment. It’s not plagued by unlimited or re-spawning zombies as some games are. It’s massively immersive and the designers are good at communicating with the community.
The levels are well designed mazes [yes you will get lost] that require team work to figure out most of the time. There is a lot of environment story told as well, the game doesn’t put you in pointless grey box rooms with zombies and call it a game instead each area looks like it was handmade carefully with precision. Clearly the map makers care about what they are doing which is a plus in my books.
There are a few bugs which are hilarious for the most part and definitely not game breaking.
The game is remarkably similar to left for dead except much, much slower paced and with weaker weapons. Don’t let that discourage you though, the weapons have very satisfying sounds and are still capable of sending zombies flying across the map if used right.
Sometimes you’ll get an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who hogs the equipment, but so far that’s about the worst you'll get.
There aren’t a lot of levels yet but the ones there are, are massive and will probably require multiple tries to complete. The animation isn’t quite done, though it’s still incredibly fun.
This is a great game if you have some friends and some mics; it’s largely strategic but not impossible to do solo.
It has a couple game types but the best is the objective mode [escape] the game combines a couple dungeon crawler elements with slight survival horror vibes but still contains much of the fun of just blasting zombies into gore.
To summarize it’s a well worth getting and a must have if you are a zombie enthusiast.
It’s also decently priced.

Let's get this out of the way first: Hotline Miami 2 is hard.  Like really hard.  Like I got the achievement for dying 1000 times when I was maybe 3/4 done with the story hard.  But it's also a fun and stylish experience with a variety of characters coupled with a once again outstanding soundtrack.  This time around there is a more coherent story, and rather than choosing from an assortment of masks at the start of each level you generally start as a different character that has his own gameplay style.  My favorite of the new styles is probably a set of twins where one carries a chainsaw that your left click will swing, while the other twin starts with a pistol that you can shoot with a right click: they're difficult to control at first but once you get the hang of it there's lots of fun to be had.  Other notable characters are the soldiers, who get a choice of a gun to start (ammo can be found in crates found in their levels) while a right click has them pull out a knife, and also a reporter who won't use guns (he will pick them up, but just unloads them and drops them immediately) and prefers to knockout his enemies rather than kill them.
Hotline 2 is a challenging game that will punish your smallest mistakes, but you will figure out the levels and be satisfied when you clear them.  The story took me around 7 hours to finish the first time through, but this is the type of game that begs to be perfected, and I can see myself coming back to it in the future.

First, I highly recommend that you play the first Hotline Miami before playing this one. It'll make a little more sense, but no promises.
Wrong Number is set after the events of the first, with the arrest of Jacket after his murder spree through the Russian mafia. You play as a group of vigilantes, known as the Fans, who emulate Jacket's actions in hopes of receiving the mysterious phone calls to give them direction, murdering hoodlums in the signature gory manner of the series.
Wrong Number is set before the events of the first, during a war against Soviet Russia, who have invaded Hawaii. You play as a member of the "Ghost Wolves", constantly being sent on dangerous missions by command to remove the Russian menace, while pining for home.
Wrong Number is set during the trial of Jacket, which is hotly debated thanks to anti-Russian factions decrying him as a American hero. You play as a reporter, who fights his way to the truth behind the group that is manipulating these murderers and what conspiracy it may be hiding.
Wrong Number is set after the events of the first, on the set of the slasher flick "Midnight Animal" obviously aping Jacket's murders. You play as a troubled actor, casted as Pig-Man, who acts out the urgings of the Director but soon begins to lose the difference between the movie and reality.
Wrong Number is set during an investigation of the Miami Mutilator, who has been brutally murdering his victims while claiming his innocence in their spilled blood. You play as a loose cannon cop, who's fighting his way through the criminal underworld while chasing this illusive killer.
All these plotlines, and more, weave through the narrative on another psychedelic spree of colorful visuals, detailed sprite work and interesting level design. While much more dialogue heavy than the first, the game still offers the lightning fast dance of mutilation, gunfire and brutality that the first one did with an emphasis on smooth action, varied style and combos to get the best ranks (don't worry, it's easy to replay specific levels, all intros and dialogue being skippable). Although, depending on your character, you won't be able to pick from a large variety of masks, most characters have either a few choices or gameplay quirk to keep every level fresh, yet give you something to master (each Fan is represented by a mask while the Reporter favors melee and can extend combos by dismantling firearms he goes, while the Soldier has a few guns to choose from before each assault).
Gameplay remains the same, with quick death and quicker restarts, melee being silent and guns attracting attention and the ability to throw weapons and stun enemies. Doors remain a fearful nether-realm to the police officers, mobsters and dogs that populate each level, but smarter AI would probably make the game impossible. Blood still splatters, executions are still brutal and weapons are varied and fun to experiment with.
Wrong Number is perhaps a perfect sequel. It keeps the razor-sharp gameplay that fans of the original will know and love, while improves the roster of options and gives you a deeper, yet still utterly bizarre narrative to feast on, if you can keep up with who's where at what time.

Sad to report that it doesn't live up to the expectations of what many fans including me might have had about it.
Hotline Miami is considered a classic. Addictive and gory gameplay, arcade like feel, and a great soundtrack to boot made the violent acid fest warrant the cult following that it had earnt. So I feel bad saying that the sequel in one word is just 'okay'.
It feels like they tried to up the ante with this one, building upon the ideas of the first game and mixing it with new ideas. Sadly, the new ideas aren't that good. For example, you play several characters instead of just one, each with their own playstyle. For example, one character gains more points for non-lethal takedowns and for disarming firearms, and another has switches between his rifle and his combat knife. While this is an interesting concept, it unfortunately betrays itself in the fact that you don't get the same freedom as you did in the first game, where before a level you can pick between 20~ masks that each have their own perks to it, allowing you to adapt your own playstyle. Here, it forcibly sets rules upon you that you may or may not like.
It's also not as polished as the last game. There are technical glitches where my swings don't connect with an enemy, causing them to return the favour with a 12-Gauge to the torso, they get perpetually stuck in walls, or that they don't hear the guy next door being mown down with an UZI. The larger levels bite itself in the♥♥♥♥♥♥as well, as often you'll get sniped by enemies you wouldn't see or know that they were there except through trial and error.
However, it's not all bad. The engine has been updated to add nice little touches like severed heads being kicked about the area, blood splatters on walls, and entrails being hung about. The soundtrack is pretty awesome as well, and there is still some fun to be found in the set rules forced upon you. If you're a fan of HM1, then definitely pick this up.

If you're reading this before buying this game, let me tell you two things I wish I knew before playing this game and the first:
1) For storyline and gameplay purposes playing the first game is required. On top of that try your best to remember what the top-down view of the characters look like because more than once you will see some characters standing some place and being able to tell it's them will help greatly in trying to decipher this somewhat vauge story.
2) No matter what the game tells you, do NOT be afraid to die or use guns! I found myself more cautious in the first game, which made the progression a LOT slower. Being loud and alerting enemies is not always a bad thing.
Now for a little pre-review backstory (not part of the review, skipable):
I only finished the original Hotline Miami a few days before the release of Hotline Miami 2. I had bought it back around christmas of 2013 but I soon gave up and moved on to other things (as I said earlier I was going through this seemingly-easy game REALLY slowly and I had started to get bored). Soon though I began craving the game again but, to my surprise, it didn't work. I tried everything I could think of at the time to get it to work (which didn't include consulting the internet) but it was still broken. Fast forward about a year later and we're a week before Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number's release. I decided to try again at Hotline Miami. I opened it up and still no luck. I went though the normal stuff but then I happened to notice and 'updated' or 'original' setting on the launcher. I set it to original to see if that would work and it did! I went into the game and beat it rather quickly. Looking back at it now I'm actually happy that I played it just a few days before the relese of HM2 because that gave me the knowlage and ability to be able to beat HM2 that I wouldn't have had otherwise.
Now for the review:
Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is by FAR one of my favorite games. Although I did find some stuff annoying, for the most part HM2 is WAY more polished than the first game. To anyone saying that HM2 is buggier than HM1 please go replay the first game then come back. The storyline is just vauge, intriguing and has lots of little hints here and there that you won't notice unless you pay attention. (Spoiler, sorta) Although the ending is a bit disappointing, I can see why the devs did it that way and I respect that.
Pros:
*More playable characters (this is debatable but I think it's a pro).
*New, more varying weapons.
*Better, more polished mechanics (with a few exeptions).
*More AMAZING music.
*Extremely Gorey (again, this is debatable if this is actually a pro or not).
Cons:
*Levels can sometimes be TOO large.
*Windows can be a ♥♥♥♥♥ and can REALLY screw you over on a good run.
*Dog and npc AI can be a bit weird sometimes.
Opinions:
(Spoilers)
*The fans are my favorite characters in this game, specifically Alex & Ash. Just the idea of a brother-sister combo going on a murder spree seems cool to me.
*I would have liked to have seen Biker In a better state. Meeting him at a bar only to find out he had just left after the first game and went crazy was really disapointing because he was my favorite character in the first game.
*At first I was sad that I didn't get to play as Jacket but now I'm glad. It makes sense from a story perspective and I'm glad they didn't include him as a playable character.
*I liked seeing Jacket and Beard(aka Soldier)'s backstory in the war. It was really cool once I realized that the silent guy with the team was jacket.
*Some levels in hard mode seemed a little TOO hard and required too much accuracy and precision.
Overall I do think this game is better than it's predecessor because of the more levels and more characters. I'm glad that this is an official ending to the saga and they're not pulling a valve and leaving us wondering where the third game is. I'm happy with this ending but I still have so many un-answered questions that I'm sure I will find the answers to later. Thank you Dennation for making such an amazing series.

I really wanted to like this game, however I get the feeling it was released just a little undercooked. At it's heart it's a L4D clone with a Warhammer flavour, and a loot system thrown in for good measure. You pick from one of five characters (Witch Hunter, Dwarf, Human soldier, Bright Wizard or Elf Waywatcher) and then choose a mission which will involve navigating the streets while being attacked by a horde of Skaven.
Like L4D the Skaven come in various flavours - from the relatively easy skavenslaves to the huge rat ogres or devastating ratling guns. You can pick up various bits of equipment along the way to help, including firer bombs, strength potions and similar. Wander off too far from the rest of the group and you risk being picked off by gutter runners.
The combat itself is fairly mediocre - most characters have the option of ranged attacks for which there's limited ammo and melee attacks which usually come in two forms (one quick slash, one stronger attack for armoured opponents). While not as sophisticated as Dark Souls or Mount and Blade it gets the job done.
I bought it on launch and found the experience marred by some pretty horrendous bugs. The AI suffers from some pathfinding issues - many times I watched the skaven simply spin rapidly on the spot, or get stuck on scenery. The same affects the friendly bots which can fill in for missing players, although they'll also just as often decide to run off like some kind of medieval Rambo until brought down by the horde; but just as often you'll find them refusing to move from a location because there's a skaven slave stuck on a nearby ledge. They refuse to assist downed players, and in fact when the host went down the AI bots seemed to simply freeze in place. This wouldn't have been a huge issue, however the matchmaking system was also flaky meaning the bots often had to make an appearance in order to get the game started.
There's a core of a good game in here, however I think it could probably have done with some additional time on the stove to really bring it out. While I've no doubt these issues will be patched out over time, it does mean rather than a recommendation I'd say "come back in a couple of months".

If you've played Left 4 Dead, you'll almost immediately have a certain level of familiarity when you start playing. You might notice one enemy pouncing a player rapidly, and you have to strike that enemy off of your team mate. You might also notice one that grabs a team mate and pulls that team mate away, around corners and such so you have to chase them to rescue your team mate. You'll notice glowing outlines of players through walls, and even two levels (that I've seen so far) where your entire goal is to gather items spread throughout the level and bring them back to the escape vehicle. Most of the levels have you going from A to B and swarms (hordes) of enemies will come at you randomly. The list goes on. However, if you enjoyed Left 4 Dead, you would likely enjoy this game.
There are plenty of differences between this and Left 4 Dead, however. Vermintide's melee combat immediately springs to mind. Although you can kill enemies with ranged weapons, most of the characters will be doing a -lot- of fighting up close and personal, including blocking, shoving while blocking, changing your position during small skirmishes to land hits and avoid them, and learning when the perfect moment it to perform a mid-range kill with your ranged weaponry, quickly switching back to melee for a block. You can even do a little quick movement left/right/back similar to Dying Light, which can help you avoid hits from enemies whose attacks would otherwise break through your defenses.
Four players can be in the game at once, and only one instance of each character can be in your game, but there are 5 characters. If someone has your character, you will need to choose between the remaining characters. This game doesn't really have a "Rochelle" character (i.e. one that is completely useless and everyone hates), so it's fun playing the different characters and trying different weapon loadouts.
Speaking of loadouts, you will start the game with very little gear. However, each time you level up (supposedly there is no level cap), you get a free piece of loot, and every time you beat a level, you get to roll dice for loot. The quality of your loot is determined by dice rolls, and you use different kinds of dice based on the level you just finished. This adds a new level of depth that it'd be fun to see the Left 4 Dead series adopt, or makes me want it to innovate with adding something really fresh to the series, at least. It's fun learning the levels and where to find the secrets to improve your loot quality, and playing on a higher difficulty gives a higher quality loot pool to base your dice rolls on. Playing on normal was netting me white items and occasionally green items, so I beat two levels on hard and got a green item and a blue item (same quality order as Borderlands games). I don't think there is purple gear, but it looks like orange gear would be possible to obtain on the higher difficulties (there are 2 above hard!).
You might think "What if I get several copies of the same weapons?" Well that's pretty awesome, because there's a forge at the inn (safe zone you can vote to load after winning/losing a level), where you can either break down the weapon into parts you can use to upgrade certain weapons, -or- you can "fuse" five weapons together to create a new weapon of the next level of rarity (5 white turn into 1 green weapon, or 5 green weapons turn into 1 blue weapon). The resulting weapon is random, but if you fuse 5 of the same weapon, you'll get the next level of quality for the -same- weapon. The only thing random will be the upgrade trait you can apply to it afterward.
Killing the enemies is quite satisfying and each character has enough differences to make if fun trying different ones. This game is so unexpectedly fun and challenging. If you think it's too easy, kick up the difficulty. My blood runs cold even considering "cataclysm," the game's highest difficulty, because hard is pretty tough, and going for the best loot means deliberately picking up hidden items that will drop the whole team's max HP down to about 25%, so it gets reeeeally nasty even on lower difficulties! I highly recommend it thus far and look forward to seeing more players online.

For an early access game, it runs and plays fluidly, like REALLY good, and is definitely an interesting and varied change of pace from the typical rhythm game, The controls are very responsive, the music, whatever your musical tastes are catered to almost a whim in this game, and with workshop support opens up another realm of customization towards the game. The learning curve is on the medium-hard side, easy to pick up , but fairly hard to master.
PROS
-Extremely fun to play your music to
-Responsive and intuitive controls
-Freedom to use whatever control scheme fits your playstyle (analog sticks, D-Pad, ABXY, Keyboard)
-Workshop opens up the potential to tailor the game to however one wants to see it (for the time being limited to just character models)
-Music detection system is nearly flawless on generation of most music tracks
-Sharp graphics
CONS
-Needs player generated tracks
-Track/Level editor to make custom levels and sequences rather than use the automated system to generate tracks (Not saying the detection is always bad, but sometimes certain tracks lack sync with specific moments in tune with the music)
-Player made level browsers (If above is implemented)
-Animation needs variety, maybe different variations of jumps, ducks and flying? It gets a tad bit boring to see Melody perform the same jumps, kicks and ducks. Stylize the game and spice it up, or hopefully add workshop support for this (Was really, really impressed with the slo-mo jumps in tune with the music, and definitely want to see more moments like this in context with the music being played)
-Level design is minimal and alright, but could use a touch of custom backgrounds, obstacles and environments, it does become a bit bland after a while
-Could use a customizable interface and music map (optionally or in tandem with the track time left)
If implemented, please make it optional, as not everyone would like this, so everyone has freedom of choice for how they want their interface to be.
With a little bit more polish, this game is well worth the price tag it's advertised for and I highly recommend anyone skeptical of trying out this rhythm game to give it a shot, because it's definitely one of the best rhythm games I've seen in a long time. I will update this review as the development of this game progresses. 9/10

Pros:
-You can play literally anything.  Pop.  Rap.  Opera.  A recording of you screaming obscenities into a microphone for two minutes.  ANYTHING.
-Beat detection is pretty darn good across a wide variety of genres.
-Graphics are appealing; there's a beauty in their simplicity.
-There are a couple different costumes and hairstyles available.  If those aren't enough for you, though, there are plenty more in the Steam Workshop.
-Melody doesn't judge your musical preferences, so feel free to play the opening of My Little Pony: Friendship is Magic.  It generates a pretty fun level.  I highly recommend it.
Cons:
-Sometimes you might get thrown off when parts that sound the same within a song (say, a chorus that repeats itself a couple times) end up making Melody go at different speeds each time.  However, this is a pretty minor complaint.
-The game doesn't seem to come with any songs as other rhythm games tend to.  Again, though, this isn't that big of a deal unless you don't have music of your own.
Conclusion:
A fun little rhythm game that's definitely worth buying and good to pass the time with.  Fast songs can be very satisfying to do well on, and slower songs are nice and relaxing.  Personally, I'd kind of like to have an option to have the song stop or get quiet when you screw up (as it is, the song keeps playing regardless of how you're doing, although you do get a little noise indicating that you derped it up along with a death animation if you missed an obstacle), just because it makes it more satisfying for me when I do well, but it's not really a priority.  If you like rhythm games, you should definitely give this one a go.  Just make sure that you have at least a halfway decent computer.  The game isn't particularly demanding, but you know how it is when you lag in a rhythm game.  A split second of computational disloyalty is all it takes to mess up a streak.

I rarely play co-op anything. I'm as much a loner in games as I am IRL. With that being said:
This is a great great great game! I suck at FPS, like really bad, but I LOVE zombies, so I buy just about every zombie game that looks worth while. I'm disapointed with some of them, say "meh.." on a few. But this one is great! As previously stated, I suck, so I played it on easy mode. I was expecting to just walk through the whole thing a few times and get the hang of it before upping the skill level.
Well, I discovered that this game is so well balanced that even in the easiest mode, there where still just a few more bullets available than there where undead. The only way to survive was to use everything available and creep forward slowly. You can't go on a rampage and you can't get careless or you will die.
Graphically, I'm impressed. At first, I was kind of put off by the chick player characters. The Skyrim Nexus has spoiled me. However. I soon realized that it didn't matter because all you see is their hands. The environment though - beautiful.
The music is stellar. It seems to flow seamlessly with what's going on in the game and it definitely sets the mood. It's that rare kind of music that you "feel" whether you want to or not.
Zombies and items are very well placed in game even though they seem to appear in different spots each time I played a level. The stiffs can and do get the drop on you because they can be sneaky. Plus, they can climb fences quickly, crawl under things and through holes. Many times it was dead silent and I turned around in a dark room to shine my flashlight in the face of one. I think I pooped a little.
The only bug I found (04NOV14), and I'll explain why I point it out, is that zombies cast shadows through walls sometimes. I am thankful for this and so are my pants. I point this out because it was the ONLY bug I found. Indi games are typically more pollished (in my experience) than major titles anyway. But this one is really, really nicely done. Not a single CTD, no magical things happening, very very very little clipping (zombies breaking down doors).. When I bought this game, I bought a finished product, and I'm thankful to the developers for that.
I'll definitely be playing this game for a long time to come!
[To the developers] Wonderful job people! Really. If you make another game that sounds like it's even remotely up my alley, I'll buy it without question! (Even if it's not, I'll use your game to give the genere a try.)

Mount & Blade: Warband is the sequel to the original Mount & Blade from 2008.
Mount &Blade: Warband –and the Mount & Blade series in general I guess- is a medieval RPG game, and where it compared with other games within the same genre lacks the magic dragons and mystic happenings, it manages to set up the mood for a realistic atmosphere with a lot of action and intensities.
You start of the game by choosing your players backstory, all the choices you make will have an effect on your skills, and you can then later on train and level up all of these by simply using the specific weapon in combat. You then start roaming around the world of Calradia, you will own nothing but the clothes on you, and your weapons, you can then slowly start raising an army and aspire to become a sworn vassal of a king, or even take castles for yourself and claim for the right of Calradia yourself!
Another great feature added to this sequel, is the multiplayer mode, you can now play online in with fellow players in several different game modes, including Capture the Flag, Team Deathmatch and many others. Apart from multiplayer, the game also includes a custom battle mode allowing you to fight any fight you want, against any enemy you want, on any map you want.
Apart from the base game being great in itself, this game is easily modable. So if you buy it and you start to think of it as too uniform, there’s many great mods out there. A few I can recommend is the “Clash of Kings” mod, (which gives the game a GoT twist) and L’aige (for multiplayer mode) and finally the graphic enhancer if you simply find it unbearable.

This game does things in two ways:
1) Avarge, like dozens of other titles.
2) Badly. Or even worse thaen badly.
Seriously, there is not a single feature in "Heroes & generals" that is somehow extraordinary. Not even a one thing that would make me say to my friends "You know, there is a cool thing in this game I played - "H&G". You know, it's...". If you played at least 3 team FPS you mostlikely seen everything "Heroes & Generals" has to offer. And most likely it was done better. And that's the good side of this game. The bad one? Balance. While I could agree that in "War Mode" (where player themselves decides on what force will fight) games can be uneven, it is ridiculous that "Staged Battles" (which should be - accoridng to game description - balanced) are pretty much the same as in "War Mode". Fresh player can be thrown in a battle against Tiger tank with no means to destroy it. Bah, one player wouldn't be bad. Butwhole your team can be matchmaked  so that nobody in your team has unlocked gear matching your opponents. So it is not rare that you will be steamrolled by tanks or bombed by planes with no means to defend yourself (couse putting some AA guns would be to much...). That's unbalanced in macro. In micro, you are screwed if you play infantry. Trying to shoot at airplanes is useless. And I mean something bigger than personal wepoans - Thomson, Garand etc. I mean Machine Guns. If it's not AA emplacement, Machine Guns sucks. Who cares that US AA is composed of 4 .30cal MGs. The same MG mounted on the back of your jeep is useless. I've spent whole ammo box (400 rounds) shooting at one plane, diving straight at me, having hit confirmations one after another... And it killed me. Kill Screen claimed I did like 10% of damage to him. Same goes for the tanks. You would think that after hard work of sneaking behind enemy medium tank with panzerfaust to launch rocket at his rear should be somehow rewarding. Well, it is not. You will receive "Armor too thick" message majority of times. And on those rare occasions when you do some damage you will learn that you will need hell a lot more hits to scorch the tank. Which is difficulot as you carry only one rocket...

On the surface, Heroes & Generals seems fine. A normal WWII free to play game. But as a player continues on, they will start to notice something. Everything is taking a while to get. "Oh well" this new player might say, "It will get better when I'm a super cool General!"
As they progress later on in the game, they soon will get tired of the constant repair costs, the cost of weapons, the pay that they get per a game, and most inportantly that just about everyone has had enough of, the ribbons.
This new player will get tired, fed up, and just downright say that the game is a pay2win, and at this point half way to general, it is.
The game itself performs from "Good" to "We can do better for 2015" such as 'Network trying to catch up' to the under the ground glitchy death screens, to zero sounds some times. I know this game is in beta, but it has been worked on since 2011.
The concept of combined strategy-part and FPS is great, and I like this game when I forget that I need to really not shoot a something to be safe beause of repair costs or that the ribbons will take a long time.
In all, I will rate this game a 70/100 on good days.

I loved the first game. I beat it in one sitting and was so blown away that I played through the whole game again the next day. Playing through Hotline Miami 2 took 4 sittings and I don't foresee myself replaying it. On just about every design choice, they tried to make things more complex. This ends up making it pale in comparison to its predecessor. With that being said, the gameplay is still similar enough to the first game that I could see how others could enjoy it more than I did.
Pros
+The soundtrack is what you would expect after playing the first game.
+The core gameplay still offers a good deal of fun.
Cons
-Unlike the open ended mask system of the first game, you're forced into using characters with combat modifiers that you may not want. Some character abilities are more abrasive than others. One won't let you pick up enemy weapons and forces you to reload your weapon at ammo crates when you run out of bullets. I don't know who the hell would have picked that if given another option.
-the story follows 10+ characters over a jumbled timeline. You won't care for any of them like you did the protagonist of the first game. To remain as vague as possible but still bring up the issue, some of those 10+ are going to die throughout the plot and you really won't care.
-The story leaves no questions unanswered. Leaving mystery around the first game's plot is what made it so good.
-The game doesn't ever feel like it's ramping up towards a final epic climax. It just kinda ends. I was surprised to see the credits start rolling on the final stage despite feeling like the game was dragging on.
-The maps are also MUCH more open than in the first game and there are windows everywhere. This makes melee weapons much less useful and leads to countless deaths from off-screen enemies shooting you. I unknowingly picked a fists only class for a mission that ended up being very open. I had to resort to dancing out in the open to get them to chase me into close quarters so I could land a killing blow.
-The AI is glitchy. Dogs get caught in loops of chasing their tails and basic enemies can get stuck in doors which makes them difficult to kill. You'll need to be standing completely on top of them for your hits to land. This is espeically awful because they could pop out of the door glitch and kill you at any moment.

+ Impressive visuals; exterior environments look incredible; water/rain effects really stand out and react wonderfully with lighting
+ Cell phone is a great feature that was integrated very well with gameplay
+ Only a handful of game-modes, but many of them are novel and fun with tons of replay value
+ Controlling zombies after death was very well implemented; devs put more thought into this than most games of the genre, and there is an unexpected amount of functionality
+ Maps are surprisingly large and easy to lose yourself in
+ Barricading mechanics are simple and intuitive
+ Game engine is very, very well-optimized; the game runs smoothly
+ Maps change every game; Objectives differ, paths close and open, item/weapon pickups are randomized
+ Voice communications operate on differing channels; survivors use one channel, and player-controlled zombies use another (this adds so much to the game, as player controlled zombies can effectively coordinate against their former companions, basically turning death into the start of a new game with new objectives, on the same map, against other players - VERY fun)

Don't get me wrong when I say I don't enjoy this game for the most part, because it's generally entertaining. However, as I play the game more it's rather apparent that many of the flaws in this game do not come from the bugs in beta, but just♥♥♥♥♥♥design choices made by the developers.
To skip over most everything, I'm going to just write out a pros and cons list (So far):
Pros:
+Entertaining gunplay
+Mixed combat, various vehicles and infantry all fighting at once makes for a neat concept and fun game
+Slow leveling system (In my opinion) so someone doesn't instantly achieve a rather powerful class
Cons:
-Unbalanced, even though devs attempt to make it a balanced game, the tank matchups tend to be tipped in favor of one faction or the other.
-Weapon durability and ammo system, i.e. you have to spend your credits on repairing and rearming your tanks/weapons after each match. (This wouldn't be a problem if anything half-decent was cheap to maintiain, but even the light tanks will cost you an arm and a leg to maintain.)
-Prone, it doesn't really work right now and I tend to rely on it a lot in most tactical shooters. (Again, this is more of a bug than design choice, but it really bothers me.)
-Map lighting, the lighting is really awful to me. The mixture of fog, darkness, and various other things scattered about make it incredibly difficult to see anything more than a hundred yards out.
-Sounds, the gun sounds are pretty bad. Enough said, they're very poorly done.
-Assault Squad System, consider that you are playing as a Tank Commander and halfway through the match you recieve at "No more Assault Squads" notification that doesn't allow you to play anymore. It's an awful mechanic that obviously has no effect to me other than to annoy me.
There are a few other things that will come up, however a lot of the issues as of now tend to bother me greatly enough to the point where I just don't really want to play it anymore.
Great concept, fun gunplay, (in my opinion)♥♥♥♥♥♥execution. I'd like to see the durability system done away with most of all, because that is the reason I don't want to play anymore. (My best tank doesn't have any profit left after matches, and just costs me money to use.)
EDIT:
Adding more cons that I thought of, sadly no new pros.

Warhammer:End Times - Vermintide is a very fun MULTIPLAYER game. If you're planning to play it in single mode (with bots) then I would recommend to wait until bot ai will be fixed (more on that later).
The game is a reskinned L4D clone with few new mechanics added on top. You can level up your heroes and gather/craft/upgrade their equipment. There are 13 lengthy and surprisingly varried and well designed maps. Interesting characters with different gameplay mechanics, and most items you'll get will give you different feeling of playing. Also game itself is pretty hard. Game looks and feels very well, it's satisfying to cut big rats in half which is the most important thing in a game like this.
There are two things I don't like about the game though - first one is the bot AI.  If you're playing with bots you'll end up being knocked down while the bots will happily stand around waiting till you'll bleed out. Even if you're playing with one friend it gets very frustrating if at the end of the map you'll both get knocked down and get defeated because bots won't help you while standing 1 meter away doing nothing. They also usually don't heal themselves - so they'll end up dying much more frequently later in the level.
Second downside is the technical state of the game- I've encountered some weird crashes, full screen fatal errors, resolution changes (eg. each time I'm launching the game even tho resolution is set to be 1920x1080 it never is so I need to change it in options to the same setting (!) and then it resets to proper one). Once I had to delete the settings config file in order to run the game since it wouldn't start anyway.
I love this game, it's like an enhanced version of l4d2. looking for skilled players to do grim runs on hard/nightmare

Let's make this clear: In my personal opinion HOTLINE MIAMI 2 is better than the first one. But this may vary on your personal preferences. If you like a more faster and arcade-like game then you shouldn't get the sequel. Basically: If you didn't like the last 4 missions of the first HOTLINE MIAMI you are not going to like this game. HOTLINE MIAMI 2 starts exactly where the first one left of (difficulty-wise).Which means that HM2 is harder than 1. 100-times harder. What HM2 is missing (most of the time) is the masks that spice up the gameplay just how you want it to be. This is a shame in my opinion. Yeah there are some levels that give you a choice which weapons you can have but there are not many. Level-design-wise the game has bigger levels which makes the player act a bit more careful. This slows the game down immensely. However I like that kind of gameplay. It makes the game feel more like a puzzle game than a reaction-based twin stick shooter.
Conclusion: If you like HOTLINE MIAMI 1 then gets the sequel. If you like HOTLINE MIAMI but you hated the last few chapters, pass this one. To me it's the superior version of HM. I am a die hard Hotline Miami fan.  I have purchased maybe 5 extra copies of HLM1 to spread to friends.  I am a huge advocate.  I loved every minute of it multiple times.
I cannot reccommend HLM2.  And it tears me up.  HLM1 rode the line of frustrating and fun.  HLM2 is just frustrating.
Why?
1: More enemies with guns means less of the melee beatdown madness that really got your blood pumping in HLM1
2: Longer/larger maps mean armed enemies will VERY often kill you from outside your view.

I don't even know where to start.  As others have said, this game is exactly what I've sought for a long time.  In a nutshell, they managed to take the positive aspects of various sandbox crafting games and made it fun and removed the tendency to become boring.
I love this game and can't stop playing it.  I can't say the concept of the game is simple because there are so many directions it can go.  There isn't a clear direction on the devs' part, and I mean that in a good way.  They've built a really solid foundation and I'm hanging on the edge of my seat waiting for the next update.
I came across this game looking for something that gives me open-world exploration and crafting.  This game delivers that and then some.  Easily one of the best games I have in my library.
It is tempting to try to compare this to games like Minecraft, Starbound, Terraria, etc., and it wouldn't be wrong to do so: there are a lot of similarities, and feels like some of the devs either worked on one of those or took a lot of inspiration from them, but then again many of these aren't really new concepts.  And in my opinion there's nothing wrong with borrowing ideas that work.
Where this game really delivers is
... and that's all above and beyond (what i find to be the very zen-like process of) mining and scavenging raw materials to build with, and doing actual exploration.  The time in-game shown as of right now (just over 38 hours) is how long it took me to get through the "story" part of the game, and several quests are incomplete, so it just goes to show that they intend to do more with that part of it.  As expected, there are plenty of bugs to work out, but the game is so engaging I barely notice them, except for the ones that break quests at which point i have to reload from a last save or something, but overall the game is amazingly well done given it's still in alpha.
This game easily gets a 10/10.
