My original hype and anticipation for this game was out the roof. As I mentioned in my Hotline Miami 1 review, I originally got HLM1 from a steam sale. For a long time, I let the game just sit in my collection, not even attempting to play it until one hot summer day, I felt like I should finally give the game a try. And to my suprise, I was absolutely amazed and taken aback at just how awesome the game was. To it's trippy soundtrack to it's fun but challenging gameplay, I practically fell in love with it.
None of these feelings however, sustain with Hotline Miami 2. Do I think it's a bad game? not the slightest. I won't get into the story here, because 1: the story is so all over the damn place I would practiclly need to write another review just to explain it, and 2: well, spoilers. Lots of them. It's hard to not explain the story without spoiling something.
So in this review I am instead going to focus on the gameplay and the music. First off, the music is FANTASTIC. I can't really seem to explain it, but despite me liking maybe 1 or two songs a lot more from HLM1's soundtrack more than the entire soundtrack of HLM2, I can tell you that in general, I found more songs enjoyable in HLM2.
It had a lot more of those "Yeah mutha!@#$%! i'm a mutha!@#$% badda$$!" Especially with great tracks such as acid spit, or roller mobster. Everytime I did a level with those songs playing I just imagined myself as some commando badass going in and wrecking peoples♥♥♥♥♥♥up. The soundtrack is so great infact, that I find myself a lot of the time replaying HLM1 with HLM2's soundtrack.
Now, before I get into the gameplay I want to talk about a few things first. So in this game you play as multiple characters. And I think the issue with this is that once you sustain too much focus on multiple characters in a game, they feel less interesting to not only play as, but in terms of just caring about them. I think this game really did strive for "bigger and better." and this is a huge problem. The problem with video game sequels in general is that they don't seem to be made anymore to continue a story, they seem to be made because the fans demand it.
And the issue with a game becoming popular is that everything great about the original goes straight down the drain. Thing is, people will complain either way,right? I mean, if you add too much, people become aggrivated because of their nostalgia from the first game and assosiate that as being "bad" but if you don't add anything then people just accuse it of being a cashcow milking ripoff that's much of the same thing.
HLM2 is different from the first game for sure(in terms of both style,story, and gameplay.) but the biggest issue was the level design, the gameplay. Which we will cover now.
In this game, they wanted to make everything bigger. They added some new weapons(I'm really loving the handguns. They had such a lack of them in HLM1) Where Hotline 1 was a difficult game, you could overcome it with enough skill and patience. The issue with HLM2 is that the levels are generally so massive now, you'll find yourself dying a lot from off screen deaths. Which is NOT a good thing. Hotline 1 was about luring enemies out, watching their patterns/walk cycles, and planning accordingly. Hotline 2 feels more like a cover based shooter at times. Where you basically have to hide and wait because you never know if that enemy half way across the level heard you and is running for you. Because if you decide to come out, you'll die and you won't even be able to see what killed you.
It's an absolutely frusterating aspect of the game. Where in HLM1 the levels were so cleverly crafted to a point where even if it was difficult, your patience and reflexes had more to do with getting a A+ in that game. But in this game it feels more like you're trying to survive/hunting other people down. Which is cool in it's own sense, however, the levels are so big to a point where they just decided to slap in tons of enemies everywhere instead of actually placing them in strategic areas. I found myself actually raging at this game because of how stupid some of the offscreen deaths were. I hope that this will be technically remedied with the level editor that's coming out soon. Which I am very excited about because the devs obviously have seem to lost their touch now with making the levels themselves. Although I feel it was more about them just wanting to make things bigger and better, as opposed to just being lazy.
Do I reccomend this game? most deffiantly. It has tons of replay value now added with an additonal hard mode after you beat the main game, some secret scenes/even a secret level. for 15$(20$ if you bought the special edition, which comes with some Payday 2 DLC and 4 extra soundtracks I believe?) Hotline Miami 2 still sees as being a fun,addictive,challenging game. The level design is pretty awful this time around. However if you can get passed that and enjoy the rocking soundtrack,visuals, and gore, this one is for you.
P.S: Stop crying about the ending. I mean, I didn't like it that much either, but did you expect anything different? look at Hotline Miami 1.

This is my first "serious" (use that term rather loosely) review of a game that I've heavily started to get invested in....little back story.
I've been following this game for awhile behind the scenes and since it was a good deal and I had a bunch of games I recently added to my wishlist within the last 2 days - I went ahead and bought it for something "different." Personally, most sandbox games are damn near zombie heavy and it just ridiculous how the market has been flooded since Walking Dead (nothing bad about the show)
...Anyways...
Here comes Planet Explorers - which I might add is a VERY interesting take on open sandbox games with a decent story mode.
If you are thinking of getting this game, let me cut to the chase and give a good rundown of what I've seen so far:
Note: I would HIGHLY advise doing the story mode first and then tinkering with the Multiplayer. Truthfully, the game is fleshing out rather nicely, but the story mode will take you a while to get through and teaches you alot about the limitations as a whole, so you can actually see what alpha is like right now.
Ok, so here it goes:
PROS
------
- Game runs superb on a high end system, and no doubt any moderate pc rig should be able to run this with no issues
- Story mode is where you want to start at (although the "tutorial" of the story mode is a little odd to catch on and learn the basics.) If you've played any other sandbox MMO then you'll be able to pick up what you need to do pretty quickly. Also, it will take you HOURS, and yes HOURS to play through the story mode if you happen to go off the path and actually have fun exploring and tinkering with stuff as you gain more options throughout the missions.
- Obviously, the game is still in alpha, so just be a bit patient as the game gets built up
- Creating in the game is a BIG plus. I have yet to do it, but planning on, hopefully, making some fun items for the community. So far, most of the designs I've been seeing are awesome looking and can't wait to try them out after full release.
- PE is a beautiful game where you can sit back and relax, watch the sun set on the beach :)
- The interface, regardless of mode, is very easy to use
-  Using sentry guns to shoot the hell out of rampaging beasts is a sweet :) Think of Aliens the Directors Cut with the senty gun scene, hehe.
- You can make scuba diving items to explorer the water!
- Found me a loot chest underground with some random items...who knows what you'll find in the most obscure places
CONS (here are some known issues)
------
- Multiplayer is a little lax since most are probably steering clear an alpha build
- Save often in single player. I only had 1 crash from nearly 10 hours of playing. Logs are written for the crash which should be sent to the devs if you like, but for the most part, this game is very stable.
- The music can get a little old and hopefully they'll add in different scores to keep it interesting. Aside from that, crank up your own music list and have at it!
- There is no tab targetting in the game, so positioning your toon to chop a tree, loot a body takes a little bit to get used too. There is an option to turn on the HP mechanic, for fighting, so you know you are actually hitting the mob, but it would be good to see the name mobs if they choose to do so in an upcoming build. Although, it DOES make it so you have to "explore" and hunt properly in the game (you really never know what you'll come in contact with) - so maybe this isn't such a con, but it's what we all are most used too.
- Finding Tin is a PITA! Just make sure you properly use your mobile scanner and it's updated properly. From there, you'll should be able to see a great 360 degree radar view in how close you are to a vein and how far you need to dig to start mining whatever it is you are searching for.
Ok, so this is a somewhat look at my experience thus far. I have to honestly say though, that someone who gets bored with games easily - this one is actually pleasant to play. Since it is still in alpha, one can only imagine what else is going to come next with the updates in 2015. I have some high hopes with this game and hope it makes it to be everything everyone wants in an interesting sandbox/massively endless open world mmo.
If you are still undecided on this game, definitely keep a watchful eye on it and with any luck, you'll buy it just for what you can do/and hopefully be able to do within the game :)

If you get frustrated by constant bugs that interfere with gameplay and progression, give it a few patches.
Here's what I think is wrong with the game:
1) PUSH TO TALK IS DISABLED BY DEFAULT. WHAT. THE. ♥♥♥♥. Not just your own voice, but you can't hear others either!! Make sure you turn this on IMMEDIATELY. Every game there's someone who can't hear the rest of the team and we have to type. This isn't the kind of game where you can stop to type.
2) Tabbing out of the game, especially when loading, can cause your cursor to stick in first person mode. If you have two monitors, it will let you click the other monitor, tabbing you out of the game. This means you can't turn to the right. Fixed by opening your inventory, which you can only do at the start of the map.
3) It's crashed several times so far. Any progress is lost. Your player slot is pretty much instantly filled, which sucks if you were playing with a friend.
4) If the host leaves, you restart the level. This happens more frequently, especially on hard difficulty if the host doesn't get their way.
5) Hook rats can pull allies through some walls. If this happens, you can't save the ally.
6) The hunter rats very often tackle a player and fly up 200 feet in the air. They come back down, but it's a ton of free damage from the duration of the jump. It's also just stupid nonense, they jump straight up into the air all glitchily.
7) There's a LOT of ledges that are maybe 2 inches tall, but you get hung up on them. Some of them are in really obvious places that you have to pass.
8) You have to watch 4-5 unskippable cutscenes every time you open the game. Even if you were just changing graphic settings or if you had just crashed. "It's unskippable because it's loading" they say. No it isn't. I've got this game on an SSD, it loads in a few seconds.

It requires a slightly different approach than the first game, but the excellence of Hotline Miami is largely repeated here with a much more involved story and an even better soundtrack.
With larger maps it is more difficult to rush into a building and improvise as you go. Larger rooms, longer hallways, more windows, and more enemies mean you'll need to use the off-center view (Shift) to scope things and building a rough gameplay before moving ahead, or holding Shift as you go and playing in the off-center view, which can leave the unaware player even more vulnerable from the sides and rear. This adds more strategy to the game, but it also interrupts the violent flow from the first Hotline Miami.
There's also more variety in level design, with stages that go outside the
building, including a jungle mission with limited weaponry and a long roof-top seige that proves a great mix of fast-pace melee and long-ranged strategy.
Masks offer FAR more variety with abilities and limitations that provide completely different gameplay experiences. Alex & Ash, for instance, allows you to control two masked characters at once, one with a chainsaw the other with a pistol, offering great firepower if you're quick enough to manage their movement.
The bottom line is that Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number changes it up from the first game, and some people may not like that because they wanted more of the same, but it is equal in quality and greater in quantity.
I thought it was great. If you liked HM1 and you genuinely care about the story of games then I think you'll enjoy this a lot.

The story is full of seemingly random, nonsensical bits which only start tying together very late in, and the dialogue is unbelievably atrocious and the characterizations almost nonexistent.  The game opens with a "movie scene" of an actor as a "pig killer" killing goonies, then randomly♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥a woman.  The♥♥♥♥♥♥option is pushed in your face at the start of the game with the offer to disable it, and absolutely nothing of value is added or lost by it.  It appears, it's not a "real"♥♥♥♥♥♥(since it's being filmed for a movie) and it's never referenced ever again throughout the game.  For a game about killing a whole lot of people in gruesome and gorey ways to a frantic high-octane soundtrack, this felt like an incredibly low and trashy attempt at shock or attention.
I could not tell the difference between half the characters save for by their hair color (or lack of hair), and even then I found myself simply NOT CARING about whatever the ♥♥♥♥ they rambled about.  Meanwhile, every time Richard appears, it sets the story going in an exciting direction, only for the next set of levels to be something completely different with someone completely different.  If it all does come together by the end, then it'd still be too little too late, and the lazy effort put into the obscenely excessive bland dialogue can't possibly be worth it.  ((Edit: Having finished the game, it's not worth it.))
For gameplay, it's essentially more of the same.  This would be a good thing if not for the fact that they've upped the difficulty curve on so many of the levels to such a degree that there's no chance at all for creativity or puzzle-solving a level like there was in the first game.  Too many of the maps involve big huge open spaces, in which shotgun-armed enemies are well beyond your line of sight, and the only way to kill them before they kill you is to blindly fire in their general direction AFTER you've respawned from being shot by them first.
Virtually every level I've played in has involved some strategy that involved hiding, waiting for an enemy to walk past, peek out of a door or a window to lure him towards me, then doing it again if needed.  This slugs the gameplay to an almost complete halt, especially if you find a hiding spot only to suddenly be shot or attacked from behind from an enemy that was out of your line of sight.  This completely destroys most attempts at combos, as the only way to advance will require you to sit and wait for enemies to lure towards you.
And there's no real chance to play the levels with a different style --- levels are divided by "Acts" and involve different characters restricted to about 3-4 minor changes in their masks/arsenals, the base one being "roll dodge" which is a perfect move for accidentally rolling out into the open and getting shot 18,000 times before you can stand ready.  The masks don't even matter anymore---the bonuses they give are almost pointless (and the Tony mask now not only gives deadly fists, but makes it so you CANNOT use ANY WEAPON at all except your fists).
So many of the levels go this route that it's impossible to get anything higher than C's for level score on a first-time around, and a single Chapter can take up to an hour to complete due to simply repeating the same♥♥♥♥♥♥over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over.
And there's no way to change up your gameplay as the vast majority of the levels FORCE you to stick to a single "hide and lure" strategy.  EVERY SINGLE LEVEL has windows, making it impossible to just walk around anymore without stopping and creeping forward foot by foot while panning the camera just to check if there's an enemy with a gun patrolling the window.  A few levels don't even let you use weapons other than what you start with, and the ones that do have very little variety in weapons around --- there aren't anymore randomly-generated weapons lying around for you to be creative with.  There's only what the enemies have, and it's always the same set each level.
Overall, the only thing good and new about this game is the amazing soundtrack.  The gameplay is fun, for the most part, but the levels are tediously drawn-out and restricting compared to Hotline Miami.

I won this in a Sonic and All-Stars Racing Transformed tournament, so I figured I'd give it a go. Well, I'm glad I didn't pay for it. What has potential to become an intriguing Metroidvania-esque apocalyptic platformer becomes kind of a muddied mess with a comfusing plot and buggy... well, everything.
You play as Randall Wayne, who has a rather interesting diary that I enjoyed reading through at the start of the game, chronicling his life before except for a few missing pages. This sets up a nice adventure game kind of feel, which is never followed through on. You find more pages, and they are about nothing important, nor do they connect dots between the existing pages. They're just random collectables. You're with a group of survivors, except you're not because they leave in the first cutscene, and you have to go find your family, who's... dead the whole time? I dunno. The Shyamalan crap doesn't work here, and just leaves the basic setup and promise that eventually, story will happen. You're trying to get to the Safe Point, which it turns out isn't safe.
The game's a basic platformer using 2.5D Metroidvania controls (think Shadow Complex, except if you haven't played that, go buy an Xbox 360 and do so instead because it's great) and gimmicks, like finding new equipment and various little items (most interesting of which are little knockoff Game and Watch's, of which I only found one, Madness Mansion and had a grand time playing around with it). Except they're all scripted. There's no freedom of choice here at all besides the occasional item in the background. The only time the 3D environment is useful is to show Shadows (zombies) wandering in and occasionally to force you to use shelves as barricades, often neglecting to show the little icon to do so and leaving you running around the room wondering why everything keeps magically killing you.
It takes an abruptly interesting spike when it completely loses it in the second act and has you taken in by a guy calling himself Ratman. He takes your weaponry, and for some reason never ever gives it back to you even when you could really use it, including when he asks you for help. So that's a♥♥♥♥♥♥move with no explanation. But you go through a basic kind of trial-and-error platformer here. No creativity allowed: It's all about timing, but it works well enough, and the environment looks really cool.
Randall kind of ruins it a little by insistently screaming at the crazy old man, calling him a "crazy old man", a "crazy old man", and a "crazy old man". Randall, in general, doesn't shut up. His voice is nice, I'll give him that, but all the dialogue feels incredibly stilted. There are very few contractions, leading to technically correct but odd sounding sentences like "I have used the first aid kit!". And then some of them actually do shut up... technically all of them, as the cutscenes, in my experience, played one second of audio and then cut out the rest for no explained reason, except at the very end.
So the plot goes nowhere. That point's hammered home. This is where the gameplay should make up for it, but it doesn't. It's basically satisfying at the beginning, but it never expands past that, forcing you to do the same things while more stuff tries to kill you. You don't grab ledges correctly, so much as jump at them and then magically teleport until he's got his hands on it. The axe occasionally does a lot of damage, but mostly doesn't. Some doors can be sprinted into, others force you to stop and calmly open them with a button press. Sometimes you can jump at Shadows and magically pass through them, sometimes you can't and they kill you. You can never take more than three hits per section, and there's never enough ammo to fight properly, which feels less like it's pushing survival and more like the game's combat system is "avoid ever getting into combat". Which mostly works except when it forces you to. There was one room I could only clear by running real, real fast through it and punching the door at the end without addressing anything in the room, and then if Randall tripped over a box and died in the next room, it sent me back to do that again.
In short, if you're looking for a platformer, a story, an accurate post-apocalyptic Seattle, a nostalgia trip, or anything but a time killer for about four or five hours, skip it. Or at least get someone else to pay for it. It starts strong and quickly peters off. (Also, for some reason Steam registers me as having way less time on it than I actually spent. I did finish it, and I don't really care to start it back up.)

Build your own kingdom, have your own banner (flag), raise your army, choose your lords, govern policies and charge into battle. Many games before this franchise have tried to create the feel of battle where you can be cut down at any time, and epically failed. Too many games were made with 12 people on each team, made in a Call of Duty "drop-in-drop-out" style. This game is great on single player and multiplayer. Best recommended to play with single player first to get the feel of it. We've all seen Lord of the Rings, Game of Thrones and Braveheart (or not, shame on you). Many large battlles take place place in them that we always want to recreate and no game ever matches those needs. Medieval Total War comes close, except they don't allow you to do any actual fighting, just to watch. Mount and Blade puts you in command of your own warband, made up of different units that you employ in different cities/villages, where you improve them through training and battle experience so that they may be upgraded, but everything costs money. You pay their wage, pay for food and equipment of your companions.
The combat is excellent, very true to proper swordsmanship, one handed, two handed and a mix. There are different factions to join and an entire economy to be aware of, with different cultures, weapons and so on. Every faction has their strengths and weaknesses and occasionally declare war on each other.
It would take too long to include everything this game offers. I say buy it and try it. Invade a castle and annhilate everyone defending it. Download modules to add improvements (such as the Floris mod, adds all new stuff, mechanics, animations and improved graphics).

In a nutshell, and for those that are hesitant or confused on what Planet Explorers truly is, it's a concoction comprised of Starbound and Minecraft, and then what Star Forge was expected to be, but has since fallen short of. If two of the three titles I mentioned ring a bell and you enjoyed them (or in Star Forge's case, didn't and wanted more), you're more than likely going to enjoy this game.
Continuing this with this thought, let me explain further, it takes its great exploration and sandbox-like feel from Minecraft, almost heavily with a lot of flare. Explore and you'll find many biomes, fantastic looking creatures that may or may not want to murder you, and land formations and villages and caves waiting to be explored, glided down from, or spelunked. The areas of land are huge, and are quite aesthetically pleasing. Adventure mode will be your friend if you want to explore with a challenge of mobs.
From Starbound it takes the great space feel with many different creatures and customization. Even though it technically looks like it would be more similar to minecraft, the building style present in the game feels much more like Starbound, the buildings can be extremely detailed and massive and amazing (I suggest you go check it out on YouTube or just the Steam Community page), and dont worry, if you want to build without threats, theres a mode just for you, no monsters to ruin your time.
And from the image of Star Forge, the look and feel of the game and combat (although not quite as… hectic). The generation, the funky mobs, the unexplained, it all fits in very well for the image I had constructed of Star Forge.
And to kick it all off, there is a pretty decent (although sometimes grindy RPG style) story to it that explains the occurrences and sends you exploring and hunting and building and saving and protecting the many people of the storyline (which, for better or worse, features almost full voice-acting). I wont spoil anything, but to give an overview of the intro, you are placed in a futuristic setting in which Earth has been browned and polluted, many of the other solar system’s planets and moons colonized and populated, and to branch out further with new hope for the human race as a whole (especially that of Earth’s), you and many many other people were sent to a planet to colonize it and research further. It was scanned and checked before arrival and there shouldn’t be any surprises, however, upon descent, your ship hits something mid-air, evacuation procedures initiate, and off you go to this planet at extreme speeds. Good luck.
: Pretty good game with a lot of content that is just magnified upon adding more than one person (although no multiplayer Story mode is very disappointing). Crazy builds available for download made by the community, which is more or less balanced in resource cost, makes it even better. Lots of exploration to be had. Good way into the story myself, and I am enjoying it, but sometimes the AI gets a little… wonky. In its current state 7/10 Would recommend, with forewarning of Early-Access. Definitely some bugs (but most can be solved by saving and reloading in Story). Worth every cent.

Off to the even worse part:
b)Terrible game design
- everything is random, except the level design. That means it's entirely repetitive, but still manages to spawn several special enemies (the kind you need to take on as a team) on one point
- the loot system: you get an item that is in the standard equipment rewarded for your level up. Now that's a smelly slap in your face. But don't worry, the rest of the loot mechanic is also nothing but artificial stretching.
Don't forget you can "craft" items which means you will have to spend many items you don't need (remember, the ones that are already a pain to even get) to have a chance to get an item for the character you want to equip, for it to be the right kind of item and for it to have the bonuses you want.
That's a pretty slim chance and since failing a map will net you exactly nothing, you will spend many hours getting there. This is exactly the kind of "randomness" that leads to frustration instead of excitement. It's like the gamble feature in Diablo, but without the supreme items and at 3000% of the cost.
- the laziness: Carry some♥♥♥♥♥♥from a to b. That's almost all of the game mechanic for objective. That, and "smash a thing that's strapped to something else". Maybe also a combination of those, in other words: they didn't really bother putting a lot of effort in.
Every class has a limited number of items that have next to zero distinctive features. There is nothing more than a handful of enemy types. The maps are mostly recycled.
Also, so far there is exactly one map that has a good ratio between time and loot. The other ones are a waste of time, so not even in that part did the developers think through.
These issues were most, if not all, already in the beta, where they were more or less acceptable. The grace period is over.
I paid, so I expect.
Unless you offer a business model that allows me to pay half the price and keep the rest until the game is finished, I expect a finished product. These aren't some minor issues I can overlook for a few weeks. This is a complete lack of quality assurance.
In essence, it feels like the developers don't play their own game. And that's a game breaker.
That being said, waiting for an addon that sets the game into 40k. Maybe the rest is going to be finished by then.

As a major fan of the first, and passenger of the hype train for this one, my review will probably be fairly biased.
I would say HM2 improves and adds a lot to the formula, but it's not all for the better. The game is very much like the first in the feelings of adrenaline it evokes. That being said however, they got rid of a lot of the swap and drop, rush your♥♥♥♥♥through a level, mayhem that made the first game so exhilirating.
The trade off isn't bad, as characters like Richter, the mafioso, (Not to be confused with the son,) Detective Pardo, and a couple others offer a similar playstyle to HM, but the game also integrates styalized characters like the fans, Evan, or the son, who all get individual abilities and unique playstyles. That being said the trade off is neither good nor bad, rather just a matter of opinion on whether you enjoy the change or not.
Next up is the story, which is a lot less buried in this game. HM2 has a story that's fed to you, meaning that as long as you dont skip all the dialogue, the game's story is pretty understandable without interpretation, while still being open enough that more information comes from paying attention. This one of those "recommend it but have serious issues with it" reviews.
TLDR: Recommend for fan(atic)s of the original game. Everyone else, buyer beware.
Do I recommend it because of the gameplay? Barely. As you've probably read somewhere already, the size of the levels, the emphasis on guns over melee, the addition of fat guys immune to either melee or ranged to almost every level, has changed the gameplay from the orginal. There are times when it all comes together like you remember from HLM1: the music, the pacing, the murder. Seamlessly chaining kills together until you were completely in the zone with the game and its theme. From top to bottom everything about it was working together until you completely bought into the idea of being a drug-crazed psychopath in the 80s, going on a killing spree. And you loved it.
HLM2 rarely achieves those moments, due in large part to the level design. Instead of the music fueling your need to lay waste to the next level RIGHT NOW, it fuels your frustration, being the background to you shouting "OH COME ON." When you do succeed, HLM2 is more about heart stopping close calls then adernaline-fueled murder sprees. Luring enemies with guns into a position where you can safely kill them is the way most of the game gets played. Using cover so you don't get your face blown off by an enemy off screen, and getting screwed by the random placement of some enemies, and the somewhat unpredictable AI, has slowed the gameplay of the sequel way down. You have to stop and scout out each level carefully, forcing the camera to its max distance and creeping along so you don't get picked off.
Is it still Hotline Miami? Absolutely. Does it produce the same kinds of moments? Not as often. It's slower, more tedious, more unpredictable and ultimately more frustrating. I beat the game in 9 hours, and it was a struggle to make myself do it.
Do I recommend it for the music? An unequivocal yes. There are over 30 songs, and while some of them seem more experimental, I like almost all the level tracks, and I think I've added more tracks from HLM2 to my own playlists than from HLM1.
Do I recommend it for the story? This is the harder question to answer. I enjoyed HLM1's story. It had me hooked as much as the music and the gameplay. The weirdness. The ambiguity. The hallucinations. HLM2's story is all of that too, but, it's scattered over 8 or 10 different characters, in three different time periods, where practically every level  you're playing a different person.
The story feels like disjointed DLC, where all the story scenes are diced up, shuffled and then stitched back together into one story. It's beyond Memento, beyond Tarantino, it's just bonkers. It feels like the story is actively fighting you trying to undestand it. It also relies heavier on HLM1's habit of using visual cues to tell you secrets. Like people standing in different scenes being significant are easy to miss because the pixel art can make it hard to tell what you're looking at. And the true "secret" parts of the story hidden are in the maps, where your best bet of finding anything is literally mashing the interact button while touching every wall and object in every scene. Missing those won't ultimately hurt your understanding of the story, but for someone trying to find them, it's a frustrating way to hide secrets, especially when all you really want to do is go on to the next level.
The ending is unexpected but not necessarily in a good way, depending on how on board you are with Dennation's message of the game. It feels kind of like a giant "♥♥♥♥ YOU" even though it probably wasn't meant that way.
And if you find the narrative trick of going "Or is it?!?!", to make every scene, statement or assertion ambiguous for mystery's sake, HLM2's story is going to♥♥♥♥♥♥you right off. Depending on your like of the story or how much you need something concrete to take away, you may or may not get the closure you want out of this game. It got to the point wher I sort of tuned out to the story near the end, as everything being said and done was probably ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t anyways.
In the end, I'm glad I played the game, because I like HLM that much, questionable story and tedious gameplay aside.  That said, while I was playing it all I could think about was how HLM1 was better on pretty much every front that matters, except the music. Having played the sequel, I find myself in the same place had I not: in love with the first game.

Vermintide takes a new look at the left for dead team fps and majorly improves melee combat and playable characters.  The combat feels weighty and powerful, and you need to dodge, block, use both strong and weak attacks, ranged, bombs, and a hefty dose of teamwork to be successful at even normal difficulty.
Positives
+Awesome melee combat!
+Fun ranged variety! Rifles, shotguns, bows, xbows, poison bows, etc.
+Classes can play very differently!
+Great game to play with friends!
+Devs listen and react to feedback!
+Characters have diologue that promotes immersion into the warhammer world!
+Weapons and perks variety add the ability to specialize!
+Tomes, grimoires, and many maps with 5 difficulty settings mean there are a lot of challenges to undertake.
+Left for Dead enemies crossed with Skaven units with some interesting twists and differences.
+Ending leaves obvious intention to add more campaigns vs. Undead, Chaos, and probably Greenskins.
+Correctly blocking, strong attacking, or just hacking whole groups of slave rats to bits all feels rewarding.
Negatives
-PUGs are often nubs that run off and get you/them killed.
(No matchmaking level requirement options, or server admin options.)
-Loot and crafting are entirely random.(debateable as a positive to some.)(EDIT now allaspects can be selected and rerolled to bring down random by a lot!)
-Some glitches or crashes may still exist and if the host drops the map reloads from start.
-Game is not terribly long content wise.
-You can possibly put infinite hours in and still not get your favorite weapon type with the slots you want.  (EDIT It seems obtainable to get very close to perfect now, but still involves some random grinding, which Offering could be perfect if you could lock skills you want.)
-Hitboxes are not perfect (did I get a headshot?)

First, if you haven't played Hotline Miami 1, get out of here. Go over there. You got no reason to be here.
On topic, most Hotline Miami 2 levels feel like excruciating chores the first time you play them. The levels are wide open, filled with gunmen, windows, criss-crossing enemy detection radiuses, and lots of wide-open spaces. Combined with HM's goofy AI and the sheer quantity of guns you're up against means you will be inching forward bit by bit, using the old "lure the enemies to one doorway" trick that allowed you to cheese HM1, only here it's mandatory.
The second time through, some of the redeemable ones will really open up to you. You'll knock out in a pleasant 10 deaths what took a dismal and boring 80 last time. You'll make a few routes that let you get some cool combos going for small parts of the levels.
That's not to say it's all daisies after the first run but the game starts annoying and ends up fun enough once you can skip the worst stuff.
Yeah yeah the music's all the same quality pseudo-80s techno-ish stuff. The plot is still a mess that's a big joke to anyone who care's about it. The gore is outstanding. It checks all the boxes. But what you will remember are windows, guns, and giant lengthy levels.
Better than the original in a lot of ways but really less fun in the one way that counts most, sadly. Still absolutely worth playing for the good parts though.

Hotline Miami 2 is the successor to a wildly popular, and fun, game that examines hyper violence and puts it within a twitch based shooter/puzzler. The game has a sharp difficulty curve. But with a stellar soundtrack to back up the fast paced, almost adrenaline inducing action the feel of Hotline Miami has been amplified and expanded upon by the sequel. The real question that matters in purchasing the game is can you put up with the glitches present in the game and the occasionally forced level design? For me the game was a must purchase but it is not a game for everyone, even potentially fans of the original.
Much like the original the gameplay and tactical decisions you make combined with a pulse pounding soundtrack make for some heart racing moments. When you complete a stage right it feels like you sprinted through hell and survived. Combined with a new story design and pacing every levels flows nicely into the next. If the glitches were less present and the enemies slightly less accurate and trigger happy the gameplay would be near perfect. But there are notable issues with level design that affected players to varying degrees. However the sense of accomplishment in after a level or even after clearing a room successfully is thrilling.
Those not familiar with the Hotline Miami may find the gameplay somewhat daunting. But for being an action and twitch based game strategy, the puzzle solving is actually the key element to the game. Memorizing levels, while somewhat helpful, is not going to net the best score nor will it keep you alive. Enemies patrols are occasionally random and the AI will shift positions after a failed chase. The challenge lies in knowing how to react to enemies and how they will in turn react to you and planning then acting around it.
The story and characters are a big positive to the game as they both exist to illustrate the proclivity of excessive violence in human nature and their representation in art. This being an overly generous analysis of course but the themes of each vignette seem to be related to the violent nature of man as well as the slipping connection between mortality and one's own sanity.  Pretentiousness aside, being unsure of what is real and not real, as well as not being totally sure if you are acting for good, evil or just doing something in your own imagination, forces the players to just act, which is somewhat reflective of the gameplay itself.
The music requires a specific mention because of how well it syncs with the game as a whole. Every level and cutscene has a great soundtrack that compliments the attitude and theme of what is going on and act to increase immersion within the levels. Even the music by itself is enough of a reason for me to buy this game.
The art style is also good but somewhat jarring. It's intentionally built like an old NES game visually but with extreme hyper violence and actions. The violence is extreme in some cases all while still appearing simplistic. It is interesting how the players imagination is used to bridge the gap between the NES style graphics and the real world violence it represents.
This list is a bit harder since many of the cons I see people mention relating to this game I am either neutral about or see in a positive light.
The first biggest complaint that most players address, and admittedly is a bit of a problem, is the larger level designs. On paper it sounds like a good idea and an improvement over the previous game. The downside being that you never quite gain a sense of control over the larger maps until they are all but cleared. This is both of a positive and a negative because it lends greatly to the sense of conflict within the game but compared to the smaller levels you feel like you're losing control of something that you would normally be in control of, specifically how the level flows by your own planning and actions.
The level designs in general are pretty good but some levels seem to boil down to forcing the npcs to act then reacting to what they always do. Actions such as shooting a gun then unloading on the waves of npcs that flow through the door to investigate leave something to be desired for strategy but sometimes they player is forced to do this else they end up dealing with too many enemies in the open combined with tougher enemies that cannot be dealt with through specific means. This breaks up the pace and makes certain levels somewhat tedious as the strategy boils down to finding a gun and using it to draw out then dispatch enemies.
While the gameplay and level design are still overall good the glitches are still pretty bad in this game. Maybe not worse than the previous one but in a longer game they stand out a bit more. Doors will twitch out especially while in use, leaving enemies practically invulnerable in situations. Enemies also get stuck in doors, sometimes able to attack and sometimes not. This leads to either an npc that can kill without risk to itself or you being able to dispatch them without any danger to yourself. Enemies will also get stuck walking in a small circle unless forced to investigate sounds or the player, this happens a lot with the dog enemies but makes them generally easy to deal with.
The biggest game bug that people noticed though was related to the Ash mask. While using the mask you play two characters, one with a chainsaw and the other with any gun you have or can pick up. Often the gunman will get stuck even before entering the level leaving you with just one character that can use a chainsaw. This is more than frustrating as a bug removes one of the most interesting new additions to the game.
With this new interation of Hotline Miami comes a change in the pacing and level styles as well as a complete change to the mask system of the game. There are less broken masks and also more useful ones. As many people say "you can't just Tony through every level." This is both good and bad but the design changes makes sense to the story. Each level you are an individual or group with only a small selection of masks based on who you are. Other levels don't use masks at all but rather have a forced gimmick related to the gameplay and story. An example being the writer, who actually does not kill anyone unless you go out of your way and who cannot use guns or knives.
An interesting note about the writer level
The other forced gameplay mode is the Hawaii levels where you are given a gun, a knife and no mask. You cannot pick up other weapons and when you run out of ammo you have to find caches that replininsh, at max, 1/4 of your ammo. This is interesting and challenging but it feels a bit like an arbitrary limitation that in later levels feels like a frustrating hinderance.
The game is much longer than the previous one and depending on your opinion of the level designs it has the potential to outstay its own welcome. In the end I loved this game and the moment to moment action. The final sequence summed up the experience of the game as a whole perfectly, but those who did not like the original or would find limiting level changes to be negative you may want to pass on this or get it on sale. This game is for the Hotline Miami enthusiast, who can look past its faults and see the core of the game they loved beneath the surface.

Honestly this game is better than the first which these days is a rarity,but hm2 pulls it of with tons of compelling story and more gun based combat.

First the POSITIVES:
In this game you take control of multiple characters with different masks, weapons and playstyles giving the game a refreshing breeze since the last one. They all have their own stories which are all related to eachother in some way or another and are pretty interesting in their own right, sometimes they actually make sense. The soundtrack is impeccable as usual and fits snuggly in its 80s/90s Miami hotpants. You can still hit a guy and his head explodes into blood and sparkles and rainbows as does the rest of his body. A level editor seems to be coming out soonish too.
Now for the NEGATIVES:
While adding more characters and ideas in comparison to the first game, it's also lost the fast paced twitch combat too. Most of the game you will find yourself luring large groups of enemies toward you to even attempt to get a decent combo started or simply to take down all the enemies with guns. The later levels also seem to make you to use guns rather than melee weapons when the area's are full of gun enemies or the fat guys that wont die unless you shoot them because they are made of metallic lard. Many of the levels force you to use a particular mask and they all limit you to a certain set of masks, while this makes sense because you keep changing characters, it limits your options largely.
There are some annoying glitches too. Enemies get stuck on doors, enemies shoot and hit through doors, you will get stuck on walls or props in the level which will lead to death and the AI will occassionally decide that it doesn't want to follow it's set path because ♥♥♥♥ you that's why.
In CONCLUSION:
I loved the first game as it allowed me to carefully plan what I was going to do before killing every enemy on the screen in one long baseball bat/machete combo. This game seems to have forgotten that to a certain degree.
Buy it on sale unless you're drowning in money.

This game was a disappointment. It contains a lot of elements that should make it a great game but instead it wastes this potential. The biggest offense is incredibly strict mechanics in an environment of shoddy controls, numerous bugs and a poor autosave feature which turns the game into a grueling ordeal of button mashing at all the "right" points. This nasty combination serves to antagonize the player and I found myself walking away from the game on numerous occasions in frustration.
This game just wasn't fun to play. I expect more from pay to play games on Steam and the reality is that I've played better zombie side-scrollers on Newgrounds. Fortunately I picked this up for a $1.50 during a steam sale so it wasn't a major loss.  4/10
Pros
- Awesome atmosphere (2.5D setting works well making the game feel less like a side-scroller)
- Artwork really is beautiful
- Character animation is very well done
- 1st act is actually worth a run-through if you can pick the game up for a dollar
Cons
- Controls are loose and wonky  (note that I played on a keyboard)
- Certain interactive items contain too small trigger locations (i.e. at one point I spent almost 5 minutes swinging my axe against a door to break the lock before finding the "just right" spot so I could advance)
- Level design is entirely linear and inconsistent (ranging from idiot simple to masochistically hard all within the same level)
- Auto-save feature is inconsistent and at times saves before long voice acting or animations
- Plot and storytelling are awful; Randall's journal is like going through the private thoughts of an angst ridden 14 year old
- Voice acting is quite poor and sound quality between scenes is inconsistent
- Game performance is surprisingly bad considering the unimpressive graphics (load times reveal poor optimization of game code)
- Many game breaking bugs which require a reload (zombies walking through walls, character getting stuck outside of a locked area and key events not triggering)

EDIT: I originally wrote a review of this game when I first purchased and played it for a couple of hours, but now I have played it much more and can more properly state my opinion.
TL;DR: This is a personal music-based runner game that really works. It's BIT.TRIP RUNNER without the pixel graphics and with your own music. It's procedurally generated and with a good amount of difficulties to keep replayability high.
Despite being, as of the time I write this review, in Early Access, it does not feel at all unfinished or unpolished. It's incredibly smooth, beautiful, and well-designed. I have found no bugs or errors in all of my playtime.
The only catch I really encountered that first set me away from this game was the difficulty. At the Medium difficulty, you must use a single set of controls to keep Melody away from danger and on the beat. However, on Intense difficulty, with which 2 achievements are associated, you must use two seperate control schemes (default WASD and arrow keys) for color orbs and obstacles respectively.
Intense difficulty, at first, was far too difficult for me to even get 50% completion on a song, let alone the 100% required for the achievements. However, I struggled through and "got gud" enough to get these hard-earned feats.
So clearly this is a difficult game for completionists such as myself, but it provides some very fun replayability that I don't see much in rhythm and music games anymore. Beat Hazard and Symphony never had me hooked like this game has, even through the "100 songs played" achievement.

I've always been a bit skeptical of Free to Play, because more often than not it is Pay to Win, and rarely there is much effort put into mechanics and gameplay. After playing the game for about 30 hours now and being a veteran of many war games i feel safe to make a proper review of the game. While still in Early Access, Heroes & Generals seems rather polished. Good graphics while not astonishing are good enough to really immerse you in the battle. Expect no real damage model to buildings like Battlefield has gotten many acustom to, as small stables and barns will hold up to tank fire and vehicles will simply fade into the ether upon being destroyed. Gun models look good, sound accurate, and have a good kick to them. Gameplay is where the real fun is for me. A good damage model where your basic Single-Action rifle will kill in two to three shots, Bolt Actions seem to kill in two, and other guns like Sub Machine, Light machine and Pistols take several well placed rounds to the chest. Headshots seem to be one hit kills on nearly all weapons. As far as the purchase model of this game, all weapons, mods and vehicles are free to be purchased with in game currency. Only cosmetics are purchased through the Gold. Naturally wanting you to spend money in the game they make buying new weapons extremely expensive for the later weapons, the Thompson Sub Machine Gun for instance is about 156k and change, and they also make you pay upkeep on your weapons, vehicles, and modifications, and also purchase new ammo between games about every two to three games depending on use. Rarely will you not cover the cost of upkeep and earn extra but Tank drivers and Pilots can get extremely expensive upkeep bills. You start with three soldiers, one for each faction (American, German, Russian as of this review) and can purchase more in game with in game currency or advanced soldiers with Gold. The Perks of Buying Gold and purchasing a Veteran status is...vast, gaining double expierance and 25% boost in in game currency and earning perks in game as well as an extra weapon/equipment slot and Badge slot. It is not completely unfair i have seen this sort of model in many other F2P games which were not imbalanced and still fun. As of this review the Soviet faction has just been released and they seem slightly imbalanced, having better weapons and possibly tanks than the other two. However as anyone who plays online games knows imbalances get patched, and you have the best weapon in the world but not be good at the game. Skill is what matters overall. The maps are big, the battles are epic and rarely one sided thus far in my 30 hours. "Call of Duty Bros" and the general "Dudebro" gamer does not seem be present in this game. I've yet to expierance trolling, very little whining in chat and above all racial slurs have hardly occured. Overall it is has been a great expierance and very enjoyable game i would recommend to anyone who wants a very gritty war FPS with solid mechanics.

First of all and perhaps the most important: I HIGHLY suggest that you do not play this game if you have not played and beaten the first one. But if you haven't, don't worry because the first one is still amazing. Many parts will be very insignificant and uninteresting if you haven't played it. However, for those of you who have played it, this game is very much worth your time and money (imo).
First let's start with the differences of this game, and beleive me when I say that there are a lot of them. Of course the game is still Hotline Miami; a blood-pumping, sociopathic, top down action game with brain melting music, however, the system and the scructure of the game is ENTIRELY different. You are no longer following around the life of a single silent protagonist receiving phonecalls. In fact, nearly every other mission you will be changing charecters with there own story and missions. Most of it takes place around two different groups of characters: The Fans, the ones who kill and steal just for the kicks, and the soldiers who are the ones who kill for "good". However, as the game progesses, you will find the truth behind these characters. While the story in the first Hotline Miami only changes it's timeline once, Wrong Number is constantly changing points in the story. The ideas of masks are different, too. Rather than the main protagonist changing masks to change/hide his identity, in this one masks already are parts of individual identities and changing them changes which character you play as. In fact, most characters don't even wear masks. Speaking of masks, they are very much improved in the way that each mask is entirely unique and are more than just power-ups, as the masks in Wrong Number entirely change your gameplay and playstyle.
One big plus for this game is, compared to the first, the increase of variety and content. First of all, the game is just straight up longer. And it doesn't just drag on each level, things happen in nearly every one and none are wasted. More music, more characters, more weapons, and more enemies to kill with the new weapons. Not to mention that music, in my opinion, is even better than the first which I though was already as good as it could get. Not only is it good, but it was also chosen very carefully and there's a lot behind the song choices than one might realise. On another positive note I feel that the story is much more interesting and easier to follow.
However, this all leads to one big complaint I've been hearing a lot about, and I have to admit that it is most certainly valid. And this complaint is the very fustrating level design you will notice as the game progresses. Do you remember the level "Assault" from the first where there would be loads of enemies completely out of your sight range? Well, expect more of that, as you will experience moments where you will feel cheated into your death. Enemies will shoot you out of your vision range and you will walk right into enemies you didn't see. Not to mention that these levels get very long. These are all very bad ways to make your game progressively more difficult. Fortunately, this problem is fixed for a couple levels with the sniper rifle but it's for such a short amount of time it barely makes a difference. It's a real shame to see things like this in the game that does so many things so well, however I do not feal in any way that it is bad enough to give it a negative review.
So, in conclusion, do I recomend this game? Well, the little blue thumbs-up at the top should answer that. It has a very interesting story, blood-pumping and unique gameplay, face melting soundtrack, great characters, and everyting that makes a great sequel. Honestly, it's one of the most well-done sequels I've ever played. However, I warn you not to play this game before beating the first, but if you have, try not to think about the story too much and just enjoy the surreal and epic experience hitting you like a wave on Miami beach.

I'm a fairly big fan of the first Hotline Miami.  I may not have played the living daylights out of it until I had a perfect rating on every level, but I very much enjoyed my time playing it, and replayed many of the stages more than once.
I was very excited about Hotline Miami 2.  I didn't have huge expectations for it.  If they just made more of what the first Hotline Miami was about, I would have been happy with that. Imagine my surprise then, to find myself strugging to enjoy HM2.
Before I played the game, I saw a review come out on PC Gamer which gave HM2 a low rating.  The reviewer complained about a wide array of perceived issues with the game, and it worried me.  I very much hoped he was wrong and was relieved to see the comments section full of links to positive reviews.
So in addition to my existing HM1 fan-boy-ism, I went in wanting to love this game against the odds detailed by the naysayers.  Despite this, I still find myself agreeing with SOME of PC Gamer's, and other's, points regarding the drawbacks of this game.  I've seen these issues mentioned in other user reviews so I'll put my two cents in on the three most common areas of complaint.
First:  technical issues.  I've seen several people cite various technical issues in the game.  I most commonly see three complaints:  dogs glitching and spinning in circles, items getting knocked outside the playable level boundaries, and enemies getting stuck on doors.  I have to admit I haven't encountered the first two glitches.  However, enemies getting stuck on door frames is a nearly CONSTANT issue that I run into.  When this happens, the enemy sprite spins in circles like a tornado, and they become invincible to melee attack.  You just have to sit there swinging until the glitch stops.  Needless to say, this is a bit of a flow-breaker, and especially annoying because I don't recall it ever happening in HM1.  I'm also somewhat annoyed that it hasn't been fixed yet in an update since release, especially because it is a very often-occuring problem which a lot of people are experiencing.  I'm no game developer, so the granular details of debugging are not known to me, but in terms of basic troubleshooting; if you can easily reproduce an issue, it's easy to find the source of the issue and correct it.  And trust me, this issue is reproduced every level, every time I load up the game.
The next common complaint I recall is the difference in the mask system.  The PCGamer reviewer didn't like how the masks now confer vastly different abilities and limitations, rather than the somewhat small bonuses and alterations they bestowed in the first game.  In addition to masks, there are also different characters who function in different ways.  I have to say that, on its own, this part doesn't bother me.  It is mostly a mechanism to force the player to approach a level in a different fashion.  For example:  not being able to use firearms, not being able to reload via dropped weapons from your enemies, having infinite access to a lethal melee weapon in addition to your ranged weapon - these are all modifications to the Hotline Miami formula that force you to step outside your comfort zone a little bit.  I normally consider this to be a good thing in gaming, as long as the modification is not obnoxious.  I don't think that it is - I think the new masks system switches things up just enough to keep it interesting without changing what most players enjoy about Hotline Miami on a fundamental level.  HOWEVER - to be continued in the paragraph below...
Speaking of fundamentals, this brings me to my personal deal breaker, and the last common complaint I want to address.  Many people have commented on HM2's difficulty being markedly increased over HM1, some saying that it more or less picks things up from the end of the ramp that HM1 was building.  This is true, and that statement, if isolated, is not an inherent problem.  I'm fine with having more of a challenge, but I'm sad to say what is manufacturing that challenge is shoddy artificial design, due to a change in level design.
HM2's stages are, for the most part, significantly different from the first.  There are less corners, bottlenecks, and more wide open spaces with unobstructed paths of visibility.  There are many stages where you will consistently get shot by enemies you never saw, far off the edge of the screen.  You will often be pegged off through a window, glass being much more prevalent in HM2 - you will also be swarmed by melee enemies as you're spotted through the panes from an off-screen corner of the room.  This is especially frustrating in the levels where your ranged capabilities are limited by the new mask system.
At first, I tried to excuse and rationalize my reaction to these occurences by thinking to myself "Well, HM1 didn't make use of the 'look' button very often, I barely used it.  This is just a gameplay improvement, because they're utilizing a previously under-served gameplay mechanic which was already present in the system.  HM2 just has more long-range gameplay, I just have to get used to thinking of that feature more often."  Unfortunately, even with that thought in the back of my brain, and a concerted effort to looking around a lot more before I leap, I have to be honest with myself that I am just not having nearly as much fun as when I played HM1.  I played HM1 compulsively, I didn't want to stop.  I'm having trouble motivating myself to even start up HM2 between play sessions, and I believe it's due to the level design.  As many people have mentioned, this new level design slows the gameplay down.  It increases difficulty in a very artificial and un-fun way, basically by taking what was great about Hotline Miami, and putting a big inhibitor on it.
I wish there was a "neutral" button on this review system, because I can neither really recommend nor condemn HM2.  Some people may not take any offense to this hide-and-go-seek snipe-y gameplay that has supplanted the familiar HM1 formula.  There are still notable moments of gameplay brilliance and carnage-induced mirth that echo the enjoyment I derived from HM1.  The soundtrack is, of course, amazing.  I'm enjoying the storyline, chock-full of fever dreams and disgusting characters, as one might expect.
Also, it's worth noting that HM2 is supposed to eventually include a level editor (originally to be available on release but removed for now, apparently due to issues), so it's entirely possible that I could eventually be granted the ability to make my own levels which match up to my own gameplay preferences, and between myself and other creators, I could wind up experiencing a nearly endless stream of fun at the hands of HM2... well, as long as they patch the bloody door glitch.
Even with the positives, I'm sorry to say that in HM2's current state, I can't positively recommend it.  The glitches break game-flow, the game-flow itself is drastically altered due to level design decisions, and the tag-team of these two problems severely affects my enjoyment of this game.  So I must click the "No" button for this review.

I actually really liked how the developers used gameplay to characterize Evan, the writer. He isn't a psychopath or a killer like most of the player characters, as such will not kill enemies unless the player forces him to. Instead he will knock them out with blunt objects, unload firearms, and refuse to pick up knives. However, if the player executes two downed enemies he will fly into a rage and kill enemies violently. You get more points for neutralizing enemies non-lethally, likely because it is better for his mental health.
The player is still given the option to play how they want, but through gameplay it is readily apparent what Evan would prefer to do, and that is pretty neat.
are actually pretty convincing and well done. And I know how hard those are to do.
I personally felt that the story was worse, and will try to say why without spoiling too much.
I felt that it takes itself too seriously, tries to explain too much of things that are irrelevant while glossing over things that would make the story a cohesive whole. The experiences of some characters are completely pointless from a story telling perspective, perhaps a casualty of having so many different playable characters. It also becomes apparent that it takes place in an alternate history, which I feel is a step down from first game being vague about the setting.
Also violates the rule of "show don't tell" far too often.
The first game encouraged recklessness, allowing the player to rely on reactions and instinct to get through levels. This was possible thanks to the tight and focused design of many of the stages, separated into small chunks. A player could reliably use walls and doors to their advantage, as very few areas were wide and open.
Hotline Miami 2 plays more like a top-down cover shooter. Single "floors" in this game can be the size of entire chapters from the first game, which severely punishes the reckless, instinctual gameplay style the first game was known for. Wide open areas, windows everywhere, extremely long hallways, and way too many dudes with guns are the culprits here. As a result, players will move towards an extremely cautous playstyle, advancing slowly and checking every angle constantly, lest they lose five or even ten minutes of progress. This is much less interesting, more frustrating, and more importantly, much less fun.
Enemies in the game act unpredictably, some will run to the source of gunfire when they hear it, others will stay still. Enemies will often melee you through walls, or shoot you from offscreen, and get caught on geometry (most often doorways) vibrating rapidly and becoming invulnerable. The one AI partner in the game also has hideous pathfinding and gets stuck on doors often as well.
Hopefully these issues will be patched in the future.
In conclusion, as someone who enjoyed the first game I find myself enjoying this game less. But as I said at the beginning, your mileage may vary.

SIKE, THAT’S THE WRONG NUMBER
Alright, now that I’ve referenced the meme everybody else who’s played this game has, it’s time for me to ramble about a game that I love. Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is the second title in the Hotline Miami series, and it is hella tight.
It’s a top down kill ‘em up where you enter a building, kill everybody, then leave. What makes it “unique” is how every enemy dies in one hit, as does yourself. However, dying in Hotline Miami isn’t something to be afraid of as you can just hit that R button to retry in an instant.
Because of the whole “nobody has any health” thing, it makes the whole game fast paced. Each moment leads into the next on what you’re going to have to do to make everybody but yourself die, planning out each step right in the moment. It’s almost a puzzle game with top-down shooter elements.
The story itself is actually really well written and aligns very nicely with HM1. It’s told in a nonlinear fashion similar to that of Tarantino’s Pulp Fiction and Vonnegut’s Slaughterhouse Five. And for people who don’t really care for it, it’s easy to just skim over it and get right back into the game.
The hard mode in the game is actually a real “hard mode”, where the enemies are smarter and the levels are altered just right to make them brutal compared to their normal mode counterparts.
However, there are a few issues that hard mode highlights in the game. This review is may be a thumbs up, but I’m going to go over what this game got wrong because that’s easier to do than what the game got right.
The first thing I noticed when playing this game was its slower than the original. At first I thought it was just the slower executions, leaving you vulnerable for longer periods of time when dealing with downed enemies, but it was more than that.
This game features a great deal more of open areas than its predecessor did, leaving you in a lot of situations where you just get shot by enemies that are off the screen as they can see farther than you can. This makes the game a bit more cautious, and as a result making it slower. Walking around in these big open spaces is a lot scarier than it was in HM1, rather than blazing your way through tightly made levels like in the first.
Also, with bigger rooms comes greater numbers of enemies. A lot of the difficulty in this game comes from just packing the level full of enemies for you to deal with. This combined with the larger areas makes it pretty scary to walk around in open hallways.
Not to mention the high number of windows as well. Windows in this game are basically just walls that can be seen through, as well as shot through. With so little walls to hide behind, you’re just begging to be shot in these levels.
There’s also a lot more gunplay rather than melee. With open areas with lots of enemies who also have guns that can see you through most of the level, there’s pretty much nothing you can use but guns. Especially with the big guys that come at you that can only be killed by bullet. Sure there’s the melee enemies that are able to dodge bullets, but those are used to sparingly compared to the big guys and really tips the scale to mostly using guns rather than melee, which is really what set the pace for HM1.
This kind of level design in the game slowed it down to just hiding behind corners with a machine gun in hand, plowing down all the idiot AIs that come around to add themselves to the massive pile of bodies.

Another separate issue, which wasn’t a big problem for me as I never really played with masks in HM1, but there was way less mask variety in this game than in the last. Since you played as characters rather than just Jacket with all this masks (the main character in HM1), you had way less choice in what specialties you had when entering a level. I’m sure for a lot of people this was a heavy hitter, but I personally didn’t mind.
The game’s difficulty is on a whole new level than what HM1 was. HM1’s difficulty is very gradual throughout the entire game, going through the entire spectrum of easy to hard, but this game starts off difficulty wise a little more than halfway through HM1’s difficulty, and it’s likely due to those slowing level design choices. I didn’t find that too particularly bad since I played the crap outta HM1, but for any newcomers it could be off putting.
A smaller gripe would be that the soundtrack didn’t really do it for me. HM1 had a lot of songs that stuck with me as favorites which led me to actually buy to music to listen to on the go, but none of the songs really stuck out for me in HM2 for listening to outside of the game. After my first playthrough of the story I muted the music and listened to my own stuff, HM1 soundtrack included.
Aside from that, the game is amazing. Just by simply being another Hotline Miami game, it more than enough makes up for the poor design choices. If I were to give the game a letter grade, I’d give it an A-. Enough for me to dedicate way too much time into score/time attacking, not to mention the level editor that’s to come out soon which I’ll probably play for only a few hundred hours.
Should you buy the game? If you’re new to the series I’d suggest starting out with the first game, really just because it’s easier and it introduces you to the Hotline Miami world. HM2 started off as a mod for HM1, later made into a standalone experience, so it was made from the ground up to be played by people who’ve already dipped their toes into the series. If you’ve already played HM1 and liked it, great! You’re going to love HM2, as it’s really just an expansion on what HM1 was.
tl;dr:
It’s Hotline Miami, just with more Hotline Miami. If you liked the first one, you’ll likely be a fan of Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number.

Bought it at early and still haven't regret it. The game is a nice zombie survival shooter, even though it has it's share of bugs and glitches it still offers a great experience.
Story
=======
The story is a little fuzzy when you start, you pick from a group of survivors and shoved in the middle of a zombie outbreak.  In most game modes you are given instructions through your phone by a unknown individual helping you escape the area but of course you need to complete certain tasks let it be taking out a fire to holding a location for a bit. There is of course a few pieces in some of the maps that hint what is going on, as more content comes out the more players will understand or piece together a story about the zombie outbreak.
The developers have also started a comic series free on their site to tell more about the story. It's rather interesting and shows a bit more about the outbreak. It's worth the read.
Gameplay
=======
The gameplay breaks down to modes  and humans vs zombies.
Mode 1 = Escape
This mode is pretty much the story driven type, as you start the map you will be thrown at the start location , from there you follow the text messages on your phone and complete tasks that will lead to your freedom. However there are a few twists, for one if you play online anyone that is killed will become a zombie creating a hard situation to deal with as they are a bit faster and annoying :P , second the objective path will change each round for example one route will have you go through a gun store to the gas station where the next round will get you to enter a threatre and push towards the bank. This randomness adds a bit more fun and reply value to enjoy.
Mode 2 = Hunted
Your shoved in the middle of a free for all. All humans are against each other nothing else matters, ammo is everywhere as well as guns so go out and murder your fellow humans because hey the world is over anyways. Remember though ...everyone you kill will become a zombie that might end up helping you become the last survivor or could be your undoing and lead to your demize.
Mode 3 = Extraction
You are randomly thrown to one of many spawn locations on the map, you may be with fellow survivors if you play online or by yourself. Your mission is straight forward head to a random location which you will find npc survivors needing help, you need to hold the location for a set amount of time then extract them...just remember the further you complete the objectives the more zombies start spawning at the next location one and anyone that dies will become a zombie and are forced to try and stop you from saving those npcs.
Mode 4 = Panic
I can't say much for this one as I haven't been able to find a room for it. It looks rather interesting.
Humans vs Zombies =
Human players have the ability to use melee weapons , guns , med kits and special items such as bolt cutters and keys to progress their story. Humans also have the ability to instant kill zombies with their melee weapon if they sneak behind a zombie which is nicely shown with a kill animation. Humans also have the ability to turn into zombies if they take enough damage or meet the random chance of luck.....as time passes your screen will become grey and your sound will become very quiet until the final moment of your scream in which you turn into those you have been killing this whole time.
Zombie players are nothing special, they aren't L4D special zombies where they take damage or dry hump the survivors to death. When you think about they are very weak, one shot to the head and your dead. However player zombies do have some abilities, one is roar which allows you to call near by zombie npcs to your aid, they will follow you and also you can give them a waypoint to charge. Zombies can also jump, crawl , break down doors and grab players biting them and giving them a chance to join your rank by infection.
Overall
=====
The game is something different , at times it does feel like the mod No room in hell which is a good thing. The concept and direction of where the game is aiming is awesome however there are many issues such as zombies getting stuck to players abusing broken mechanics such as throwing keys or cards under desks or objects that will force players to a halt as they can't progress forward . The story is also non-existence until the comics came out but then again what zombie game really has the full picture as the concept of a zombie outbreak is always based on the idea of pure chaos and pieces of information which does work out.
Should you buy it
============
For coop = Yes it's rather fun and enjoyable
For singleplayer = Not really worth it as it becomes very dry after the second run.
For PVP = if you can get into the 20 player servers it can get pretty crazy and fun. But if your just going for pvp and not big on coop then might want to wait until a sale day.
Final Remark:
My fellow survivor decided to be a jerk by taking all the ammo for everytime of weapon even the ones he didn't have....so I decided to show him the reason why not to be greedy by dragging a mob of zombies into one room which killed me and then grabbed another mob and fellowed the survivor....the end was rather enjoyable as he finally understood that a bathroom wasn't the safest place to hide during a zombie outbreak.
