I've always been a bit skeptical of Free to Play, because more often than not it is Pay to Win, and rarely there is much effort put into mechanics and gameplay. After playing the game for about 30 hours now and being a veteran of many war games i feel safe to make a proper review of the game. While still in Early Access, Heroes & Generals seems rather polished. Good graphics while not astonishing are good enough to really immerse you in the battle. Expect no real damage model to buildings like Battlefield has gotten many acustom to, as small stables and barns will hold up to tank fire and vehicles will simply fade into the ether upon being destroyed. Gun models look good, sound accurate, and have a good kick to them. Gameplay is where the real fun is for me. A good damage model where your basic Single-Action rifle will kill in two to three shots, Bolt Actions seem to kill in two, and other guns like Sub Machine, Light machine and Pistols take several well placed rounds to the chest. Headshots seem to be one hit kills on nearly all weapons. As far as the purchase model of this game, all weapons, mods and vehicles are free to be purchased with in game currency. Only cosmetics are purchased through the Gold. Naturally wanting you to spend money in the game they make buying new weapons extremely expensive for the later weapons, the Thompson Sub Machine Gun for instance is about 156k and change, and they also make you pay upkeep on your weapons, vehicles, and modifications, and also purchase new ammo between games about every two to three games depending on use. Rarely will you not cover the cost of upkeep and earn extra but Tank drivers and Pilots can get extremely expensive upkeep bills. You start with three soldiers, one for each faction (American, German, Russian as of this review) and can purchase more in game with in game currency or advanced soldiers with Gold. The Perks of Buying Gold and purchasing a Veteran status is...vast, gaining double expierance and 25% boost in in game currency and earning perks in game as well as an extra weapon/equipment slot and Badge slot. It is not completely unfair i have seen this sort of model in many other F2P games which were not imbalanced and still fun. As of this review the Soviet faction has just been released and they seem slightly imbalanced, having better weapons and possibly tanks than the other two. However as anyone who plays online games knows imbalances get patched, and you have the best weapon in the world but not be good at the game. Skill is what matters overall. The maps are big, the battles are epic and rarely one sided thus far in my 30 hours. "Call of Duty Bros" and the general "Dudebro" gamer does not seem be present in this game. I've yet to expierance trolling, very little whining in chat and above all racial slurs have hardly occured. Overall it is has been a great expierance and very enjoyable game i would recommend to anyone who wants a very gritty war FPS with solid mechanics.

I actually really liked how the developers used gameplay to characterize Evan, the writer. He isn't a psychopath or a killer like most of the player characters, as such will not kill enemies unless the player forces him to. Instead he will knock them out with blunt objects, unload firearms, and refuse to pick up knives. are actually pretty convincing and well done. And I know how hard those are to do.
I personally felt that the story was worse, and will try to say why without spoiling too much.
I felt that it takes itself too seriously, tries to explain too much of things that are irrelevant while glossing over things that would make the story a cohesive whole. The experiences of some characters are completely pointless from a story telling perspective, perhaps a casualty of having so many different playable characters. It also becomes apparent that it takes place in an alternate history, which I feel is a step down from first game being vague about the setting.
Also violates the rule of "show don't tell" far too often.
The first game encouraged recklessness, allowing the player to rely on reactions and instinct to get through levels. This was possible thanks to the tight and focused design of many of the stages, separated into small chunks. A player could reliably use walls and doors to their advantage, as very few areas were wide and open.
Hotline Miami 2 plays more like a top-down cover shooter. Single "floors" in this game can be the size of entire chapters from the first game, which severely punishes the reckless, instinctual gameplay style the first game was known for. Wide open areas, windows everywhere, extremely long hallways, and way too many dudes with guns are the culprits here. As a result, players will move towards an extremely cautous playstyle, advancing slowly and checking every angle constantly, lest they lose five or even ten minutes of progress. This is much less interesting, more frustrating, and more importantly, much less fun.
Enemies in the game act unpredictably, some will run to the source of gunfire when they hear it, others will stay still. Enemies will often melee you through walls, or shoot you from offscreen, and get caught on geometry (most often doorways) vibrating rapidly and becoming invulnerable. The one AI partner in the game also has hideous pathfinding and gets stuck on doors often as well.
Hopefully these issues will be patched in the future.

SIKE, THAT’S THE WRONG NUMBER
Alright, now that I’ve referenced the meme everybody else who’s played this game has, it’s time for me to ramble about a game that I love. Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is the second title in the Hotline Miami series, and it is hella tight.
It’s a top down kill ‘em up where you enter a building, kill everybody, then leave. What makes it “unique” is how every enemy dies in one hit, as does yourself. However, dying in Hotline Miami isn’t something to be afraid of as you can just hit that R button to retry in an instant.
Because of the whole “nobody has any health” thing, it makes the whole game fast paced. Each moment leads into the next on what you’re going to have to do to make everybody but yourself die, planning out each step right in the moment. It’s almost a puzzle game with top-down shooter elements.
The story itself is actually really well written and aligns very nicely with HM1. It’s told in a nonlinear fashion similar to that of Tarantino’s Pulp Fiction and Vonnegut’s Slaughterhouse Five. And for people who don’t really care for it, it’s easy to just skim over it and get right back into the game.
The hard mode in the game is actually a real “hard mode”, where the enemies are smarter and the levels are altered just right to make them brutal compared to their normal mode counterparts.
However, there are a few issues that hard mode highlights in the game. This review is may be a thumbs up, but I’m going to go over what this game got wrong because that’s easier to do than what the game got right.
The first thing I noticed when playing this game was its slower than the original. At first I thought it was just the slower executions, leaving you vulnerable for longer periods of time when dealing with downed enemies, but it was more than that.
This game features a great deal more of open areas than its predecessor did, leaving you in a lot of situations where you just get shot by enemies that are off the screen as they can see farther than you can. This makes the game a bit more cautious, and as a result making it slower. Walking around in these big open spaces is a lot scarier than it was in HM1, rather than blazing your way through tightly made levels like in the first.
Also, with bigger rooms comes greater numbers of enemies. A lot of the difficulty in this game comes from just packing the level full of enemies for you to deal with. This combined with the larger areas makes it pretty scary to walk around in open hallways.
Not to mention the high number of windows as well. Windows in this game are basically just walls that can be seen through, as well as shot through. With so little walls to hide behind, you’re just begging to be shot in these levels.
There’s also a lot more gunplay rather than melee. With open areas with lots of enemies who also have guns that can see you through most of the level, there’s pretty much nothing you can use but guns. Especially with the big guys that come at you that can only be killed by bullet. Sure there’s the melee enemies that are able to dodge bullets, but those are used to sparingly compared to the big guys and really tips the scale to mostly using guns rather than melee, which is really what set the pace for HM1.
This kind of level design in the game slowed it down to just hiding behind corners with a machine gun in hand, plowing down all the idiot AIs that come around to add themselves to the massive pile of bodies.

Another separate issue, which wasn’t a big problem for me as I never really played with masks in HM1, but there was way less mask variety in this game than in the last. Since you played as characters rather than just Jacket with all this masks (the main character in HM1), you had way less choice in what specialties you had when entering a level. I’m sure for a lot of people this was a heavy hitter, but I personally didn’t mind.
The game’s difficulty is on a whole new level than what HM1 was. HM1’s difficulty is very gradual throughout the entire game, going through the entire spectrum of easy to hard, but this game starts off difficulty wise a little more than halfway through HM1’s difficulty, and it’s likely due to those slowing level design choices. I didn’t find that too particularly bad since I played the crap outta HM1, but for any newcomers it could be off putting.
A smaller gripe would be that the soundtrack didn’t really do it for me. HM1 had a lot of songs that stuck with me as favorites which led me to actually buy to music to listen to on the go, but none of the songs really stuck out for me in HM2 for listening to outside of the game. After my first playthrough of the story I muted the music and listened to my own stuff, HM1 soundtrack included.
Aside from that, the game is amazing. Just by simply being another Hotline Miami game, it more than enough makes up for the poor design choices. If I were to give the game a letter grade, I’d give it an A-. Enough for me to dedicate way too much time into score/time attacking, not to mention the level editor that’s to come out soon which I’ll probably play for only a few hundred hours.
Should you buy the game? If you’re new to the series I’d suggest starting out with the first game, really just because it’s easier and it introduces you to the Hotline Miami world. HM2 started off as a mod for HM1, later made into a standalone experience, so it was made from the ground up to be played by people who’ve already dipped their toes into the series. If you’ve already played HM1 and liked it, great! You’re going to love HM2, as it’s really just an expansion on what HM1 was.
tl;dr:
It’s Hotline Miami, just with more Hotline Miami. If you liked the first one, you’ll likely be a fan of Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number.

I initially had high hopes for a game set in the Warhammer universe as we don't really get enough games set in this universe. I have to say albeit only around 12 hours into the game, I'm thoroughly pleased with the game so far.
The comparisons to Left 4 Dead are obvious and fair but I think the game does enough new things that it can safely differentiate itself from L4D.
The biggest distinction is obviously the focus on melee combat with blocking, heavy and light attacks and ripostes make combat extremely satisfying to execute especially vs some of the tougher enemies. In addition, each hero also has access to a secondary weapon that are very powerful but consume your ammo and resources. Futhermore, of the 5 heroes currently available, each play differently, have different weapons and strengths and weaknesses.
The other big distinction to make is the rewarding loot system. After each level, you're rewarded with an item that can range from common to exotic but you can increase your odds by completing side objectives. Rarer loot has better stats and better bonuses in combat. Your loot also customises the way you play, for example, you can equip a two-handed weapon or a sword and shield on some heroes that change their roles. Loot is the focus of this game and each item transforms the way you play and complete levels. While a little on the RNG side, loot is still satisfying to acquire but good loot isn't a requirement to complete most levels on the lower difficulties.
Overall, if you like the horde/cooperative style games similar to Killing Floor and Left 4 Dead, you can't go wrong with Vermintide. Combat feels great, there's great variety in the loot systems and each hero plays differently. There's also plenty of levels and a wide range of difficulties to complete them on. While lacking any form of PvP similar to Killing Floor, the game offers enough challenge and progression to keep you occupied for many more hours to come.
The game is still fairly buggy and glitchy though, AI can be a little odd, running into walls, glitching through walls, weird ragdoll physics. In addition, the game isn't well optimised at the moment and while my PC isn't cutting edge, its mid-range and I struggle to keep this game above 60 consistently on lower settings despite the game not looking amazing, its looks fine enough. All I recommend is that you check the system requirements before considering a purchase or get a steam refund if you struggle to run the game at all.

As expected for an Early Release it still has a few hiccups and glitches here and there, but over all it is a good game. I have played other "Rythm-Runners"   but they tended to pre built levels to set songs, which got boring after awhile. This game allows me to pick the songs I want to play then generates a level based on it, it feels like if AudioSurf and BitRunner had a child. Now I will explain what I like about the game.
1.Choice) The ability to choose which songs I want to play is a nice feature, but then to allow me to through in my own songs makes the game more player oriented which allows for a better experience.
2.Personalization) This games does somthing that AudioSurf didn't, customizable character. The fact that there are A good starting number of options for customization is alright, but with the addition of steam workshop you can go in and make your own charcter or find one you like that others have made.
3.Depth) The way that the game is divided into teirs isn't a new thing, but it helps. It makes it so someone just starting to play can get used to it, and those that know it can push their skills to the limit. The addition of the visualization mode is also nice. It lets you not only listen to the song, but see how the level would look if you would play it.
Now on to the not so fun bit, what I found laking or distracting from the game.
1.Menu) While getting through the menus isn't bad, the lack of BGM in them displeases me. I get that it is about my music, but an option to allow the game to cycle through tracks I have already played in the menus could be a nice touch, or just nice looping ambient music/sounds would be better than the the silence there is now.
2.Levels) Having the levels generated from the music is awseome, the lack of variaty with the desing of the obstacles makes the longer songs seem more repetitive and less interesting. I'm not saying to change what they are but adding different designs of/on the obstacles would help keep the screen interesting. Maybe even adding a few varying obstacles could help with this so its not as repetitive, like a skating sequence to help balance out the flying sequences.
Other than those few things I find nothing else wrong with the game besides a few loading hiccups when playing a song for the first time, or key presses not regestering(could just be I'm that bad) which for an early access are forgivable. If I had to rate it I would give an 8/10 right now on the grounds that the Replayability and personalizatin are there, but the levels feel to similar with the obsticles and the menus while are visualy appealing lack ambient sound.

If you have scrolled down this far, you probably already know that Melody's Escape is a casual rhythm game that uses your own music.
I just wanted to say that while it does only one thing, it does it well. It has only one game mode, it doesn't have multiplayer or online leaderboards, but it does the casual single player game thing almost flawlessly.
The generated track matches the music very well, the art style is practical and convenient, loading times are really short. There are multiple difficulty levels, and if you don't like them, you can create your own difficulty level. A failure doesn't interrupt the flow of the game, music keeps playing and you're back on track where you are expected to be within a second. Both keyboard and controller work fine, I prefer the controller, but it doesn't make much difference.
All you need is a collection of music on your disk. Music videos are fine too.
The only minor annoyance is that the game doesn't render all characters in Asian or Central European languages correctly, so if you have a collection of K-pop labelled in Korean, you're gonna have a bad time. But apart from that, everything works fine.
A simple, well-done game. If all you want is a simple rhythm game and increasing your scores for your own satisfaction, this is it.

The REAL selling point for this is the novelty of getting to play your favorite songs. I tried piano pieces, theme songs, arhythmic experimental tracks, video game soundtracks - they all work, and it's a marvelous feeling getting to choose what song to play to.
I admire the programming's ability to detect the beat of songs. The arrows/notes don't fall into the typical predictable beat of the song, instead there is a degree of complexity to it, a synchopation.
Like I said, the only downside is the intense side-scrolling can strain your eyes badly. If you're a fan of rhythm & beat games, this is the first one on Steam which I think really captures the spirit of the genre.
Intense and Overload difficulties are great for those times when you feel like patting your head and rubbing your belly at the same time are just too easy.

Melody's Escape is my favorite rhythm game, and one of my favorite games of all time (Steam or otherwise). It's a 2D running/escape game set to the rhythm of your music; a must have for fans of rhythm games like Beat Hazard and Audiosurf and lovers of music (especially EDM). If you're not sure whether or not you'd like rhythm games, there's a free demo of Audiosurf you can try
I was able to pick this game up on sale for about 8$, but I would easily pay double that if I had the money.
Melody's Escape has considerable room for improvement (which is to be expected since it's early access), but the core gameplay is extremely enjoyable and polished.
Pros:
+Works with your music collection
+Works well with a wide range of music, best with EDM and marches (e.g. Sports Song by Weird Al)
+Melody and the color scheme can be customized with the Steam Workshop
+Difficulty is customizable to suit your style
+4 difficulty levels provide a good learning curve and make the game suitable for casual and expert players alike
+Good control scheme, including controller support
+Music can be dragged and dropped from your computer to get around the limitations of the game's built in file browser
+Very nice graphics considering it's 2D
+Music matching algorithm is quite good, though there is still some room for improvement. Some of the claims made by the devs about it seem exaggerated
+I once got Melody to run in midair and I have no idea how
Cons:
-Doesn't come with any music, you have to provide your own files
-Can't bookmark folders on your computer for easy access in the built in file browser (but you can favorite songs)
-Anti-aliasing will cause bad lag, and isn't really needed. Make sure you have it disabled
-Post-processing is buggy in some cases. Try disabling it if the motion seems choppy or the game seems to be going too fast or slow
-Doesn't work with internet radio like Beat Hazard does, though that may not be possible for Melody's Escape since the songs need to be analyzed before play.
-Game can become repetitive if you frequently use the same genre of music
-No story mode, though any story they do make should/would come second to the freeplay you can do now
-No multiplayer features like high scores or head-to-head

I wanted to like this game. I did like it for about the first hour of gameplay. Then I slowly but surely began to hate it.
Here is why:
The narrative is tired and predictable and end with a disappointing revelation.
The cutscenes have a bug which has persisted for far too long which cuts the audio and ruins all the atmosphere the artists had been so elegantly crafting during the gameplay.
The combat is satisfying when it works, but too often I found myself swinging at an enemy that had just barely failed to appear on the action plane of the game and which then proceded to make a tasty snack out of my neck. Other times I found myself swinging my axe at a hoard and hoping and praying that non of them clipped through the weapon, unphased.
The platforming... just no. This game had nice strategic and suspenseful platforming in the first half. In the second half, it devolved into unintuitive, trial and error, instadeath scenarios where if you didn't make the exact move at the exact appropriate time you had to reload the game just far enough back to frustrate you even more than the ridiculous death you just experienced had done.
...*ahem*...
let's not forget that it even implements completely inconsistent mechanics. Throughout the entire game, the character becomes accustomed to vaulting over short walls and fences. But as soon as there is a time constraint (such as a helicopter gunship on your♥♥♥♥♥ you suddenly have to painstakingly climb over them like you're a toddler figuring out how to use a ladder for the first time. The controls often don't make sense either, like when you're hanging from a ledge, if you press down and jump, the character will jump back UP onto the ledge.
I tried to like this game. I didn't want to feel like I had wasted my money. By the end of it I was simply gritting my teeth to make it to the end for the story, but even the ending was a disappointment. Its a shame that the gameplay programmers couldn't hold a candle to the artists for this title because it is very atmospheric and there is a surprising amount of detail in the environment. Unfortunately, art doesn't make a good game and I cannot recommend this one. Don't waste your time or money, even on a sale. play something else such as Limbo or Braid. You'll have a better time than I did.

Deadlight is mainly a platformer game with minor combat and puzzle elements spread throughout its 3 hour run. The protagonist is in search of his disappeared wife and daughter in the midst of a zombie apocalypse in Canada. The story is nothing to write home about and any "twist" it tries to throw at you simply falls flat. There are two reasons for this: 1- The cutscenes are presented with a semi-dynamic comic book look which look acceptable but never convey the sense of danger or excitement that the game wants to go for. 2- The voice acting is HORRENDOUS. The protagonist and every living person he comes across are extremely annoying characters always ready to spout poetic sentences about how everything has gone to hell. The zombies themselves are actually very well voiced.
Graphically, the game looks very good. The animations are smooth and the artistic environment design is top-notch. I had a major framerate dips when things became a little too chaotic though. The game uses physx for some nice destuction and ragdoll effects. The developers talk so much about this game being set in the 80s, but other than being reminded in a single monologue and the load screen (which resembles a cassette tape) I couldn't really define a specific era for the game. It just seemed like another current-day world to me.
You can think of the gameplay as a poor man's Shadow Complex (a little Shank as well). And by poor, I mean extremely shallow and linear. All you ever need to do 99% of the game is run and jump. Sometimes there's the random box pushing puzzle, switch pushing, shooting a lock, but you're constantly moving forward. You can do a little scavenging to find useless secrets though which don't add to the experience one bit.
Deadlight has a few bugs but mostly it's smooth sailing. I didn't have audio in the cutscenes at first which was fixed by re-installing the game.
The detailed animations mean that your character will be reacting to your button presses with a bit of lag which definitely lead to some frustrating deaths. What's unique about this game is that most of the time, you shouldn't fight the zombies but rather run away from them which leads to some very exciting scenarios where you are running away from a hungry horde. You get to wield a revolver, a shotgun and a slingshot (only used in a single chapter) but never enough ammo to stand by and start picking off the zombies.
The game can be finished in under 3 hours and you unlock Nightmare mode that doesn't have any saves. As extras, you get concept pictures and "making of" videos which I found to be utterly boring and not worth the time.
If you don't care about the lackluster story, short length and some minor bugs, I actually think you'd enjoy Deadlight. You probably won't care for it after the 3 hours spent to finish it but those 3 hours will be an exciting albeit lackluster experience. Thumbs up for a developer with potential.

This review is pretty hard to write...
Let's start with the basics (Pros and cons will be listed at the end).
Yes, the game is recommended and if (like me) you loved the first "Hotline Miami" you'll enjoy this game, even only for the fact that it's more "Hotline Miami" action.
So overall this is a good sequel, worth playing; for players who played the first one, this is still a must-buy.
Now the sour stuff...
Hotline Miami 2 only has one big problem...it feels way less "Polished" than the first one.
The game rightfully tries to add as many gameplay elements as possible to make the formula more "fresh" and when the game plays well it definitely is a lot of fun...
Unfortunately some other gamplay elements, a frustrating level design and many bugs put this game a step below the original title.
The main problems i encountered with the game are these:
1- The game makes you use different characters, with different abilities, which is neat. Unfortunately not all characters play well and many times you end up wishing you had a chance to use a different character.
2- The masks mechanic is almost fully removed...only a couple of characters can use masks and the selection of them in really really small. Unexplainable, considering how fun having all the masks was in the first game.
3- The level design is a big problem here. The developers tried to make the locations more varied and they did it! The game offers a lot of different kind of stages.
Half of them are great but the other 50% are frustrating as hell.
The first game offered small but well crafted stages which allowed great strategic freedom, while the sequel too often relies on wide areas in which you are always exposed to enemy fire (particullary frustrating when it comes from enemies you can't see yet). On top of that almost every level is filled with glass windows which make you visible and vulnerable every time...
This approach kills the strategic freedom of the first game and most of the time the only way to win is luring all the enemies inside a room...
4- Unlike the first game this sequel is filled with nasty bugs...nothing "Game-Breaking", but almost all of them cause some "cheap deaths". Sometimes enemies far away react to shots while foes nearby stand still...sometimes dogs keep moving in a 360° motion until triggered, sometimes enemies get stuck into walls, sometimes enemies get glitchy and unvulnerable while passing through doors and many more...
In the end the game is still fun, but the brutal level design and the numerous bugs sometimes make the game too frustrating and insanely (and unfairly) difficult...
As i said at the beginning it's a must buy for harcore fans like me, but if you're new to the game go get the first one! It's better in every way and really cheap.
Pros:
- Amazing Soundtrack (Even better than the first game's one)
- Some stages are very well crafted
- Increased Longevity
- Great overall variety
- Still "Hotline Miami" afterall
- Still confusing, but better storytelling
- Level Editor with workshop support
Cons: All described in the paragraphs above.

The million dollar question:
Is Hotline Miami 2 better or worse than the original?
Here's a simple answer. They're both awesome. Why the hell does that question need answering, and why are people trying to answer it? Which is best for a newcomer? I'll say the original game, so you comparatively know what's going on should you get the sequel (You don't need to play the first game to follow what's going on, but it provides context) and can get a taste for the gameplay. However, if you own the first game, and liked it, you will probably like it's sequel.
What about all the people who loved the original and hate this one? I have no idea if you'll be one of those people or not. Just play the game. If you constantly think of comparisons to the original, you will most likely decide this one is of slightly worse quality. If you can let a game not being one of the greatest games ever made lower your enjoyment of it, I doubt you enjoy most games.
Overall: This game is worth your time, and probably worth your money should your budget allow. If you're new to Hotline Miami, I still reccomend the first over this, but if you liked the original you will most likely like this one too.

I'm not recommending this game because of the uneven difficulty, at least at launch. Now if you are one of those people that whenever someone comments about difficulty you quickly post, "oh that's so easy, I beat that encounter in 20 seconds with the starter weapons only using the basic attack," then this review is not for you so don't waste your time reading it; you'll likely love this game.
My wife and I are not what I'd call "hardcore" gamers but we've been playing a wide variety of games together for many years (including some L4D so the game type is not new to us). I'm just saying that we are not noobs. We started Vermintide on easy just to get a feel for the gameplay and try different characters. The first scenario was a bit hectic since we didn't know how anything worked and there is no tutorial, but we made it through just with a couple deaths. The second scenario (opening some sewers) went better - we were getting the hang of it and didn't die at all.
Then we went to the mission where you collect barrels of gunpowder, still on easy. We hop down from the initial area and immediately get mobbed by special units and the roving "elite" pack and totally wipe. Okay, bad luck, we try it again. Same thing. At this point we are very frustrated - we are playing on EASY mode FFS, just trying to get the feel of the game.
Now perhaps part of this is due to us having 2 of the party manned by bots, but we aren't interested in playing with random people and would only recommend this to our friends if we tried it and liked it. If the game is balanced to require 4 humans for success, then I feel it should state that in the description.
We probably would have returned the game at this point but I bought the steam keys from a third party site (lesson learned). We will keep an eye on it to see if later patches iron some of this out, but for now I'd say skip this one if you aren't up for a challenge or are allergic to frustration.

TL;DR: Buy this.  It's hard but fun and customizable.  There's a lot of replay value.
Rest of review:
I bought this as a kind of cheap impulse buy during the Winter sale.  I was pleasantly surprised by how awesome the game was and still is.  After playing for over an hour and getting the easiest of the achievements and messing with difficulty settings and changing skins multiple times, I must say I enjoy this game.  I'm going to keep it installed as a casual time-waster.
The game has some flaws which really did not bother me at all.  First, the difficulty levels aren't really changing the gameplay at all except for the "relaxing" mode, so in order to really get into the game, you need to find some very fast-paced songs.  I highly recommend Final Fantasy's battle music on medium difficulty as a start.  Second, the character mods are just skins, modified texture sheets.  This limits the amount of character customization you could possibly have.  That said, the game offers Steam Workshop support for character skins, so you can find some nice skin mods and install them very easily.  Finally, a lot of my button presses don't register when using the Xbox 360 controller, so I missed a lot of key presses just because they were too close to each other and I couldn't press them fast enough.
The overall feel of the game is fast-paced.  it has its slow moments, but it relies on your own music files to generate the game's obstacles and pace, so as long as you avoid slow-paced songs, you should have a very fun time with this game.

While this may work better for some songs then others I have found the overall effect and performance of the system to be quite satisfactory. Since I’m not very good at these games I have trouble actually enjoying watching the character while trying to concentrate on hitting all the buttons on time. That is when auto play mode comes in. You can select this play mode to have the character automatically play threw the game for you while you sit back and watch. It may sound silly but it is actually a lot of fun. Even though this review is written in early access I feel the game already provides all that it advertises and is well worth the cost. While I’m really looking forward to further improvements I would not feel cheated at all if the game was made 1.0 right now.

Deadlight is a very interesting and skill challenging game. The game may appear to be a simple sidescroller (which in I have not played too many myself), but does provide a challenge of timing and reflexes when going through the game. The game play can be a little awkward at times if you're using a keyboard and mouse, but nothing unbearable. I would recommend a controller if you're going to play this game. The graphics for the game are quite spectacular and provides an interesting playing experience, especially with the various camera zooms.
The one negative about this game is that the game does appear to be a bit short and lacking on content. The game can completed in anywhere between 3-4 hours depending on how much time you take to find collectibles and that of the sorts. Also as I previously mentioned, the game can be a bit tricky if you're running a keyboard and mouse due to the fact there are points in the game where you'll have to dodge obsticles and time jumps correctly in order to advance.
Overall, I would recommend this game for anyone looking to try out a different stlye dystopian fiction game.

I bought this game and liked it quite a lot so heres my pros and cons breakdown
PROS
> The story line is immersive and pretty cool, I found myself really getting into the storyline which added to the game yet still leaves scope for you to just saunter off and do whatever you want.
> You can download all kinds of cool weapons and items made buy players streight into your game as well as make total monstrositys yourself
> Early on the creatures on the planet are a clear and present danger and its not rare to be killed by some uber creature if you stray off to far.
> I like how you can recruit npcs to accompany and help you, as well as how the game expands into colony management late game
> Getting someones already pretty cool ISO then modifying it to make your own improved mega awesome version is really fun, I did that with a helicopter and a gun (new paint job and added functionality) The laser gun ended up being incredibly powerful and pretty game breaking really.
CONS:
> The storyline isnt finished yet and it seems to end abruptly on a bit of a cliffhanger
> You HAVE to use the design system in the game to make stuff and the game heavily penalises you if you dont. Some people see this as the best aspect of the game but I would like to see some default isos included in teh game that you can just use early on. I am not good at 3d design and I dont really want to be. The tool seems incredibly complicated to me and for me personally it subtracts heavily from my enjoyment of the game. You can download other peoples ISOS but many of them you cant use until youve got further into teh storyline and found the npcs with the nessecary parts and many others are just overly fancy, wasting materials that are scarce early game.
> Development seems slow to me, whats already there is really enjoyable and a good game already but I'd like to see a big update (maybe open more of the map) soon
> making buildings is a pain in the rear end, boiling down to dragging out big squares unless you choose to use the in game 3D engine to make some (which again is incredibly complicated and takes FOREVER) please give us some prefabs
> I found helicopters a real pain to use
> The inventory system just makes no sense at all and for me it completely ruins immersion. As well as being finiky to find what you want to find, for some reason your guy is able to hold  50 zillion tons of weigh, yet run around completely unhindered.
> The hostile creatures get very easy very quickly. At the start of the game they are a threat, but early mid game nothing is a threat to you at all as you have vehicles and a manajory of heavily armed bodyguards.
> The multiplayer servers are pretty much dead
> The only players that seem to remain as this game has just been in development so long are fan boys who dont want anything at all to change. They are happy being able to carry unlimited amounts of weight etc.... I feel the small hardcore fanboy player base is actually holding back development of this game as the devs seem to pander to them. Its nice for devs to listen to feedback from their community, however listening to people who are killing your game and holding back any progress is just silly.
initially I reccomended this game but the vision the devs seem to have for it falls well short of my initial expectations and I feel that they are throwing away an opportunity to make a truely amazing game. Having seen how this game has developed and will develop I feel I can no longer reccomend it... its just not going to be the epic game I imagined it being and it completely ill equipped for a large player base. With no real restrictions on what players can carry, and seeing that you can hit near teh top of teh tech tree in a few hours of play, every multiplayer server on the game would be reduced to ashes in a day if there was a sudden influx of players.

So I'm actually kind of on the verge of recommending and not recommending Melody's Escape. I'll explain, of course, but in the end I do recommend this - just to a certain crowd of gamers.
Now, I have previously reviewed Audiosurf, and after finishing everything I wanted to do in Melody's Escape I moved on to Beat Hazard. All three of these games are similar in the whole "play your own music" motif, but each game has vastly different gameplay mechanics. And I have to admit, out of these three "play your own music" games, Melody's Escape did the least for me. Don't get me wrong, it's not a terrible game, just not a fantastic one in my eyes.
In short, Melody's Escape is a running game set to your music. You control a female protagonist named Melody and tap certain directional keys to correspond with obstacles, such as sliding, jumping, and kicking through blocks. There are sections for each type of intensity, as well. The background changes to a slightly hotter color and the scenery moves faster as the intensity of a song builds up. On top of this, there are also slow-motion sections of long jumps for cooldown segments of songs, which I think is quite a nice touch despite being rare, as I've only encountered such sections maybe 3 or 4 times out of the hundred-ish songs I played. Finally, there are multiple difficulties you can choose from. The easiest has you press only one directional key for each section of a song, and the hardest has you use
WASD and arrow controls for certain types of obstacles, which poses a substantial challenge.
However, besides the decent gameplay, this game has a few issues for me. First off, the visuals in this game are very basic and bland, and the game isn't nearly as visually appealing as Audiosurf or Beat Hazard. Even the menu looks rather boring. Unlike other rhythm games I've played, Melody's Escape features no music on the menu, and I think that's a nice facet that rhythm games ought to have. In Melody's Escape, the menu is just silence, save for the minimal "beep" sounds that you hear when selecting options on the menu.
There is also very little to do in this game and minimal incentives. There isn't a sort of leveling up system or anything to unlock, nor leaderboards for songs, rendering your high score on songs to not have much purpose. The only real incentive in this game is the 8 achievements, which are all relatively easy to get if you're going for them. It only took me around 8 hours to get them all. After that, it comes down to merely playing for fun. And I'm not a huge fan of games that are solely made to pass time unless there's actual incentives or things you can do afterwards.
Anyways, if you want more of a "for-fun" rhythm game customized to your music to pass the time with, Melody's Escape would be a good purchase for you. If you're into games with more of an incentive and contain more for you to do, consider Audiosurf or Beat Hazard instead. However, keep in mind this game is still in Early Access as I write this and is probably awaiting a few changes, so I can hope that some of its issues will get fixed in forthcoming updates.

Im giving this a thumbs up for the creative and original idea, and dispite the flaws of it being Early Access. However, I do not recomend it if you will have issues with the following cons.
The first one is the motion blur. Yes, the motion blur from the "markers" and obstacles is really irritating. Because of it my eyes hurt and therfore I am distracted from enjoying the music and game. And this is due to the fact my eyes perceive the objects blurry, and have issues with tracking. This is worsen by the running and faster speeds, as the obstacles are seen only as colored blurry "things". A partial fix to this is to use your peripheral vision and focus on the runner.
Second is the Sync and Track Speed. And I will compare this part to Audiosurf.
Well, the game(Melody Escape) does scan the music quite accurately, but, the obstacles are place only on the bass or beat parts of the music. Whilist the speed, intended to be in the music is quite off.
I used the soundtrack from UT2004 - Level 8, which has a more calm, jogging like nature, which smoothly transfers to a bit faster pace.
First I tested it on Audiosurf(Ninja Mono). It went just as I expected, it started of slowly in the purple tone(slow pace), then the beats came up, making the road bounce a little, then the speed again smoothly changed to a blue tone, and this perfect sync with the temp went to the end, AND most importantly, the pace was changing in this way (purple-blue-blue/green-green/greenish yellow-blue-purple).
Now if we take Melody Escape on Relaxing! difficulty. The beginning starts off with me ramming one button, then jogging, then running, then jogging again and these two speeds accompanied me almost the whole part with a very unsync transfer between each other, but I didn't finish, and this is where the 3rd con comes up.
Obstacles are either too close, or too fast, even on slow speed option. Yep, in addition to the 1st con this makes the game unplayable. No matter what, you WILL miss.
So, in the end I wish the devs could find out how Audiosurf was made, or rather how it syncs the music, and add more speed temps in addition to fixing the 1st and 3rd con.
But still, I think the game is great, and it does have potential.

First, as I'm writing this review it states my playtime in Deadlight as 12.7 hrs. This is because the game has been sitting in standby for at the very least 4 hours.
Now, the review: Deadlight starts off with a great atmosphere and with pretty solid feeling controls. The visuals are good, with moving backgrounds giving the 2D game some feeling of deapth.
The game does, however, not live up to it's first impressions throughout. At some point it just becomes try-and-die, which I found very frustrating.
The flaws of the controls also started to shine through as the game progressed and the difficulty increased. (I did play with a gamepad, so that may have been at least part of the problem) There is this particular section in the middle (which all Deadlight players remember dearly i reckon) where you for some spoilerific reason have to run over some rooftops, jumping gaps and traversing walls and fenses. The problem is that the character only on rare occasions determine that he should jump over the fense quickly. Instead he most often leisurely climbs up one side, steps over, and then seems to sit there admiring the view for a moment while the deadly thing closes in before he recognizes your frantic mashing on the jump button. I don't remember the last time I raged at a game like I did during that part.
The story overall is also kind of dumb. A lot of things just leaves you wondering why on earth they think THAT was a good idea. The story has some potential, but it's not delivered very well and the ending felt puzzling and pretty unsatisfying.
The game is buggy. It worked mostly fine for me, but sometimes when i tried to pause it it froze for some time. I always got it going again through alt-tabbing to desktop and then back.
At one moment I was supposed to swith on a device, but the interaction prompt just made me pick up bullets?!? I reloded last ceckpoint and then the interaction prompt activated the device, the bullets were gone. Weird...
As for recommendations. At full price? No way! I got it for around 1.19€ and that, I think, seems fair. But that's why I wont recommend it, it won't be available for -90% all the time.

This is a very neat game as far as potential.  There is little doubt that this CAN replace Minecraft and Starbound as well as perhaps some others.  There are a few warts that need to be resolve very quickly though:
1) Study Guild Wars 2 and Minecraft controls thoroughly.  It is very hard to control this game in relation to the camera.  First person is also ESSENTIAL (like Skyrim).  Resolving the control and camera issues will make this game improve by at least an order of magnitude.  We've bought this for our entire family and that is the #1 thing that everyone keeps coming back with.
2) Get some diversity of music going.  Right now the music just gets old very quickly.  It is beautiful, but very quickly starts to grind on the player.  Follow the lead of Minecraft again on this.
3) Make it more clear of how to create your creations (the export process is clunky).  There should perhaps be a better tutorial system.  In the inventory, make it easier to search for things.
4) Make an option to allow players to start together in a community.  It is very hard to get to each other and cooperative playing is SO fun in this game.
5)  Tree environments should have more interactive options.  Example, the rope gun should allow scaling of trees and tree houses sould be buildable.  Would be so fun in forrest and jungle environments.
6) Digging underground structures and cities should be refined via some control locks that allow side views or different perspective views to be leveraged to really create proper carved structures out of the ground, hills, mountains, etc.
Overall this game is incredibly fun and has immense potential.  If these items can be addressed it will generate a huge amount of additional desire to play this game.

Im giving this a thumbs up for the creative and original idea, and dispite the flaws of it being Early Access. However, I do not recomend it if you will have issues with the following cons.
The first one is the motion blur. Yes, the motion blur from the "markers" and obstacles is really irritating. Because of it my eyes hurt and therfore I am distracted from enjoying the music and game. And this is due to the fact my eyes perceive the objects blurry, and have issues with tracking. This is worsen by the running and faster speeds, as the obstacles are seen only as colored blurry "things". A partial fix to this is to use your peripheral vision and focus on the runner.
Second is the Sync and Track Speed. And I will compare this part to Audiosurf.
Well, the game(Melody Escape) does scan the music quite accurately, but, the obstacles are place only on the bass or beat parts of the music. Whilist the speed, intended to be in the music is quite off.
I used the soundtrack from UT2004 - Level 8, which has a more calm, jogging like nature, which smoothly transfers to a bit faster pace.
First I tested it on Audiosurf(Ninja Mono). It went just as I expected, it started of slowly in the purple tone(slow pace), then the beats came up, making the road bounce a little, then the speed again smoothly changed to a blue tone, and this perfect sync with the temp went to the end, AND most importantly, the pace was changing in this way (purple-blue-blue/green-green/greenish yellow-blue-purple).
Now if we take Melody Escape on Relaxing! difficulty. The beginning starts off with me ramming one button, then jogging, then running, then jogging again and these two speeds accompanied me almost the whole part with a very unsync transfer between each other, but I didn't finish, and this is where the 3rd con comes up.
Obstacles are either too close, or too fast, even on slow speed option. Yep, in addition to the 1st con this makes the game unplayable. No matter what, you WILL miss.
So, in the end I wish the devs could find out how Audiosurf was made, or rather how it syncs the music, and add more speed temps in addition to fixing the 1st and 3rd con.
But still, I think the game is great, and it does have potential.

Ridiculously fun! But not without its issues.
- Combat is visceral and feels like it has some real weight to it.
- The weapons themselves provide several different playstyles for each class; the Bright Wizard has a slew of staves at her disposal, for rapid-fire peppering of Skaven or intermittent obliteration of large groups, for example.
-Loot is only rewarded when you level up or successfully finish a level, which is a bit of a double-edged sword; on one hand it means that you feel you have earned your loot because this game holds
back, but on the other hand you can be left feeling a bit cheated (particularly in single-player with AI, but I'll come onto that later) when you fall at the last hurdle and have nothing to show for it but a handful of exp.
- Classes are varied enough to keep things interesting, yet not so different as to pigeonhole players.
- Gameplay is tough as old boots as you are almost constantly under attack by hordes of ratmen. While this can seem unfair at times, it adds a lot to the sense of urgency and the scale of the infestation.
- My biggest gripe is with the co-operative AI; oftentimes they will just
, or all become suddenly very anti-Skaven when you fall, rather than having one of them trying to revive you. They also aren't the best at following you to objectives, and are very easily distracted by a single ratman. For this reason I would avoid single-player when possible, and stick to playing with friends or matchmaking; single-player is doable, but the game really shines when you have 4 humans playing, rather than 1 human and 3 statues.
- The game also suffers from a few bugs; I had a problem in an online game where I revived a player and they fell down into an inaccessible portion of the map, and the game insisted I try to revive them. Thankfully they eventually died and were able to be rescued elsewhere in the map.
- As well as this, the resolution seems to reset every time I launch the game; although this is easily fixed with a quick trip to the options menu, it's still an inconvenience which can become quite tedious.
-I've also had the game crash my computer a few times, requiring a system restart, though thankfully this is rare.
Hopefully Fatshark can get the major bugs ironed out with a patch soon, because this game is fun as hell and hard as nails, and damn if I don't want to kill
of those damn Thaggoraki.

Awful execution belies otherwise solid mechanics. I want to love this game, but it's a one-way relationship.
The first hour-or-so will be an enjoyable stealth-based platformer, before you're introduced to The Rat and his one-hit-kill maze of twitch platforming, relying on millisecond-perfect reactions to make progress. Expect to die 20+ times per trap.
After this area, you'll begin to see small issues with the game itself... Odd checkpoints placing your further back than your progress, requiring you to bring lifts back down for you to proceed; Audio being reliably cut off, losing huge chunks of dialogue and replies; Awful hitbox detection that allows you to be hit from behind an enemy, and equally bad enemy AI that will ignore specifically placed distractions and beat you to death while you're being held by another; A broken standing-jump mechanic that will send you flying to the side if you're not perfectly still; and an interactable environment that is impossible to tell foreground from background, leaving you plummeting to your death where you thought there was a walkway.
So what's good about the game? Well, it's not the story as told by the cutscenes or the overly-raspy voice-actor, but the journal was a delight to read, and hidden pages of it, though making no sense, are a nice collectable to have and tell you more about your character than the game itself every will, besides the odd grunt of his wife and daughter's names.
A gritty, 3D side-scroller based on luring and evading enemies is a rare commodity, as far as I know, and this game captures the world and its parkor exploration very nicely, though the liklihood of your character actually being able to move like that is questionable. The enemies themselves are your typical zombie-type, but feature eyes that glow red when they're being aggroed, which I suppose is nice, if a bit too 'gamey' for the real world they're trying to create. And once again, this is some magical universe where zombies have never been conceived of, and are instead known as 'Shadows'.
I will let you make your own mind up about this game. If you're a big fan of platformers and zombie survival, you might find something you like... but for the casual player, there is far too much confusion and overly-punishing mechanics for me to recommend this game.

An excellent addition to the sandbox adventure/miner sub-genre, Planet Explorers is, in a nutshell, what people who fell for the hype over StarForge were and still are looking for.
Where Starbound is basically Terraria in space, Planet Explorers has that same relationship with Minecraft but manages to be better. While Minecraft uses block-based voxels to construct its landscapes, Planet Explorers uses OpenCL. This enables the terrain to be just as malleable as that of Minecraft, but look a damn sight better. Though admittedly OpenCL, being a prototype, has a few bugs, one of which is that vehicles travelling at high speed over rough ground have a tendency to clip through the terrain as of 0.85. That said, the bugs present in the alpha of Planet Explorers, albeit slightly frustrating at times, are easily more forgivable than those in
(*stares viciously at EA and Ubisoft*) and barely put a scratch into the rest of the game.
Story mode is easily the best of the three game modes, the other two being Adventure (basically Minecraft Survival) and Build (creative mode). Beneath the magnificent visuals - not to mention the aliens themselves (which look
less silly than those in Starbound) - there is a surprisingly well-crafted storyline with interesting lore and bright characters to explore. Item crafting in Story is tiered depending on how far you are into the story, with simple wooden equipment available for use at the start and more powerful armour and weapons being available for manufacture later on.
Speaking of crafting, Planet Explorers has what far too few games of this genre have in my honest opinion - a fleshed-out  and incredibly detailed item creation system that is easily mastered to boot. One can create a huge amount of useful, fully personalised items and vehicles - swords, guns, bikes, tanks, helicopters, boats and airborne dreadnoughts, to name but a few. Unfortunately, it is not possible to create custom tools or armour, and firearms are limited to pistols, assault rifles and laser rifles (but this might change soon). Nonetheless, Planet Explorers' powerful item creation system gives it a big leverage over other games of its genre.
To conclude: do I recommend this game? Of course I do. If you can forgive the glitches and bugs (take into account that this is an alpha, and not a fully released game yet), a wonderful sandbox adventure that has the potential to surpass even Minecraft in its scope awaits the lenient.

Off Screen Sniping: The biggest ♥♥♥♥ing problem in this game that didn't exist in the first. More enemies have guns now, and have a huge ♥♥♥♥ing FOV, moreso than you do, which means sometimes you'll get your face ♥♥♥♥ed by a bullet seemingly out of nowhere.
Terrible Enemy AI: Enemies often do random♥♥♥♥♥♥ which makes your runs through the levels painful. they'll often get stuck in doors, and flail about for a set period of time, or just straight up mong out and do nothing.
Generally Bad Level Design: Levels are often spawling and huge, which seems like a fun idea, right? nope. it just lends well to the 'getting shot out of nowhere' problem of the game, as you often can't see the enemies that will be shooting at you.
Some levels also start with an enemy immediately running at you, which to me just seems like♥♥♥♥♥♥poor level design.
It's not like the first game where you generally knew where you ♥♥♥♥ed up, and you knew you could do better the second time. It's more a case of 'imma try to progress in this level, but get murked by something that has nothing to do with my level of skill at the game smdh'

Some of my freinds mocked me for picking this game up. They agreed (almost unanimously) that it looked like something a 12 year old would enjoy. Thats kind of what drew me to the game to begin with, its cutesy sci-fi theming. So they will not pick it up in case a friend of theirs sees it in their library and judges them non adults or some other social convention i dont fully understand.
Ill tell you what keeps me playing though, this game rocks! and dirts! and sands! and you can craft almost anything you can imagine. If the item you want is not something you can get a recipe from an npc for, then you can open the object creator and create it. if you have the materials in your inventory, you just export it to the game and BAM! your imagination, now realised. I mean anything too, need a weapon? no problem. need a car? no problem! need a chopper? no problem! need a town? easy as pie!
Admitedly, the object creator portion of this game could use some better tutorial in game... but there are a good number of youtube videos showing exactly how to use it (and some tips to using it more efficiently) so really the community has come together where the developers have delayed their efforts.
Remembering also that this game is still in alpha (currently at version 0.85a as of this writing), and plans to include items the fans have taken it upon themselves to create and share (tutorials, ISOs, and the like) may be in the works still, this game still plays really well. Ive had to restart the story a few times now, due to saves not being compatible with features added/removed in version patches, but i enjoy it (after the first few missions, anyway) each time since i generally notice something in the story line that i didnt pick up on before.
All in all, i would give this game 7/10. The music is♥♥♥♥♥♥♥(its easy enough to turn off though), and the grass is distracting at best (the blades are too fat, and obscure the terrain too well imho) but again, easy enough to turn off... The game plays well, but without these 2 features enabled looses a lot of its gloss (themed music that isnt annoying as all get out would increase immersion, and better grass would make surface deposits more visible). I would reccomend this game to anyone who likes this builder/survival genre.

Gameplay was fun, if repetitive. I played with my keyboard and mouse, and while I didn't have the timing issues most people seem to have, aiming was a nightmare. So I tended to rely on the ax, which might give you an indication of how little combat is in the game. The voice acting was stale and the story brought nothing new to the table - it was actually pretty terrible, predictable, and the ending reeked of "I Know Best" Dude Heroism (if you've played FNV and done Boone's companion quest to the point where he tells you about Carla, well, then you probably know what I mean).
Hooowever, the atmosphere, music, and backgrounds were all very very well done. Post-apoc Seattle was the best part of the game.

Deadlight is a 2.5D sidescroller game which takes place in a typical zombie apocalypse world where "shadows" (as the people in the game call zombies) have taken over all the major cities. The idea of the game is admirable - a zombie platformer - but that idea can't carry the whole game when the story is very mediocre at its best and the clunky controls cause occasional frustration, not mentioning how campy most of the voice actors sound. Also it lasts barely three hours and there even is one 30 minutes lasting part which is completely pointless and out of place, something what the creators should have cut out before the final version of the game and replace it with actually a relevant sequence. So why do I recommend this after all these negative things? Deadlight's graphics look great considering it's a sidescroller game, and some scenes are really enjoyable when the controls and the story's lousy writing aren't bothering you. You could spend your two hours in a worse way than playing this game. The main point is the price of Deadlight: if you can buy it with some pocket change, go for it, especially if you're always ready for another zombie adventure. At full price? Not worth it.
*After you finish the game a difficulty mode called "Nightmare mode" unlocks, urging you to repeat the game. It contains an alternative ending, but I didn't feel like wanting to play the game again any time soon so I watched it on YouTube. I prefer it to the original ending, so if you want to experience Deadlight again with a better ending you should, or you can just do as I did.

Update: 31/10/15
- Since the last edit, the developers have released some minor patches to remove some of the exploits. This is a step in the right direction but falls far short of expectations. None of the major problems have been addressed.
Should you buy it?
- No, not yet
Why?
The game is not ready for release.
- Terrible netcode, horrible p2p latency issues, numerous drop out, no host migration, unpredicatable AI, unpredicatable hitboxes, unpredicatable and unrewarding loot.
Let me first apologise for the long review. i want to give a fair critque of the current state of the game and to explain why i would not recommend this game. This game has great features, but the major problem is not with the feature but the poor way they are implemented. Think of someone having great ideas but says "Meh, ♥♥♥♥ it, this will i do" when implementing them. This is the game i am reviewing. This review will warn you about the frustration this game will cause, possibily because of those features but mainly due to the terrible state of the game.
Intro:
Do you like melee? Do you like ranged combat? how about leveling and getting loot? All these sound like great things in a game right? Well, they are, Vermintide is basically a very good game. The ranged combat is good but not as good as other dedicated ranged combat games. The melee is tactile but not a good as a dedicated melee game. And, the combination of the two mechanics are inferior to games such as Killing Floor 2, but better than other game that are not heavily focused on pure combat mechanics like Skyrim.
What about interesting character classes? A teamwork-centric experience? Well the game is also these things. The classes are differentiated but are not as clearly as other co-op roleplaying games like Dungeon Defenders but is more varied than Left4Dead and other horde mode games.
So would i recommend this game?
- If the game worked properly: Yes. It does most things quite well, like a jack of all trades, but it is a master of none. Fun when it works, a well balanced game with a number of interesting features that have great potential, but mostly it doesnt. Allow me to explain.
Poor Net-Code:
- Imagine a challenging experience where you have the chance of great reward. You work hard, co-ordinate with friends or strangers to complete very difficult tasks, but near the end of the challenge... BAM!!!! ♥♥♥♥ YOU, YOU GET NOTHING! Why? Because the host disconnected? Because the host is a troll and disbanded the party on purpose? You Disconnected? You could experience any number of these issues.
Poor-Graphics Optimisation:
- For anyone without a high-end PC you will be playing on medium at best. Even then, you will experience severe drops in framerate. From 60+ to low 10's during combat. In addition to this, the poo optimisation has lead to GPU's over-heating, and hence, crashing the game.
P2P Stability:
- Most, if not all players, have experienced disconnections and latency issues. How often do these things happen will vary depending on your connection. If your internet is perfect this will still affect you. If your internet is average, then often. If your internet is very good in almost every circumstance and does no experience any of these issues in any other game, still often.
Un-Polished Mechanics:
- How about you avoid these issues most of the time? Do you like killing vermin? How about killing a rat but moments later your screen flashes and notifies you that you have taken damage. Why? Because of the horribly unpredictable latency. Swing your Axe/Sword/Mace: every now and again, nothing happens. Shoot your Gun/Bow/Staff: same problem.
Poor Game Design:
- Challenging games like Dark Souls are challenging but fair. Good mechanics, learning the game,  patience, and practice, will result in the game becoming more enjoyable. But in Vermintide, these things are irrelevant from time to time. If the game decides you take copious amounts of damages you will. Can you block the damage? No, Can you dodge the damage? No. Can the player control any of the variables in the game that will prevent this damage? No. The game has unblockable, undodgeable, randomly generated enemies that can spawn during opening-cut scenes, behind walls, under the map, or any number of unacceptable cricumstance that will wipe your entire party.
RNG (random number generation) Hell:
- The loot system is far too unpredicatable and unrewarding. When you (If you) complete a map, you have to roll a set of 7 dice; this will determine which of the 7 objects you receive. The 7 possible objects are all randomly generated. Once you receive the item, there is randomly selected trait out of a possible 30 traits, most of which are not that useful, but a select few that are ridciously overpowered and game changing. Then you 'unlock' the traits which randomly determines the % change of it proc'ing. So far, that is 4 RNG hoops to jump through when receiving an item. This is more random and annoying than Diablo 3's loot system at launch which was heavily critised. You cannot control the loot in any meaningful way. The game does not take your preferred or weapon choice into account when determine the 7 possible reward items. Completing objectives only increases the possibility of an increase in of item quality (white, green, blue, orange, red) but you can still end up with trash/white loot in the second hardest difficulty.
Conclusion:
I want to spend 50, 100, 500, hours on this game. i really do. Can i? yes, of course i can, but it will probably lose my♥♥♥♥♥♥ The game has potential, but it's the same potential as a wild animal. It may be cute and welcoming at first but be prepared as they will likely ♥♥♥♥ your♥♥♥♥♥♥up after a while.

Vermintide is a great addition to the Warhammer storyline, set in an apocalyptic wasteland of vermin rats. A group of four characters, chosen from five, will fight together to go through quests and accomplish feats.
The pros:
-Intrigiuing loot system which rewards you for finding hidden Tomes and Loot Dice.
-Crafting system is interesting, and allows buildup towards exotic weapons the longer the playthrough.
-No microtransactions that make it a 'pay-to-win'. Simply gameplay driven.
-Combat is strong, fast-paced, and requires your individed attention, lest a pack-rat or assassin rat make your life a living hell.
-Enemy AI makes combat fun an interesting.
-An alright diversity of enemies makes combat thrilling.
The cons:
-Nowhere near enough different kinds of weapons.
-A lot of the classes, due to a limitted amount of weapons, feel very restricted in their build pattern. For example, the waywatcher only really ever has a bow for ranged.
-The friendly AI suck miserably. Very miserably. They're just♥♥♥♥♥♥ Always, always play with friends instead. Numerous times, the farther into missions you go, the AI will just sit there and do absolutely nothing. Sometimes they'll just wait in one spot while you progress through the map, and do LITERALLY nothing. Their combat skills are god-awful, often never taking advantage of DPS or anything, and just hold the block button. They get stuck in walls like it's nobody's business, and have no concept of navigation.
-Even in full release, almost all of the bugs from pre-release stayed. For example, many players experience vertice glitches, where one or two vertices of characters will be in the floor, whereas the rest of the body will be either above it, or elsewhere if they've been ragdolled. Also, character models sometimes just have disappearing bodyparts.
Conclusion: All in all, I still love the game. The problems are counteracted by the thrilling combat and intriguing crafting system, which puts a lot of other games to shame. Even still, though, I'd highly recommend playing with friends. The friendly AI are more cancer than I can describe. They just don't function.

First, I need to say this: The graphics aren't great. Need to get that out of the way. Oh and the music. That also sucks, although you can change it if you play around with the sound files. However, its the gameplay that makes up for it. M&B:W is a third person hack & slach, a RTS and a market sim. You create your charecter and you are ploped into caladria. You choose a faction (6 I Belive) and start there. The tutorial isn't one. You start getting attacked by bandits. The combat is simple Depending on how you swing, you swing in a diffrent direction. There is also a First Person mode, but its only use is if you are crosbow sniping. Then a tradesman helps you out asks you to resque his brother from bandits and then you are off on your own. The world is huge. To move in the map, you click where you want to go and then your party moves there. You can hire vilagers from towns and train them. If you run into a lord they'll talk to you (Or Attempt to destroy you if you have a bad relation with them). Runing into bandits causes a battle. You can also make a living off being a bandit yourself. You can also buy land and make an enterprise. There are often tournaments of some towns. You should start by going to a King and getting a mercanary contract. Gain some renown and become a vassal/jarl/Something. Or instead of the contract gain renown and get a claimant to thier throne. Or make your own faction. Just a warning: this game can get a little addictive.

More platformer than adventure, Deadlight puts you into the cliched boots of a gravel-voiced, grizzled protagonist who is trying to survive while also searching for his family (who may or may not actually be alive) during a zombie outbreak. Set in 1986 Seattle, the game's environs are almost entirely urban, though (especially in the sewer levels) exaggerated to foster interesting gameplay. The actions you perform are typical of a puzzle platformer and involve jumping onto and hanging from ledges, pulling switches, and pushing boxes. It's all handled rather well and the game's zombies (or "shadows" as they call them) are used to decent effect in creating obstacles throughout the game.
Weapon combat is mostly downplayed with firearms being available at certain intervals, but with limited ammo and even then maybe only for a third of the game as a whole. A fire ax is supplied to help deal with zombies and certain obstacles, but in proper zombie fiction style it's easy to become overwhelmed by a group of zombies and/or lose stamina while fending them off and find yourself helpless.
Deadlight is a short game and little about the story or characterizations is very original in the realm of zombie fiction, but they stick to the established tropes well so it's hard to argue. Visually, the game is a pleasure to look at and the audio is well handled too, though dialogue was either too loud or too soft in many places. Overall I enjoyed the game and for a 3-4 hour experience, think it's worth picking up.

The combat gameplay is dull when it's not clumsy, but this is a survival-horror platformer, so I suppose I can excuse that. The player character moves realistically, like a human would, but I don't play platformers for the realism.
All of this I could excuse if the story and the writing kept me interested, but they don't. The story is a pile of post-"Walking Dead" cliches, while the voice acting is a "Max Payne" knockoff without the sense of humor. Not that any voice actor on the planet could have made this dialogue sound good, anyway -- the writing is BAD. Just try reading the  super-serious Diary of the protagonist without your eyes rolling back in your head, I dare you.
Good thing that I spent only a couple of bucks on this in a Steam sale, otherwise I'd be angry instead of mildly nonplussed. The three hours I spent beating it, however -- those I will never get back.

I thought i would share my thoughts with anyone who is thinking about purchasing the game.
Gameplay: So, like with most shooter games, there is no real flow to the story. There are several maps that you can play in different modes of gameplay.
*  Hunted: Which is player vs player to see who can survive to the last man.
*  Escape: Where you are given a series of tasks to complete via text message in order to     complete the map.
*  Extraction: Where you are given directions to a random location to save citizens from a onslaught of zombies.
*  Panic Classic and Objective: Where a Survivor player turns into a zombie and you need to try and stay alive and aviod being turned (or if you are a zombie kill all the survivors). Classic is basially a free for all PVP situation where objective is where you have to complete the escape mission while avoiding the Survivor turned Zombie.
I find that your gaming experience will depend on the people you play with. I wouldn't recommend the solo play as for myself i found it quite boring (but that could just be because i played multiplayer first) The one gripe i have is that the servers have no vote to kick function so games tend to fill up with alot of testosterone filled teens who play the i have a bigger e-peen then you game.
Graphics:
The graphics are not too bad. I have only experienced one bug within the graphics where when i am a zombie and switched to blended mode the zombie model glitches basically letting me see its insides and only the top portion of the model floating around. However, i have experienced a bug where the game will constantly crash with no error report although this has not happened recently.
Sound:
Sound can be a bit glitchy sometimes. The directional sound sometimes bugs up and makes it sound like there is a zombie right next to you when they are on the floor above you or in the next room over. At the same time sometimes there is absolutely no sound and zombies come out of nowhere to eat you alive.
In conclusion, this game is quite fun to play for awhile. Its best played in the multiplayer setting. As long as monochrome follow through with their promise of free DLC. Worth the $20 if you are looking for a game to fill up some time.

I hate early access games. I think that whilst the principle is nice, it's far too tempting for devs to take the money and not deliver on their promises. But this game has interested me from the time I first saw it. I've been looking for a good survival and crafting experience that doesn't rely on multiplayer and all the griefers that come with it. This game offers that in what is already an impressive array of single player and co-op experiences.
Yes it is still noticeably alpha in some areas but the important things all work well and the graphics are good for a game of this type. I'm still discovering new creatures and elements and it sounds like there will be more added by the time it's finished. Building and crafting is very simple and intuitive. I was impressed that the story mode had at least some voice acting, hopefully they finish it off for all the quests and maybe add more than just the 2 or 3 soundtracks they've got.
But yes looking at the other games offering similar experiences I am satisfied that at the moment this one offers the best experience for those who want an exploration game without forced multiplayer. The direction it's heading at the moment it seems it will end up as a combination of Elder Scrolls, DayZ and Minecraft, blending them all together for something unique.
