Just a heads-up: I'm writing this review on 15 October 2014. As of today, Melody's Escape is still in Early Access, so this review might not be accurate if the game undergoes more development.
Melody's Escape has heart, and its base concept is so simple that I'm surprised at how challenging it is. The problem is that a good portion of the challenge doesn't come from the gameplay, but from the interface and the bugs.
In full screen mode, the game doesn't register button/key-presses worth a damn, so I played it in windowed mode instead. It works much better in windowed mode, but the timing of key presses still feels somewhat arbitrary. This is most notable in sections that have evenly spaced single notes that, by rights, should have a regular 4/4 beat, but even tapping right along with the song yields a hit only 80% of the time at best. This includes Relaxed mode, where (supposedly) you can LITERALLY just tap one button in time with the song for most of the prompts. I get the distinct impression that this is not because the prompts aren't timed right, but rather, the game still isn't registering all of my key-presses correctly.
In sections that mix "button" prompts (orbs) with "direction" prompts (obstacles), the game tends to ignore between 30-50% of all my "direction" presses, even on difficulty modes where the directions and buttons are interchangeable (The lowest two difficulties). Additionally, when two "long-note" sections, which require you to hold the button, are back to back, the game tends to ignore my button press on the second prompt. For most of these issues, I find that if I press the key a split second early, it tends to register more often, but what is the point of a rhythm game if you have to force yourself to ignore the rhythm in order to play?
On top of this, the process of respawning after you die is not very forgiving. I find that most of my deaths come in twos, because Melody will fall down, reappear, and immediately trip over something else because the game isn't ready to register key presses yet, or something.
My last major point of contention is that the difficulty level of the game, even without the bugs, is off the charts. Personally, I can't imagine how anybody referred to this game as "relaxing". Even some of my most drifty, relaxing music was face-meltingly difficult at anything other than "Relaxed" difficulty, which just requires you to tap away at the same key for most of a song. I don't know if the devs read reviews, but I'd suggest changing, or implementing a setting to allow the player to adjust, the speed at which the stage goes by (or the speed at which Melody runs, if you prefer). A follow-on suggestion to that would be two sliding scales of difficulty. The current one changes the fundamental game mechanics so that you either have to use one button at a time, four buttons, or four buttons AND four directions. I'd like to see a second difficulty setting that simply lets me adjust how frequently the prompts appear. Only having to press the B button doesn't help me if I have to press it 16 times in one syncopated measure.
Finally, and this is NOT a complaint but a suggestion, I would really like to see the "AutoPlay" mode be able to play more than one song consecutively. If you're going to play it up as a visualizer, why not let Melody just run her way through an entire folder?
If the timing/sync issues could be resolved, and if I could play it fullscreen, I'd probably give the game an 8/10 or 9/10 even with the insane difficulty level. It has style, the concept is simple and proven, and honestly, who doesn't like games that respond to your personal music library? As it stands, though, it gets one point for style, one point for letting me use my music library, one point for having polished visuals (or, if you want to be brutally honest, an aesthetic so simple that the visuals couldn't be anything other than polished), one point for the solid concept, and an extra point for the music thing (because I REALLY like games that let me use my music library), for a wobbly 5/10. I look forward to seeing where this game goes. I do recommend it, but I also recommend not expecting a perfect game. It's still in Early Access and I like it, but it definitely needs work.

Currently I'd only recommend the hunted game mode. Hunted is PVP, last man standing with zombies thrown in. It has a really nice dynamic that I haven't seen before, dodging player zombies leading AI hordes while hunting down other players using your phone which shows players when they are close. Hunted was worth the price of admission for me.
The other game modes (extraction, and escape) need a lot of work and aren't good in their current state unless you get a good group of players. Especially escape, since it has overly vague objectives that aren't really a whole ton of fun (scavange for a key ring for 40 minutes so you can open a door). Better indications of where to go in general on that mode would be great.
Perhaps the game's greatest weakness (which ties in with the above) is that it explains almost nothing. The only hints you get are on the loading screens, and those aren't even specific to the game mode you're loading. For example, in hunted the phone is an essential tool. It tells you when human players and player zombies are near and lets you buzz their phone so you can hear where they are. This is not explained at all outside of a minor blurb on the loading screen, and even then it doesn't tell you that you can see zombies (many new players think it's telling them where players died - but that isn't the case).
They have improved the game greatly from when I played it 8 months ago. Whether or not you could hit something was a matter of luck. Now shots register nicely on everything except moving player zombies (human players seem fine for some reason). Also melee works in all cases now except against player zombies (melee wasn't even an option before due to detection). They've also added a couple great maps in that time.
I have no idea what the plans are for the future of the game (at the moment it looks like the devs are actively working on it), but I feel I've gotten my money's worth.

This game has a more realistic approach to the zombie apocalypse than L4D. It's just you and other survivors, ordinary zombies, and limited ammo that you have to scrounge and scavenge. I've had a good bit of fun playing it, since it is fairly unique. It is worth noting, however, that it is a bit light on the content and features and perhaps a little rough around the edges, feeling more like an older game than a current title. I would recommend that you wait until it's on sale, and then at that point, by all means buy it.
Hunted mode is PVP - the last survivor standing wins! Thus, you not only have to worry about the zombies that want your brain, but also every other gun-wielding survivor. I've been in some pretty brutal firefights - plenty of tense fun, and the most popular game mode.
Escape mode is a coop puzzle mode - solve the puzzles (how do I get to <location>? where can I find a pair of bolt cutters?) and complete the objectives to escape. I recommend playing solo or with a group of people you know - I've just had better luck that way. On public servers, everyone scrambles to get the loot before it's all grabbed up, leaving zombies alive to sneak up behind everyone, getting themselves killed in their rush for loot, and not working as a cohesive team. Then, the players who are killed due to this  come back as zombies, substantially reducing the odds of survivors escaping. This mode needs to be played methodically - stick together, kill all the zombies in an area, loot, then proceed to the next area at the same time as a group. When this happens, it's pretty fun - otherwise, it's frustrating.
I found Extraction mode to be kind of frustrating. Any lack of teamwork is even more problematic than in Escape, the AI survivors are dumb as rocks, and the zombie hordes are hard to keep at bay.

Good:

Powerful item maker (although somewhat limited) allows for creation of your own weapons/vehicles
Vast amounts of resources that can be combined into other parts etc making for a rich and rewarding crafting system
Seemingly active Dev team
Neutral:
Ok voice acting, not the best but still not bad
Sometimes NPC's can be annoying or in your way other times very helpful
lack of ability to make your own armor types (in creative mode)
Adventure mode (the free roam survival) is somewhat lacking in depth
Build mode devoid of NPC's and animals
Still in Alpha
Bad:
Can be somewhat glitchy (rubberbanding NPCs, sometimes textures disappear from ground)
Adventure/Build mode procedural generation distance appears to be fairly close so lots of stuff "popping" in including the landscape
Conclusion: Excellent for an alpha/early access with lots of features implemented and working well. Shows extreme amounts of promise/potential as long as devs keep working hard at it. October 16th, 2014.
Planet Explorers is a game with great potential.  However this is how every Early access game starts out.
As of right now I can say it -IS- worth the asking price, as the game is fun regardless however I do have a few personal contretemps regarding the game.
The biggest one being it's been far too long without an update/patch.   They have plenty of communication but most games I play with early access pump off a patch a month, at least.  But rather then randomly pointing out fails and wins, I'll make a list.  Just remember, this is MY personal opinion, an opinion someone else might share.
Pros
-  Scenery is beautiful as is, though after a few patches, assuming it'll be even further improved, makes me excited to see just what amazing wonders this game can pull off.  Even the Random adventure mode is pretty nice on the eyes, day or night.
-  Although limited, I DO like where they're going with the combat system.  A little clunky, yes. But it feels less like the other generic fps crafting survival games and instead takes a 3rd person approach which makes the game feel far different. making sure not to force you into a choice between this game and one just like it.  You can easily enjoy both to the same extent without feeling like you made a redundant purchase.
- Being able to create and download blueprints for other vehicles and buildings.  I can't possibly praise this feature enough.   Not only can you duplicate something you spent hours making, but you can tweak a design others have already imagined.  To construct the masterpiece is even easier, only needing the basic materials it lists to make it.
-  Terraforming.  What turned me off about most crafting/terraforming games is the blocky or jagged earth you're left with when you take a pickaxe to the dirt.  When something looks too reticules, it takes you away from the immersion and just makes you want to get the digging over with.  Not the case with this game.  Not only does everything seems smooth and manageable but you can find yourself digging into a chasm below, falling into a dark cave, water to your waste.  Lighting a torch you would stand in awe at the amazing/beautiful situation you've found yourself.
-  My personal guilty pleasure.  I enjoy nothing more then making a defensive structure, armed to the♥♥♥♥♥♥with rocket turrets, jobbers.  Only to use a craftable item that lets you call out the most dangerous creatures to challenge your amazing armada.
CONS
-   The music in the game is dreadful.  I found myself disabling music in-game, tabbing out, opening YouTube, just to find my own adventure music to play in the background.   (this is obviously easy to counter with a quick patch)
-   Turrets shoot at the ground, walls, friends, or whatever, trying to shoot an enemy that might be behind said obstacle.  Because Turrets have limited ammo, this is bad... very bad.
-  Lacking plenty of sound effects.  this is to be expected though.  Since this is on the same topic, I have to mention that the voice acting in this game is dreadful. it honestly makes me roll my eyes out of their sockets when I actually try and grasp the storyline.
-  Lacking a worthwhile tutorial.  They are working on one now but I already know they're going to mess it up.  No one likes to sit/play through a tutorial for 15 - 20 minutes.  people like to see what they can do on their own, with the option of learning should they be stuck or inquisitive.  Making a colony for your people as an example, is needlessly complicated .  Not so much setting up a colony, but rather utilizing it.
-  Being stuck on an island small as my♥♥♥♥♥♥in adventure mode.  I just don't understand it.  I loaded multiple games to see if it was just an unlucky seed generation but no, I was doomed to be an island
Again, MY opinion.  Love it or hate it but let me know if you have anything to add because my perspective CAN be swayed.  From the bottom of my heart, I hope this game ends up being everything it was meant to be.
Update:  Nov 11.  2016.

I don't usually write reviews, but this game is a place where I think an opinion from one who plays lots of first person/third person blade games (i.e. Chivalry) might be handy. So this review is going to focus on combat mechanics rather than the overall feel (which is great by the way).
Starting off with melee weapons, I can confidently say the melee system in this game is extremely satisfying. Even for one that likes a skill curve in games. Melee weapons have that clunk to it that you don't usually see in games. When you hit a wall with an axe/hammer you'll see it get caught on the wall, similar to Chivalry. But not just walls, but the Skaven (the rat people) as well. When you hit Skaven, you'll see your axe get caught in their arm/chest/neck and it's satisfying as hell. The hit boxes in this game are extremely tight, so managing the direction and distance of your swings is nessecary. Because all the melee weapons attack with a preset combo when hitting lmb is succession, you get a predictable move set. This allows place to aim for parts of the enemy which will cause higher damage. Similar to dragging in Chivalry, you can aim your weapon's swing so that it'll hit the neck the neck only for a high chance of decapitation (ultimately a 1 hit KO) which is usually only seen consistently with the large war hammer. This is great because a skilled player could be spending potentially 50% less time on each enemy since they're taking 1 hit to kill their enemy instead of 2 (which is common with swords/rapiers).
Blocking in this game is about right. The way it works is that you have a certain amount of block points. Different enemies will take up more block points when hitting you shield/weapon. It goes without saying that shields will have more block points but sacrifices your melee weapon since you'll only be able to 1 hand the sword/axe. You can shield/weapon bash which'll knock enemies back leaving openings in swarms of enemies which you wouldn't have otherwise (similar to L4D). But these will also take up one block point. Effectively managing your blocking and bashing allows for interesting teamwork since shield users can use shield bash to attract attention onto them, then tank with the shield, while friendlies clean up the attackers.
Ranged weapons are satisfying enough to the point where nailing an enemy in the head is risky, yet rewarding. Most ranged weapons (such as pistols/bows) will take 2 hits or more to kill an enemy in the body. But in higher levels or in bigger enemies, you can aim for the head for a 1 hit KO. Althought effective, it is risky. More often than not you'll see yourself missing because of such slim hit boxes and fast enemy momvement speeds. Thus creating an especially steep skill curve with most ranged weapons. For those without real skill in aim, they can still use shotgun like weapons which help mow down multiple enemies at a time.
Now onto how stats effect gameplay. The main stats in this game are:
number of enemies that can be hit at a time
damage
speed
knockback
For the most part it's self explanatory. However it's still fun to mess with different weapons since it vastly determines the way you fight. Hammers and other blunt weapons will have lots of knock back with their charge attack and be able to hit many enemies at a time. Thus allowing for major crowd contol. However 1 handed weapons such as daggers or axes will have trouble attacking large groups of enemies because you're going to find your weapon getting stuck in enemies every hit. These stats allow for different varities of gameplay because you're going to be moving differently. When using 1 handed weapons, I find myself not bashing as much, but dodging and waiting to single out 1-2 enemies while the others are recovering. However with large weapons such as hammers, you'll find yourself charging attacks and using it to take out 6+ enemies at a time while not having to move too much. The skill curve with each weapon seems to be there, and it's fair to say each type of weapon is an experience in of itself, and can be, to some extent, mastered.
tl;dr
+Skill can increase performance in-game greatly
+Doesn't heavily rely on skill, and there are tools for everyone
+Combat is extremely satisfying and visual feedback is there to show high performance (i.e. gore)

I have only played the Prologue thus far. Entered a public lobby with random people and played as the Bright Wizard.
First Impressions:
It's Left 4 Dead with Warhammer lore.
Similarities:
Cooperative team play versus hordes of enemies. There are special enemies that can incapacitate a player requiring assistance from a team member. You can carry a medpack in the form of a potion or healing bandages. There are bombs in place of pipebombs. Instead of adrenaline shots, you have speed or strength potions. Even familiar phrases such as, "Ammo here", are intact in the form of, "Ammunition here".
Differences:
No versus mode. There are different classes with different playstyles. I have only played the Bright Wizard so far. Your hero can be equipped with different items and weapons. Each class does have a melee option and a ranged option.
Conclusion:
I think this will be a fun game to explore and play especially if you have some friends that are also picking up the game.

EDIT: The crashes and progress bugs appear to have been resolved, based on my last 5 hours of play. The host issues remain, so I still cannot change the reccommended status on this review.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This game is entertaining, but sadly suffers from numerous problems, many which just carried over from Beta without being addressed. Fatally, crashes upon launch and during play are common, with progress breaking bugs happening with frequency also. Being that you receive loot at the end of each run, this is especially irritating.
Furthermore, when the host drops, the instance is reset and all progress is lost. Why not just have another party members resume host and continue the instance? Either this or a crash has stopped me from finishing a run at least 10 times in as many hours of play, and nullified each run.
On top of this, after just 10 hours the game is already getting very repetitive. There are only 5 regular enemies to fight, with most of them just being standard melee enemies who run at you and do the same charged attack. Minor issues for me include the extremly slow acquisition of gear (subjective as to whether this is good or not), lack of weapon reloading animations (cmon just making the gun dissapear below view is not up to scratch for 2015), sloppy AI pathing and movement, and somewhat basic movesets. Most melee fighting comes down to spamming left click to hit the rats before they land their charge attack, (they are either 1 shotted or stunned, so it defeats the purpose of using other tactics in most cases) and if they pile up the occasional sweep attack or push back. The epitome here for developer laziness is the fact that you cannot turn off music or alter individual audio levels. If I want to play some music as I grind away, I have to mute the entire sound for the game. What year are we in again?
Coming from other melee games like Chivalry, or other multiplayer coop shooters like Killing Floor 2, it feels lazy, and like a major step backwards. You'll get fun out of this game, but in my opinion it's one to pick up on sale, 50% or less.

Feels like stepping back into the 90's playing this game, and not in a particularly good way. Everything this game does, Battlefield 1942 did better, and looks about the same in terms of graphics. With the hoards of FPS WWII games out there, there's nothing particularly enticing about this game.

Good game, Especially for being in beta, It looks like it has a loving community, and, at first glance, looks on par (in the FPS part) to The Acclaimed Battlefield or CoD series (at first glance I thought it was just Battlefield 1945 re-mastered) It is very good, and very intimate, each victory (in the War part of the game) effects the entire war, be it losing a major city, maybe costing your team say Berlin or Moscow, or Winning a city and maybe driving the Americans out of Mainland Europe leaving them stuck in Britain at the whim of your evil German hands... As it stands right now, the game is graphically appealing, especially for a FPS (and RTS) Veteran like myself. It is lacking in variation (you are very likely to experience every single map battle in a few hours of game time) but as most of the community is hoping for, that will be changed and fixed. At beginning you may think one team is more imbalanced than another, though it is very much at the hands of the players, as they choose who they wish to fight for in the war (While technically you can play anyone at any time, choosing an allegiance and sticking with it can level you up amazingly fast). The RTS part of the game I can't say much on as of yet, but the leveling system makes it an achievement to play the RTS part (Must be Level 12 to field assault teams, the first taste of the RTS, and level 18 to become a general and command armies). This is, shockingly the first Free to Play I have tried that isn't Pay to Win, you can level up easily by just playing the game (while paying does level you faster, and buying you goodies, you can do the same just playing). The Designers have, so far, done a very good job at keeping the game easy to play without paying a dime. Due to the way the game plays and it's affinity for Large battles, (max right now being 18 per team, with every so often all three factions, US, Germany, And Soviets right now, playing at once) the more players the better the game, so I very much recommend it. And due to its current Free to Play status, there is no reason not to just try it, a few battles, maybe leveling up a bit, and changing history!

I'm sure you play a lot of rhythm games. I'm sure you do. Many will like a way to actually feel what happens when certain parts of a song come up. Melody's Escape is just that.
Melody's Escape is like a "runner game meets Audiosurf". You take control of a girl named Melody and you need to guide her trough your own music library. Her speed adapts to the intensity of the music, from walking on calm parts, to flying when the music reaches it's peak intensity. The only limit is how many songs are in your music library.
Even while running on my low-end computer, the frame rate is amazing. Sure, you have to tweak some options, but when you do, it becomes really smooth.
The music tracking is still not perfect but hey! It's Early Access! It will get better!
Melody's Escape single-handedly made it to my favorites list in less than an hour of gameplay and I must say: I hope it becomes the perfect game.

More action, more gore and more story.
Meanwhile, we're treated to fewer masks, fewer weapons, severe level-design-problems, frustrating enemies, more pretentiousness, less overall fun and what generally seems like false advertisement:
You like the dual-wielding in the trailer? Well, only two characters can do that, they are only in select missions and they can only use two clips in each gun before they have to ditch them and switch weapons, making them unable to do the trick again for the duration of the level.
That covers the Bear character, "Mark", of the Fan faction, but what about the others?
The Zebra, "Corey", is able to "dodge roll", but not only is the action mapped to the same button as finishing moves - meaning that you're unable to do so when an enemy is downed near you - the direction seems to be basically chosen at random and the roll does not, as a matter of fact, prevent you from getting shot dead.
The Tiger, "Tony", has the same killing punches as the incarnation from the first game, but is now COMPLETELY UNABLE TO USE WEAPONS.
The Swans, "Alex and Ash", are interesting, because you play both of them - the left mouse button makes the first guy swing his chainsaw, and the right mouse button prompts the second (who will try, and sometimes fail, to follow the first) to fire his ranged weapon. When he's out of ammo, at least he can pick up discarded weapons, but I have found that making him do so can sometimes be a frustrating experience of walking over weapons several times, and he has gotten stuck going through doors - even more frustrating on levels where you are unable to exit the main building after you initally enter - meaning he will REMAIN stuck outside.
This covers the most diverse "faction", with the others consisting of fewer characters with (usually) less originality.
The Russian mob has two characters, the son of the mobster boss from the first game and his bodyguard. The new mobster boss has three different "styles", "Bodyguard" which gives him the roll of the Zebra, "Dirty Hands" which gives him the punches and weapon restriction of the Tiger and "Bloodline", which gives him "fire power", meaning he has the abilities of the Bear. The bodyguard gets nothing to choose from in his levels.
Then there's Detective Pardo and the writer Evan - possibly representing the most nonsensical end of things as well as the most original, respectively; Pardo brutally murders hordes of people and associates with the Russian mob, but walks out of crime scenes with fresh blood on his shoes using just the words "Don't shoot, I'm a detective. Here's my badge!" He also investigates inhumane murder cases by the "Miami Mutilator" (who is hinted to be himself) and grudgingly provides inside information to Evan, who wants to write a best-seller about these murders. Evan, on the other hand, is a standard, friendly guy, his only apparent flaw being that he is a workaholic neglecting his wife and kids to write his book - oh, and he also has the fighting skills of Bruce Lee. Not only does he have plenty of action sequences, himself, which he can handle for no discernable reason, but he has enough skill to handle them NON-LETHALLY. While this gameplay mechanic is interesting (melee weapons knocking enemies out instead of killing them and picking up ranged weapons simply unloading them and rendering them unusable while providing you with a boost to your score, much like finishing moves), there is no explanation OR consistency to this - you are fully capable of murdering everyone as Evan, but gain no benefit from doing so.
Then there's the fourth faction, consisting of "patriots". They (chronologically) start out deployed in Hawaii, where only a single character is playable: The Lieutenant, "James", who will later go on to become the ever-present shopkeeper from the first game. He gets a choice between several weapons (unlocked as you progress) - an assault rifle, a shotgun, a machine gun, a sniper rifle and a flamethrower. No matter which weapon you pick, it is the weapon you will use for the duration of the mission - you are unable to use the weapons of your enemies. The right mouse button, instead of dropping your weapon, simply switches back and forth between your selected weapon and a knife. Your ranged weapon has limited ammo, which can only be replenished when COMPLETELY OUT of ammo at few-and-far-between ammo crates, which the game designers saw fit to only allow you a partial ammo refill - the sniper rifle, for example, starts out with ten bullets ready to use and ten in a spare magazine - but if refilled at an ammo crate when these twenty are spent, you are given a measly FOUR bullets. Once these are spent, you will have to go back to the crate - if at all possible - and restock, reload and gain another whopping four bullets. Rinse and repeat.
The second playable character from this faction is only playable in Miami proper - he is an overweight teacher from the Lieutenant's squad, constantly raving about patriotism and doing his duty - meaning that he wants to murder as many Russian Americans as possible. He gets a choice of three different snake-masks, "Jake" (similar to the cobra-mask in the first game) making thrown items instantly kill enemies, "Iruin" starting with a nail gun - an inaccurate, but silent ranged weapon with limited ammo - and "Dallas"... which turns him into a nunchuck-swinging speedster with its "inner warrior" ability... ♥♥♥♥ knows why. While using Dallas, he is unable to use regular weapons, but his short-range punches can kill, and right-clicking causes him to start wildly swinging his nunchucks about while significantly increasing his speed for a while. The nunchuck is a regular one-hit-kill melee weapon, albeit short-ranged, and he will stop swinging it after a while to take a moment to pack it away - giving him yet another weakness. Other characters in or related to this faction - The Colonel (later Lieutenant General) whose exploits are mainly providing missions for the four-man crew while in Hawaii and apparently ripping the face off of a purple panther to wear it as a mask while he raves. Then there's Barnes and an a blonde guy who, as far as I recall, neither has a portrait shown at any time, or is mentioned by name. Only the Lieutenant and the overweight patriot are playable.
Then, finally, there's the factionless characters:
Richter, the rat-mask-wearing criminal from the first game, who is playable when he tells Evan his side of the events before AND after the first game - I would always kill him in the first game, so I don't even know how he should be alive in this one, considering we're given the choice to actually kill him. Anyway, we follow the story of the man trying his best to support himself and his very ill mother, only to ignore one too many ominous phone calls and having his car torched with further threats forcing him to take on the Rat persona.
Finally, there's "Martin Brown", the Pig-mask-killer. His small part of the story is viewed from his perspective - he appears to at least partially believe the brutal murders he's executing are part of a slasher-flick, "Midnight Animal", all the way up to his sudden, violent death.
All in all, what made Hotline Miami great is not present often in Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number.
The flexibility the masks provided you - all the different little twists it gave to the different levels - is more or less gone, providing only a shallow difference between playthroughs.
The levels are littered with enemies that ignore certain weapon types, some enemies can attack and brutally murder you through doors, the AI is horribly inconsistent - especially in terms of when enemies notice you - there is still no mechanic in place to let enemies react AT ALL to corpses of their fallen kin and the characters are just generally unlikeable - except for the Bodyguard and, possibly, Evan.
In my humble opinion, Dennaton failed big time with this one.

This is one of those games where you play it for two hours, think it's alright, and then come back to it a year later. Which is
what I did. But when I returned and got farther into the story, I have to admit that I became really impressed with the game and questioned why I left it for so long. While the main characters are very cliche, I feel that this adds to the reality that these are regular every-day people stuck on this island. Meanwhile there are very unique characters, such as Sam, Hoyt, Buck, Citra, and the
psychopath Vaas. This contrast serves to make very interesting relationships between the characters, which of course adds to the story. Now in the beginning, the game was actually pretty boring to me, hence why I left it after not feeling very captivated, but it honestly picked up quickly after that and soon I was sucked in (and on my second playthrough I really had a better appreciation for the beginning, so maybe you'd like it better than I did). Through the game, as I improved new abilities I was discovering such as paragliding, boating, racing, looting, challenges, completing bounties, capturing camps, crafting, collecting, exploring, hunting, and my all-time favorite, poker, I became more and more comfortable with the environment, to the extent of being completely satisfied with everything the game offers. But legit guys, the poker in this game is pretty immersive. Besides all of that though, I enjoy the soundtrack and especially the game's main theme (though Make It Bun' Dem is definitely up there). The moods of each song echo the feeling of the game in that moment or mission, and I can really appreciate that in all games. Now onto general gameplay, it's solid. I don't see any problems with the fps aspects, and I find driving extremely fun with the realism of it, having your camera angle in a place that makes it feel as if you are actually driving (it's more on the side and not centered). And while events in the game may not always be realistic, specific story elements are always there to back it up, with the plot constantly improving as the game progresses (though there
a point where it slows down a bit, but it's a spoiler so I can't say~).
All in all, I definitely recommend this game. It has to be one of my favorites, and I'm still going back to it every now and then just to hunt, drive, and kick Tyrone's♥♥♥♥♥in poker.

I have found this game incredibly fun and fulfilling, even with the more limited content available. The slightly slower pacing compared to a run-n-gun zombie shoot-em-up is refreshing as you have to actually scavenge for your ammo and supplies and, especially on harder modes, conserve as much as you can.
If you like cooperative play like I do, the escape and extraction modes are fun, especially if you find a good group of people. In escape, you have to navigate a level with some objectives and obstacles that rotate through a couple different scenarios, and in extraction you locate NPC survivors, hold out for a time against hordes, and then escort them to a drop off point. As with any online game, you will probably get in several games with people that aren't as cooperative or skilled, but when you have a good team it's very fun.
If you favor competitive play, there's always hunted and panic modes. Hunted is your basic pvp, where players killed become zombies and when there's two left, all NPC zombies charge at the two remaining players. In Panic, one player begins the game infected but may not know it for a few minutes, and the only zombies in the level are the player zombies, while the first player zombie respawns as a SWAT zombie. Human players have to kill the zombies a certain number of times, or survive for like 20-30 minutes to win.
All in all, I got the game on sale for $5, and I would say it's the best 5 I've spent in a long time. Yes, some graphics aren't as up-to-date and some animations can be wonky, but it's not distracting to me at all. I would recommend this game even at the 20 price if you think this sort of thing appeals to you.

More action, more gore and more story.
Meanwhile, we're treated to fewer masks, fewer weapons, severe level-design-problems, frustrating enemies, more pretentiousness, less overall fun and what generally seems like false advertisement:
You like the dual-wielding in the trailer? Well, only two characters can do that, they are only in select missions and they can only use two clips in each gun before they have to ditch them and switch weapons, making them unable to do the trick again for the duration of the level.
That covers the Bear character, "Mark", of the Fan faction, but what about the others?
The Zebra, "Corey", is able to "dodge roll", but not only is the action mapped to the same button as finishing moves - meaning that you're unable to do so when an enemy is downed near you - the direction seems to be basically chosen at random and the roll does not, as a matter of fact, prevent you from getting shot dead.
The Tiger, "Tony", has the same killing punches as the incarnation from the first game, but is now COMPLETELY UNABLE TO USE WEAPONS.
The Swans, "Alex and Ash", are interesting, because you play both of them - the left mouse button makes the first guy swing his chainsaw, and the right mouse button prompts the second (who will try, and sometimes fail, to follow the first) to fire his ranged weapon. When he's out of ammo, at least he can pick up discarded weapons, but I have found that making him do so can sometimes be a frustrating experience of walking over weapons several times, and he has gotten stuck going through doors - even more frustrating on levels where you are unable to exit the main building after you initally enter - meaning he will REMAIN stuck outside.
This covers the most diverse "faction", with the others consisting of fewer characters with (usually) less originality.
The Russian mob has two characters, the son of the mobster boss from the first game and his bodyguard. The new mobster boss has three different "styles", "Bodyguard" which gives him the roll of the Zebra, "Dirty Hands" which gives him the punches and weapon restriction of the Tiger and "Bloodline", which gives him "fire power", meaning he has the abilities of the Bear. The bodyguard gets nothing to choose from in his levels.
Then there's Detective Pardo and the writer Evan - possibly representing the most nonsensical end of things as well as the most original, respectively; Pardo brutally murders hordes of people and associates with the Russian mob, but walks out of crime scenes with fresh blood on his shoes using just the words "Don't shoot, I'm a detective. Here's my badge!" He also investigates inhumane murder cases by the "Miami Mutilator" (who is hinted to be himself) and grudgingly provides inside information to Evan, who wants to write a best-seller about these murders. Evan, on the other hand, is a standard, friendly guy, his only apparent flaw being that he is a workaholic neglecting his wife and kids to write his book - oh, and he also has the fighting skills of Bruce Lee. Not only does he have plenty of action sequences, himself, which he can handle for no discernable reason, but he has enough skill to handle them NON-LETHALLY. While this gameplay mechanic is interesting (melee weapons knocking enemies out instead of killing them and picking up ranged weapons simply unloading them and rendering them unusable while providing you with a boost to your score, much like finishing moves), there is no explanation OR consistency to this - you are fully capable of murdering everyone as Evan, but gain no benefit from doing so.
Then there's the fourth faction, consisting of "patriots". They (chronologically) start out deployed in Hawaii, where only a single character is playable: The Lieutenant, "James", who will later go on to become the ever-present shopkeeper from the first game. He gets a choice between several weapons (unlocked as you progress) - an assault rifle, a shotgun, a machine gun, a sniper rifle and a flamethrower. No matter which weapon you pick, it is the weapon you will use for the duration of the mission - you are unable to use the weapons of your enemies. The right mouse button, instead of dropping your weapon, simply switches back and forth between your selected weapon and a knife. Your ranged weapon has limited ammo, which can only be replenished when COMPLETELY OUT of ammo at few-and-far-between ammo crates, which the game designers saw fit to only allow you a partial ammo refill - the sniper rifle, for example, starts out with ten bullets ready to use and ten in a spare magazine - but if refilled at an ammo crate when these twenty are spent, you are given a measly FOUR bullets. Once these are spent, you will have to go back to the crate - if at all possible - and restock, reload and gain another whopping four bullets. Rinse and repeat.
The second playable character from this faction is only playable in Miami proper - he is an overweight teacher from the Lieutenant's squad, constantly raving about patriotism and doing his duty - meaning that he wants to murder as many Russian Americans as possible. He gets a choice of three different snake-masks, "Jake" (similar to the cobra-mask in the first game) making thrown items instantly kill enemies, "Iruin" starting with a nail gun - an inaccurate, but silent ranged weapon with limited ammo - and "Dallas"... which turns him into a nunchuck-swinging speedster with its "inner warrior" ability... ♥♥♥♥ knows why. While using Dallas, he is unable to use regular weapons, but his short-range punches can kill, and right-clicking causes him to start wildly swinging his nunchucks about while significantly increasing his speed for a while. The nunchuck is a regular one-hit-kill melee weapon, albeit short-ranged, and he will stop swinging it after a while to take a moment to pack it away - giving him yet another weakness. Other characters in or related to this faction - The Colonel (later Lieutenant General) whose exploits are mainly providing missions for the four-man crew while in Hawaii and apparently ripping the face off of a purple panther to wear it as a mask while he raves. Then there's Barnes and an a blonde guy who, as far as I recall, neither has a portrait shown at any time, or is mentioned by name. Only the Lieutenant and the overweight patriot are playable.
Then, finally, there's the factionless characters:
Richter, the rat-mask-wearing criminal from the first game, who is playable when he tells Evan his side of the events before AND after the first game - I would always kill him in the first game, so I don't even know how he should be alive in this one, considering we're given the choice to actually kill him. Anyway, we follow the story of the man trying his best to support himself and his very ill mother, only to ignore one too many ominous phone calls and having his car torched with further threats forcing him to take on the Rat persona.
Finally, there's "Martin Brown", the Pig-mask-killer. His small part of the story is viewed from his perspective - he appears to at least partially believe the brutal murders he's executing are part of a slasher-flick, "Midnight Animal", all the way up to his sudden, violent death.
All in all, what made Hotline Miami great is not present often in Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number.
The flexibility the masks provided you - all the different little twists it gave to the different levels - is more or less gone, providing only a shallow difference between playthroughs.
The levels are littered with enemies that ignore certain weapon types, some enemies can attack and brutally murder you through doors, the AI is horribly inconsistent - especially in terms of when enemies notice you - there is still no mechanic in place to let enemies react AT ALL to corpses of their fallen kin and the characters are just generally unlikeable - except for the Bodyguard and, possibly, Evan.
In my humble opinion, Dennaton failed big time with this one.

The original Hotline Miami was like a puzzle game, and the puzzle was working out how you were going to burst into a room and murder everything within the next three seconds.
Hotline Miami 2 is also like a puzzle game, but it's a memory puzzle, where you have to die constantly, and remember on your next play the direction each gunshot came from; because Hotline Miami 2 is a top down sniper duel where you can't see the other participants; the levels are huge, and you're going to be shot by a lot of enemies from three screens away;  Your finger is going to be constantly on the look button, and even that's not going to be nearly enough to see where the shots are coming from. Hotline Miami 2 actively encourages a lot of cheesy gameplay; blindly firing at people you can't see, and aggroing enemies and hiding round corners for them to come to you.
This game is a great expansion on the first in nearly every other way, the art direction and music are great. I actually like having the mask choices rebalanced and restricted; but the major problem is that the level design is very poor in this sequel; and redesigning the entire game is something that's not going to be fixed by a patch.
If you've never played Hotline Miami before, get the first game. If you played the first and really, really want some more, get this, but don't expect it to be as polished as the first. It's like they didn't understand what made the first game good.

Note: Summary at the bottom of the review.
Your colony ship just hit something in orbit, just as you arrived at your destination. Your lifeboat pod has crashed down, and the only other human occupant is injured and need medical attention. You have no weapons, barely any food, and your only tool is a simple knife. Welcome to Planet Explorers.
Luckily, the above is not a huge problem, because this game lets you craft all of the above, and not just craft it, you can actually build your own guns and transport, chosing exactly how they should look by adding base parts (a gun has to have at least one muzzle and a grip) and then building the shape of your gun piece by piece from there.
This is an Alpha game, and like all games still in early access, that means that things are not optimized. You will experience lag. You will find bugs (both the kind that tries to eat you, and the kind that just annoys you). And the grass...is awful. I recommend turning it off. Look beyond that though, and you find an exellent sandbox game that gives you a lot of freedom as to how you play and what you do. It is, even in its current "rough" state, a better game than many similar games that are considered a finished product. In short, it is a FUN game, that hopefully has a bright future!
Pro:
*A huge sandbox game with deformable terrain.
*A very good (if a bit complex) crafting system.
*An interesting setting.
Con (these may be fixed before launch):
*The grass is simply awful, but can be turned off.
*Lag is not uncommon, especially if you've built a lot.
*Still needs polish and optimization.
Summary:
If you are in the market for a 3D survival Sci-Fi Sandbox game, this is a solid choice that shows a lot of promise, even in its current unfinished state. If the developers sticks to it, this could easily become THE survival sandbox game to play. Even "as is" there is a lot to explore and do, and you'll likely have fun doing it! 6/10 -Recommended.

This is the best co-op game I have played in a long time. If you're a fan of Left 4 Dead, you'll probably like this game. It's pretty much L4D, but with a heavier emphasis on melee as opposed to ranged weapons. The focus on melee combat as opposed to ranged can be a bit tough since you actually have to manage your ammo (unless you're a Bright Mage, then you manage your heat) and there are other mechanics not present in L4D. You can guard, push enemies away, and dodge. There is also a charged melee attack you can use and vary depending on the weapon type. Some charged attacks are very effective in dealing with armored enemies while others are very useful in pushing back hordes of enemies. Mastering these mechanics are essential in doing well at higher difficulties.
There are currently five different heroes with their own strengths and weaknesses as well as varied playstyles depending on the weapons you equip. There is a loot system in which there is a dice roll at the end of each mission to determine which piece of equipment you'll obtain. In each level, there are 3 tomes and 2 grimoires hidden somewhere on the map (the locations of these items never change). Each tome adds another die while the grimoires add a guaranteed success die. Though, tomes take up a healing slot (you can drop the tome and pick it back up to heal) while grimoires take up a potion slot (you cannot drop the grimoire to pick up a potion, doing so makes you lose the grimoire) and reduce the party's maximum life by 25% per grimoire. There will be times where you'll know where both grimoires are, but may elect to not pick one or both up due to how difficult the level is. The loot system isn't perfect though since items you roll at the end of each mission is random and might not even be relevant for the hero you are currently playing. However, personally I can look past those flaws since the game itself is very fun, especially with friends.
Don't take this game lightly. This game is difficult, especially when playing with random people since you are likely to have little to no coordination. Coordination with your team is very important if you want to successfully finish a mission. One thing to note is that VOIP communication is off by default so you may want to turn that on if you want to communicate with your team better. Sticking together as a group is key since you need to watch each other's back. You know how in L4D2, sometimes you have situations where there is a spitter, smoker, and hunter about all at the same time? This game does that too, but to a higher degree in that multiple of the same type of special rat can spawn at the same time. On difficulties higher than "Hard", there is friendly fire for ranged weapons. For those starting out, I would recommend starting off on easy or normal just to get a feel for the game. Understanding the mechanics and using them well are key in succeeding in "Hard" and higher difficulties. There is nothing wrong with playing on "Easy" in order to figure out and master the game's mechanics, memorize the locations of all the tomes and grimoires, and know where the good chokepoint areas are for hordes. In fact, it's encouraged to do so because wiping at any point in a mission causes you to fail entirely, losing all progress, and forcing you to start over from the very beginning should you opt to try again.

Zombies done right! This isn't too different from the other FPS Zombie shooters that you'll find out there. There are zombies and non-zombies, commonly referred to as humans. Humans have guns, and zombies have hands and teeth (and sometimes body armour found on riot squad police). There are numerous modes of gameplay with no real story line, offering any gamer the ability to jump right in and just shoot decaying bodies in the head. My favourite 'perk' about the game though is you don't have to worry about dying too much. No longer do you have to be upset about dying and losing your place among the survivors, because now you get to have your time to shine as a zombie! Take control of one of the mindless, scream out of your decaying lungs and summon other A.I. zombies to follow you as you hunt down your friends and make them lose as well!

Contagion, the game I love the most.
This is my review on a little game called Contagion.  It's had alot of work put into it and I find it to be my faviorite game. It may not be the game I give a reword on for being greatly put together, but it sure has become adictive.
TO A PERSPECTIVE(NOT IMPORTANT)
Contagion is one of those games that you'll meet intresting people on. Mostly people from diffrent contrys who don't know what your saying like Gemens and "Vikings" but people all the less. Contagion was released in the time of zombie games, and was one of the most inhabited by diffrent races looking for a good goul game to play.  I started playing when my brother bought me the game when on sale. I found myself trapped in a dark place the first time I played it. Surrounded by people saying things like (UNCIARR) and (TOLLA CARBIAC TUE?) I was realy confused. Then one day I found myself a translator, someone speaking both english, spanish, and german! He guided me through the small frazes that they used and most important tought me how to survive the harsh world full of sludge monsters that ooze blood when you shoot them. I was and still am young at the "video gaming experience" so at every sight of one of the monsters I felt myself fill with cold shivers. But then when I learned the game everything came to a stop, than rewinded and made me what I think is a "pro player" and am now playing this game more than any other. Anyway on to my review.
GAMEPLAY
Contagion fits into a catigory of a "Team Work Game" meaning you usualy in most of Contagions gamemodes need to work together. It has a survival of the team and not a survival of the fitest feel at most times, and is enjoyable with friends. They have fixed most glitches from the first time I played and it feels to run nicely. It has a fair amount of gamemodes with their own original touch to them. New maps would be great, as their are not that many courently in the game.
PROBLEMS/GLITCHES
This game seems to have grown from the first time I played it in that it does'nt seem to have many glitches. Yes, ocasionaly you will find a zombie stuck in the stairs or a zombie to be walking on water like it was Jesus, but overal I havent seen many at all in the last few hours I've played.
COMBATE
The combate in this game is dull, it seems to lack what its potentual leads on to seem in that its worse than it seems. Trying to melee a zombie easily is imposible, but it does make up for this with its smart takedowns ability. The weapons are great and fairly acurate to what it would seem like when firing in other first person shooters. At times the zombies melee is a bit to fast for the player and thier speed is a bit to out of hand, but besides that it seems "ok".
ABILITY/LIMITS
The graphics are quite decent for a game like this, and then running first person view animation is fantastic.
REPLAYABILITY
Its diffrent gamemodes alow it to be played many times, and since its all different depending on what kind of team you get or what kind of weapons you find, it gives it lots of replayability. No glitches rune it making it very playable, and in the next year I could find myself dropping time like a bomb on this one game.
ONLINE
The servers can be played on very easily and even with bad internet you can still play it quite well. The other players on it seem to be very kind and acceptable, especialy considering you don't know what they are saying most of the time with thier strange little accents.
REVIEW
I gave this game 88.9/100 on this game because of its replayability and online formate.

This game gets zombies right.

The infection mechanic is what really makes this game stand out; anytime a zombie attacks you, your character has a chance to become infected. Shortly after your character becomes infected your screen will gradually turn gray and your audio will become distorted until your become a zombie. This creates an atmosphere where your afraid of zombies and you can't just wade through them carelessly taking damage. Before playing this game I had always assumed that a mechanic like this wouldn't work because I wouldn't want to turn on my former teammates. This, however, was not the case and now turning into a zombie is one of the funnest moments in a match for me. As a player zombie you can deliberately infect survivors by biting them from behind, you can control groups of up to 15 npc zombies and you have far more mobility than a survivor. All these things allow the player zombie to create ambushes and attempt to make a victory out of the defeat of being killed as a survivor.

Pros: Very tactical. Feels like the zombie apocalypse, with that atmosphere, the ability to board up entrances, infection, and a mode that allows humans to fight each other over resources. Tense, addictive. Challenging, so satisfying, hard won victories. Escape Mode plays like a proper single-player survival horror, but with co-op, and player zombies: look for the way to proceed, find objective items like fire extinguishers and keys, etc. Allows players fighting each other as Humans, zombies. Varied, dynamic modes. Randomized objectives means you can't predict quite where to go, or what to do, even after playing levels many times. Solid co-op, with 2-16 players. Good alternative to Left 4 Dead, which it is a clone of.
Cons: Some awkward elements, such as glitches and bugs. Exploits that some players abuse. Players that are zombies are not quite equal to 'human' players, the way it is in, say, Aliens vs Predator. Too little content. Not as refined as Left 4 Dead. No "easy" way to play, and steep learning curve, and rarely winning does get frustrating.
My recommendation: Get this if you want an alternative to Left 4 Dead that is not streamlined, and even more realistic and dynamic.

I highly recommend this game. It's quite annoying at times, but the building possibilities and systems for building allow for endlass expansion and imagination, higher than that of Minecraft. While Minecraft is a rather frowned upon game, you can't help but to admit the possibilities of that game, as it is a very profitable sandbox. Planet Explorers is not like Minecraft in any other way than the limitless life span that the game can provide. You are able to make your own custom shield, sword or even rifle. Adventure, story and a mode similar to creative.

You also start of with quite a few revival shots, which are require to get up out on the battlefield to continue the fight. If you run out, don't worry. You will just spawn back at the colony.

In Creative mode, it is as the title suggests. You travel the planet sculpting and constructing upon it to your hearts desire with no fear of losing it to those wretched aliens. The possibilities are endless in Planet Explorers.

More action, more gore and more story.
Meanwhile, we're treated to fewer masks, fewer weapons, severe level-design-problems, frustrating enemies, more pretentiousness, less overall fun and what generally seems like false advertisement:
You like the dual-wielding in the trailer? Well, only two characters can do that, they are only in select missions and they can only use two clips in each gun before they have to ditch them and switch weapons, making them unable to do the trick again for the duration of the level.
That covers the Bear character, "Mark", of the Fan faction, but what about the others?
The Zebra, "Corey", is able to "dodge roll", but not only is the action mapped to the same button as finishing moves - meaning that you're unable to do so when an enemy is downed near you - the direction seems to be basically chosen at random and the roll does not, as a matter of fact, prevent you from getting shot dead.
The Tiger, "Tony", has the same killing punches as the incarnation from the first game, but is now COMPLETELY UNABLE TO USE WEAPONS.
The Swans, "Alex and Ash", are interesting, because you play both of them - the left mouse button makes the first guy swing his chainsaw, and the right mouse button prompts the second (who will try, and sometimes fail, to follow the first) to fire his ranged weapon. When he's out of ammo, at least he can pick up discarded weapons, but I have found that making him do so can sometimes be a frustrating experience of walking over weapons several times, and he has gotten stuck going through doors - even more frustrating on levels where you are unable to exit the main building after you initally enter - meaning he will REMAIN stuck outside.
This covers the most diverse "faction", with the others consisting of fewer characters with (usually) less originality.
The Russian mob has two characters, the son of the mobster boss from the first game and his bodyguard. The new mobster boss has three different "styles", "Bodyguard" which gives him the roll of the Zebra, "Dirty Hands" which gives him the punches and weapon restriction of the Tiger and "Bloodline", which gives him "fire power", meaning he has the abilities of the Bear. The bodyguard gets nothing to choose from in his levels.
Then there's Detective Pardo and the writer Evan - possibly representing the most nonsensical end of things as well as the most original, respectively; Pardo brutally murders hordes of people and associates with the Russian mob, but walks out of crime scenes with fresh blood on his shoes using just the words "Don't shoot, I'm a detective. Here's my badge!" He also investigates inhumane murder cases by the "Miami Mutilator" (who is hinted to be himself) and grudgingly provides inside information to Evan, who wants to write a best-seller about these murders. Evan, on the other hand, is a standard, friendly guy, his only apparent flaw being that he is a workaholic neglecting his wife and kids to write his book - oh, and he also has the fighting skills of Bruce Lee. Not only does he have plenty of action sequences, himself, which he can handle for no discernable reason, but he has enough skill to handle them NON-LETHALLY. While this gameplay mechanic is interesting (melee weapons knocking enemies out instead of killing them and picking up ranged weapons simply unloading them and rendering them unusable while providing you with a boost to your score, much like finishing moves), there is no explanation OR consistency to this - you are fully capable of murdering everyone as Evan, but gain no benefit from doing so.
Then there's the fourth faction, consisting of "patriots". They (chronologically) start out deployed in Hawaii, where only a single character is playable: The Lieutenant, "James", who will later go on to become the ever-present shopkeeper from the first game. He gets a choice between several weapons (unlocked as you progress) - an assault rifle, a shotgun, a machine gun, a sniper rifle and a flamethrower. No matter which weapon you pick, it is the weapon you will use for the duration of the mission - you are unable to use the weapons of your enemies. The right mouse button, instead of dropping your weapon, simply switches back and forth between your selected weapon and a knife. Your ranged weapon has limited ammo, which can only be replenished when COMPLETELY OUT of ammo at few-and-far-between ammo crates, which the game designers saw fit to only allow you a partial ammo refill - the sniper rifle, for example, starts out with ten bullets ready to use and ten in a spare magazine - but if refilled at an ammo crate when these twenty are spent, you are given a measly FOUR bullets. Once these are spent, you will have to go back to the crate - if at all possible - and restock, reload and gain another whopping four bullets. Rinse and repeat.
The second playable character from this faction is only playable in Miami proper - he is an overweight teacher from the Lieutenant's squad, constantly raving about patriotism and doing his duty - meaning that he wants to murder as many Russian Americans as possible. He gets a choice of three different snake-masks, "Jake" (similar to the cobra-mask in the first game) making thrown items instantly kill enemies, "Iruin" starting with a nail gun - an inaccurate, but silent ranged weapon with limited ammo - and "Dallas"... which turns him into a nunchuck-swinging speedster with its "inner warrior" ability... ♥♥♥♥ knows why. While using Dallas, he is unable to use regular weapons, but his short-range punches can kill, and right-clicking causes him to start wildly swinging his nunchucks about while significantly increasing his speed for a while. The nunchuck is a regular one-hit-kill melee weapon, albeit short-ranged, and he will stop swinging it after a while to take a moment to pack it away - giving him yet another weakness. Other characters in or related to this faction - The Colonel (later Lieutenant General) whose exploits are mainly providing missions for the four-man crew while in Hawaii and apparently ripping the face off of a purple panther to wear it as a mask while he raves. Then there's Barnes and an a blonde guy who, as far as I recall, neither has a portrait shown at any time, or is mentioned by name. Only the Lieutenant and the overweight patriot are playable.
Then, finally, there's the factionless characters:
Richter, the rat-mask-wearing criminal from the first game, who is playable when he tells Evan his side of the events before AND after the first game - I would always kill him in the first game, so I don't even know how he should be alive in this one, considering we're given the choice to actually kill him. Anyway, we follow the story of the man trying his best to support himself and his very ill mother, only to ignore one too many ominous phone calls and having his car torched with further threats forcing him to take on the Rat persona.
Finally, there's "Martin Brown", the Pig-mask-killer. His small part of the story is viewed from his perspective - he appears to at least partially believe the brutal murders he's executing are part of a slasher-flick, "Midnight Animal", all the way up to his sudden, violent death.
All in all, what made Hotline Miami great is not present often in Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number.
The flexibility the masks provided you - all the different little twists it gave to the different levels - is more or less gone, providing only a shallow difference between playthroughs.
The levels are littered with enemies that ignore certain weapon types, some enemies can attack and brutally murder you through doors, the AI is horribly inconsistent - especially in terms of when enemies notice you - there is still no mechanic in place to let enemies react AT ALL to corpses of their fallen kin and the characters are just generally unlikeable - except for the Bodyguard and, possibly, Evan.
In my humble opinion, Dennaton failed big time with this one.

The original Hotline Miami was like a puzzle game, and the puzzle was working out how you were going to burst into a room and murder everything within the next three seconds.
Hotline Miami 2 is also like a puzzle game, but it's a memory puzzle, where you have to die constantly, and remember on your next play the direction each gunshot came from; because Hotline Miami 2 is a top down sniper duel where you can't see the other participants; the levels are huge, and you're going to be shot by a lot of enemies from three screens away;  Your finger is going to be constantly on the look button, and even that's not going to be nearly enough to see where the shots are coming from. Hotline Miami 2 actively encourages a lot of cheesy gameplay; blindly firing at people you can't see, and aggroing enemies and hiding round corners for them to come to you.
This game is a great expansion on the first in nearly every other way, the art direction and music are great. I actually like having the mask choices rebalanced and restricted; but the major problem is that the level design is very poor in this sequel; and redesigning the entire game is something that's not going to be fixed by a patch.
If you've never played Hotline Miami before, get the first game. If you played the first and really, really want some more, get this, but don't expect it to be as polished as the first. It's like they didn't understand what made the first game good.

Melody's Escape is a pretty game, with clean and simple visuals that utilise colour instead of detail to create its aesthetic. The game lets your music be the driving force and doesn't seek to fill the screen with crap and distract you. All of the rhythm games I have played, it is probably the one I like the look of the most. The style of the game, however, comes at a cost, as the visuals are horizontally based meaning that your eyes have to keep track of colours and shapes moving across the screen at often quite high speeds. This movement will cause blur and will quickly tire out your eyes and, if you are like me and are light sensitive or are prone to headaches, the may be game very unpleasant to play for anything but a short amount of time.
The audio detection is hit and miss. Sometimes it works really well and sometimes it completely fails and leaves you trying to keep up with an entirely different beat to the song you are listening too. All rhythm games that utilise the user's music are like this to a certain extent but Melody's Escape seems to keep to these extremes a lot more than other games, meaning it is likely that you will just have to keep a list of what songs you have that work and don't work. This is especially true due to the fact that the game isn't predictable at all: I've had acoustic, vocal-dominated songs work perfectly and electronic dance music with a very clear and repetitive beat fail.
The gameplay is fun and addictive and, providing the game doesn't induce a migraine, can easily be played for long sessions. Best of all, the game has a good variety of difficulty levels allowing for varied gameplay.
Another, albeit small, negative that I should mention is a lack of compatibility with non-Latin script. It recognises Hiragana/Katakana and a certain amount of Chinese characters, usually this is enough for you to be able to find the right song but it is annoying for have half the title or artist's name displayed  in blocks. I haven't got a lot of Korean music but it is possible that it doesn't recognise Korean characters at all, as all my Korean music  is displayed in blocks.

This game is without a doubt one of the greatest games created for PC. It gives the player complete control of his destiny, there is no main quest, you do not start as some great hero that must save the world. You create a backstory for you character that ranges from a simple peasant to the son of a powerless noble. You have a small introduction quest that will show you the basics of how to move about the world and recruit men to your cause, then it leaves you alone. There is no giant marker on the map that tells you what to do, it simply leaves you to do as you wish.
Now once you finish your little intro quest (which technically you dont have to finish but i recommend you do as it gives you some money to start off with) You then can do anything you please. Want to become a raider and destroy villages and pillage the riches? Go ahead. Want to become a rebel and help a claimant take the throne of a tyrant? Do it. Or perhaps you want to rule these lands in your own name, go right ahead.
Now on to the mods for this game, the mods are absolutely astounding. Each mod can change every single aspect of the game. Most are complete overhauls to the game which may take you anywhere from, Middle Earth to feudal Japan. Each mod is a completely new experience with brand new maps, items, people, races, one even adds in magic to the game. Not even skyrims mods can compare to the quality of these mods. Never have mods seemed so well done. Each one feels like a DLC made by the devs themselves. My personal favorites is Phantasy Calradia which adds in tons of fantasy aspects to the games such as magic, orcs dwarves elfs ect. It really completely changes the game. I would also recommend using the sub mod *Diplomacy* on your first playthrough of the game as it adds lots of new features to the vanilla game that feel like they should have been there in the first place. Its on the workshop and only take a few seconds to download.
I cannot recommend this game more.

Easily one of the best team combat games I've ever played.  This game's single player takes the free campaigns from Star Wars Battlefront II to a whole new level, the combat as well.  This game is so unique and so amazingly open and one in which you can set your own limits and really rewards you the higher you go.  The difficulty is so customizable that any level of player would be able to enjoy this game for a long time
Now, the mods.  The mods are where this game truly shines.  Not to say that the vanilla game isn't amazing, but the mods can take this game, a diamond in the rough that really shows the limitations of it not being a big-name developer, and makes it shine.  The mods act like sequels, adding features and new locations and new items, new units and new quests, new characters, and new worlds even.  The mods for this game are as amazing in Mount & Blade as they are in the major Paradox-developed games.
The game is very easy to get into and very easy, as I said before, to build up the difficulty to your personal taste.  The game also allows you to choose different routes.  You could choose to be an honorable and chivalrous lord, helping the peasants and cleansing the crime-ridden realm like an exterminator to rats.  You could choose to be a bandit leader, slaughtering the innocent and burning their homes taking for yourself their valuables.  You could choose to be a trader, leading a caravan from town to town, maneuvering through mine fields of banditry and hostility.  You could be a mercenary captain, a king, the options really are diverse.
The versatility and the lack of structure gives this game an extreme level of replayability.  I've been playing this game regularly on and off since the release of the first Mount and Blade back in 2008.  I fell in love the day I discovered it and that love has done nothing but grow.
I haven't played too much multiplayer due to constraints on my end but from what I've had of it it is fun and very challenging.  There are some very good players out there, taking you from slaughterer in the single player to swine in the multiplayer.  I think that could go for most any game though.
Over all, this game is an 8.5/10 for me, 10/10 with mods.  I'm a pretty strict grader too I like to think.  If you liked Star Wars Battlefront, I would absolutely recommend this game.  Even if you didn't, it is still worth a shot.  Warband polishes up and adds a lot of features to the old Mount & blade and also has a much stronger mod community due to cumulation over time.  If you're going to spend your money on mount & blade, go with Warband.  They recently ported the TLD (Lord of the RIngs) mod to Warband, making the original kind of pointless.
Sufficed to say, I am looking forward to the Banner Lords sequel.

This is the best co-op game I have played in a long time. If you're a fan of Left 4 Dead, you'll probably like this game. It's pretty much L4D, but with a heavier emphasis on melee as opposed to ranged weapons. The focus on melee combat as opposed to ranged can be a bit tough since you actually have to manage your ammo (unless you're a Bright Mage, then you manage your heat) and there are other mechanics not present in L4D. You can guard, push enemies away, and dodge. There is also a charged melee attack you can use and vary depending on the weapon type. Some charged attacks are very effective in dealing with armored enemies while others are very useful in pushing back hordes of enemies. Mastering these mechanics are essential in doing well at higher difficulties.
There are currently five different heroes with their own strengths and weaknesses as well as varied playstyles depending on the weapons you equip. There is a loot system in which there is a dice roll at the end of each mission to determine which piece of equipment you'll obtain. In each level, there are 3 tomes and 2 grimoires hidden somewhere on the map (the locations of these items never change). Each tome adds another die while the grimoires add a guaranteed success die. Though, tomes take up a healing slot (you can drop the tome and pick it back up to heal) while grimoires take up a potion slot (you cannot drop the grimoire to pick up a potion, doing so makes you lose the grimoire) and reduce the party's maximum life by 25% per grimoire. There will be times where you'll know where both grimoires are, but may elect to not pick one or both up due to how difficult the level is. The loot system isn't perfect though since items you roll at the end of each mission is random and might not even be relevant for the hero you are currently playing. However, personally I can look past those flaws since the game itself is very fun, especially with friends.
Don't take this game lightly. This game is difficult, especially when playing with random people since you are likely to have little to no coordination. Coordination with your team is very important if you want to successfully finish a mission. One thing to note is that VOIP communication is off by default so you may want to turn that on if you want to communicate with your team better. Sticking together as a group is key since you need to watch each other's back. You know how in L4D2, sometimes you have situations where there is a spitter, smoker, and hunter about all at the same time? This game does that too, but to a higher degree in that multiple of the same type of special rat can spawn at the same time. On difficulties higher than "Hard", there is friendly fire for ranged weapons. For those starting out, I would recommend starting off on easy or normal just to get a feel for the game. Understanding the mechanics and using them well are key in succeeding in "Hard" and higher difficulties. There is nothing wrong with playing on "Easy" in order to figure out and master the game's mechanics, memorize the locations of all the tomes and grimoires, and know where the good chokepoint areas are for hordes. In fact, it's encouraged to do so because wiping at any point in a mission causes you to fail entirely, losing all progress, and forcing you to start over from the very beginning should you opt to try again.
