I blew through normal mode today, so time to write a review I guess.
If you've come here after playing Hotline 1, you want to know how it holds up on two fronts.
Combat is still visceral and fun, although I found myself missing the level design from the first game. It feels more restricted, although that's likely due in part to the character system present here. While the personalities do add to the story, I feel like the mask system from 1 worked better. I can see why they didn't use it though-so moving on.
The story in Wrong Number left me cold. The characters all work, and as a writer I can't argue against them. There will be some spoilers from here in-minor ones that you'll probably see coming anyhow. If you don't want any spoilers at all, please skip down to "CONCLUSIONS."
Ready?
I didn't feel that I had enough time to really grow to like (too strong a word for most of the sociopaths) the characters before their untimely deaths. While the structure works-flipping between characters to get the big picture-the ending didn't really leave it open to interpretation like 1 did, which I felt was a defining moment for the first game, as we were given reasons to "like" each character making it hard to internally decide who survived the events of 50 blessings.
HOWEVER
Having done some minor research and putting a lot of thought into it, the entire game is an interpretation.
Super spoilers ahead guys. You may want to skip ahead to the conclusion down there.
In Hotline Miami, Jacket ends up following a false lead from the 50 Blessings group, which lead him to his attack on the Mafia tower. This takes him to the wrong address and is why Richard said Jacket would never find the answers he wanted. Only Biker's path-where Jacket dies-takes a good turn, where he finds and unmasks 50 Blessings for what is really is with the puzzle pieces. This takes him to the other side of town, and a different address. The "Right" number.
Still, the ending of this game sort of whacked me-it definitively shows Jacket's death. As a generally pro-Jacket guy, this means that no matter which ending of Hotline 1 you preferred, Jacket is still dead. More's the pity for me, although I think we can all agree it was bound to happen eventually. Just not like this.
CONCLUSIONS
I blasted through normal in six hours or so, and despite not enjoying it overall as much as I did with the original, I still had a blast and a half. Hotline fans, rejoice, for the sequel is indeed good. Just prepare to be crushed a few times over the course of the story.
Oh, and there's an unlockable hard mode which does add to the story-and it lives up to the name. You can't go wrong with this game if you liked the first.

This game is actually pretty damn good for an indie game in Early Access, no less. I just have to give credit where credit is due here.
When I first picked up this game, I expected it to be another half-decent "play to your own music" game that's being put on the Steam category, so as a music addict, I had to buy it and see what this game was capable of. When I picked out my first track and as soon as the game finished calculating the audio, the gameplay itself began. And needless to say, my expectations were passed.
Melody's Escape is a sort of "rhythm platformer" as I like to call it which reminds me of a rather underrated game of the same genre called "Vib-Ribbon" for the PS1. It's just as easy to play, but it's also as hard to master.
The only buttons in this game are the WASD keys, shich are used to input multiple actions according to the direction and color of the obstacle. You break orbs, hop across gaps, break through walls, and even fly with stylish beauty. The game runs at a perfect and smooth 60 FPS, which perfectly compliments the game's vivid and colorful graphics.
The first thing that caught my attention when I played my first song was how accurate the obstacles were to the tempo and beat. This is by far one of, if not the best audio detections in a procedrual music game that I've seen.
If that's not reason enough to get this game, it does have Steam Workshop support to add some neat little aesthetic touches.
Overall, is Melody's Escape worth your time? Yes. Especially if you love music.

An interesting take on the zombie genre although not without some flaws:
The Good:
- The atmosphere is one of the best yet I've ever experienced in a zombie themed game.
- Has a pretty killer soundtrack.
- The animation and art design is really good! Plus points for the art style!
- The action is adequate and the thrills and horror elements of the zombies are well put to use, most of the time.
- It feels mostly like a spinoff of the series everybody loves to watch or read although with Solid Snake as a protagonist.
The Bad:
- Clunky controls. The controls can fail at the most crucial times.
- The game is awfully short.
- The other characters are flat and generic.
- The story can cram too much in such a short time that the player would end up not giving a crap at all.
- The collectibles can be a pain to gather as well.
Overall Deadlight is a slightly above average game with its moments but in the end it is pretty forgettable. 7/10.

While overall it is a pretty game and I enjoyed my playthrough of it, Deadlight has some frustrating elements and I see no reason to play through it a second time. The controls are alright but sometimes can be clumsy, most of my deaths were from that, especially since it is not always visually clear if you are at the top of a wall you are climbing over or just below the top. Little annoyiances like that which trip you up and cause you to fail (die), sometimes literally tripping you up when you are running and don't notice the small chair or a couple of boxes you should be able to just hop over or run to the side of... although those aren't game breaking at all. Just annoying. Several sections are timed but very unforgiving, and sometimes a tad inconsistant, I ended up being a second or two too fast to run through a section and somehow that made the ceiling cave in FASTER. Which is odd. The ending was also, okay, there was a sacrifice I didn't feel was necessary but whatever, that character had just sentanced a lot of people, innocent and guilty, to death to try and save another character.
Also I lol'd at how your character "can't swim" so he just sinsk to the bottom of water like a rock, and doesn't make a splash.
The first act of the game is pretty good though, very well done and set a post-zombie (sorry, "shadow") apopcalypse feel, but it did get a bit more disjointed and weird after that. The end was much less of a platforming game, although I don't think it that is necessarily bad it just could have been a bit more polished.
The main character is clearly suffering from emotional and mental issues, your diary (which you collect parts of throughout the game, which is a bit weird but w/e) is very, very weird though. Also an FYI to the devs, Canada doesn't have a national guard. It was really neat that the main character is from Hope, BC though, I didn't expect that.
I think I got this in a bundle, and it at least was good for one play through, but eh I'm not seeing the "Amazing game" or "GOTY" quality people are raving about. The developers have promise though! I hope they can build upon this experience for their next games.

Deadlight is a game with an inspired visual style and fluid, natural animations. Some areas do a good job creating a creepy ambiance. The use of 3D environments for 2D interaction worked well most of the time, making environments feel more like rooms and streets and less like boxes and planes.
Fluid animations make the game look nice when you're not in combat situations. But when you have to fight zombies (which, thankfully, is less than it could be) they get in the way. Hit detection on axe swings/pushes is, no pun intended, hit or miss. You're as likely to swing when you want to push and vice-versa, and enemy distance only vaguely informs what Randall will do. Expect to die because you intended to do one thing, but your character does another.
3D invironments work against you in zombie situations as well. It's frequently unclear when zombies are on the active plane, and they can approach you from the background to close distance while maintaining invulnerability. You end up running back and forth to put enough distance between you and the zombie while it comes in from the background.
While the guns feel impressively explosive, poor animations frequently cause Randall to spend a long time not aiming at your target. I've died dozens of times because; despite aiming left, Randall still wants to face right.
This game starts rather smooth, but the longer you play it the less fun it becomes. While the game generally uses transference well, by the end of the game it devolves into a mire of unclear objectives and trail-and-error gameplay. The last half-hour is essentially "I Wanna Be The Guy: Zombie Survival Edition". The floor drops unexpectedly, and you die. The cieling drops unexpectedly, and you die. I spent a ten minutes in a two-screen wide area fighting endlessly generating zombies because there was a glass window I needed to shoot that could only be shot from one side for some reason. Deadlight starts fun, and ends a mess.
Someone forgot to remind Tequila Works that zombies are supposed to be metaphoric. They have been since Romero.  The choice not to have any meaning behind the zombies is a huge wasted opportunity, and generally makes for dumb stories.
There were lots of meaningless gestures in Deadlight. Randall as a dangerous misanthrope with a gradually revealed diary documenting his psychosis? Nothing really comes of it. The Rat and his son? Not really relevant to anything outside of the annoying, out-of-place Rat level. Randall's friendship with Ben? Not really important, he's just some dude Randall likes. Spoiler about the ending ->
.
As for flow, there's barely anything that keeps things on track. The first third of the game is meaningless terrain treading. The second third is a huge non-sequitur through a trap-filled maze that has nothing to do with zombies. There's not even a reason for you to go through the traps, as the guy who runs the maze has non-trapped passages and he isn't antagonistic or afraid. The final third is the only part where the story of Deadlight makes any progress, and it's the worst gameplay wise.
I'm no social justice warrior. I don't think women always need to be portrayed positively, or that they need to be in every game. But literally every woman in Deadlight begs for Randall to kill them. No men do this, and it's not played as some sort of unreliable narrator device due to Randall's misanthropy or psychosis or something. They're just all terribly written characters. The one woman you get to spend time with is the traditional "bad escort" scenario, complete with the woman needing to be protected and helped up ledges that Randall has been climbing all game. Randall even has to rescue her from being sexually threatened by men with guns. To top it all off, all the women have notably bad voice acting in a game with generally bad voice acting. Deadlight reads like a textbook for especially bad female characters. I read/watch/play a lot of zombie fiction, and Deadlight has the worst female characters I've seen in ages.
If you don't have Deadlight, you probably shouldn't get Deadlight. It's only a little fun for about two hours. If you already have Deadlight and haven't played it yet, I hope this saves you a few hours of frustration. Steam is a big wide place, and there are other games to enjoy.

*Much longer soundtrack than HM1, and just as amazing.
*Hard mode option (after beating the game)
Cons:

invincible.
*Far less mask variation (however there is much more character playstyle variation as mentioned earlier)
*AI are buggy at times--not as responsive or don't attack when they should.
(Hopefully the bugs stated will be fixed at some point)

not sure yet. i will edit this review in time. i havent played it to full extend. but there are some poor design choices that make it hard to enjoy at times.
maps are huge. there is barely any guidance. on objective maps you get vague infos where to go through your cellphone serving as a mission log, sometimes with an indicator telling you the distance to your goal, sometimes not, most of the time it's not reachable by direct means anyway. people quickly get lost, both humans and player zombies. some level have built-in "You are here" location guides, and there is a map showing up before a level loads, but its still hard.
on the other hand it may encourage more teamplay than usual. people are put into the need to communicate to find their way through. at least when people with varying skill level are thrown together. but perhaps this is teamplay for the wrong reason, by forced means and simply lack of explanation. if people know their way they sometimes seem to rush ahead and leave some people behind. there are no real barriers (sometimes people need to find keys or tools to get on, but usually it's the skilled player who will find it and not the newbie) or any real incentives to drag people along, not that i would have noticed thus far. ammo hoarding does not seem to slow you down, and unlike no more room in hell or zombie panic source you cannot see and select individual ammo you are carrying but simply drop all the ammo for guns you don't have. and why would you want to share if people waste their ammo and tend to attract more zombies than what's good? i have seen this issue in no more room in hell too. as soon as people know their way they do that way, you can hope for them to "teach" the newbies but not everyone is going to show that patience. people can advance ahead and trigger temporary escape vehicles on objective maps dooming every slowpoke.
if you die or get infected and turn you become a player zombie. in all modes. even in objective maps there are player-controlled zombies. this is probably the most unique thing about contagion. there are always player controlled zombies. but this is also a poorly developed aspect of this game. there is little incentive or motivation for some people to engage their prior teammates. they may just go afk or do that "friendly zombie" thing and basically just screw around. if they even manage to find the survivors. as mentioned the maps are huge. zombies can spawn far away from humans. they can climb fences (which feels a bit buggy at times though, and the animations to do so could need polish as well) they have zombie vision to see footsteps. but they seem somewhat inconsistent. if you see them they could be "outdated" and the survivors who made them have advanced far beyond. zombies cannot know which objectives the humans are currently following/which location they go for. their only way to locate humans besides following vague footsteps is listening to gunshots, by roaming and guessing around and by hoping to see some npc or other player zombies lunge around at bigger speed presumably hunting someone down. even if you play pvp matches where there are no strict objectives to follow other than kill all you see rounds can still take forever because people simply won't find each other.
contagion feels a bit like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of zombie panic source and no more room in hell. it has some nice ideas like the cellphones as objective logs and using them to "call" living and dead players and locating them by their ringtones, and player zombies have interesting abilites like making npc zombies gather around and follow them, but controlling these can be just a pain the same because they won't run as fast as player zombies do, you need to drag them along, their pathfinding is subpar, which can be tedious on the huge maps. some modes like hunted can be fun, but even there frustration can sneak in when you spawn in bad places or when humans team up even though they are supposed to slaughter each other at first sight.
a few interersting thoughts went into the game, but i think they just aren't executed as well. if someone asked me "why would i want to pay for contagion if i can play no more room in hell or zombie panic source for free?" i couldn't give any too great answer. thats like my biggest issue with contagion. i got exhausted on both nrmih and zps, and those games aren't perfect either, but at least they have more convenient and polished mechanics like proper inside into the things you are carrying or a more satisfying melee system (melee in contagion feels imprecise and like half a pain) and they won't torture you with huge maps and no clue where you should be going to. nothing of what i've seen of contagion seems uniquely enough to justify it being a stand-alone title. if you want co-op you could very well jump at no more room in hell. if you want pvp you could very well jump at zombie panic source. if you want something of both without necessarily of the same good quality and level of polish you may be fine with contagion.

This is an excellent game, and it is still in alpha. And I am downplaying my recommendation, as I want you to read this:

But what I recommend, is the advanced (or Build) crafting method, in which you can build YOUR OWN ship, boat, car, bike, sword, shield or gun. My first car was a wooden table with wheels, but now I have a TRON-like glider, a boat, and a five seated rover.
- Graphics: Are great. I would have recommended the game without impressive graphics, but this game has AWESOME graphics. Granted, it is kind of idylic. But it looks f@#$ing great.
- Base/Colony: You can build a colony, and have the NPC to move over. You can assign jobs to them, automatize the farming of vegetables. Put automatic weapons to defend the base and the NPC, etc, etc.
Extra bits:

- Steam workshop allows to share what other people and you build in the advanced crafting interface. There is a ship build like Battlestar Galactica!!!
- The Story is awesome. Even though is linear, is still an awesome story.

This is the first review I've ever written and after playing more than 50 hours with Planet Explorers, I felt compelled to write this review.  First, the specs:  I'm playing the latest build, A0.831, on an i7-2600K, 16Gg RAM, and a GeForce 760 Ti.  I absolutely love playing Planet Explorers.  The combination of creativity, exploration, and surprises are what do it for me.  The huge world seems filled with so much potential and I'm constantly being pleased with the next "big thing to do".  The game is graphically beautiful, and I've only crashed maybe twice in the 50+ hours I've played it. The progression from simple tools and resources, to building a colony is smoothly done, such that I never feel overwhelmed.
I enjoy building structures, fortifying them, defending them, and expanding them.  I've only played in Story mode and I like how the story expands the gameplay for you.
Even though the game is Alpha, I highly recommend it.  I got this game on sale for $15.00 and have had over 50 hours of enjoyment from it.  How can you beat that deal?
When I'm away from the game I find myself coming up with ideas for what I'll try and do next in Planet Explorers.
For instance:  I made a crude heliocopter and was flying back to my colony one fine day when I was attacked by some dragon-like, vulture, flying creature.  He destroyed my helicopter!  So later on while having lunch, I thought "I'm going to build a much bigger, attack chopper, with a front-mounted cannon.  I'll show that flying freak who's the boss!"
It's these kinds of experiences both unscripted, and scripted, that keep me coming back to PE!

a comprehensive review on all features and I
explored every feature availble to the game currently, just most of them. I likely will not explore too much more of the game and it's features but, as I support this game, I will closely monitor it's patches and development.
PROS: For the most part, in it's current state, this game is very fun to play.
-Multiplayer; being able to gather materials faster and more efficiently to be able to build helicopter gunships for decimating alien encampments is far too much fun. Honestly, after my experience playing the game with my friends, the fun we had was almost criminal.
-Hunting; when it comes to hunting these large-scale dinosaur-like creatures, this game really shines. Especially when you have access to better gear so you don't have to rely on hit and run tactics to lure the beasts towards your substantially better equipped AI.
-Crafting; holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ Being able to craft
technology is amazing. No more of that unnecessarily complicated, unreasonably restrictive redstone fluffy flutter from Minecraft.
with a
on gameplay and progression. The list of available recipes is gigantic and, at first, very overwhelming. But it makes the game really something to behold.

CONS: That's right, you knew we would get to this part as soon as you saw the word "pros". And to a great degree of sadness, this list is much larger than the other one. So much larger, it's hard to pick a good starting place.
-Multiplayer; ♥♥♥♥ing port-forwarding. Everyone's least favorite chore. I
have friends who would rather pay me their hard-earned, broke college student funds than do their own port-forwarding. Ironically, even I don't like doing it. It's bizarre; it's complicated and simple at the same time. Usually you just go to your router's browser page at 192.168.1.1 and follow some simple directions to get the port forwarded. Combine that with some firewall exceptions and you've got yourself an open port for some multiplayer madness. Assuming it actually works. Which, most of the time, is the problem. There's almost
a layman's solution to port-forwarding without buying a program to forward the ports for you. You can't just strap in and forward the ports without having to learn the arbitrary process first, it rapidly gets you very involved and educated on how to do it like a professional through a mind-numbing few hours of trial and error. And unless you do it the mythical
which is different per router, you'll find that before long your ports are closed again. tl;dr port forwarding for multiplayer is a bad solution, but a cheap one. Invest a little in better multiplayer and watch the crowds eat up your game.
-Hunting; oh boy. Want to hunt something that can't
you like it's name was Ralph? Really boring and offers almost nothing you'll need to build decent survival gear or buy it. Want to hunt something that
gives a worthwhile supply of necessary materials like animal skins and fat or isn't just plain boring to fight? Well be prepared to overly rely on your AI or multiplayer comrades because otherwise it will kill you and♥♥♥♥♥♥your corpse into the ocean. For most of the entire game, it's usually a far safer idea to simply avoid almost everything and mine for materials in vast quantities to be able to emerge from the earth as the most powerful entity on the planet. But then the game is boring because nothing provides a challenge anymore.
-Crafting; bore chore. As excellent as the crafting system of this game is at delivering impacful technology that feels as good as it performs... Actually crafting it is obnoxiously boring. It's all about making excessively vast quantities of little materials to be able to make smaller and smaller quantities of larger and larger materials until you have everything you need. The only redeeming feature here is that you can produce things in bulk, which you'll quite often rely on because otherwise you'll have to make
of the necessary materials over and over again until you no longer need to make whatever oddity you're crafting to begin with. It takes such a long time to make anything worthwhile or important,
the various vehicles in the game.
-Vehicles; I didn't sign up for this. The vehicle creation menu/functionality is a very frustrating feature of the game. Especially for those like myself that aren't very creative-minded and
when presented that much crafting freedom. As much as I like the freedom offered in the feature, you need to at least present some guidelines or most players will just be lost in the age old question of "Where the ♥♥♥♥ do I even start?" Let's not even get that much into the controls of the vehicle crafting feature because all that needs to be said is prepare to rely on the undo function heavily as you constantly mutter "I didn't want to do that". -Gathering; so many problems. Wood gathering? Takes too damn long if you want to get any worthwhile amount of wood that is determined seemingly
based on the size of the tree you're chopping down. Mineral gathering? Prepare to scour every inch of the planet trying to even
these materials. They're arbitrarily hard to locate; but I guess that's not so bad when you can mine them in the thousands if you're willing to spend the time doing it once you actually find a vein. Underwater/Oceanic gathering? Unfortunately necessary for the later parts of the game. To make matters worse, to build a boat for easy/safe underwater/oceanic gathering you need oil/petroleum. To get this, you need a boat to be able to safely traverse the waters without getting immediately killed by a dino-shark-demon. I'm sure you see the cycle here.
-Voxels/Vertices/Whatever; the last, but greatest con.
You'll mine voxels/vertices/whatever so finely that creating a mine to work in that isn't game breaking or safe to actually stand in is next to impossible unless you're really diligent and have the time on hand to actually do it. Copper pickaxes are one of the first pickaxes that actually mine larger voxels/vertices so you can make flat surfaces for mining much more easily. job.

I want to start by saying that I really enjoy playing this game. I had recently been wanting to play a WWII game but I didn't feel like spending $20 on CoD:WaW which is also an outdated game. This came in perfectly as it cost nothing and is still being worked on, which is why I wanted to write this review.
Overall, this game is great. I love the ballistics, there is nothing more satifying than getting a long range headshot on a moving target. I hear a lot of people complain about Soviets being OP but it hasn't been that way for me. There are times when it seems like it, but I still win games against them and can kill them just like any other faction. I love the fact that maps can be different, especially the weather. I don't know what makes fighting in the fog so much fun but I always get excited when the maps are anything but sunny. But, I'd still like a few more maps to play on.
The things that really bother me aren't even huge issues and I hope they get fixed before this game is finished. I've adapted my driving ability for this game but sometimes the wonky driving physics either get me killed or detroy my vehicle. Also, I hate not being able to shoot while jumping or just in the air. I've been killed so many times because I was standing on something weird and the game thought I was in mid-air and wouldn't let me shoot. I believe my other complaint to be circumstantial as it pertains to the queue time. I keep searching for a game and end up waiting in the queue for 2-3 minutes before I get into games that started a minute ago, or are almost over. This wasn't happening when I first downloaded the game so I can only assume there are more people playing than before and the servers need an upgrade.
There are quite a few minor things I would change about this game, but as it stands it is good enough to keep playing. I even liked this game enough to spend the $20 I saved on WaW, on this game to show my support for what I think is one of, if not the best WWII games out right now.
P.S. Don't forget to bring your panzerschreck!

NOTE: I may sound like I hate this game, but it is actually still one of the most fun (I use that word loosely) and by far the most creative rhythm game I have ever played, so keep that in mind while you read my rant.
Edit: Oh, and ANOTHER problem. Whatever generates the notes in the map is sort of... not all that great. I can't count the times that I've been tripped or clothslined by an object that doesn't even have a place in the song. It's annoying as Hell, that's all I'm saying about that. And another problem (that maybe others are experiencing) is the fact that you have to play basically two different songs with two different hands. It's just not practical. Imagine two songs going on in your head (on top of other random notes) that you really like then trying to sing along to one but being constantly interrupted by the other. That's sort of how it feels. But again, that may just be another personal problem. Oh, and another thing I feel the need to say again, the timing is so brutal. It doesn't give you any breathing room at all because God forbid you concentrate on ANYTHING while you are playing. I feel that you should actually have to think about what you are playing rather than just winging it every time you play (Which is what you have to do in this game because of the note system and it's need to throw random things at you) And again I state, I'm no stranger to rhythm games, so I think I know what I'm talking about.
End of Edit
So many things I would already like to say about this game... I guess all of my issues are personal, but they may also relate to other people. So, first off, it's a little freaking hard! Now, you are probably screaming at your monitor 'Try a lower difficulty ya' moron!' Well, the problem with that is that any difficulty below Intense doesn't feel like the actual game. Mainly because when you hover over Intense mode, it says 'Complete gameplay experience'. Now I feel like playing on anything but Intense is not getting the whole experience. (Which so far isn't a great one) And on top of that, I have serious coordination issues when it comes to this game for some reason. I mean, I played Extreme songs on Hatsune Miku: Project DIVA F that were easier than this. (And for those of who know what that is, you ESPECIALLY understand what I'm saying)  But that's just a personal problem. Also, I have quite a bit of rhythm game experience under my belt (I've played osu!, Frets on Fire,  Project DIVA F, and Audiosurf very extensively) so it's not like I'm a complete stranger to the genre. But anyways, that's really all of the bad I have to say about it. Oh, wait, and it's not forgiving in your timing AT ALL. Okay, NOW that's it.
Other than that, it is a VERY good rhythm game in general. It's beats usually make sense, the controls seem fun for someone who can actually use them, and the graphics don't look too horrible for a rhythm game. And that's all I have to compliment it by. Overall though, I would definitely recommend this game just to give a try.  Hope this review helped and thank you for reading!

If you're looking at this you're probably wondering if the game is worth a buy, 20$ may seem very expensive to those who don't have the luxury to just go out and buy games without a doubt while it may seem like pocket change to others.
You should buy Contagion because It's fun, it provides an environment where cooperation is key, while that may seem like a generic statement across all sorts of zombie survival games, seriously, in this one, it is. If your friends die they become zombies and ultimately that makes your gameplay a whole lot more difficult because that one player zombie can infect another player and they're count goes up one by one until the last person is left cowering in a corner before she/he is mauled to death by a horde. A lot of players who prefer the old slow zombies and freakish hordes of them will like this game in its entirety.
Contagion challenges the players in a multitude of gamemodes such as...
Stopping with the possibly ranting non-sense, lets get on with this review. First of all, the store page in comparison to real gameplay.
If you've read the section "What they're saying about Contagion" which is the first section of the store page for reviewers it's basically saying that Contagion is a good game that has gone back to the old style slow zombie game that is worth the 20$ it's worth. But is that really true?
Yes, Contagion has done that and so far I've liked the game, even in the most frustrating moments I've had fun running around popping zombies in the head once or beating them with a melee weapon of my choice. But that is me however, how would it be for you the player?
Contagion may be fun for a good majority of the possible people willing to throw money at the developers so that they can play however a there is also the fact a lot of people have said that the game is terrible, the graphics are bad, the gameplay sucks, gore is 'meh' and it's been an overall bad experience. Hell, the two first reviews I saw of Contagion had said that it was a bad game and there was only one good review. But these reviews were a bit old, like, months back old so I decided to write one myself.
In all seriousness, if you have a problem with graphics, any game developed for the Source Engine is gonna look bad in some way so you should save yourself the time and money and just ignore this game all together. If you're cool with it, enjoy.
Gameplay wise, if you have everything going for you and you have a smart team to play with, even on the most hardest difficulties you will steam roll through zombie hordes and make it to the end with minimum casualties if not zero. That is probably the biggest aspect of the game I consider that makes it fun for anyone to play it really. Teamwork is essential in this game and if you're not a teamplayer, you're gonna get wiped quick and you'll probably get mad very easily at this game because being mauled by a horde of zombies isn't fun, not for you, not for anyone and not even for your teammates across the map. Because when you die, they'll have to deal with you and any player zombie is more fiendish than an NPC in a horde.
The Gore is decent, it's not gonna rock you and have blood spraying everywhere but the limbs will fall off I assure you this. It's also toggable so if you have children who want to play feel free to turn of it. Then again, why are you subjecting your child to such a violent gorish videogame like Contagion?
Overall Experience of Contagion? It's pretty good, I wouldn't say 'decent' because the only time I would ever say 'decent' if it was a 50/50 that everything was going right and everything was going wrong at that point. With my 'small' experience of Contagion gameplay I can only say this. It's good because discluding the idiotic players, the twit taking things he doesn't need and the relatively low chance of getting trolled by a zombie because you've emptied a magazine into his head, it's pretty good.
The only things you need to worry about in the game is the things I just discluded, the dumb or should I say, learning players, the trolls, the hoarder of ammo and the trollish hitboxes preventing you from ending the zombies life. Those are the only things that are going to ruin your day, mostly the trollish hitboxes on the zombies. Other than that, the players tend to listen and stick together but you will usually always have the one guy who decided to hoard everything and not share one bit of it.
What they've said is true in terms of finding weapons or objectives but the map layout tends to be the same and you will usually have a deja vu moment here and there. It will always be new in terms of trying to find the objective in the various places they put it as well as the pathways you take to that objective but other than that the map will remain the same. I honestly thought the map would be different like they made blocks of the maps that would interlock easily and would create a whole new environment all together.
Edit 9/2/2014 - Added a little bit concerning the pathways to objectives will always be different.
I would say that this would be true in terms of it described but I honestly don't think it's state of the art, you could really compare this to Deadspace's limbic system when you utterly destroyed the monsters.
This I would consider to be definetly true, I never got to a point where I ran through the game without even thinking, I was always cautious because the obvious zombie moans around the corner usually prepared me to get mauled to death.

Quick summary at bottom of review.
Planet Explorers is a good game with even greater potential. Yes the game is Early Access and it wont be released/completed for a while yet, but it's certainly worth supporting the developers and watching the game evolve.
In it's current state it is playable, though you'll encounter alot of bugs and such. One of the worst examples is the Adventure Mode randomly generated worlds. You choose 1 of 4 biomes to be your main biome to play in, the others you'll practically never see in game. Not only this but the original spawn point and camp is normally on it's own island surrounded by a large crevice on all sides (imagine Avatar's floating islands, except these are connected to the world vertically). Not too much of a problem, just build a make-shift bridge out of dirt or something. But it does cause alot of annoyance.
Story Mode seem relatively good, though I have barely touched it as it is at this point a long tutorial which you can get the over all feel and mechanics of the game within an hour.
As for custom content, this is where the game shines. You can create a nice variety of items and weapons in game at this time. Here's a quick list of 'functional' things you can create; Swords, Shields, Firearms, Boats, Wheeled Vehicles (any type on land transport), Helicopters and Planes. Now when I say functional I mean things that you can use. You can also create in-animate objects, wether it be a flag or a wall decoration, the option is there.
As for the construction mechanic, it works well. Everything is built with blocks and easy to place with good camera controls, and your buildings don't look blocky at all they are smooth. Though the gathering of these resources is very tedious. Just scan for ores and mine them or just stand in one spot and hold LMB and keep mining. That's it. There is a scanner that can tell you the location of ores in the world within a short radius, but I rarely use it as the most needed ore can be found in stone alot of the time.

I couldnt decide what to write in this review , so im gonna share with you guys my favorite apple pie recipe Enjoy! :D
Pastry
2 cups all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon salt
2/3 cup plus 2 tablespoons shortening
4 to 6 tablespoons cold water
Filling
1/3 to 1/2 cup sugar
1/4 cup all-purpose flour
1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon
1/2 teaspoon ground nutmeg
1/8 teaspoon salt
8 cups thinly sliced peeled tart apples (8 medium)
2 tablespoons butter or margarine
1) In medium bowl, mix 2 cups flour and 1 teaspoon salt. Cut in shortening, using pastry blender (or pulling 2 table knives through ingredients in opposite directions), until particles are size of small peas. Sprinkle with cold water, 1 tablespoon at a time, tossing with fork until all flour is moistened and pastry almost cleans side of bowl (1 to 2 teaspoons more water can be added if necessary).
2) Gather pastry into a ball. Divide in half; shape into 2 flattened rounds on lightly floured surface. Wrap in plastic wrap; refrigerate about 45 minutes or until dough is firm and cold, yet pliable. This allows the shortening to become slightly firm, which helps make the baked pastry more flaky. If refrigerated longer, let pastry soften slightly before rolling.
3) Heat oven to 425°F. With floured rolling pin, roll one pastry round into round 2 inches larger than upside-down 9-inch glass pie plate. Fold pastry into fourths; place in pie plate. Unfold and ease into plate, pressing firmly against bottom and side.
4) In large bowl, mix sugar, 1/4 cup flour, the cinnamon, nutmeg and 1/8 teaspoon salt. Stir in apples until well mixed. Spoon into pastry-lined pie plate. Cut butter into small pieces; sprinkle over filling. Trim overhanging edge of pastry 1/2 inch from rim of plate.
5) Roll other round of pastry into 10-inch round. Fold into fourths and cut slits so steam can escape. Unfold top pastry over filling; trim overhanging edge 1 inch from rim of plate. Fold and roll top edge under lower edge, pressing on rim to seal; flute as desired. Cover edge with 2- to 3-inch strip of foil to prevent excessive browning.
6) Bake 40 to 50 minutes or until crust is brown and juice begins to bubble through slits in crust, removing foil for last 15 minutes of baking. Serve warm if desired.

This game has a fantastic concept, good execution, and fun mechanics. The world is enormous and there is a lot to explore, but that being said, I cannot recommend the game in its current state.
Most new players will attempt story mode first as it is a very good introduction into the games mechanics and general lore. Story mode, however, is barely functional. Every single mission I played glitched out in some way, whether it was people running into trees and getting stuck, or they had no clue what to do. Along with the glitches, the side missions are utterly boring, requiring you to collect random herbs, protect people from ridiculously overpowered monsters (the grind in early game is very very difficult), or just visiting somewhere with no interest.
The combat is possibly my biggest gripe with the game in its current state. The game has an ABSOLUTELY HORRIBLE combat system. Early and mid game monsters are ridiculously overpowered, destroying any chance of combat being fair. While the stock weapons that are sold are horrible, even if you made weapons, they can barely damage monsters. Beyond the grind, the combat is boring, consisting of you standing still and clicking enemies that also stand still to attack. Beyond health bars, there is ZERO indication that you are even hurting monsters or people. No flinching, no blood, no visible damage at all. Needless to say, this gets really repetitive and boring.
Overall, it's a decent game with a very interesting concept, but unless the developers revamp the gameplay, combat, and questing aspects, this game will die very quickly. It's a great game and it would be a shame to see it die, but in its current state its awful.      6/10
TL;DR Interesting game with great concept, but gameplay, combat, and questing is awful and desperately needs reworking.

I recently purchased this game when it was on sale for $15.  I feel it was worth that.  I have completed the story line for as far as it goes once, and logged most of the rest of my hours on the Adventure mode.  I tried the multi player for just a couple of hours.
Pros:
It's a beautiful game.  I really enjoy the look of the world.
I like the basic crafting.  It's easy to find what you want in your recipes, and the resources are automatically selected if you have them, or indicated if you don't.
I like the potential of the ISO creation tool. But as I will mention below it has drawbacks.
I love the rope gun.
I love the jet pack.
I love the glider.
I love being able to create a settlement.
I like being able to recruit villagers to participate in my base.
I like the farming.
I like the resource gathering.
Cons:
The ISO creation tool was to difficult for me to figure out.  (the good news is there are sites available to download other peoples creations, and many of those are just beautiful)
Weapons and monsters aren't well balanced.  Early weapons are nearly useless, ISO created weapons are too devastating.
Vehicles run out power/become damaged too quickly.  It's usually easier to just use your jet pack and glider than to bother pulling out a vehicle to get where you are going.
Vehicle weapons are too weak.  It's quicker to just get out and kill the monster with your rifle, than to try blasting it with your vehicle cannons.
There is a lack of sentient creature aggression.  Aliens attack if you run into them, but the never attack your base.  Animals will attack.  But they aren't a challenge.  The toughest thing is looting all the corpses that litter the field before they disappear.
Settlement mechanics are still pretty sparce.  I am looking forward to those being fleshed out  in the future.
There are a lack of building machines for tunneling, leveling, and raising land.  It's all done with a pick and a shovel.  I am looking forward to heavy equipment to speed up the beautification of my base.
You can't replace natural earth that is removed.  So if you are trying to make a level spot for your garden and you accidentally hit the wrong spot, there is no way to fix it short of loading a previous save.

-NOTE: This review is for a game in alpha!
Very unique game with tons of creative ideas, but as it is in alpha, these ideas lack a lot of flare, and are very underdeveloped. In fact, all the game's ideas (not to mention the whole game itself) is packed to the brim with bugs and errors. The story mode is something I consider awful. The voice acting for all NPC's and keystory characters is annoying, and really feels like something you'd find at a high school acting club. The missions are all tedious, and rarely go beyond the MMORPG tropes of "kill X of Y" or "Collect X of Y". This is especially disheartening considering this is a singleplayer storyline, and yet it lacks anything to really intrigue me for longer than an hour. The multiplayer is glitchy as hell. Sometimes I'd be able to join a server, but most of the time this wouldn't be the case. Even when hosting my own server, something I've had a lot of experience with, the connection is very unreliable, working around 50% of the time. Now I'm positive this isn't an error on my end, as I actually have a personal server in my home, have hosted private servers for numerous games, and followed the game dev's official server setup instructions to the letter.... twice. Even if I am able to connect to a server, be it my own or someone elses, in multiplayer, there is no way to control where you spawn, meaning you and your friends will be in entirely different villages and required to shlepp around until you find each other making it very, very tedious. The create mode is the true selling point of this game. The create mode is incredibly easy to use, and almost reminds me of a dumbed down version of Solidworks, a 3D modeling program I used to use quite a lot. That being said, it is still very unrefined and lacks a lot of the flare to create anything more than some basic cars or guns without spending hours in it. There are so many tools missing from the overall creation experience, that many things are so complex to create in this 3D modeling software. This is extremely frustrating since I know that I could easily make a lot of this stuff using the vastly more advanced tools of something like Solidworks, or hell, even the Microsoft 3D modeling software. Also, there is no options for zooming besides using a mouse wheel which is annoying since I'm so used to modeling with a trackpad. This game does have a lot of potential for sure, and I will be looking at it again in beta and the final version, but as it stands right now I couldn't reccomend this at all. If I had to give this game a score, which I probably shouldn't given it's not even in beta, I'd have to give it a 4/10. Avoid this game like the expensive plague. Also, a word of advice to all "early release" developers. Please sell your alpha games at a discount. Usually you have to pay people to play such glitchy monstrosities, and it's something I deeply regret that I paid full retail for this junk heap.

To you folks out there in gaming land, this is what you want - smart developers that refine and improve, providing you with ever better gaming experiences. It's like SCIENCE!
So, what do we have? Left 4 Dead, framed with a Warhammer context, and then some.
What's been added?
- gambling/unlock system, itemisation and customisation. In the good way, as oppossed to the ever popular 'milk your fanbase's playtime by hiding the goodies behind a time wall'. The core experience is delievered from the start, the rest is simply tinkering things to suit your playstyle.
- focus on melee. Blocking is an important part of play. Not everyone needs to get up close and personal and a shield isn't required to succeed, but oh yes does it help. If you were the type to pick up the fireaxe in L4D, damn everything else, and boldy take point, slaughtering all the deadheads that dared oppossed you, then you're gonna love this game.
- better signalling. You can tag specials for your team mates, helping you cooridinate your efforts. Likewise, the sound effects triggered before a special enemy attacks are clear and add to the atmosphere.
- which brings me to the specials. We've basically got the smoker (pack master), hunter (assassin), spitter (poisonwind globadier.. with less floor-splash, more in-your-face gas distortion and the tendency to self destruct on death), and tanks (rat ogres). Thankfully there's no jockey but we do get the awesome Storm Vermin, who have a habit of clumping up and giving you grief, thanks to their armour.
- Warhammer. Grimdark. Dirt. Rats. Cracks. Stains. It's all there. If you've ever wanted to virtually sniff the docks of an Imperial city, or stain your boots in its fetid sewers, or perhaps simply chill in a gloomy tavern with a very ugly bar tenders, then this is the game for you.
What are we missing?
- Sadly, we can't play as the Skaven.
- There's a crippling shortage of rednecks.
- The colour palette seems washed out, though I figure this is more to do with the confusing Gamma settings instructions. Personally, I wacked things down till they were gloomy and never could find the second symbol...
TL:DR
4 players. Ideally friends. Fighting hordes of ratmen. With axes, swords, fire, guns and bow. In a lavish gothic-fantasy setting.
Good fun. Bring friends!

Vermintide is pretty blatant with how much it was "inspired by" Left 4 Dead, but that definitely isn't a negative.
The game takes the very core game from Left 4 Dead, refocuses the combat to be mainly melee-based,  then adds in a class system for variety and loot for both variety and incentive for replayability. How extremely well the Warhammer skin is done is just a solid bonus.
Pros -
The melee combat is fun and feels quite impactful.
The game looks amazing, doubly so for a $30 title. It's easily the best looking Warhammer game out there, at any rate.
Classes feel different and varied, but not so much so where there's a noticeably power disparity between any of them.
Item system lets you have varying ways of playing each class, and definitely adds to the replayability factor.
Plenty of maps, with a large variety of areas from city streets to the sewers to the forests outside the city.
The Warhammer theme is very well executed - everything looks, sounds, and feels appropriate for a Warhammer Fantasy game.
Cons -
Minor connection issues. Mainly the matchmaking can be kind of slow at times, but primarily it's the fact that if the host's game crashes it boots everyone back to the start of the mission with a new host.
FPS drops: the game runs extremely well on my rig - which is a moderately high end one - but every so often the FPS will just die. Sometime it's only a minor drop from my solid 60 (capped at 60) down to 45-50, but other times it goes into slideshow mode for a second or two before coming out of it and going back to normal.
The cons are annoying, but nothing too game breaking. Overall I would definitely recomment the game, especially for people who played and enjoyed L4D.

What begins as an intriguing and atmospheric side-scroller soon degenerates into an extremely frustrating experience from the moment you meet one of the most annoying characters (the Rat) since that Aussie bad guy in Far Cry 3. From then on, Deadlight's imprecise controls and unfair deaths make the game more of an endurance test than a tense survival horror. You can't react to events in a bid to survive; you wander into a trap, get killed, retry, get killed again, and then after a few more deaths finally realise there is one, and ONLY ONE, specific way to progress to the next checkpoint. I can only imagine the fury this game must conjure in all but the most tolerant and persistent of gamers who dare to try Nightmare mode.
To add insult to injury, the dialogue and voice acting is stupefyingly awful, and I'm not being overdramatic here: it's frequently of the forehead-smacking or eye-rolling level of terribleness. The story is bog-standard for the genre, but because the game quickly becomes more frustrating than fun you don't care what happens to protagonist Randall Wayne (who, annoyingly, talks and refers to himself in the third person) and simply want to finish the game so you can remove the install from your hard drive, space that could be taken up by a more worthy gaming experience. That tired old "nightmare flashback" style, as seen in Max Payne et al, makes frequent appearances along your journey, adding virtually nothing to the plotline.
It's a shame, because Deadlight's visuals are stunning, but it's sunken by simplistic game mechanics, a frustrating hodge-podge of trial-and-error gameplay and truly terrible writing. In no way should you purchase this for the full asking price; at the very least, wait for a sale, but even then it's hard to recommend Deadlight even for a few dollars.

Back when I first played Hotline Miami, I fell in love with it. The quick, versatile gameplay accompanied by an 80s style retro soundtrack was amazing and really complimented the game.  This isn't about the first Hotline, however, this is about the second. Hotline Miami 2 fails to live up to its predecessor; however, it does have some interesting features that makes it feel a bit more fun at times.
I’ll jump right into the pros, the soundtrack, for one, is amazing. Just like the first game, the soundtrack really drags you into the gameplay and just feels great. Whether you’re simply playing peek-a-boo with the enemies or running down a hallway guns blazing, the music blasting will certainly pump some blood in your veins.
The graphics, although very similar to the first game, have improved. It still has that arcade feel, but more refined. Along with that, the developers have really made the levels feel less bland overall. The detail in the game is immense and really adds to vibe of the game overall.
The last real good thing I can say is the different characters you can play as. Whereas Hotline 1 was restricted to just Jacket and Biker, there are so many other characters you can play in this one. Most of them have something that makes them different from the others, whether it’s rolling around or using two characters at the same time (my personal favorite.)
Unfortunately, there are only so many good things you can say about this game. One of the core elements of a video game is the gameplay itself. Hotline Miami 2’s gameplay is extremely disappointing. Hotline Miami 2 is centered around guns like crazy and it’s gets to a point where the whole game is frustrating in itself. Whereas Hotline Miami made guns an ineffective way to the finish the level, and even frowned upon at times, Hotline Miami 2’s levels have most if not all enemies wielding guns. Pair that up with terrible shooting controls and extremely open levels and you got a recipe for disaster.
Speaking of levels, the level design in terms of gameplay is far from great. The levels feel so big and open that it makes it very hard to spot enemies, forcing the game into a game of peek-a-boo and sometimes even blind shooting just to bring out enemies.
Honestly, I really want to like this game because there are so many fun things about it. But even then, the sheer gameplay and hollow story brings the game down. Hotline Miami was never meant to be a gun game with tedious levels and terrible design; it was meant to be fun arcade style mess-em-up with a vague, but compelling story. As much as I want to give this game a good rating, Hotline Miami 2 is ultimately a disappointment that doesn’t live up to its hype.

Completed this game in about 11 hours, and oh my god I loved it the whole way through.
But, let's start with cons to get them out of the way.
Level design has apparently been a major issue for people, and with a heavy heart, I agree. It's simply too open in some areas, as opposed to the first game where you felt like a beast when you charged in and racked up huge combos by beating in heads and gunning down mobsters. This game simply feels like a cover shooter at times, especially with certain Hawaii missions (that damn power plant), with people shooting you through windows off-screen, so you're forced to move sparsely and poke your head out of cover. I can't really think of any other cons since I love this game and its predecessor so damn much.
Pros - so many good things. The soundtrack is spot-on, if not better, with over 50 songs featured throughout. Every level has a different song. Every level. The gameplay, aside from level design, is also brilliant. In the original, you had one character with different masks (and Biker I guess). This game has a huge array of characters and playstyles that are completely fresh and new. For example, Corey lets you dodge and roll through areas to avoid gunfire and look like a badass, while Mark lets you dual-wield submachine guns and shoot enemies side-on. Unfortunately some characters feel the same, like the Writer, who doesn't have any abilities aside from... not being able to kill people? There are characters without masks now, and simply have different abilities.
But the main thing to comment on here is the story. The story is what's been focused on the most in this game, tying up loose ends with the story, as well as providing explanations and making you gasp with realisation. The game bounces back between many characters, where stories may intertwine, with characters seeing or killing each other through missions. The story is incredibly surreal in the first as well as its sequel, but makes a surprising amount of sense by the end of the game, each character being important or serving a role. The ending hits you like a train when it all comes together as well.
So overall, while gameplay is slightly slower-paced than its original, it still stands as an amazing game, worthy of being a sequel, with everything you could expect out of it and more.

I am torn apart by this game (like most of the enemies you will meet). For everything good that it does, there is almost always something annoying happening to counteract it, whether it be glitches or game mechanics. Towards the end of the game, I questioned whether I was actually playing it because I liked it, or just playing it to see it to the end.
The gameplay. You will be killed by an offscreen enemy many times, and while you can do the same to them, I would rather be able to see where I am shooting instead of firing blind. The huge turning point between this game and the first is that the levels are larger, meaning the gameplay has turned into a "lure and kill" strategy game. You will not be able to run into a room and spray gunfire everywhere (in most of the levels). Something else that really irked me is that you can't effectively pick up a weapon that you want. This seems like a minor detail at first, but when you have certain types of enemies that can't be shot or bludgeoned rushing at you, it's a different story. Enemies will get caught in doorways and twitch non-stop, as if they are telling you to hold the door for them next time. They will also randomly spin in place, and I'm not sure whether this is intentional or not because it happens to the same enemies everytime. I also feel like there wasn't as much thought put into the enemy placement; it feels like they went the Dark Souls II route and just put enemies everywhere in order to make the game feel harder than it really should be. Whenever I saw I unlocked hard mode after beating the game I just laughed and thought: "...Well I'm never playing that."
The music. What can I say? It was universally accepted that the soundtrack to this game would be excellent... and it is! However, sometimes the music can get obnoxiously loud. I'm talking take-your-headphones-off-loud. The first time this happened was so unexpected I nearly jumped out of my seat. This seems like it should be a good thing, and to be honest you can really get into the music at first, but then you die 50 times and hear it loop 37 times. This is especially noticeable in the final stage of an act. It's as if it's trying to tell you, "AM I GOOD? YOU KNOW I AM." You're probably wondering why I didn't just turn it down. I could have, but the fact of the matter is that I shouldn't have to.
The plot. Hotline Miami 1's story intrigued me, and the mystery surrounding Jacket and the phone calls are what pulled me in. I am pleased to say the plot in Hotline Miami 2 is fleshed out more than the first. There is a lot more dialogue this time around, adding personalities to the many characters in the story. The story is very hard to understand your first time, unless you're really good at paying attention to minute details and keeping track of dates. Think about it like if the movies "Memento" and "Pulp Fiction," had a baby and it was addicted to cocaine.
Overall, I feel like the story and music alone are not enough to make you want to play the game; and you realize just how repetitive the game is because it feels like it drags out near the end. So did I have a positive or negative experience with Hotline Miami 2? To be perfectly honest, I really don't know. When the music and plot are the more enjoyable elements of your game, maybe you should just make a visual novel instead.

Initially, the game has a very steep learning curve, and is really quite difficult. That might have been how I chose to start my character off, but I was constantly asking one of my buddies how to advance in that situation and what to do next.

Mount & Blade is a historical simulation and RPG set in a fictional realm of warring kingdoms called Calradia, each of which seems to be based on a different historical nation (Vikings, Saracens, Mongols, etc). You play an individual who is free to roam this world and carve their own path.
When you begin the game, you create a character in a similar manner to many RPGs, adjusting your apperance, name, gender and a backstory which (presumably) affects your starting stats, as well as choosing your starting location. After a short introductory quest, you are free to travel around the continent, recruit followers, do quests for villages and lords, join a kingdom and rising up the ranks and so on.
Overall, I strongly recommend Mount & Blade: Warband. There is a great amount of depth and the world is very open, thus there are lots of different ways in which you can gain renown, experience and or gold, including trading, robery and raiding, hunting bandits and taking them prisoner and selling them, quests, setting up and running a series of businesses (brewery for example), and once you gain a fief (a village or town which a king can give to their vassals) you can gain money through taxes and tarrifs, as well as spending money to upgrade your fief through various buildings. The fact that you are not forced down a particular path is one of the good things about this game, it also gives the game a high level of replayability. Furthermore, as becoming the ruler of even one faction, let alone the entire continent, is not a quick process which further adds to the longevity of this game.
Battles are one of the main parts of the game and they are quite fun. You have a degree of tactical control over your followers although once a battle enters a melee stage, it can get quite chaotic. Nevertheless, battles are visually quite impressive with large numbers of individual soldiers represented, including infantry, cavalry, archers and siege weapons. Sieges are particularly impressive and the fighting on the walls of a castle is often particularly fierce. At the beginning of the game, you are quite weak and often need to stick with your men. While it's possible to single-handedly defeat multiple enemies in melee combat, it can be quite difficult, often requring you to block an onslaught of attacks before an opportunity to attack presents itself. This means you can't go charging in Rambo style, as against three or more enemies, it's difficult to block all of the attacks against you.
Graphically, Mount & Blade: Warband is very nice. It's not brilliant but it's certainly nice which is evident in the visual detail of soldiers, and skies are quite visually appealling as well, particular at dawn and dusk.
Overall:
I'd give it 9/10
And for a breakdown:
Gameplay: 9/10
Range of content (including mods): 10/10
Replayability: 9/10
Graphics: 7/10
Sound: 8/10
Value for money: 10/10

While the comparison to Left 4 Dead is an easy one to make, it's also deeply unfair to do so without taking the major differences into account. Vermintide takes the concept of fighting through masses of enemies while completing various and varied goals along the way, and manages to do it better than L4D by including collectibles, randomized loot and witty dialogue between the characters which blows valve's zombie counterpart out of the water.
Not only is every level well-crafted, fun and challenging on any difficulty, the addition of tomes, grimores and dice that gives you an extra chance on loot makes the temptation to check every room and chest nearly unbearable, well-knowing that slowing down or separating is likely a death sentence. "Is a peek in that storehouse and a potential extra loot roll worth the chance of being carried off by a skaven packmaster?", you'll ask yourself.
After each completed game, your efforts culminate in a dice roll determining what goodies you get for your contribution, a very satisfying game mechanic which comes as the cherry on top of a well-earned victory. This is how you put together a horde survival game and ensure that it'll be popular for a good, long while. Have yet to be bored even for a second while playing, and stoked to see what might be added in the future.

First off I want to say this game is a really good WW2 Themed shooter, but, like all games, it has it's flaws.
A note before all my whineing about how unfair this game can get: This game likes to enforce 1 key detail. "War isn't fair." remember that. You may get wrecked the first time you play, but don't get discouraged.
It is essentially just your regular shooter, but with some twists. For one, the leveling up and currency system is alot like World Of Tanks, you don't HAVE to spend money to unlock content, but leveling up and saveing up for new weapons or training for a new class takes ages. I have played for 10 hours and I am only level 3.
I throughly enjoy this game, but sometimes it can be a pain. Like when the enemy team decides to not cap a place and instead spawncamp the crap out of it. Snipers are a massive pain to track down and tanks are really hard to kill when you are just starting, as to unlock new weapons you have to earn ranks on Ribbons.
Instead of leveling up and gaining the ability to buy any weapon you want, you instead have to use certain weapons and do certain things to unlock ribbon ranks, then allowing you to buy the item. Also, Ribbons don't carry over between characters, even if they are in the same army.
Like I mentioned before, snipers feel overpowered on some maps (Like Airfield), and tanks can be very difficult as not many people like to carry a Panzercheck, which weights alot and uses alot loadout space.
To balance this, however, you don't get infinate spawns. Everytime you spawn in a Vechical or spawn in as a certain class, it uses a "Spawn Ticket" each time. Meaning, the enemy team can only have a limited snipers (Lets say 10) throughout the round. Meaning, if you spawned in as a sniper, you only have 9 tickets for sniper left. You die and respawn as sniper, 8.
So if you run out of tickets, you can't play sniper anymore. Tanks, Paratroopers, Infantry (Though you have a ton of them), Paratroopers, Planes, pilots, basically anything you spawn in, IS LIMITED.
One major flaw is how overpriced and expensive everything is. Unless you plan on spending real world money, it will take you forever to reach General and unlock stuff along the way. This game will eat up hours to get good at.

If you enjoyed the first game, you will almost certainly enjoy this sequel.  It remains true to the general formula of its predecessor while changing enough of how it presents itself to distinguish itself from its former title.  This isn't really a good point or a bad point, it just makes the game different from the first.  If you are looking for the fast paced, largely melee combat of the first game with a minimalistic story based more around attention to detail than narrative, then you will be slightly dissapointed with this installment.  There are cutscenes galore with walls of text to be had in a complex and time-weaving plotline that leaves much more up to interpretation than Hotline Miami.  Overall larger environments and firearm-clad enemies mean you will have to rely more on shooting your way through levels, which is an aspect of the gameplay that still holds residual interface difficulty from the first game.  The music is still great like the last game, although I found it to be far less memorable this time around.  That could just be because the tracklist is greater and more varied this time around though.
I much prefer the first Hotline Miami game to Wrong Number but that doesn't mean that this sequel is a bad game, not by any means.  It is still a boatload of fun, and with a longer campaign is worth $15, especially if you plan on revisiting the game on its harder difficulty and obtaining the highest scores in all of the levels.  Notice how I mention the first game in pretty much every sentence in the first paragraph of this review: Hotline Miami, to me, is pretty much a perfect top down beat-em-up from which I compare all similar game experences.  Hotline Miami 2 is merely a step down from perfection, which is still better than many games can claim.
If you haven't played Hotline Miami, then you should certainly pick it up prior to considering Wrong Number.  Also, shame on you for never having played Hotline Miami.
EDIT: After listening to the soundtrack for a few months after playing HM2, I've found it more heart-pounding and entertaining than the first game's soundtrack.  Some tracks are certainly better than others but the ones that stand out on top are truly pheonmenal.

The game is in an alpha - so the story line is not complete.  There is about 20 hours of playable story content, and what I have seen is extremely interesting. They have the potential to weave a great story out of this game and are headed in the right direction.
It is a hybrid of a FPS/BF1942 (Yes, the old one) land, sea, air combat - mixed into the crafty style of minecraft, splashed with colony/base management & building.
The game uses a Voxel engine, written in Unity, and while I am not always a fan of Unity 3D based engines (Mainly due to it having such a low barrier to entry - so you get alot of shotty development teams using it), but this game is written so that you would think it's using CryEngine or some custom engine. It has no signs of Unity slowness.
There is a huge technology / crafting tree..  Its not perfectly balanced, but it is so engrossing, that I think they will have no trouble balancing it. The crafting works well.. the UI is intuitive and makes it a good experience.
They have a unique system for 'scanning' for minerals - which makes finding materials much easier and helps with base/colony planning. A great idea.. and it also looks amazing.
There is a great system for crafting your own items/weapons/aircraft/boats/cars - the system is easy to use, reminds me a bit of Google Sketchup, except with voxels - and is fairly realistic in material usage, weight, and physics (IE.. heavy planes don't fly)
They allow you to import models from other users in ISO format - which is a great feature if you are lazy like me and really don't wan to spend hours painting and building a really cool ship. All of the importing is integrated using Steam Workshop - so its' very seamless.. It reminds me of the model importing from Spore.
The multiplayer is still immature - most servers are lowly populated - but it is an Alpha game, so I suspect that will change in the future.  It has a bit of the DayZ appeal in multiplayer, so I think this part will come around as game development progresses.  It offers Adventure, Surival, and Coop modes - but there  is no Coop for Story mode.
The game does not feel like an Alpha at all..  The game is fairly stable. I have seen a few crashes due to array indexing issues, but for the most part, its not bad.
The developers have pushed content on a regular basis and seem to be a very worthy team capable of completing this project. I have no fears that my cash used on this project will yield a solid product.
This is one of the few Early Access projects that I have jumped on where I feel like I immediately got a return on my investment. There is a playable demo available at their main site too..  It would be nice if they would add it to steam and maintain it, but that may not be easily done.
The game uses Unity - but the graphics are quite nice.  I've done a bit of indie work with Unity 3D and until I read about it on the forums, I couldn't tell it was a Unity based game. The only real visual hint is that the frill is batched, which shows up in open plains areas.
The terrain blending is done to perfection.. mineral types make sense, the textures look realistic to the terrain (IE.. no gold rock sticking up in the middle of the terrain).  The forests are lush and all of the models are well done. The animations are 'ok' - though they could use a bit of work, but it is an Alpha, so no worries on that getting cleaned up.
On my system, it runs very smoothly - renders distant terrain without issue and feels very well optomized. It is processor intensive and uses a large amount of RAM (4gb after playing a while) - so if you have a system with less than 8gb - you will likely see some slowness loading the areas (They make heavy use of caching..)
The minimum system specs are really low.. I don't see how you could have a fun play experience with just those specs.
The gameplay is fun..  even the crafting isn't bad (I'm not a fan of minecraft/free form building). It has several game modes, Adventure, Story, and Free Build (unlimited resources) -  so it caters to a variety of play styles.
I see alot of potential in the story - if they can pull it off..   Multi-content base battles.. large battleships (all destructible), very similar to the combat of BF 1942 or PlanetFall.  The best part is that it is voxel base, so the entire world is destructible/buildable.
The story starts off very slow.. I had this game in my library a few times.. thought it was just another voxel garbage game - so I didn't give it much of a chance.  If you play the story, give it atleast two hours as it can be very overwhelming at first and will easily turn you away.
However, consider the story to be more of a tutorial on the interface.  It gets better after you get into the vehicle/guns part and actually turns into an intrigueing story of alien races/who did it/why are we here..
This game is lightyears ahead of Landmark - the only other engine I've seen come close to doing what it does.
Overall.. this is one of the best games I've seen in 2014 and has so much potential and seems to be backed by the developers who can pull it off.
If you understand that the game is an alpha and that your story will most likely be spoiled by playing early (before it is complete) then this a definate buy for your library.
However, I would recommend waiting on the story to be complete as my only disappointment in this game was reaching the point in the story where it was incomplete (I really wanted to play on.. it was addicting, fun and a great experience)

Almost everything in this alpha is awsome! Most stuffs are polished .... let me list out the ups and down for y'all:
Alright, for all you skeptic lads out there, I'll start with the down:
Down:
Bugs (at the state of an Alpha, this is pretty damn small)
- Turret falling through grounds
- Some funky clipping sometimes
- Moster Beacon *** not disappearing or removable.
Combat(melee) system could be polished some more ... somewhat stiff.
And perhaps some optimization ... might hurt a bit if you do not have a decent PC, my laptop overheated every once in a while ... but perhaps because I might have been playing for too long ;)
And now, for the good part ... I could go on with this for hours ... however, here're the highlights:
Voxel based construction & destruction (Has according stats, not only for cosmetics)
- The crafting (editor) system is brilliant, it is freaking brilliant! you can make your own:
[VEHICLES] cars, bikes, boats, planes, airships, a flying shoe, etc.
[ITEMS] Shields, guns ... you name it. But mind you, all voxel placements and materials EFFECTS THE ITEM'S Stats. (Sadly, you can't make your own ammo yet ... hope it is added though :) )
["Objects"] Want to make a decoration? Go ahead! Custom fence? Sure! Some dolphin you want to cuddle in game? Go ahead!
RPG elements and Colony system:
Putting this in the alpha persepective ... the Colony system looks quite promising ... though could use a bit of polishing.

Npcs

All in all, this is a brilliant game ... if you are looking for something to sink your teeth in, if you like games the allow you to desgin your own ways ... of travelling, fighting, living .... this is totally the game for you! However, mind you ... in order to thrive in this new world ... there are challenges to the mind ... if you think you got what it takes, then hop abroad the ship and off we go!
See you soon, and safe space faring Colonists.

My second review for this game. My first attempt felt terrible, mainly due to frustrate issues and weirdly synced songs.
However, after the developer contacted me and offered help I retried the game with his advice.
The second play through proved far more enjoyable. With more stable frame rates and using better synced songs I enjoyed the game thoroughly. The Beat detector seems decent, and will work about 80-90% of the time.
Keyboard controls are reasonable, but I found it more responsive with an Xbox Controller, (I haven't tried the PS controller).
Loading up a level (accompanied to Chicane's Poppiholla), I found the beat syncing to within a reasonable level, there were a few mistakes, but because this in Early Access, plus the uniquely generated levels, I let this slide. The timing was okay, but it seemed difficult to gauge when to accurately press the needed key, but, the game play is functional enough to adapt to, and obviously, as mentioned before, this is, essentially, an almost finished beta, so this may be fixed in later iterations.
The game features alternating backgrounds based on the dynamics of the song. Quieter sections feature Melody walking slowly through the rain with a nice cityscape backdrop. The loudest sections can have Melody flying through space.
All in all, the game fells and plays well enough to be enjoyable. It could do with a little polishing, but these issues my be resolved in later versions. The graphics options will obviously need to be tweaked for optimisation, but it looks as if it would work in universal PCs.
I feel I can recommend this game.
