So far I've noticed two three things about this game:
1: It looks and feels fantastic. The visuals are very polished and make for a fun experience in a musical game.
2: As a game; it's just as fun as Audiosurf, but with a different style to it. It doesn't feel at all like a cash-in or knock off of Audiosurf either.
3: THIS GAME IS HARD AS BALLS. the detection is Razor-edge precise, so if you screw up it's usually because you messed up the timing, couple that with multi-handed directional "Button-mashing" and it can be hard at first.
All I have to say is this is a good game, maybe not for ten dollars, but still ok. It definately needs some tinkering in the Control aspect though, allong with full controller support.

I've played this before it came on steam for a lot of hours, and I mean ALOT.
With about 24 hours already played (I've given the game a break for a bit, came back to see how Timoshenko is) on Soviet, I've got to say they've improved it massively since the last time I played. There really isn't any 'pay 2 win' in this game since there is nothing a non-paying player can not get, not paying only makes you need to grind, and even then you might not be good with what you buy. A friend of mine bought Lietunant for USSR and he is absolutely horrendous (He was just level 2 before he bought Lt).
Although many people seem to claim the USSR being too overpowered, I've seen them lose the past 2 - 4 wars in a row (Probably because our generals are horrible and provide us with few resources to counter the panzers and tigers). I usually play with a group of friends, 6 maximum and 3 usually, and we never find the game lacking in entertainment, may it be swimming across a river and launching geurrila attacks with mines near the enemy spawn or driving arround on a GAZ with panzerfausts tank busting.
The whole 'USSR too op devs plehs nerf' is probably the most innaccurate I've ever heard yet. In most games I'm in the best tank we'd get is 1 T-34 1942 model and a ♥♥♥♥♥on of those midget machine gun tanks against the enemy who usually always have the medium tier Panzer tank, tiger tanks and machine gun mounted cars. In one game they had 3 or 4 Panzers against our 2 T-26s. We've lost most of our battles on Staged and a crapload on War, and then the US comes in with the Roflmpson submachine gun and takes out an entire car crew in a matter of seconds, or we get roflstomped by the Stuart tank of ebolastan. I don't think any other faction has had to endure being spawn camped by 2 fighters in a War battle for the entire game having all your cars blown up, but hey, Soviets are OP amirite.
The system specs are quite demanding, a friend of mine even has his graphic card crash every game (Remember the guy who bought Lt from level 2? Yeah that's him). Before I got my new doomsday machine from Mars PC I would run a solid 7 FPS on lowest, but now I run this on 140 FPS minimum on max. You can run a system spec check to see if your computer will be able to run the game on its minimum or recommended
.
Don't know if the sound glitches a bit, you'd sometimes get shot and killed and you wouldn't even hear the gunshot. Bolt action rifles are extremely underpowered (You'd expect to 1 - 2 shot kill someone, not 2 - 3 shots on the Torso with sniper bullets or anything higher). SMG's need to have their recoil a lot higher, especially for the lolmspon sub machine gun. I'd rather put the bolt action rifles as the default spawn weapons instead of the Semi-Automatic ones.
Gameplay is somewhat smooth and requires heavy amount of teamplay, or you won't be going anywhere, lone wolfing is only somethign I'd do as Recon tbh.
Although still not a completed product, it's amazing fun but it does have missing elements, which the developers will hopefully fix in the (hopefully near) future. Oh and please we need better Soviet generals in war :'(

Hotline Miami holds an extremely special place in my heart. It is the first game that compelled me to tell others how fantastic it is, and the reason I started my Lets Play channel. In the past year, some clever marketing by Devolver Digital has revved up the anticipation for Hotline Miami 2 beyond belief. It went from a nicely polished but largely unknown gorefest to a game nearing “mainstream” success while retaining the edge that is quite literally shaping the series. The game wasn’t just carried by marketing of course, the slick controls serve the top-down shooter/stealth/brawler hybrid extremely well. As I danced my way through the stages, I found myself painting like Pollock, on every inch of screen available. Punch a guy in the head, use his gun until it’s spent, fling said gun through a window and kill another dude with it. Glorious. Dance the dance of death with me while I dig a little deeper into Hotline Miami 2.
The best part about both games is undoubtedly the music. I could write for days on how well the pulsing synth and kicking bass positively accentuates the glorious neon frenzy that is unfolding on the screen. Aside from fantastic electro, Hotline Miami 2 features a number of ambient tracks during the dialogue scenes. The ambient music is generally rather eerie, and while I don’t particularly enjoy them as much as some of the more banging tracks, they do serve the aesthetic of a mask-wearing psychopath extremely well. The level of detail in this game is as impressive as ever too. My mind was absolutely blown when I walked by a rack of clothing and it spun as I brushed by it. It doesn’t affect anything about the gameplay, it’s purely meant to immerse you deeper and such small details carry the game a very long way in that regard.
The original Hotline Miami offered masks which had a variety of effects from augmenting your walking speed to spawning you with a weapon. Hotline Miami 2 takes this mechanic to a whole new extreme with a massive load of new masks and abilities. Some do seem a bit gimmicky, such the twin swans who operate as a unit, but overall the slew of new masks to pick from is extremely satisfying. Some masks are inherently better than others, but that was also true in the original game. Then again, what is inherently better for a character who enjoys brawling might not suit a player who prefers an old-fashioned shooting rampage. This freedom is what defined the original Hotline Miami, and unfortunately some of that was stripped away in the sequel. When playing as the swans you aren’t able to pick up any new weapons. Ammo can only be found in specified crates, and this castrates much of the freedom the original offered.
While the gimmicks involved with a few of the masks seems to be a poor choice, there is very little else to nitpick about this game. Some of the sound effects are a bit generic or repetitive, and the fun factor is knocked down a bit due to the frustrating difficulty. Overall Hotline Miami 2 is a blast to play and will keep me coming back to try and top the global scoreboard for a long time to come. The actual gameplay feels a lot less luck-based than the original installment. The storyline is also much more gripping this time around, though it does Tarantino around an awful lot. There is some controversy over a♥♥♥♥♥♥scene that appears in the game, but after stomping a series of five bad guy’s heads like grapes in an old I Love Lucy episode, I didn’t find myself overly phased by it. The entire game is a trip, and one totally worth experience. Just be sure to hide it from your kids.

Unfortunately, this sequel of the awesome Hotline Miami 1 is quite bad. Almost in all aspects, I have to say.
How is that possible? The developer has apparently decided to emphasize the weak points of the game while neglecting the strong points.
First of all, the control scheme is mediocre. You can either play with mouse and keyboard, getting better precision, but the problem is that you aim via a near-invisible cursor that easy to lose sight off. Because mouse aiming is relative, you must know which direction you are aiming - and with twitch aiming, this just does not work. Gamepad has the "lock nearest enemy" function that almost feels like cheating, and the analog stick aiming is absolute, but the precision is far worse.
Another problem is that the game is horribly pixelated and thus the artificially low resolution can cover only a small part of the battlefield. The solution is to SHIFT - peek out of your normal vision range in a given direction that is both clunky and unfit for a fast-paced, twitchy game.
That all is less of a problem in small, close quarters map, where stealth, melee and careful planning is most important. That's why the developer has decided to go for large maps with tons of automatic guns, where you get shot from beyond your visual range most of the time, so you must carefully shift-creep through the levels. Frustrating, slow, bad.
The syndrom of the sequel is the prevalent American "MORE" - more player characters, more guns, more enemies, bigger levels, more story threads. Unfortunately, it all results in a worse game - big levels are tedious to play, ranged gunplay emphasizes poor controls, too many storylines shatter the focus of the game narrative without really going anywhere. The gruesome acts of violence get exhausted fast as a shocker.
4/10 - Disappointing.

I had great expectations for a sequel to Hotline Miami and unfortunately I have many issues with its sequel.  Though the game follows the same mechanics as the first (rewarding for fast execution of levels, rapid restart of levels, choice of weapons) the way the game delivers it makes very little logical sense.
-Punishing gameplay or frustrating gameplay?:  Hotline Miami 2 continues in the same style of merciless gameplay as the first.  However, where the first rewarded you for figuring out the easiest/fasting/most satisfying way to clear levels, Hotline Miami 2 seems focused on simply driving the player to frustration.  Attracting attention with guns is inconsistent and the same shot done in the same location on fresh level restarts will not consistently attract the same mobs or the same number of mobs, eliminating your ability to plan ahead properly.  The overt use of windows also ensures that you will be shot from multiple rooms away without warning, preventing a gradual learning of levels.
-Door agro:  One of the biggest issues I had was luring mobs closer to be executed.  Unlike in Hotline Miami 1, where if they saw you they gave chase, Hotline Miami 2 has restricted this to a range of approximately 1 screen - and only if you're in the same room.  Many times even if a mob sees you through a doorway they won't take notice of you until you physically enter the room, resulting in the ridiculousness of entering and exiting a doorless rooms and exiting them.
-Door Glitch:  Mobs will get stuck on doors.  In doors.  In doorways.  On door frames.  They will get stuck and spin.  They will get stuck and be unhitable for several attacks.  They will result in your death.  Alot.
-Confused AI:  Particularly on later levels, you will find several mobs stuck circling a specific point rather than an area, which appears to be a symptom of bad pathing scripted within the levels.
-Non-linear story and game progression:  Throughout the game the story bounces between different characters, revealing snipits of their stories without context and without a real order, leaving you to question what the hell is going on half the time.  This also leads restrictions of characters, weapons, and playstyles across all levels as different masks/abilities do not carry over between the different characters.  This ensures you will feel no attachment to any of the characters throughout the game, their stories, or a specific gameplay style.
-Poor Level Design:  This is connected to the former point; however, in general the game is balanced to favour specific weapons and abilities, restricting the player options in completed specific levels in a way that makes sense to them.  The design reflects a heavy use of guns and punishes the use of melee weapons on several levels, preventing you from repeating a specific style of play.  This may not seem like an issue at first but if you enjoy playing a specific way, you will find yourself restricted.
-Very limited unlockables:  Besides the 3-ish masks unlocked per character story, and restricted to said character (and some of them repeating between characters), the unlocking of progressively more interesting weapons from Hotline Miami 1 has been removed completely.  The fact that some of these starting abilities run out thus deffying the logic of picking level perks.
-Limited weapons choices:  The selection of weapons has been drastically cut down, with only key weapons being available for pickup based on level.
-Unfinished story:  The story remains incomplete for many of the characters, resulting in multiple instances where their story just ends.  It quite literally feels like they created too many stories and could no correct them all, literally just throwing their stories away at the end.
Overall:  Great soundtrack.  Okay gameplay that could be better.  Prepare for gamebreaking frustration.

When I first heard about this game, it was from a friend. I watch him as he played it while on skype. I was interested in it, but I didn't know to much about it. For the longest time it was only for Windows. I being a Mac user, had to wait until it became available for Mac. Now, This game is absolutely stunning. The ability to customize your character in somewhat the same style as an Elder Scrolls Game. Unique armors and weapons that can be looted or bought from cities in the game. Mounts that allow you to ride into battle with your army behind you. Tactical commands, allowing you to take your armies fighting prowess to new heights. This game is sure to give anyone who plays a unique experience. So much so, even my girlfriend has taken to it. (She flies a unicorn banner in her save) (I fly the Black Stag Banner) What I couldn't stress more enough is while playing this game talk to everyone, even the bartenders. Get your reputation up with place you plan on conquesting before actually taking over. Don't flip flop from one alliegence to another, it will leave you with a lot of bad standing with other faction members. When in battle, think strategically. If you happen to be fighting in the mountains on hilly slopes, I would suggest holding your men and letting your enemy run down hill at you allowing you to take advantage of the plains with your archers. 3 main types of troops, Infantry, Archers, Chalvery. All having important roles in your kingdom. Tournaments galore throughout the kingdoms of Calradia. Mount & Blade is a historical simulation and RPG set in a fictional realm of warring kingdoms called Calradia, each of which seems to be based on a different historical nation (Vikings, Saracens, Mongols, etc). You play an individual who is free to roam this world and carve their own path.
When you begin the game, you create a character in a similar manner to many RPGs, adjusting your apperance, name, gender and a backstory which (presumably) affects your starting stats, as well as choosing your starting location. After a short introductory quest, you are free to travel around the continent, recruit followers, do quests for villages and lords, join a kingdom and rising up the ranks and so on.
Overall, I strongly recommend Mount & Blade: Warband. There is a great amount of depth and the world is very open, thus there are lots of different ways in which you can gain renown, experience and or gold, including trading, robery and raiding, hunting bandits and taking them prisoner and selling them, quests, setting up and running a series of businesses (brewery for example), and once you gain a fief (a village or town which a king can give to their vassals) you can gain money through taxes and tarrifs, as well as spending money to upgrade your fief through various buildings. The fact that you are not forced down a particular path is one of the good things about this game, it also gives the game a high level of replayability. Furthermore, as becoming the ruler of even one faction, let alone the entire continent, is not a quick process which further adds to the longevity of this game.
Battles are one of the main parts of the game and they are quite fun. You have a degree of tactical control over your followers although once a battle enters a melee stage, it can get quite chaotic. Nevertheless, battles are visually quite impressive with large numbers of individual soldiers represented, including infantry, cavalry, archers and siege weapons. Sieges are particularly impressive and the fighting on the walls of a castle is often particularly fierce. At the beginning of the game, you are quite weak and often need to stick with your men. While it's possible to single-handedly defeat multiple enemies in melee combat, it can be quite difficult, often requring you to block an onslaught of attacks before an opportunity to attack presents itself. This means you can't go charging in Rambo style, as against three or more enemies, it's difficult to block all of the attacks against you.
Graphically, Mount & Blade: Warband is very nice. It's not brilliant but it's certainly nice which is evident in the visual detail of soldiers, and skies are quite visually appealling as well, particular at dawn and dusk.
Overall:
I'd give it 9/10

All of my Steam friends probably know that I love rhythm games. And games with pretty colors. This game has (or claims to have) both.
Before I start, please note this is the Early Access version. Things can change in the future, I'll try to change my review later.
So, why am I not recommending Melody's Escape? Because this game actually doesn't have both things I love. Reasons:
1) Rhythm detection just doesn't work for most songs. Most songs were discarded when I tried it (which means almost all random beats), just a few of them had confidence over 40%. And probably only 1 over 70%.
2) Even if confidence is higher, you are pressing buttons outside of beats in most cases. Or you expect to press the same keys when music repeats, but no - they are mostly different and you easily miss a button because of this.
3) When you miss a button which is related to an obstacle, you die and respawn in a few seconds. This is bad. Especially when beat detection isn't the best, because this means you are dying too often.
It really isn't fun to watch the screen sometimes for 10 seconds (mostly less, but yes, this can happen too if there's a really long slide or jump) without being able to do anything. I want to play, not wait until I respawn.
4) Putting beats right after you jump and land is awful. You have pretty much a few milliseconds to react. No. This is bad.
5) Difficulty. Relaxing is too easy and boring (no, pressing the same button for a few minutes isn't relaxing, sorry), normal is sometimes too hard (but that's mostly because of weird beats).
6) The game looks pretty on screenshots, but it gets boring really fast. At least change the background more often. Just look at Audiosurf - there's always something cool to see. Do it like that.
7) Blur. This is a big no in a rhythm game. I need to see clearly what is coming.
I really wanted to like Melody's Escape. I will definitely give it a try in the future, but it's a thumb down from me for now.

Amazingly good for an early access game. I haven't played through the entire story mode yet, and haven't messed around with the build or survival modes yet, but Planetary Explorers currently looks and feels like it could be a fully developed game. It has good graphics and a well thought-out, if very loose, beginning to a story so far with a very imaginative setting and good mechanics. I definitely like the crafting system better than games like minecraft, and the voxel mining system looks very natural relative to a lot of other games I've played, although I wish the camera didn't track the character's motions quite so  precisely. The environment is wonderful and fairly varied once you venture beyond your starting area
My biggest complaints for the game so far are that A) there needs to be a bit more detail in the starting missions or at least a more in-depth help screen to describe some of the controls (such as that you can toggle running with "r" or that, yes, those ARE herbs that you can harvest by facing them and right-clicking) and B) that the game becomes exponentially more memory-intensive as you progress and begin actually exploring the island. The second one is by far the most serious, because so far I've explored less than a tenth of the massive continent you start on but have encountered the error that my fairly high-quality, memory-rich expensive laptop has run out of memory to run the game on. At the moment, the game is trying to store too much awesome for my computer to handle at the same time. Much as I am in favor and awe of the good graphics and incredibly huge open map, I would settle for a bit less of it if it meant I could finish the game.
That said, the game shows great promise and I would definitely buy it again just for what I've seen so far.

I really want to like this game, but I simply can't.
The concept is awesome, I love Warhammer and a coop game in the fantasy universe is a great idea. The theme with the Scaven is inventive, usually developers are lazy and go Orcs or Chaos, so a change of pace is nice.
However, everything other than the universe and theme simply feels unfinished,
First off, framerate is a huge issue. I cannot get the game to stabilize at 60fps no matter what I do (within reason, I wont go below 1920x1080). Hovers around the upper 50s most of the time, plummets to mid 40s whenever there are more than 4 enemies on the screen. Not only that, but the game looks awful. I was not expecting much, but mostly everything except the lighting looks dated. Skypboxes are awful and anything at a distance is just ugly, hell, even most things right up in your face are ugly (weapons are the exception). Animations are sloppy at best, terrbile at worst. And the "weight" to melee that you've seen mentioned in all the previews is just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. It simply feels disconnected, like your clicks are only good for turning models of enemies into ragdolls.
I love the variety of Scave, it rare to find a game where the PR-hype of "no enemies look the same" has a basis in truth. You won't see the same models, or at least notice them very often, unless it is special enemies (Stormvermin, Gunner, Ratogre, etc.). But at the same time, they do look rather terrible. I do not know if the animations or the character models are worse, or if everything is just dragged down by the framerate, but the game just doesn't look good.
AI is also a huge issue, you can visibly see the range at which enemies react to your presence (about 10 meters or so). Once they react, their reactions are just not very interesting, they usually run straight for you, sometimes get stuck. Once they are just right infront of you, they pause, and then do an attack. They do not feel aggressive, more like sheep going to slaughter. The exceptions are the specials, these feel more dangerous, but still, they don't seem "responsive".
With that said, the game is far from easy. I failed the first map on all 3 of my tries on Normal with a team that actually seemed to stick together. We were not excellent, but not bad, and the game still got us. This did not feel unfair though, so that is a plus.
One last nitpick: You pass through friendly characters. Now, this is not a mortal sin, but it just feels sloppy and irksome. I understand that there would be chokes where the player characters just get stuck on each other if there was collision detection on the characters, but they should have designed the game with this in mind.
As I mentioned, I only played 3 matches, so keep that in mind. But as I intend to refund the game, I can't justify spending more time with it.
Another 6 months in development and the game might have been ok. Now it is subpar.
Edit: Just wanted to clarify that my system is "ok" at worst. I run an i7 3770k, GTX 970 ad 16 gb ram. I think that it is not unrealistic to expect the game to be chugging along at a stable 60fps with this system.

I figured I would give this game a chance since it was up for free for the weekend. Now, I'm a big fan of killing zombies, I rarely get tired of putting a shot or a axe in the skull of a zombie. With this in mind, I like what Contagion is, but there are things about it I'm not too crazy about it. Before I go about posting what I think is great about the game, I will start with the things I'm not too crazy about.
1. Forgettable characters - Aside from picking the character you like, that is really about all there is to character selection. There just isn't anything that makes you remember the character beyond it's appearance.
2. Lack of a story - Now I know the game isn't a RPG or anything, but a little bit of story would be nice. Matter of fact it would be a nice way for the character's to be rememberable.
3. Flashlight needs work - Now the flashlight is very handy and by no means am I saying it's useless. However, why can the flashlight not light up rooms? It just seems to light up a small area and jeebus don't get too close to anything in particular with it. The light at the center can just about block out the view of items. You cannot even light up a room for a fellow survivor whose weapon doesn't allow a flashlight fitting.
4. Lack of Zombie variations - Aside from the standard Zombie, player Zombie, and Riot armored zombie. There really isn't anything else of danger around. A Zombie dog would have been a great addition to this game, or even enviromental hazards like falling buildings, out of control cars crashing, or something. A well organized team can easily put down a army of zombies, unless of course they're out of ammo.
5. Ammo hoarders - Don't get me wrong, when you need ammo badly, you need it badly. However, there are people that will pick up ammo for every gun BUT the gun they actually have. I cannot tell you how many times I've been down to one bullet and cannot even get a person to throw a magazine or ammo box my way.
6. Terrible Iron Sights - Now you don't need to serve a tour of duty in a war to tell some of these weapons have terrible iron sights. I've had times where I've woundered if it was easier to shoot from the hip or just aim down sights. Obviously it's better to aim down the sights, but some weapons just have such terrible iron sights it renders players ineffective at times. However, if you get use to the iron sights, you can easily work your way around their terrible design. Out of all the guns, your best bets are on the Pistols, the shotgun, and the hunting rifle. Pistols are semi-automatic, so you can control your rate of fire with them. Shotgun has bad iron sights, but it makes up for it with a wide shot spread so you just need to aim for the head. Heck you may even take down more than one zombie with a single shell. The Hunting rifle zooms in and it's the sniper rifle, so you don't have to deal with iron sights with it.
7. Getting stuck on stuff - This is more of a minor complaint, but there are times that it feels like I get stuck in doorways at times. It looks like I got enough room to enter, but some how I still get stuck.
Now for the things I like about the game.
1. The Enviroment - It actually feels like a proper zombie apocalypse. Nothing is clean, nothing is overly destroyed. Things feel just right.
2. Zombies are true to nature - Short of shooting them in the head, blowing them up with a grenade, or hitting them with a melee weapon. A zombie will keep coming after you. Thank you devs, these are true Zombies!
3. Sound effects  - The sound effects in this game are really good in my opinion. Since there is no real map to use, you can listen for the gun shots of your fellow survivors to actually tell you a general idea of what direction they're at. Or as a Zombie you can use it to find where your targets are at (short of using the vision sight for foot prints.) Overall everything sounds good in this game.
4. Limited resources - Nothing worse than playing a survival game and finding every little thing you need in the world in no time. Ammo, weapons, and medical kits are so hard to find. You actually have to concern yourself on how you approach the streets, corners, buildings, and rooms.
5. Infection - There is a chance when you get hit by a zombie that you actually get infected. If you're infected, there is a limit of time before you start to feel it and eventually turn against your fellow survivors. You won't know you're infected till it's too late. Some people may find this annoying, but I love it. Even if you die as a survivor, the game isn't over for you. Because now you can fight against them as a zombie and lead Hordes of zombies towards them. (Nice way of getting payback on those Ammo hoaders)
6. Board up and hold out - Now I know everyone likes base building, but honestly it get's old seeing player made sky forts or whatever. Contagion may not have base building, but boarding up windows is one of the most logical ways of keeping the zombies out. I just wish the boards didn't fall inbetween line of sights. If a Zombie gets close enough to try and break into the building, it's hard to get them off the window boards without shooting the defense itself.
7. Plenty of maps and game modes - The game isn't limited to just your typical "Start at A and get to C by moving through B" (Though ti does have a escape mode which is fun still), but you also have a PVP game mode where players start off killing each other, then holding out against zombie palyers in a game of Hide and seek. A objective based game where players locate survivors and take them to be extracted across zombie infested streets or neighborhoods. Also with players seemingly able to make their own playable maps, it's no real concern about there ever really being a feeling of a lack of enviroments to play in.
8. Maps change - Nothing better than playing a map that can change from another playthrough. I've had games where doors that were usually unlocked, were actually blocked off. So really you cannot predict what route you must take to get to a objective, you sort of have to learn on the fly.
9. Random starting gear - Our survivors may be all different, but the nice thing is that they start out with random gear. You may have just a pistol at first one game, then the next you may have a pistol and a SMG. I just feel this is a nice way to keep things feeling interesting.
Overall Contagion isn't a bad game, but it doesn't do too many things great. With some stuff fixed, a few improvements made, and some other little things. The game can honestly stand toe to toe with the Left 4 Dead games. Don't take this as me saying "i want it to be more like Left 4 Dead." I just want to see some more stuff that will pull me into the game more. One more zombie type, fixed weapon iron sights (or at least a visual zoom in), and some other little things would just be perfect for someone like me. While I cannot stand playing the game for hours on end. I can at least say what time I do play, I enjoy greatly.
If you see this game on sale and you want a good little Zombie shooter game, I would highly suggest picking this game up. I only paid five bucks and don't regret it.

Hotline Miami holds an extremely special place in my heart. It is the first game that compelled me to tell others how fantastic it is, and the reason I started my Lets Play channel. In the past year, some clever marketing by Devolver Digital has revved up the anticipation for Hotline Miami 2 beyond belief. It went from a nicely polished but largely unknown gorefest to a game nearing “mainstream” success while retaining the edge that is quite literally shaping the series. The game wasn’t just carried by marketing of course, the slick controls serve the top-down shooter/stealth/brawler hybrid extremely well. As I danced my way through the stages, I found myself painting like Pollock, on every inch of screen available. Punch a guy in the head, use his gun until it’s spent, fling said gun through a window and kill another dude with it. Glorious. Dance the dance of death with me while I dig a little deeper into Hotline Miami 2.
The best part about both games is undoubtedly the music. I could write for days on how well the pulsing synth and kicking bass positively accentuates the glorious neon frenzy that is unfolding on the screen. Aside from fantastic electro, Hotline Miami 2 features a number of ambient tracks during the dialogue scenes. The ambient music is generally rather eerie, and while I don’t particularly enjoy them as much as some of the more banging tracks, they do serve the aesthetic of a mask-wearing psychopath extremely well. The level of detail in this game is as impressive as ever too. My mind was absolutely blown when I walked by a rack of clothing and it spun as I brushed by it. It doesn’t affect anything about the gameplay, it’s purely meant to immerse you deeper and such small details carry the game a very long way in that regard.
The original Hotline Miami offered masks which had a variety of effects from augmenting your walking speed to spawning you with a weapon. Hotline Miami 2 takes this mechanic to a whole new extreme with a massive load of new masks and abilities. Some do seem a bit gimmicky, such the twin swans who operate as a unit, but overall the slew of new masks to pick from is extremely satisfying. Some masks are inherently better than others, but that was also true in the original game. Then again, what is inherently better for a character who enjoys brawling might not suit a player who prefers an old-fashioned shooting rampage. This freedom is what defined the original Hotline Miami, and unfortunately some of that was stripped away in the sequel. When playing as the swans you aren’t able to pick up any new weapons. Ammo can only be found in specified crates, and this castrates much of the freedom the original offered.
While the gimmicks involved with a few of the masks seems to be a poor choice, there is very little else to nitpick about this game. Some of the sound effects are a bit generic or repetitive, and the fun factor is knocked down a bit due to the frustrating difficulty. Overall Hotline Miami 2 is a blast to play and will keep me coming back to try and top the global scoreboard for a long time to come. The actual gameplay feels a lot less luck-based than the original installment. The storyline is also much more gripping this time around, though it does Tarantino around an awful lot. There is some controversy over a♥♥♥♥♥♥scene that appears in the game, but after stomping a series of five bad guy’s heads like grapes in an old I Love Lucy episode, I didn’t find myself overly phased by it. The entire game is a trip, and one totally worth experience. Just be sure to hide it from your kids.

Unfortunately, this sequel of the awesome Hotline Miami 1 is quite bad. Almost in all aspects, I have to say.
How is that possible? The developer has apparently decided to emphasize the weak points of the game while neglecting the strong points.
First of all, the control scheme is mediocre. You can either play with mouse and keyboard, getting better precision, but the problem is that you aim via a near-invisible cursor that easy to lose sight off. Because mouse aiming is relative, you must know which direction you are aiming - and with twitch aiming, this just does not work. Gamepad has the "lock nearest enemy" function that almost feels like cheating, and the analog stick aiming is absolute, but the precision is far worse.
Another problem is that the game is horribly pixelated and thus the artificially low resolution can cover only a small part of the battlefield. The solution is to SHIFT - peek out of your normal vision range in a given direction that is both clunky and unfit for a fast-paced, twitchy game.
That all is less of a problem in small, close quarters map, where stealth, melee and careful planning is most important. That's why the developer has decided to go for large maps with tons of automatic guns, where you get shot from beyond your visual range most of the time, so you must carefully shift-creep through the levels. Frustrating, slow, bad.
The syndrom of the sequel is the prevalent American "MORE" - more player characters, more guns, more enemies, bigger levels, more story threads. Unfortunately, it all results in a worse game - big levels are tedious to play, ranged gunplay emphasizes poor controls, too many storylines shatter the focus of the game narrative without really going anywhere. The gruesome acts of violence get exhausted fast as a shocker.
4/10 - Disappointing.

I had great expectations for a sequel to Hotline Miami and unfortunately I have many issues with its sequel.  Though the game follows the same mechanics as the first (rewarding for fast execution of levels, rapid restart of levels, choice of weapons) the way the game delivers it makes very little logical sense.
-Punishing gameplay or frustrating gameplay?:  Hotline Miami 2 continues in the same style of merciless gameplay as the first.  However, where the first rewarded you for figuring out the easiest/fasting/most satisfying way to clear levels, Hotline Miami 2 seems focused on simply driving the player to frustration.  Attracting attention with guns is inconsistent and the same shot done in the same location on fresh level restarts will not consistently attract the same mobs or the same number of mobs, eliminating your ability to plan ahead properly.  The overt use of windows also ensures that you will be shot from multiple rooms away without warning, preventing a gradual learning of levels.
-Door agro:  One of the biggest issues I had was luring mobs closer to be executed.  Unlike in Hotline Miami 1, where if they saw you they gave chase, Hotline Miami 2 has restricted this to a range of approximately 1 screen - and only if you're in the same room.  Many times even if a mob sees you through a doorway they won't take notice of you until you physically enter the room, resulting in the ridiculousness of entering and exiting a doorless rooms and exiting them.
-Door Glitch:  Mobs will get stuck on doors.  In doors.  In doorways.  On door frames.  They will get stuck and spin.  They will get stuck and be unhitable for several attacks.  They will result in your death.  Alot.
-Confused AI:  Particularly on later levels, you will find several mobs stuck circling a specific point rather than an area, which appears to be a symptom of bad pathing scripted within the levels.
-Non-linear story and game progression:  Throughout the game the story bounces between different characters, revealing snipits of their stories without context and without a real order, leaving you to question what the hell is going on half the time.  This also leads restrictions of characters, weapons, and playstyles across all levels as different masks/abilities do not carry over between the different characters.  This ensures you will feel no attachment to any of the characters throughout the game, their stories, or a specific gameplay style.
-Poor Level Design:  This is connected to the former point; however, in general the game is balanced to favour specific weapons and abilities, restricting the player options in completed specific levels in a way that makes sense to them.  The design reflects a heavy use of guns and punishes the use of melee weapons on several levels, preventing you from repeating a specific style of play.  This may not seem like an issue at first but if you enjoy playing a specific way, you will find yourself restricted.
-Very limited unlockables:  Besides the 3-ish masks unlocked per character story, and restricted to said character (and some of them repeating between characters), the unlocking of progressively more interesting weapons from Hotline Miami 1 has been removed completely.  The fact that some of these starting abilities run out thus deffying the logic of picking level perks.
-Limited weapons choices:  The selection of weapons has been drastically cut down, with only key weapons being available for pickup based on level.
-Unfinished story:  The story remains incomplete for many of the characters, resulting in multiple instances where their story just ends.  It quite literally feels like they created too many stories and could no correct them all, literally just throwing their stories away at the end.
Overall:  Great soundtrack.  Okay gameplay that could be better.  Prepare for gamebreaking frustration.

I've only been playing for a dozen hours but so far I'm immensely impressed by the quality and originality of the game. In recent years (due to the success of MineCraft) the game market has become saturated with sandbox survival games, with few titles delivering a compelling experience. Starting off in story mode, the game plays and functions very much like a normal 3d RPG, the fact that you can alter your surroundings in this world hardly ever registers as its quality is similar to that of any MMORPG of around 2008 (WoW, Guild Wars, etc.). Although the visuals don't (currently) feature HD graphics the world of Maria still manages to be brilliantly beautiful and captivating, relying more on ambiance, flora, lighting, and simplistic symmetry to carve out an idyllic image on various unique landscapes.
From the moment you crash land on Maria you will be immersed in the whole world and evolving storyline. The game seamlessly blends sci-fi and medieval elements, making you feel as though you are struggling to survive when beginning with nothing. While you may start off running about with a knife, very soon you will upgrade yourself to a sword and shield, and later laser guns. The combat itself is rather simplistic, point and shoot or stand and stab, but there's enough large monsters to keep you on your toes as you frantically attempt to run between camp on the open plains. (Frankly I'm not sure if the dark forest with lurking wolves or the open tundra with giant warbirds is more terrifying).
Of course at the stage of development there are some bugs, but the only game breaking one seems to be an issue with NPC "following" which may disrupt certain quests in the storyline, resulting in a little bit of frustration in trying to escort a glitchy zig-zaging NPC stuck in the ground. Most of the other bugs are pretty minor and I've seen a lot worse in games that put out on the market, so it seems like Pathea is dead set on making a high quality game. While it probably won't see as much success as Minecraft, it'll definetley make a great showing and is a fantastic first game for the publisher.

Cons:
Complete inability to remap controls and existing controls are pretty bad (notably the location of crouch)
Game completely falls off by the end, leaving you constantly repeating trial and error scenarios. This is where the flow of the game breaks hard. Whereas early on it is fairly intuitive, expect a lot of 'bs' deaths by the end due to bad pacing.
Sound refuses to work on some cut scenes. This is a problem other Deadlight players have had, as well.
Lack of logic interferes with the game. Example: Bullets magically can't shoot through glass when that's what the design wants. Main character is a forest ranger who can for whatever reason parkor like a god, but can't swim- no explanation given for this. Gets disarmed of his weapons and despite being right next to an assault rifle, he ignores it.
Controls are weirdly unresponsive at times. This is critical in a tension paced platformer.
Utter lack of direction of what/where you're supposed to do or where to go. This is a hassle in a game where it is very difficult to determine what platforms you can walk on and what is background. Some environmental targets have context based highlighting, but only when you're particularly near them instead of being readily available. Considering you 'interact' with these at range, that's a nuisance.
No real care taken in the port to PC. You will see gamepad directions everywhere. There's a general lack of polish here.
Basically, I don't regret playing the game but this is unachieved potential- it could have been sooo much better with just a little more care put into the port.

I like my zombie apocalypses, though i can be a bit particular about it. Non of that 28 Days Later stuff  for me, i want to see the classic slow walking stumbling rotting corpses kind of zombie world, and Deadlight captures that world perfectly and does so in 2D as well!
So it's a 2D platformer. You're character starts out being cut of from his friends and needs to find a way out of the building he is in which is being swarmed by zombies and find a way to reunite with your fellow survivors. By climbing up ledges, jumping over gaps from platform to platform to rooftop, dragging crates and throwing switches to activate traps and open up passage ways you make your way through a very convincing post apocalyptic scenery thanks to some nifty looking graphics and a gloomy atmosphere. And a honorable mention for the stylefully done comic cutscenes by the way. You are far from invincible so you will have to rely on your wits by staying high of the ground  and luring any potentially dangerous zombies in to traps. You do get a melee weapon and a gun, but as with most zombie survivors ammo is scarce and you can only swim a fire-axe so many times.
On the gameplay side everything is pretty solid. I did here some complaints here and there that the controls aren't all that great or responsive and it makes you miss a jump and fall to your death, but i have to say i haven't had any problems with that really. I might have messed up a couple of times here and there but checkpoints are never far away so repeating your action isn't all that big of a deal.
Is the game perfect? Well i wouldn't say that. It's good and i've enjoyed it but as many have mentioned it is a bit on the short side. You'll be through it in between 4 to 5 hours, depending on the collectibles like diary pages and id-cards you went out of your way looking for.  You can however unlock some extra like artwork and making of videos so that is a nice extra for those who really liked the game. Next to that i have relatively some minor complaints that didn't let me enjoy the experience completely. Now the story isn't anything to write home about, it's fairly straight forward, but that's fine. I've even enjoyed reading some of the diary pages which i found were quite well written. But when your character starts talking it just changes things. The voice acting is overdone and makes him sound like a cheesy action hero, not at all fitting to the writing. I even think that all the writing of the diary pages and the collectables like post cards have been done by a completely different team then the dialogue writers.
But as i said, minor gripes on a otherwise good title. Definitly recommend it. Although i will say that i find the full price a bit steep so i suggest to wait until it comes by on sale. I've scene it pop up for $3 or so on occasion.

Since the game is still in early access quite a few more change can be expected to come along to improve the game.

THE DIFFERENCES BETWEEN HOTLINE MIAMI 1 AND 2
I just beat the game so I'll try to tell you. HM2 is bloodier, and it's much harder. However, I think it's harder due to poor level design. The best way to put it is most of the levels are like the really hard floor in the chapter "Hot & Heavy" (you know the one). Most levels have long corridors and lots of windows, so most of the time you won't know there's an enemy till it's too late.
HM2 has a much more complex storyline, as it involves around a dozen playable characters, and I'm considering playing through it multiple times just to understand it.
My main gripe is that there is much less unlockable content in this game. HM had tons of weapons and masks that you could use on EVERY LEVEL. HM2 has around 10 unlockable masks and 3 unlockable weapons that you can use on certain levels. You could argue that the new masks are cool, quality over quantity and all that, but I think there should've been more masks.
However, whether you should buy Hotline Miami 2 all depends on ONE THING. How in-depth is the level editor? That level editor can easily make or break the game for me. Can you imagine playing a recreation of Doom, with a custom Doom Guy mask?
In conclusion, if you REALLY need more Hotline Miami, you should get this game. It's no where near as good as the first one, but it's still pretty good I guess. If you really don't want to risk your money on this, wait for the level editor to come out, and then see what people think of the level editor. It should be out sometime this spring.

After getting to about the 3rd or 4th act in this game I can safely say, just stick to the first game if you're considering which one to purchase.
This game sticks to a very similar gameplay/ graphics style of the first which I love - as well as the overwhelmingly awesome levels of gore! The soundtrack is also a really cool concept to this game. It's as good as the first but not just copied and pasted from its predecessor - which I thought was great because it shows they're very capable of creating a good set of music to suit the games' atmosphere.
Then, there's the negatives...
This game's overall level design, contrary to the first game, is really not that great. There are horrible amounts of enemies in massive compounds of floors. That really isn't the worst part. Many of them have to quite literally be lured in by the everchanging (I'll get on to that later) character. It feels stupid to have to outsmart almost every enemy by bating them in so you can steal their weapon and fight off the rest of them, presuming you even succeed in doing so. Another huge problem with the massive floors is the god forsaken camera. If I had a Pound for the amount of times I would get shot from across the map without even being able to see my enemy... and of course, I would have to fight them ALL off again the next time around - which wouldn't be a problem if it wasn't for the sheer amount of enemies.
Now, the story I'd imagine is somewhat interesting with the whole idea of the tape recordings. But, the fact is, if you thought the first games' story was hard to understand, have a go at understanding this one. This game has huge amounts of dialogue that I try my best to read. But that's not the problem...
This game changes character almost every level, allowing for lots of different styles of play, granted, but also a hugely complicated storyline that ultimately makes little sense to what I'd imagine to be quite a lot of people. You can see for yourself the backstories of all these people if you so wish.
Also, in my opinion, the mask system is abysmal compared to the first. Some masks are somewhat overpowered. Others are completely and utterly useless and very frustrating to use. Most of them only allow you to use a couple of weapons or none at all out of the 4 i've seen so far - which really isn't good because I like variety and flexibility in Hotline Miami - it's argubly a huge aspect to the game.
Overall, I would not recommend this game until after you have thoroughly played through the first - which is one of my favourite games on steam.

Medieval gameplay done best. This game has politics, marriage, and strategy in moving up the ranks of the feudal system. Embark on a journey to become Emperor of Calradia. Unite with other lords and gain vassals as you build an army to take your place as ruler. Things are rarely peaceful and the combat makes that fact a very good thing. With amazing mounted combat and sieges that actually feel epic, you might think you were actually experiencing the middle ages. With tons of armor, weapons, and horses to choose from all with unique stats, you build a character all your own. Manage your food supply for your band of mercenaries and keep morale up or they just might leave. Recruit special hero units with unique back stories to help you on your quest. Host feasts in a castle or town that you own and participate in tournaments for fortune and fame. You will spend hours of your life playing this game. It will grab you and hold you in the same way that Civilization keeps you playing just one... more... turn.
The graphics aren't very stunning, but honestly, you likely won't mind and it actually helps as some of the battles can get pretty large.

This game is SO much fun. I've been having a blast playing it in both single player (adventure and story mode) and multiplayer with friends over the past week. REALLY glad I bought this- for an alpha version of the game it's surprisingly polished, and so far I haven't found any bugs at all which is amazing. I've beta tested a TON of games over the past 15 years and I'm always finding bugs to report, but so far, I've found nothing. The dev's are really quick to update it too when something breaks, they're really on their game which is a refreshing change from a lot of the 'early access' games on steam that don't see updates for months at a time. One evening, the animation for chopping trees broke. I went to sleep, and it was fixed the next day! I got this on sale, but I dare say, it's worth the full price for how much time and care thats being put into this. It's like Minecraft and Landmark had a baby with the space adventures of Terraria/Starbound thrown into the mix. All my friends who play Minecraft with me love this game to pieces and we've actually been playing this a lot instead! The ONLY thing I would add is that I wish there was more weapon/armor variety IN the game, BUT with the ability to create stuff out of voxels (called/saved as ISO's) you can make or download a TON of fantastic stuff that have been made by users, so it's not even a big issue really. The game doesn't have some decor you want? Build it, or find it on the workshop! Absolutly amazing. And so far, the community has been VERY friendly and helpful- I really hope it stays that way.

What I want added to the game
-Pets
-Personal socialization with NPC's (like marriage or something)
-More weaponary (although there is quite a bit of that already)
-Classes you can choose would be an amazing addition. (Just like most RPGs)
-Endless mode possibly as the game does in fact, have an ending
What they should improve on
-Although I truly understand that this game is still early access, there are quite a few easily noticable bugs. For example, the first time I stepped into the ocean, I kept glitching back and forth.
-I don't know if this is just unfinished or they accidently left it out, but some things that NPC's say, you can actually hear it in the audio. However, some things they say can't be heard in the audio. I have even encountered a speech where the NPC was talking halfway, and then he just stopped, so I had to read the rest of it.

You may see the thousands of reviews praising Warband as one of the best games of it's kind. It probably is, as good RPGs are pretty scarce these days. But Warband is not the perfect RPG that these thousands of people make it look like. It's flaws are plenty, some of them being way too annoying, up to the point that some people considered them game-breaking and created mods to "fix" the game.
Well, that should be enough for an introduction. Let's get on with the game itself.
What always defines an RPG is it's single player mode and Warband is not the exception. Warband's campaign is pretty unique in the way of letting you choose your own way to reach the throne of Calradia, the fictional land where the game takes place. Be a mercenary, pledge an oath to an existent lord (more specifically, a King), start a rebellion by supporting a claimant to the throne or by supporting yourself.
Warband has tons of quests to help you gain renown, exp, money and improve your relations with lords and cities. One lord could hire you to break into a town/castle and rescue his family member, other could just hire you to track and kill outlaws. Some might, if they trust you enough, even entrust their wife to you for an escort mission to a town.
Don't like being a mercenary or just wanna win lots of money quickly? Become a travelling merchant. Discover trade routes and become rich without meddling on Lords affairs.
Unfortunately, that's where good things end. Although some people claim that you have complete freedom to do whatever you like (someone here compared it to Skyrim), the game's obvious goal is solely to reach the throne. Otherwise you will just be doing the same things over and over again until the you get bored. The inability to die or loose in any way, besides supporting this goal, just kills immersion and realism to the game and makes it too easy. It's just a plain stupid feature. A known sadistic Lord could capture you, retain you in his castle for weeks and then you go free like if nothing would have happened. No penalization of any sorts.
Another thing to notice is the horrendous political system. Without mods -- specially Diplomacy mod -- politics are just "nobles can control fiefs and get different missions than the commoner". There's no actual political game on Warband. You only declare war, ask for piece and make "friends" that you can make vassals for your kingdom. And even then, you don't need to make friends. Defecting Lords from other kingdoms will just spam your court and fill all your possible NPC spawning spaces, even if they hate you, you don't have any fiefs to give and you're a dishonourable ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. That's how bad politics are in this game.
The last nail in the coffin are the battles and sieges. The game has a limit on the number of soldiers that can appear at once, which is 100 if I remember correctly. This completely ruins large-scale battles, like lord vs lord or king vs king battles. To make matters worse, the deployment of your troops is mostly random and they all just charge at the start of a battle. You literally have to babysit them each time you start a new battle.
So, if you were planning on using each and every soldier for a good tactic combining everyone's weaknesses and strong points or just to rush the other guy and win by numeric superiority, too bad.
If the campaign is the heart of M&B, then the combat is the backbone. In that case, Warband is the 300 movie hunchback. It's ugly, it can barely stand or walk and can't fight for sh*t. In other words, Warband's combat sucks. PvP is, literally, grabbing the largest non-spear polearm you can get, wear no armor (it doesn't even protects you that much and slows you a lot) to move fast and make circular moves while using horizontal attacks. If this tactic(?) isn't getting used, then it becomes a feinting-fest. Both players abuse the feinting mechanics to bypass the horrendous and extremely complicated blocking mechanics until one of them dies.
Cavalry? Use a spear, both for being a rider and for killing cavalry. That's the only use you will give to the spears. Try to use any other weapon as a rider and people will keep killing your horse on a single blow.
Why do I make spears look like crap? Because stabbing attacks barely work on this game and most spears only have a stab attack. Stabs doesn't do damage if the weapon's pointy end isn't half a meter away from the enemy. If it's too close, no damage or extremely few damage (if you do 4 damage, you were really lucky) is done. If it's too far, you do less damage. Also, blocking a spear it's a cakewalk, since it just has one attack direction. Trying to stab someone in Warband is a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥ rendering spears useless for anything but cavalry.
Finally, clumsy character's movement mechanics doesn't help out the fighting mechanics. No sprinting, no dodging, no rolling, no crouching, kicks are useless, etc. As the rest of the gameplay on this game, it was overly simplified.
Overall, Warband could have been a lot better if the developers cared to improve the combat from M&B. Hopefully, they will improve it on M&B2.
Finally, the part where I compile everything worth mentioning that doesn't require a topic on their own. These being mods, music, graphics, story.
Mods are the reason this game is alive after so many years. Anyone who ever plays a modded campaign or a custom multiplayer mod on Warband doesn't ever gets back to native (vanilla). The problem is that the game gets updated way too often -- honestly idk why since the game is stable as it is -- and most of the time, mods won't work on newer versions of the game. You will need the mod's author or authors to update it, which could take time, depending on the modders's personal schedule. It's a hassle, for both the modders and the players. But it's the best feature of this game.
Music is plain bad. Not much to say here. You will find yourself turning off the music after the first 5 hours and putting your own as a playlist.
In the graphics department, this game is very ugly. Armors, weapons, blood, landscapes, cities, everything on this game looks horrible. Even with graphical overhaul mods, it's still ugly.
Though graphics doesn't need to affect your view on a game, it's pretty annoying that there are no facial expressions for the campaign mode. It would be much more immersive if I could tell what a person thinks of me by just watching his/her face, or how my questions and answers affects him/her. And of course that it would be impressive to watch the amazing landscape surrounding the towns and villages, or the villages and towns themselves. Saddly, it's not possible. If you want impressive looks, get mods that change the whole map, like 1429: la Guerre de Cent Ans.
Story is almost non-existant, and the few story the game has it's nothing new or innovative. There was an Empire ruled by Emperors, the Empire crumbled and 6 factions appeared, each ruled by 1 individual who claims to be the legitimate ruler of Calradia. That's it, nothing special about it.
Again, if you want a good story, get mods. The only way to get this game to be impressive is by installing mods.
5/10 without mods
7/10 - 8/10 depending on the mod
Warband needs a lot of work to be a decent game; work that the community is already doing. It's sad that modders have to develop what we paid the developers to do, but that's how things are.
As I said already, buy it on a good sale and mod it as soon as you get it.
Hope this review helped you make a decision. Also, don't just read reviews. Check gameplays too and make an opinion for yourself.

So far, I'm quite pleased with the state this is in, in Alpha. I was an avid Minecraft player though less on the "elaborate builds" and more on the "exploration and live in a hollowed out cave" side, so initially this is pretty good for indulging your Exploratory side, and building looks customizable enough that it'll be a decent-sized learning curve vs simple blocks/pixel recreation; ergo, it'll be more in-depth and nice looking than Blocky builds would, but also harder to tweak just right than simply slapping one block/lego onto another in some cases.
It is an Alpha though at the time of this review, so there's some minor bugs/issues; movement can be wonky sometimes(it was worse, but they actually made it better in a recent update), I had a quest to escort an npc to a place and had to kill 3 monsters at the location, but they spawned underground or something and, while still being marked on my map, weren't killable, breaking the quest. The NPC went ahead and acted like I'd beaten them, but since I hadn't, couldn't complete. This was in Story Mode, though, and will likely be fixed at the rate they work.
Server-based Multiplayer is available, though still finicky in it's current iteration. I tried to create a game with a friend and it simply wasn't showing up in the list, and vice versa. I assume/hope that they'll be working on that and making hosting & joining a little easier for the average joe to do without having to learn to set up "actual" servers for small-numbers co-op play with a friend or two.
TL;DR: If you like Survival/Exploration/Building games a la Minecraft, Terraria, or even similar to Everquest Landmark, with a solid single player experience as well as Multiplayer options, this is worth a shot for ya. I'm eager to see where it goes as it progresses into a more stable Beta and eventual Launch.

Another great indie game (set in Canada and developped by a Spanish team lol) with fantastic visuals despite it being a 2D side-scrawling game. The game manages to create a believable post-apocalyptic universe where 'shadows' (aka zombies with red glowing eyes) have taken over the world and people are just trying to survive amidst the chaos and fear. The story is compelling and well-narrated by the main character as you progress through the environments and his journal and other collectibles you find along the way help to fully flesh out his character and the situation that he finds himself in. If you pay close attention you may realize that all is not as it seems and that the alternate ending is the 'real' ending.
The combat is refreshingly different as it's in your best interest to avoid the infected as much as possible and cleverly lure them into specific positions so as to better circumvent them or gleefully watch them stupidly plummet to their deaths (second deaths? True deaths? bah, damn zombies screwing things up again!) as you taunt them into following you into deadly pitfalls. You will shimmy across telephones lines while below dozens of undead reach towards you only to have the cable snap and have you rushing like a madman away from the monstrous horde. At other times you'll be tasked with using elements of the environment to help you navigate safely through roaming zombies or fleeing from an attacking helicopter intent on turning you into ground beef across the rooftops of a ruined city. You do get access to powerful guns (and melee weapons) at various points in the game but these sections are rare and never last very long, forcing you to never get too comfortable or feel too safe :P
Can be completed in 5 hours or so, a bit longer if you're a completionist. Worth every penny.

Probably one of the best 2D indie games I've ever played. But you probably already know trhat. What you're really wondering is, how does it compare to Hotline Miami?
Well, it's harder. I mean, a lot harder. The level design is way more open, much bigger, and much more of a puzzle than the first. Think you can just run in with Tony and punch your way out of everything? Not this time. Death is absolutely needed to figure out where you're going. Whether this is a good thing, or a bad thing, it's up to you, but I think they're equally great in different ways.
Music wise, this is hands down the better soundtrack. Sure, the first has some classics, and there are a few misses on this one, but when it hits, it hits hard. And there are over 40 tracks. There are more hits on this soundtrack than there are songs in the first.
Storywise, absolutely it's better. First game? All we had was some janitors prank calling people to kill mobsters. Now, I won't spoil it, but it's way more fleshed out, way more thought out, and way more crucial to playing the game. I wish the organization was better though. And don't get me started on that ending, it was an amazing trip.
Overall, is this better than the first? I can't answer that, each is good in their own right. Is it a worthy successor? Absolutely, 100% yes.

This game delivers very well for what it has to offer and I would definitely recommend this game to someone who is intrigued by cooperatively-driven gameplay. I shall continue to play because it offers a very entertaining and somewhat rewarding experience that I enjoy very much.
Presentation: This game has a low production value, but that doesn't really negate from the overall package. Monochrome has delivered a reasonably enjoyable title that differs greatly from other titles that are similar too it. Generally speaking, the game has a nice and slow pace, but picks up progressively as you immerse yourself into the game modes that it has to offer. The game modes are all worth playing. They paid a legitimate amount of attention to detail. Many environments are dark, the zombies can be fierce, and you feel as if you must really fight for your survival. And that's what it's all about.
Graphics: The Source Engine has been on the market for quite some time now, but that doesn't mean that the graphics are unimpressive. The graphics are still very nice and there are a lot of options you can adjust to get it to how you'd like. This game does not push the Source Engine to its limits in terms of visual aesthetics, but there is a sufficient amount of visuals to keep you immersed in each environment. The lighting can be a little-bipolar - either extremely dark or extremely bright, but the flashlight lighting was done very well. It even alarms the zombies quite a bit. The frame rate also holds together very well when tons of zombies drop in on you and your partners' location.
Sound: They did a fantastic job with the audio system. You can hear rain drop onto tin roofs of surrounding shacks or drop onto plastic tents and the differences in sound are all there. You can even hear the rain trickle off of buildings and onto the ground. The voice overs were done okay, but the players can be a little annoying when they say the same thing over and over about keycards or how every door separates "US" (players) from "THEM" (zombies). Because of the fact that the GPS system is not an absolute pinpoint marker to locate other players, you must really do well to communicate with other players, but with that said, you'll also learn to appreciate the sounds of other players' gunshots, bones cracking from falling, and other sounds as well. Music is also there and it is very appropriate. It's subtle, but enough to enhance the overall feel.
Gameplay: This is where the game stands out. I'd definitely recommend playing with people you know and play it with the intent of wanting to succeed, otherwise you will crumble. Alone, you might not even enjoy the experience at all.  You cannot run and gun through this game. You have to plan routes together, find and conserve resources, as well as ration them fairly. Knowing what you NEED to take versus what you WANT to take can make the difference in having to put bullets in the heads of a legion of zombies or just wiping a huge chunk of them out with an IED. This is one of those games where you will be highly tempted to wander off alone, but doing so can be extremely dangerous and may cost you the game. Stick together and you will find that it is a much more rewarding experience, even if it is possible to succeed scrambled. That would be a no-no.
Lasting Appeal: The gameplay formula is sufficient enough to provide for definite replayability, but the ice-breaker is content. The small number of maps and game modes may feel limited to many people who have played or decide to play this game. If Monochrome adds more content to this videogame, this will definitely be a much more longer-lasting game. However, the maps and modes are very fun when played as they should be, and the overall experience does not have a bad aftertaste. On the contrary, it may feel natural to want to play multiple sessions on the same map. Aside from it being fun, there is also a modest level of randomization on each map, which allows for some unique playthroughs each time.
I'd say play it, but play it with the right people. :)

It's alpha. you'll need to reference the wiki to find out what different items do, how to control the game, and what you ought to be doing.
But even with that, it's fun. The item/vehicle/weapon creation system is pretty unique amongst this type of game, and is done reasonably well (a part of me ached to have more Blender-like controls, since modifying existing objects is a bit rough at the moment). Combat is decent, though most of the time I tended to lure monsters to a colony so the colonists killed them for me.
After an hour or two of resource collection you won't need to do it again, which is good. It's got a great mining system that smoothly deforms the ground as you mine (it's actually the best implementation of that I've ever seen), but the animation is slow and controlling the camera underground is an exercise unto itself.
Building a colony is fun, I appreciate that there's finally a minecrafty game that emphasizes that you're not alone, and allows you to recruit NPCs to work at your colony. There do seem to be some bugs with it, but nothing insurmountable. My biggest gripe is how *small* your colony has to be. It's not feasible to build dwellings and houses for your people, because if you put their beds too far away (read: like 50m away) from the colony center, it won't count towards your colony.
Overall, it's definitely rough, but I like where it's going. I'd recommend that if you're uneasy about the "early access" pricetag, that you wait 6 months and give it another go - i expect it'll be more fully-featured at that point. If you want something cool to play *right now*, i'd still go for minecraft or starbound. But this is one to keep an eye on.

A lot of the AI and animations has a lot of polishing left to do, the combat's hilariously clunky, and the 'storyline' isn't terribly well-balanced.  But that said, it's a fantastic start.  There's plenty to do, plenty to build, and lots of frightening spore-creator kinds of creatures to roam about and kill vicariously.  If you want a game that gives you enormous amounts of space and room for creativity, this is it.
All that aside, though, there's a hell of a lot you can do with building up your base and your armaments.  Shields and swords can be custom-designed with the voxel editor.  Buildings can be given lovely cornering and layouts, with plenty of accessories already avaioable for use.  The cars are just that perfect blend of controllable and completely bonkers to drive, making your bouts of ATVing hilarious, wonky, and yet not actually frustrating.  This game picks -way- up once you start getting into vehicles and colony control.  That said, to get the resources needed to get there, you're probably gonna have to look at the wiki. Medieval gameplay done best. This game has politics, marriage, and strategy in moving up the ranks of the feudal system. Embark on a journey to become Emperor of Calradia. Unite with other lords and gain vassals as you build an army to take your place as ruler. Things are rarely peaceful and the combat makes that fact a very good thing. With amazing mounted combat and sieges that actually feel epic, you might think you were actually experiencing the middle ages. With tons of armor, weapons, and horses to choose from all with unique stats, you build a character all your own. Manage your food supply for your band of mercenaries and keep morale up or they just might leave. Recruit special hero units with unique back stories to help you on your quest. Host feasts in a castle or town that you own and participate in tournaments for fortune and fame. You will spend hours of your life playing this game. It will grab you and hold you in the same way that Civilization keeps you playing just one... more... turn.
The graphics aren't very stunning, but honestly, you likely won't mind and it actually helps as some of the battles can get pretty large.

"Do you know what time it is?"
It's time for a bloodbath...
Hotline Miami is back ! And Wrong Number starts where the previous one finished.
It acts around many new characters, levels, dialogues and stories that clear out the reasons of the massacre you perpetrated in the first one.
By talking about dialogues and stories, this next (and final) chapter is deeper, darker and stronger.
It's a real pleasure to follow the destinies of these new characters and (at last !) find the truth about everything.
Because Hotline Miami 1 was very short in terms of narration and immersion, even if you could play as one of the bosses and change the story to find who was behind the contracts.
With new skills and ways to kill your targets, the game is much more varied and complex than the previous one.
New masks, weapons and bonus, i didn't espected less from Dennaton.
But the most interresting feature of Wrong Number is the ability of some characters to receive the help of an other hitman and couple their weapons to increase your combo rate.
You can even, depending of the character and the level, start with a reloadable firearm and a knife.
Or the fact that with some  masks you have movements skills that makes you move agile and bring new ways to do combos.
Because Hotline Miami is all about scoring, accuracy and death.
You select a mask or a weapon, a level and go for points.
Every take downs gives you points  which depends of the variety, the speed and the number of kills you will do in your combo window.
And this is the soul of the game.
In this order: You ente ra level, spot and learn enemies locations, find the appropriate path... and start your combos bloodbaths. And you will die alot.
Depending of the characters or the masks, you can't receive more than one or two bullets in the body. Even if your targets are weak, they die with one hit and you too.
To bring more difficulty, enemies are different: the fat gansters can endure 2 gun shots, the dog spots you from a far and attacks quicker or more simply the weapons enemies holds forces you to find a differend approach.
The marvelous thing, you feel like a real hitman: quick, accurate, deadly... and the finnest, silent. And scoring is not only for leaderboards, it unlocks achievements, new items, levels and secrets.
In Hotline Miami 1 you could find a mask that gave you a drill to kill and get tons of points.
Here it's better, cooler and ... well in fact everything has been increased.
Even the number of possible kills, the soundtrack or the overall design of the game, which is amazing has been reworked. Like when you pause the game and stop the screen as if it was a video tape.
Or as the story itself wich tries to lost you into the madness of the hitmans and the dark atmosphere of this Miami of the 90's where blood and murders are common.
We have few bugs such as enemies blocked near doors or the poor A.I level wich is still the same from Hotline Miami 1.
But the really questionnable aspect of the game is sex. You can disable sexual scenes at the beginning. They are few and, of course, brings a much more mature atmosphere than the previous one. Like the gory pixel art of the number 1, this will make people debate about games and the way they deal with violence in general. The overall "murky" atmosphere has been respected and it won't let anyone insensible.
To conclude:
Gameplay cooked at its finnest, design so well reworked that the number 1 goes to the past, very long and funny. Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is a masterpiece.
And like all masterpieces, in a way or an other it will affect you.
"Do you know what time it is ?"
It's time for a bloodbath. The madness has returned and it's good to be mad...
Brilliant.
N.B: Note that if you've pre-ordered the game, you will receive new items like masks, weapons or even a new character in Payday 2. And at 13 bucks... this game is a steal.
A must buy.
