I really love Hotline Miami, I say that people should play this. I beat it and it took me within 2 days (counting my AFK). I do recommend this game to others. I am a big fan of the first game, but things in this sequel aren't doing it any justice. First I really want to get the things out of my chest of what I didn't like about this game. I am simply gonna state what I didn't like about the game. (I will say nothing about the story to prevent spoilers)
One thing that I didn't like. You didn't get to play as the fans as much. There were levels of them but there weren't a fair amount of them. So don't expect to play as Tony the Tiger, those chainsaw/gun twin pair, and that double machine gun bear. That is because they have an oversaturated amount of characters which you didn't feel much for.
Also the reason why this game is difficult is because there literally is no room to be reckless or take risks. The first game was "recklessness is rewarded." But this game "stay very close in corners, camp, bait those dumb enemies in and kill them one by one. And memorize that dude at the window with a shotgun miles away which you cannot see". The way they used the large scale map concept didn't help at all because it just got frustrating.
Now I believe that if a game is gonna be difficult, it needs to give you plenty of options. This one, nope! You have to play the game by the rules. I do love difficult games that motivate me to think more with fast real time reflexes, but when a gameplay is so structured and so forcefull, it really holds itself back and destroys its own potential.
Okay, enough with the flaws. I loved playing as the fans although their levels were short lived. Once you start to play Alex and Ash (chainsaw/gun twins), spend the time to master them, and they are just fun to play. You will get the same theme from the first game if you loved it. The electronic beat and discordant color pallete and the 80s feel. The gore and violence is bumped up for the best. I mean you literally ripped out one of the enemie's spinal cord with head out of the body "FATALITY"! The dead body sprites have more of a nice touch.
So I know I said more of the cons than the pros of this game, but give this game a chance. It's worth playing. But to summarize what I said, the fun times are fun, the boring parts are boring, and the frustrating parts are just unfair. The good does sometimes outweigh the bad.

Everything in life is about death and taxes. Mount and Blade is no exception, though it does manage to make it fun. Years before I bought this game, it was recommended I get it as soon as possible. I did look at it sure, but from the store page it looks like an old RPG that didn't age well and isn't relevant any more. I see now how wrong I was.
Sure I don't have a lot of hours into, but it's been a real blast to play and I've seen people with thousands of hours into it, so I don't see it getting any older any time soon. I bought it during the 2014 Summer Sale, I can't quite remember why. One of my friends was with me and we spent a good majority of our night laughing at how bad the enemy AI was, or the outdated graphics, or the war cries after winning a battle. There was something about riding into battle on a horse singlehandedly against 100 enemy horsemen just to be dragged around for days as a prisoner that was just funny. The entire game seemed like a big joke or parody towards the "European RPG" genre. I put it down not expecting to play it again until my friend bought it himself.
I restarted and decided to actually do the first quest and not go on suicide missions the entire time. What I was met with was a surprisingly open ended RPG that was fun to invest time into. I can't really explain it while writing it down, so I won't even try. I'll put it in a some kind of faux chart because everyone loves charts.

I've barely played this for 10 minutes and I'm already in love with it. Not even because of the gameplay but because of the masterful lore. I instantly fell in love with this game after reading through the existing pages in the journal. It reads like any proper story. This is how it familiarizes you with the protagonist and really does a better job in text than many games do in an hour origin story level. You learn that he's a gruff, loner, traditionalist ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but at the same time an artist, poet and atheistic thinker.
The visuals are great too. They're that really nifty 2.5D style that Trine popularized. Unreal's signature high specularity rendering style is easy to screw up when you're writing a grim and dark game but they did a really good job here from what I've seen so far.
The gameplay isn't something I've really focused on so far but I'm liking it. You could do worse when it comes to a zombie game. The jumping and such feels kind of loose but from the looks of things there won't be any platforming that is too bad. Otherwise fine though.
Why yes, I am a sucker for good lore. How did you notice?
P.S. The game comes with its OST all in one directory. Look at your install dir.

Before you go all "ugh, zombies again", give this game a shot; I don't remember there being any zombie-oriented 2.5D platformers. The puzzles are not overly complicated, but require some very satisfying brainwork. There is a lot of resource management and cautiousness involved, as combat against more than two zombies is usually a bad idea. Myself, I was very satisfied with the game.
Oh, there's just one thing I will take issue with: the controls. Not that they're badly mapped and unintuitive; they're just annoyingly unresponsive at times, which led me to a lot of unfair deaths.
Still, if you persevere, you'll have a very satisfying experience on your hands.

It feels thrown in for the hell of it, like the levels that involve the soldiers- you can tell that these were taken from a scrapped idea for another game because the mechanics don't even match up, you're stuck with one gun and you can't pick up other guns- if you don't play like the game wants you to play (do melee kills and save your ammo for the invincible fat guys and the snipers that hide and take potshots at you) congratulations, you've just wasted several minutes of your life in this game with huge sprawling levels- and no checkpoints.
In the original game, the inconsistant AI gave every playthrough a sense of unpredictability, here it often results in enemies that randomly show up and kill you just for the sake of wasting your time- screw all that planning and carefull playing you did, this guy/dog magically sees you all of a sudden.  The original Hotline Miami was difficult, but not cheap- this game is downright unfair.  I find my self screaming ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t constantly at this game, something I never did when I died in the last game.
This game's story is cryptic for the sake of being cryptic.  There are many loose threads that just start and end, you never get time to actually care about any of the characters and it jumps around from past to future... the game never bothers to endear you to any of the people you actually play- I got to know Jacket and Biker, here I'm just playing as mess of pixels guy number 5 with a dumb mechanic attatched to him and a story I don't really care about.
The game's sole saving grace is the music, the soundtrack is yet again brilliant- I have nothing bad to say about it... except that I have to hear the same song again and again because I have to restart a level 100 times because the game just kills me when it feels like it.
If you've never played Hotline Miami, play the first.  If you really, really, really like it give this game a spin for the sake of the soundtrack alone.  Otherwise prepare to be disapointed.

Remember all those fun times you had quickly skirting from room to room, frantically picking up weapons to throw at one guy before shooting another and then running into the next room to dodge the guy patrolling out in the hall so you can deal with him a bit differently? Yeah ♥♥♥♥ all that noise this is now a cover based shooter.
No seriously, a good deal of the levels now deal with essentially finding the best form of cover and then luring baddies nearby to shoot at them. Thats bad AI and level design in a -THIRD PERSON- cover based shooter. Top down its sometimes just literally impossible. You will find yourself wondering, in a way that only video games provide, if a Lamborghini is in fact merely something that impedes forward movement (hint: yes) or if it is the magical type of thing that also impedes bullets (hint: somehow no).
You will also have levels where you start off with enemies pathing directly into your start zone. Meaning that if you don't have those starting positions memorized you will inevitably die on your first ever go around, simply because there is no way for you to look up fast enough to see them.
Also remember how in HM1 sometimes the "I heard a gunshot" AI was kinda finnicky and would lead to some frustrating deaths when you swore you were far enough away but he came charging at you anyway? Yeah, thats not fixed. And in the HUGE OPEN levels of HM2 its even more prevalent and obnoxious!
Also remember how you could chose which mask to wear to best fit with your gamestyle? Jake was great wasn't he, what with the ability to toss things lethally. Made all those levels in HM1 where you had those tricky hallways a lot easier when you could toss a bat down a hall and knock out three guys like you were playing bowling. Yeah mask choice isn't really a thing anymore. I mean it is, but not really. You can do it ocassionally and when the game lets you because this is their silly overwrought narrative dammit.
Ugh. This game should have been great. I mean for christ sake its still Hotline Miami! In those moments where you have masks and nice tight spaces and and can do those quick decisions to scoot into here and then there and get off one of those long chain combos from just doing the thing quickly, its still utterly brilliant. But when you are abusing the AI, waiting back and using Shift to desperately search for the next baddy, you aren't playing Hotline Miami anymore, you're playing ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Gears of War.
Loved every second of this. Simply an amazing game that I will not forget anytime soon.

You want to know what's a great example of what Ubisoft's development team can do? This gem right here.
Far Cry 3 doesn't ever forget its roots in action and non-linearity the original and second were praised for, but it takes all the garbage vehicle driving and repetitive gameplay of 2, fixes it, and throws it into the pacific.
You can spend dozens of hours just exploring the Rakyat Islands and find cool stuff and doing side quests, hang glide across the ocean, or go knee deep into the storyline, which is what I suggest doing. Far Cry 3 does an excellent job of blending realistic and (occasionally) silly elements (you'll be fighting a human trafficking ring by...burning down their weed production.) but never feels forced or boring to play. gunplay is as fast and fluid as you want it to be, and the excellent branching skill tree system gives you multiple ways to play and approach the game. Everything oozes replayability and action in a well done package. My only real complaint is that the last 1/3 of the story doesn't feel like it transitioned smoothly. Vaas Montenegro is an expertly done villain (he's on the bloody game art) yet he's not even the main antagonist, and it feels like a weird closing act of the game.
Despite the small flaws and the requirement to use Uplay, the game is excellent and one I can heartily recommend. I hope someone makes a mod of this to turn the acid trip that is Far Cry 2 into something like this.

This is a 2D zombie survival platformer in a 3D style, with more emphasize on "flight" rather than "fight".
Advantages:
-Great art
-Decent music
-Mostly fluid animations
-Consistent 60 fps in game, (locked 30 fps in cut scenes)
Disadvantages:
-Controls can be fidgety, not very tight (not even close to Meat Boy level)
-Voice acting isn't very good
-Cut scenes are sepia toned slideshows
-Story isn't unique or very compelling
I enjoyed this game until I got to the Rat's labyrinth. The Rat is an unrealistic character in a highly realistic game, his voice acting is the worst of all of the characters, and his platforming level is absolutely infuriating.
At the beginning, the game tries not to hold your hand and gives you reasonable clues as to what your supposed to do and it was fun and is rarely frustrating. But that all changes in the Rat's labyrinth, where all the traps are obvious but really difficult to maneuver because of the slippery controls. Since the route is obvious and linear, you don't get the pleasure of figuring out where to go because of your own wit. And since the traps require very precise movements (and are even timed at some points), but the controls don't allow for very precise movement, it becomes a chore instead of a game.
At this price, it's not worth the hour and a half I got out of it before I had to endure the Rat's labyrinth.
Maybe get it if it's really cheap, or you have a gaming rage youtube channel.

This is a 2D zombie survival platformer in a 3D style, with more emphasize on "flight" rather than "fight".
Advantages:
-Great art
-Decent music
-Mostly fluid animations
-Consistent 60 fps in game, (locked 30 fps in cut scenes)
Disadvantages:
-Controls can be fidgety, not very tight (not even close to Meat Boy level)
-Voice acting isn't very good
-Cut scenes are sepia toned slideshows
-Story isn't unique or very compelling
I enjoyed this game until I got to the Rat's labyrinth. The Rat is an unrealistic character in a highly realistic game, his voice acting is the worst of all of the characters, and his platforming level is absolutely infuriating.
At the beginning, the game tries not to hold your hand and gives you reasonable clues as to what your supposed to do and it was fun and is rarely frustrating. But that all changes in the Rat's labyrinth, where all the traps are obvious but really difficult to maneuver because of the slippery controls. Since the route is obvious and linear, you don't get the pleasure of figuring out where to go because of your own wit. And since the traps require very precise movements (and are even timed at some points), but the controls don't allow for very precise movement, it becomes a chore instead of a game.
At this price, it's not worth the hour and a half I got out of it before I had to endure the Rat's labyrinth.
Maybe get it if it's really cheap, or you have a gaming rage youtube channel.

Note: I played through the whole game before actually getting in Steam, I don't even know why I bought it, compulsive spending I guess.
Overall Impressions
I expected this game to be better, first of all, there are a lot of issues are which are making the experience less enjoyable. I'll start with gameplay, the controls themselves are good, but the overall platforming feels slow and clunky, things easily blend in with the background and make it harder to see where you need to jump to.
Animations aren't so good when platforming too which makes the game feel even more awkward while jumping around. Sometimes you have to stop and carefully place your character right above an object (which takes time and zombies are almost always following you)  in order to jump and trigger a grabbing animation.
The shooting is kinda fun, despite the clunky aiming and platforming, the so-called game "secrets" are simply obvious, but the atmosphere is really good.
Puzzles are boring and generic (pull this here to climb over there), the game difficulty and feeling of despair you get when you see the world easily become obsolete when the game saves every five seconds and gives you full health every time you re-spawn.
Soundtrack isn't anything mind blowing, but it isn't bad either. The graphics are gorgeous though, but the game lacks simple options to control them (I'll talk more about that later). The story is your generic zombie apocalypse kind of thing, the characters are barely likeable and voice acting is terrible.
The cutscenes look like they are scaled down to 720p, you can clearly see some artifacts here and there and are not really enjoyable, seems like they saved money on rendering actual cutscenes and just went for the comic slide-show type of narration here.
Port
The port is where it gets really bad, the game is locked at 30 FPS, the menu has barely any video settings at all, FPS drop in certain places for no reason and the game sometimes freezes for a couple of seconds and unfreezes on its own. Optimization is really bad overall.
Controls are fully rebindable, so we have that going for us. There is an audio settings menu with basic options as well, which is always nice. The game also supports a gamepad (It would be strange if it didn't, considering it's an Xbox port).
I can't believe they couldn't make a decent PC port out of a Platfromer/Shooter kind of game.
Quick Version:
- Lack of Basic Graphics Options
- Bad Optimization
- 30FPS Cap
- Awkward Platforming
- Clunky Mechanics
- Bad Voice Acting
- Generic Characters and Story
+ Great Atmosphere
+ Beautiful Graphics
+ Shooting Things Is Somewhat Fun
+ Fully Rebindable Controls
+ Gamepad Support
Would I recommend this game?..uhm not really, I expected more and even if you like the game itself the port will definitely ruin your experience to some degree.

That was truly a beautiful and dark journey! You are playing as Randall Wayne, who is searching for his wife and daughter. You could say that it is nothing incredible, despite the fact the world is over. Unknown virus spread through Randall's homeland, turning people into wild beasts called "ghosts". In this post-apocalyptic environment Randall wants to survive and to find his family members, being surrounded by infected from one side, and by his flashbacks on the another side.
"Deadlight" is a classic platform game which includes puzzle riddles and some tasks requiring agility to pass them. Apart from that, the graphic and whole atmosphere is noteworthy. You can see beautiful landscapes of the city, suburbs or sewers, making a great background to the actual game area on which you can climb, run, hit... or even whistle to drag enemies' attention. There are also cutscenes made in drawn-slideshow style that tell the story in it's crucial moments. Randall can also fight with different weapons: fireaxe, gun or rifle. Ammunition is limited, so even when you get shotgun, you won't turn into a person who defeats all enemies without much effort.
I must also say some words about the achievements. I enjoyed getting them. Some of them are easy (like beating a certain chapter of the story) or harder (like beating the game on nightmare difficulty), but in general you can get over in my oppinion 50% achievements unlocked easily by just finishing the game.
The difficulty level is balanced - the game is not too easy, but it's not too hard to pass either.
About disadvantages... well, I can say it was maybe too short. It might be worse if the story kept on extend, so (oh well)  I believe the creators calculated the time needed to pass this game correctly. These several hours spent in post-zombie apocalypse world and atmosphere of being hunted are enough to love this game (at least that's my oppinion).
What will be the end of Randall's history? Will he find his family, or is there any cure for that terrible illness that brought apocalypse to Deadlight's world?
To know the answers, you must check it out by yourself by beating this game, 'cause it's totally worth it!

You want to know what's a great example of what Ubisoft's development team can do? This gem right here.
Far Cry 3 doesn't ever forget its roots in action and non-linearity the original and second were praised for, but it takes all the garbage vehicle driving and repetitive gameplay of 2, fixes it, and throws it into the pacific.
You can spend dozens of hours just exploring the Rakyat Islands and find cool stuff and doing side quests, hang glide across the ocean, or go knee deep into the storyline, which is what I suggest doing. Far Cry 3 does an excellent job of blending realistic and (occasionally) silly elements (you'll be fighting a human trafficking ring by...burning down their weed production.) but never feels forced or boring to play. gunplay is as fast and fluid as you want it to be, and the excellent branching skill tree system gives you multiple ways to play and approach the game. Everything oozes replayability and action in a well done package. My only real complaint is that the last 1/3 of the story doesn't feel like it transitioned smoothly. Vaas Montenegro is an expertly done villain (he's on the bloody game art) yet he's not even the main antagonist, and it feels like a weird closing act of the game.
Despite the small flaws and the requirement to use Uplay, the game is excellent and one I can heartily recommend. I hope someone makes a mod of this to turn the acid trip that is Far Cry 2 into something like this.

When I first beat Hotline Miami 2, I felt like it was a disappointing mixed bag. Now that I've had time to think, I think...it's still sort of a mixed bag. Here's another review.
The Good:
-The Soundtrack. It's Hotline Miami. It's ♥♥♥♥ing amazing. Seriously.
-The Graphics. It's Hotline Miami. It's ♥♥♥♥ig amazing It's still got that cool retro feel, and now with larger maps and better technology, it looks really good, both effect and detail-wise.
-The Weapon/Character Variety. I was a bit surprised to find that there actually was this character, ability, and weapons variety. All of the abilities seem useful in at least some sense, and the many takedowns and melee weapons are especially satisfying.
-The story...sort of. I'm glad it brings every character we wanted to see, no matter how short their time was, together for "closure". Granted, some of them get too short a time, and the individual endings for each character are disappointing, but I'm impressed with how Dennaton managed to keep everything generally together. It really ends the only way it can, with psychotics and explosions, not to spoil anything. And to see everyone get what they deserved but to stil make you sad, that's a feat.
-That. Last. Level.
-The Level Designer. That is all.
The Bad:
-Level Design. Sigh...this is my, and several other's biggest problem with the game. First, this game focuses way to much on guns, and not enough on melee. Melee was encouraged for a lot of the first game, but here they scrapped that just to make things more epic as you get closer to the end. Second, there is way too much of four things. Fat Guys, Windows, Open Spaces, and Hallways. Seriously, those four things essentially become artificial difficulty nodes towards the end, and they are half of the reason why guns are so encouraged. Level Design feels a lot more Mobile and "lively", but at the cost of making it seem more shallow. Third, the levels are too. I don't actually mind the length of the game in "scenes" too much, but the levels get so long and tedious it almost becomes unbearable, like Mark.
-Lack of focus and poor character paths. I and many others were most hyped for a few. Pig Butcher, and The Fans, and maybe Jake. Yes, The Fans get the most levels, but they just stop only about halfway (lengthwise, not actwise) in. And I felt the game really should have centered around them. They never learned anything or changed, they were just there to make you feel like it was HM1 again, and it's really sad because I liked Tony. The Pig Butcher is a tutorial character with two missions. He deserved better and his story went nowhere. Jake also got two levels, which is especially sad considering he also has the two best "Masks", Jake and Dallas. His story went nowhere. The Son felt like a copy of The Fans at times, and while his story went cool places and ended the game with a bang, he didn't have much of a character. The Henchman went nowhere. Evan had some cool gameplay, but his story just went nowhere too. Pardo's story ALMOST got a great, disturbing conclusion but was interrupted by the ending. Jacket had no story. Richter was more of the "make you feel like HM1" characters, but at least he got somewhere.
-Beard. I really feel bad for Beard in this game. He's my favorite character from the first, and his story was actually one of my favorite arcs, despite it's flaws. But his gameplay...is bad. It feels like a top down Battlefield at times with him. I was expecting his levels to be a cross between Metal Gear Solid 3 and Rambo, but no. Elite Unit, burst in guns a blazin. Can't even pick up weapons and actually STARTS with guns. He has GUN unlocks. It just feels...wrong and poorly done.
-Richard. I just wanted everyone to have some interaction with him, cuz he's cool.
The Ugly:
-Nothing. Nothing in this game is truly bad. Just disappointing. I still think it's a good game on it's own, just very underwhelming.
Conclusion: Still buy this game, just be aware of the facts.

If you're a returning Hotline Miami player, do you remember those 1 or 2 unfairly designed levels towards the end of the game? Those hallways far too long to see the gunmen before they shot you? Of course, they weren't that big of a deal because of how rarely that happened. Unfortunately, almost every level in the latter half of Wrong Number is designed around using the view limits against you and frequently spawning you in an enemy's line of sight. If that kind of trial and murder is a turn-off, (and it should be) then I'd say skip this one, at least until the level editor is live but even then it'll be a gamble.
It's very similar to Hotline Miami - as can be expected - but there is more of a focus on guns in Wrong Number, to the point of including several levels where apart from shooting you only have a knife that can't be thrown. I wouldn't mind this if the enemies with weapons weren't so deliberately placed outside the visible area and as such, I found myself getting irritated way more quickly than in the original game. The problem is the fairness just isn't there. It felt like my fault before, now I have to remember where off-screen I got shot from because even though I found myself holding the SHIFT key for most of the game, it didn't help. Except now there's no George mask to help with that.
Speaking of masks, they're different now. Many levels in the game don't let you choose one and when you do, they're very specific in function. The variety in abilities isn't really there compared to the first game, though there is some. A couple of the choices yielded interesting and fun gameplay changes but I don't want to spoil them, as they were great fun to discover and use for the first time.
I hope you're patient because I've got a lot more to complain about with Wrong Number so let's get this done. Way too often I found my character dying right after restarting, as enemies would spawn in the same room and immediately rush them, prompting yet ANOTHER restart. I don't know what possessed them to design the levels like this, I can only assume it was their inelegant attempt to extend the game's length. Even with this almost NES-era level of sadism, I still found myself under the "one-more-level" hook and turned a late evening into an early morning.
Unfortunately those aren't the only problems with how the game plays, though those are the biggest. Enemies get stuck in doorways, the doors themselves get in the way more than they ever help, walls have many invisible edges to get stuck on, dogs run in circles, there are new "special" enemies, enemy reaction time varies wildly, a lot of levels are full of randomly moving/unpredictable enemies, enemies frequently occupy the same space as there are no enemy-enemy collisions and shotgun blasts don't always actually hit 2 people at once, even though melee can do that every time.
The lack of enemy-enemy collisions has been the most infuriating though. Since most levels are gun oriented, you'll likely be doing a bit of shooting and thus, like the first game, hiding behind corners and waiting for the conga line. Imagine doing that but one of the enemies is actually two enemies, and the one underneath won't get hit by the first bullet. Of course they also have a gun and will shoot before you can again.
Though lesser, this seemed deliberate and is getting a call-out. Those new "special" enemies aren't fun to deal with. Remember the fat black men who took longer to die? Now there are versions of that but with guns. Now (though briefly) there are guys that have to have a weapon thrown at them, cannot be shot and are faster than you. It's annoying just to think about, though not the last thing I want to bring up.
Later on, the difficulty spikes in a new way. Wrong Number will make you learn enemy patterns (by dying of course) and execute perfect sequences of actions in open areas. By that I mean running through, clearing out rooms of enemies with perfect aim, no lock-on (due to the multiple enemies) and perfect timing. Caught on a wall? Dead. Took 0.1 seconds too long to line up a shot? Dead, do it again. I assure you that there's no other way in these levels. It's difficult, yes, but it's not fun. There's no tension, just rising irritation. Where Hotline Miami progressed on a room-by-room basis, letting you plan ahead and see what's next, this often just throws you in the deep end and expects you to deal with it.
Very similar to the original, with a few added effects (raindrops, flags waving in the wind, more character animations) and several huge levels set outdoors without the neon background. There is a marked increase in mundane colours as opposed to the high-contrast palette from Hotline Miami. This might just be me but I had trouble noticing a lot of enemies in certain levels just because they looked like part of the environment. The new colours and frequent white/beige floors also make the white reticle easier to lose. Thankfully all of the character portraits are still ugly.
Great. I love the soundtrack, more than the original because of the increase in dirty, dark synths and loud, fast and frantic tracks that distracted my attention from the level design. The soundtrack might have actually been the biggest reason I kept playing.
Batfeces insane. It jumps all over the place, letting you play as at least 11 different characters throughout the game and being vague, ominous and just all around strange, even compared to Hotline Miami's story. I don't really mind, it's been interesting.
While I did have fun with it for a time and it certainly has a few redeeming elements, nothing can change the poor level design. Instead, go to Devolver's soundcloud, turn on Wrong Number's soundtrack and go play the original Hotline Miami again. That is, unless you need new Hotline Miami levels no matter what.
While I've played a good deal of Wrong Number and feel close to the end at roughly 6-7 hours, I haven't completed the game yet. I'll update this review if anything changes.

That is Mount and Blade: Warband in a nutshell. Fun. Mount and Blade: Warband is the sequel to the open world action adventure RPG Mount and Blade. It has a large environment for you to explore, take quests, and fight bandits in. The exploration generally comes down to you riding around with your army (more on that later), introducing yourself to lords and recruiting soldiers. While crossing the landscape of Calradia to find these lords and towns where you can hire these soldiers, you may come across bandits, who, when attack you, start an "instance", where you battle these bandits on a large, open plain, using your weapons such as bows, axes, spears, and more to take out your opponents. It is good to hire farmers so over time you can upgrade them into strong infantry, cavalry, or archers. This game has some of the best medieval combat I've ever seen. Relying on timing and blocking, you can sometimes be an absolute hero and take on an army with a crossbow. Some of the quests are repetetive, the graphics are dated, and it is slightly buggy.
Overall, a good game, but rough around the edges.

Avoid if:
-You want really deep mechanical systems.
-You won't play with randoms and you don't have 3 friends.
-You hate randomized loot with a fiery passion.
-You hate typos.

If you're a returning Hotline Miami player, do you remember those 1 or 2 unfairly designed levels towards the end of the game? Those hallways far too long to see the gunmen before they shot you? Of course, they weren't that big of a deal because of how rarely that happened. Unfortunately, almost every level in the latter half of Wrong Number is designed around using the view limits against you and frequently spawning you in an enemy's line of sight. If that kind of trial and murder is a turn-off, (and it should be) then I'd say skip this one, at least until the level editor is live but even then it'll be a gamble.
It's very similar to Hotline Miami - as can be expected - but there is more of a focus on guns in Wrong Number, to the point of including several levels where apart from shooting you only have a knife that can't be thrown. I wouldn't mind this if the enemies with weapons weren't so deliberately placed outside the visible area and as such, I found myself getting irritated way more quickly than in the original game. The problem is the fairness just isn't there. It felt like my fault before, now I have to remember where off-screen I got shot from because even though I found myself holding the SHIFT key for most of the game, it didn't help. Except now there's no George mask to help with that.
Speaking of masks, they're different now. Many levels in the game don't let you choose one and when you do, they're very specific in function. The variety in abilities isn't really there compared to the first game, though there is some. A couple of the choices yielded interesting and fun gameplay changes but I don't want to spoil them, as they were great fun to discover and use for the first time.
I hope you're patient because I've got a lot more to complain about with Wrong Number so let's get this done. Way too often I found my character dying right after restarting, as enemies would spawn in the same room and immediately rush them, prompting yet ANOTHER restart. I don't know what possessed them to design the levels like this, I can only assume it was their inelegant attempt to extend the game's length. Even with this almost NES-era level of sadism, I still found myself under the "one-more-level" hook and turned a late evening into an early morning.
Unfortunately those aren't the only problems with how the game plays, though those are the biggest. Enemies get stuck in doorways, the doors themselves get in the way more than they ever help, walls have many invisible edges to get stuck on, dogs run in circles, there are new "special" enemies, enemy reaction time varies wildly, a lot of levels are full of randomly moving/unpredictable enemies, enemies frequently occupy the same space as there are no enemy-enemy collisions and shotgun blasts don't always actually hit 2 people at once, even though melee can do that every time.
The lack of enemy-enemy collisions has been the most infuriating though. Since most levels are gun oriented, you'll likely be doing a bit of shooting and thus, like the first game, hiding behind corners and waiting for the conga line. Imagine doing that but one of the enemies is actually two enemies, and the one underneath won't get hit by the first bullet. Of course they also have a gun and will shoot before you can again.
Though lesser, this seemed deliberate and is getting a call-out. Those new "special" enemies aren't fun to deal with. Remember the fat black men who took longer to die? Now there are versions of that but with guns. Now (though briefly) there are guys that have to have a weapon thrown at them, cannot be shot and are faster than you. It's annoying just to think about, though not the last thing I want to bring up.
Later on, the difficulty spikes in a new way. Wrong Number will make you learn enemy patterns (by dying of course) and execute perfect sequences of actions in open areas. By that I mean running through, clearing out rooms of enemies with perfect aim, no lock-on (due to the multiple enemies) and perfect timing. Caught on a wall? Dead. Took 0.1 seconds too long to line up a shot? Dead, do it again. I assure you that there's no other way in these levels. It's difficult, yes, but it's not fun. There's no tension, just rising irritation. Where Hotline Miami progressed on a room-by-room basis, letting you plan ahead and see what's next, this often just throws you in the deep end and expects you to deal with it.
Very similar to the original, with a few added effects (raindrops, flags waving in the wind, more character animations) and several huge levels set outdoors without the neon background. There is a marked increase in mundane colours as opposed to the high-contrast palette from Hotline Miami. This might just be me but I had trouble noticing a lot of enemies in certain levels just because they looked like part of the environment. The new colours and frequent white/beige floors also make the white reticle easier to lose. Thankfully all of the character portraits are still ugly.
Great. I love the soundtrack, more than the original because of the increase in dirty, dark synths and loud, fast and frantic tracks that distracted my attention from the level design. The soundtrack might have actually been the biggest reason I kept playing.
Batfeces insane. It jumps all over the place, letting you play as at least 11 different characters throughout the game and being vague, ominous and just all around strange, even compared to Hotline Miami's story. I don't really mind, it's been interesting.
While I did have fun with it for a time and it certainly has a few redeeming elements, nothing can change the poor level design. Instead, go to Devolver's soundcloud, turn on Wrong Number's soundtrack and go play the original Hotline Miami again. That is, unless you need new Hotline Miami levels no matter what.
While I've played a good deal of Wrong Number and feel close to the end at roughly 6-7 hours, I haven't completed the game yet. I'll update this review if anything changes.

What is Melody's Escape?
Melody's Escape is a runner/rhythm PC game with gameplay synchronized to your own music library! (MP3s, WMAs, iTunes, FLAC, etc.)
When you're running outside with a portable music player blasting music through your headphones, have you ever felt a sudden burst of energy when a specific part of a song started playing?
In Melody's Escape, advanced audio detection algorithms transcribes the energy that you feel when listening to music and synchronizes that experience with the game.
It will adapt in real-time to the intensity of the music and change the movement mode accordingly, from walking during very slow calm parts up to all-out flying when your music explodes!
Melody's Escape features 4 different intensity movement modes, each with their own obstacles:
Walking
Jogging
Running
Flying
Your goal is the help Melody avoid obstacles and collect floating orbs (all of which are in sync with the beats of the music, thanks to powerful BPM/tempo detection) by pressing buttons in rhythm. Depending on your own personnal preferences, you can choose to have a relaxing experience or a very intense one thanks to 3 difficulty settings:
Relaxing - Each intensity movement mode requires the same button/key press for all obstacles; a relaxing way to enjoy your music.
Normal - The type of obstacles (and associated color input) depends on the musical key of each specific beat.
Intense - The complete gameplay experience, keeping you on your toes! :)
Melody's Escape also has a strong focus on voices and long held notes (wether it's violin or dubstep wub-wubs), giving you the opportunity to slide alongside the voice while it is held in the song. This makes playing on beautiful songs even more enthralling!

ORIGINAL REVIEW 2/28/14: I want to like this game more than I do. That sounds confusing, so let me explain. The game is a nice, fresh take on the "play your music" genre. However, the game's music-to-level system is not completely functional. This isn't the worst thing, as it's an early acess game with time to fix it, and the level creator does seem to work fine on some songs. However, the result is an extremely difficult game, even on the lowest difficulty setting, as the beats are just slightly off from where you'd expect them to be. All in all, this game has potential, and if you want to get in early to help test it, you should. If you're deterred by the bugs, put this game on your wishlist. You can forget about it, and in a little while, when it's fixed, you can come back and receive what should be a quality experience.
EDIT 3/16/14: After coming back to this game, I've found the detection to be better but still not perfect. I do like the custom difficulties, as making it lenient but a reasonable speed can offset the slightly faulty beat detection. Overall, I still think it's a fine game, but if you're not sold I would recommend waiting until it's out of beta.

Melody's Escape.
Wow. This game's mechanics are impressive to say the least, and the aesthetics are so cleverly done, it's hard to beleive the game is in early release. I can't wait to see what the developer has in store for us in future updates. The game is very user friendly, and the interface is simple and clean. I could get straight into the game with no confusion whatsoever. The particle effects particularly stood out to me as looking really great.
Any criticism i have, is entirely constructive, and does not lean this towards a negative view of the game from my part. This may simply be my screen, but i find that a lot of motion blur occurs, and makes it difficult to see upcoming colour instructions, and it makes the game quite hard on the eyes. I find that trying to press a key to either touch an orb, or to overcome an obstacle is really inconsistent. I don't know whether if this is really my incompetance, but it seems that if you press it directly above the arrows, it fails to work. It seems you need to actually press it before you reach it, and then when you reach the obstacle it will then perform the action. This really confuses me, and i don't know if it's just me being bad at the game, or is a feature. I personally find the intense mode kind of arbitrary, as it simply requires you to press 2 keys at once, rather than one. Perhaps including more complexity and requiring quickly fingers and reflexes into the levels would make for a more "intense" gamemode. The algorithms are just really awesome, but they tend to be the most compatible with techno. Slower songs like instrumentals and classicals feel very out of place, as if a slow song is to a very fast game. A final criticism (a constructive one, i urge) is that when Melody is performing an action, like a long drop or a long slide, the game says "Error" even if your move was "perfect" or any other.
After looking back at this review i seem to have portrayed the game with an overwhelming area of faults, but this is really not the case. Melody's Escape is an origional and fun game, which is worth every penny, even in this early stages of that game. Especially recommended for music lovers, one of the best games of 2014 so far!

Hotline Miami 2 is an interesting game with very interesting charecters, but very boring level design. The game has six acts in which each act contains for levels, each level will be played as a different charecter with a different style. The problem comes in with the each charecter style isnt really a mechanic more of restriction. For example, the charecter "Beard" can only use a certian gun and has only a limited ammo, he cant pick up other guns, this wouldnt be a problem if the design of each level didnt come into play with this. Levels seem to work against the charecters mechanics rather than with them, an example is level 12, death wish, you play as each of the fans through each floor, and when you get to corey, whose mechanic is to dodge roll, you'll find a table that stops the roll, and you'll probably get shot in the process making it quite useless to use. This isnt the only problem with the levels, each level seems to contain a large amount of windows and excessive amounts of AI, most of the time I was worried where the AI was so I wouldnt get shot from across the screen. Another issue with the level design is that it is way to larger, when I hold shift to see the rest of the map, I hardly see the whole thing, Im seeing so little of the map because its so huge, while I do that I also have to make sure no AI is going to snipe me with a shotgun from a wall of windows across the other side of the map that I cant even see. While these mechanics are difficult to work with, the games story and music are far superior to the first game, it's hard to say whether or not I recommend HM2, but Im maybe with a level editor we will see some far more interesting things happen with the levels.

An exercise in frustration.
The original Hotline Miami was a strange game. At its core, it was a top-down action game, where the goal was to brutally kill all the enemies in the level. Enemies died in a single hit, but so did you; the player quickly got in an entrancing loop of dying and respawning, over and over, until the level was beat.
It stood out due to its fast and ultra violent gameplay, its eclectic and nostalgic soundtrack, and its deliberately ugly yet colorful visual design.
Hotline Miami 2 uses the same mechanics as its predecessor, and expands upon them. Unfortunately, the gameplay took a turn for the worse.
Due to the fact that the camera is fixed straight above the characters' heads, you can't see very far in these games. You can extend your field of view using the Shift key to look ahead, but not by much.
In HM1, this shortcoming was remedied by having most levels being in-doors, within tight corridors, so the player could run from room to room, dodging gunfire and outrunning mobsters; enabling (and encouraging) to be brash and ballsy.
In HM2, there is an overabundance of wide open spaces, windows everywhere, armed goons stationed at every single one of them. Instead of going on a bloody blitzkrieg, the player is forced to tiptoe about and try to lure enemies around a corner, killing them off one by one, lest he gets shot by some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sitting out sight.
This kiting tactic doesn't always work out, since the AI is very inconsistent. Either they're oblivious to the twenty corpses lying on the floor; or they're said telepathic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that snipes you with a shotgun from the other side of the level. Or the dog that jumps at your throat before you can react. Or the fat bodyguard that is immune to melee attacks, and forces you to run into the sights of the aforementioned gunmen. All of this forces the player to slow down and to be extremely careful; behaviour which isn't associated with Hotline Miami at all.
Putting gameplay grievances aside, the presentation of HM2 is as strange as the original's, and comes together just as well. The visuals are still simultaneously ugly and beautiful, with gorgeous neon and pastel bumpers between levels being offset by deliberately repugnant character portraits; not to mention gore galore during gameplay.
The story itself isn't particularly deep, but it's told in an interesting fashion. It constantly switches between characters, back and forth between events before and after Hotline Miami 1.
The soundtrack is definitely the game's best aspect. Artists such as Perturbator, Carpenter Brut, and M.O.O.N. provided for a brilliant score, with a fitting late 80's/early 90's vibe. Unfortunately, their talent ain't cheap: the Digital Deluxe Edition of the game only contains a few remixed tracks. The OST can be bought separately, for the same price as the base game.
Hotline Miami 2 is the type of sequel that attempts to go above and beyond its predecessor, but forgets what made the original come together. Level design shifted from small and tight environments, to wide open spaces. Players can no longer go all-out, and are forced to tiptoe around, hoping to not get shot by an enemy they can't see.
You'd be better off just buying its soundtrack, or getting the original instead.

Having played and enjoyed the first, this one is subpar in comparison. The levels in this one are far more open and rather than blast your way through each level, patience is the name of the game here. The accompanying story is also kind of uninteresting and convoluted. The new soundtrack is ♥♥♥♥ing fantastic though!

Is Hotline Miami 2 better or worse than its predecessor?  It's different, and I appreciate it for that. Having achieved critical and fan success with their first game, I applaud the developers for doing something different. They could have slapped together 20 new levels and new masks and weapons and call it a day, but they wanted to make something unique, risking a more negative reaction.
Now, with that out of the way, I love HM2. It keeps most of the gameplay from the previous game, still fast-paced, ultra-violent, high-risk brawls with a top down perspective. The main difference is that now the story gets priority, you don't get to choose from your arsenal of masks before every level, but follow the story of the different characters before, during and after the events that took place in Hotline Miami 1.
Levels are longer and harder, so if you're looking for a challenge, you won't be disappointed. As the game progress, the ramping difficulty forces you to re-think your steps and forge strategies. Barging into rooms like a destructive force, rushing through levels, killing everyone, that's something that happens less frequently than it did in HM1.
My biggest critique, is that a lot of levels feature really long open spaces, which force you to move around with the SHIFT key pressed, in order to scout the enemies before they shoot you off-screen.
In conclusion, I liked the story, and appreciated the changes in the gameplay, even if I might still prefer the style of the classic one. I'm satisfied with what I've got. Oh, and the Soundtrack is simply amazing.

-You have no patience for day 1 scrubs ruining your run. They'll learn or quit, but not this week.
Avoid if:
-You want really deep mechanical systems.
-You won't play with randoms and you don't have 3 friends.
-You hate randomized loot with a fiery passion.
-You hate typos.

I forgot how I got my hands on this game, to be honest. I found it in my library one day and after watching the trailer I decided to give it a try. It somehow reminded me of Mark Of The Ninja, S.T.A.L.K.E.R. and Left4Dead all together and this couldn't be a bad thing.
This being said, it's not much to say about the game.
The game looks great and has an awesome artistic direction as well as a nice story (wouldn't call it good but it's enjoyable. The soundtrack is very good and fits perfectly with the somber atmosphere of this game.
Naturally, being a platformer,  there are a lot of simple puzzles to solve. In fact, the second chapter (the game is split into 3 chapters) of the game is full of them and it feels like it was especially designed to have as many puzzles as possible.
Unfortunately, the game has it's issues.
The most annoying thing is the clunky controls that can make the game frustrating since it has many trial-and-error moments
Button response is slow and extremely unresponsive. Same goes for the aiming system.
Trying to jump of a fence can make you jump back to the side you're coming from, in the middle of the zombies.
Trying to make a sprint right after jumping down from a fence or windows usually doesn't work and you have to try holding the sprint key a few times.
Jumping while you are sliding down on a wall or floor doesn't work as it should or takes too long to respond, making you miss the jump window and retry again and again. Sometimes, jumping when running won't work so you'll find yourself stumbling upon boxed all the time. And since getting up is slow, you'll most likely end up being eaten by shadows.
It also has some bugs in the last chapter of the game. Reaching the top of the stairs that end up with a shaft causes the shaft to close before you get out, pushing you out of the map. Also, this happens when you try to get inside a building or room through a window. The window opens before you can get on the other side and you get stuck there so you need to restart the checkpoint.
The last chapter unfortunately is full of bugs and the controls feel worse here. Escaping the military base is a nightmare. I encountered all those bugs there. Also, the interact button as well as using the ax to break things are extremely unresponsive here.
Of course, these problems won't occur when you use a controller showing that this game was designed with a controller in mind, something you can see in the videos in the extras menu, after you finish the game.
However, leaving all these problems aside and the fact that the game is very short (you can finish it in less than 2 hours on your second playthrough), the game is enjoyable and fun to play and definitely worth a few bucks.

Besides the fact that it can takes hours and hours of farming in order to get something (Or you could just spend real money to buy it... because its THAT kinda game!), I would have to say this game sucks. From the "realistic" gameplay, the completely "balanced" factions, or maybe the "realtime" wars that players influence, I would have to say that it doesn't really live up to anything that it says!
Lets start with the free to play part! It, as stated above, can take upto weeks just to get enough money and XP to buy a weapon. However! If you think that you're above this, and don't want to wait, you can just spend the ~10 US dollars to buy it right there and then. (Buying it with credits even allows you to COMPLETELY skip over the XP requirements, along with the money!)
Then comes the "realistic" and "Simulation" battles- IF one could call them that! I believe that the biggest contender here is the movement model, which although had some nice hopes... is for lack of better words, sh*t. Many a times I have been in open fields or with large arm movement areas, when I get into a firefight with another soldier. Mid shooting, my gun pulls up and does the action that it does when your muzzle isn't in position (Because APPARENTLY my gun was running into some invisible force?) for firing. Then theres the maps... Oh! how I hate ALL of the maps. From large open areas with almost no cover from base to base, to the maps where it looks as though you must camp in order to be successful, or maybe the maps with overgrown areas with large amounts of fog? All in all, the maps aren't that great either, simply compounding upon everything else that is wrong in this game.
After that, there goes the "balance" which just as everything before is little but existent. I'd like to paint a little picture for you here...
American Bombing Planes: 2 bombs
German Bombing Planes: 1 bomb
Soviet Bombing Planes: 4 bombs! (Kinda crazy right?)
But, the German plane must have SOME redeeming qualities right? Like better mobility, or stronger bullets? Nope, its the exact same as the other, if not worse. After the planes comes the tanks and weapons. (I'd like to just say real quick, Germany is EASILY the most underpowered, and it seems that the developers neither intend to make it better, or debuff the other factions as they just recently added the Soviets into the game, which look to have the best weapons.) From the poor guns of the German, to the crazy one shot rifles and ludacris fire rate and accuracy of the American weapons, to the overly good starting Soviet guns, its blatantly obvious that the developers favor some faction WELL over others. Tanks/vehicles, while pretty well balanced, are VERY overpriced, and some seem to have the sole function of spinning in circles or denying friction. All in all, the game's balance seems to be lacking, and its actually rather annoying to see the devs. favor some factions over others...
Those "real-time" wars you were expecting? Or that "huge scale" battles that you thought you were going to get? Wrong again! While yes, there is a mega server that most of the battles take place on, and are ranked, most battles are only 16 V 16. This looks to be a rather small amount of people for all of the "class variety" that the game has, leading to searching for game up to 10 minutes (And thats without a squad... being in a squad can take AGES). Finally, after getting into a game, you may notice that THE WHOLE SERVER consist of just THAT class, or very few other... You can see that this leads to frustrating gameplay, and overly long searching time for a game that it may 'plop' you in, which ends roughly a minute after your joining! (Also, I'm not really going to approach the whole, campaign thing, as its seems to literally be pointless. Wars end within a day and most of the time it doesn't give props to the right faction... but you can almost always bet the Germans lose, even when they win?)
All in all, this game really in a trainwreck, that yes, I have had SOME fun playing, needs A LOT (and I cant stress enough how much I mean that) of work. Also, before you say, "Oh well you've spent almost 100 hours playing the game, it MUST be good!" I would like to state that I have only spent that much time in game because I wanted to be able to expierence a large portion of it so that I may give a proper rating and suggestions!

Some people complain that not having a huge selection of masks is too restricting. I would argue that Dennaton Games made the game this way in order to force the player to step out of their comfort zone and learn how to play the game multiple ways, instead of just picking Tony the Tiger every single level.
Also, a lot of people are complaining that Hotline Miami 2 suffers from "bad level design." However, I would argue that the levels are just different from the first Hotline Miami. In Hotline Miami 1 it was a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to use guns, becuase as soon as you would shoot, every enemy would rush you since they are all in earshot. In Hotline Miami 2, the levels are much much larger and enemies are more spaced out and as a result, using a gun won't lead to being bum rushed by 40 different people, only a few enemies. So basically, the levels offer a different kind of challenge. If you did miss the old style of gameplay, there are a few levels that focus on melee combat (notably Richter and the Writer's levels).
Essentially, this is a great game that adds more of what was loved in Hotline Miami (like a great soundtrack, personally I like the tracks "Guided Meditation", "Sexualizer", "Rust" and "Divide" to name a few) and also adds a nice story (albiet a little hard to follow your first time through), a hard mode for extra replayablitiy (Hard mode really lives up to its name), and a lot of other nice touches that make the game look really impressive (like physics objects, being able to dismember heads that you can kick around, and the level select screen is a cool VHS box set thing.)
Final verdict:
Buy the game, but be prepared to get a replacement R key for your PC.

Its rather differrent than the first game. But not in a good way. But If you really want to see how it all ends, by all means, buy the game. If you loved the first one, you will be dissappointed by the sequel. if you did not like the first one that much, well, then this isn't the game to buy.
First off the movement is now sluggish. Instead of a fast-paced movement and turning; you now have a much more noticably reduced speed. This forces you to plan out nearly every section of a level, roughly room-by-room. it was kind of like this in the first game, but its forced more in HLM2. No, you cannot change this in the controls or settings. You also attack like a coma-patient that just woke up after 20 years of being in bed. There are no varried weapons speeds, everything is as slow as the Ax from the first game.
Secondly, each character,mask or other "play-styles," are bland. you will have less of these to work with and the differences between them are non-existant. The same abilities are recycled between some new characters too. yes, the same ones characters had in the same game. Gameplay variaty was turned down, or rather stretched to the extremes. Most new styles are rather awkward and to be frank, suck.
The third. Music. The qualitiy of the selected music for this game is defanatly worse than the first. Some are pure ambience or glitch-ambience with some dub-step in there. You will only hear about 2(?) new-retro-wave songs and thats it. The music  that is in the game is rather trippy or kind-of depressing. I know its the last installment of the series, but geez. Now I'm not gonna say I can make better music, but I definatly could've choosen better music. This is my biggest gear to grind with this game.
Fourthly, the level design was kind of bad. This would lead to levels being pretty easy or hard. The easy levels were not always the shortest or the longest, same applies to the hard levels. In the leves where you are forced to play as a specific character, you were often faced with levels that did not suit their play-style. The few that did were easy, too easy.
Lastly, the story, oh god the story. Well I'm not going to spoil anything but, it was quite dissappointing. People will tell you it "makes no sense." But it does. Its almost as if they had alot of things they wanted to do and either: 1. Ran out of time or 2. Ran out of money. In the end it comes off kind-of half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
To sum it up. Game play is slower, not as fun. No variaty with the masks and other styles. The new music is♥♥♥♥♥♥ The levels are not intuative (thats probably why we get a level editor, but I have yet to see it.) The story starts off ok, but ends in a very rushed and lazy way.

Well, they've done it again, managing to release yet another in a long line of horrible PC ports and getting paid to do it. The Call of Duty franchise seems to be based largely on repitition, so-so story to burn a little time coupled with the multiplayer that seems to be the title's real selling point. This is where we get to the fun part, though. Multiplayer is largely the same as last year's, and the year before, and the years before that, spare a couple bells and whistles here and there. Some weapons are horribly overpowered making skill far less than a requirement. Performance is much like other failed PC ports of late: poorly optimized RAM hogs with a bad taste for your video memory (12... cores... not... enough). SLI support is virtually non-existent (the game would have been better off without it) and stuttering issues require tweaking just to get acceptable framerates. On top of this, it is usual for my system to bluescreen or for my video driver to stop responding (and sometimes in a sort of chain reaction!). In short, you are paying for last year's Call of Duty minus acceptable framerates and any pretense of stability.

Craft/sandbox games are popping up everywhere since the success of Mincecraft.
Many of them arn't bad, but are nothing more then "meh" MC clones (I have tried alot of them, and most couldn't keep me interested for very long.)
Then there is this beauty.
You can mine, chop, and dig, but the landscape isn't "cubed" but adapts dynamically.
And ofcourseyou can craft a vast amount of items, build tools, houses, bases, vehicles, etc...
But wait ! There is more ! you also have a spore-style editor in-game to craft blueprints for your own custom <any item>.
When you are finished building your blueprint (in the game called an "ISO") the game calculates what parts and materials you need to build it, and you can create and use it in-game.
Exploration is encouraged, and is much more fun then most MC-style games, because the landscape actually is pretty. You spot alien creatures are ripe for the hunting, but carefull, some might just hunt you. Or work in packs.
It looks good, it plays good, and it even has story mode ! (also, adventure, build, ...)
If you enjoy Crafting/sandbox/survival games, this one is a must-try.

On concept alone, PE already is many a gamers dream game: Getting dropped on an alien world with almost complete freedom of what to do there afterwards. While I haven't played Minecraft myself, the comparisons in regards to gameplay seem acurate as a lot of the early stages of the game consist of getting tools to acquire resources and mining/chopping/hunting what you need. At this moment, Combat is very basic though and I hope that it will be improved over the course of development since most of the other elements in the game are already perfectly viable like movement, exploration, the aforementioned resource gathering as well as building structures and, one of the games coolest features, vehicles.
At the time I am writing this, my only real misgivings with the game are the AI of some of the followers as well as the scripting for the quests, since some quests are structured in a way that make it hard or even impossible to complete some quests without abusing the apparant invulnerability of some NPCs or having to fast-travel in order to make some monsters respawn.
I bought PE for full price after having it on my wishlist fo some time and I dont regret it, if theres even a small part of you that likes the concept, I suggest getting at least on sale since I honestly think there isn't any early access title right now that shows more promise.

An exercise in frustration.
The original Hotline Miami was a strange game. At its core, it was a top-down action game, where the goal was to brutally kill all the enemies in the level. Enemies died in a single hit, but so did you; the player quickly got in an entrancing loop of dying and respawning, over and over, until the level was beat.
It stood out due to its fast and ultra violent gameplay, its eclectic and nostalgic soundtrack, and its deliberately ugly yet colorful visual design.
Hotline Miami 2 uses the same mechanics as its predecessor, and expands upon them. Unfortunately, the gameplay took a turn for the worse.
Due to the fact that the camera is fixed straight above the characters' heads, you can't see very far in these games. You can extend your field of view using the Shift key to look ahead, but not by much.
In HM1, this shortcoming was remedied by having most levels being in-doors, within tight corridors, so the player could run from room to room, dodging gunfire and outrunning mobsters; enabling (and encouraging) to be brash and ballsy.
In HM2, there is an overabundance of wide open spaces, windows everywhere, armed goons stationed at every single one of them. Instead of going on a bloody blitzkrieg, the player is forced to tiptoe about and try to lure enemies around a corner, killing them off one by one, lest he gets shot by some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sitting out sight.
This kiting tactic doesn't always work out, since the AI is very inconsistent. Either they're oblivious to the twenty corpses lying on the floor; or they're said telepathic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that snipes you with a shotgun from the other side of the level. Or the dog that jumps at your throat before you can react. Or the fat bodyguard that is immune to melee attacks, and forces you to run into the sights of the aforementioned gunmen. All of this forces the player to slow down and to be extremely careful; behaviour which isn't associated with Hotline Miami at all.
Putting gameplay grievances aside, the presentation of HM2 is as strange as the original's, and comes together just as well. The visuals are still simultaneously ugly and beautiful, with gorgeous neon and pastel bumpers between levels being offset by deliberately repugnant character portraits; not to mention gore galore during gameplay.
The story itself isn't particularly deep, but it's told in an interesting fashion. It constantly switches between characters, back and forth between events before and after Hotline Miami 1.
The soundtrack is definitely the game's best aspect. Artists such as Perturbator, Carpenter Brut, and M.O.O.N. provided for a brilliant score, with a fitting late 80's/early 90's vibe. Unfortunately, their talent ain't cheap: the Digital Deluxe Edition of the game only contains a few remixed tracks. The OST can be bought separately, for the same price as the base game.
Hotline Miami 2 is the type of sequel that attempts to go above and beyond its predecessor, but forgets what made the original come together. Level design shifted from small and tight environments, to wide open spaces. Players can no longer go all-out, and are forced to tiptoe around, hoping to not get shot by an enemy they can't see.
You'd be better off just buying its soundtrack, or getting the original instead.

The new soundtrack is ♥♥♥♥ing fantastic though!

Is Hotline Miami 2 better or worse than its predecessor?  It's different, and I appreciate it for that. Having achieved critical and fan success with their first game, I applaud the developers for doing something different. They could have slapped together 20 new levels and new masks and weapons and call it a day, but they wanted to make something unique, risking a more negative reaction.
Now, with that out of the way, I love HM2. It keeps most of the gameplay from the previous game, still fast-paced, ultra-violent, high-risk brawls with a top down perspective. The main difference is that now the story gets priority, you don't get to choose from your arsenal of masks before every level, but follow the story of the different characters before, during and after the events that took place in Hotline Miami 1.
Levels are longer and harder, so if you're looking for a challenge, you won't be disappointed. As the game progress, the ramping difficulty forces you to re-think your steps and forge strategies. Barging into rooms like a destructive force, rushing through levels, killing everyone, that's something that happens less frequently than it did in HM1.
My biggest critique, is that a lot of levels feature really long open spaces, which force you to move around with the SHIFT key pressed, in order to scout the enemies before they shoot you off-screen.
In conclusion, I liked the story, and appreciated the changes in the gameplay, even if I might still prefer the style of the classic one. I'm satisfied with what I've got. Oh, and the Soundtrack is simply amazing.

TLDR - Good idea and premise but horrible execution and playability. Cannot recommend.
Long version:
First thing to slap me in the face was the horrible controls, moving, aiming and shooting. Moving around felt blocky and sticky. It's hard to describe in words but those would be the best words to describe it. You're trying to walk forward but you cannot because the invisible borders of a table or such is blocking you. Move a tiny bit to the side and you can walk forward. Shooting stuff.. just eww. Firstly Contagion uses the (now) standard ADS for aiming and shooting. But how it actually feels and behaves as you play will drive you insane. It is the most frustrating thing ever when you are aiming at the head of a zombie around a car length away, fire and you miss. Zombie is only slightly wobbling from side to side, not moving and you miss. You aim a second time, ever carefully aiming and aligning the sights, fire and miss a second time. At this point you cuss, throw the mouse across the room, smack ESC and promptly exit the game. It is really hard to put into words how frustrating and annoying the aiming and shooting is in this game but maybe just saying it does not feel "natural" or comfortable would suffice. Anyone who has ever shot a handgun or a rifle in real life can relate to the next issue. When the game is trolling you with stuff like "There is no automatic reload" and then you shoulder an AR-15.. facepalm immediately. Feels like you're trying to shoulder it but at the same time you move your head as back as possible while pushing the rifle as far as possible from you and then you're trying to squint through the sights. I cannot understand how they could mess up so badly the main idea of ANY zombie shooter, the actual shooting.
Some other things to note (in bad or good, you decide). There are only two zombie types, regular and "riot", where the latter is "armored" (Yes a riot helmet and vest will totally resists several rounds of intermediate cartridges or higher). The maps are quite nice and realistic looking. Realistic in the sense of how one would imagine it to be in this type of situation. Graphics look quite outdated (In my opinion Left 4 Dead looks much better, yes the first). Game modes are pretty "standard" with the usual PvE (escape and civilian rescue)/PvP and mixed modes of those two.
The few hours that I've played Contagion I really do not recommend it. The idea and premise seem promising but the execution and playability is horrible that it will frustrate you to no end. For the money there are better alternatives.

I've been following this game for a couple years now, and it continues to get better and better. It takes a bit of time to warm up to it, but if you give it a chance, you'll find it a deeply satisfying blend of RPG, sandbox, base building, exploration, crafting, and open world survival. The AI NPC's are a fantastic addition, as well as the built-in object editor, where you can download patterns other people have created from within the game. Honestly, it's hard to recommend this game to anyone. The premise is great. WWII full on tank plus plane plus ground battles. However, like most others in it's genre, it falls flat.

Staircases are also a nightmare, especially when others are with you.
Vehicles. Personally, I have no experience in planes, so I won't be talking about them, but I have driven every land vehicle from bikes, to tanks, to standard 4-6 person vehicles. Drving is OK. Typically you have alright control over the vehicle in terms of turning to avoid debris, sandbags, etc. It's the bumps and hills that bother me, since you're going, like, 50 kph and going over a slope sends you flying.
Now, the weapons. I tend to not be very picky with weapons, as most of the time, they're what you'd expect. Decent bullet drop, reasonable reload times, realistic stability, etc. It's the melee that bothers me in particular. Shovels. ♥♥♥♥. Shovels. I swear they're broken. I've heard knives work, but I haven't seen nor tried myself, so I wouldn't know.
Overall, it's an OK shooter. It's still in some phase of beta, but it's been in development for four years and still has a LOT to work on. Up to interpretation, I guess.

Fantastic rhythm game, very good beat detection with imported songs. I've tried a very wide variety of genres and the only genre the game seems to have trouble with is metal, in every case I tested the song took place 90% of the time in air sequences. All other genres are detected without issue, and the commands follow the beat.
There are rhythm games on Steam where the song doesn't seem to have much impact on the game, like Beat Hazard, or when it tries to generate commands it doesn't do it very well and often times doesn't match the song, like Rhythm Zone. Melody's Escape is up there with Audiosurf as a well-programmed, unique and very fun rhythm experience. If you're a fan of the genre you owe it to yourself to pick this one up.
It's also worth noting that even though the game is in Early Access right now, it feels very complete. At the moment there aren't global leaderboards and the game seems sparse on options, I'm not sure if either of those will be expanded on. But as it is right now, it does everything it sets out to do without issue. Coming from someone who has reservations about buying Early Access games, this one is well worth it.

Recommendations for Development Team:
Define off-beat and on-beat notes seperately, to make it more a reaction-rhythm than a music-based guessing game.

Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is the prime example of "If it ain't broke, don't fix it." The gameplay is very similar to the first however new characters means new abilities to play around with that add a nice change to keep the game from feeling like a copy paste. If you have a weak stomach for difficult games, stop now, this is your last warning as Hotline Miami 2 is true to the original in that some sections of this game will make you want to punch your monitor. While I recommend not doing that I could understand why during some sections. However the great part about this game is that while certain levels seem REALLY hard, it's always extremely satisfying to figure out the correct solution and you really do feel like a total badass when you conquer a particularly hard area. Combat is quick, hectic and very gory, to the point where I know it has been banned is Australia. As for the game's soundtrack.......my god. I thought the original Hotline Miami had an amazing soundtrack, which it does, Hotline Miami 2's is better in my opinion and it is definitely worth the extra money to pick up. The story in Hotline Miami 2 is, well, I've beaten the game and tbh I have entirely no idea what any of it meant. While playing the game the story felt incredibly pretentious, however the amazing art had me still intrigued by every new cutscene. That being said the ending really left a sour taste in my mouth, I felt that it didn't wrap up the epic Hotline Miami saga as I hoped it would. Others may feel differently but I personally didn't like the ending and for the sake of not spoiling anything I'll refrain from doing so and I'd ask people in the comments to take the same consideration. My playtime for the game was around 5 and a half hours to beat the story including cutscenes, if you don't care about the story and skip the cutscenes the game could take you anywhere from 4 to 5 hours depending on how good you are at the game. I completely understand if people are put off by this short runtime however the game offers a score attack mode to keep completeionists playing for many hours as well as a harder difficulty if you're a sadist. However if you aren't interested in either of these I'd hold off until a sale because paying $15 for around 5 hours of gameplay is too much in my opinion. That being said it's very hard to dictate how much time this game takes as it completely depends on your skill level. If you are, let's just say "Less than stellar" at this game it will definitely take you longer to beat, I personally have a friend who has put in around 9 hours and hasn't made it to the final chapter yet. In conclusion I'd recommend this game not for the story or length, but just for how amazing the gameplay and soundtrack are. This game is essentially a quality over quanity situation, each level is awesome and if your desire is to just beat each one once I wouldn't recommend the game as replay value will be low for you until the level editor comes out. However if you are like me and you desire to see that A+ next to every level this game will easily offer you dozens of hours of gameplay.
