A good sequel to the first Hotline Miami game, although I find it hard to call it a better game than the first one. The core gameplay has been kept mostly the same, with the player taking down floors filled enemies in a top-down view, with both you and your enemies able to take a hit or two before going down. The soundtrack is once again excellent and fits the game's presentation perfectly. The game is also noticeably longer without overstaying its welcome (at least in my opinion). It is also a lot harder, although not always in a good way.
However, there are some notable differences to the first game, which might disappoint those who enjoyed the first game.
- There is a lot less room for different play styles, especially during the latter half of the game. While in the first game you could play each level differently, be it strictly gun or melee oriented or something in between, you could finish the level any way you wanted. Not so in Hotline Miami 2. As the game goes on, most of the levels get larger, more open and filled with more enemies, most equipped with guns. Trying to go melee only in these levels will only get you showered in bullets from multiple cardinal directions, reducing you to a bloody pulp before you are even able to kill more than one mobster. This is made worse by the later levels having more windows than walls and some enemies staying off-screen even when you are looking farther using Shift, making it difficult to survive certain situations except by blindly firing bullets across hallways and open areas, hoping you'll kill whoever is on the other side before they are able to kill you. Not all levels are like this and only a few are truly frustrating in terms of level design, but if you enjoyed the first Hotline Miami because of the ability to mow down entire floors with only your fists or a beer bottle, you might be sorely disappointed.
- The narrative and gameplay focuses on multiple characters. While in the first game you could choose a different mask for each level, in this game you are sometimes limited to a choice between three or four different masks, your starting weapon or in some levels, you don't get to choose at all. Hotline Miami 2 is a bold sequel both in terms of scope and execution, which may surprise people who expected just more Hotline Miami. If the differences in level design and gameplay don't bother you too much, go for it.

I don’t know how I could have missed this jewel of a game. It’s rough and partly unpolished, but heavyweight and, well, precious.
This is advertised as a ‘medieval combat simulator’. While this may be true, the combat is actually only one facet of the whole entertainment package. If I was to compare this game to other titles, I’d say it’s a mix of the venerable Darklands and Total War with a bit of Rune thrown in for a good measure.
THE SETTING
Europe and Middle East in around 12-13th century. We immerse ourselves in the everyday life of a medieval kingdom, set in a vast territory shared with five other sovereign states.  The kingdoms are fictional and loosely based on (then) existing cultures such as Nordic, Russian, Italian or Arab. The architecture and general appearance differs from place to place and towns and villages actually feel medieval-ish, cramped and dirty.
The world is uncaring and, in turn, requires no player’s care or attention to function. Things like war and peace, trade and robbery, death and love are common and part of everyday life. The castles and towns change hands, the Jarls and Lords are captured and released, freelancers raid and are being chased off. Whether you decide to sit quietly on the sidelines or jump straight in, the fate of the world is usually not affected… not by much in any case. Even after you reach your goal and become the king of everything, the world remains in the same dire state as before. Bandits will roam the countryside and the peasants will be worked to death by their lords. You are not a glorious saviour. You are not the chosen one 'that the prophecy spoke of’. Oh no, you are there to simply take your own slice of the pie, wallow in riches and become famous.
Most aspects of the game are historically correct (in fact surprisingly correct for a fictitious setting), albeit not in a great detail, ie. the feudal relationships are there but much simplified. Clothes, armour and weapons are mostly correct as well - and abundant.
GAME MECHANICS
A perfect combination of strategy, TPS/FPS and role-playing game.
The strategic part includes hiring, training and commanding troops. There are several troops to choose from, each with a specific ‘career path’, strengths and weaknesses. There are mercs that aren’t cheap but come fully equipped from day one. There are ‘heroes’ or companions, that serve as skill boosters and/or additional powerful melee or ranged units. Apart from training, you have to keep the ever-growing army fed, paid and happy. In turn they help you accomplish personal goals by killing, and dying, in your name. This element of the game I am very fond of, as it helps build and bind the army according to personal preferences. After several weeks and numerous bouts with bandits your band becomes less of a number and more of a personal asset, especially when that peasant woman you’ve rescued from bandits some time ago becomes a veteran warrior.
Somewhere around mid-game, the balance changes and you start dealing with wider problems, such as managing your towns, castles and villages and planning greater politics. Struggle for power goes hand in hand with struggle for money and you have to be both an entrepreneur and a grand strategist to succeed. Setting up industries and taking care of your fiefs seem to be the only ways to earn enough money for the upkeep of your grand armies of conquest…
The RP aspect is limited to the character development, interactions with various lords, politics, courtship etc. The character development is not overcomplicated and rather intuitively focuses on skills and weapon proficiencies rather than attributes. I particularly like the fact that the hit points pool is kept within realistic boundaries. However, this element is rather bare and would not satisfy a hardcore RP gamer: the conversations are standard canned responses (you get a sense of déjà-vu – I think I’ve spoken to this guy before?) and the quests are repetitive (and not very imaginative either).
First/third person perspective is for many crème-de-la-crème of the game. The activities range from taking a stroll through a village, to shopping, to large scale battles where you have to command troops and keep situational awareness, as well as prove your prowess in battle, be it on foot or from horseback. The orders are simple and advanced tactics is next to impossible, mainly because of the limited controls, but on the other hand it simulates well the chaos of a medieval bout. All of a sudden we find ourselves charging alongside heavy lancers, while bolts and arrows whistle overhead or get stuck in the shield. On more than one occasion I had the horse killed under my character, and had to continue on foot… The fight mechanics are simple but intuitive and not difficult to learn. Fights one on one are as exciting as big battles, especially against well armed opponents - different weapons have different speeds and reach, forcing various tactics. This part of the game is well designed and exciting.
Unfortunately, late game experience is repetitive and rather tedious. Micromanagement is ripe and painful as one needs to travel back and forth to adjust garrisons of castles, train new troops etc.
SPARKLES
Nothing to see here, move along.
The engine is clearly dated and, although incorporating modern-ish eye candy like HDR, looks like something out of previous era. This is not necessarily a bad thing as for most part it’s clean, readable, functional and on more than one occasion – beautiful (sunsets!). Great diversity in scenery and varying weather (fighting in the fog - a host of heavy cavalry suddenly appearing in front of you is a sight to behold!) really add to the flavour!
The models are not overly high polygon ones and this is actually a good thing, as the battles can incorporate anything up to 100 troops at a time, and even on high-end rigs the game can be a bit jittery. The animations are, again, serviceable. Collision detection is quirky.
Sound effects do their job. There may be nothing really epic in the dull thumps, meaty crunches, whistling arrows and throaty death screams, but they do help to immerse in the game. The game lacks voice acting – only few lines of text (out of the hundreds) are actually voiced, you have to read the rest yourself. Some consider it an outrageous downfall, some other – simply old-school.
The ever-present background music is exactly that – background music.
JEWEL POLISH
This game truly shines when user-made mods are applied. There are all kinds of those readily available, ranging from armour addons, to graphic enhancements to complete overhauls (Game of Thrones setting, Warhammer setting, Ancient Rome, feudal Japan, Thirty Years' War etc). The latter are particularly useful, as they bring out what truly makes this game magnificent. In my humble opinion, to experience the M&B in full scope, one should use the the Floris Expanded mod. It doesn’t change the game experience too much, while improving existing features and adding tons of new ones.
IN SHORT
Pros: Immersive, addictive, sometimes adrenaline pumping game. Taking the character from rags to riches. Army training feature.
Cons: Repetitiveness (at some point). Slightly dated graphics.
P.S. Excuse any strange grammar constructs - English is not my first language...

It's truly a terrifying game, but for all the wrong reasons. Deadlight starts really well with a good set piece of survivors dealing with the transformation of one of their own. It sets a good tone, and I wanted to know more about their story prior to their predicament. However, this good start is cut short as the game's mechanics do not work very well at all.
Console-style platforms require precision and a good flow of movement in order to give the player a sense of development as they pass increasingly difficult obstacles. When a player fails a test of skill, they should feel responsible for that mistake. But this game does not have the right feel. The momentum from jumping or running just does not feel right at all. The rules and spaces of play are never conveyed very well, and that's what really drags this game down.
I never felt as though I was learning as I played the game. It was a constant roll of the dice (metaphorically speaking) or a practice of trial-and-error in advancing from level to level. With two hours on record, I just could not go any further with Deadlight. While the atmosphere, themes and characters were interesting, the shoddy systems and mechanics negated any positive feelings I could have for it.

This game is great however it could use much refining. It is understandable that this game is merely an Alpha which makes it reasonable for flaws to be in the game but, nonetheless, the game is very fun. I enjoy this game a lot in almost every aspect, save for a few, from creating vehicles to collecting resources. There are some issues in the game like how a monster will hit you through walls, which causes stupid deaths, but the issues like that are being resolved with each passing patch.
In this game, you can do almost anything you want. You can drive around in completely customized vehicles, creating the vehicles through voxels in the creator, and even build your own colony within the online servers with other players. You can design your own sword, gun, vtol, truck, tank, boats, etc. which allows this game to be completely based on your actions. The ground can be shaped the way you want to make it. All trees can be cut down and even buildings demolished. Anything you want to you in Minecraft, you can do here with much more interraction in a non-block world.
I would have to say, despite how much I love this game, the major flaw that ruins it for me would have to be the servers. There are no official servers for multiplayer and, if you wish to have a reliable server, you're pretty much out of luck unless you make your own. Almost all of the servers are locked for groups of friends and the public ones are laggy and, if they go down, everything you did on them is lost. Anything you do on a server is confined to that server. This means that if you gather the best weapons and armor and make a civilization on a server, you cannot take them to a different server. It is recommended that you make your own server so that everything you make is saved.
All in all, this game is one of the best games I have played in a long time and I will play it a lot more when more content is added. For an Alpha, I give it a 9/10 but i expect that to hit 10 once the bugs are fixed.

I've had this game for quite some time. I put it down a while ago because my friends decided to play something else.
And then Vermintide 2 was announced.
So I decided to hop back in with my trusty dwarf shield wall armed with a hammer.
I forgot the thrill of hearing the "Horde Horn", the whipser of the assassin rats, the rattling of the "choker", the whining gattling gun of the "gat rat". And I watched as the streets piled up with dead rat corpses, and as my hammer dripped with blood. And then I thought, "God dammit, I love this game."
Matchmaking works! Lots of maps to fight through, each with secrets and challenges of their own. The difficulty settings ease you into the game. Easy for newbies, cataclysm for those who want the video game equivalent of getting kicked in the nuts for not blocking. There's a robust loot system that scales off of difficulty and the amount of collectibles you acquire while wading through rat corpses. The combat is deep. So deep that a character that you've played one way will completely change once you equip a different weapon. Blocking, dodging, and striking need to be timed carefully in higher difficulties. There's no shame in spending a few hours in the lower difficulties to practice, because you WILL need it. Weapon diversity is extensive. They can range from daggers to flamberges to hammers; pistols, AUTO-pistols, shotguns, rifles, bows; each with their own strengths and weaknesses, and each can be upgraded. Each character plays drastically different than the other 4, and each serve an important roll within the group, no matter the combination.
There is a high skill-cap, and a large learning curve. If you go into this game thinking that it's a L4D reskin (the core is there but it's in a league of its own), then you won't have a good time. Even the weakest rat can give you a bad day.
I bought this game while it was still in its beta state, and it's come so far in the 2 years since then. THIS is what this game was meant to be. Grab some friends, stock up on booze, and go kill some vermin. Also, the DLCs are pretty dope.
Remember: If you like it a lot, Vermintide 2 is coming during the first quarter of 2018; and it boasts a deeper story, deeper character customization, and the same thrilling combat.

A fun rythm game. Once you choose a song to play, the game lets you know how good of a job it's done in converting the song into a stage. If a song scores a 70% or above, it will be really fun to play and you'll totally get the sense of rhythm that the game is going for. At 40-50%, it'll still be fun to play. But if a song receives a score of 30% or below, then it will feel chaotic and messy to play.
At its best, Melody's Escape feels a lot more rhythmic than Audiosurf does. But it does have some drawbacks. The visual cues are confusing at first because they're based on the Xbox controller's button layout (a yellow symbol means press your "up" button, for instance, while a green symbol means press "down"), and I was using a PS3 controller so it didn't really connect with me. There aren't many options in the game yet, and hopefully they will offer more color palettes as the game is developed. The "rosy" color palette, I noticed, was far too fuzzy-looking and it hurt my eyes to play.
Ultimately though, it's a fun rhythm game with a cute graphical style.

Even in this early stage, Melody's Escape is a great game. It feels to me like the generated level is far more influenced by the music than in similar games like AudioSurf or 1... 2... 3... KICK IT!, which might just be because the gameplay is more connected to the rhythm of the song than AS's puzzle mechanics or Kick It's city generation. It reminds me more of "classic" rhythm games like BeatMania instead of other music-based procedural generation games (that's a word).
If you've got a couple of minutes, there's more thoughts on the game in this video, including what is missing from the game in it's current form, and why it is really hard to get used to the game at first:
No Audiosurf in either gameplay or tempo algorythm, that's for sure. Yet Melody's Escape has its moments. Hopefully the developers will sort it all out before final build.

Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is the prime example of "If it ain't broke, don't fix it." The gameplay is very similar to the first however new characters means new abilities to play around with that add a nice change to keep the game from feeling like a copy paste. If you have a weak stomach for difficult games, stop now, this is your last warning as Hotline Miami 2 is true to the original in that some sections of this game will make you want to punch your monitor. While I recommend not doing that I could understand why during some sections. However the great part about this game is that while certain levels seem REALLY hard, it's always extremely satisfying to figure out the correct solution and you really do feel like a total badass when you conquer a particularly hard area. Combat is quick, hectic and very gory, to the point where I know it has been banned is Australia. As for the game's soundtrack.......my god. I thought the original Hotline Miami had an amazing soundtrack, which it does, Hotline Miami 2's is better in my opinion and it is definitely worth the extra money to pick up. The story in Hotline Miami 2 is, well, I've beaten the game and tbh I have entirely no idea what any of it meant. While playing the game the story felt incredibly pretentious, however the amazing art had me still intrigued by every new cutscene. That being said the ending really left a sour taste in my mouth, I felt that it didn't wrap up the epic Hotline Miami saga as I hoped it would. Others may feel differently but I personally didn't like the ending and for the sake of not spoiling anything I'll refrain from doing so and I'd ask people in the comments to take the same consideration. My playtime for the game was around 5 and a half hours to beat the story including cutscenes, if you don't care about the story and skip the cutscenes the game could take you anywhere from 4 to 5 hours depending on how good you are at the game. I completely understand if people are put off by this short runtime however the game offers a score attack mode to keep completeionists playing for many hours as well as a harder difficulty if you're a sadist. However if you aren't interested in either of these I'd hold off until a sale because paying $15 for around 5 hours of gameplay is too much in my opinion. That being said it's very hard to dictate how much time this game takes as it completely depends on your skill level. If you are, let's just say "Less than stellar" at this game it will definitely take you longer to beat, I personally have a friend who has put in around 9 hours and hasn't made it to the final chapter yet. In conclusion I'd recommend this game not for the story or length, but just for how amazing the gameplay and soundtrack are. This game is essentially a quality over quanity situation, each level is awesome and if your desire is to just beat each one once I wouldn't recommend the game as replay value will be low for you until the level editor comes out. However if you are like me and you desire to see that A+ next to every level this game will easily offer you dozens of hours of gameplay.

Ok so i got hotline 2 thinking this will just be more of the good old fast paced mass murdering rampage that hotline 1 had. All i has to say is HOLY CRAP. This game is soooooo much better than Hotline 1 in almost every way.
Pros:
1) Story
This game Actually ties who certain people in hotline 1 were and how they ended up the way they did. It also has many different people whose stories are in depth on why they go on killing sprees. It also makes one players death switch to another persons story seemlessly. Also The ending IS AMAZING it ends soooooo goooood. I wont spoil but all i have to say is thats a ending for hotline.
2)Violence
This game made the violence in hotline 1 look like call of duty compared to Splatterhouse. They made custom kill mechanics for many of the different weapons such as a chainsaw that can gruesomely rip apart a knocked down foe. You then see his guts spill out and slash the next dude. They also added silenced pistols, Katanas, Heavy MG's and much more.
3) Player classes
The game improved the Amount of masks from the first game and actually made each class unique. you can use ash and his bro while weilding a chainsaw with one and a pistol with the other. You can even dual weild SMGS and reck havoc on your prey. It feels so satisfying to be able to have the classes all balanced. Along with this the enemies are varied with some being fat and hard to kill or fast and heavy.
4) sounds
While hotline 2 has a nice soundtrack i think i enjoyed 1 more but 2 still sets the mood very well. Along with this many of the weapons sound great when shot or sliced and i think that they did a outstanding job with it.
5) Length
This game was so much longer than hotline 1 yet it still felt well paced. I loved how the game was extended and how open the levels were. In most missions you had multiple ways to get around to a good killing spot and it did very nice places of cover. It also Did a well job of showing the cutscenes and made your mind spin on how crazy things get.
Now every game has its pros as well as cons
Cons
1) Glitches
There were plenty of glitches while playing hotline 2 that frustrated me deeply. Enemies would glitch in doors and would spin not being able to be hit. You'd either get a lucky hit and kill him or you would get hit and die. Another thing is the fast enemies in the prison level would run at you and glitch through the wall/door and kill you. This also happened with a dog. Also a enemy with a shotty decided he didnt want to die and walked through a wall and out of the map. I couldnt kill him so i had to restart the mission.
2)Ai
another issue with hotline 2 is that while it is still has decent ai some of the ai is stupid. They can see you across the map but cant see you in a doorway. Along with this a shotgun blast makes people run towards the noise but then they just look around and ignore.
After beating hotline 2 in about 11 hrs or so I have to say that this game is great and i highly reccomend it plays better than hotline 1 in many regards and has just a few problems that i am sure will be fixed. Along with this i heard workshop support will be added so this can show the communities love of the game. I give this game a 8.6/10 and think its a must buy for any fans of the first game or anyone who wants to have a great time

Despite being a little broken ( I hope they fix it soon, they have been rolling out patches quite frequently, so there is hope) and some levels plainly poorly designed (for example: you start unarmed with a normal baddie, a fatty and gun baddie pretty close, so you must try several times to get weapon and kill the fatty), this game is pretty awesome.
It looks the same, but the gameplay is quite different (less quick melee action on narrow spaces Vs slow hide and seek action, with emphasis on guns, on wider rooms), but it still has some levels which are like taken from the first one.
The story development is also different: that nihilistic storytelling has been replaced with a proper narrative squeme, so expect less psychedelic inner monologues and more narrative around different characters. There is a lot less of ambiguity too (there is some present too, this is still a HM game!). I found it to be pretty nice, so not a bad thing.
The characters are refreshingly varied, covering a spectrum which goes from new masked characters with a complete new set of abilities, some returning characters which play exactly as Jacket to new innovative characters, one with fixed weapons you select prior starting the action and replenish its ammo during the level and even one with a non-lethal approach!
The music and art is as good as in the first one, if not better. Totally fits the new feeling, and in general is less fast techno and more dark synth.
The only bad things, once you have understood this is not Hotline Miami 1 are:
+ You can't make baddies kill other baddies
+ Some levels are plain♥♥♥♥♥♥br> + In general, I see a more "trial and error" approach
+ The swans are pretty neat, but the one with guns cannot die and clips a lot, which worsens the experience a tiny bit.
+ Enemies are either deaf or can hear you from Uranus.
+ Speaking of Uranus, their "buttocks" [steam filter prevents anatomical rigor]  seem to behave like a literal third eye, so they will pop you even if they were facing the wall
+ Spinning dogs
+ Baddies clipping through doors cannot be knifed and sometimes pop you while trying, making you scream curse words and smashing that l33t keyboard in rage.
+ Minor issues I forgot/ too lazy to write them down
I think (most of) these shall be fixed soon, so I give it a 8.5/10 (9.5 if they fix everything above). Even if somewhat different, this is a masterpiece of a game and 3 levels aside (which are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥, you will have, at least, as much fun as you had with HM 1 (that's if you like this thing, psycho...).
So go ahead, buy this and enjoy. I did.

Deadlight is a great little game to knock over on a weekend. It's essentially a puzzle platformer in which you have to avoid zombies and get to a safe point to meet up with your group - pretty standard zombie stuff really, but there's nothing wrong with that if it's done well and Deadlight does everything well except for voice-acting and script-writing. The motions feel fluid and nicely animated and you really get a feel for the bleak post-apocalyptic cityscape that you're traversing. The cut scenes have a nice art-style, even though they are essentially moving cut-outs with (groan-inducing) dialogue. There's a rather annoying spikey trap zone, but every good game has it's frustrating moments just to remind you that it's not all easy. Playing through Deadlight was a very pleasurable experience, and even though the dialogue was horrible I'd still recommend it. 7 out of 10, would traverse.

Yeah, yeah, yeah - Left 4 Dead with rat-men.
But it's so much better than that. With melee focussed combat and a variety of classes, not to mention persistent loot to make said classes stronger, this game takes the genre to the next level.
Combat feels tight and satisfying. Each swing of your weapon collides in a satisfying way, backed up by the excellent sound FX. There's plenty of depth, with the block, push and heavy attack system, all of which will take some time to master - a necessary feat to tackle the games devilish higher difficulties.
The loot system is a great way to keep things feeling fresh, and makes every win that much more satisfying - However, with the way it works, players are definitely going to start min-maxing and running the same level over and over in order to achieve the optimal loot chance. This is already somewhat of a problem in the beta, however the developers have stated they're looking at ways to prevent this from becoming too much of a problem.
The graphics and setting themselves are fantastic, particularly if you're a fan of Warhammer. The environments have a great feel to them. The city is a wholly believable location.
Whilst there are still some kinks to be worked out, and there are a fair few bugs (many of which I haven't personally encountered), the dev team seem dedicated, already rolling out two patches in the three days I've played. I wholly recommend this game, particularly if your friends pick it up.

Since this is an Early Access game and as a result, may get large changes pushed through due to patches, my review might miss some things. I'll try to keep it up to date with changes patched in.
I'm a total sucker for games that work based off your own music - the entire reason I first joined Steam was for Audiosurf. I've been excited for Melody's Escape ever since I first saw it on Greenlight, and now that it's finally released I have to say that it definitely meets my expectations.
In terms of gameplay I would best describe it as a "sidescrolling DDR" - the focus is on hitting notes corresponding to arrow keys (as well as WASD on higher difficulties), while running. The 2d platformer style is definitely different from the other rhythm games that I've personally played, and it adds a nice bit of variety to the genre.
The game itself is really pretty, with focuses on monochrome and splashes of color that give it a really vivid look. Unfortunately I had to turn off some of the more intensive settings to be able to get the best performance but I find that the game still looks striking without all the extras. The animation is very smooth and the transitions between actions (ie, going from somersaulting over a barrier to flying off a cliff) are nice and fluid.
The difficulty curve is steep but not impossible. After a few hours I was pretty consistently able to get 3 and 4 hearts on whatever song I played. It requires a bit more finesse when it comes to hitting notes compared to other music-based games I've played - the hitboxes for notes are very tight and require a fair amount of precision, a lot of which is dependent on the FPS you get. I found I had to turn the resolution way down and turn off several of the extra graphics effects in order to get a good framerate and to be able to consistently hit notes, but if you have good hardware this shouldn't be too much of a problem.
However, it's also very forgiving of mistakes, simply regenerating you whenever you miss an obstacle without stopping the song - a very welcome design considering that half the reason I play music games is to listen to the song, so stopping me in the middle of a track when I die is not a good thing!
The game also allows the setting of a "custom" difficulty which allows you to configure what type of button-presses and the density of obstacles, among other things. So, if you find that you're not being challenged enough, or if you're having issues moving from Relaxed to Normal, using the Custom difficulty should make for an enjoyable experience.
One issue that I had with other music games is that either every song tended to feel the same in terms of gameplay, or that it was very easy to predict what type of course you would get which meant that for a challenge you ended up having to play the same sorts of music. This is not an issue with Melody's Escape - I listen to a fairly wide variety of music, a lot of which doesn't normally play well on games like Audiosurf, but almost every single track I tried produced a great level. Obviously like all music games some tracks will still play much better than others - a few songs that I found to be good in other music games didn't really provide the best experience, while others were absolutely
, even on Relaxing difficulty.
For an Early Access game, Melody's Escape is incredibly polished - if I had bought it as a regular, non-EA game I would still be impressed. The only missing features that I would like to have (Last.fm integration, etc) are things that have been confirmed to be added in the future. There's also support for custom skins, hairs, and color schemes via Workshop, which while I don't find incredibly necessary is still a great option to have.
All in all, this game is well worth the wait and the money I paid for it. If you're already a fan of music based games like Audiosurf and want to try something new I would highly recommend checking it out.

As to why, it's because the visuals really hamper the player's ability to notice and react to oncoming notes (relying on sound is good but there's different buttons).
The speed of the game ( mostly when melody's sprinting ) really drives it to become more reaction-based though, and the visuals just add fuel to the fire and makes it almost impossible for anyone starting out to get used to the game easily.

Hotline MIami 2 covers a lot of the same philosophical grounds as the first game, constantly trying to get the player the question why all this violence is enjoyable. The tutorial opens with a depiction of a violent♥♥♥♥♥♥ fading to black and then panning to a director yelling "Cut!". Richard (the chicken mask, a character who makes a lot more sense if you remember he is constantly talking to the player) then appears, almost mocking the player character at this time who is trying to justify the violence in the movie by saying "it's just a film".
This is Hotline Miami 2's thesis statement. Is all of this violence OK because it's a video game? Does media have any real repercussions on our psyche, and if so, shouldn't it be treated more seriously?
The actual gameplay is a fun but the artificial difficulty, especially in later levels, made this game feel significantly less satisfying and more frustrating than the original Hotline Miami. While weapons have been added and you now have more methods to take on the challenges presented, none of it feels integral to the gameplay. Instead many of the additions feel tacked on, I could imagine the sentence "This is Hotline Miami 2, so we need more!" being said during development, and I don't think that's what I personally wanted from the sequel.
Story is a larger focus in Hotline Miami 2 than it's predecessor, or more specifically the story is told in more depth by multiple characters. Much of the same ground is covered in this story, but with more characters (MANY more) and more interactions between them.
Hotline Miami 2 is a great game with some serious flaws. If you want more hotline miami this is the game for you, but if you want more of what hotline miami did best you might want to skip this. Despite all of this, I am still recommending Hotline Miami 2, because at the end of the day it is still fun.

Deadlight is a game I actually really enjoyed, for the most part, because it does have its issue, but let’s start out with the positives. Firstly, the music! I really enjoyed the soundtrack for this game and I’m actually in the process of listening to the OST as I write this review as I can’t get enough of it.

Next up is the gameplay! (sort of!) You’ll be doing two things when it comes to this game. One of them is fighting, and the other is running, and one is considerably more fun than the other. The whole platforming side of the game I really enjoyed in its 2.5D setting and was something I rather enjoyed, the combat not so much. The combat was more or less hit this button, then hold the button once the enemy is on the ground. Now, that’s okay for a one on one fight, but as the zombies pile onto you more and more, melee combat becomes somewhat redundant and not effective at all. It just becomes a struggle, and an annoying and frustrating one at that.
The story isn’t something revolutionary and completely original, but I liked how it was told, and when a game goes for the emotional side of things when it comes to stories then you have me hooked, which made me realise how much I actually enjoyed the game once I had finished it.
Another thing the game does well is the setting and the art. The setting is dark and somewhat gruesome, which can be expected when it revolves around a zombie apocalypse. The cutscenes are hand drawn and look great. They may not have been full motion, but they told the story well while looking beautiful at the same time.
Now, one thing that had bugged me consistently throughout the game, and I don’t just mean the combat was the bugs that I had encountered. A couple of times there were zombies clipping through the door that I had just shut, which didn’t make too much of a difference but wasn’t exactly great either. But the real thing that was a real problem was the majority of the cutscenes had no sound. No sound, no voice acting, no nothing. It was just silence as the cutscene played its way through. I don’t know what the problem is and why some were left unaffected but it did put a damper on the experience for me, since it had occurred so regularly.
Overall though I really enjoyed my time with Deadlight. It had its moments where it had frustrated, thanks to the combat and the lack of audio for the cutscenes, but it did nowhere near tarnish how I felt about the game. Music was brilliant; the hand drawn cutscenes looked great, the story was emotional. Deadlight was just an all-around good game that I would happily recommend and happily play again!

This game is a overall A, not an A+ though... here's some negatives/positives
Positives:
- Realistic sense of danger, when not cheating, starting out bandits (and even looters) are a real threat to your company
- Things like food and money REALLY take into account your actions early on
- When playing on full damage, Moral is extremely important.. if you have an army of 20 go against 25 deserters and lose 10 guys (which is likely) then they will hate the high casualities
- There are many different battle tatics you can use depending on your situation, you don't just have to 'charge' the enemy
- The game lets you cheat when you first start, without this it'd be insanely hard to learn the game
- Interactive factions/NPCs - if you get a lot of renown or honor people will comment on it
- Tournaments are super fun and hard (playing on full damage), it's just really exciting when you finally win one
- Good companions, and their abilities affect the party
- Even at a high level (well, at least 28) your character does not become super-human.. they become stronger, but you still need to watch out
Cons:
- There should be more ransom brokers
- There should be more basic talk options (like to manhunters, travelers,etc)
-  Joining a faction should be beneficial.. in my experiences factions hold you back - they give you 1 town which is always on the border of the faction, which is frequently looted (even as Swadian or Sarranid, which tend to be the strongest)
- Factions are not even, in every game I've played Rhodoks/Khergit/Vaegirs are crushed by day 60, not dead, but have lost 70%+ of their territory... It's happened in 6 games so I'm inclined to believe it always does so
- The entire "prisoner management" system is flawed... I've seen NPC Lords carrying 80+ prisoners, I can only carry 20 (and at level 28)
- Certain bandits are much harder then others, but the loot is not equal - for example Sea Raiders can drop Lordly armor and frequently mail shirts while also selling for 112 gold each, they are all on foot, while Desert Bandits drop horses/crap and sell for 80 each (not to mention you can barely catch them, even with Borcha)
- Swadian and Sarrinid factions are unbalanced with others, Mamluks and Knights are much stronger then anything else on the field - they are beatable while using orders, but facing a high-renown lord from either faction is nearly impossible until very late game

After a while of playing this and I have played more than my game time says becuase I've played it quite a bit offline I finally completed the main story mode for the first time. What I can I say other than the fact that the game is fantastic. Not without flaws mind you but I'll get to those.
The single player mode is full of variety and they give you tons of stuff to do. It's not a game where it's an open world just for the sake of being an open world they give you a lot to do and it's fun exoloring the island and taking part in activities that are a lot of fun whether you're activating towers or you're taking over outposts and espicialoy hunting it always remains a lot of fun.  The island is also huge and even after you've beaten the game's story mode you can still spend a lot of time exploring parts of the island you haven't looked too much into yet.
There's also a crafting system which works well but you do find that you don't really need all the items that you can craft so it comes as bit of a drawback.
The campaign mode is even better. With a really strong story line that goes in places you don't expect. Likeable main character and a fantastic villian in Vaas.
What I love about the game and what really appeals to me is that you have a choice of how you can take out your opponents. You can either live out your fantasty and shoot all of them up or you can be a bit more smart and use stealth and the enviroment to your advantage. Once you gradually level up your character you become more powerful and unclock new moves. This isn't a game where they start you off really overpowered your constally building yourself up and making yourself more powerful which means you can really take your time to get a certain upgrade and it means that doing the activies arojnd the island is really benefictial if you want to level up your character.
This is where I get my biggest complaint about the game which is the multiplayer and co-op modes. I really don't feel this were necessary becuase the single player mode already gives you tons of stuff of do and both of the modes just feel generic and not really that fun.
But overrall this is one of the best open world games you can get and if you can get it on sale buy it you won't regret. Even getting it a full price it's still well worth it.

A rather good rhythm game with a unique system of creating patterns to songs. The audio detection algorithm is amazing, letting you play any music you like and be able to play the game to it. Not all songs are created equal though, there is a stability indicator that says how fluid a song will be, with anything over 50% in my mind being rather good, and anything 80% and above being so fluid that you would think someone manually timed and perfected the notes. It does have a couple drawbacks:
The blur is rather annoying and makes hitting precision targets difficult. The second oddity being that when I go to autoplay my controller rumbles to the song. It's in alpha and those are the worst things I can find, which mean it’s a pretty good game. The pros are the unlimited song bank, the fluid feel of the game, the cool visuals and the convenient interface. No quarrels over hit detection.
For under $10 this is definitely a game to pick up if your fan of rhythm games. And it's only going to get better.

Oh man, I still don't know how I fell about this one. First of all, I'm not a big fan of the level design. Many levels are much more open that I'm used to. This change made me drop my style from the first game and be really careful. Sometimes (when I picked Tony, who can't use any weapons now) I had to bait enemies one after the other so I won't get shot. On this kind of levels I don't feel like I did throughout Hotline Miami 1. It was hard, but if you gave it enough time, you were starting to feel confident and could rush through levels min-maxing your completion time (around 40 minutes for me). I don't think this is going to work here. Much more gunplay is required; the balance betwen melee and guns is about 30-70 for me.
On the other hand, visual aesthetic and soundtrack is still rocking, with a great surreal sequence near the end. Oh, in this one there's much more dialogue and story. There are multiple playable characters, some of whom had restrictions or bonuses. It's much more vital than masks in the first game. For example, one character doesn't use guns at all, and another can only equip ammo to his one weapon of choice. This is another reason why I didn't feel too confident - the story jumps around and sometimes I had a hard time adapting to new rules. I think the main reason I would come back to HM2 is the level editor coming up this spring.
Overall, if you enjoyed the first game, I think you should at least give it a try - maybe you'll love it, maybe you'll think it's okay. It misses the strong, fast style of Hotline Miami 1, but this game can still be a lot of fun. So, like, that's good. RIP Tony.

This is another one of those games that has a lot of style to it but ultimately sacrifices everything else for it. For the first third of the game the atmosphere is great and it really manages to draw you in. What you're drawn into, however, is a total mess.
I think the game suffers from "devs not having others try their own game" during design phase. Everything works, but one can certainly be forgiven for thinking it doesn't. There are not enough mechanics explained so when it comes time to use them the player hits a wall until they figure it out. A good example of this is the tutorial flashback where it shows you to fire a gun.  It tells you the button to load the gun, then says to shoot the can. It doesn't tell you that you use the right stick and RT to do so, it just tells you to shoot it. So if you're dumb like me you mash the buttons until you realize you actually aim the gun using the analog stick (why would I presume that devs?). This isn't so bad in a tutorial with no danger, but combat and running past zombies suffers from this as well. And then there are certain bad design ideas like mysteriously jumping up higher when there's a ledge to grab onto.
Unfortunately the controls are pretty clunky even if you do know what to do. This isn't really a surprise since it is an analog stick platformer and going for a horror setting and there's this ridiculous notion that a "good" horror game needs bad controls. Even if you know what to do hand-to-hand combat is extremely frustrating. You'll swing in the wrong direction all the time. While you're attacking you'll move forward but the enemy won't and they'll end up on the other side of you. To jump straight up you seemingly need no momentum at all instead of just taking your hand off the stick, things like that.
All this combined with some gotcha gaming level design leads to you dying a lot. And dying a lot WILL destroy the atmosphere, especially when it's in the same place over and over. Keep in mind this is with the game TELLING you what to do, more or less. What you need to do or where you need to go is often flat out pointed to with an arrow or highlighted with blue. The running sequences should be scary. I mean, there's a horde behind you. Unfortunately they're just annoying because you get tripped by chairs or get blocked by a zombie and the game doesn't tell you outright how to get around them. And when you figure out the game's already over because it's so short.
There are also some technical issues. I hope you're not like me and use in-game volume controls. Said in-game volume controls do not apply to cutscenes. If you are unfortunate to find this out the hard way enjoy being deaf. The second is that pausing often causes extreme hangs. I've found the only way to fix them is to ctrl+alt+delete, then alt+tab back in.
I did enjoy everything quite a lot before the Rat Labyrinth (you'll see if you play...) but after that the game just felt like a disaster. Very unfortunate. Wasted Potential/10

DO NOT BUY THIS GAME.
Okay, please, read the whole (or at least most) of the review, I might save you some money or at least let you go into it informed.
This is a fantastic concept. If it weren't for a single, glaring issue, I would easily put this as one of my favorite games of all time. It's a FANTASTIC idea. But, do not buy it, or at least not for the single-player mode.
Why?
The. AI. Is. An. Abomination.
Let me give you a quick comparison that'll tell you easily whether you want to deal with it.
Have you ever played League of Legends? Or any MOBA? If you haven't, skip this paragraph.  If you have, remember that worst teammate you've ever had? The one who didn't have items till level 6? The one who tried to solo dragon at level 3? Who went 0/17 in your Gold promos? That one? Yeah. Imagine something twice as dumb, and then imagine you're 1 person in a team of 100, and have to win. That's what this is.
The AI gets stuck on terrain CONSTANTLY. Like everywhere. They do not understand unit priority or what threats to them are, so EVERY SINGLE FIGHT, unless you manually control every single group of units at all times and do not take part in the fight yourself (because you do not have time), they will just die repeatedly. Your cavalry will charge directly into their pikemen line if they get too close. Your infantry will sit there, fighting with spears (which bounce off of units too close to you) in the middle of a massive mob instead of switching to the 3x more effective swords they have, and all the while will ignore the line of archers literally 2-3 feet away from them taking hundreds of free shots at their unguarded backs.
Your archers will insist on trying to snipe halfway across the map at other archers, instead of firing at the infantry 3 feet away moving ultra slow coming up a hill straight at them.
The AI will make you more infuriated than (almost) any game you've ever played.
Now, I'm sure you're thinking “well, it's a really dated game! This is kinda to be expected! Be fair!”. Well, you'd be right, it's old, and old games have worse AI. BUT, this game has seen fairly regular updates since it's release. It's on version 1.158. The AI could have been fixed, or at least far more options given (did I mention you can't tell your units to attack a certain unit type with any sort of efficiency?) sometime in the last several years.
Lastly, the game is basically terrifying without mods. Like if nothing else, the face textures are just horrifying. You need to mod the hell out of it (if you do get it I heavily suggest the “Floris Mod Pack”, and if you like Game of Thrones there's a mod called A Clash of Kings, and one called A World of Ice and Fire, both of which are pretty good).
Now, thanks a ton for reading all of this. I will say, despite my complaints, if one day they DID make the AI not the most rage-fueling, hate-filling, want-to-throw-your-computer-into-a-wall thing you've ever experienced, this game would be one of the most amazing games in gaming history. If you want to risk that feeling of literal hours wasted just because your units can't figure out how to attack an archer, go for it. If you can get past that (even though it will be there in every fight you ever do), it's a wonderful game.
Wouldn't be bad if you can get past dodgy controls, but that is the last thing you should be "getting past" in a platformer.

This game just simply isn't remarkable.  There is nothing you haven't seen and some of the standard elements you might find in a game like this are missing.
1.  There are only about 8 character models - one for each character you can choose from and one infected version of these characters.  These are recylced over and over making for a stale, non-emersive experience.
2.  The models are all low res and don't have the visceral feel of something like Dead Island or Dead Rising.  Not a lot of blood.  No dangling body parts.  Sorta like the bad painted face zombies of the early 1980s.
3.  The mechanics are a little clunky.  I don'y know how you can take the source engine and make it less elegant but they managed it.
4.  Resources are limited and this is good and bad.  I did feel the need to scrounge and save resources but this was partially due to the fact that standard things you might expect are not in the game.   Example - see all that food in the cafeteria?  You might want to eat it to gain some health or at least some stamina buff.  Nope.  Non-interactable.  There is literally no way to heal yourself - that I found - in the game.  Perhaps there is a particular character that is a medic, which would increase team play, but that is not made clear to you in the character selection if so.  I found no method of healing in the game itself - no food, med packs, etc.
5.  The environment is bland and interaction options limited making for a non-emersive experience.  Kill a cop zmobie?  no ammo or gun on him.  See that knife sticking out of the dead zombie's head?  Yeah you can't use that.  Unlike most half-life/source mods, you can't even pickup and throw any objects in the room.
6.  Stamina system is fine but is pretty unimaginative.  It's a standard mechanic in a lot of survival games now and it makes sense.  But then you have other standard survival horror mechanics missing.  Example - your flashlights have unlimited batteries.
7.  Probably the most disappointing part of this game is melee combat.  You have a regular attack and a charge attack.  While you reel from being hit, the zmobies do not.  Even wielding a large sledge hammer, your melee range is about the length of a small toothpick.   The sneak attack thing is highly buggy and this is exasperated by a really underdeveloped stealth system.  If the dev. wanted this to be a part of the game play, the execution needs to be on par with something like State of Decay, Skyrim, or Dishonored.  No stealth or awareness indicator.  The stealth attack can only be executed when you are directly behind the zombie and this often still doesn't work due to environment clipping issues.
Final analysis - pass on this.  I gave it a try on the free weekened and glad I didn't spend a dime on it.  With so many other titles in the zombie genre that are quite solid (although I am still waiting for that perfect zombie game), this one is rather forgetable.

Hotline Miami 2 is a very fragmented game in many aspects. The story (which is now far more prominent compared to the first game) is a multi-perspective, non-linear telling of events which ends up being near indecipherable if you do not find the optional text segments scattered around areas. What's there is certainly interesting, but the extra bits and pieces can be very hard to distinguish as they lack the signature arrows that distinguish everything else in the game.
The gameplay, while initially seeming to be more of the same has some heavy departure from the original game with your score being dependent on keeping a streak far more then any other option, which makes score attack a much more fast-paced affair but heavily penalizes any other playstyle. The mask system was also heavily revamped with quality over quantity changes, although a good third of the available unlocks are more or less copies of earlier unlocks but for another character.
By far the worst change, however, comes in the form of the level design. Corridors stretch far and wide with enemies waiting to snipe you the second you take one misstep, which makes holding your streak impossible until you know every nook and cranny of the level. It also heavily discourages certain playstyles over sniping enemies over long distances, which sometimes makes every enemy on the map hunt for you and sometimes does not. The variety of enemies is bigger than the original game (by about 4-5 new types), but they are utilized far too sparingly.
All in all, Hotline Miami 2 is still a good game, but it is a lot less focused compared to the original and has a few design decisions that detract more then they add. The level design is the deal breaker, but as there is a level editor in the works perhaps fans can use the game to create a larger variety of levels in the future.

It's gone over half a year since I found a pretty long game to play, and Farcry 3 is the name!
First of all...I just love the size of the Islands and the game, and how you can (almost) at all times move freely around with different vehicles, boats or just running. Your character never gets tired either, so you can run limitless. There are also some ways of getting to places, which I will not spoil here. It's awesome!
There are two kinds of people I'll guess. Those who finish the main story fast, or those who explore and try to find every possible hidden item. I am the last one, so I did very few main missions, until the first Island was cleared of almost any box, treasure or letters. The only drawback by doing this, is that you don't get full access to the tattoo, and end up with tons of points you cannot use.
I recommend doing the game until the first or second tattoo skill bundle unlocks, so it's much more fun to capture the bases, and sneaking around.
The story and graphics of Farcry 3 is very good, and my 2012 laptop could almost run it on full graphics. FX effects was put on medium, and is the bottleneck if you start lagging. Having no FX after effects is a bad thing as things will look very taggy, like the ends of some close up items having a zigzaw pattern. In the end medium on it was good enough.
I did also try the multiplayer, to get the last achievements, and it's kinda messy at first, but I'll talk about that later. The MP is alot more than I thought, with level systems, weapon and item upgrades, and I did actually have fun the hours I played it. The messy part is that you can only create a lobby, if you are the leader. You more or less get thrown into a random game, with random people. There is a way to also make private games, but if you don't have friends, just stick with the normal MP. MP levels are really fun, but the only drawback is the skill level of certain people. Some run away from the group, some leave, and at some point you end up just being 2 people playing out of 4.
To end this review. Farcry 3 is an excellent and awesome game, with lots of variety, and I would recommend playing it to the full length, doing as much as you can.

Monster Hunter is one of my favorite franchises.
I also love Dark Souls.
I also love Terraria, Dwarf Fortress, Minecraft, etc.
I love jRPGs, open world games, survival, exploration, etc.
I also love MMOs.
At a glance, this game seems to be all of those things (minus the massively multiplayer part).
Execution-wise, it still has a bit to go.
I'm aware it's early access, so I'm just hoping all these things get addressed soon.
Large monsters walking about, and you have the ability to craft weapons and fight them which looks like a typical
Monster Hunter battle or a Dark Souls boss -- only mechanics have yet to catch up.
It feels clunky at best. The hit boxes are unclear, and the enemies don't seem to follow a set logic.
Also the lack of real movement options for the player -- rolling being the key one, and the lack of attack animations
that are conducive to this kind of gameplay really pulls the experience down.
I found myself avoiding these fights more than not.
It's not a skill issue, either. I would classify myself as "good" to "Very good" at monster hunter, and "well-versed" in Dark Souls.
I appreciate a challenging game and a challenging control interface. I like to take difficult encounters and learn them
until I can beat them untouched and unharmed.
That being said, I found that next to impossible to do even on the easiest of enemies.
The method of combat thus far does not seem to be to outskill your prey, but rather to out-tech it with armor and weapons
until its damage and defense becomes negligible to your own.
Exploration is fun, but could be streamlined a bit and sped up.
Being that it is not massivelty multiplayer, making mining and chopping wood take arbirtarily long amounts of time don't have
any meaningful reason. It's a single player game that focuses on mining and exploration, so let the exploration feel fun.
Tune the amount you dig, the way you dig, and how fast you dig to better reflect this.
Though that sounds like a lot of criticsm, I do in fact enjoy this game. I played it a lot before picking it up on Steam. I still continue to jump in and play every now and then.
I am looking forward greatly to upcoming patches.
This has potential to be one of my favorite games.
I'm hoping the developers pull through.

Because the game uses a bit more aggressive gpu computation, it will appreciate a flaky gpu less than some lucky games. This is likely to remain the case, and even become true of more other games as time passes anyway, though. :p
Personally, I'd prefer if the design editor felt more integrated with the game - right now it feels much more like a meta process which messes with one's feel of existing in the world a bit. not sure how much this can be improved, given that the editor needs to be usable from *outside* of play as well. If you kill a man in this game, it will be because you have driven sharpened metal into him, and your swordarm will be bloodier for it.  There is no fast travel.  There are no magic spells.
This is not a fantasy sandbox RPG, nor is it a medieval empire simulator.  Instead it is something impossibly balanced between the two.  The game world takes (in game) days to cross, even with fast horses and good pathfinding, and each of the dozens of lords, towns, and villages that inhabit it have separate goals, gifts, and opinions of you.  Wars will be fought between factions whether you join one side or not, and the soldiers you lead will prove a far deadlier tool than any weapon you can swing.
And you will lead soldiers, a stunning variety of vikings, knights, crossbowmen and keshiks.  What you lead them to do is entirely your decision.  Noble hero of the people?  Sure, be nice to some villagers.  Murderous brigand?  Go back and raze that village, taking everything you can tear from the peasant's hands.  Loyal vassal?  Ruthless mercenary?  Upstart ruler?  There is no main quest, no scripted events, just a world of chaos, and the choices you make.
Also, bugs, and some very unwieldy interface design. But there are mods that turn this game into Westeros and Middle Earth.  Mods that let you join an army as a raw recruit or engage in politics like a Kennedy-Lannister hybrid.  This game is as close to a freeform, low-magic D&D campaign as currently exists.
Oh alright, there are also mods that add magic.

Mixed reviews for this one.
I'll start with the negatives. First of all, 9 out of 10 cutscenes didn't have any audio. So I'd be engrossed in some sort of 'run from the zombies!' moment, then silence during the cutscene. It took away from the experience quite a bit. I briefly looked into the problem, and it seems like it was a common bug in the earlier release. The patch was supposed to fix it, but it didn't for me. Second, lots and lots of bugs. I wasn't even trying to go anywhere in the game other than the intended route, and I still got stuck a few times (and once flew straight up through the roof of a building and died). This stuff shouldn't happen on a full release. Third (and probably the most annoying), some of the scenes were practically unplayable. I'm not a pro-gamer by any stretch of the imagination, but it shouldn't take the average player-base 10-15 tries to get through a scene (I've looked through the forums and I'm not the only frsutrated gamer out there). A few of the scenes were just plain long and boring, and some of them were just way too finicky. Also, since you can't save the game, every single time you die you have to restart at a pre-determined checkpoint. Throw in some really unresponsive controls, and you have yourself a bit of a frustrating experience. Also, the story was so-so, and the voice acting was mediocre at best.
Ok, now for the good. I loved the concept. It's kind of a 'Limbo' meets 'Walking Dead'. It had so much potential, it's just to bad it missed the mark (see above). Secondly, the visuals. The levels looked really cool (especially the backgrounds).
All in all, it's a fun little game (4 hrs of gameplay) if you can pick it up on special or as part of a bundle.

It starts out decently enough, if a bit dull. Set in a zombie-apocalypse scenario in 1980's Seattle, it seems like it has some originality to it that discerns it from the horde of other zombie games out there, as well as the "2D" sidescroller format.
However, the game quickly went from dull to plain boring, but I kept playing because I figured it wouldn't be a long game, so I might as well push through and get it over with. I was wrong.
Normally being longer than expected would be a benefit, but this game overstayed its welcome very fast, and by the end, you just want to be done. Some of the end puzzles and areas are also among the most frustrating, so much so that you just want to strangle whoever came up with them.
The controls are a problem all the way through the game, although you probably won't notice it too much at first. They are sluggish, and doing several things at once are something the game is very bad at handling. I've tried both KB+M and an xbox controller, I can't actually say which is superior, as the controls just plain suck when using either.
Then there's the story. Between the often outright cringe-inducing lines ("the blood in your saliva is the only real thing left!"), horrible acting that just gets progressively worse, the protagonist odd choices like deciding to hold a speech for a friend right when hundres of zombies are meters away, or the plot "twist" that everyone should see coming from half a mile away, I don't know whats worse.
It tries to be somewhat original, but the writing, acting and way it is told is just plain bad. Calling zombies "shadows" just seems like a lame attempt at calling them something else just for the sake of being original, and you quickly find yourself simply not caring about the protagonist, his missing family, or any of his buddies. He is boring and unlikeable, so are his friends and allies, and the acting for them is mediocre at best, outright bad most of the time. Several characters try to be deep, but they end up only being deep like a puddle, or a like how a high schoolers essay is "deep". There are also plenty of inconsistencies, as well as things that just don't make sense.
There is pretty much no immersion present, due to the boring and badly written characters as well as the poor acting and inconsistencies, and the diary you find often reads like it could have been written by a middle-schooler.
The soundtrack is not noteworthy either, it's just there. Several puzzles are frustrating to execute, not in the way that they're hard to figure out, but in the way that making the protagonist actually do what you want to do quickly becomes an infuriating experience in poor game design. Sometimes you even have to execute them perfectly, with no margin for error, not even a tiny bit, leaving you trying the same "puzzle" over and over until you get the timing right. This is again due to the bad controls that can't figure out how to do more things at one time, nor will allow you to start an action before the previous one is completely finished.
Despite writing so much already, I still haven't mentioned the bugs, of which you'll surely run into some as well.
So to sum it up:
+ It tries to be original rather than just another zombie game (although the execution is bad)
+ Graphics are okay, nothing amazing though
- Bad and boring story
- Boring and unlikable characters
- The writing sucks in general
- Horrible controls
- Game quickly becomes boring and a chore to play through
- Too long, due to the tedious gameplay
- Bugs
All in all, my recommendation is that you save your money and buy something else.

Deadlight, at its simplist, was simply more frustration, cheesiness, and poor design choices than fun. I wanted the game to be over by the end, rather than wanting to see how it concluded. More often than not, you will see the way something should be done in this game, only to be forced to do something a certain way - a way that often does not work.
Deadlight is a zombie game, and a platformer, which is a great idea for a game. The visuals are very good, as the backgrounds make you feel like you are in a post-apocolyptic city. Some of the platforming sections are viably interesting and offer some challenge. A few of the earlier sequences that teach you how to interact with the world and its possibilities gave me high hopes that this would continue into later sequences that were very satisfying.
After this though, the game goes downhill very quickly. The character development is really bad, the lines they deliver in awkward cutscenes and in game both are cheesy, and the story feels very unenthusiastic. Deadlight can't quite decide if it wants to be a platformer that focues more on action, puzzles, or speed; in the end, it winds up doing all 3 poorly. Cheap death mechanics combined with a poor checkpoint system will have you playing the same sequences over and over, even if you have already figured out how to do it.
The action part irritated me the most though. You can only move sideways, but zombies can move in a 3D landscape. This means that zombies, when moving from deep in the frame, can get right next to you without you being able to defend yourself. When this happens in tight quarters with an endless zombie spawn spot while you are trying to complete an objective, it becomes fairly infuriating.
Overall, this to me felt like a waste of time. This game is more of a wasted opportunity than anything else, and I recommend saving your money. There are better zombie games, and better platforming games; hopefully, someone in the future will make a high quality combo of the two, but this isn't it.

Hotline Miami 2 is a very fragmented game in many aspects. The story (which is now far more prominent compared to the first game) is a multi-perspective, non-linear telling of events which ends up being near indecipherable if you do not find the optional text segments scattered around areas. What's there is certainly interesting, but the extra bits and pieces can be very hard to distinguish as they lack the signature arrows that distinguish everything else in the game.
The gameplay, while initially seeming to be more of the same has some heavy departure from the original game with your score being dependent on keeping a streak far more then any other option, which makes score attack a much more fast-paced affair but heavily penalizes any other playstyle. The mask system was also heavily revamped with quality over quantity changes, although a good third of the available unlocks are more or less copies of earlier unlocks but for another character.
By far the worst change, however, comes in the form of the level design. Corridors stretch far and wide with enemies waiting to snipe you the second you take one misstep, which makes holding your streak impossible until you know every nook and cranny of the level. It also heavily discourages certain playstyles over sniping enemies over long distances, which sometimes makes every enemy on the map hunt for you and sometimes does not. The variety of enemies is bigger than the original game (by about 4-5 new types), but they are utilized far too sparingly.
All in all, Hotline Miami 2 is still a good game, but it is a lot less focused compared to the original and has a few design decisions that detract more then they add. The level design is the deal breaker, but as there is a level editor in the works perhaps fans can use the game to create a larger variety of levels in the future.

While it's technically a good game, it's just not better than the first game. A lot of changes in design are mostly what came out during my repeated playthroughs. It's less about having a sandbox to tear through, and more about solving floors that are more like puzzles now. Many levels boil down to firing a gun to lure enemies, and killing them safely. Risky behavior isn't rewarded like it used to be, as just about every single level has gun-weilding enemies, usually in excess.
The characters are more interesting this time around, and there's some fun mechanics that were added. The Swan Siblings are the coolest, but they are extremely buggy in pathing. Dual MP5s are also fun to use. However, this game has less melee weapons than the first game; some weapons were even removed, such as sledge hammer, dart, scissors, etc. Tons of guns got added, though.
I feel like this game will be more worth it when the level editor comes out, and the design issue can be fixed with crowd-sourcing some campaigns out. The story itself is interesting (I like it, anyway), and the music is amazing, but the gameplay is somewhat flawed compared to the original. Many bugs persist from the first game, like glitchy dogs and pathing through doors getting wonky. No crashes, though.
Still: it's not a bad game. It's just not really an improvement or expansion for how long it took to develop. If you really want more of Hotline Miami, this isn't a bad investment. If you haven't played Hotline Miami, play that one first, if only to better understand the story.

I'll keep this review simple:
Pros:
- Excellent fluid animations
- Timing algorithm seems to work like a charm in terms of the buttons syncing up
Cons:
- The fast movement of the camera when the song gets more intense can distort the screen and make it hard to see incoming buttons
- Difficulty ramps up a lot when you move from relaxing to normal. I assume this is because there is a random assortment of the WASD keys instead of a believable rythym like W-A-W-A.
- The actual timing itself is a bit weird; the perfect rating is at the edge of the character's model, not the middle where I assumed it to be. This gets hard to control when the game moves much faster.
- Having to hit a series of keys at X BPM for given amount of time can absolutely destroy your fingers. A 6 minute song will require about 3 minutes of relaxation to get your fingers ready for the next song.
I like the concept but the fast camera and the difficulty in normal seems like it should be Intense. Other than these two points, I'd say this is game has potential.

Being the first Far Cry game I have ever played, I can proudly say that I am extremely satisfied with Far Cry 3.
As a gamer that loves stories in games, I find the story that Far Cry 3 is telling is very intriguing and thrilling as I progressed through the game. The sheer hatred of how psychotic Vaas is, the abduction of your friends and the needs to save them. It all blends very well, from the start of game until the very end. The back story of the unfortunate experience for Jason and his friends  on the Rook Islands is very interesting to me. Who would've thought a skydiving trip could turn into a long, long trip of captivity (at least for Jason's friends).
Being a person that doesn't really care about graphics, Far Cry 3 however has a very, very, beautiful and stunning graphical experience. Although there may be imperfections, say like grass sprite being drawn way over a cliff, the lighting of the game, the water, basically everything, is cool enough to actually make you want to stop doing something in the game and appreciate the scenery. Whew.
AI wise the game excels very well in making the AI of NPCs work brilliantly, maximising interactivity and minimising cringe lol.
If anything related to gameplay, I would certainly say that I really like how stealth actually works really well in the game
Sure, there are shortcomings to the game too. One of which is the difficulty to actually stumble on an animal that you are trying to hunt (for crafting). It would take me a number of times of going away from a particular area, wait a few minutes, and return to see if the animal i wanted would spawn. Another one is that often times when you are trying to liberate an outpost, suddenly the AI of the pirates are kind of unfair, given of how they exactly know where you are hiding. Since I love sniping them from afar, this can be seen a lot clearer as you spectate those pirates running towards your place of camping.
This review isn't meant to be a full fledged review, so take it with a table spoon of salt. Rather, they are just reflections of my opinion and experience on the game. Also that is also part of the reason why my review seems incomplete.

Music is solid and sound effects are terrific. Devs seems to really care about the game, I think they know they have a hit here and want it to do well. Teams can have many different strategies, min/maxing will happen but thankfully the devs did not make the good items rediculously overpowered, you still need skill to win at the higher difficulties.
Tough to continue playing after a while. The crafting system and achievements can keep you motivated, but ultimately a game like this survives on new maps and new gametypes. Hopefully we will see some further development in that direction. Still recommended.

There are still some bugs to work out, but I wouldn't say they're a major hindrance to enjoying Planet Explorers.
I played several hours of the campaign and a bit of the exploration mode.  The mining, crafting, gathering and cooking systems are very solid.  The 3D resource scanner system takes a lot of the guess work out of things, which is very welcome, and the inventory system isn't oppressive with encumberance or backpack limitations.  Upgrading gear between schematics and resource quality was very rewarding and interesting - eventually taking huge chunks of a mountain out at a time felt really good after plinking away at it with a low tier copper pickaxe.
The combat has a lot of flexibility and is entirely gear dependent, and if you have the right minerals, you have the best gear.  The follower systems ensures very good balance for most situations.  Multiplayer was a blast, and buildin my own settement was very rewarding.  As was building my own vehicle from a blueprint starting with no template, only key parts.
The game's seeds are not impossibly large, and have a lot going on to the point where you'll never have to trudge for a long distance totally bored, unless you want to just to explore.  Very interesting wildlife designs and behaviors, lots of predator/prey ambient stuff going on that you can watch.  The giant antagonists are rightfully dangerous and intimidating, very challenging but not impossible to overcome with a solid team.
I very much enjoy this game.  If I had to complain, I'd say that I wish there was more to the character customization, and some of the storyline quests have some annoying bugs, mostly relating to friendly AI behavior.  The game can be gorgeous in places, but only if you ignore some of the low res, constantly repeating ground textures.
Regardless, I still highly recommend Planet Explorers.
