Wait.  If you play this game now, you'll very likely ruin the experience for yourself later.  It's similar to hearing a spoiler for a good movie or sneaking a peak at your presents before Christmas.
Here's an example.  There are two epic items to craft in this game: the glider and the jetpack.  Most importantly, there's only one
you'll build either of them.  If you really have to struggle and strive for it, then it's an extraordinary reward.  Conversely, as in my experience, if you're able to build both of them in the same session, after less than an hour of mining, then it cheapens the whole experience.
Speaking in generalities, the game lacks ballance.  Gameplay jumps up sharply and then plateaus for a long time -- jump, plateau, repeat.
For crafting, the game started well, but soon became boring.  I spent a few days hacking at trees, trading, and crafting simple items.  Much too quickly, though, I gained access to advanced recipes, thereby skipping about 80% of the game's content.
Difficulty is similarly unbalanced, with roughly 3 levels: wild animals, aliens, and giant robots.  Leaning how to kill the aliens was a fun challenge.  The giant robots, however, are perhaps 10-times more difficult to kill, and there are no enemies between these two levels of difficulty.
Survival is way too easy, and without that pressure, gameplay has no tension or excitement.
A.I. feels very basic.  The wild animals exhibit no complex behaviors; they don't socialize, eat, sleep, or communicate.  They are nothing more than wandering bags of meat.  The aliens, who
be intelligent, are glaringly stupid, and this ruins immersion.
Visually, the game is gorgeous, and I absolutely love exploring the fantasy world.  Just be warned, though, that gameplay is loose and sloppy.  I've stopped playing because I don't want to spoil the game for myself.

This game is a overall A, not an A+ though... here's some negatives/positives
Positives:
- Realistic sense of danger, when not cheating, starting out bandits (and even looters) are a real threat to your company
- Things like food and money REALLY take into account your actions early on
- When playing on full damage, Moral is extremely important.. if you have an army of 20 go against 25 deserters and lose 10 guys (which is likely) then they will hate the high casualities
- There are many different battle tatics you can use depending on your situation, you don't just have to 'charge' the enemy
- The game lets you cheat when you first start, without this it'd be insanely hard to learn the game
- Interactive factions/NPCs - if you get a lot of renown or honor people will comment on it
- Tournaments are super fun and hard (playing on full damage), it's just really exciting when you finally win one
- Good companions, and their abilities affect the party
- Even at a high level (well, at least 28) your character does not become super-human.. they become stronger, but you still need to watch out
Cons:
- There should be more ransom brokers
- There should be more basic talk options (like to manhunters, travelers,etc)
-  Joining a faction should be beneficial.. in my experiences factions hold you back - they give you 1 town which is always on the border of the faction, which is frequently looted (even as Swadian or Sarranid, which tend to be the strongest)
- Factions are not even, in every game I've played Rhodoks/Khergit/Vaegirs are crushed by day 60, not dead, but have lost 70%+ of their territory... It's happened in 6 games so I'm inclined to believe it always does so
- The entire "prisoner management" system is flawed... I've seen NPC Lords carrying 80+ prisoners, I can only carry 20 (and at level 28)
- Certain bandits are much harder then others, but the loot is not equal - for example Sea Raiders can drop Lordly armor and frequently mail shirts while also selling for 112 gold each, they are all on foot, while Desert Bandits drop horses/crap and sell for 80 each (not to mention you can barely catch them, even with Borcha)
- Swadian and Sarrinid factions are unbalanced with others, Mamluks and Knights are much stronger then anything else on the field - they are beatable while using orders, but facing a high-renown lord from either faction is nearly impossible until very late game

Is it good? 
-YES
Is it good for everyone?
-NO... - depends!
Why?
...well it's a good mixture of: 
- L4D game mechanics (4 players vs AI with those special enemies, swarming hordes, but no PVP)
- Chivalry: Medieval Warfare melee combat style with charged attacks, parry and dodge
- Kinda pure ranged combat is possible with mage class, limited ranged capabilities due to ammo with others (might change with good loot luck)
Features atm:
- Good graphics (GTX770, i5-4x4.2ghz, 16gig RAM here playing smoothly on high settings – and I know folks that run the game on a first gen i7-860 with a gtx460 on low but are able to play ok'ish)
- Responsive and smooth game engine if the hosting player is in the same region and has a decent connection (play with friends!)
- Nice and atmospheric maps so far
- Random map events you need to deal with keeping the same map re playable (as there where only 3 later 4 maps in beta)
- On the run adjustable difficulty (Grimoires to pick up or not - more loot but group debuffs)
-Team play is key – all loot improving items are shared at the end of the round no matter who carries them home!
Stuff to be aware before buying this game:
- The game play features getting permanently swarmed, little room to breathe or mistakes, it's hard survival after all even on normal difficulty. this is not a game to chill out and snipe some AI's off on a cake walk... no no no it is not!
- Playing the game public may be kinda frustrating due to some players still have no clue what to do at all, run off and get killed quickly so having friends playing the game is a big difference to difficulty and success in general. You should join/form a group/clan in the long run or just be fine with those random dudes in public games – it's not impossible to master higher difficulties in public games but it's less likely for sure in WH:Vermintide.
- 1st person melee combat may not be liked by everyone - but I was surprised how many of my friends who disliked the combat in Chivalry: Medieval Warfare now enjoy this game as it is PvE not PvP. A big difference!
- hard difficulty means HARD DIFFICULTY atm, epic and legendary loot tiers require high game difficulties to get any chance at all rolling them ... you need a team of capable FPS/Chivalry players to proceed to those nice and shiny loot things! (I hope it stays this way... good loot should always be a challenge to get not only a matter play time and pure grind)
- "head bobbing" can't be turned off yet so ppl with motion/simulation sickness be aware of this (or avoid 2H-weapons to minimize the shaking effect)
- No color blind mode yet
- Just one master volume slider meaning loud music all the time or low game volume... I got used to it but meh
- No dedi servers yet (but promised)
- Once again: playing public games is not ideal as some ppl (as like in any game) may not care about team play that much or have (yet) no clue how to react to certain events - I recommend to play it with friends or to quickly make friends with good players along your runs to master that learning curve together! Individual player skill is one thing, to form a successful permanent team needs time but it's very rewarding.
- The loot system is very very random atm. If you're unlucky you won't get a good item for your preferred class after days of game time.
State of game development: 
-The game has still some flaws with stability that might need treatment by the user...
for e.g.: GTX680/GTX770 users might need to down clock their GPU by 40mhz with nvidiainspector.exe to avoid crashes (common problem in a lot of games these days...)
-The game does not feel finished and polished balance and hit box wise, but it's playable - good luck finding another good COOP vs AI game those days so it's ok for me :)
- The game Devs seem to care and fix stuff kinda quickly - so that's promising for existing and future issues.
To sum it up:
This game is an awesome TEAM CHALLENGE!
L4D and L4D2 PvE are a cake walk compared to this.
Like it or not, you will first fail, then hopefully learn, group up, maybe give up (!) or succeed through higher tiers of swarming PvE COOP madness!
Or you don't care about good loot, (get drunk) play it on easy with friends and have a good time for some hours - totally fine too ;)

I would highly recommend this game to fans of the CoD series, for those who want a fairly interesting and gripping single player game full of action and high octane gameplay. But honestly - this game is not worth the full price of £40/$50. You'd be wise to pick this game up cheap on a sale or reduced price!

This is a game for fans of the original hotline miami. If you haven't played it or didn't like it, don't buy this game. If you liked hotline miami 1, consider getting it. Just wanted to give you the short version first, I tend to ramble.
My first run took roughly 9,5 hours, though there are plenty of replay ability with getting achievements, getting high scores and trying to beat the game again on hard difficulty.
Hard difficulty flips the map (which might not sound like much, but it does make it disorienting when you come back to missions you've played before), reduces ammo on guns and gives you notibly tougher enemies to fight.
Though the graphics, animations and soundtrack are as good, if not better in some cases, as in hotline miami (now referred to HM1), hotline miami 2 (HM2) has multiple issues that need to be addressed.
The 4 main issues with this game is: Too many long halways and open spaces where you can't see the enemy, but they can see you. This leads to more deaths than is healthy being based on not being able to see them because they were too far away. This encourages not a speedy and violent approach to a level, but a slow and paranoid one, which also hurts your end score.
2: Too much glass windows. Both enemies and you can see eachother through glass windows, and both you and enemies can shoot through them. This leads to a huge amount of frustration, as nearly every single level has multiple layers of glass. It is more realistic, I suppose, but stil, it will become very frustrating as you play through the game.
3: The cursor gets stuck on invisible walls on the screen all the time. This is (I assume) a very serious bug. When the cursor gets stuck on the screen, you can't look around, and often you can't aim or fight against enemies because they come from a blind spot and your cursor is stuck! You can sometimes free it by jerking the mouse across the screen a few times, but it is stil very frustrating.
4: The story is pretty difficult to follow, aswell as confusing. Though it might be on my part, not memorizing all the dates, months and years the game shows, its still annoying. I am assuming the game takes place as a movie or recording (they reveal this in the first mission, don't worry about spoilers), but its stil a little fuzzy. People have complained about the ending too.
That was most of the negative. Now to the possitive!
1: This game has more variety than HM1. While HM1 had the general theme of each level being chose a mask for a bonus and walk in and kill everything in sight with the same general tactics, this game throws far more characters at you! You have the reporter, whom doesn't want to kill people and tries to be careful, the fan club whom wear animal masks just like jacket, all of which get different bonuses.
One of the fans are 2 siblings (brother and sister), one is controlled directly and uses a chainsaw, while the other follows you and can use guns to shoot, very cool concept, though fairly awkward to control.
You have the soldier, whom dual wields a gun and a knife, and some other characters. The soundtrack (stil has some great songs, so you can likely appreciate that at the very least) also feels more varying in the theme of its songs, from upbeat pop to threatening party music and all the way to creepy and sad tunes.
HM2 is much more difficult than HM1 (partly because of long hallways and glass window overload), so getting good scores takes notibly more skill and practice than before (my lowest rank on HM1 was usually a C-, and that was rare).
The ending is very strange. It comes out of nowhere after a very interesting and unique mission, but it doesn't answer any questions, and is fairly unclear of what really is happening (though it is likely that they don't want to make a 3rd game in the series).
The concept and ideas for this game are very good, the variety is nice and the gameplay is more hotline miami, though that is more or less what we hoped for in the first place. As I said in the beginning, don't buy this if you haven't played or disliked hotline miami 1, as this game has little mercy for newer players. Consider waiting for the game to get fixed and perhaps for the price to drop. Other than that, its great for hotline miami fans!

I haven't finished the game yet but I can already say that it has been a disappointment. So much so that I even felt I had to write a review (something I've never done before).
Like many others have pointed out before, Hotline Miami 2 is lacking in almost every respect when compared to HM 1.
You are constantly fighting enemies off screen, unloading guns down hallways and huge rooms hoping to kill enemies you cannot see because if you don't, they will kill you immediately. As a result, you are constantly moving around looking for enemies off screen who will snipe you. It's tedious and doesn't feel in the spirit of the first game which was frantic but still felt fair.
Cheesing the AI plays a much larger role too, since there are so many enemies armed with firearms, that your best bet is to lure them into kill rooms and just unload your magazine into the doorway. While this also true in part for HM 1, it was mostly a last resort. In HM 2 you'll find yourself using this tactic much more often, which has never been the fun part of the game.
The fun part was to plan how to tackle each room in advance and then try to execute that plan with precision and speed. Now most rooms are full of gunmen some of which you can't even see, so you are forced to either shoot them all, or again lure them into a funnel or kill room. No variety there.
This also aplies to amount of melee weapons in the game. MUCH less choices there and thus less variety in the execution  animations.
Also, AI doesn't seem as consistent anymore. Shooting a gun won't automatically make everyone run towards where you are, making it much easier to get away with not being stealthy. Even so the game seems more difficult, but it does so because of the wrong reasons: larger levels focused on gunplay, much more enemies. It all becomes more focused on twitch reactions, not on planning and executing.
While presentation overall is still great, the sequel takes a poor direction in terms of design in my opinion. Just replay part 1.

This is an excellent game.  I am actually quite impressed with the depth of this game and the variety of play styles available.  It is possible to play this game from a militaristic angle or a diplomatic angle and both are quite difficult and dynamic styles of play.  The combat system is pretty good, though I get a bit of stuttering sometimes in the larger battles.  It is unclear why since the graphics shouldn't a problem (even when I turn the graphics down).  At the same time, you could play a romantic, trade goods to make money, avoid all combat and marry into a dynasty.  It is very interesting to see so many different ways to play this game.
The politics are quite complex and allow a variety of ways to engage the leaders and lords.  Cultivate relations with one or all the lords, support an usurper to regain a throne, or just make enemies of everyone by looting caravans and harrassing peasants.
The battles are also dynamic, though a bit easy at times.  You can move troops tactically, though most of the time, they just run straight at the enemy.  It is sometimes hard to control the troop movements.  I recommend you stop everyone first, if you plan on making real tactical movements during battles.
At the same time, on horseback, I can pretty much dominate any battle I am in, which makes it a bit too easy.  The only enemies that can even start to damage me are those with very large numbers of crossbow and bow units.  Even these have trouble if I keep moving in the right directions and have a working shield.  So, the combat can become a bit tedius.  In addition, if you don't enter combat with your troops you will lose more than if you enter.  It always happens, so I am stuck entering pretty much every combat situation, though it is usually not completely boring.
Overall I think this is a great game and allows great depth.  I have only begun to gain several castles, and I can see a very long road to becoming king, if ever.  So, it is really is a long game and allows a lot of different styles.
Note that I have not played much MP or DLC on this game.  I found the Nepoleon expansion relatively uninteresting and the MP scenarios under Nepoleon expansion rather strange.  However, I have not played them enough to comment much further.

This game is very good, period.  Loading music into it is a snap - you can either find the file on your drive, or you can just open your music player and drag-and-drop the file right into the game window.  The load times are very quick, even when uploading a song for the first time.  Sound quality is crystal-clear, animation is smooth.  This game did surprise me though - some sections of songs that are normally slow-paced (like the intro to Free Bird by Lynyrd Skynyrd, for example) have Melody running at a higher speed.  Not exactly a bad thing - the game still runs smoothly as the beat changes.  If you happen to flub up, it's not bad either - you get placed back on the course at exactly the right spot every time, without hindering the music.
If you like rhythm games, I highly recommend this one.  $10 (or until March, $9) is a fair price for this title.

What can I say? Melody's Escape has the potential to be the best rhythm game of this generation; The concept is simple, like any game of this genre - press the right buttons with the right timing, with the hardest difficulty adding an additional directional button press in songs. It works well, my only problem is that it's EXTREMELY easy to get confused at first - you'll be pressing B instead of X instead of A instead of Y for a good long time, worsened by the exactness of the timing. This can be mitigated with practice though, and that's the name of the game for this genre.
The music detection is as spot on as I've ever seen, especially nice is that it changes the algorithm used depending on what kind of music you're playing. It handles almost every song I throw at with aplomb - from metal to electronic even to more downtempo, ambient stuff.
The aesthetic is minimal - the screenspace is mostly black, with a soft, dark background to add a little contrast - a good choice as you want minimal distractions from the demanding gameplay. Melody herself is generally very fluid in her animations, flowing from one maneuvre to the next easily, while her hair adds a welcome splash of colour as it changes through the song. As of right now there isn't much in the way of personalisation but that has been declared as one of the things to be added shortly.
My main beef on the graphical side is that it starts to hurt the eyes after a while because of the motion blur - if you have a 120Hz monitor the game will shine but for 60Hz plebs like me it can get a bit painful over extended periods.
On the audio front, it's quiet. Aside from the menu music and effects you don't hear much in the way of ingame effects, with your music being the absolute focus of the game.
Overall, Melody's Escape is a very good rhythm game and well worth trying out for fans of the genre. It's feature set is a bit minimal but that's to the plus - it's focused on what it does and it does it well.

(40 hours into a0.82) I was very very surprised at how much I liked this game and I look forward to it reaching full release at some point. Compared to my 50 hours of time put into Starbound (100 hours into Terraria), I think PE has a lot more going for it. The only clear negatives right now would be an out-of-memory CTD every 40-80 minutes of playtime, and the obvious, sudden "work in progress" placeholders for the story mode missions about 30-40 hours into the game (but suggests maybe another 10-40 hours of story mode at least). Other rough spots include game balancing and some issues w/ colony (micro)management and crafting/block placement.
Those kinda pale in comparison to the sense of awe inspired by exploring the (story mode) landscape though. The graphics tend to be a bit cartoony but not much more so than Starbound/Terraria (but in 3D), but the landscape and views can be pretty breathtaking, and (spoiler alert) you can eventually buy/craft a jetpack and a glider, and along w/ a rope gun which gets some use, it reminds me a lot of the awesome feels coming out of Just Cause 2's parachute and grappling hook. The first time I crafted a simple flyer sled put an easy grin on my face too, and I had the odd but welcome reminder of how I felt when I enchanted some uber gear back in Daggerfall and Morrowind to do silly awesome things in a game, or the rush I felt realizing I could fly the jumbo jets in San Andreas.
The game has an MMO-inspired mission progression and exploration/open world feel to it, with action gameplay that feels like Minecraft or Terraria/Starbound, married to gathering/crafting partly inspired by Minecraft, with an object-modeling/crafting system that feels both relatively powerful for a game while also being a bit limited in terms of a 3D modeler (even a partly voxel-based modeler). Most of your time will probably be spent exploring the breadth of the oft-times breathtaking landscape in story mode, and some of your time digging out ores (after finding deposits using your trusty ground-penetrating scanner). Story mode also has pretty nicely-written NPC dialogue that fits the graphical style of the game, scifi-ey with just enough cartoon feel to make it feel kinda epic w/o being too serious.
Other (good) comparisons I could think of: Spore's exploration gameplay. Mining/gathering in the game isn't too bad either, but I'm not that into that kind of play, and tunneling isn't too satisfying b/c of the slower animation (but you get multiple resource units per swing). There's also no need-based survival-type management, aside from keeping your inventory stocked w/ hp and stamina consumables and ammo/repair mats, but this is similar to Terraria and Starbound which are still nice games without having Wayward or Don't Starve's emphasis on survival.
Enough tangents though, PE is a fun game, as long as you can forgive the CTDs and current balancing issues w/ some of the alien creatures you have to fight from time to time (oh yeah, minimal flashbacks to Monster Hunter, at least seeing the size of some of those beasts, but don't get me wrong, combat is fairly straightforward in PE). I'm still starting out in adventure mode, so I don't know if PE's story mode strengths carry over, but my initial impression is that landscape/map generation could probably use some work.
BTW, the map is pretty big, as in it take a while to hoof it from place to place even in one biome. There's Fast Travel to landmarks, but you also eventually get the ability to build cars, boats, or flying vehicles if you like (even making them into gun platforms), or as I said up top, you could jetpack into the sky then switch to glider to take to the skies (plus rope gun if you want to scale mountains w/o burning (camp-rechargeable but also craftable) battery).

At first, I was mildly excited for a voxel based Minecraft clone, with real combat and a few other
advances. To say I have been pleasantly surprised is a gross understatement. I wildly underestimated both the technical expertise of the developers and the coherence and beauty of their vision.
BUILDING
To get a sense of their intent; take Minecraft construction and speed it up a bit, make it take
significantly less gathering time, and shrink the scale of any project. In other words, the world of Planet Explorers lends itself to building more things faster, and toward those things feeling like part of a bigger world. (this is not meant as universal praise)
TERRAIN
The biomes in Planet Explorers (story mode) are gargantuan. You truly feel totally immersed in an alien world, hoofing it across grassy plains. Your character will witness the sun rise and set
behind massive mountains that actually sometimes require planning to bypass them to reach your destination quicker or safer! In other words, the terrain achieves relevance AS TERRAIN while at the same time being fully terraformable.
WILDLIFE
Adding to this are the herds of fauna. In addition to the large number of different types of
creatures, there is a huge number of types of AI. You will witness flyers ganging up on prey, troops of monkey creatures fighting off predators, those same predators catching lone monkeys, and many other realistic situations.
CRAFTING
So you take this mix; quick construction, living, breathing fauna, and a gorgeous natural
environment, and to it add a heavy layer of crafting. Crafting is very well done, leaning toward
recipe trees that make harvesting always fun and profitable, while reducing the actual act of
crafting to a minimum (for good or ill). This causes occasional lulls in the frenzied bouts of
construction, while allowing one to get back to it after a refreshing harvest period.
COMBAT
Combat is odd. It fufills its function properly; requiring you to watch your back, but not too much, allowing some experimentation and failure without too heavy a penalty, and giving a sense of progress and empowerment over time. The combat itself is fairly clunky at the moment. One's character is required to completely stop moving to perform a combat action (swing, shoot, throw) so it isn't super fast paced action twitch combat. It is however often frenetic and thrilling. My only objection is that healing items are instantly applied and heal for huge amounts, often 70% of your HP. Personally I'd prefer they back off on instant huge heals and, like combat, go for slightly slower action, requiring planning and preparation.
SUMMARY
Overall, better than I ever imagined I'd get in a game featuring heavy terraforming and
construction. To have so many and such varied systems layered atop an already well executed creation game is, frankly, dreamy.
PROS & CONS
- wildlife view distance is fairly low, leading to some pop-in and unrealistic situations
- voxel technology has a ways to go; your creations have a far smaller draw distance than everything else. Again, pop-in.
- players who enjoy this type of slower combat don't want to monitor their HP bars for sudden
precipitous drops; they want to monitor the RATE of DECREASE of their HP. Conversely, allow movement during combat actions to move toward more action oriented combat.
- runs pretty heavily on my SSD, 3+ghz multi-core, decent gfx card system. Not sure if it needs
optimization or it's just a heavy game, but either way it wants a beefy system.
- texture detail is varied. some are goregous and sharp, others are, hopefully, placeholders.
- the humanoid characters look fantastic in terms of animation and graphics. really top notch.
- bullets and lasers should really be far faster.
- lighting is fantastic both indoors and out. doesn't hog up my FPS, either. (how the hell?!?)
- water looks great, needs physics based waves. keeping my fingers crossed.
SPECIAL MENTION
- billboard grass done right! The view distance on the 3d grass is mind-blowing, and the way they animated it is perfection. Wow.
- flowers that bloom at certain times of day! huge boost to immersion
- the person behind the "ambience" features in this game is a genius. floating petals and flowery debris is such a subtle but effective addition to the plains biome.

First time doing a serious review of a game, so please bear with me.
NOTE: This review is for version A0.82 so my opinion may change for better or worse over time.
With that all over with, let's get to the review.
Planet explorers is a voxel based open world building/RPG game with Singleplayer/multiplayer support. The game is very playable for an alpha game, and deserves all the credit possible for that feat alone. It's one of the best games I've played this year, and has lots of replay value through the creation system on its own. The building system in this game is one of its strong points. It improves upon something that games like Minecraft fall short on. It gives you the ability to enter a free cam mode and build as you see fit, with support for curved edges, slopes, ramps, and everything else of the sort. The creation system is fun to use, but really flimsy with its actual usage ingame. So far I've seen little use for ground vehicles, aside from being cool looking sometimes. The weapons are terribly weak and could be improved upon. When my 1000 meat pistol does more damage than 20,000 meat tank, then you have a problem. But all that aside, I've spent a majority of my time on this game making vehicles and weapons. It truly gives the power to the players. With admins stating that they plan to add extensive mod support for this game in later builds, I see it having a very long and prosperous life. Instant classic.
The combat system in Planet Explorers is very clumsy to say the least. You lunge forward with melee weapons and flail around like an idiot hoping you hit something, while the massively overpowered giant monsters make scraps of you. I've used 3+ revival shots on fights that should'nt even need healing. The ranged weapons are bearable, but the Ocarina of Time camera angle it throws you into makes moving and shooting very annoying. In the end I found myself relying on grenades and placing down my Artillary cannons to deal with monsters instead of actually fighting them.

Amazing game in it's current early access state and I'm really looking forward to see what else the developer might add to the game. Having a lot of fun exploring the world while going on my own little adventures!

Call of Duty: Ghosts is, in a word, pathetic. It is a Call of Duty game that not even the Call of Duty fan will enjoy, let alone anyone whose cynicism for the series has prevented them from playing previous games. How did we get here from the magnificent Modern Warfare back in 2007? I don't know either. And yet here we are.
Infinity Ward's latest at bat definitively proves them to be the total incompetents we thought they were after their latest outing. Right from the amazingly dumb opening through to a trite and stupid twist, Call of Duty: Ghosts provides the low mark for the series with aplomb and panache, ably making the boring and poorly made Modern Warfare 3 look good by comparison.
From the outset, the game initially looks promising. During the loading screen of the first mission we are treated to a dumb introduction in which the narrator introduces some silly and foolish legend about a group of soldiers called "ghosts" complete with hyperbole and unnecessary mysticism that makes them seem farcical. Before long (though the story is one you've heard a thousand times before, yet never quite so tritely), the introduction cutscene mercifully ends, and we are treated to one of the worst opening sequences in Call of Duty memory in which you realize the narrator telling the story was the protagonists father. Before long, something awful happens and the protagonist, his father, and his brother leave their campfire and run along aimlessly yelling about tremors before we are introduced to ODIN - an orbital weapons platform. Suddenly, we find ourselves in control of a US space commando - literally - hovering in space around the ODIN station now under attack by foreign saboteurs determined to take control of the station and destroy the US military with it.
We later learn that these enemies are from "The Federation," a South American super state that has implausibly grown in power to challenge the US. The enemies succeed in wresting control of the station and using it to bombard the US, and as this space commando you are tasked with taking back control of the station, or scuttling it if you are meant to do so. The sequence is phenomenally cool, and when it abruptly ends two minutes later you will probably think to yourself "Wait! No! I want to be in space again!" Save for one glorious moment right at the end of the campaign that does take you back there, and save for a few short sequences in which you take control of Riley, an adorable and bloodthirsty German Shepard who moonlights as a mass murderer and who is the games only likeable character, the game begins a sharp slide into stupidity from which it never recovers. The few moments with whacky high tech doodads are nothing you haven't seen before, and the hardware in the game varies from "boring" to "Black Ops 2 did it better."
As is typical of Call of Duty these days, you will find yourself faced with enormous numbers of explosions and uninteresting characters. Uniquely, there are two opposing plotlines - saving the crippled remains of the United States from The Federation, and hunting down and killing Rorke, who is himself busy with hunting down and killing the aforementioned ghosts, who develop into some ridiculous kind of brotherhood. While the setting may be interesting, it is badly bungled, and the actual story of the game is truly dumb. The game features a number of twists, each and every one of which you will have predicted long before the reveal.
From a gameplay standpoint, it seems like there was precisely zero playtesting of any kind. The familiar "flinch" when shot is worse than ever, and makes it a chore to play in the fast paced style you'd like to. The checkpointing is also truly terrible, even by the low standards the series has set. I can recall many times - enough that I've forgotten several and yet still couldn't count them all on the fingers of both hands - where you will die, then be treated to sitting through a five to twenty second scripted sequence before the ensuing firefight. Infinity Ward is not skilled at their game, obviously, and the weapon balance is woefully off kilter. Shotguns are unusuable garbage, pistols offer absolutely nothing, assault rifles do nothing that a sub machine gun does not do better, and light machine guns are so vastly superior to everything else that you wonder why you'd bother. Save for a few scripted sequences, you wont want to touch any of the sniper rifles either, as none of the games battles take place over long enough distances to warrant their use.
The awful campaign meanders along until one glorious section in space, where you are given the proper extra-planetary encounter you wanted at the start of the game. It isn't long enough by half, features more of the same dumb flinch and bad checkpointing you remember (although even here it seems like it was done better), but it is totally cool and makes you wonder why they bothered to have any of the levels on the ground at all. While it is glorious, this five to ten minute segment absolutely does not redeem the stupendously bad single player campaign.
The games multiplayer is as you'd expect for an Infinity Ward game, featuring lousy maps, a bunch of stupid gimmicky extras, and as usual, overpowered defensive tools that turn the game into a campground that will infuriate players who want the kind of frenetic multiplayer that the series can provide at its best. As it was in the campaign, the weapon balance is totally off, and the remixes to the basics will do nothing to thrill vets on the series, who should probably just play Advanced Warfare or the pretty excellent Black Ops 2.
Packaged as an extra is something called "extinction," which provides a Zombies-esque wave survival mode against creepy crawlies, but instead your opponents are alien creatures. It features a more defined campaign style setting with a pretty explicit story that is a major step up from the standard Zombies games, and there is a lot to like here if you're determined to play more Call of Duty. I was not, personally, but it will likely appeal to someone with a little less Call of Duty fatigue.
On thing worth noting is that Call of Duty looks like a game from 2008, but runs like a game from 2018. It's confusing options defaulted to the absolute lowest on my rig (of course, the game runs at a stable 30 FPS on high settings). While I was tinkering with the graphics options, my biggest challenge wasn't finding a good mix of graphical fidelity and performance, though - it was finding a good mix of graphical fidelity and not-crashing-to-desktop. Consider yourself duly warned.

Contagion is a first person shooter/survival horror game. Contagion is the first game developed by Monochrome LLC. The game takes another perspective on zombie survival. You can’t wildly shoot zombies. You have to learn to conserve ammo and aim for the head.
Contagion has some major elements to the game. It can be either played online or solo. The weapon, ammo and item drops are completely random. Each time I played, things were in a different spot. The zombies behave like you would expect them to. They wander around meaninglessly like a zombie should. If you make noise, the zombies will notice you and you will be swarmed by a horde of them. Each time you load up the game, the location objectives you have to go to will be different. You may have to go to cell block 1 the first play through and cell block 2 the second.
The concept and zombie AI are amazing in Contagion. You use a cell phone to communicate with teammates. The phone looks like an actual cell phone. Another thing, I wasn’t expecting to be able to shoot a zombie in the head through a door, but when I did it was fun and satisfying. I found myself doing that over and over from that point on. The in-game sound is really good. The zombies sounded creepy and immersed me into the game. With a headset, when a zombie is right next to you, you can hear them as if they are next to your chair. The graphics in the game are beautiful and very impressive for Monochrome’s first game.
Although the graphics are amazing, in order for it to be playable, I had to turn all my settings down. In the process of turning my settings down, the game froze and I had to force close the game. When I read the system requirements, my PC could more than handle the recommended system requirements. When you first install the game, the graphics are on the absolute lowest settings. These observations lead me to believe that there is a bug in the coding. Another bug I found was that head shots sometimes didn’t register as a head shot. Sometimes the bullet would miss completely, and others it would take 4-6 shots between the eyes for the zombie to fall. This had me very frustrated because of the fact that ammo is very, very rare. The ammo drops sometimes feel too rare, and then you see that an abundance of ammo is laying around in one room. I found myself aggravated at that fact because I had to melee my way around since I ran out of ammo.
To wrap things up, the concept for Contagion is great. The idea of using your cell phone to view a GPS of the map is exciting. The game seems very slow paced, and seems more like an exploration game once you have killed everything. In my opinion, if you would like to support the developer, purchase the game. That’s how I am viewing my purchase. If money is tight or you have other games that you are interested in, I would suggest waiting until Monochrome irons out all the kinks.

This is an amazing rhythmic-platforming game. You basically tap along the beat in accordance with the color and directional ques on the screen.
Melody Escape has, let me tell you this frankly, just about the best beat detection in a music game I have EVER played! It is also a "true" rhythm game, unlike stuff like Audiosurf which merely masquerade as one.
Game is not easy, and it will take just a while for even seasoned rhythm gamers to get warmed up. You start off at Relaxing difficulty, move up to Normal and then all hell breaks loose (or is it your fingers go out of control?) in Intense difficulty.
The game uses your own music and doesn't have any built-in music for now. I've played across a range of BPMs, and some songs with varying tempos....and the game takes them all on its chin.
Controls can be edited to your liking, as can the visual effects be tuned.
So yeah, this one here is a resounding recommendation on my part if you like rhythm games. It is almost a no-brainer given its amazing and revolutionary I might say beat detection technology.

The music genre is a shadow of its former self; we used to see yearly iterative titles and silly spin-off here and there. So what happened? A mix of oversaturation and minimal innovation led to one of the quickest booms and bust for a gaming genre. Recently we’ve seen PC take centre stage with games such as Osu! and Audiosurf being front runners, they’re extremely affordable and include a huge range of playable songs without the need of some ridiculous peripheral. So where does Melody’s Escape fit in here?
Melody’s Escape's only limitation is the size of your music library. It is able to detect your audio files (FLAC works, Audiophiles rejoice!) and then convert them into a playable song. The gameplay is simple enough to pick up and go, while still being somewhat hard to get a perfect score in songs with higher BPMs. The goal is simple; get the highest score possible.
Now one thing that may turn you off after looking at gameplay may be the fast movement of Melody. The game moves incredibly quick at times and your song of choice may not always help you concentrate. It's for the most part easy to read due to the great colour palette, the black objects help bring out the colours of the notes, also obstacles share a certain input and as such you can even use them as a second point of reference. Though it's easy to read it doesn't mean it's not strenuous on the eyes, there's a little to much going on screen at any one time and it destorys anyone who uses peripheral vision as a main tool.
While it may be fun to play it does lack one key thing which music games are greatly known for,  improving one’s self and being able to display your improvements through scores. It’s hard to know what song is harder than another and two people could play the same song but if one is playing at a different bit rate you could get different tracks.
In saying that I still think it has its spot in the music game genre. While it may not be as hard as Osu! or have a great group experience like Rock Band. It allows you to play any song you want, whenever and presents you with a clear and easy goal.

Thought it would be alright for $15. What a rip. Super buggy - what FPS have you played where scopes actually glitch and become useless? Hit detection and lag issues are many times worse than the initial problems plaguing BF4 when it launched. Those are just the most glaring issues.
Graphically, it's rather disgusting. I assumed that everything had defaulted to Low settings for some reason, but upon inspection, it was all set to High. It basically looks like Duke Nukem Forever and plays like Quake 3 Arena.
The whole game is generally a mess; it's split up into three different parts: Single Player, Competitive Multiplayer, and Co-Op Extinction. It doesn't even feel like one unified product which is very strange.
Single player features the typical Call Of Duty style large set pieces void of any interactivity and instead of letting you explore these environments, you are hurried to the next whatever to shoot more stuff. In some cases if you hang back to explore, you automatically fail the mission. Even the objectives you are pushed around to are unclear and not interesting except for bringing you closer to the next loading screen cutscene and towards the end of the game. I played for a few hours and decided it was just too dumb to waste my time with.
Multiplayer is pretty much Team Deathmatch since the majority of players (less than 400) were playing this. Due to the lack of dedicated servers, you have no control over what game you are entering. This sucks so hard. The time to kill for pretty much every weapon is super fast and due to lag, things can get really weird. Dying after running behind a wall, or getting killed before even hearing the multiple shots that took you out. It's gross. Watching the deathcam replays even shows in slow motion how janky the hit detection is - it is pretty damn funny.
Extinction has crashed every time I tried to play it, so maybe I'm missing out on why this game deserves more than $5?
If you are into early-access alpha versions of games, you might like this. Otherwise, save your cash.

If you're looking for a medieval game that lets you work your way up from nothing to a king, then this is the game for you. You're rewarded for patience and loyalty by the lords and kings you serve until you're able to declare sovereign right. You can be punished or praised if you're a warmonger. And even if you work your way up, you can still be torn down and stripped of pretty much everything.
It can be punishing, time consuming, and at times tedious. However if you're a fan of strategy games, fantasy, and the Elder Scrolls genre, I believe this is the game for you.

(Current main version at the time of this review: 0.8, just played singleplayer)
I bought the game when it was doing its kickstarter after seeing it on YouTube, been following devopment since.
Updates come every few months, but contain a lot of features and advance the story significantly, the devs regularly post updates.
Overall impression: Pretty far developed for a early access game, nice and immersive artstyle (barely anything looks out of place). (The trailers/screenshots are gameplay footage, not rendered CGI unlike many games these days)
Story: The current storyline (advances with every update) got me occupied around 18-20 hours the last playthrough, probably a lot more when going blind and not rushing it (restarted with 0.8 update, did not spend much time designing/making weapons/vehicles/building).
Gameplay: Not much time has to be spent grinding, you can use the shop to skip some parts of the "tech tree"(there is no real techtree, you can get almost everything with tier-1 stuff), like faster tools or vehicle parts, as you get more meat (currency) then you need.
Creation System: Although it is not really intuitive (i recomment looking for tutorial) it is really powerful and allows to create really detailed things that change their stats(damage/speed/...) based on shape and material used. You can also paint everything so you can recreate your favorite gun/car. If that is not your style, there are many community-created creations to download, like detailed gun-replicas, various furniture and futuristic helicopters.
Bugs: I had a few bugs and graphical glitches here and there but nothing really gamebreaking, completely acceptable for a Early Access game.
Performance (i7 2630QM/GT 555M):  Just runnable(15-20 fps) when setting everything to
and runs fine while still looking nice if i lower it a bit on my
, honestly expected worse.
Remember: This is a Early-Acess game so what i wrote might be outdated, i recommend playing the beta (older version, availble on the website) and watching some gameplay footage of the full version to see if it fits your style.

I've been saying for a while that my perfect game would be a cross between Skyrim and Minecraft:  I want big, beautiful graphics, quests and plenty of monsters to kill, and an open world I can dig up in 3D to build my house brick-by-brick.  And I have to say that so far Planet Explorers is already coming pretty close!  I love the planet's megafauna and that there's a predator/prey system in place.  I love that plants apparently have a life cycle.  And the premise of the story is just fantastic.  (Did I mention how much I love that a sandbox game has an actual story?)
And there's a Thing editor.  Vehicles, swords, shields, random arts and crafts:  THINGS.  I honestly didn't expect to like it, because I'm not what you'd call an architect, or an engineer.  And then I built this car.  It was an awful car, but the next one I built was twice as awesome in half the time.  And then I built a helicopter.  A helicopter, okay?  It was magic.  (Okay, it was awful.  But the ability to make a helicopter?  THAT was magic.)
Yes, the game still has its issues; it's in alpha after all, so that's to be expected.  In A0.82, farming is a little iffy (I suggest you start with a 5x5 plot of non-organic and work your way up from there) and I've had some crashing problems, but the answer to this is so simple I've actually played through until there are no more quests at present to play, my base is complete, and I have all the things.  In a nutshell:  save religiously.  Once I got out of the habit of relying on autosave, I was golden.
Tl;dr:  this is an awesome game for many, many reasons, only requiring a modicum of patience, and will only get better.

The sequel to the amazing Hotline Miami.  This game definitely changes things up, but I wouldn't say it changes in a bad way.  A lot of the levels have fairly open designs, forcing you to play differently than you might in the first game.  There is also a bit more focus on guns in my opinion, but you can still get through a lot of it with melee.  Unlike the previous game, over the course of Wrong Number you play as quite a few different people and it seems there is much more to the story this time around, quite a lot going on.  Although Jacket isn't playable in Wrong Number and doesn't even have a big role directly, his actions from the previous title have caused/inspired many of the events you play through.
There are also some pretty awesome masks to wear (which aren't just cosmetic for those who havn't played either game before, they all give you a different ability).  The best example is one that actually lets you play as two people at once; a girl with a chainsaw, and a guy with a gun, wearing goose masks.  <3 Alex the chainsaw wielding goose lady.
Overall it's pretty awesome and definitely worth buying along with the first one if you don't already have it.  The soundtrack is amazing (duh), the action is awesome, the story is interesting.  A good buy.  Also the Special Edition gives you six remixed tracks and some special Payday 2 stuff if you're into that kinda thing.

This game is not only very pretty but has an excellent skill curve where gear is never more important than skill and experience.
Its a v entertaining game, the Warhammer world is beautifully realized and the screaming endless hordes of clan rats coupled with the specialized units such as globadiers, ratling gunners, pack masters, gutter runners, storm vermin and the horrifically brutal Rat ogres mean the game feels different every time you play it.

If you enjoy L4D, you will very likely enjoy this game. If you enjoy Warhammer, you will very likely enjoy this game. If you enjoy Killing Floor, you will very likely enjoy this game. If you enjoy Chivalry... the list goes on.
Things to be aware of:
- Super satisfying combat: lopping off rat heads, knocking over swathes of mobs at a time, annihilating huge groups with incendiary grenades... they really nailed the combat here. It's not all melee - you can get a multitude of ranged weapons, including some spells, bows and assorted guns. The combat system allows for charged attacks, pushes, blocks and some special attacks - which allow you to be pretty tactical with how you engage enemies.
- Rewarding loot system: you get an item at the end of a successful mission from a list of random weapons, which you can then equip.  Certain items you can collect throughout the map increase your chance to get better items in the list of items at the end of a level. It's a bit more complicated than that, but that sort of covers it.
- Useful consumables: Bombs, potions of speed/strength, healing poultices, health packs, ammo - each of the consumables has it's own utility, and you're rewarded for exploring the map by finding them. Hobbling around on 5% health after fighting a rat ogre (the equivalent of a L4D tank) and finding a health kit tucked away in a bookshelf behind a door is incredibly satisfying - so is popping a speed potion and darting between rats before they can hit you, or a strength potion and cutting down huge amounts of vermin in one satisfying slice.
- Weapons change up your play style: Each weapon will change how you approach enemies, and many will have very different traits. One weapon might be able to pierce armour with a normal attack, some will require a charged attack; some charged attacks might hit huge groups, some might be single target. In some cases it's literally the difference between a crossbow and two flintlock pistols.
- Lore and voice lines: They really put the effort in here. I'm not a huge Warhammer fan, but I can already tell there's a lot to appreciate here - with references to mechanics and characters that you might recognise if you know the lore. But my favourite part is the effort they put in with the voice lines - if you jump around too much, the Sergeant will ask 'What's with the Bretonnian dance? Keep your feet on the ground will you!' and so on. Each of the characters has multiple reactions to these sorts of thing, and people will comment on headshots, killing sprees, being knocked down etc. It might be something you expect from any decent-quality game out there, but these lines are especially good.
- Real replayability value: I've got 9.3hrs in the early-access version of the game, which was (until last night) 3 maps in total. On release they'll have 13 (I think?) levels - and I dread to think how many hours I'm going to sink into them. All the major levels have collectibles you can find to increase your loot chances, on top of hidden secrets, alternating routes and huge variability in enemy and loot spawns. No two playthroughs of the same map are the same - and that's a very good thing.
My only negative comment, which will likely be reiterated elsewhere is: the NPC AI is awful. Just like L4D, bots will try to help you up if you're downed - even when you're surrounded by 10 rats and your friend is being dragged off by a special rat - or they'll sometimes wander off and find a special rat to challenge to a one-on-one duel. If you're expecting to play this solo, I'd maybe avoid it. I've not tried it - and maybe at least one bot will stay beside you at all times or something, they're usually pretty good at sticking close - but my tendency to get annoyed by bots would put me off. I'm expecting to play this with one other human player pretty much every single game.

The last CoD I played was MW3 (I have BO2 but have about 3 - 4 hours in it) and it was a cheat fest - lobbies with flying people, spawning in the middle of the game instantly dieing, people with endless granade lunchers and so on. There are cheaters in Ghosts quite often but you can definetly feel the difference and you can play the Multiplayer allmost felling secure that the people in the lobby depend on skill only.
After getting to lvl 60 (max lvl) I am starting to really like this game. The co op - Squads part is amaizing. You have your squad that you customise the name, the look and everything also you can jump and play as any of the soldiers and level it up. When you set up your squad you select the map and the mod that will be played if someone attacs your squad while you are offline. When you do that you can start playing against other peoples squads on their therms, you can play 1v1 pvp you and your squad against another player and his squad, you can play a "Wargame" that is random mod and random map against bots or you can survive against waves of enemies.
The levels are interactive and fun every level has its unique event that usually changes the map a bit and its unique mission event. The mission event usually acts like the old MOAB but it is not achieved only by getting kills without dieing. Some times when you or someone from your team dies they drop a briefcase that contains a mission that you have to complete on pick up before you die or you lose it. The mission is usually something as simple as Kill an enemy while jumping, or Humiliate the next person you kill. If you complete the mission you get a care pacage that may contain the mission event. My personal favorite mission event is on the map FOG where you get the mask and the axe from the movie HALOWEEN and you start running and chopping people's heads while a creepy music playis.
Summary: I was more of a CoD hater after they screwd us with MW3 and so on. But For less than 10 euro Ghosts is a pretty good game. And a must if you like co op like me. The cheater problem is somewhat handeled and with a hand on my heard I can state that about 70% the lobbies I have played didn't have cheaters but when you get a cheater you can just quit and go play against squads.
Rating: 7/10 The reason for that high rating from me is that all the cons from the game can be overcome by the excelent co op and squads mod. You can enjoy your game without having to worry about cheaters or people to play with.

Gameplay
This game is like a milk shake, it has a little bit of everything, FPS, Strategy, RPG, ect... The world is very large, with six different factions with their own problems and every single one of them are joinable. It is recommended to join one in the early bit to help in the late game. Each faction has pros and cons that will make you or brake you in the late game. You start as a weak level 1 to a level 62 with an empire. One of the main gameplay elements is the ability to hire people from villages to form an army. Eventually you will create an epic army, starting with people with pitch forks to people with every weapon imaginable! So gameplay get's a 9!
AI
The AI is average at best. They run around like a chicken with their head's chopped off when faced with hills or dips in the terrain. They do what you want them to do, they kill enemies. The path finding is pretty good, they will charge the enemy and attack them without mercy. Pressing the 1 key will give you the ability to command them with basic orders like "Hold Fire" and "Charge". So the AI get's a 8!
Combat
The combat is pretty good, I found the best way to kill an enemy is to block then attack right after blocking. The AI will use the different attack angles to attack you. You can use the different angles as well by moving the mouse in a direction you want and left clicking. So combat is very solid and takes a bit of practice to understand. Combat get's an 8!
Cities/towns/fortresses/villages
All of the cities, towns ect, can be entered. Most missions require to enter the city or fortresses in their keeps, and villages have what you would expect in them as well. Not much to say about them, but they are mostly there to immersion, because they cannot be entered. So cities, fortresses, ect, get a 7!
Graphics
The graphics are okay, the aren't HORRIBLE but not great. The game runs very solid on any computer, but the graphics are bad. If your looking for a pretty looking game, this is not one of them. This game runs off of gameplay more then anything. So the graphics get a 5!

Don't let the collective salt of people getting sniped and leaving bad reviews on here dissuade you; Hotline Miami 2 is a true sequel in every way. It improves upon the things that made the first one great, it dangles more story in front of us for us to digest, it still has probably the best video game soundtrack to date.
A lot of people currently are shouting "bad level design, bad level design!" like some kind of collective hive mind because the levels this time around seem to favor bigger areas with a lot of windows. I honestly don't think this is bad level design, in fact, I'm really enjoying it.  It's clearly a design choice and one I stand behind. Yeah it's more difficult and I've had to pause and take breaks due to rage, but the fact that I keep coming back says something about the game. After dying, and dying, and dying, and dying, and you finally find a way that works for you, fail a few times, and then manage to pull it off at the end.. Nothing beats that. You will find yourself mentally high-fiving yourself and doing a little fist pump motion while saying "yes" either loudly, or at least just under your breath.
If you loved Hotline Miami, and you wanted more of the same, well, that's not *exactly* what this offers. It offers more! More characters, more difficulty, new moves. Screw the reviews and watch some flat gameplay footage if you still can't make up your mind. I guaruntee the moment you load this baby up and get your first kill, veteran or no, you'll be hooked (all over again)

It has more features than the first game. Some are great, others aren't. There are a surprising number of bugs. It's still really fun.
There are more characters with interesting new abilities, and also certain story missions that choose unique abilities for you. I won't spoil any of them, but I think it adds some welcome variety, and requires you to adapt new strategies in different levels. Others may not like it because you don't always have the same complete freedom to approach every level your own way like you did in the first Hotline Miami. Still, I think it kept things interesting.
Level/enemy design can be odd. A lot of the levels are big and open, so you can get shot from offscreen and have no chance to see the enemy or react to it. It stalls your momentum in a lot of levels, as you pause behind cover and use the ZOOM function to scout around the edge of the map, only moving when you think you're clear. This wasn't what the first Hotline Miami was about. In the first game you would be able to see most of the map and go on a rampage with just a little planning but mostly reflexes. It was fast, had rhythm, and it you could really feel the brutal animal ferocity that drove the main character. Now, you kind of have to pause and think about your next move every now and then. It feels less exciting.
Some reviews have criticized some of the new enemy types. There are big melee proof bad guys that can only be taken down with bullets, super fast movers (on at least one level), and others I may not have seen yet since I haven't finished the game. I think they're ok. You need to die a few times to figure them out, but once you know how to challenge them, it really adds a layer of strategy to your movements through the levels. You may realize that you have to get a firearm early before you deal with the big dudes, for instance.
One thing I didn't like about the enemies is that they can blend into the backgrounds. This is a problem. The look of the game is very pixelated with a lot of colors, and sometimes the enemy sprites get lost in all the chaos. This wouldn't be as much of an issue if the enemies always move, since moving sprites are easy to see. HOWEVER, a lot of enemies stay stationary until you alert them to your presence. I have suffered many deaths because I thought I cleared an area but there was a bad guy standing still around the next corner who was blending into the background. There are also some objects in certain levels that enemies can walk UNDER, disappearing from view. These are things like foliage/bushes. While they are underneath them, you can't see them but they can still kill you. Overall, enemy visibility could have been better.
Also, some barriers in the game act as walls/cover, both against enemy sightlines and bullets. However, because the art style of the game is 2D and top down, it's impossible to tell at first what actually is a wall vs. what is just a table that won't block anything. There is also a level where some parts of walls CAN be shot through, but it isn't visually obvious at first. Again, you often need to die a lot to figure out what is what within a level. You'll figure it out, but it's annoying during your first few attempts at a level.
Also, others have already mentioned this but there seem to be a lot of bugs that I don't remember experiencing in the first Hotline Miami. Enemies get stuck in doors and fizzle around. Dogs spin around in circles. Sometimes enemies hear your gunshots and come running but other times they don't. It's very inconsistent. Also, there's a cool playable character that is actually TWO characters that move as a pair. However, the second character who follows behind the first character often gets stuck in the doorway as you enter a level (clearly a glitch). This leaves the first character in front with no backup and only short range attacks. The game just doesn't seem airtight, and funny things happen. I wasn't expecting this from the sequel of the very smooth Hotline Miami.
Soundtrack is still great, probably even better than the first game.
Overall, still fun and really cool. WAY more flawed than I expected, but still (narrowly) recommended. Definitely during a sale.

I got Deadlight through Humble Bundle like a lot of my library on this account. What amazed me picking this game at random to try out was how solid a platformer this was. I've been gaming since way back on the Master System and the original Prince of Persia game. Back then PoP was a really solid game. It was tough, puzzling and took lots of skill to get through.
Deadlight is the first game I've played that comes close to a similar experience. It's got a lot of nice and neat little puzzles which require a good think about. I've come across little things that have stuck me for ages, and relatively complex things that I've solved first time round.

Every aspect of the movement is simple. It would've been great if there was an element of the original Tomb Raider in there. All in all though, a fantastic little platformer.

If you enjoy L4D, you will very likely enjoy this game. If you enjoy Warhammer, you will very likely enjoy this game. If you enjoy Killing Floor, you will very likely enjoy this game. If you enjoy Chivalry... the list goes on.
Things to be aware of:
- Super satisfying combat: lopping off rat heads, knocking over swathes of mobs at a time, annihilating huge groups with incendiary grenades... they really nailed the combat here. It's not all melee - you can get a multitude of ranged weapons, including some spells, bows and assorted guns. The combat system allows for charged attacks, pushes, blocks and some special attacks - which allow you to be pretty tactical with how you engage enemies.
- Rewarding loot system: you get an item at the end of a successful mission from a list of random weapons, which you can then equip.  Certain items you can collect throughout the map increase your chance to get better items in the list of items at the end of a level. It's a bit more complicated than that, but that sort of covers it.
- Useful consumables: Bombs, potions of speed/strength, healing poultices, health packs, ammo - each of the consumables has it's own utility, and you're rewarded for exploring the map by finding them. Hobbling around on 5% health after fighting a rat ogre (the equivalent of a L4D tank) and finding a health kit tucked away in a bookshelf behind a door is incredibly satisfying - so is popping a speed potion and darting between rats before they can hit you, or a strength potion and cutting down huge amounts of vermin in one satisfying slice.
- Weapons change up your play style: Each weapon will change how you approach enemies, and many will have very different traits. One weapon might be able to pierce armour with a normal attack, some will require a charged attack; some charged attacks might hit huge groups, some might be single target. In some cases it's literally the difference between a crossbow and two flintlock pistols.
- Lore and voice lines: They really put the effort in here. I'm not a huge Warhammer fan, but I can already tell there's a lot to appreciate here - with references to mechanics and characters that you might recognise if you know the lore. But my favourite part is the effort they put in with the voice lines - if you jump around too much, the Sergeant will ask 'What's with the Bretonnian dance? Keep your feet on the ground will you!' and so on. Each of the characters has multiple reactions to these sorts of thing, and people will comment on headshots, killing sprees, being knocked down etc. It might be something you expect from any decent-quality game out there, but these lines are especially good.
- Real replayability value: I've got 9.3hrs in the early-access version of the game, which was (until last night) 3 maps in total. On release they'll have 13 (I think?) levels - and I dread to think how many hours I'm going to sink into them. All the major levels have collectibles you can find to increase your loot chances, on top of hidden secrets, alternating routes and huge variability in enemy and loot spawns. No two playthroughs of the same map are the same - and that's a very good thing.
My only negative comment, which will likely be reiterated elsewhere is: the NPC AI is awful. Just like L4D, bots will try to help you up if you're downed - even when you're surrounded by 10 rats and your friend is being dragged off by a special rat - or they'll sometimes wander off and find a special rat to challenge to a one-on-one duel. If you're expecting to play this solo, I'd maybe avoid it. I've not tried it - and maybe at least one bot will stay beside you at all times or something, they're usually pretty good at sticking close - but my tendency to get annoyed by bots would put me off. I'm expecting to play this with one other human player pretty much every single game.
For an indie studio, this game is a massive achievement. For £23, it is a ridiculous steal.

Contagion had much going for it and I gave it high hopes when I initially purchased it, for I believed it to be a wonderful game and I believed it to have a clear path to success paved with hard survival, high playerbase, and heavy loads of content; however, instead we recieved an abandoned video game.
The playerbase has decreased from hundreds to null since I first purchased it. I find it difficult to discover players without resorting to friends or asking people to play on the Community Hub that is shrinking.
What gave me hope for this game was its Workshop. I always had a firm belief that, if a video game is given the ability to be modified and the community is allowed to publically create mods, the community would last tenfold than what it would have without mods, but this was the video game that made me question my belief. The majority of mods for this game are ripped pictures from the internet to create a new wallpaper for the phone that one would have to use throughout this game; there are little amounts of quality mods.
The phone - this is an interesting mechanic that I truly loved in this game. It was better than simply following points and being forced to see where you have to go; it encourages exploration with little information.
Like many video games created by small groups, they are abandoned. It is a sad sight to see; hell, even I felt bad when I discovered Dead Island: Epidemic was shutting down, but it was worse discovering information from the players themselves rather than the developers that this video game was abandoned. It has been one year since its last update, and I do believe that the most recent update was its final one.
Do you remember when people were whining about Resident Evil 4 through 6, believing that Capcom ruined their survival games and replaced them with an action franchise? (I still love these games, though.) Contagion managed to fit survival with action - there scarce weapons and rare ammunition, thus forcing the players to conserve their guns, and in one shot hordes will run toward you, forcing you to become desperate and give you a choice: fight or flight. Usually retreating is never chosen as these zombies are slow, in small groups, and can be killed in one shot, but issues do rise when you find yourself surrounded due to your poor situational analysis and you would surely die because of your actions.
Verdict----> 2/10
Just save your money and buy Left 4 Dead 2. It is a much better video game of zombie survival even if it is more action-packed. The community there is still alive, there are quality mods everywhere, and it is a finished game. I wish there was a way to contain this contagion then send it back to the people whom created this game to get my money back, but it's too late now - it already infected my library.

Time for a 'Kiss, Marry or Avoid'!
Pros:
- The aesthetics are clean, crisp and very pleasing. The dark, almost silouette style of the characters paired with a grim, bloomed atmosphere are eye candy. If you liked Limbo, it's up your street.
- The cutscenes are created in a delightful comic strip style setting that help portray the environment and setting very nicely.
- There is a nice sense of progression and a meaning between each environment you push through. Generous checkpoints and varying locales and obstacles keep things going.
Cons:
- The controls suuuu~ck. They feel completely backwards. For instance, Running is on RB and Crouching is LT. Firing your weapon is RT and reloading is LB. I mean, what? Why would you put the physical skills on completely opposite buttons and the same for the weapon skills??
- Trial and error. It's not an overall criticism but there are many times where you will die due to not having time to react or knowing what you will run into.
- The plot is a mess. There are several times where you will question "Why?" at some plot lines.
- The game can NOT handle close quarters combat. If Zombies get too close (and sometimes, you have no choice), you're as good as dead. The problem gets to be is that Randall can take two hits during his stagger animation before you take control again and his only close attack seems to be random from being useful to just a waste of time. This begets frustration and a tinge of unfair.
Other:
- Short game, about 3-4 hrs. Neither good nor bad. For an indie game, pretty good.
Final impression?
KISS

Sadness fills me, as of writing this review, I have beaten most fantastic game, called Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number. This game was well worth the wait. Many postponements, angered me, but in the end, this game was ♥♥♥♥ing amazing. I loved it. When I saw the credits roll, I was so sad to see it end, I almost cried. I love this series and I'd love to see another one, please make another one.
Hotline Miami 2 takes place it seems after Hotline Miami 1. Masked people, like Jacket, are popping up everywhere. That's what one of the characters are in this game. The fans, fans of the mass murder sprees with masks on. There's four of them, I don't remember their names, but I'll call them by their mask. Each character has its unique ability also. Zebra has combat rolls, Bear has dual submachine guns, Gooses, are two people, you control both. One has a chainsaw and the other has a gun. Last, is Tony, his punches kill, but since they do that, you can't pick up weapons. This is only one of the character stories there are in the game and I'm only going to name the ones that are obvious, the others you find out later on. There's the writer, he's trying to write a book about the masked killer. He attended a court, trying to get info, but he didn't get any, but he tries anything to get info. What's unique about him, is he can't kill people. You can only pick up blunt weapons. You can pick up guns, but he just disarms them. I hated playing as him, but he was a cool and totally different character. There's the soldier and the police officer. Not going to touch on those characters, you have to play the game to find out who they are and what their campaign is like. :)
The gameplay is the same, but a little bit more polished than Hotline Miami 1. What's new to this game, is probably the whole characters, and their abilities. Also, the aim system has changed a little bit, instead of some sort of free aim in the old one, it runs on like a swivel, seems to be made for the console version. But, also the new addition, would be the lock on. You can use aim and when you're using a gun, you can press the lock on button (most likely middle mouse, I changed it because mine is broken.) and it locks on to that person. It's useful, but if you want to unlock, you have to aim and press the button. Not so good in sticky situtations.
The music is as good as it's ever been and maybe even better. Artists like Perturbator, Carpenter Brut, and many more. I can list all the songs in the game in this review. The songs in this game, make this game fun and exciting. The music pumps you up and makes you want to kill those ♥♥♥♥ing mobsters or whatever you're killing. The music is one of the best things of this game, besides you know, the game.
Hotline Miami 2, was a great and wonderfully designed game, I loved it as much as I loved the first one. I plan to play it a lot more, beat it a couple more times, and maybe even try to speed run it. Though, the levels are a lot more challenging, in my opinion than the first game. If you don't have this masterpiece of a game already, go get it right now. I don't care if you want Battlefield Hardline or someother ♥♥♥♥ing game. ♥♥♥♥ those games, pick this game and the first one in a bundle pack for ♥♥♥♥s sake. 9.5/10 I would buy this game again.

Did you love the first Hotline Miami?
Good. You'll love this one.
+ Bigger levels (the levels in Vietnam were a nice departure)
+ The main cast: You've got more characters here, each with their own motives and styles of play, including one that does not enjoy killing; he'll knock his enemies out and he'll pick up and destroy the weapon, but he won't use it. It really switches things up between levels and keeps things from growing tedious.
+ More interesting weapons. Some may disagree with me on this, but I loved the nail gun and the double fisted sub-machine guns. Most of all I loved playing as the chainsaw and pistol wielding male/female duo.
+ The music. The first game was hailed for its soundtrack and this certainly lives up to and builds on that reputation.
- It's a little too easy to exploit the AI, kiting them around a corner and just popping them as they poke their heads around. What's unfortunate is there are instances where it feels almost neccessary in order to pass a level. Yes, I love that the levels are bigger, but the lock on feature is clumsy and there are a lot of blind spots which can lead to getting shot off screen and a lot of trial and error gameplay.
Really, there isn't much to complain about. This is an evolution of the first game. I know the developers say this is the last one, but I'm hoping they decide to go in for a trilogy.
