The only reason I bought this was because it offered split screen coop, and it didn't disappoint.
For those who don't know what the game is, it plays like a slower, more realistic version of left for dead. There aren't hordes of zombies that rush you, no special creatures. The zombies amble, rather than run, but they can only be taken down with head shots, and you have very limited ammo, which means if you get cornered, you are screwed.
The stage also changes, so this time you can get through a gate, next time the gate is locked and you have to go through a building, opening up an area you have never seen before
It has high ram requirements- 4GB, but you can turn down the memory cache setting (I think it was) and it ran perfectly with 3GB on my 32 bit machine.
Over all a fun coop experience and even single player is a blast. Highly recommended.

This review introduces the whole game, and considers the clichés one could have heard. If you want more details, comments are free.
What can we say about that game, beacuse it can change so easliy...
Let's start with the beginning : Heroes And Generals is a free2play MMOFPS which takes place during the WW II (around 1944 considering the available equipments, including some anachronisms). You can play as German, American, Russian or even the three at the same time (however that's not recommended). Control a character on the battlefield (FPS), or/and assault teams on the generals' map (RTS).
The graphics arn't ugly, but sounds are currently... meh (for example, the PPSh-41 sounds like a vacuum cup...), the gameplay isn't that bad (and the devs seem to decide to upgrade it).
Let's talk about the free2play/pay2win aspect. It is NOT P2W unlike what some reviews could say, because you can buy EVERYTHING (including the premium membership) with the money of the game (credits : weapons, modifications, or even those flahy camouflages everyone seems to like. The main default, for casual-gamers, is that the credits are won quite slowly if you don't have a cheap and effective build....
Now, the pros and cons :
PROS :
- Free, no P2W but a bit Pay Or Farm
- Both RTS and FPS
- Possibility to play various types of infantry, tankists, plane pilots, snipers, paratroopers at the
same time.
- A lot of available weapons, explosives and gears for a lot of vatious builds.
- Possibility to have several characters of all the tree factions on the same account, and to switch between them during a game (of the faction you're playing, if the type is available).
- Quite "all ages" : no gore, no real violence, not hardcore (but noob alert).
CONS :
- Sounds as realistic as those form Excalibur 2555 A.D
- Experience and money come slowly...
- The RTS part comes when you have a lv12 character (but that's not unattainable)
- OneShotOneKill weapons not always working because of this filthy medal that can reduce the damages (if the enemy equiped it)
- Sometimes, you'll enter a game with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥... a lot of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥... fu** those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
Nonwithstanding all of this, weapons can also be modded to increase the damages, the accuracy etc... while decreasing other stats. This is a really good point because you can have several gameplay with a single weapon, depending on how you mod it. For example, the starter semi-automatic rifle, which is bad (stock), can be upgraded to be deadly accurate (scope) or to have high rate of fire and damages (cqc). But beware, some builds could be expensive.
I also want to open a parenthesis about those who say that factions arn't balanced : that's false. Indeed, weapons can have different stats, but each weapon is better than its ounterparts in certain situations : The karabiner has correct damages and a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ sight (1 pixel, go buy glasses), but can have a very good infantry scope, the Mosin Nagant 1891/30 has correct damages and correct infantry scope, but has a very good iron sight and the M1903 has a good sight, a scope like the one you built with a paper roll when you were 6, but its damages are a bit better than the 2 others, and its helpfull against that filthy badge I talked about earlier.
This is quite the same thing with every weapons. So you'll be disadvantaged against a PPSh-41 in CQC, but you'll beat it during a middle-range shooting.
So, why do I give a blue thumb? Even if I rage each ime I play a bad game, it really worth it (1500+h, not for nothing). Don't really read reviews written by people with less than 200h because this game is far mor complex that it seems to be. The funometer is quite sinusoidal but well, sometimes you can have a very good time.
I would recommend to play with friends, because you can be far more efficient when you communicate with someone else than XCyka-BliatX.
If you are interested in more details about the game or some specific part, write a little comment. Thanks for wasting your time on my review!

I've only tried the Story Mode so far, and after that, I don't know if I'll be up for trying the other modes.
The game has potential but it's still very early to determine what the end result will be. Playing, it feels like the developers are still unclear on what they want to do with some features. From what I've played, quests have been simply going from point A to a very far point B then back, or gather X amount of resources A, B and C, or a combination of the two. They are long, tedious and do little to keep you wanting to play more.
The crafting system is decent, but very early on, you'll get very complicated scripts that require you to create many different materials from many different resources in order to create a single Item. It wouldn't be so bad, if resource gathering was fast and entertaining, which it's not. early tools take ages to gather resources, and you're stuck with them until you figure you have to buy more scripts from an NPC.
The combat system is barely worth speaking about. If you don't notice the little enemy health bar that appears in the upper left corner of the screen, you won't even know if you're landing any strikes or not, until either you or your enemy are down.
You can put items for use in the 1-9 bar, a la Minecraft, and it works well, but the only way to know which Item you have equipped is by looking at the square left of button 1, which shows what you're currently using. I guess that's ok, but it'd be less confusing if it just highlighted the Item you've selected. Another problem is that if you're using a sword and Shield and you change to a pickaxe to do some mining, when you switch  back to the sword, the shield will stay unequipped, forcing you to go and equip it again, which can be annoying considering how you can be attacked at any time.
One other problem I had is that throughout the time I spent playing, I felt like I was doing something (or rather everything) wrong. Following the questline brought me to face enemies against whom I had no chance. I constantly wondered if there was something I missed, something that should have prepared me for the challenge, but there seemed to be nothing there.
Overall, the game has potential, but I cannot recommend it to anyone, simply because it's too unfinished. I wish I had waited a year or two more to play it in a much more polished state. I know I'll have to wait at least that long to come back to it.

Update: the game will no longer start on my computer. I have tried reinstalling it and it didn't work. If anyone has a possible fix, please let me know.
Ok, let me just vent for a moment, because the game gave me no relief for the adrenaline pumping through my body right now. I lost my motivation for finishing the game just before the ending mission, but was invested again all too soon. After that, no spoilers, I won the game. That's it. Barely more than a, "congratulations," message on an arcade machine. There is no payoff, no indication as to what happens after the fact. You just make your choice (really trying not to spoil here) and some stuff happens and Jason Brody starts talking about the future. Why couldn't I see what happened in the future? Why? I just need something to either chill me out or get me pumped to get rid of all this useless adrenaline, but all I got was the ending credits. What!
Alright, I think I've calmed down enough to talk about the rest of the game. Let me start off by saying that the game is awesome and you should totally buy it. I feel like this marks a point in time when Ubisoft wasn't dedicated to screwing over its customer base.
You start out as some rich snot on vacation to a tropical island. Unfortunately, the island is infested with pirates. So many pirates. And somehow nobody in your group found this out while planning the trip. Things swiftly go awry and you and your friends are all kidnapped to be sold into slavery. You escape, however, and begin your metamorphasis into a cold-blooded murderer.
If I had to sum-up the game in one word, it would be, "immersive." I don't play many fps's, so it took me some time to get used to the game's controls. This works perfectly into the plot, which starts out with you as a scared-stiff tourist, suddenly handed a gun, and told to fight trained killers. Throughout the game, I feel like the emotional roller coaster I was on was entirely parallel to Jason Brody's. As he learned how to hunt and survive, so did I, until we were both looking at bringing down a pirate stronghold with bored competence. I would, however, say that I only actually became bored when I had been playing the game for too many hours at one time and was just running down a checklist. I'd say that's on me, not the game.
Writing is another thing I look for in a game. That being said, the dialogue is pretty pedestrian and nothing to write home about. Far Cry 3 compensates for that, along with its other flaws, by focusing on its strengths and covering it up. This game has some of the most effective voice acting I've ever come across in a game. When the main antagonist, Vas, is talking, I'm glue to the screen with actual chills running down my spine. I can't say I was ever as invested in saving my friends as I was in sticking a knife in Vas. The majority of Jason's friends don't get much fleshing out, so I never really cared about most of them, but I did reach the conclusion by the end that I was siding with them more than the warrior tribe that had been sponsoring me. From that, I guess they did an alright job making me invested in their safety.
Aside from the story, half of the game's appeal and overall substance is the combat. Where do I start on the combat? I guess I could start by saying that you can acquire a bow and arrow. I shouldn't have to say anything more after that. They give you a bow and you can fire arrows into people and watch them curl their spine back and plummet face-first into the dirt! It's more satisfying to watch than the half-baked sex scene in the middle!
Right, as I said, the combat is incredibly satisfying and intense. The world has a bunch of strongholds for you to liberate, by which, I mean, sneak around the pirates' homes, wreck their alarm system, and knife, snipe, and arrow every one of them until you can raise the flag of freedom. USA! The combat is fantastic and I don't have any major issues with it, except for the heavy armor ****ers who take three grenades to put down. They're a chore to fight and I don't care if their armor is a foot thick and made of adamantium. No one can survive a grenade literally being thrown at their face.
Getting back to the story, two problems arise. *SPOILER WARNING* *SPOILER WARNING*
Throughout the first half of the game, Vas is the only main bad guy we've encountered. Killing him is the end goal, along with rescuing all of our friends. After we kill Vas, we are then introduced to another main bad guy who is apparently Vas's boss. That's right. The main villain has a boss. It's like if Bowser was taking orders from Cthulhu. To top it off, the new guy isn't even as interesting as Vas. Where Vas was directly involved in many of the plot point in the game, the new guy, Hoyt, has done nothing to us directly and seems to be content to sit at a desk and let his mercenaries take care of everything. So it's more like if Cthulhu was taking orders from Kim Jong Un.
The second problem is what I already vented over in the beginning of this review, but I'll go into greater detail now that I've put up a spoiler warning. After you've rescued all of your friends, you then have to rescue them from the tribe of native warriors who have sort of been training you, but mostly they've just been giving you drugs. It's all a bit confusing. Through a very effective cinematic cutscene, you are given the choice of whether to save your friends or stay with a tribe. I decided to go home with my friends, because I was ready for things to start making sense again. Some stuff happens and the scene cuts to an overview of a boat, presumably taking you and your friends home.
That's it.
There is virtually no payoff for the literal gallons of suspense the game dumps on you from the point where you kill Hoyt to when you're reuniting with your friends. I suppose the alternative ending might be better, but I have it on good authority that it isn't.
That aside, however, if you've made it through this entire review to this point or if you just read the beginning and are skipping to the end to see the conclusion like a cheater, then I should still point out that the game is absolutely worth picking up. It only falls apart at the climaxes, which is admittedly one of the worst places for a game to fail, but everything else is rock solid and I would not now have a pair of massively swollen blue balls if the game hadn't been great.

Did you love the first Hotline Miami?
Good. You'll love this one.
+ Bigger levels (the levels in Vietnam were a nice departure)
+ The main cast: You've got more characters here, each with their own motives and styles of play, including one that does not enjoy killing; he'll knock his enemies out and he'll pick up and destroy the weapon, but he won't use it. It really switches things up between levels and keeps things from growing tedious.
+ More interesting weapons. Some may disagree with me on this, but I loved the nail gun and the double fisted sub-machine guns. Most of all I loved playing as the chainsaw and pistol wielding male/female duo.
+ The music. The first game was hailed for its soundtrack and this certainly lives up to and builds on that reputation.
- It's a little too easy to exploit the AI, kiting them around a corner and just popping them as they poke their heads around. What's unfortunate is there are instances where it feels almost neccessary in order to pass a level. Yes, I love that the levels are bigger, but the lock on feature is clumsy and there are a lot of blind spots which can lead to getting shot off screen and a lot of trial and error gameplay.
Really, there isn't much to complain about. This is an evolution of the first game. I know the developers say this is the last one, but I'm hoping they decide to go in for a trilogy.

I loved the first Hotline Miami and it is easily one of my favorite games. The second installment adds so much to the game and gives it an amazing new soundtrack and a really great, deep, and thought provoking story; unlike the first game whose story was mostly left up to interpretation (not saying that's a bad thing). Honestly this game feels like a direct finish to the first game, and that's not exactly a good thing.

First off this game is hard, like extremely hard. The Hawaii missions are some of the hardest and a lot of peoples least favorite missions (including myself), because they are so... broken...
Yes broken.
The first game was hard, but it was fair. Everytime you died you knew why you died and how to correct it next time.
This game on the other hand is very unfair. You die from things off screen like guys with shotguns, rifles, pistols, and worst of all... Dogs (RANDY ORTON R-K-O OUTTA NO WHERE). Even shift looking doesn't help most of the time.
The level design is honestly just brutal, windows everywhere, and (as mentioned above) enemies you can't see.
The game is good, but the level design is terrible. And Hotline Miami is all about the level design.
It feels like the levels went from a non-linear, complete how you want kinda deal to feeling like a hyper consentrated puzzle, with only one way to solve it.
This game expects that you have played the first game, as the first level (not the prologue) is already very hard, and the difficulty doesn't get any easier. The missions only get harder and harder.
The game on normal difficulty is already tough as nails, but hard mode... Oh boy...
Did you beat Hotline Miami 1 only using the Richard mask without dying once? Then hard mode is for you!
Like losing ammo when you drop your gun? Neither do I.
... I will still recommend this game.
The story is fantastic and pieces itself together at the end extremely well, the story also leads for a lot of discussion. But this game truly concludes the whole Hotline Miami series. So no more Hotline Miami (sadly :c)!
The characters are mostly really well thought out and each have an awesome backstory.

I'm torn apart about this game really and I don't mean by being mutilated by chainsaw, I mean I'm still not sure if I should recommend it or not. If there was a "mixed bag" button for reviews, I'd press it. There were many things that I enjoyed in Hotline Miami 2 but there was also an equal amount of things that irritated me. Let's start with the good stuff for now.
I thoroughly enjoyed the music and atmosphere of Hotline Miami 2, which matches if not surpasses the first game by a little bit. The story was interesting, even though I didn't understand it the first time. Little details like the VHS pause menu and other effects are nice. Enemies telegraph their attacks a bit more to make dodging easier. New characters freshen up the experience and have their own strategy to them. Some of the levels are very creative and have a personality to them.
Speaking of which, leads to the negative part of the review, the levels. There are way, way too many levels that are overly populated with enemies and are placed in wide areas. Having so many enemies in a wide open area makes it extremely difficult to chain together kills without resorting to the "lure and corner kill" technique. Being killed offscreen by a distant enemy is not my idea of entertainment. The game requires a lot of paitence which is bizarre considering that the first game is best played with good reaction time rather than crowd control. Aside from that, there are several times in HM2 where you have to die several times before you can even get a grasp of your surroundings. By that I mean enemies are already charging at you the moment the level loads up! This next point is a personal opinion more than anything else but I felt like the game was a bit too long. Is there such a thing as too much of a good thing? well to me the answer is yes. The game was a blast to play starting out but eventually it just over stays its welcome. It didn't help that almost every level is like what I mentioned before, enemies galore spaced in an open area.
At the time of this review I have also experienced my fair share of glitches. Enemies would get stuck on doors or spin erratically in place, dogs & enemies jumping through walls, enemies leaving the map, etc. How many times was this game play tested? I feel like these glitches should have been called out and some levels taken out by enough play testing.
So should you buy Hotline Miami 2? Personally I'd say buy the soundtrack instead but if you really want to play it, don't let me stop you. There is definitely some enjoyment in the sequel but not enough for me to deal with the issues I mentioned earlier. One last thing to mention is at the time of this review, March 3rd, 2015, the Level Editor is not in the launch game. I thought it was already in the game? I guess I should pay more attention to the game news instead of just the advertisments.

Initially Deadlight appears to be a slow burn: the combat is scarce and tense, the platforming is contextually sensible and the 1980s dystopian Seattle setting is beautifully realized both visually and atmospherically. I spent the entirety of the first act, about 45 minutes give or take, pleasantly surprised and had been fully immersed and engaged; sure there are a variety of control issues and the keyboard setup in general could be irritating at times, but rarely did the game venture into territory where the difficulties were prominent and in the foreground.
When the second act came around I was introduced to a character named The Rat who inexplicably stole my items and in spite of professing an interest in helping me, made me traverse a series of makeshift traps in his underground lair. I tried to suspend disbelief and bear with the jarring transition into Crash Bandicoot insta-death and artificial difficulty induced by repeated (and clearly intentional) blindsiding moments/fake outs and I tried not to think much of it when my character decided to just go along with it in spite of risking his life for no discernable reason, going so far as to helping the man find his teenage son after the gauntlet was through. It's a game afterall and though it seemed uncharacteristic of the entire introductory segment, perhaps it'd be a detour and I'd get back to the funereal feel of what came before.
Unfortunately that's not the case. Led by The Rat and his pseudo-philosophical banter I dodged saw blades, pushed about a dozen blocks in order to traverse ledges, and spanned an impossible arena of challenges he was the architect of, each one becoming less and less about building tone or a convincing universe, and more and more about throwing out visual stimuli and a kitchen sink approach to finding methods to incorporate the game mechanics. Problem is, there's no depth when you turn the maps into obstacle courses that discourage skill in favour for trial and error, and faced with the irritation of both the change of pace and the rehashing of the same mechanics ad infinitum (wall jump awkwardly onto hanging wires, push blocks, barrel through doors) it became apparent that I had clearly mistaken the game's intentions.
The platforming is never fleshed out to require player aptitude; everything is so specific as to almost be a button prompt or a quicktime. Nowhere in the game did I feel like it was anything akin to what you'd find satisfying about any old school side scroller because it's less about precision and timing and more about whether there's an unfair obstacle that could come as a surprise, usually resulting in death. You follow linear corridors, do plodding "puzzles" and repeat the same motions over and over, sometimes with combat smashed awkwardly in between.
The argument could be made that, due to the theme, the platforming isn't intended to be in the same vein as its forefathers, but that brings up the question "Why is it a platformer then?" and Deadlight refuses to answer more often than not. If early Survival Horror utilized tank controls and shoddy combat mechanics in order to heighten tension perhaps Deadlight's messy controls and atypical form could be attributed to a similar notion, but I think that'd be incredibly generous. What it mostly comes down to is that the game happens to not be good at much, and the faster the tempo the more clear the blemishes tend to be as a result of it actually having to rely on the platforming for core gameplay as opposed the situationally pragmatic fashion it was initially applied in, in spite it not being fun, nuanced or fluid enough to do so potently.
Your character will refuse to do things you've seen him do prior in identical situations at times, failing to make a jump or spinning ridiculously while you're being torn limb from limb. The levels are nonsensical set pieces after the first act and none of them feel particularly thrilling or earned for that matter, just a bunch of archetypal content strewn and spattered about without rhyme or reason so your protagonist has an excuse to jump onto buses suspended from wires, evade helicopters and bounce off walls.
I could discuss the hollow plot, the fact that there's a substantial bug that cut my audio out in every cutscene, or the platforming animations largely consisting of you missing jumps and being teleported toward the ledge anyway, and I could elaborate on the inconsistent characterizations, the lack of direction or the complete misuse of the gameplay resources and so on but ultimately Deadlight is a game that had an amazing amount of promise and squandered it by the time its demo length intro has finished only to repeatedly remind you that what you anticipated and likely even enjoyed at first is not what Deadlight truly is, even if it's afraid to admit it or ultimately (and likely) isn't even aware of it.
Recommended Instead:
Limbo
Shinobi III
Eating Out Of The Trash

One word sums this game up: Frustrating.
The controls are clunky and unresponsive. The collision detection is finicky, sometimes requiring you to keep doing minor adjustments to be able to use an object.  The game is going for a photo-realistic look, which makes platforming much harder than it needs to be. It's often hard to make out where you're supposed to go--the game works around this by displaying little "arrow" indicators at edges you can climb, but there many places where there are no such indicators.
The zombie-related gameplay involves a lot of trial and error. Often times you have to go through an area and die several times before figuring out the "optimal" path and actions to take to go through. This, coupled with the rather horrendous checkpointing combine to make the game mostly an unpleasant experience.
Halfway through the game you get the good old "Let's strip the player of his weapons" gimmick, and you endure it on the hopes of getting them back from the person who took them (He promises to do so once you save a person related to him). However, once you actually do what he wants, you don't get your weapons back.
There's an infuriating helicopter chase scene that is not fun, drags on for too long, and is buggy to boot.
There's a diary for the protagonist that's supposed to provide a backstory or something, but it's nonesensically scattered throughout the game, and there's no motivation to read it whatsoever.
There are technical issues, too. Many people, myself included, suffer from a cutscene glitch where the BINK-encoded custcenes stutter midway, making it impossible to watch. You have to skip them and use the bink player provided by RAD Game Tools to watch them yourself.
Don't get this game unless you've run out of platformers, or bought it in some sale or bundle. It's not worth it.

Deadlight had potential. It has a cool art style and the platforming puzzles are fun. But the experience is hampered by a shallow story and a steep difficulty spike mid game that is worsened by spotty controls.
Even the story had a good premise: in an alternate history of the USA, the cold war ended when a zombie uprising led to a little bit of nuclear war. Zombies and nuclear winter in a 1980's America? I can work with that, even if zombies (called "Shadows" in this game) are overused nowadays.
Instead of expanding on this setting, Deadlight chooses to make a character driven story. The main character is a Canadian park ranger trying to find his friends and family in Seattle. The problem with Deadlight is that if it wanted to make a character driven story, it should have made its characters interesting or at least consistent. The story presents it's characters as somewhat naive of their surroundings at best and bipolar at worse. The voice acting, often delivered dead-panned, doesn't help.
The platforming is the star of the game. It plays somewhat like the original 2D Prince of Persia. You have your wall jumping and a bunch of climbing and running. You have a stamina that dictates how long you can hang off a ledge, sprint and use your melee weapon. The game haves you jumping on top of air conditioners on high rise buildings, running through crumbling buildings and evanding traps. Ignoring the fact that this park ranger knows parkour, it's satifying to finish one of these puzzles.
Making it harder to accomplish this endeavor are the controls, which are somewhat spotty and lag sometimes during inputs. This can make your life miserable on some sections of the game where the difficulty spikes. The game sometimes puts too many obstacles during sections where you're asked to run to your goal. With no room for error, having unresposive controls can lead to you dying dozens of times.
I wouldn't recommend getting Deadlight unless you have a steep discount. When you ignore the story and the game works, it's fun. But it's so short that I feel it wasn't worth it to suffer through the frustrations and get to the good parts.

From a guy tht doesnt like WW2 games:
The Good:
A good game, with some features that are unique. Love the paradropping and 3 way battles with 3 different factions on same battlefield.
The bad:
Lots of problems and bugs. Balance not too bad, but sniping a problem with poorly developed maps that only favour sniping and tanks/planes. Tanks reverse in a way that makes people who play other tanks games rage.
Climate seems like "PayToSnipe". You cant grind a recon in any reasonable time, so after you get sniped a dozen times, you start wanting to counter snipe, which you cant. Solution? buy a sniper for 2k gold (real money currency)
The Ugly:
Banning people with good KDR (above 3+) with under 50 matches is grounds for ban. Friend put a couple bucks, bought a sniper, FG-42 rifle and started going to town on people with starter kit. His rewards for developer poor planning was a ban wave.
TLDR- Not recommended unless you're willing to put lots of time or money to get sniper/tank/plane. Bad map design favours those. If you plan to play the game well, make sure to do so after a few bad games so you dont get in the ban wave.

Beautiful game with a great concept.  This game holds all the attributes that sandbox games need to have: a vast wourld with nearly endless freedom.  The game shows great potential evn for an early access game.

Note: At the time of this writing, the game is on Alpha version 0.82.
I like that you can download objects from other players from right in the game. I haven't been able to try out the multiplayer yet but I'm looking forward to it. The NPCs in the story do a great job of giving you the scripts you need to build almost everything as long as you do the side quests. It's also nice that I can sell my extra wood and marble to them before buying an item to 'trade' my wood/marble for newer tools.
I am enjoying the story missions, when I don't run into a quest stopping bug (Up! Up! Up!). The game has its share of bugs like not locking the mouse into the game window during fullscreen. For dual monitor setups, this means your game will go into window mode every time you click outside of it. I change my setup to single monitor when playing. My game has not crashed at all since the 0.82 update.
One of the tricks for a few of the bugs you'll encounter is to save your game often. IF you hit a bug, load up your last save and try again. If you get stuck on a quest ad don't have a save; save, quit, load. I got stuck on a quest to rescue some survivors from a stuck ship and almost gave up after reloading a few times and then it suddenly worked without explanation.
tl;dr: It's a great game with a few bugs. The game has great potential. If you like sandbox builders and save often, you'll love this game.

More music, more story, more characters, more difficult, and overall just more content. I really hope this isn't the last game, and hopefully we at least get DLC at a later date! As expected, the game remains tough to beat, if not tougher than its predecessor. The game stays true to the old formula while still managing to feel new. The old mask system was sort of removed, in a way. You don't get to choose what mask you want to wear at the start of each level. Instead, because the game is much more story-driven, you get to play as certain characters. However, some levels will allow you to choose between masks, which allow you to uniquely complete a level. The soundtrack in the game is as great as ever, feeling very atmospheric, and gets my blood pumping when I'm going around slaughtering people. It eases the frustration of the game, because even when you die, at least you'll still get to listen to some sweet music. The one issue I have with this game is level design, as enemies can and will shoot you from off screen, while others still will be shooting at you through hundreds of glass panes while others STILL will charge at you from behind. The main reason it takes so long to complete the levels is due to some things like this, but it is not a dealbreaker for me. I rather like that sort of challenge, though. Sometimes, you'll find that the usually strategy doesn't seem to work, and that absentmindedly charging in and killing people ruthlessly is a much better option. Believe it or not, it DOES work to an extent, even if you're completely unaware of enemies around you. And every once in a while you'll have to play peekaboo with a guy or two.
As for the story, I will admit I found it hard to follow, but I feel like this was one of those games where they slap a story on it and call it a day. However, with the way this game is played, I can excuse that, because I feel that this game is more about just going around killing things as opposed to a game that's more narrative driven. Though it does help to know the story. As I mentioned earlier, the game is considerably more difficult than the first one, so if you had trouble with the first game, you'll be in for a world of hurt. It can take a long time to finish some levels, and it nearly took me an hour to beat the second to last level because I kept on dying. If you're the type of gamer who does not enjoy difficulty games then DO NOT GET THIS GAME, or it will make you cry every last tear you have. Other than that, this game is just about perfect. Lots of action, lots of adrenaline, lots of frustration and anger. But with that frustration and anger comes lots of satisfaction once you overcome a level.
Now, about that wall glitch.
I finished one of the levels (I forget which) that took me about 15 to 20 minutes of frustration to beat. Right as I'm walking down a flight of stairs to leave, I accidentally walk back up, and for some reason that results in me getting stuck in the wall. As I am unable to move, I was forced to quit. :( Hopefully this won't happen again.
Besides that one glitch I've encountered, Hotline Miami 2 seems to be a very well polished game, with no other issues thus far. With amazing mechanics and gameplay, and a superb soundtrack, Dennaton Games has impressed me yet again with this amazing sequel to Hotline Miami.

Don't get me wrong, I actually liked Deadlight, as a whole.
It is just that with what the game makes itself out to be, and with a price of over ten Euro, you should be warned of basically two things:
1) The game is not exactly what it appears to be. Sure, it is atmosperic, has a good story, nice characters, interesting blend of jump-and-run and horror survival and builds a dark world, that feels very genuine. Until the Platformer-Part kicks in. At some Point the game just stops feeling realistic and starts to subject it's level design to "We want to have more platformer-elements". Plus it had a suprisingly high frustration factor, and even the best voice acting sounds stupid when you hear it for the tenth time because you keep dying for reasons beyond your comprehension.
2) Deadlight is very short. I finished it in under 4 hours, and while I probably missed a lot of the collectable stuff, I did so on purpose. I generally dislike using collectables as a means to prolong the game. If the story takes four hours, that's how long the game is.
So if you do like platformers even if they get proposterous in terms of level design, and happen to get this game for a low prize, or in some bundle: Go for it! It definitely is a step into an interesting direction.

As a beta tester I couldn't enjoy this game as much as I would have liked because the developers were undoubtably lazy in polishing the mechanics of this game.
First off, the hit detection for melee is broken, you can't hit a zombie that's a centimeter into the background despite performing a horizontal swing that clearly would've connected, zombies have no problems attacking you from the background however.
It also randomly decides not to hit zombies who are perfectly in range of getting hit. Zombies have no problem at all with hitting you while you're at least a half meter out of their range or taking a swing at you when you're prone on the floor, said swing being performed at shoulder height and somehow manages to hit a target a whole meter below that.
Getting grabbed by a zombie is almost always a death sentence if there are other zombies nearby as it is impossible to push multiple zombies away, they'll pass through others as if they were ghosts, giving you no option of crowd control or getting out of a bad situation, this also didn't make the areas with infinitely spawning zombies any easier. If the whole point of the game was meant to evade the zombies at all cost, why even bother giving the broken option of trying to fight them off in melee?
The controls sometimes decide to do whatever they feel like, swinging back and forth over a fence instead of dropping down and sometimes climbing back up a ledge I'm trying to climb down.
Certain areas of the game were very annoying as it required you to do things in a very fluid and nigh-perfectly executed and predetermined manner. One area in particular had a warehouse that would collapse bit by bit, I was stuck on this area for far too long because the game did not like me trying to be too fast by performing a running jump over a pit and continuing to run, doing this would result in the final piece of debris killing me a mere centimeter away from the next segment. Instead the game forced you to make a normal jump over the pit and then sprint in order to clear this area. Stupid.
The main character is supposedly a park warden, who can't swim, not only can he not swim but he also sinks like a rock straight to the bottom where he will drown standing almost immediately. This did not help with my immersion into the game at all as it was a poor excuse to have some water based obstacles in the game.
I'm not surprised none of my friends bothered playing this game to the end, all of them appear to have stopped playing at the exact same spot as well, I wonder why.

Im a 40k fan so when I hearx about this game it didnt register on my radar. However, I dont think I have ever enjoyed a compulsive buy as much as I have this game. Be warned, its a LFD clone to the T, but I couldnt care less and im glad it is in many ways.
If you have played LFD1-2 than you will recognize the style of gameplay. Vermintide adds alot of depth by making the levels much more interactive and adding a great loot system with all types of upgrades and sidegrades. The reward system is unique as well and adds a great element to the game; do you want to risk not being able to finish the level or do you want to go for the potential for more loot? Everything about it makes the levels much more replayable than either LFD games.
The combat is great, its much more dynamic than I thought it would be. You wont be successfull in melee fighting by blindly clicking the mouse button. When 50-100 rat warriors are bearing down on you, you have to be able to think and position yourself quick or your going to get wiped out.
All in all, you dont have to be a fan of Warhammer to enjoy this game but if you are it makes it that much sweeter. I highly recommend this game for a fun game to play with feidnds.

Of all the sandbox early access games on Steam, this seems so far the most promising. And indeed, the most complete ~ *cough* DayZ *cough*
I was entirely taken aback by the MMORPG-like feel from the get go, and it initially made me weary. It took exactly five minutes to forget any of that, thanks to the addictive harvesting, mining, building and just generally extremely well-done crafting in this game. This game so far has *the* best customization that I have seen, and knocks Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri and Galactic Civilizations 2 down from their previously shared throne in this aspect IMO.
The parallells to Minecraft are also subdued - thankfully.
Apart from The Secret World, I don't think I've ever been more immersed in an over-the-shoulder perspective game. Sure, the music is mostly licenseware, the voice acting sounds like a school class project, and some textures are extremely flat; but I find myself ignoring a lot of what would otherwise be real annoyances for me because of the overall charm this game has.
Probably the main strength this game has is the authentic-feeling world. Multiplayer has some procedural niggles that I hope will be gone after alpha, but the single player (and selectable in multiplayer) "canon" world quite possibly is the most authentic, immersive "alien looking" world I've seen since The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind. And to be sure, Planet Explorer's flora and fauna has a lot in common with Morrowind, to the point that it feels like an homage, if a slightly more colourful one.
There are a few things left to really fix for me to give this top marks. For example, I feel the multiplayer progression is way too fast compared to the single player, and people will get easily burnt out if they start out with multiplayer first. PLAY SINGLE PLAYER FIRST! The music is repetitive, and I hope a placeholder - but the choice of music, even if it's sparse, at least was a good one. Voice acting is campy and of low technical and artistic quality - which is kind of charming, actually. And I don't think many care in this sort of game. Also, I wish harvesting, woodcutting and mining were a bit more agile. Currently, herbs have too small "pick up zones" where you have to stand realllllllllyyyy close to the center, the woodcutting is tedious because you have to hold down the right mousebutton, sometimes for MINUTES if it's a big tree, and finally the mining animation is slow as heck and hard to abort to precision mine.
Lots of minor issues, no major issues - except one:
Most of all the dedicated server launcher could use a lot of work, and the parameters the worlds is created from need to be expanded. For example drop rate. Well... ESPECIALLY drop rate. Ha. Current default multiplayer servers will let you get full steel armour and a helicopter within 2 hours. AWFUL. But hey, it's alpha.

For an early access game that is still in its beta, the game is VERY well polised. I have not seen any bugs or glitches yet that might cause issues. The crafting system and mouse abilities, might need some tweaking for easier crafting and access to those options, but from the very start there is so much you can do that it is impossible to be bored and with all the content now and to come the game will be very very popular for multiplayer/co op with friends! A sure win and a sure buy!

Summary: Very short (4 hours gameplay). Very nice aesthetics. Very bad gameplay mechanics.
The gameplay is too short for the money asked. If you buy this cheap, it's a better bargain.
The graphics style is amazing, I loved how the world looked like, I loved the still-picture-style sequences, character animations are very fluent.
The story is fine. But finding pieces of a diary all over the world is weird and unrealistic, and it seems to be just a gimmick to fill the world with some interesting objects.
The gameplay mechanics... oh my.
Let's start with saving - there are two types of checkpoints, first of them which save the progress even when you exit the game, second which only save progress during gameplay. It is never indicated well which is which, so you never know how much of the game you are going to repeat if you quit it. The very check point location is badly executed as well, sometimes they are _before_ an in-game cinematic (non-skippable, *of course*!), so if you die shortly afterward, you're going to see the cinametic again, and again, and again.
The 2.5D platforming - is problematic as usual. Especially with that black-outline graphic style. You never know what is the foreground, what is the background. There are several places where you can spend 15 minutes looking for a way out, just because it's so damn confusing which objects can be used and which can not. Also the zombies coming from the background are invulnerable until they are fully foreground, which you never know when it happens. So they'll bite you to the neck.
Picking up objects - so annoying. Usually you can pick up several things from a body. But you can't pick up everything at once, there is a delay, and you never know how many objects are there. So you pick up the first object, and then you have to wait 5-10 seconds whether a new pick-up indicator appears. If it does, you pick a second object, and wait again. If you've waited long enough and no indicator appeared, there are no more objects. Why on earth make it so annoying and unusable?
Action scenes - sometimes there is an even when you need to run, avoid objects, kill a few zombies, all in a certain time interval (a chopper flying behind you, closing in, and shooting). That could be fun. But it isn't. The way it is implemented, there is only a single correct solution how to perform this. You can't make a wrong step. You can't delay yourself by 0.1 second. There is literally zero time to spare. Jump on a fence just a little bit too early, which means you need to spend another 0.3 seconds pulling yourself up, and you're dead. And you need to learn every step the hard way, dying and repeating. Combine that with bad checkpoint location and inskippable in-game animations, and you'll get seriously annoyed.
Fighting mechanics - I like the energy concept. You're just an ordinary guy - swing the axe a few times and you're so tired you can hardly swing once more. The guns are OK, but aiming isn't. You don't get a crosshair, so you never know which way the characters is going to aim when hitting the aim button. Adjusting the aim is slow and I always tried to swap the direction (left or right) using the mouse (used to it from other games), which doesn't work. That makes gun fighting more tedious than it should be. You're not playing against the game, you're playing against the controls. Which is not good.
Moving mechanics - You're just an ordinary guy, who's weak, can't swim, but can do wall jumps, Prince of Persia style? How does that fit in? It doesn't. Breaking objects is yet another story. In order to increase the number of gameplay concepts, the developers allowed us to kick doors, smash them open while running, or smash them with an axe. But don't you try to do something else than they allowed. Wan't to kick doors which are supposed to be smashed open? No. Want to smash open doors which are supposed to be kicked out? No. Want to break them with an axe? No. When running against a door, can you jump to put a bit more weight behind you? No. You get the idea. So usually you need to look really carefully for the symbols and then hit the right button and never any other button. That's the only way it works. Really ruining the experience.
Overall, I think there are better games of this genre out there, and this one has too many flaws to deserve a recommendation.

I enjoy this game alot.  Full disclosure, I did not play the Left For Dead games so I am unable to compare, but so far, the experience is just fun. 2 1/2 stars (out of 5).  Extremely disappointing that this game has such great potential but is frequently ruined by bad implentation or poor gameplay decisions. It's a sin, really.
Pros:
The graphics are drop dead gorgeous, as are the various models and they way they interact with the world.
Explosions are awesome.
The weapons are great, and have a solid feel and sound, as well as effect.
The story is also very good, and the voice acting overall is superb;  actually, the best I've ever heard.
The physics are very good, overall, though there are some issues that I assume are with the engine, such as picking up cash or looting bodies.
Now for the Cons:
I hate the annoying weapon swap prompt everytime I want to loot a body.  That is, if the game even detects I'm hovering over a body in the first place. You waste so much time trying to get it to figure out what you want, and where you ponit the cursor makes no difference.. and sometimes you get shot or attacked while futzing with the stupid finicky loot system.  There should be an option to disable weapon swapping entirely at some point; why on earth would I want to swap my tricked out P416 for an AK-47?  It's ridiculous. It's also hard to pick up cash sometimes.
The menu from long pressing of "1" is very awkward.  The 1 key?  Really? Terrible design.
The Rakyat Challenges screw up your in-game weapon selection.  Then you have to go back to a safe house and get the right ones back. That's not extremely annoying or anything, since you can only carry 4 weapons. Actually, yes it is.
Bodies often just vanish before you can loot them.
I've also seen weapon glitches:  random remapping of key assignment,  keys not working, or throwing a grenade and it doesn't explode (only once).  The whole weapons system is pathetic.
The Map behaves terriblly too, it ofen starts drifting out of control, as the mouse cursor will just appear to the edge of the map for no good reason.  Fail.
There is no way to skip cutscenes.  That sucks for 2nd or 3rd playthroughs.
The Save system sucks possibly the most, but most especially during "missions", where they choose to disable it, and leave you at the mercy of their chosen checkpoints.  Usually the checkpoints aren't too bad, but the last mission, right after you kill Hoyt and try to escape, they're too far between.
Even worse, if you quit the game, it won't remember your checkpoint, you have to do the entire mission over again from the beginning.    F$%#$# that!
Speaking of killing Hoyt, when you're trying to escape the base on the helicopter, you've got half a dozen guys firing rockets at you from the extreme left side of the screen (on freaking easy mode!), such that the gun doesn't move that far over, you can't take them out before they hit you.  You're a sitting duck.  It's a no win situation. My second playthrough, I couldn't get past it. 6 tries.  I gave up.
There are other gameplay annoyances I can't think of off the top of my head.
It's as if the engine, audio, and graphics teams were loaded with the industry's top notch designers, as the graphics, models, engine, voices, storyline  etc.. are just among the best of any game.  But the abysmal teams that worked on the menu system and gameplay choices had no business working alongside this talent, they significantly damaged what would otherwise have been a fantastic game.

As expected, the game remains tough to beat, if not tougher than its predecessor. The game stays true to the old formula while still managing to feel new. The old mask system was sort of removed, in a way. You don't get to choose what mask you want to wear at the start of each level. Instead, because the game is much more story-driven, you get to play as certain characters. However, some levels will allow you to choose between masks, which allow you to uniquely complete a level. The soundtrack in the game is as great as ever, feeling very atmospheric, and gets my blood pumping when I'm going around slaughtering people. It eases the frustration of the game, because even when you die, at least you'll still get to listen to some sweet music. The one issue I have with this game is level design, as enemies can and will shoot you from off screen, while others still will be shooting at you through hundreds of glass panes while others STILL will charge at you from behind. The main reason it takes so long to complete the levels is due to some things like this, but it is not a dealbreaker for me. I rather like that sort of challenge, though. Sometimes, you'll find that the usually strategy doesn't seem to work, and that absentmindedly charging in and killing people ruthlessly is a much better option. Believe it or not, it DOES work to an extent, even if you're completely unaware of enemies around you. And every once in a while you'll have to play peekaboo with a guy or two.
As for the story, I will admit I found it hard to follow, but I feel like this was one of those games where they slap a story on it and call it a day. However, with the way this game is played, I can excuse that, because I feel that this game is more about just going around killing things as opposed to a game that's more narrative driven. Though it does help to know the story. As I mentioned earlier, the game is considerably more difficult than the first one, so if you had trouble with the first game, you'll be in for a world of hurt. It can take a long time to finish some levels, and it nearly took me an hour to beat the second to last level because I kept on dying. If you're the type of gamer who does not enjoy difficulty games then DO NOT GET THIS GAME, or it will make you cry every last tear you have. Other than that, this game is just about perfect. Lots of action, lots of adrenaline, lots of frustration and anger. But with that frustration and anger comes lots of satisfaction once you overcome a level.
Now, about that wall glitch.
I finished one of the levels (I forget which) that took me about 15 to 20 minutes of frustration to beat. Right as I'm walking down a flight of stairs to leave, I accidentally walk back up, and for some reason that results in me getting stuck in the wall. As I am unable to move, I was forced to quit. :( Hopefully this won't happen again.
Besides that one glitch I've encountered, Hotline Miami 2 seems to be a very well polished game, with no other issues thus far. With amazing mechanics and gameplay, and a superb soundtrack, Dennaton Games has impressed me yet again with this amazing sequel to Hotline Miami.
This game is a grand departure from the first however it still maintains tight controls and interesting, if confusing, story.

Tagline statement to garner immediate thumbs up/thumbs down that is shamelessly stolen from a professional review:
"If Hotline Miami was Drive, Hotline Miami 2 is Only God Forgives."
Brief bullet pointy list:
- A colder, more calculated killing experience; a slower pace necessitated by level design and enemy types, sometimes to the detriment of the game.
- A fleshed out Hotline Miami lore.
- A cast of both familiar and new faces, each with their own twisted and convoluted storyline.
- A major departure from the first game; do not buy it because it carries the Hotline Miami name or because you have fond memories of the frag-em-up gameplay style of the first one.
Rambling statement about what I find best about the game:
In the first game, you flew through the levels like a hammer-wielding tornado, crushing skulls to the tempo and briefly slowing down to inspect the carnage on your way back to the car. Hotline Miami 2 takes an entirely different approach, forcing you to take in the scenery, not just using it as a canvas for your bloodsoaked work of art.
From the second you exit the car, you're either encouraged to carefully plan out your assault, or immediately kick in the door and start killing. Either way, you will be aware of the level - and the settings can take a bit of the sting of poor level design (in some cases, see other reviews). While Hotline Miami featured mostly apartment blocks and residential areas, Hotline Miami 2 departs very early from the tried and true - you'll wreck a department store, storm a ship in rough waters, assault a resort in Hawaii; all while having the atmosphere enhanced further by what amounts to possibly the best OST we'll hear in a video game all year.
Hotline Miami 2 is, in my honest opinion, less of a game about being an unstoppable death machine, and more of a game about the set design/character concepts/atmosphere. It's a far stretch from the first game conceptually, but it certainly stands on its own as a successful experiment.

On the surface Planet Explorers seems like a quick cash-in on the Crafting/Exploration genre, which is not to imply it doesn't succeed at what it intends to do. While still in Early Access this title performs very well on both fronts, and should not be dismissed for the bugs/flaws currently in-game.  The attempt at exploration Planet Explorers makes is impressive, and although the graphics may be a little dated, the scenery can be downright beautiful at times.  Even with a map as vast as the one in Planet Explorers moving forward is not always the best option, with vast cave networks easily discovered using you Handheld PC, you won't have to venture far to discover the unknown.  One flaw that currently is plaguing this title is the draw distance, and the rate at which the landscape appears, while easily written off as an Early Access issue, it is one that will need to be addressed before official release.
Crafting in Planet Explorers can feel like the usual fanfare, resource tiers(wood, rock, copper, iron, etc), but the Creations Editor is where the crafting in this title moves beyond what I've encountered so far in my gaming experience. Yes, other games have had content creation, map editors, etc, but Planet Explorers brings it right to the forefront of its systems.  While the Creations Editor(a more accurate name would be Blueprint Editor) can seem daunting and unwieldy, spending time learning it's nuances will quickly show you just how robust this tool can be.  I have had a blast buidling new vehicles and testing them in Build Mode to see how well they perform, and the experience brings me back to my childhood playing with legos.
While Planet Explorers is on the right path towards what, in my eyes, is the next evolution of the Crafting/Exploration genre, it is not without it's bugs. I previously mentioned the draw distance, which is an issue for immersion, but also for traversing the map in aircrafts, or other very fast moving vehicles. While travelling around the map you will have trees, animals, mountains, and more appear in front of you, often leading to emergency meneuvers.  With the robust Creation Editor, and Steam Workshop support this title has the potential to develop a large following, and create many memorable moments.  Other bugs do occur, and not all game elements are currently implemented, but I feel with our support this could be a title to throw up on the board with Minecraft, and if all the kinks are worked out it will surpass it in what it does.

Update: Changed to negative review as I'm just sick of the bad design in this sequel. The first one was great, and more like a melee action-puzzle game. This one is mostly about getting shot from offscreen while holding a gun with no bullets and fighting with the awful camera (which is too zoomed in, puts you in the middle of the screen instead of looking ahead, can be moved but then messes up your ability to aim or even SEE YOURSELF, and is too often having you face off-screen enemies up or down vertical corridors you can't see down because the game is in widescreen and too zoomed in).
Instead of action, and the non-stop moving from room to room slaying enemy after enemy like in the first one, you will instead spend most of your time waiting & trying to lure enemies by getting just close enough to them that they run at you. You'll die randomly if you get too close and they shoot you with their aim-bot aim (and they can magically detect you even if they are not facing you, and will magically 360 no-scope you across longer distances than you can even see; yet at other times you will fire a shotgun right next to them and they will stand there oblivious for some reason, while much farther enemies rush to your position). You will get snagged on the poorly designed scenery A LOT. You'll sit around waiting for enemies to randomly walk to where you need them to be, which makes frequent retrying tedious. The enemy AI and patrol paths are terrible, on enemies that aren't scripted to walk set paths, as they randomly change directions at 45 or 180 degree offsets and act like they're balls bouncing off walls. Dogs often literally spin around in circles. Humans get stuck in doors all the time. You'll spawn outside the level and be walking around in walls unable to do anything but retry in places. So many bugs you will see so often.
The dialog and plot in between action levels is beyond tedious. I don't even know why it is there. It was OK in the first game but it seems more padded out in this one, and it's very poorly written.
You cannot save mid-scene, and some scenes require you to clear multiple floors and will make you want to ragequit mid-scene but then punish you by making you do the earlier parts again. When you do re-launch the game and click Continue, it won't automatically select the stage you were up to; you have to scroll through the list of acts, select the last act you unlocked, then scroll through the list of scenes within the act and do the same. Basic stuff that is a bit inexplicable.
I do keep coming back for more, largely thanks to the instant retry, but I can't say I'm really enjoying it. I'm considering uninstalling it, which is rare for me, but I'll probably make myself finish it.
Man they messed this game up compared to the previous one, IMO. Way too many situations where you're being shot at by enemies off-screen you can't see (even if you move the camera out, sometimes, and doing so then means you can't see *yourself* and can't aim properly). Too much focus on guns (yet very little ammo, which in some ways makes things a puzzle but, since the guns are so haphazard and bullets often go into a door instead of an enemy, ends up making things quite random at times).
In HM1 you'd work out how to move through a level and kill everyone. In HM2, you work out how to pick a couple of people off silently, and then lure everyone else to a choke point, or snipe them from cover. Lots more waiting. Lots more depending on AI which is unpredictable (and not in a good way; many times things get stuck in doors or, the dogs especially, just walk around in circles on the spot).
Some other problems on certain levels indicate a slight lack of polish, but it's the general level-design philosophy which really messes things up, sadly. And unlike the odd bug (1 crash, and multiple levels where I kept spawning inside the walls instead of the corridors) or the odd annoyance (a level where the action is under parts of the HUD which don't become translucent or move; also huge, bold, coloured point numbers appearing over killed enemies on top of other enemies you are trying to fight so you can't see WTF you're doing)... ... ...unlike those, the level design probably can't/won't be patched by updates, unless the devs are willing to change things quite significantly by reducing enemy sight distance (seems doubtful; presumably they playtested it and like it how it is, although god knows why). Maybe the option of zooming out farther could make things less frustrating/unfair, or making the camera point ahead of you instead of putting you in the middle of the screen.
I don't mind hard games, and parts of the game are hard-but-fair... However, parts just feel like utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and make me ragequit, which isn't something games make me do often these days (and HM1 never did, until the stupid end boss fight with the cut-scene you had to watch on each retry). But I do keep going back for more, for some reason.

Warhammer: Vermintide,
Is a good replacement if you're still hoping for the game Hellraid which is on hold.
At least, if you like games similar to Left 4 Dead. Because that's what Warhammer: Vermintide basically is.
A group of 4 heroes (Players/Bots) embark on missions and after they completed them there's some small XP reward and the occasional loot in the form of a weapon for one of the five available classes.
Depending on how many treasures you take with you to the end of the map it might result in a better weapon as loot.
At its core Vermintide is a good game. The idea, although completely copied from Left 4 Dead, except for the loot and XP system, does work.
But, to be honest, the things Vermintide does are not very well executed and could use some serious tweaking and testing to keep it interesting in the long run.
For instance, the loot system does provide a random weapon for one the five hero classes. So, if you like just two or maybe three of the available heroes it could mean that you get most of the equipment for the other, not so liked, classes.
Even if you recycle those weapons at the forge to get a new weapon, it doesn't mean you get a better item.
At first glance this seems okay, but the more you play, the more annoying it becomes. Because, getting new weapons means you'll have to play a mission and complete it.
And that's the other weaker point of Vermintide. The maps look nice and set a certain mood. Nothing wrong with that, but the objectives are: Survive Wave, Destroy X, Bring A to B. Spread across 13 maps this does provide a certain boredom. Especially when the enemies are rat versions of Left 4 Dead.
Zombies are rats which can be slaughtered by the hundreds. (Though they do fight) Rat ogres are just a Tank in rat form, pack masters are rats that act as smokers and assassins are hunters.
They are nicely modeled, but we've seen that type of enemy before and for me it doesn't really ad to the fun.
Okay, there're gas rats, ratling gunners and commanders. Those are different, but are not enough to lift the game above the mediocre and dull experience which it provides after a couple of hours.

As a huge fan of the first game, I was overjoyed with excitement when this finally came out. Does the sequel live up to the first? Yes and no.
Firstoff, the good stuff.
Dennaton has made a number of improvements on an already near perfect game formula. Gameplay is pretty much the same. Combat is still fast paced and keeps you on your toes. The lock-on system is also more functional than before. The new characters and masks/abilities allow for various, fun ways to slaughter thugs. Length-wise, HM2 is much longer than the first providing a decent-lengthed playthrough that is longer than some AAA titles today (around 6 hours).
The story is spread among the different characters, providing different viewpoints and taking place in different time periods. It also includes a large amount of back and sidestory in the environments, requiring you to keep your eyes open if you want to understand everything going on and receive some closure. And of course, the new soundtrack is just as good if not better than the first, fueling your bloodlust with pumping bass.
But what did the developers do wrong?
Some levels here can be character-biased. What I mean is that, in the first game, some masks were better than others for completing levels, but each level could be completed with whatever mask you liked. Here, some levels are near impossible if you choose the wrong character/mask/ability. This restricts your freedom a bit and can lead to massive frustration.
The level design is greatly frustrating as well. It's as if all the architects in Miami decided that every building needed a hundred windows on the inside. You'll often be shot at from across the room. Remember that one room in Hot & Heavy from the first game, with the four mini-rooms and glass windows? A ton of levels feel like they're copied off that one.
Some bad levels don't ruin this game. If you're a fan of the first, chances are you'll love this second and last entry of the series. It improves upon nearly everything the first had to offer. Can't go wrong with that.

If you're a fan of the original Hotline Miami like I am then you're probably the kind of person that likes a game that actually challenges them. Well I've got good news for you, Hotline Miami 2 picks up where the original game left off in difficulty and amps it up all the way to the end culminating in one of the most insanely difficult and satisfying ends to a game I've ever played. The game has over 24 levels that span about 5-7 hours or more depending on how experienced you are along with an additional hard mode which about doubles the difficulty of every level and can extend out for many more hours. At a price of $15 it is well worth it for the quality playtime you will get out of the game especially when compared to more expensive titles that often clock in below 6 hours in playtime and don't challenge the player like Hotline Miami.

As a fan of the first game, and having beaten the second game, I can say Hotline Miami 2 disappointed me. Only the last third is on par with HL1.  It was a decent game with a terrible story.  If Hotline Miami hadn't been an incredibly game with a great story, I probably would have a higher opinion of the sequel.  Yes, I recommend it.  No, you won't think of it as more than an average game, play-wise, bogged down with bad storytelling but inexplicably blessed with a fantastic soundtrack.
If you don't like long reviews, you can stop reading here.
HL2 plays like a hard mode expansion for HL1.  "Hard" meaning
rather than
Off-screen deaths, fatguys, wide-open levels, and being constantly forced to lure enemies to their death or use guns instead of having melee as a viable option lead to repetitive play and low scores (especially for some characters).  I also have to add something I was surprised not to see in other reviews: the mouse sensitive starts out dangerously slow, but if you increase it distance-looking becomes nearly impossible to control the distance of.
Besides bad map design, the game is incredibly linear for all the timeframe jumping it does.  There's one, maybe two ways to beat any given map, and both of those ways make combos very difficult.  Even in HL1, where a map might be crowded with enemies, it would usually be small enough that taking unnecessary risks to destroy everyone in a wave of melee attacks was worth considering.  With the gigantic, enemy-filled maps, you will either clear them using guns at a distance or peek-and-lure style melee.  They're both time consuming, lousy for combos, and result in you feeling punished when your score is tallied.
The original also had levels interrupted without warning, which broke up any feeling of "Different Day, Same ****".  2/3 of the way through Crackdown and all of a sudden you're dealing with
when you thought you were just killing mobsters again.  It sort-of kinda happens once in HL2 in a way you won't care about.
As for the story, HL2 seems like it was written by fans working separately on each part, none of whom understood what made the original so damn good.  When they finished, and crammed their work together as best they could, they knew it was problematic but released it anyways.  The fact that this was made by the same team that did the first one astounds me.  How did they screw up so fast?  To be frank, this situation reminds me of how a number of TV shows go into an unwatchable death spiral because they have good qualities but also "push-the-boundaries."  At some point the creators somehow get it in their heads that pushing boundaries is what made their show popular, rather than those good qualities which are so much more time-consuming to write than just making it gorier, grosser, or trying to offend as many people as possible.
(Tiger Mask) An improved version of the tiger mask from HL1.  He can survive one light round, punches out fatguys, and (if he hasn't been wounded) attacking a dog with melee too late results in him catching the dog and killing it rather than dying.  His limitation is he can't pick up weapons.
(Zebra Mask) Has a combat roll that is worthless when used on purpose.  It's less than worthless when used on accident, because it was tied to spacebar, meaning you may roll into the an enemy's path when you meant to finish off a prone enemy.
(Bear Mask) Starts out dual-wielding machine guns.  Until they run out of ammo, you'll destroy anything in front of him.  His worthless special is he can slowly hold his guns akimbo by holding right-click, which is a good way to shoot far too many bullets to kill a small number of enemies while keeping your hand in an uncomfortable position.
(Swan Masks) One has a chainsaw, the other has a gun (replaced automatically with one off the floor when it is empty).  You control Ash (chainsaw) with the movement keys and Alex tries to echo the movements.  Ash attacks with left-click, Alex fires with the right-click and aims with the mouse cursor.  Once you get the hang of playing them they are easily the best new gameplay mechanic introduced in HL2.
(Pig Mask) Plays like Jacket, except he can survive a light round (or two?).  Killed off(?) so early it's not even a spoiler to say that.  I'm serious.
Plays exactly like Jacket.
(Snake Mask) Much like the snake mask in HL1, except thanks to the inertia nerf, thrown objects go about half as far.  The wide level design, enemy grouping, and windows make what was one of the best tactical masks in the first game surprisingly ineffective in the second.  He also seems to have a shorter reach with unarmed melee attacks, which seems like a shockingly poor decision for a character whose special is
.
Plays exactly like Jacket.
Basically Jacket + (Mark, Corey, or Tony).
Plays like Jacket, but his levels are conspicuously prone to providing him with silenced weapons.
(the writer) A pacifist (emphasis on the fist) who uses non-lethal combat and empties any guns he picks up unless you choose to have him lose his temper.   A surprisingly enjoyable challenge to play because it's optional.
(the soldier) Limited to one gun and a combat knife, which you switch using right-click.  Despite poor map design in a number of his levels, I actually liked playing as him.  I've read there are ammo boxes he can use (would have been FANTASTIC if the game told me that), but even if you don't find any (or know they exist) you may enjoy the challenge of conserving ammo like I did.  Like Ash and Alex, you get the convenience of having a melee and ranged weapon available at all times.  Unfortunately, limiting Nicklas' ammo so severely means you're pretty much never going to get a significant amount of points on his levels.
HL2 is basically a bad existentialism/sci-fi movie that goes on for way too long.  It's the kind of bad story that people try to defend by claiming you didn't understand it, when really they didn't understand it well enough to realize it was badly-delivered utter nonsense.  There is no biggest problem, so I will just list all of the major problems with the game:
You jump around in time without any sense of when you're at (unless you're really good at memorizing dates), seeing disjointed, meaningless things happen to characters you won't like or miss.  Nothing is resolved or introduced properly.
(who was a welcome surprise in this game) and Nicklas are the only exceptions to these rules.

You need little more proof than Deadlight to see that Metacritic is useless and either very fickle or easily manipulated, bordering on scam.
At 78/100, its rating is almost identical with Fallout: New Vegas (the sub-80 rating of which cost Obsidian Entertainment a well-deserved part of their pay).
Just like Fallout: New Vegas deserved a higher rating, this deserves a far lower one.
Deadlight is a game with an interesting premise - Parkour elements, a dense atmosphere in the trailers and screenshots, some pretty cool "alternate history - Cold War goes Zombie Apocalypse" idea behind it... It's not until you actually play the game that you realize a few things:
1) The cool setting is treated as a bait - it's supposed to get you interested but isn't explored in any meaningful way and it could just as well be the present.
2) The parkour mostly consists of the same few puzzle elements you execute to follow the linear path. But unlike other games that are mainly based on movement as gameplay, it doesn't exactly feel amazing and you are not going to feel challenged at any point.
3) Jumping and running aside, the combat system (and thus the rest of the gameplay) has only two or three moments where you can enjoy it; the rest of the time, it's tolerable at best and adds little to the experience.
4) The atmosphere wears off very quickly. Yes, you're running and jumping around a zombie-infested city but then, suddenly, you're (
) running around the trap-riddled sewer kingdom (and it really has the proportions of a small Central-European monarchy) of Mr. Hobo McTinfoilhead who, apparently, anticipated all of this and started building his own city (but apparently without the blackjack or hookers to make it worth your time). That section is disgustingly ugly (it's not the poop, it's the fact that no sewer ever looked like that, anywhere, ever, and it barely looks like it's part of the same game) and it is pretty frickin' long. Oh, and the comic cutscenes... Well, they're not bad themselves but that style does not go well with how the rest of the game looks (or, to put it differently: "That dress with those shoes?!").
5) As the previous point suggests, the story and characters are no selling point. No, the Hoboking is much funnier in my description than he actually is in the game.
6) For 12 bucks, and even without all the gripes stated above, this game is insultingly short (at only 2-3 hours).
If you have to see this game, watch a Let's Play. If you absolutely HAVE to play it, then
1) pick it up when it goes on sale and
2) may God have mercy on your soul.
