I thought Zombie Panic: Source was a mess. An earnest mess with plenty of chances to grief other players. Such as taking all the ammo in the house the survivors are holed up in and throwing it out the window at the zombie horde. Glitching the door to keep the zombies out of my hiding spot so the round continues forever. Knocking over zombie-built ledges so the zombies can't have any soft, lovely human flesh.
Contagion is a much more developed take on Zombie Panic: Source. And the only reason I've wanted to play it beyond the first moment was because of the Hunted game mode. Hunted is where players fight zombies, temporarily team up to find safe places, and then turn on each other. Or you can play it like I do, which is shoot everybody I see while reading their angry text through a drunk voice. It allows for developer-sponsored griefing, and that's a plus.
Unfortunately the rest of the game outside of Hunted is pretty damn boring and riddled with flaws. The most egregious flaw for me would be the mapping. The mapping is pretty wasteful, having entire stretches of street and all these buildings and not really doing anything with them except using them as scenery. I'd rather have smaller, more functional maps than wide ones with nothing to really offer. What's more, they make the objective-based missions tedious and confusing to navigate. We knew there was a gun shop, but we had no idea where to go, which meant we had to spend ten minutes to locate the shop and then take another ten just to get there.
The part of the game that made me stop playing was the netcode freezing the game. It wasn't lag, but something in the netcode that made the game freeze and wait for the server to catch up and give everybody the game data. This got extremely annoying when I was scoring headshots up close and personal with a zombie horde. I was popping my gat at zombie heads, then my game froze, and then the game told me I had stood there while the zombies nibbled at my gun hand and now I was a zombie. The kind of thing that makes me want to eat my mouse in frustration.
And worst of all: Zombies are still a god damn chore to play. Even with the ability to control hordes, order them around, jump on other players from behind and give them a big old kiss! They are still so damn boring, because you have to find the human players to kill them, which means you have to hoof your decaying♥♥♥♥♥towards gun noises and hope there's a tasty human to kill. Which is why I kill every human player I see. I say I am friendly and then shoot them, because my bullets are friendly too. They are like tiny little lead puppy dogs.
Anyway, don't bother.

Mount & Blade: Warband is a great game, in it's singleplayer you can play for many hours trying to conquer all of Calradia, fighting battles and wars from snowy mountains to desert sands. Not only is Warband's original singleplayer fun to play, it is also one of the best modded games on steam, there is mods to transform your original medieval setting of a fictious land into the actual European ages, complete with an accurate map of Europe and its factions. Moreover, if you're a Game of Thrones/ASOIAF fan, you can download one of the two great mods for the game, you can try to become King of Westeros as you fight during the War of Five Kings. There is many more great mods for warband, which all can get your many hours of playtime if you like them.
Overall, Mount & Blade: Warband is a little bit old, so the graphics won't be spectacular, but they are bearable. The singeplayer is good once you get into it, multiplayer can be quite goofy or serious and is fun especially with a group. The mods are one of the things that make Warband shine, and should be given a try if you buy the game.

An excellent game. At first, I forgot the game was even Early Access, it was so good, for me, at least. The storyline was interesting, and while at some places it appeared to start getting a little bit boring, other things come along, like those maddeningly-hard 3 giant Warbots that guarded one of the storyline's main objective!
While the game was, overall, quite good, there are some things that I can see improvement on- but not nearly as much as I would see in other Early Access games. I've played in all three modes: Story, Adventure, and Build, and mainly play in Story, since you can actually talk to people, look at a map, find people to trade with, etc etc etc. I also like Build because it gives more options in terms of experimenting: without a colony, it can be quite fustrating if you make a Creation, and find out that you did something wrong. However, here are the things that I think could have a bit of touching up on, or reworking:
- AI, both in Colonists, and, say, your Followers. It's aggravating to have to go out of your way so that your Followers can actually follow you, and player-made buildings are worthless with Colonists, since they just walk up to a wall, and then appear on the roof.
- Mining. I say this because, even at more advanced levels, it's a pain to mine. While sometimes you can just get caught up in seeing the massive amounts of items coming into your inventory, and having plenty of space to do so [Since Minecraft is one-item-per-block, and this is 20-items-for-half-a-block]. Drills might be useful: a mining machine would be much appreciated. Slopes would be helpful as well: the voxel system is awesome, just a pain to go up and down the mines, you know?
- Movement. Ever played, say, Red Faction: Armageddon? If you were to introduce a movement system similar to that, I would be so bloody grateful. While everything is very, very nice, such as the running and attacking animations, RF:A has a much more versatile character movement, with lots of running and jumping, and you can change what you're doing mid-action, whether just turning or jumping away.
- Colony. I don't know the plans, but I'd see it as very useful if you could have your colonists also work with mines and the like. If the Colony could generate an output, a production, instead of constant need of attention, both in the form of adding military might through turrets to keep the bad guys away, and in keeping everything running.

Look I wanted to like this game, I really wanted to like it. I played the original Hotline Miami, and though it didn't matter at the time, I got mostly a ranks in the missions going back in and playing a second, third time.
And then I played through Hotline Miami 2 on normal. It wasn't bad, sure, but it had some problems. There's a bit of a focus on gunplay that becomes more than a bit annoying as you play.
Most of my deaths came from off-screen, from a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ with a shotgun that I couldn't see.
Many times I played a level I would just stop and think instead of running through and thinking on my feet, just because of those off-screen deaths.
Using shift look became so integral to my experience, despite the fact that it rarely helped, and the fact that I never ♥♥♥♥ing used it in Hotline Miami 2.
Despite what everyone's saying, I found the levels with the journalist to be the most fun, and I have no idea why people are complaining about not being able to use guns, since most of the levels he's in aren't gun-centric anyway.
There are too many guns in the game and too many thugs that can only be killed by guns. There are also too many windows that guards can shoot through immediately.

Mount and Blade Warband is a true classic of a game.It is an RPG game where you choose what your character looks like, their name, and their background. Once you do that, you choose from six nations in the fanciful land of Calradia to spawn at. You are but a poor peasant at the start, but you will eventually become rich by completing side-quests given to you by NPCs and by defeating enemies and taking their crap. You will hire fresh recruits from villages, which can be upgraded into more powerful units as they get more experience, You can hire hero characters and already-powerful mercenaries from taverns in major cities. You can conquer or pillage other towns, and can actually fight battle alongside your troops.
Once you have your own little army, the possibilities are endless. Will you become the servant of powerful lords and kings? Will you join the manhunters and fight the many groups of bandits in Calradia? Will you become a murderer and a thief? Will you pledge alleigance to one of the six nations in Calradia, and become a lord of villages, castles and cities in times of peace, and be a general in times of war? Or will you forge your own destiny, and became the all-powerful ruler of your very own nation?????

Choose wisely.

So far, I think this is an absolutely fantastic game.  It's a very fun and well designed side-scrolling platformer with basic but enjoyable combat.  The thrill of the game is not fighting zombies, but running from them, executing acrobatic skills and solving rudimentary puzzles to get from Point A to Point B to Point C as quickly and safely as possible.  Don't worry, this isn't just a free running side scroller dressed up with a zombie theme.  The zombie elements were very well implemented.  The atmosphere, dialogue and storytelling, and the purposefully limited but fine-tuned combat make you really feel like you're running for your life--and for your friends--in a post-apocalyptic zombie world.  It's a refreshing addition to the zombie themed games in that the focus is not on mowing down waves of zombies or barricading yourself up to last as long as possible, but parkouring your way through a zombie infested Seattle in order to survive an unwinnable war against the undead.  It's fast paced, but still gives you enough of a break from time to time to catch your breath and plan your next moves.  Definitely worth picking up.

I suppose now that the game is released and the hype train has ended, the question is: does it hold up? Has this game earned the title of being a fitting successor to the Hotline Miami we all know and love?
Pros:
• Very fun characters, especially the fans.
• A wider narrative.
• Not much has changed in terms of overall gameplay. Unlike some cases with sequels, this is a good thing.
• Very challenging without being brutally unfair (except in some circumstances).
Cons:
• Level design has a lot to be desired. It's not terrible for the most part, but some levels could definitely have used a lot of polish and redesigning.
• In HM1 you could use any mask on any level. You can only use certain characters on certain levels in HM2, as they each have their own stories and viewpoints.
• Less melee variety. The weapons in HM1 might have been almost the same, but it was still nice to have a wide choice of objects to smash people's heads in.
• This game was released a few days before I made this review. It is currently very buggy.
Is this game as good as Hotline Miami 2? In some cases it's better, but overall I'd say HM1 is the better game. However, that does not mean that this game is not worth playing. If you were a fan of HM1, then I recommend playing this game.

There's a sweet spot between "cynical rehash" and "absolutely nothing like the original" that a proper sequel resides in. A proper sequel doesn't have to reinvent the wheel, it just has to improve upon the previous installment and mix up the gameplay just enough to feel fresh... while also not degrading or neglecting any existing, successful features.
This is a proper sequel. The music is still great, with returning artists such as M|O|O|N and Pertubator contributing tracks alongside numerous newcomers. The trippy neon aesthetic is still here, along with the graphic, over-the-top violence. The same basic gameplay framework remains, but the missions offer much more variety. Choosing a mask tends to have greater impact on the gameplay than in HM1- one allows you to control two characters at once, while another might grant instakill punches (but prohibit using any weapons). The existing elements that made Hotline Miami an enjoyable experience are either just as good as you remember or even better this time around.
- Did you like HM1? Do you want to play more? Pick up this game.

Planet Explorers is simultaneously like Minecraft, 7 Days to Die and other crafting/adventure games, but completely different.
For one, it's in space! On a planet called Maria, which really does look beautiful and, combined with the soundtrack, I felt immersed in this strange new world as soon as I started playing. You can select from a Story Mode (where you do the story, duh), Adventure Mode (where you can...uh, adventure) and Build Mode (guess what you can do in this one).
You can speak with NPC's and do the main mission if you like, or any number of the side missions that are available. Or you can roam the countryside, looking for a defenceless animal to slaughter for their sweet, sweet meat. Oh yeah, about the meat: it is your primary trading resource. No coins, no bottle caps, no human trafficking- just the dessecated remains of your victims.
Can't afford that tool or clothing? Go kill some more animals. No conscience, no worries!
The crafting system is great. You can 'shop' with some NPC's to buy your items, or you can buy their scripts. Scripts are like the blueprints of that item, and are usually a lot cheaper than buying that item outright. So it makes sense to pay for the script, learn how to craft that item by right-clicking it and then gathering the resources needed to craft it. You can gather different plants from the world (easy to tell apart because of their vibrant colours), dig huge pits in the ground in your search for minerals and cut down trees just to give Mother Nature the middle finger with both hands.
NPC's will follow you as part of your team (because you always need help in butchering helpless herbivores), usually after completing a short mission for them. I have two followers at the moment, and there's nothing sweeter than hitting an enemy once before running away and letting your followers swarm them, giggling with child-like glee.
The developers are releasing updates that are quite regular, and packed with content. If you visit the Planet Explorers Steam page you can see the list of current features and ones that are being developed. An up-and-coming feature that really caught my eye: fishing. Fishing! In space! It seems this is the game that keeps on giving, especially if you want to rule over the food chain of Maria with an iron fist and make the mother of every creature stand at the window, teary-eyed and hoping their sons and daughters will make it home for another day.
Finally, there is the Creation Menu. You can access this in-game, and you can pretty much build whatever your dark abscess of an imagination can conjur up. This includes guns, tools, swords, vehicles, whatever. You build something according to your desires, and it will give you a list of the material needed. If you have that material, great! The game will save it as an .iso file and then you can attempt to 'export' it into your current game. Again, you require the materials, but if you want to build a nuclear-powered, animal-chewing, meat-spitting, telekinetically-controlled orbiting Death Star that rains down medpacks evey hour, on the hour, you probably can't build that.
But you can build pretty much anything else!

A Worthy Homage to L4D, and a Worthy Warhammer Game
The parallels with L4D are unmistakable, and it's a licensed game, yet it rapidly claims it's own identity with an effective combination of:
-Brutal, swift and decisive mix of melee and ranged combat
-Clever, entertaining writing of dialogue between the player characters and not-unpleasant voice acting
-Detailed levels, rich in sound and light, resplendent in the decaying glory of a high-medieval fantasy version of a Germanic empire
-Foul, skittering Skaven. They can be cowardly when few in numbers, but this game is called Vermintide for a reason. Pouring forth from the ceiling, the walls and the floors, the common rat-kin foe is voracious, but it is the more specially-trained and equipped troops amongst the rabble that can prove the most deadly.
In the Grimdark Fantasy, There is Only War
Based upon my limited experiences with this game and the nascent community, I would strongly recommend this title to my friends, and to anyone who liked L4D and/or decent Warhammer games I would recommend at least checking it out, as there is a better-than-average chance that you too will dig this game.

I've recently gotten into atmospheric platformers, and this game fills that hunger pretty well.
If you like atmospheric platformers, the zombie theme, and dark, gritty settings, then you will like Deadlight.
The aesthetics are great - the detail in the environment is very well-done. The screenshots do not do the game justice, and if you are able to play on medium to max settings, you will be greeted by a beautiful, dark world resulting from a zombie apocalypse. The sound and music is also very good, and adds to the seemingly hopeless aura projected by the story. The cutscenes are nice, however, if you have problems with the sound playing, make sure to check out the steam guide detailing how to fix this - you don't want to miss out on the writing.
The controls are pretty straighforward, and you are reminded of the controls whenever a new mechanic is introduced (or if you appear to be stucked). The tutorial (control) popups can be a bit noisy/intrusive, as they will appear in the middle of the screen and will show both the xbox controller and keyboard controls. The learning curve is minimal to moderate - the puzzles are not very challenging, and the game seems to be more of a storytelling narrative. You can choose to fight the zombies - referred to as "shadows" - but most of the time it is more efficient to dodge them with some light parkour tricks (like jumping over vehicles or leaping across large gaps. The game provides checkpoints pretty regularly.
Overall, the gameplay and feel of the game is quite fluid - strengthening the atmospheric element as you continue to experience the story. For the achievement hunters, there are a number of "secrets" and collectibles, however, most of them are easy to find if you just explore the entirety of the levels (which usually consists of jumping across to a ledge you don't need to use). The feedback in the game is very helpful, always showing you when there is an object you can interact with.
When using melee attacks, your stamina bar will deplete - when you have low stamina, the screen will have a beating, tunnel vision effect, which I found to be a very nice touch. Headshots with the revolver are also cool to see. You can also taunt enemies to draw them toward you (so you can jump over them, or use traps like dropping a car).
Personally, one of the coolest, most rewarding things to do in this game is to progress through an area quickly, continuously leaping and wall jumping until you get to the next checkpoint. The smoothness and fluidity of the gameplay makes these speedruns look amazing. You might, however, also miss collectibles if you proceed too quickly.
If you are into the zombie theme and enjoy atmospheric puzzlers with a nice story, give this game a try.
Recommend!

I suppose now that the game is released and the hype train has ended, the question is: does it hold up? Has this game earned the title of being a fitting successor to the Hotline Miami we all know and love?
Pros:
• Very fun characters, especially the fans.
• A wider narrative.
• Not much has changed in terms of overall gameplay. Unlike some cases with sequels, this is a good thing.
• Very challenging without being brutally unfair (except in some circumstances).
Cons:
• Level design has a lot to be desired. It's not terrible for the most part, but some levels could definitely have used a lot of polish and redesigning.
• In HM1 you could use any mask on any level. You can only use certain characters on certain levels in HM2, as they each have their own stories and viewpoints.
• Less melee variety. The weapons in HM1 might have been almost the same, but it was still nice to have a wide choice of objects to smash people's heads in.
• This game was released a few days before I made this review. It is currently very buggy.
Is this game as good as Hotline Miami 2? In some cases it's better, but overall I'd say HM1 is the better game. However, that does not mean that this game is not worth playing. If you were a fan of HM1, then I recommend playing this game.

Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide is a great co-operative survival / slash'em up game for up to four players but has some room for improvement.
The game is quite similiar to other games like Left 4 Dead, but is instead set in a grimdark medieval world.
The games combat mechanics are very agile, every weapon, staff and shield feel like they connect as they should, and every weapon also feels equal to its counterpart. All the classes are distinct from each other and each class feels different from the other. The class haracters all have distinct and funny personalities which I quite enjoyed. While the gameplay is very enjoyable, there are some problems I feel could be worked on.
The loot system rewards players with a new item after completing every stage, by using a dice system. You can obtain more dice depending on how many collectibles (tomes & grimoires) you found during the level. There are 3 tomes and 1 grimoire in ever level. This is a good system that motivates you to complete a level. However, I have experienced that, since I know the location of all the 3 tomes and the one grimoire in a certain stage, I will just replay that stage over and over. There is little actual motivation to try any of the other levels once you know the optimal way to run one stage, since the loot system only gives you one item at the end of the level, and each level only has 3 tomes and one grimoire to collect anyway.
As for the technical aspects, some have reported poor performance. I am able to run the game at a constant 80+ FPS, but will experience frequent frame drops, something I believe will be fixed in the future, with the addition of new drivers, and such. The graphics are pretty, but nothing out of the ordinary, so the framerate should be a lot smoother.
In conclusion, the loot system and variety could be improved, but Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide is still a great and fun game that I definitely recommend you pick up and try if you have a couple of friends willing to play with you. It comes at 28€ which is a great value for this game.

Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number may not be for everyone but it is an amazing experience for those that choose to brave the challenge. It not only expands on everything the first game brought to the table, but adds unique gameplay features and unbridled difficulty. In comparison to the first game, the gameplay is much more varied. Instead of masks simply giving you a weapon to start with or changing your character's speed they'll completely change the way you play. From the chainsaw and gun wielding duo, Alex & Ash to using a long range sniper and close quarters knife combo this game really explores the possibilities of a top-down shooter. You'll hear some complaints about difficulty but as someone who loved the first game, it's pretty welcomed. The original Hotline Miami was one of my go-to favourite games. I'd just sit down and kill some mobsters for 15 or 20 minutes, Over the course of a few years I put quite a bit of time into the original Hotline Miami and it became pretty easy. Wrong Number realized this and knew that there had to be a steeper difficulty curve. It starts to bar on the difficulty of old NES and SNES games which may seem unfair to some people but was more of reminiscent or nostalgic feeling for me. The game never feels impossible but rather incredibly challenging.
The music is just as good (if not better than the first game) and alone is worth the purchase. You'll find the soundtrack pumping you up to clear the next room or just chill you out while you're selecting a chapter to replay. I purchased the vinyl soundtrack and it was worth every penny.
As for the story; Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number keeps the retro 1980s (and early 1990s) vibe the first game established and drives it home with a mosaic of eighties and nineties movie tropes. In true Hotline Miami tradition they paint the whole picture through disjointed and hazy visuals in cut-scenes as well as subtle background imagery allowing for you to still come up with wild theories and discuss the story with your friends. The games art is unmistakeably beautiful and tranquil at times while being disturbing, gory & over-the-top violent the rest of time. Dennaton has said this will be their last Hotline Miami instalment and they manage to send the series off in a melancholy, dark and beautiful tone.
To sum everything up, Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number will probably not appeal to those who are faint of heart or are seeking a more relaxing experience. But will be very satisfying for those who a looking for a insanely challenging retro game. Especially to who enjoy the 80s/90s neon blood-spattered world. Hotline Miami 2 will go down as one of my absolute favourite games of all time.

To conclude, Hotline Miami 2, yes ! Definitly. Despict having a different level design, this is everything you can expect from Hotline Miami in even better !

I don't really like thumbing down games unless I think the game deserves a negative review 100%. You can probably guess which category this game belongs to. Congratulations, you've done it! Now you might as well stop considering buying this game right here, at this point. Do it. Trust me. You'll get more entertainment out of spreading peanut butter over your nipples while playing Shadow Complex with one hand and singing "I Love It" by Icona Pop. It'd be a lot more worth your time and money.
Still here? Fine. Let me elaborate on why this game is a waste of your time: it lasts around 3 or so hours, has a lackluster, flimsy and predictable story full of plot holes, is riddled with weird bugs (people with lower system specs and possibly Nvidia cards have it the worst), has cringeworthy voice acting, sometimes completely unintuitive (as in, "Why is THIS even over THERE?") level design and in the end makes absolutely no sense whatsoever, but boy, does it try. It tries so hard, but then just kinda tumbles over and faceplants into the ground. And stays there. Forever.
It's like a terrible Hollywood SF/action flick with zombies. Overdramatic, cliche and simply badly written.
, the atmosphere is hauntingly beautiful and the concept art is gorgeous, and that's about it. By the looks of it, a lot of cool stuff was cut out of the game, I'm not sure for what reason (I doubt it was budget constraints), and so this is what we all get in the end. I could spend a lot of time praising the art direction (Have I mentioned that it's great? I know I did, but it's GREAT), but the art direction alone couldn't save this game from being an almost out-and-out flop. Which is a real shame. It could have been something SO much better.
If you're a hardcore zombie apocalypse fan, sure, give it a whirl, but for the love of god, don't buy this at its full price. Or just stick to peanut butter till something better gets released. Damn, now I'm hungry.

I hear how some people complain that it is pay to win, which I can understand that to an extent. But on the contrary it would cost you a lot of money, and I'm talking hundreds of $$$ (not an exageration) to simply pay-grind your ribbons, then pay to unlock them, then pay to equip modifications, then pay for everything else.
On top of this everything, and I mean everything is behind a level or ribbon level grind. Vehicles, Guns, Equipment, even camo choices.
Now gameplay is great, but you need to focus on teamplay and not confuse this with Call of Duty where you can solo your way to success. This game is heavily focused on the ability of a team to work together to complete objectives and it is obvious in their use of Squads and Squad leaders who can issue commands.
I know I have not mentioned much, but I am getting ready to play it again and I'll probably edit this review. But overall it's a great game that is Free to play, has a War feature played out over a large campaign map, has great graphics for a free to play game, and is not abandoned by it's developers which seems to be a trend with games on Steam. If you want someone to help show you the ropes or just to play with MrLeMaster is my in-game name.

Far Cry 3 is the pinnacle of the Far Cry series, still unsurpassed by later offerings. It is the perfection of the Far Cry formula, which is basically a run’n'gun romp through various exotic locales. Attack outposts. Unlock cool guns. Gain new abilities. Abuse the silenced sniper rifles. Launch grenades at enemy vehicles.
Compared to its predecessor, Far Cry 2, FC3 is in a whole different ballpark of gameplay. It is an improvement over FC2 in every way, with the one possible exception being that it is much easier. Compared to its offspring, Far Cry 4, FC3 still reigns supreme, although the gameplay mechanics in FC4 are marginally better. FC3 triumphs over FC4 largely due to the fact that it has some semblance of a story, whereas FC4 has no such thing. Furthermore, the tropical island theme is a mainstay of the series, and fits the overarching Far Cry theme better than the Himalayas.
A near perfect FPS experience, with a few quibbles here and there. Inventory management is a chore. The AI can be gamed pretty easily, especially on anything other than Master difficulty. If you level a few key skills early on, you can become game-breakingly powerful. Still, Far Cry 3 is a landmark experience, and one that you owe yourself if you enjoy shooters.
My biggest complaint about Far Cry 3 is in relation to the terrible endings, of which one is merely awful and the other is exceptionally subpar. Without delving any spoilers, the story of FC3 is good to great right up until the final mission, then immediately tanks with either of the aforementioned endings. To add insult to injury, if you Google "WTF Far Cry 3 ending" or something to that effect after feeling left empty as the credits roll, you'll come to discover the head writer is a pompous, pretentious toff who claims Far Cry 3's endings are an "exploration of the nature of misogyny" amongst other colorful sociological explanations. One surmises that the blindingly overt glomming on of social justice to an otherwise enjoyable video game is the writer’s less than brilliant attempt to cover up the fact that he wrote two pretty **** endings. I highly recommend not Googling anything about FC3’s endings, even after experiencing them, as you will find maddening idiocy at every turn, from Ubisoft’s never-ending embrace of all things PC to the lead writer spewing forth some seriously disturbed bile about the people who enjoyed (mostly) his work.
Nevertheless, Far Cry 3 is a great experience, right up until the bitter end. There are complaints to be made, but it is still the flagship of the series, and I highly recommend it. Crappy endings and Uplay aside, there are few FPS games that reach this level of refinement, beauty, and fun.

Updated Review:
After the devs started undertaking an overhall of the game, I tabled it for a while.  I had already completed the story, had my save wiped, and completed it again, so I didn't feel I was missing much.  18 months later, with a0.9 out, i picked it up again... and it's boring.  NOTHING CHANGED!  The view is exactly the same and the graphics don't feel any different.  I looked up a screen shot of my last save, and they look nearly identical, with a few slight differences.  Before the view distances were synced properly, but now the grass can go on forever with no terrain beneath it, making it look like the grass can fly.  There's a weird haze over anything further than ten feet, and the close plants don't appear as vibrant either.  Loading times are longer, and lag spikes are more frequent, but watching my computer performance, not linked to high hardware demands.  So I take it back, it doesn't look the same as before 0.9, it actually looks a bit worse.
Sounds now detract from immersion.  Ambient noises like the ocean waves cannot be turned down without turning down sound effects as well.  Voices are hard to hear, and the text font sometimes goes blurry.  The music used to be nice, but after hearing the same thing for hours, it gets monotonous.  The tracks are short and there's little diversity if you're staying in the same area for a long while.
Weapons are put away in the middle of combat because you changed your view angle.  Bows are so weak you might as well be throwing rocks, but you get guns and laser pistols soon enough.  Those also suck until you spend the time upgrading, which I highly recommend.  The turrets are more fond of shooting your own base than any enemy, and there's no quick way to refill them.  Axes won't start hacking at trees unless you have them drawn, not just equiped but drawn.
The interactions to harvest plants are choppy and irritating.  Monsters will despawn while you're still trying to empty their inventory.  Trees magically regain all of their durability if you stop hacking at them for more than a second.
The creator tool is still awesome, but at the same time aggravating.  You can create many amazing things, like if you want to spend hours making a sword or carving out a shield, or possibly days on something bigger.  You can change your view angle, and camera locationg, but working intricate designs is extremely difficult.  Even curves are a pain, so most initial designs come out looking like boxes.  I'm not really into moschism, so I just use the scripts or workshop.
I did build my own helicopter though, and let me tell you that's a challenge.  The softest landings damage it, despite tires and iron struts.  That's fine, helicopters are delicate.  So delicate that if you ram into an invisible tree, your creation is dead.  There are also invisible walls marking the edge of the story zone.  No semi-transparent warning, nope, just flaming death.
The camps have been changed since I last played though.  Before, the martian camp was decorated with everything they could want or need, which is in line with the story, and I happily stole it all.  Yeah, suck it martians.  I guess the devs didn't like that tactic because now the martians have the same camp, but with skeleton buildings.  No doors, no stairs, no pretty plants, nothing.  And the buildings themselves didn't change to accomodate, they just stripped them bare.
The pathing has been improved slightly (very slightly).  Now my followers don't get stuck in a cave, but they do still walk off plateaus, get trapped in rivers ten feet from the beach, get stuck inside buildings, or inside trees, or rarely stuck in an empty field with nothing around.  If you have them assigned to a work station they'll sometimes teleport though, so yay I guess.
Okay, so I ragged on it a bit, but that's mostly due to the devs spending a year getting 0.9 out, and the transition being less than stellar.
The price has gone up a bit since I first bought it, but for those that have never played it before, I still recommend the purchase (currently $25).
Yes, it's incomplete and the movements aren't fluid, and mining is slow and painful, but your first dive in will be to an incredible new world with a story that actually makes you curious about why the martians and earthlings hate eachother.  I don't think I ever really found out besides there was a war or something, but I hope there's more (otherwise the backstory sucks and needs some filling out).

Great game, especially for being in alpha. No major bugs that I found, but at the same time not everything is working yet, which is to be expected. The scanner is the only real pain right now as minerals don't always show up. Combat is as expected, though a first person view would be great for those tighter areas. The story is engaging as I'm trying to solve the internal human problems as well as slowly imagining a history for the alien species. The graphics are amazing, even on low settings, and while there are very different regions, they transition smoothly.

At a glance, Planet Explorers feels a lot like another MMO.  This is especially true if you play Adventure mode.  Not being all that into MMOs myself, I was at first a little wary.  Soon enough, however, the lovely scenery, interesting aliens, and a crafting system that has a variety of levels of depth, and I was already humming along and happily harvesting plants.
The crafting system is excellent.  There is a basic level, where you learn "scrips" and then build objects out of stuff that is in our inventory.  Then there is a deep level, where you can build any 3D object you want and it becomes available in the game.
I also really enjoyed the aliens.  Especially at first, you never know what an alien is going to do till it sees you.  Then you learn really quick.  The scale of aliens is also great.  There are beings tiny like us meek humans, and towering giants that either ignore you, or quickly put you out of your alleged mysery.
This game can only go up as it gets more and more polished.  I'm happy to be in somewhere near the ground floor!

Basically, the basic smgs of the germany and usa are getting slaughtered by the ppd's with 71 round mags and so on. I could list way more of problems but this one i'll use to picture the problem i have in mind. We play a game that's having ol' battlefield mechanics, it's not aiming to be realistic. So the balance should be the main concern of the game developers. It is not, obviously. You're not equal in the engagment. You should expect being in a disadvantage because your weapon is going to be most likely ♥♥♥♥♥♥. And that's how it is in more that half of situations. Mount and Blade Warband is a true classic of a game.It is an RPG game where you choose what your character looks like, their name, and their background. Once you do that, you choose from six nations in the fanciful land of Calradia to spawn at. You are but a poor peasant at the start, but you will eventually become rich by completing side-quests given to you by NPCs and by defeating enemies and taking their crap. You will hire fresh recruits from villages, which can be upgraded into more powerful units as they get more experience, You can hire hero characters and already-powerful mercenaries from taverns in major cities. You can conquer or pillage other towns, and can actually fight battle alongside your troops.
Once you have your own little army, the possibilities are endless. Will you become the servant of powerful lords and kings? Will you join the manhunters and fight the many groups of bandits in Calradia? Will you become a murderer and a thief? Will you pledge alleigance to one of the six nations in Calradia, and become a lord of villages, castles and cities in times of peace, and be a general in times of war? Or will you forge your own destiny, and became the all-powerful ruler of your very own nation?????

Choose wisely.

Survivors vs Zombies gameplay is fun but gets old quick if stuck on the same map with no cycling. It is a $$ knockoff of the FREE Zombie Panic! Source mod on Steam:
I would only recommend this game if it were free or had significant overhaul/expansion of features to explain the price increase from a free mod. Some constructive criticism for the devs based on my gameplay experience follows:
-Zombies get tired? No ranged attack? WTFrack?? Get rid of the stamina guage for the Zombie run or use it instead for a spit attack (minor damage+chance to infect+momentary blurred vision?). The undead don't tire, but it does take time to cough up more corruption+parasites from their dead lungs. Make it an unlock if you think Zombies with ranged weapon is unbalanced - refillable only by devouring Surviors perhaps (minor health gain)?
-Insanely difficult to track down survivors on the larger maps as a zombie, especially if you are new to a map and don't know the layout. The pathing/tracking blood sight system needs to be improved badly.
-Royal Pain to sneak up on anyone as a zombie, especially with the constant moaning an groaning. Maybe limit the noise zombies make to only when they are attacking and/or running quickly. It should be much easier to get one good stealth bite in and would definitely increase the suspense factor.
-Remove the Nail Gun + Boards or make them easier to use. Easier currently to just defend an area yourself than board it up, as it is very non-intuitive.
-Survivors should be able to scale fences just like Zombies, faster even but using their stamina meter, same as jumping or running. Very annoying when the undead are climbing over fences and cars but you cannot. Other option is to take away Zombie ability to scale anything and instead allow them to knock fences down especially when zombie buddies helping, similar to the destructible doors.
-The physics engine felt blocky with most of the movement - maybe smooth it out? I don't know if collision can be tweaked, but I found myself frequently getting snagged on corner of cars, buildings, dumpsters, etc. Definitely breaks the mood when you are running someone down or trying to run from a horde.
-No anti-camping mechanism. All roofs should have multiple access points but do not currently. Zombie spit attack (see above) would also help with this. The other option would be to make all survivors spawn in an infected state with life steadily decreasing. When it hits zero, they die and turn. Obviously you would have to have more med kits and/or food/drink items laying about to counteract this. It would add a definite sense of urgency to scavenging items besides ammo.
-Headshotting zombies is a guaranteed one-shot kill. The only difficulty with this is the zombies which have broken necks or otherwise move their head down or to the side when shambling about - also the riot gear zombies. Grappling+biting survivors should be a guaranteed infection to balance things out. Didn't seem to be the case.
-Nothing sucks worse than running from a horde shrieking like a lil girl because you have no weapon with which to defend yourself. Sometimea your teammate is hogging all the drops or just got to them first because you're new to the map. More variety and availability of improvised weapons would take care of this problem - ie screwdrivers, broom handle, ice pick, meat cleaver, molotovs, hairspray+lighter, etc. There should be an improvised weapon in almost every room if you looked closely enough. This doesn't mean they cannot be depleted, snap off in or get lodged in a zombie carcass, forcing you to obtain another. This increases the need to scavenge.
-Plenty of weapons in game, but I'd like to see more, so long as they are not too similar to existing weapons - ie flamethrowers, katanas, crossbows, etc. Permanent weapon mods/unlocks such as extended mags, flash supressors, vertical foregrips, silencers, laser sights, extra magnifcation scopes, etc would be awesome but should be rare finds or purchased DLC unlocks. Also more ammo types per weapon - ie hollow points or shotgun slugs to blow thru the SWAT zombies.
-Varying reach and delay for different melee weapons. It felt as if all melee attacks were pretty much the same and equally susceptible to getting your arm chewed off. Only thing that seemed to help was higher ground and timing. Close quarters should be knives and Grapple+Bite only (quickest). Everything else requres room+time to swing and thus 1-2 meters more reach. Also additional effects such as block, knockback, dazed or impaired runspeed dependant on what was struck by which weapon. Zombies don't feel pain but they lose limbs fairly easily. Its all that corruptive rot setting in.
I did enjoy the few flaming zombies I saw, but did not get to see how long they could last running about like that - they caught a round to the head far too quickly. Saved my assault rifle ammo for when I ran into SWAT zombies or all my other ammo ran dry. Also got infected twice and the blurred vision was a good indication I was turning. IMHO it should be more nauseating and/or disgusting to watch them turn, within the existing ESRB rating ofc.  Chance to infect seemed random but may have been based on how many times I was gnawed on.

For those who haven't played the first game in the series, Hotline Miami was a splendid retro-looking birdseye shooter which was merciless towards player mistakes with a storyline which would make you question your own intelligence as it was so mindbogglingly  brilliant. It wasn't however with its flaws. At launch, it had extremely limited resolution options and the amount of flashing in the background upon killing an enemy made my eyes want to commit suicide, a problem it seems only I actually cared about.
The second removes all the issues the first had,  follows pursuit by taking what was good in the first game and yet somehow improves it in almost every aspect. There are far more story scenes, characters, bosses and most suprisingly- levels. I expected to complete this game far earlier than I actually did as the amount of content provided was most suprising, especially if compared to the first.
In regards to the story, without trying to sound like a preacher, it's very rare a game can truly speak to you, especially one as simple as this, yet Hotline Miami 2 made me somewhat remindful of my own mortality during some of its scenes and evokes emotion often underexplored. Though I cannot say the same will occur to you, perhaps it will at least leave you with a few questions and thoughts as it did myself. However- it does leave a lot to be answered too and the plotline has many loose ends which is extremely confusing as a spectator and because of this I found the ending quite disappointing.
With that being said, It's amusing how the combonation of disco music and 2D gore is suprisingly glorious. This game features by far some of the best beats I've ever heard from a game, whilst delivering some clutch combat with some stealth elements- both traits shared by its predecessesor.  I've heard lots of people complain about being shot by "invisible" men outside of their characters point of view and suddenly dying, crying that it is bugged. Due to the games larger and far more diverse maps, tactical planning is an upmost requirement, more so than its predecessor. If you run in first and think later, you'll be met constantly with the face of defeat. This is a game that should require many attempts to beat, if you fail to accept you make mistakes, you may as well stop reading now whilst you're ahead, as this game will make you more frustrated than entertained.
Overall, it provides 10ish hours of entertaining simple to grasp fun and provides a sense of accomplishment due to its difficulty that most games fail to provide. The amount of content received for the price more than justifies it and though the developers stated this will be the last official game in the series, hopefully the upcoming level editor will be able to breathe new life into the game upon completion.
To sum up this game quite swiftly: it's a must buy.

This game is a lot of fun...up until you make rank 3.  Regardless of which faction you chose you will eventually hit rank 3.  At this point you gain the ability to enter the War campaign or continue in random battle style matches.  What the game doesn't tell you is that once you make rank 3 you will primarily be fighting rank 5 and above players.  At first I thought no big deal, it's only a few ranks they can't be that much more powerful.  Boy was I wrong.  I went from being a dominant force on the battlefield to being an absolute sheep.  Let me put this in perspective for you folks.  At rank 3 my best soldier had a submachine gun and some basic frag grenades.  That's it.  Once I started joining matches I was fighting nothing but tanks and guys using way more advanced weapons (sniper rifles, LMGs, etc...).  I went from averaging 500xp per game to maybe breaking 100.  The character advancement curve in this game is intentionally bad.  It's so that you will become frustrated with going up against tanks which by the way you probably won't have any anti tank weapons unlocked if you're primarily a gun user like me.  This game simply does not care that you have far inferior weapons and sometimes no weapons at all to damage your opponents.  Why would they develop a free to play game this way you ask?  Simple, you can unlock literally anything in the game for real money.  The highest tier weapons, vehicles, equipment, or aircraft.  Am I saying that it is impossible to play this game as a purely free to play?  No, but be warned that unless you plan to suffer for a very, very, very long time then you better be willing to bust out your wallet.  Plenty of people will tell you that pure free to play is possible, but I'm willing to bet they shelled out some cash at some point and from what I've seen you would have to shell out enough to buy a real game for the money it would take.

It's essentially a l4D with less content and polish but with better graphics and a fresh Warhammer mordheim-esque setting.
Is it fun? Yes. Is it worth 20-30 bucks? I think so.
Will it be dead a few months from now? I think so : I but would love to be proven wrong.
Update:
This game desperately needs a reworked itemization system along with daily quests, achievements and cosmetic items (aside from just hats, which are ridiculously hard to get btw) to make me wanna keep playing it. There's just no sense of progression and even WITH exploits the progression is too slow.
Not complaining though, for 20 bucks that I invested in it I still got a solid 20-30hrs worth of gameplay which isn't too bad.
The game is top tier in many aspects but an outright dissapointment in others.
Also, whilst the levels themselves are beautiful, whilst you're basically running down corridors they're well designed to make you not feel that way. Unfortunately they're nearly all plagued with the same mediocre mechanics: carrying X bags or barrels to Y or defending/attacking X things on the map or surviving for X minutes. As such nearly every level plays the same pretty much.
Final verdict: Good bang for the buck, not gonna last long unless they are quick to improve the content.

For those who haven't played the first game in the series, Hotline Miami was a splendid retro-looking birdseye shooter which was merciless towards player mistakes with a storyline which would make you question your own intelligence as it was so mindbogglingly  brilliant. It wasn't however with its flaws. At launch, it had extremely limited resolution options and the amount of flashing in the background upon killing an enemy made my eyes want to commit suicide, a problem it seems only I actually cared about.
The second removes all the issues the first had,  follows pursuit by taking what was good in the first game and yet somehow improves it in almost every aspect. There are far more story scenes, characters, bosses and most suprisingly- levels. I expected to complete this game far earlier than I actually did as the amount of content provided was most suprising, especially if compared to the first.
In regards to the story, without trying to sound like a preacher, it's very rare a game can truly speak to you, especially one as simple as this, yet Hotline Miami 2 made me somewhat remindful of my own mortality during some of its scenes and evokes emotion often underexplored. Though I cannot say the same will occur to you, perhaps it will at least leave you with a few questions and thoughts as it did myself. However- it does leave a lot to be answered too and the plotline has many loose ends which is extremely confusing as a spectator and because of this I found the ending quite disappointing.
With that being said, It's amusing how the combonation of disco music and 2D gore is suprisingly glorious. This game features by far some of the best beats I've ever heard from a game, whilst delivering some clutch combat with some stealth elements- both traits shared by its predecessesor.  I've heard lots of people complain about being shot by "invisible" men outside of their characters point of view and suddenly dying, crying that it is bugged. Due to the games larger and far more diverse maps, tactical planning is an upmost requirement, more so than its predecessor. If you run in first and think later, you'll be met constantly with the face of defeat. This is a game that should require many attempts to beat, if you fail to accept you make mistakes, you may as well stop reading now whilst you're ahead, as this game will make you more frustrated than entertained.
Overall, it provides 10ish hours of entertaining simple to grasp fun and provides a sense of accomplishment due to its difficulty that most games fail to provide. The amount of content received for the price more than justifies it and though the developers stated this will be the last official game in the series, hopefully the upcoming level editor will be able to breathe new life into the game upon completion.
To sum up this game quite swiftly: it's a must buy.
Fantastic sequel, does everything the first game did, adds new twists and variety and has another phenomenal soundtrack by some very talented artists.
"Bloody" good fun and challenge. Not for the faint hearted or people that normaly don't play hard games.

Borderline Yes, but only if you like zombie-related stories enough to forgive well-trodden tropes, or if it's $2 tops. It's a 2.5D platformer (gameplay in 2D but with 3D graphics), but the controls are sloppy and the game's presentation favors graphics over easy recognition of what's a solid thing to platform on or interact with, and what's mechanically open space. Short story, I did my first playthrough in 4 hours, and that's with the repeated die-reloads from wrestling with controls and trying to make sense of some of the level design. Honestly, I remember hard NES 8-bit platformers that felt more fair--there I could at least see where I'm supposed to go and the controls were tight enough that I could only blame myself.
Linear gameplay, this is no Metroidvania that lets you revisit map areas, nor does it offer >1 way to advance through the levels, and much of the game relies on the player knowing how to execute some platforming or otherwise do some interactions with the right timing, order, and precision, at times so much so I wish I'd rather have gotten quicktime events since we're basically railroaded and I'd rather not have to try and figure out what exactly the designers expected out of me.
Replay's probably limited to a 2nd playthrough to get collectibles (more if you happen to miss something but trigger a hard checkpoint that keeps you from going back in an area), and a 3rd bunch of playthroughs if you choose to tackle the permadeath Nightmare mode (I'm not saying it's impossible, or even very hard, but you've got to know the game very well and have an excellent handle on the controls to complete Nightmare mode).
The placement of save checkpoints (it's all auto-save, no manual save) favors chunking along story beats *too* much, considering how gameplay in some areas will likely call for about a dozen retries, each time replaying that extra bit of story in that scene unnecessarily. I guess it wouldn't have been so bad if there were no voiceovers that get repeated over and over until you get the hang of the action challenge.
The platforming, story-through-collectibles, and graphics fight for player attention and clutter up the experience. Platforming requires good attention to figure out how to advance properly (you'll be punished with reloads if you don't do it right), but if you're also looking for collectibles, each time you pick one up there'll be a popup on the screen and a narration that plays as a distraction (some collectibles are picked up in the middle of rush rush action segments).
Overall I think the experience is a lot like putting together a bog-standard "serious" zombie survivor 3-4 hour movie (think 70s-80s zombie movie cliches but with Walking Dead seriousness), except you're the only actor and stuntman, and your director calls CUT every 4-10 minutes to reshoot an entire scene from the beginning b/c you screwed up a stunt. And some of those reshoots need 10 or more retries to get it right and move on. I'm tempted to say that the most memorable "highlights" of the game were the reloads...
Really really makes me wish Shadow Complex was on PC, now *that* was a pretty good 2.5D platformer that did Metroidvania gameplay and graphics very well. Similar graphical vibe too if you're just in it to see 2.5D at work, "realistic". No zombies in Shadow Complex, but it does have techno-shooty-spy action.

Like most early access games, Planet Explorers has a ton of potential. However I think this one stands out from the rest because of its custom builder workshop. You can build swords, shields, guns; land, air, and sea vehicles; as well as other misc items like furniture. The builder is fairly limited right now but I think they could make it VERY legit. I've already built the buster sword from Final Fantasy and a very tiny melee shurukin.
Aside from the builder the game has voice acting (not very great, but it's better than nothing right?) and an amazing soundtrack, though it is quite limited at the moment. The singleplayer is sort of bland with lots of running around ( I only played like 30 minutes so it may get better) but it helps you get the basics nailed down. I haven't tried multiplayer yet but I'm sure within a few updates it could be really fun, especially in build mode.
Speaking of modes there is currently 3 different ones. Campaign, adventure, and free build. Campaign is pretty straight forward. Adventure is basically free roam/do whatever and free build is the sandbox part of the game where you have unlimited supplies and can do pretty well whatever you like.
All in all if you like building vehicles, weapons, and other things, then you will probably enjoy this game longer than most early access ones because of the time it takes to build when you get started. The game is fun to fool around in once you get some things built, and you can even go onto the forums and use other peoples stuff. Also I can see myself coming back to this game after every semi-substantial update to see what new goodies they brought in for each mode.
For now, I'll stick with building weapons because it's something I've always enjoyed and this game offers that freedom (somewhat :P).

I didn't read any info about the game before I started it, so I didn't really know what to expect.
I started the game, and went into solo-adventurer mode, here I found myself in a camp with some other people (shopkeepers it seemed, some had quests). I bought a shovel, ran out of the camp, and dug a small cave, neat! Then I equipped my dagger (I think it was) and attacked a creature that handed me my genitals on a silver platter. Then I started using some of the materials I dug up when making the cave to make a small hut (creatures are obviously not to be trifled with). About 5min into this I ran out of stamina, and I had no idea how to get it back.
In story mode I found that there were some questlines to follow, they explained some of the basics, so I no longer want for stamina (or hp).
The story mode led me from hub to hub, but I'm still only scratching the surface of this because I was distracted by a looming mountain; "I wonder if I can dig a tunnel through that mountain" *2 hours later* "yeah!". There is a progression in what schematics you have available, which follows the questline. For example, the first schematics for weapons available are wooden ones, then stone, then iron.
The quests I did so far were mainly gather x/kill y/escort z ones, which for me would normally be a big "thumbs down", but in this game the backdrop steals the show, and the quests are (imo) mainly there to give you a purpose for why you venture out. I got a quest to gather 20 copper and 5 tin (I think it was) for some guy, and I ended up making a huge underground cave (mining 1000's of copper and tin in the process). I could have finished this quest in 5 minutes, and it would have been a boring gather quest, but because of how the backdrop is made I lost myself in it, and spent literally hours making my very own cave.
Most early access games hold great potential, but Planet explorers, I feel, already has the fundamental basics covered, and this is why I recommend it. It's evident that the people making this know what they are doing, and with the content I've seen so far I don't doubt that they can flesh out the rest.
It lacks polish (detailed below), but it has a solid engine. In my first 10 hours of gameplay I haven't had any crashes, and I did stuff like tunnelling through a mountain for fun (this was ~2 hours worth of drilling straight into rock), and then made a big cave where there was a copper deposit.
For anyone who can enjoy the simple pleasure it is to shape the world with your mining pick and shovel, there is already a lot of hours worth of gameplay in this game.
I wouldn't recommend it yet to someone who is only/mainly in it for the combat, although this does show promise, it's definitely not balanced - you can build 10 (portable) sentries and wipe out pretty much anything by placing them quickly on the ground near the creature while it's aggressive towards you. It will however cost a lot of bullets having 10 sentry turrets firing away at the same time.
- not all game modes are quite ready, I recommend you start in story mode, this seems to be the most polished
- some of the models lack the detail some other models have (people are very low-poly, but some of the creatures are gorgeous)
- there is a help/tutorial system, but it's not very detailed, especially for some of the complex things you can do, like making your own craftable ISOs (blueprints)
- a basic tutorial for how to "live" is needed (how to regain hp/stamina), there is a quest that explains some of it in story mode, but if you start out in adventurer mode you will be out of luck when you run out of stamina and don't know what to do (sleeping in a bed currently doesn't give stamina, I think it's intended to though)
- a few features are not enabled yet
- melee combat feels clunky
The help/tutorial system will likely be lackluster till much later in the developement. It doesn't make much sense to create elaborate explanations of how to do stuff when it is likely to be changed.

Loose controls, mediocre graphics, and terrible animations galore... but Planet Explorers easily manages to do what it says on the tin: set you loose on an alien planet and leave you to your devices. For all its alpha-stage clunkiness, the game regularly pulls off moments of sheer wonder (the art design does triumph over the so-so graphics) and somehow manages to throw survivalist challenges at the player while still maintaining a serene, natural atmosphere that tugs at your curiosity. With so many more features still to come and the game already as stable as most finished titles, you will want to keep an eye on this one.

I said Hotline Miami was a piece of art .
And holy♥♥♥♥♥♥, Hotline Miami 2 was a blast as well .
Let's start with the most essential point :
Basically the same mechanics as the first episode , mostly .
The difference comes from the variety of characters you have . Among them : A soldier who chooses a main weapon between five ; the fans , who each have a unique skill (which are all useful as long as you're not awful in this game . Yeah , sorry , fan haters) ...
One interesting addition is the writer , with his non-lethal style , where you only have to knock off the ennemies , either with bare hands or with melee swing . Picking up ennemy guns will make the character empty the weapon , leaving it unusable so no ennemy can pick it up .
As before , you have the choice between melee and weapons , BUT some ennemies will require you to switch of style . Remember those fat guys only vulnerable to bullets ? Now there is -in extremely rare occasions though- ennemies who only dies from melee attacks , somehow dodging bullets . The lovely dogs are still here too . The devs knew you wanted them . One issue with the melee system , however , is the executions . They take quite much more time than in the previous game , and supposing you don't finish an ennemy the moment after you killed another , your combo will be broken , so you better be sure all your swings are lethal and that you don't abuse doors too much .
But going fully melee isn't recommended anyway , giving the enormous floors . You WILL have to use guns sometime .  Remember the Assault level in the first game ? Well there are several levels this big in HM2 . Full of windows that allows the ennemies to see you and shoot you dead before you can say FU** .
Which brings another point : The difficulty .
So far , I've only cleared the game on Normal difficulty .
This game is pure Trial & Error . You're going to need skill , level knowledge and both patience and nerves to get through the game . Because holy♥♥♥♥♥♥,
But that's part of the game . The feeling of satisfaction after completing a level is that great .
So , maybe there are different mechanics , but that's part of the work ! When you want a sequel , you want something different , not just a refresh , right ? It's not that the level design is poor . It's purposely made to make you try again and again , until you can clear the perfect run .
Especially if you go for the A+/S rank in each level .
I don't know where to begin . It's both satisfying and disapointing . Just by the way it ended .
It's not a focus about one character we have , but around many , quite like the everyday life of an apocalyptic Miami threatened by the conflict between 50 blessings and the Russian mafia , after the traumatism caused by Jacket's actions , that more or less started it all . The storyline happens to be way more tragic than the first episode (Just look at the contrast between HM1 and HM2's menu theme) and
.
There is a lot of new characters and story arcs , which or all more or less connected , and all related to Jacket in some way . The latter is not playable , but you're going to hear about him .
The backstory is complete , mostly with little elements this and there (the dates and the journals) that might confuse the player who didn't look for them before the ending .
Last point for the scenario part :
Holy mother of Jesus . I didn't know till there that ears could have an erection . It's no less than 49 tracks in there , for the pure pleasure of your ears , and each level plays a different one , unlike the first Hotline Miami . 30 artists joined this massive ear candy made of electro , with some veterans of the first such as M|O|O|N , Jasper Byrne , Perturbator and El Huervo . You'd guess , as I'm writing all of this , I'm still listening to the OST . I don't really have words for it , they wouldn't be able to represent the greatness of those sounds .
EDIT: It's been two years since I wrote this review and I still regularly listen to the soundtrack while driving. That's how good it is.
I do believe the main points have all been exposed . There are a few cons to the game though - even though minor ones. Some bugs involving doors , where some ennemies will happen to get stuck and have ... what seems to be a seizure , I don't know . There has been report of dogs going through walls , but it didn't happened to me .
The IA is still like before , with some ennemies stopping to chase you after a certain point
.
Overall , Hotline Miami 2 is an over-the-top game , and strongly recommended for those who loved Hotline Miami 1 . Why not to newbies ? Because they should first play Hotline Miami 1 , so they can understand the context , and be trained for what is going to be a hard , hard trip .
Yes , there were some changes , without completely metamorphozing the game mechanics , but that's what make it a whole new episode rather than an extension . There were answers , there was a completion and explanation to HM1's events , there was a solid gameplay , an insane difficulty and a lot of pixelated blood : All the elements that makes a Hotline Miami .

This game is perfect proof that atmosphere isn't everything. While the suspenseful setting and uniquely dramatic score make for an interesting ride, sloppy parkour mechanics and an uninspired gameplay core will leave you bored within a couple hours. Amusing at first, the platforming and traps quickly become severe annoyances. While these parkour aspects are a decent take on an already sound system, it is not uncommon to find yourself dying repeatedly at the same point from missing a jump by mere pixels, solely because your leap was off by an attosecond or two. On top of that, the "puzzle" aspect of the game is really nothing more than a speed bump to prevent you from shooting through the remarkably short game in under an hour. For each of these traps, you are virtually guaranteed to die the first attempt, and again nearly guaranteed to beat it on the second attempt. This is due to the puzzles not being puzzling in any sense, but more 'unforeseeable deathtraps' that are completely ineffective once you know of their location and MO.
TLDR: If you can stand constantly revisiting the 3 minute gameover loading screen, and are not easily discouraged by excessive and unimaginative 'puzzles' that can be solved only by repetition (rather than wit and skill), then the atmosphere and  combat of this game will be an enjoyable experience.

The game had some good qualities.  The atmosphere was decent, the graphics were nice, and the level design was pretty creative.  The bad aspects however, outshine the good stuff heavily.  The controls on the keyboard are terrible (have fun pressing Lshift and Lctrl at the same time), slow to respond (Quick-Draw McGraw Randall is not), and lack some basic functions like executing a zombie while it's on the ground.  Speaking of the zombies, they're frustratingly resilient if you're using your axe and trying to conserve ammo, you'll spend minutes swinging away only to knock them over, and given the inability to execute, waiting for them to get back up.  Stack on top of that a plot riddled with holes, dumb, and cliche, and you have yourself an unenjoyable and noticably short experience.  The worst part for me though, was the combination of the 2-D with the background.  2-D games are just fine, but you have to be careful about the backdrops otherwise you end up damaging the suspension of disbelief.  For example, you shouldn't find yourself trapped by a closed door when the one immediately next to it is open.  Nor should you be forced to slide down slopes equipped with spikes and traps when there are perfectly good stairs next to them.  Nor should certain transients run off into the background, presumably taking the safe route, leaving you unable to follow and doomed to dance your way through a gauntlet of aggravating death.  All in all I get it a 4/10

When I first saw the trailer and images on the store page for "Planet Explorers" I thought to myself wow this game has lots of potential, and it looks like lots of fun to play, but to my dismay this is what I got:

In short term let me make Pros & Cons,--
Pros
-----
Good Concept & Idea
Fun Digging
You can climb any mountain by hugging the wall
Creation Mode
Cons
-------
Friendly Npc's are completey useless & redundent
Villages feel extremely dull and dead
Enemy Npcs are too strong (Even at starting level, some enemies can even 1 shot you)
Obtaining easy weapons/gear is quite frustrating

Multiplayer Digging/Mining Glitches (Cant see other player tunnel)

Melee Combat aiming is awful
Lighting Glitches while in Mines/Digged holes
The time it takes to get places on foot
General Glitches (Falling through world/underground)

Multiplayer Search System is terrible
etc........
Overall this game is definatly not worth its Early Access price of $20, I bought it for $15 on sale, and its not even worth that. I would say at its current stage the game is worth no more than $5, because they still have alot to prove and bring to the table.

Very entertaining. Whistling at comprades to signal the approach of an enemy tank, or to point out the location of an enemy sniper is sure to put a smile on anyones face. Circling around an enemy encampment via pedal bike while you and your passenger frantically duck for cover - guaranteed to form new, awesome memories with your friends. Bullet drop calculation, crosshair-leading and strategy win more battles here than outright run-n-gun tactics - and when your team finally captures that base - the feeling of pride and accomplishment is sure to strike hard.
However, it is extremely difficult to get into this game. Without prior knowledge of Web-based interfaces in the MMO genre (navigating the menu, store, ranks, weapons mods and misc options), you will surely find yourself needing to refer to the H&G FAQ - which I have found to be not very helpful. The main menu screen is extremely non-user friendly, and it took me half an hour to find the button for modifying weapons after referring to the FAQ and being disappointed in finding no answer as to its location. There is no readily available explanation of your soldier's Rank or experience, so you will spend much of your time *assuming* you simply dont have enough experience or rank to buy that weapon modification because it still appears as "Locked".
Furthermore, it is difficult to discover how to unlock weapons, soldiers, and classes - period. There are plenty of Tables and graphs online to google, but there are no descriptions of how you can actually obtain the various in-game rewards. And much of the in-game rewards are ONLY PURCHASABLE WITH REAL CASH.
All in all:
- Fun game, guaranteed fun factor of at least an 8/10. Coupled with some friends who utilize strategy, you will feel awesome when you manage to annihilate an incoming convoy of enemy players, capture bases and finally win the match.
- Interface is not user friendly at all, and much of the games mechanics/rewards are hidden( though seemingly in plain sight), with little to no help in guiding you in the right direction towards certain aspects of the game.
- Very little incentive to play - after going on several 15-0 kill streaks, various ribbons and rewards, an 18-0 kill streak with MVP status for the match via capturing bases - I still have yet to unlock anything *AT ALL* and have yet to reach tier 2, which is where the massive battles take place. I have loads of "Credits" saved from my battles, and have NOTHING to spend it on.
I recommend holding off on playing this until they've made the game smoother and more easily accessible.

When I first saw the trailer for Deadlight, I was stoked. I have a weakness for post-apocalyptic settings, grungy feelings, and character-driven stories (basically the Last of Us). I love platformers, and I couldn't wait to give this a try.
I am both disappointed and impressed with what this game has to offer.
Firstly, the visuals are stunning. This game presents the post-apocalyptic setting in a realistic and gloomy way. The zombies, while limited in their animations, are superb. Little details like grafitti and a wind-blown newspaper don't go unnoticed.
The gameplay is in the middle-ground between good and bad, in my opinion. Like I said, I love platformers and side scrollers. Growing up, those games were all I was able to get my hands on. I feel like the execution of the game's controls and playability is a little off. Don't get me wrong - as a whole, I love it. I really do. But there are random things that throw me for a loop every once and a while. For instance, I didn't know I couldn't stand on this platform without it breaking and falling to my doom. There were no visual hints or anything to lead me to reconsider jumping there. Many occurences like this create a trial-and-error feel to the game.
I simply don't like the voice acting in this. Some of the lines -- writers, really? "That is the helicopter that is chasing my friends. I have to find my friends."
Listen. We've watched the video -- we know they're our friends. We aren't stupid. We know of the objective. Give the player some creative thinking space instead of having everything filled in by a chessily-voiced steriotypical male radio-announcer character.
Overall: I'm enjoying Deadlight -- I'm a little over halfway through. I would recommend it. However, it doesn't play without its flaws. If you can get over them, go for it. Definitely worth the $3, and if you're a big fan of the genera, it'll be worth the $15, too.
