Vermintide gives you something to progress with: Loot, EXP, customization --> addiction.
The gameplay is impressively fluid and responsive, the hitboxes are from time to time a bit off, but mostly feel just right and reward every hit/shot with a proper, gory and satisfying animation.
The sheer amount of potential for this title is amazing, even though i highly doubt, that most of my desires won't ever come true. Some exaples, which i persoanlly think would benefit the game greatly:
- An experience based Skillsystem for each of the Heroes

- Bossmonsters (Not talking about the specials) - Maybe for the end of each chapter
- Perhaps bossfight mechanics which require more than just hitting the thing untill it dies
Bottom Line: Out of all games which roam this genre, i've gotto admit:
Vermitide does it the best way.

When the game was first released to everyone it was actually pretty good, a semi good balance of gameplay mechanics made the game tolerable from the bugs present and you actually got a lot from playing and earning weapons, attachments and extra characters with additional roles like Recon, Tank Crew etc. However with the new update, Timonshenko, you can throw all of that out of the window.
Timonshenko is one of those classic updates that free-2-play games do that totally destroy the original fan base, utterly exclude anyone that doesn't have/want to spend money on the game and majorly unbalances the game that is practically unfixable for them. You're probably wondering how and why it is unfixable? Well, because of the new update, Timonshenko, which introduces one of the main military forces during WW2, the Russians, it has made them horrendously over-powered by making them machine gun orientated and very powerful weapons introduced exclusive to the Russians. The PTRD 1941 is one of those weapons that a game probably shouldn't introduce for a good many reasons. Since the update and the lack of people wanting to switch over to the Russians to start the new chracters previous to their already grinded, bought out ones the developers added a deal to entice people into joining the Russians, a 50% off gold deal on new academy trained characters within the Russian faction. Now this gives people who bought them a massive advantage over the rest and able to purchase the dreaded over-powered weapons currently plaguing the game, this is where the the PTRD 1941 comes into play, players are not using them for what it is meant for, tank destruction, instead using it for anti-personnel which it excels at. One shotting anyone at any range means it is a weapon to be feared. The only down side(s) to the weapon are the default iron sights so sniping is actually quite difficult, but not impossible and the slightly long reload time as you only have one shot that has to be chambered manually. No magazine. It can also one-shot jeeps which I have done many times with a full complement of troops on board of which I got the weapon from a player I killed.
The first new grenades you get with the Russian faction is also again (surprise, surprise) very overpowered as the ridiculous blast radius and damage output puts other grenades to shame, chuck one in the room and you're garunteed to exterminate anyone in said room while other starter grenades would most likely only heavily injure players.
All in all the Russian faction seems to be the death of Heroes & Generals respective to the fact Reto-Moto has became greedy for the pay-2-win scene, while the game has always had pay-2-win aspects it has never been 'too' (and I say that lightly) intrusive to the over-all playability. Also while the starting SMG, the PPD-40 starts the over-powered parade of which the Russians blitzkreig all capture points you can bet when ever facing the Russians the only way you can possibly win is by having a Veteran team with highly upgraded weapons and vehicles other than that, prepare to die many times and have a quick defeat.
Fixing the game after all that has been done due to the Timonshenko update will be for nought as they are already starting to lose some of its veteran community base and only growing due to players wanting an easy and unchallenged start that the Russian faction provides changing the balance of the Russians would only alienate the people that spent money for that specific reason and would more than likely lose those supporters too, I do however think they would not care as they already have your money now and as a fellow veteran that has bought the veteran membership, to support the game with minimal benefits (never bought any weapons attachments etc with Gold, only earnt them) I am too very disappointed with Reto-Moto with the decision on taking the game in a new, unfavourable path.
While before I would have recommended Heroes & Generals to anyone that likes WW2 style FPS shooters and a strong strategy aspect that requires good players acting as Generals to supply assault teams to different battlefields that can change the tide of the war for their faction I can not however do this now because Reto-Moto has turned into one of those dreaded developers that sacrifice a well respected community of people, supporting the game from the start, for people that has an excess amount of money and an unspoiling credit card.

Hotline Miami 2 attempts to make a strong sequel to Hotline Miami 1, and fails at almost every aspect. This game shows that the developers didn't really understand what made the original game so appealing.
The main thing that made the first game so appealing, in my opinion anyway, wasn't so much the story, setting or visuals, as much as it was the "flow", that abstract gameplay concept in which you move around the level, from room to room, dispatching enemies using whatever means you could find. Be it doors, guns, punches, melee weapons or throws, the gameplay, done right, was about improvization and quick reactions. Executed right, it was IMMENSELY satisfying.
This concept is hard to achieve, and was maintained through smart map design. The map was small, or at the very least, at any given point, you could easily see to the end of a room, as it was within your field of vision. Windows were scarce, as were corridors. This allowed you to find many choke points, and limited the ways in which enemies could kill you from outside your field of vision, thus resulting in the player's ability to move (relatively) freely, and rack up combos along the way, because you were always able to see where the enemies were. The bottom line to take from this is that "flow" comes from player agency. The maps were created in such a clever way that they allowed for creativity and various playstyles. Improvization and quick reflexes were enabled by clever maps. It was simple and elegant. The bad players could, of course, choose the cowardly route, hiding and baiting, but the better you got at the game, the more you could improvise, the cooler you became.
This game screws the pooch completely, and throws the flow out the window by increasing the difficulty in the most unsatisfactory way possible. The game is now about giant maps, with many, many windows and open areas. The enemies have a FoV which is about as far as your shift - view, meaning that they can see you, but you can't see them without having to hold down shift, something which severely limits your own field of vision, causing frequent deaths from behind. Even worse, several missions were designed for you to have a limited ammo count, meaning that if you run out of ammo, you're forced down a path of baiting the stupid AI to follow you down a path, and sneaking up on them with a melee weapon in order to kill them. Essentially, as a result of these map changes, your ability to move about is severely reduced. The increased amount of "special enemies" (enemies that can only be killed with a gun, or enemies that can only be killed with a melee weapon) only adds to the frustration. One level, which has you invade a dance club, which is unbearably dark, has you fight against dogs, whose color is almost the same as the dark floor, and the only way you can see them is by baiting them to run into the somewhat better lit rooms.
This game completely loses the "flow", and as a result, falls short of its predecessor. Based on this alone, and the fact that the game becomes unenjoyable about halfway through, I wouldn't recommend it, but there's more.
Many people complain about the increased emphasis on the plot. I found the plot interesting, albeit nowhere near as "fragmented" and deep as some reviews claim. It's quaint, occasionally funny, but usually just mildly interesting. I will say that the ending is one of the boldest statements that I've seen in gaming, but that, in the end, it doesn't work. It left me retrospective, but not in the positive sense of digesting the experience so much as in the sense of game design, and the sacrifices that Dennaton took in order to make this game more plot heavy. They sacrificed the style (which could be coupled with the flow) for substance, AKA, a more substantial plot, with thicker lines between the real and the surreal. Some might like it, I don't, and I feel like the ending, which I won't spoil, leaves you with a giant, sour note, and feels like it's a big joke played at the expense of the player. The first game attempted a similar theme, but the first game pulled it off perfectly, with the minimalist story and setting. This game, with the enhanced emphasis on plot and background setting, simply can't pull the same tricks as the first. It tried, and ended up falling flat on its face.
Last but not least, are the bugs, which are utterly hilarious at times, and downright infuriating at others. Doors are buggy as hell, will frequently get in the way of your bullets and prevent you from hitting enemies if you dare to stand in a doorway. Enemies get stuck in doors and become unkillable for some periods of time. Dogs tend to run around in circles trying to catch their own tails. Key items get stuck in areas that you can't reach. Mouse movement feels extremely rigid at times, and I'm told this has something to do with v-sync, which keeps turning itself on. The level editor wasn't shipped with the game, and I fear for the community, as the longer they'll take to ship it, the more they'll lose the launch date momentum. There's some big pathfinding bugs with the Swan Siblings, where the gun wielding sibling will get stuck on terrain, having you finagle the chainsaw sibling around back and forth to get the stupid gun wielder out.
There are some good things to say about this game. The music is still great, some tracks being very memorable, particularly the very talented Perturbator's work. The aesthetic is as good as ever, with some fantastic settings and truly unique enemies towards the end. The earlier levels are quite enjoyable, and capture the Hotline Miami game style quite well. It's unfortunate that they don't last.  Some of the new characters (mainly the fans) are a ton of fun to play.
I can't recommend this game in whole heart, as it is just not satisfying.  Speaking as a big Hotline Miami fan, I didn't want a carbon copy of the first game, I just wanted Dennaton to recreate what was good in the first game. They didn't, and as such, all I can say is this: Just play Hotline Miami 1.

Mount and Blade Warband is a great Medieval Role Playing Game. In singleplayer one can choose a variety of goals from becoming an honorable lord, a despicable bandit, or even the King of everyone and everything. Recruit peasants to form your warband and train them into elite soldiers. Fight in great battles during wars between 5 diverse factions and conquer vast lands. The choice is yours. Combat is unique and exciting but can be frustrating at times in multiplayer. Attacks can be executed in 4 different directions based upon your mouse movement. For example moving your mouse upwards while left clicking will cause an up attack. In multiplayer you must block (by right clicking) in the same direction as the incoming attack to successfully block it. Besides the native singleplayer and multiplayer, warband has a surprising amount of detailed mods entailing everything from persistent worlds to even lord of the rings themed singeplayers. Not to mention the fantastic DLC for the game, Napoleonic Wars. Participate in early 19th century warfare and fire a volley into your opponents or run down retreating infantry as cavalry. You can even join a regiment for this DLC and participate in line battles. If you are interested in joining a regiment contact me. Overall mount and blade warband is an excellent game and features excellent mods and dlc. If this game is on sale it is defenitely worth your money to pick it up and give it a go.

This is definitely a great game with a bright future. Even though it's in Alpha, it still has a lot of content and things to explore.
The in-game creation editor allows you to make pretty much whatever your heart desires in terms of weapons, shields, vehicles, and decorations. I was never an artsy kind of guy in terms of drawing or modeling, but it is fairly simple to figure out how to work the controls for the editor. Also, there is a small built-in tutorial along with of a bunch of help amongst the community.
There is also a build mode that allows you to place blocks and build structures. Unlike many other games of this type, it allows you to build multiple blocks at once through dragging vertically / horizontally, and offers you various shapes such as cubes, spheres, cylinders, cones, and much more. Along with this, you can also enter a free-view mode, which makes building much easier to control and look over.
I haven't played the single-player campaign to its fullest yet, but it has been nice so far. I have primarily been playing on my multiplayer server with a couple of friends, and have been creating and exploring for many hours. Personally, the game is much more fun when you have others to play with, since you can go on adventures or see what others created themselves.
I personally prefer hosting a server from the game itself by going to Multiplayer > Host. I say this because the server controls are a bit iffy right now, and from what I understand, the "correct" way to shut down the server is to find it in the multiplayer list, select it and hit 'Delete'. With this being the case, the admin of the server is whichever character created it, and thus, they are the only ones who can do the process stated above. However, when hosting it from a .BAT file or whatnot, there is no specified character as an owner. As such, the only way I've found to shut it down is to either just exit out of it, or kill the process if using batchmode. Of course, there could be something I'm missing entirely, and I'm sure this will be refined more in the future.

When the game was first released to everyone it was actually pretty good, a semi good balance of gameplay mechanics made the game tolerable from the bugs present and you actually got a lot from playing and earning weapons, attachments and extra characters with additional roles like Recon, Tank Crew etc. However with the new update, Timonshenko, you can throw all of that out of the window.
Timonshenko is one of those classic updates that free-2-play games do that totally destroy the original fan base, utterly exclude anyone that doesn't have/want to spend money on the game and majorly unbalances the game that is practically unfixable for them. You're probably wondering how and why it is unfixable? Well, because of the new update, Timonshenko, which introduces one of the main military forces during WW2, the Russians, it has made them horrendously over-powered by making them machine gun orientated and very powerful weapons introduced exclusive to the Russians. The PTRD 1941 is one of those weapons that a game probably shouldn't introduce for a good many reasons. Since the update and the lack of people wanting to switch over to the Russians to start the new chracters previous to their already grinded, bought out ones the developers added a deal to entice people into joining the Russians, a 50% off gold deal on new academy trained characters within the Russian faction. Now this gives people who bought them a massive advantage over the rest and able to purchase the dreaded over-powered weapons currently plaguing the game, this is where the the PTRD 1941 comes into play, players are not using them for what it is meant for, tank destruction, instead using it for anti-personnel which it excels at. One shotting anyone at any range means it is a weapon to be feared. The only down side(s) to the weapon are the default iron sights so sniping is actually quite difficult, but not impossible and the slightly long reload time as you only have one shot that has to be chambered manually. No magazine. It can also one-shot jeeps which I have done many times with a full complement of troops on board of which I got the weapon from a player I killed.
The first new grenades you get with the Russian faction is also again (surprise, surprise) very overpowered as the ridiculous blast radius and damage output puts other grenades to shame, chuck one in the room and you're garunteed to exterminate anyone in said room while other starter grenades would most likely only heavily injure players.
All in all the Russian faction seems to be the death of Heroes & Generals respective to the fact Reto-Moto has became greedy for the pay-2-win scene, while the game has always had pay-2-win aspects it has never been 'too' (and I say that lightly) intrusive to the over-all playability. Also while the starting SMG, the PPD-40 starts the over-powered parade of which the Russians blitzkreig all capture points you can bet when ever facing the Russians the only way you can possibly win is by having a Veteran team with highly upgraded weapons and vehicles other than that, prepare to die many times and have a quick defeat.
Fixing the game after all that has been done due to the Timonshenko update will be for nought as they are already starting to lose some of its veteran community base and only growing due to players wanting an easy and unchallenged start that the Russian faction provides changing the balance of the Russians would only alienate the people that spent money for that specific reason and would more than likely lose those supporters too, I do however think they would not care as they already have your money now and as a fellow veteran that has bought the veteran membership, to support the game with minimal benefits (never bought any weapons attachments etc with Gold, only earnt them) I am too very disappointed with Reto-Moto with the decision on taking the game in a new, unfavourable path.
While before I would have recommended Heroes & Generals to anyone that likes WW2 style FPS shooters and a strong strategy aspect that requires good players acting as Generals to supply assault teams to different battlefields that can change the tide of the war for their faction I can not however do this now because Reto-Moto has turned into one of those dreaded developers that sacrifice a well respected community of people, supporting the game from the start, for people that has an excess amount of money and an unspoiling credit card.

So, since this game is free for the weekend, I decided to give it a try, see if it's worth it, and maybe even buy it. So, it IS worth it or not? Let's see.
First of all, this is more of a remake of the well-known mod for HL2, "Zombie Panic; Source". I played the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of that mod, and I did like it! If you don't know if you will like this game, you should check and play the mod first, since it's the same with new stuff.
So, Contagion is a mix between the old Zombie Panic, adding Left 4 Dead and State of Decay (I swear, that game was a huge dissapointment). The game is mainly multiplayer, but it can also be played alone in some modes. There are a few gamemodes, but it goes like this:
In one of them, all the players are left in a map, most of them spawn split, and must find items in the houses, where they are send to save civilians. You first must arrive there using your Iphone (really? Iphones?), find all the survivors, gather all the stuff that's left on it, and escort them to safety. If all the survivors die, it's over, for some reason, and the ones that survive and climb over the fence, will drop their stuff to the players. The other mode reminds me of the L4D stories. The survivors spawn in one area, and must escape, getting to somewhere else. The final mode, though...I might have to talk more about it, since it's one of the mayor problems this game has.
The most played mode, is called "Hunted" or something like that, I don't remember the name right now. Mainly, it's like the classic Zombie Panic mode: Most of the players spawn human, and 1 or 2 as zombies. If a player dies, he turns into one of them. There are also non-stopping zombies that keep spawning forever, and end up flooding parts of the map later on. So, what's the problem? Isn't this the best mode?
No. Sadly, the mode I was looking up to, turned out to be like playing DayZ all over again. You see, there's friendly fire. And I'm okay with that, but on this mode, humans tend to KILL OTHER HUMANS, to take their stuff, so they can survive longer. What the hell? Not only that, the game has the tools to kill other players, and even the devs tell people to do it on the trailers.
Basically, on this mode, since you don't have to use the GPS on your Iphone ,you can instead call other players who are near you. When you do it, you can hear their phones, and so secure their location. Once you do it, you can murder them in cold blood. And sadly, this happend to me the first time I played. I got killed on the first minute, of a 20 minutes long game. I wasn't♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off, just seriously confused by what the point of this gamemode even is. And you know what? I called a friend to play together, and we went in a murder-spree with the entire server afterwards. We literally killed every player, and them camped in the top of a building with crossbows and grenades. And they got♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off. And we had fun.
The game also has a random system, like the one in L4D, making each game different. Sadly, though, it doesn't really have that much maps to be worth the full price of the game. Since you might be playing this Hunted mode a lot as well, you might as well get a friend to play it, since being alone is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ If you find this game at a sale, like this weekend, like zombie games, and have someone to play it with, I do recommend buying it. But for me, I'm just gonna stay this weekend, killing people in cold blood, and return to Zombie Panic.
Oh, and what's up with the voices? Some characters sound drunk, bored, or both. Was it what they tried to do? At least it was nice to find a Zombie Panic pinball in one map...

I consider this game having three acts, the first starting out on the island and hunting down Vaas, the second having you reach the second island, and the third having you complete the game.
It has 38 story missions total, so about 12-13 missions for each act. The game is also split between two islands, the first two acts take place on the first island with the final act taking place on the second. The game starts off great, I was really enjoying the first act, and the side missions were fun enough to keep me doing them. However, after a while the side missions just get boring, as unfortunately they fall into the Ubisoft formula of "Go here, kill this, come back." that plagues their games. I completed about 2/3 of the side missions before I just started ignoring them, and strangely all of the side missions you can do to get special animal skins to craft the best upgrades are all on the first island, so you'll have every upgrade before you finish the first act. Also for the first act you talk a lot with your new buddy, Dennis, and he helps you through learning the ropes of the island. I really liked Dennis, and by the end of the game I really felt bad for him.
The second act is where I found the game really fell flat. I quite enjoyed Vaas and his role in the game, but unfortunately he doesn't stick around until even the end of the second act. After him you have to deal with his boss, Hoyt, who has hardly even been mentioned until this point in the game and isn't nearly as interesting. Along with losing interest in the side missions, I was also losing interest with the story. There wasn't really much keeping me going at this point, even Jason was starting to irk me, as I just couldn't understand a lot of his decisions and most of what was even coming out of his mouth anymore.
However, I feel the third act is where the game really shines. The last 10 missions are fantastic, and your new new buddy, Sam, is a really fun character and adds a lot of spice back to the game. I definitely like Sam more than Dennis, and the story missions with him are by far the best. Fortunately Jason was getting a little better in my eyes and I was liking him again, and a lot of the stupid things he was saying in the second act have passed. The final few missions were amazing and I finished the game with a significantly higher opinion of it than I had by the end of the second act.
Meanwhile, there are lots of collectibles, as is to be expected from a Ubisoft game. This game seems to try and one-up Assassin's Creed by having at least a thousand chests scattered around the two islands (this is probably an exaggeration, but good lord there has got to be at least 500), not to mention 120 relics, 20 Japanese WWII letters, and 20 drug dealer memory cards to collect. As with all Assassin's Creed games, you can purchase maps to show you where everything is, then you just have to collect them.
Overall, the game is very fun despite the weak middle part. Though keep in mind that it will be a test of endurance if you plan on achieving 100% completion as the collectibles and side missions are an exercise in tedium.

is one of the only games I have ever played that has been consistently entertaining throughout multiple playthroughs. This is a game that can be played in both doses and marathons, without losing its appeal.
The game takes place in the fictional region of “Calradia,” a land dominated by 6 factions, all with their own unique units, armors, and fighting styles. You play as a lone adventurer, who leads his/her army throughout their adventures in the realm.
Once you begin your game, you are taught the basics of the gameplay mechanics and then given your first mission, which will begin your adventure.
The game has three distinct sections:
1.	The Overhead/Strategic Map
2.	 “Scenes”
3.	Battle Mode
From the overhead map, you can see settlements and their owners, enemy war parties, and bandit lairs. From this view, you may move your party across the map to any of these locations, where you can interact with NPCs or, in the case of settlements, walk around the area.
Scenes are the locations where the player controls their character outright. These take place in either Settlement or Dialogue form.
Settlements are large areas where other NPCs (primarily villagers and townsmen) roam. These areas also lead into smaller scenes, such as Taverns, Castles, and Prisons.
Dialogue scenes primarily take place between the character and any other party encountered on the map, but can also take place within Settlements. As is expected, these scenes allow the player to interact with NPCs to perform a variety of actions.
In the case of Lords/Ladies, you can perform certain actions to increase your relation with them, such as quests or simple conversation.
In the case of others, you can ask questions, purchase items, receive quests, and recruit mercenaries and companions to your party.
Battle mode is where the major chunk of the gameplay is found. Here, your character and his/her army engage in combat with a variety of enemies.
The game’s combat mechanic is simple:
Your character can carry 4 items, Melee and Ranged Weapons, and Ammunition and Shields.
You can form any combination of these, including multiple shields, to combat your enemies. Certain weapons are more effective against certain enemies, such as a spear vs. cavalry, or a sword vs. archers.
Your character becomes more effective with certain weapon types over time, and develops skills as they level up, which provide multiple bonuses to yourself or your party.
If you have any of the aforementioned companions, you can personally outfit them as you like, making your own unique soldiers.
Battle’s are going to be your early source of income, as they produce loot, as well as small amounts of money, and in some cases, prisoners.
Armies are comprised of 4 types of units:
Infantry, Archers, Cavalry, and Horse Archers (considered Cavalry, but work much differently than other Cavalry units).
Each faction has their own unique units in each of these classes, or in some cases, none at all. (Some factions may not have Cavalry, but have stronger Infantry or Archers)
Each of these units perform as you would imagine. Archers get in damage from a range and can help thin an attacker’s numbers before they reach your infantry.
Infantry are your footsoldiers, who deal the most damage and form the backbone of your army.
Cavalry are used to charge an enemy and break their formations, and certain cavalry units are capable of defeating enemy cavalry.
Horse Archers, reminiscent of the Mongol and Hunnic hordes are a big threat against infantry-based armies. They can easily ride around your troops, firing arrows while staying out of range.
Your units are each assigned to different sections of your army, numbered 1-9, which can be renamed as you like. If you want Knights in your Archers group, the game won’t stop you.
Companions are recruited in Taverns, for varying prices.
They all have unique backstories and personalities, and some get along better than others.
Your companions will have different opinions of each other and, consequently, you based on their behaviour. They can be outfitted as you like, and assigned to certain number groups, like other units. This way, should you want to, you can make Lancers, Skirmishers, Legionaries, Berserkers, Javelineers, or even Clubbers. (No, not the kind you find on Thursday nights when you’re not on your computer.)
These Companions can also be sent on missions for you.
The game is comprised of 6 kingdoms, with multiple fiefs yours for the taking.
You can accomplish this through direct conquest or, should you be well renowned, vassalisation. Joining a faction gives you a relation boost with its vassals, and gives you a bit more security than if you started your own faction.
Conquering fiefs expands your kingdom’s borders, and helps your character gain power.
Castles and Towns require Garrisons, which require wages. These troops defend your fiefs when you are not present, and depending on their strength, are more or less likely to be successful at this. 100 Recruits are less likely to successfully defend than 100 Swordsmen.
The game also allows marriage, some diplomatic interaction between factions, vassalisation of companions, trade (entirely player-managed. No missions, prices vary between towns), Arena Combat, Duels (between lords), Tournaments, Prisoner Sales/Ransoms, Looting of villages, Feasts, and Training montages with the Villagers.
--
The Multiplayer modes utilize all of the game’s combat features, however your character is outfitted as certain soldier types, and you “purchase” your equipment with gold received from killing players and achieving goals. (mostly killing, though. :D)
Game modes can range from epic Battles and Sieges to calm Duels.
--
All of these features are present in the Vanilla game. The
DLC adds a multiplayer Gunpowder-Era mode (which has a thriving player-base). The modding community is expansive, creating multiple worlds within the engine, ranging from Feudal Japan, to 11th Century Europe, to Rome, to the American Frontier.
This is a game that any PC gamer needs to play at least once. It is one of the few Gems of the PC Gaming archive, and deserves most if not all of the hype it has received from fans.

If you played the original, you know what you are in for. What you might not be aware of are the awesome tweaks that make Wrong Number even more of a blast. 9 hours, 20 stages and over 1000 deaths later, I can't get enough of this game.
The story jumps around a bit more this time through multiple, sometimes-intersecting groups/characters and each of them has their own unique gimmick that changes the gameplay up a bit. The army guy picks a weapon and sticks with it (and a knife) for the entire level. You'll need to find ammo stashes to reload when you run low. The fans all have the familiar masks, but they are also tied to the individual, so sometimes you are forced to play with a certain style. Maybe your punches are lethal but you can't pick up weapons, or maybe you are playing as a duo (at the same time) armed with a pistol and chainsaw.
I'm not even close to done with this game yet, but I heavily recommend it. And I would be remiss if I didn't mention the awesome soundtrack. Great job to everyone that worked on this title!

Get this game. No seriously, get it. If you had any doubts before getting this game, as a person that just finished the game, believe me you'll want to experiance it.
Let me start off however by saying that in terms of favorites, Hotline Miami 2 is not. I actually profusely enjoyed Hotline Miami, despite it's short length of 3-5 hours.
Why? Well first let me get into what Hotline Miami 2 does right.
For starters, it is the true escence of what a sequel of any game should be: adding new things without taking away what made the first game great... gameplay wise.
I'll get to the story in just a second, but gameplay wise, the additions are fresh and welcome in the Hotline Miami universe. Instead of playing as Jacket from the original HM, you will be filling the shoes of multiple characters such as the Fans, a pacifist writer, a dirty cop, and more. All of whom having different gameplay styles and strategies you'll have to adapt to, making sure the already fluid gameplay does not feel TOO familiar.
But fear not, there's still the classic Hotline Miami gameplay of planning around how to kill your enemies in the most brutal way possible. The game still rewards you for both carefully planning your route as well as placing various well placed shots to rack up your score multiplier. And it always feels good.
Speaking of feeling good, the weapons feel amazing to shoot. Just as good as the first game, in any case. There is also a slightly larger variety of weapons to choose from as well. That said, some of the guns from the game are ones that you will instantly be able to tell are best for trailers, and showing off. Particularly one of the Fans which I will not spoil for you here. They don't play badly, but their abilities are "gimicky" at best, and disappointing at worst.
As for levels, there are a ton here. Okay, maybe there aren't hundreds upon hundreds (yet... I'll get to that later) but there are enough to definately warrent the price tag of even 15 bucks. Those hours that I've plugged in so far? 12? That was over one playthrough. Give or take an hour or two I might have been idle, that's 9-12 hours of gameplay, which is twice the amount of some 60 dollar titles that have come out this year (*cough* Order 1886 *cough*). And once again, most, if not all the levels have some sort of manner that changes up the formula.
So as a game, especially a challenging arcade game, this game is definately worth your money.
The presentation and asthetic is also nice. Trust me. Just pause the game and you'll get an example of what I mean.
As for the music... do you even need to ask? It's fantastic, hosting a variety of artists. While the first game may have had a better choice in music, (nothing beats Musik per Automatick, yo) this soundtrack is definately something you need to hear.
Now, if you were looking for the same trip you found in Hotline Miami in Jacket's story... here's the thing. It's not as good.
Don't get me wrong, the story of Hotline Miami 2 is still great. But it falls flat in places because unlike the first one, there are times where you don't know if it wants to be a schizophrenic narrative like the movie Memento, or if it wants to be the surreal experiance Jacket's story was. The story will hop around time frequently, so if you plan to start making sense of the story, be sure to get a pen and paper because you're going to need to put together some dates to figure out where you are.
Because I've only played through the game once, I can only speak from what I know. After all, this is the type of game where replaying the story will do you benefit for understanding it. But the main story that was being told, I found the backstory of Hotline Miami more interesting. Rather, the origins of Jacket and the convenience store clerk. It was interesting to watch unfold and even begin to draw conclusions as to Jacket's motivations in the original game. As well as explaining where his lack of empathy stemed from. Even allowing a meta look at the storyline of the first game.
As you can tell, that's the most interesting part. Learning and experiancing the world outside of Jacket's own. The other story with the Fans, and the remnents of the Russian Mafia and Columbists is interesting enough where you won't be itching to skip through all their dialouge, but it just falls flat... ironically because some of the stories are simply too uniform and lack the same charm and surreal quality of the first game.
Still, it's enough where it'll keep your attention, and in some cases drive you to keep dying over and over to see what happens next.
That's the end of the bad news however. The good news is that once you beat the game once, it's not the end. For those who loved the game enough, there's an additonal Hard Mode after you play through the game once on Normal, taking away the lock on and making the enemies smarter, faster, and tougher than before. This is easily another 10 hours to gameplay.
But not only that, there is the upcomming level editor. While the quality of this editor is unknown at this point, and the amount of heart in the modding community is unknown as well, assuming the best scenario there could be a potentially infinite number of Hotline Miami levels for you to keep playing, and coming back for more. At worst, it will at least be a brief distraction for those who want to mess around with it.
-----
In short, Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is far from a perfect game. Some may argue that it has too much and that takes away from the experiance. But one cannot deny that it is a step up in many ways from the previous game. And while the developers said that this was the final game in the series, if enough folk give this game a try, one way or another the game will live on for a lengtly lifetime.
Or something. I don't know, I wanted to end this review with something beautiful. But ♥♥♥♥ it. Buy the game if you like to hurt people. Or if you just like really good games.
TL;DR
Pros:
-Varying Level Design
-Numerous Characters and Playstyles

I cannot recommend this game.  This makes me sad.
First the Good:
Price: I got it as part of a humble bundle and I wanted to like it.  I can forgive a lot for an indie game that sells itself so cheaply.  This is where I want to future of gaming to go.
Art: The art is phenominal. The 3D backdrops are very detailed with lush animation, and the comic book style cut scenes are wonderfully expressive, although more on those in a minute.  The overall effect is to make the game feel less like a 2d platformer and more like a rail game.  This is only slightly dampened by situations where you have to do something convoluded to reach a platform when there are clearly well constructed stairs leading up to it in the background.  Wat... Still the art is very impressive indeed.
Animation: The animation is a little over long in melee strikes hampering control, but overall Randell moves smoothly and only occationally becomes incongruous.  The zombies are not so fortunate and frequently do not interact with the environment correctly.  Not Assassin's Creed smooth, but rarely outright bad.
The bad
Gameplay: I have to say Deadlight's gameplay is very poorly thought out and above all inconsistent.  Despite being a near copy of the controls from 2d Prince of Persia games, Deadlight's controls are neither intuitive now precise.  I often had Randell dropping when I wanted him to jump and jumping when I wanted him to drop.  Zombies would sometimes latch on to me when I ran past them and sometimes they wouldn't bother.  My axe would sometimes hit zombies in it's arc and sometimes it would pretend they weren't there and they would latch onto me.  With one exception the puzzles were pretty obvious once you discovered the surprise element they frequently throw at you in the middle and the "moving wall" style escape the chopper and the parkour through a collapsing warehouse scenes wore out their welcome before they were done.    The game was frequently tedious to play which is odd considering how short it is.
The story.  Yeah.  Randell is a mountain park ranger from Canada who inexplicably doesn't know how to swim.  Or shoot a gun.  Wat?  Wait, he can parkour like a stuntman?!  Where did he learn that?  Still what he does know is his family "must" be out there waiting for him and he must find them at all costs.  Also he is pretty obviously mentally ill.  The twist ending seems to have taken a lot of people by surprise, but I saw it coming from the first flashback and was irritated to be proven right in a way that was even less entertaining than I imagined.  By the end Randell has accomplished nothing but losing his only friend and realizing how messed up he is.  Not a very satifying narrative arc at all.  Finally the villains are cardboard cutouts out of place even in a 2d game.  They have exactly zero motivation beyond some vague "dominance" assertions and♥♥♥♥♥♥  I had several wall banger moments toward the end of the game.  Ug.
The Neutral
Music and VA:  The vocal talent in Deadlight was pretty average for an indie game.  It wasn't really high quality but neither was it ear gougingly bad.  However due to the way the checkpoints in a couple of locations are arranged you may be forced to endure the same lines many many times.  None of them stand up to that kind of scrutiny.  The music was average to good and never seemed out of place or especially noteworthy.  The epidomy of solid but not exceptional.  Both are severely let down by a bug that occationally turns off all sound during those comic book style cut scenes.  There is a workaround but one should not be required.
Overall:
It was short at 5 hours but still managed to wear out its welcome before it ended.  I can't complain about it too much considering what I paid for it, but I really wouldn't recommend anyone buy this game.  An HD let's play or playing another game that is better thought out would be a more enjoyable use of your time.

I consider this game having three acts, the first starting out on the island and hunting down Vaas, the second having you reach the second island, and the third having you complete the game.
It has 38 story missions total, so about 12-13 missions for each act. The game is also split between two islands, the first two acts take place on the first island with the final act taking place on the second. The game starts off great, I was really enjoying the first act, and the side missions were fun enough to keep me doing them. However, after a while the side missions just get boring, as unfortunately they fall into the Ubisoft formula of "Go here, kill this, come back." that plagues their games. I completed about 2/3 of the side missions before I just started ignoring them, and strangely all of the side missions you can do to get special animal skins to craft the best upgrades are all on the first island, so you'll have every upgrade before you finish the first act. Also for the first act you talk a lot with your new buddy, Dennis, and he helps you through learning the ropes of the island. I really liked Dennis, and by the end of the game I really felt bad for him.
The second act is where I found the game really fell flat. I quite enjoyed Vaas and his role in the game, but unfortunately he doesn't stick around until even the end of the second act. After him you have to deal with his boss, Hoyt, who has hardly even been mentioned until this point in the game and isn't nearly as interesting. Along with losing interest in the side missions, I was also losing interest with the story. There wasn't really much keeping me going at this point, even Jason was starting to irk me, as I just couldn't understand a lot of his decisions and most of what was even coming out of his mouth anymore.
However, I feel the third act is where the game really shines. The last 10 missions are fantastic, and your new new buddy, Sam, is a really fun character and adds a lot of spice back to the game. I definitely like Sam more than Dennis, and the story missions with him are by far the best. Fortunately Jason was getting a little better in my eyes and I was liking him again, and a lot of the stupid things he was saying in the second act have passed. The final few missions were amazing and I finished the game with a significantly higher opinion of it than I had by the end of the second act.
Meanwhile, there are lots of collectibles, as is to be expected from a Ubisoft game. This game seems to try and one-up Assassin's Creed by having at least a thousand chests scattered around the two islands (this is probably an exaggeration, but good lord there has got to be at least 500), not to mention 120 relics, 20 Japanese WWII letters, and 20 drug dealer memory cards to collect. As with all Assassin's Creed games, you can purchase maps to show you where everything is, then you just have to collect them.
Overall, the game is very fun despite the weak middle part. Though keep in mind that it will be a test of endurance if you plan on achieving 100% completion as the collectibles and side missions are an exercise in tedium.

Trying to shoot at someone while having simulated hand spasms is damn hard. Gameplay generally felt sluggish and heavy when using the guns, and somewhat unresponsive in tight situations.

"It's like Skyrim with guns"... yeah not really. FC3 is more like Assassin's Creed on an island but not as good. In fact, the format is essentially the same, but FC3 finds a way to be even more redundant. Besides a couple noteworthy main story missions, you are basically just running around liberating enemy outposts again and again.
The story isn't redeeming either. Granted I haven't played the other Far Cry games, but there is almost no explanation about why everyone is killing each other. The storyline from the perspective of Jason who you play as is shallow. He is trying to save his friends, but other than that, the details are just filler. Otherwise, you go kill a bunch of people because reasons. Maybe fun at first, but becomes old.
Graphic detailing is weak. On a tropical island, you'd imagine there would be lots of opportunities to create lush landscapes and immersive environments. Instead, it's mainly dirt roads with hazy, blurred mountains in the distance.
Crafting is also a major component, but it finds ways to be oversimplified and somehow tedious. For instance, to get the first wallet upgrade you need two pig hides to craft it, but you don't get to areas of the map that have pigs until after several missions when you've had your wallet completely full since the first hour of the game. Then, you have to get deer hides for the next wallet upgrade, which you have to go to the complete other side of the map into enemy territory to find. When the bad guys find you hunting in their territory, they'll kill you and you respawn a mile away without your deer hides. For the last wallet upgrade, you need two shark skins. Since when do you need to hunt two sharks just to make a wallet? The stores only sell weapons and maps, and animals will kill you often. I've been killed by a Warthog.
But it's bearable for a few hours, and there were some moments worth playing through. Ultimately it's just a lazy game. If you like FPS and Assassin's Creed and have low standards this is the game for you

A quick example being the Hawaii acts, where the player is handed a gun of there choosing and a knife. Due to it's focused nature, the levels are designed with these pre-requisites in mind and do a fair job of compensating for whatever handicaps the player.
On the other hand, we are also subjugated to a mandatory play-style that we may not enjoy. An example being Evan's levels, which are focused around non-lethal combat that can be a bit confusing to those who haven't played it before.
A few small gripes I have however:
*The game relies far to much on level memorization.
*The AI pathing acts like it's entirely random at times
*Levels are stupidly large; with far more enemies then the original. Which has lead to several occasions of burnout while playing.
*(Might be a bug) When attempting to pick up a weapon, certain characters seem to favor some weapons over others; which has lead to many frustrating deaths when I want a knife instead of a rifle.
The original game had tight buildings which were much easier to navigate and memorize. I for one prefer the more focused style of the original, but I can see the appeal of the more open arena style level design.
Story:
When first playing, I claimed that the plot was very misplaced and seemed cheesy; Overall I was disappointed, but not really a big deal; this game was not made to convey a story.
Music:
Overall, I enjoy the new soundtrack. There are one or two tracks that seem to drag on however and can get obnoxious when repeating the same level over and over again. Furthermore, some of the looping feels lazy and can break my murder high.
Conclusion:
In the end, It took about 11 hours for me to bullhead through this game. The adrenalin rush you get from the original is back and very powerful. Many of the levels added are jam packed of those tense moments that we all craved from the original and the sequel offers these moments in spades. I suggest playing in short bursts; as I for one burned out multiple times on my first play through.
Did you like the Original? You'll like Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number.

Preclaim: I am a Hotline Miami fan who is willing to wear an animal mask and kill people. I enjoyed Hotline Miami and grew crazy with it. Hotline Miami 2 though, is not as good as Hotline Miami.
So what is wrong with HM2 as a game? Nothing. Really nothing is wrong. You can have bugs and glitches sometimes but the game itself is still very very very fun. It got all the guns and bullets and killings and blood and dying. A really good game to play, if you haven't played HM.
What is wrong with HM2 is that it is a sequel, a bad one. In short, it took away the good things in HM. In long, HM2 tried to add new mechnics and stuff to the game, but failed to keep what was already there.
In HM, you have all these masks with all these different skills. In HM2, you only have 3-4 "styles" to choose from, and not all characters can choose styles. This eliminated the "you can do the level however you want" feeling in HM, as you seldomly choose styles in HM2. Even if you can choose, some different characters have the "same" styles to play with. The Fan's masks and the Son's techniques are exactly the same (except for the siblings style).
The crazy (and probably the most effective) way of "charge in and kill everyone recklessly" is no more in HM2, because of its bad level design. In some levels you HAVE to wait for an opening to charge in, wait for lure your enemies, and wait so you don't die. You can no longer run&kill through the entire level, which is what makes HM crazy good. In HM2 you are more like an assassin waiting for the perfect moment to strike, but HM is all about fast, no thinking, craziness.
Back to style, when you play as a character without styles to choose from, you are playing the same, plain character. The effect from this is that you can't feel the different characters. Dennaton added new playable characters to the game, but he didn't give them different styles (except for the Writer, the only well-established character). What the developer should have done was to give every playable character their own, unique combat styles so we the players can get more immersed with the characters.
Still about style, the styles in HM2 are poor. Dodge Roll is only useful of getting you killed - Corey should keep his Killing Door style from HM, instead of this useless "Dodge". Killing Punch but No Weapon means you literally can't beat some levels with it, plus it takes so long to execute the animation - Tony is a Tiger, he is not using weapon because he is one. But it doesn't make sense for him to spend a entire second (more than enough for you to die three times in HM) to execute anyone. The Siblings is a good idea but badly designed - Chainsaw guy is like Tony, with too much animations to get yourself killed. Gun guy follows you like a flail which is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ also he shoots the gun he picks up. Dual Machinegun is the worst style ever - you can't reload until you are out, can't melee until you are completely out.
All in all, Dennaton tried to create "the new" in HM2, but failed to preserve "the old" from HM.
So, would I recommend this game? Yes, because I just love Hotline Miami, and I want you to like it too.

is one of the only games I have ever played that has been consistently entertaining throughout multiple playthroughs. This is a game that can be played in both doses and marathons, without losing its appeal.
The game takes place in the fictional region of “Calradia,” a land dominated by 6 factions, all with their own unique units, armors, and fighting styles. You play as a lone adventurer, who leads his/her army throughout their adventures in the realm.
Once you begin your game, you are taught the basics of the gameplay mechanics and then given your first mission, which will begin your adventure.
The game has three distinct sections:
1.	The Overhead/Strategic Map
2.	 “Scenes”
3.	Battle Mode
From the overhead map, you can see settlements and their owners, enemy war parties, and bandit lairs. From this view, you may move your party across the map to any of these locations, where you can interact with NPCs or, in the case of settlements, walk around the area.
Scenes are the locations where the player controls their character outright. These take place in either Settlement or Dialogue form.
Settlements are large areas where other NPCs (primarily villagers and townsmen) roam. These areas also lead into smaller scenes, such as Taverns, Castles, and Prisons.
Dialogue scenes primarily take place between the character and any other party encountered on the map, but can also take place within Settlements. As is expected, these scenes allow the player to interact with NPCs to perform a variety of actions.
In the case of Lords/Ladies, you can perform certain actions to increase your relation with them, such as quests or simple conversation.
In the case of others, you can ask questions, purchase items, receive quests, and recruit mercenaries and companions to your party.
Battle mode is where the major chunk of the gameplay is found. Here, your character and his/her army engage in combat with a variety of enemies.
The game’s combat mechanic is simple:
Your character can carry 4 items, Melee and Ranged Weapons, and Ammunition and Shields.
You can form any combination of these, including multiple shields, to combat your enemies. Certain weapons are more effective against certain enemies, such as a spear vs. cavalry, or a sword vs. archers.
Your character becomes more effective with certain weapon types over time, and develops skills as they level up, which provide multiple bonuses to yourself or your party.
If you have any of the aforementioned companions, you can personally outfit them as you like, making your own unique soldiers.
Battle’s are going to be your early source of income, as they produce loot, as well as small amounts of money, and in some cases, prisoners.
Armies are comprised of 4 types of units:
Infantry, Archers, Cavalry, and Horse Archers (considered Cavalry, but work much differently than other Cavalry units).
Each faction has their own unique units in each of these classes, or in some cases, none at all. (Some factions may not have Cavalry, but have stronger Infantry or Archers)
Each of these units perform as you would imagine. Archers get in damage from a range and can help thin an attacker’s numbers before they reach your infantry.
Infantry are your footsoldiers, who deal the most damage and form the backbone of your army.
Cavalry are used to charge an enemy and break their formations, and certain cavalry units are capable of defeating enemy cavalry.
Horse Archers, reminiscent of the Mongol and Hunnic hordes are a big threat against infantry-based armies. They can easily ride around your troops, firing arrows while staying out of range.
Your units are each assigned to different sections of your army, numbered 1-9, which can be renamed as you like. If you want Knights in your Archers group, the game won’t stop you.
Companions are recruited in Taverns, for varying prices.
They all have unique backstories and personalities, and some get along better than others.
Your companions will have different opinions of each other and, consequently, you based on their behaviour. They can be outfitted as you like, and assigned to certain number groups, like other units. This way, should you want to, you can make Lancers, Skirmishers, Legionaries, Berserkers, Javelineers, or even Clubbers. (No, not the kind you find on Thursday nights when you’re not on your computer.)
These Companions can also be sent on missions for you.
The game is comprised of 6 kingdoms, with multiple fiefs yours for the taking.
You can accomplish this through direct conquest or, should you be well renowned, vassalisation. Joining a faction gives you a relation boost with its vassals, and gives you a bit more security than if you started your own faction.
Conquering fiefs expands your kingdom’s borders, and helps your character gain power.
Castles and Towns require Garrisons, which require wages. These troops defend your fiefs when you are not present, and depending on their strength, are more or less likely to be successful at this. 100 Recruits are less likely to successfully defend than 100 Swordsmen.
The game also allows marriage, some diplomatic interaction between factions, vassalisation of companions, trade (entirely player-managed. No missions, prices vary between towns), Arena Combat, Duels (between lords), Tournaments, Prisoner Sales/Ransoms, Looting of villages, Feasts, and Training montages with the Villagers.
--
The Multiplayer modes utilize all of the game’s combat features, however your character is outfitted as certain soldier types, and you “purchase” your equipment with gold received from killing players and achieving goals. (mostly killing, though. :D)
Game modes can range from epic Battles and Sieges to calm Duels.
--
All of these features are present in the Vanilla game. The
DLC adds a multiplayer Gunpowder-Era mode (which has a thriving player-base). The modding community is expansive, creating multiple worlds within the engine, ranging from Feudal Japan, to 11th Century Europe, to Rome, to the American Frontier.
This is a game that any PC gamer needs to play at least once. It is one of the few Gems of the PC Gaming archive, and deserves most if not all of the hype it has received from fans.

I was stuck on a level for a few minutes cause I was used to looking for the clues to the next step not realizing I had to croutch in order to go under some debris blocking a doorway.
Over all though I'd recommend the game for a good side scrolling zombie adventure.

To also compare it to other video-games: Battlefield 4, the 'other' big shooter of last year which direclty competed with Ghosts, runs at maximum settings and 1080p with always above 60 FPS for most new machines. If you take the same rig for a spin on Ghosts you actually have to tone down the graphics a notch to get into CoD-playable regions, since CoD also - always - had strong disadvantages if your FPS is all over the place and not at a rock solid 60+. A fantastic cooperative campaign-based game where you have to fight through hordes of Rats with your 3 other teammates, L4D(2)-esque.
This is certainly a competent game, as the meat of the game, the melee combat, immediately feels satisfying. This was especailly important to get right, as you will be spending most of your time slashing away at incoming hordes, and a huge Hammer sending a wave of incoming Rats flying back won't get tiring anytime soon.
After 40+ hours I'm still thoroughly enjoying the feedback you get when using your melee weapons, and the game has an extremely challenging difficulty too, way more challenging than L4D2's Expert difficulty (imho).
The gloomy environments, set in a dark fantasy world, and the change from Zombies to hordes of Rats are certainly welcome.
This game has a lot of potential, on top of its already substantial base game, and there can be done so much with future content. At the time of this review, there are only 3 maps released (pre-order beta), and I already feel satisfied with my decision to get this game. The addition of 10 more maps at release is most likely only going to confirm that feeling, so I can, without a doubt, give this game a thumbs up, and I hope it does well, so the developer can build on top of the base game and keep adding features to enhance it further.

This was my most anticipated game for 2015, and in general, and its... dissappointing, to say the least.  I love Hotline Miami 1, I have about 75 hours into it, and I used to casually speedrun it.  Hotline Miami 2's graphics, music and overall atmosphere are on par with the first game's, but that's where the positive comparisons stop.  HM2's gameplay, story and overall execution are worse than the first game's.  Now let's go into detail-
Story:  I won't talk much about the story, because I don't really play games for the story, but there are way too many characters (I believe there are 13), and the ending is anti-climactic.
Graphics:  Same graphics as HM1, still amazing.
Music:  Fantastic, but I preferred HM1's soundtrack.
Gameplay:  Oh boy, here we go...  I would like to start out by saying that a game that got delayed for around 6-8 months should not have MORE bugs than its predecessor...   So, the gameplay..
-Too much focus on gunplay, melee weapons are basically useless.  There are way too many guys with guns, and the only way to take them out is with guns.
-Levels are WAY too big (almost all of the later levels are bigger than your SHIFT-camera will allow you to see, so many times you have to almost get yourself killed trying to look ahead.)  And you are punished for recklessness.  In HM1, "Recklessness is rewarded", but being reckless in HM2 will only get you killed.
-There are small invisible walls around basically every single solid object or wall, which make it really difficult to kill guys who are directly around the corner.  I presume they did this in order to prevent some of the glitches from HM1 from occuring again (like being able to shoot through certain walls, and being able to kill the guy in the prison cell on Assault from outside the cell), but it makes melee combat even more frustrating.
-The range of your fists is slightly shorter, thus making melee combat even MORE frustrating.
-The AI is even worse than in HM1.  People get stuck on doors WAY too often, dogs AND humans both randomly go in circles for no reason, baiting is still as frustrating as HM1 (using guns to bait is STILL completely random, but peeking around corners seems to work more often than before).  The two swan fans (one uses a chainsaw, and one uses a gun)  seem awesome in theory, but execution is once again poor.  The gun guy gets stuck on EVERYTHING, and he is never where you need him to be.
-Not sure if this is a glitch, but sometimes guys with guns who are running at you will stop directly in front of you, right out of your melee range, and then shoot you.  It feels extremely unfair.
-If you use the characters who have "killing fists" and cant use weapons, they will sometimes randomly do an animation that takes approximately 3 seconds while killing dogs, thus getting you killed as a result.  I cant figure out what causes the animation, but sometimes it leaves you vulnerable to other dogs or people
-Game overall feels way slower than HM1.  It's like the devs forgot what made HM1 so great.
So overall, I would not recommend this game.  The devs lost sight of what made the first game so great, and what they did differently was executed extremely poorly.  Later levels felt like a chore, abilities weren't as interesting or fun to use, AI is even more glitchy, too much focus on guns, punished for using melee weapons, and punished for being reckless.  Oh, and it did not ship with a level editor... wtf?
EDIT:  Some things I forgot...
-no random weapon pickups within stages, which makes this game even less interesting
-weapon spread is still random (only a problem with shotguns, really)

is one of the only games I have ever played that has been consistently entertaining throughout multiple playthroughs. This is a game that can be played in both doses and marathons, without losing its appeal.
The game takes place in the fictional region of “Calradia,” a land dominated by 6 factions, all with their own unique units, armors, and fighting styles. You play as a lone adventurer, who leads his/her army throughout their adventures in the realm.
Once you begin your game, you are taught the basics of the gameplay mechanics and then given your first mission, which will begin your adventure.
The game has three distinct sections:
1.	The Overhead/Strategic Map
2.	 “Scenes”
3.	Battle Mode
From the overhead map, you can see settlements and their owners, enemy war parties, and bandit lairs. From this view, you may move your party across the map to any of these locations, where you can interact with NPCs or, in the case of settlements, walk around the area.
Scenes are the locations where the player controls their character outright. These take place in either Settlement or Dialogue form.
Settlements are large areas where other NPCs (primarily villagers and townsmen) roam. These areas also lead into smaller scenes, such as Taverns, Castles, and Prisons.
Dialogue scenes primarily take place between the character and any other party encountered on the map, but can also take place within Settlements. As is expected, these scenes allow the player to interact with NPCs to perform a variety of actions.
In the case of Lords/Ladies, you can perform certain actions to increase your relation with them, such as quests or simple conversation.
In the case of others, you can ask questions, purchase items, receive quests, and recruit mercenaries and companions to your party.
Battle mode is where the major chunk of the gameplay is found. Here, your character and his/her army engage in combat with a variety of enemies.
The game’s combat mechanic is simple:
Your character can carry 4 items, Melee and Ranged Weapons, and Ammunition and Shields.
You can form any combination of these, including multiple shields, to combat your enemies. Certain weapons are more effective against certain enemies, such as a spear vs. cavalry, or a sword vs. archers.
Your character becomes more effective with certain weapon types over time, and develops skills as they level up, which provide multiple bonuses to yourself or your party.
If you have any of the aforementioned companions, you can personally outfit them as you like, making your own unique soldiers.
Battle’s are going to be your early source of income, as they produce loot, as well as small amounts of money, and in some cases, prisoners.
Armies are comprised of 4 types of units:
Infantry, Archers, Cavalry, and Horse Archers (considered Cavalry, but work much differently than other Cavalry units).
Each faction has their own unique units in each of these classes, or in some cases, none at all. (Some factions may not have Cavalry, but have stronger Infantry or Archers)
Each of these units perform as you would imagine. Archers get in damage from a range and can help thin an attacker’s numbers before they reach your infantry.
Infantry are your footsoldiers, who deal the most damage and form the backbone of your army.
Cavalry are used to charge an enemy and break their formations, and certain cavalry units are capable of defeating enemy cavalry.
Horse Archers, reminiscent of the Mongol and Hunnic hordes are a big threat against infantry-based armies. They can easily ride around your troops, firing arrows while staying out of range.
Your units are each assigned to different sections of your army, numbered 1-9, which can be renamed as you like. If you want Knights in your Archers group, the game won’t stop you.
Companions are recruited in Taverns, for varying prices.
They all have unique backstories and personalities, and some get along better than others.
Your companions will have different opinions of each other and, consequently, you based on their behaviour. They can be outfitted as you like, and assigned to certain number groups, like other units. This way, should you want to, you can make Lancers, Skirmishers, Legionaries, Berserkers, Javelineers, or even Clubbers. (No, not the kind you find on Thursday nights when you’re not on your computer.)
These Companions can also be sent on missions for you.
The game is comprised of 6 kingdoms, with multiple fiefs yours for the taking.
You can accomplish this through direct conquest or, should you be well renowned, vassalisation. Joining a faction gives you a relation boost with its vassals, and gives you a bit more security than if you started your own faction.
Conquering fiefs expands your kingdom’s borders, and helps your character gain power.
Castles and Towns require Garrisons, which require wages. These troops defend your fiefs when you are not present, and depending on their strength, are more or less likely to be successful at this. 100 Recruits are less likely to successfully defend than 100 Swordsmen.
The game also allows marriage, some diplomatic interaction between factions, vassalisation of companions, trade (entirely player-managed. No missions, prices vary between towns), Arena Combat, Duels (between lords), Tournaments, Prisoner Sales/Ransoms, Looting of villages, Feasts, and Training montages with the Villagers.
--
The Multiplayer modes utilize all of the game’s combat features, however your character is outfitted as certain soldier types, and you “purchase” your equipment with gold received from killing players and achieving goals. (mostly killing, though. :D)
Game modes can range from epic Battles and Sieges to calm Duels.
--
All of these features are present in the Vanilla game. The
DLC adds a multiplayer Gunpowder-Era mode (which has a thriving player-base). The modding community is expansive, creating multiple worlds within the engine, ranging from Feudal Japan, to 11th Century Europe, to Rome, to the American Frontier.
This is a game that any PC gamer needs to play at least once. It is one of the few Gems of the PC Gaming archive, and deserves most if not all of the hype it has received from fans.

Call of Duty: Ghosts is the 10th installment in the long-running Call of Duty franchise. This installment takes place after a catastrophic event leaves the United States and its military in a weakened state. A small squad of deadly killers known as the 'Ghosts' is ultimately tasked with the destruction of the Federation and restoring freedom to their homeland.
While this game doesn't offer a vastly new experience over other titles in the series, Call of Duty: Ghosts is still a solid experience that manages to fulfill the various traits associated with typical action games. You can expect some solid gameplay, acceptable graphics and a continuously awesome multiplayer mode with this - plus, you get a badass alien invasion game mode.
Gameplay consists of running, gunning, crouching, sliding, jumping, using your iron sights, and using some gadgets; everything works the way its supposed to, and firefights feel the way they should. If you've played any other Call of Duty titles before, you'll fall right into the familiar groove of sprinting and popping baddies with your assault rifle. The nice array of weapons and attachments allows you to go with varied loadouts unique to your playstyle; I especially liked the attention made to many of the new rifles included in this installment. The gun sounds (while unrealistic) sound extremely awesome in this game, as they are sufficiently loud/explosive enough to make you feel like a badass.
The visuals in this game are somewhat inconistent and are rarely outstanding, however. Many levels in the game are the same murky-brown environments we've grown accustomed to in this genre; despite this, one or two levels that dared indulge in some greenery and varied landscapes actually looked quite beautiful thanks to the impressive lighting. The visuals are never terrible, it's just that they don't exactly rise to the standards of newer games like The Witcher and other impressive titles.
The campaign mode, while quite short, offers everything you've come to expect from the franchise and will take you up to 10 hours to complete. The story and character development is completely disposable here, but the campaign is still a good 'tutorial' mode for new players. Call of Duty veterans should feel free to skip this mode completely.
The Extinction game mode allows players to fight off waves of bug-like aliens in several different maps; this is a co-op experience where players have to destroy enemy nests using drills, all the while ensuring that the invading aliens don't get too close. While this mode isn't particularly inventive, I thought it was a good bit of fun to enjoy with friends.
The Multiplayer mode is still your standard fare, and will definitely entice veterans of the franchise. The usual unlocks, levelling up system and customisation options are still here, and the addition of new game modes is certainly a welcome change. Nothing particularly new here, but it still feels fun to play if you enjoyed previous Call of Duty titles.
Overall, Call of Duty: Ghosts is a solid title despite its lack of innovation. If you enjoy Call of Duty or are looking for a decent multiplayer game, you might consider picking this up for $20 in a sale. If you have grown tired of the franchise, however, you would not enjoy this game as it offers little change over previous titles. A good romp to enjoy by yourself or with friends! 7.5 / 10

This has to be one of the prettiest open-world sandbox games. While others sandbox games fill themselves with the 2D or voxel art styles, this game concentrates it on the 3D world like another similar game, Windborne. While Windborne concerns itself within a magical realm and makes everything centered around building defenses for your new kingdom, Planet Explorers sets you down as a human colonist on the planet Maria. There's a more sci-fi/modern twist to an already saturated genre.
Also, there's an Adventure Mode. Minecraft lets you do whatever you want as they just plop you into the game mode. Planet Explorers is trying to give you a story. Since it's a beta, the word 'engaging' is far from it. The quests in Adventure Mode mirrors predecessors like World of Warcraft. Fetch, kill, escort, harvest - it's tedium faced from other games in a Single Player  environment. The only difference between World of Warcraft and Planet Explorers is that there is the allowance of creativity that WoW cannot afford in its multiplayer experience.
I have yet to play the other two modes but when I do, I will give my full review here.

You're trying to seed human life on a new world. As you descend, your ship collides with what looks like some sort of magic hover city, destroying both it and your ship. Small life pods eject, sending those who weren't killed in the first explosion down to the surface to try their damndest to survive.
That's where you begin.
Help your fellow crewmates heal their injuries and collect together, defend against the occasional monster stampede and assemble a fortress to protect those who remain as you struggle to secure life, and begin the existence you intended from the start. Will you make friends with the indingenous sentient species? Can you even survive their outrunners long enough to try? Learn designs to assemble all the things needed to live well and comfortably, from huge laser cannons that rest on top of your most vulerable buildings to eggshell chairs like people loved in the 1970s, you eventually learn it all from your friends and potential new allies.
But there is more danger than you might think at first.
Beware, explorer, the depths of the forests for they hold creatures I can only refer to as like the Chimeras of S.T.A.L.K.E.R. fame. Oceans, fish that could eat blue whales in 5 bites. The skies conceal huge birds, but a quick wit and a well-maintianed rifle can nearly keep you even from being harmed by them.
What will you build? An impenetrable steel fortress with 30 foot walls that stand in mocking defiance of the local beasts? An underground compound filled with laberynthine passages and high-tech facilities? A huge golden tower gleaming in the sun, staring down from a huge mesa or mountainrange?
That's for you to decide.
The only thing the makers of the game care about, is you enjoy their carefully crafted world of make-believe.
