Hotline Miami asked players a simple question; "
". If you answered yes, that's good. Being brutal and throwing caution to the wind rewarded the player with a higher score (seriously, there's a score catagory called "Boldness"). Most levels were designed in a way that alowed to to take a bold approach, killing each mobster that came at you with a baseball bat that you had forcefully taken from its previous owner. Gun weilding mobsters were (almost) always in range of a thrown weapon, and nothing felt better than gutting a mobster with a knife thrown across the room, picking it back up, and continuing on your rampage.
Hotline Miami 2 askes players a different question; "
". The second game felt less about "how fast can I kill this room full of mobsters?", and more about "Let's stand by this corner and see how many mobsters I can lure over to me". I have to worry if enemies will see me as I quietly slash their friends to bits, as I have limited ammunition and the only ammo box is half way across the stage. One level (Death Wish, I believe), I was playing as Alex & Ash, and
thought to myself "If I shoot here, I can attract some mobsters towards me and kill them as they come around the corner".
(but not Revengence; that's what this game
be).
You'll notice this "stealth" mentality most often during chapters where you play as the soldier. The soldier starts every level with a gun of the players choice and a knife. You can switch between the two weapons on the fly, which makes dealing with fat guys and their friends much easier. The downside to this is that you can not pick up droped guns, even after your starting gun has run dry. To use your gun again, you are required to find ammo boxes that are in set locations in each level. Not exactly the best mechanic ever, as in most of these levels you are requied to take out ranged enemies as well as fat guys, who are immune to melee weapons.
If you haven't figured out by now, I'll say this; I'm a melee guy. Give me the option between a uzi and a golf club, and I'll start hitting hole-in-ones with my foes heads. Rarely did I ever use a gun in HLM 1, or ever feel the need to (except for the fat guys (thugs); ♥♥♥♥ those guys). Fastforward to Wrong Number, where melee is not a viable option. Foes are armed with guns and put at the end of narrow hallways and other open areas, forcing you to put down your trusty buldgeing object and pick up a pistol, lock on from a distance, and try to hit them. Better yet, try shooting them with Ash.
.
I'll ignore the problems with the buggy AI (helicopter dogs, deaf mobsters, and Ash the not-so-great follower), as those can (hopefully) be patched in a later update.
The one saving grace that this game has is it's soundtrack (which I'm actually listening to it as I write this). For every amazing song that HLM 1 had, Wrong Number has one that's even greater (Roller Mobster, Sexualizer, Richard(by Dubmood)). Each scene has a song that matches it perfectly.
Overall, is it as good as the first game? No. Does it have it's flaws? Yes. Are fat guys still anoying as hell?
. But is it good as a game in general? Yes (well, actually the answer depends on the person but screw you this is my review). Compaired to it's predecessor, Wrong Number falls flat. But mabey the community can fix part of that when the level editor is released.
ADHD Version: It's not as good as the first game, but it still has it's moments (and that soundtrack).
Sure, levels are bigger and harder and provide annoyances, but this game is FUN. It is on the same quality level as the original and much longer.

God, it physically pains me to write this, but...
I just cannot recommend Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number.
I love the original Hotline Miami, I think it is one of the best games I have ever played. Incredibly invigorating through its amazing visual design, soundtrack, and fast-paced, strategic in the "think on your feet" kind of way. The second game has the first two made even better, but destroyed the gameplay, sadly.
How did it do that? Through the god-awful level design and shift of focus from fast-paced combat with a mix of ranged and melee attacks to the slow-paced, repetitive gameplay that is a mixture of unfair and punishing.
The levels in the new Hotline Miami game are all extremely large, and are generally so big that enemies will shoot you from outside of your maximum vision range while holding shift. In addition to this, there are way more windows than before, so you get murdered by enemies that you had no clue even existed. The first game was difficult, sure, but in a fair way. Theoretically, someone who was really good at the game could play through the whole thing the first time and never die. It doesn't happen, of course, because nearly no one could be that good on their first try, but it's possible. That is not the case here. In HM2, you will die. A lot. You need to die, a lot, so you can memorize the location of all the enemies in the map. Its slow, repetitive, and frustrating. If you ♥♥♥♥ up your plan even a little bit, you will not be able to do like in the first and improvise your way out of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ situation. You'll get shot from across the map or killed by a dog when there are no melee weapons around.
Speaking of "when there are no melee weapons around": There are never any goddamn melee weapons around. HM2 is now almost entirely focused on gunplay. The first game had incredibly powerful guns that could completely screw you over by firing just a single shot, with attracting tons of enemies to kill you. Of course, in that game, you could improvise and kill all of the approaching enemies. No longer is this something that happens in HM2. Guns are everywhere in the new game, and melee weapons are almost entirely forgotten. And guns aren't fun anymore. Guns are still loud, but the enemy AI only hears the gunfire half the time, and there is no more improvisation and clever, emergent gameplay that comes from shooting a gun. Now, you either shoot all the other enemies, or you die.  There is no juxtaposition between the quiet, knife throwing and stabby fast gameplay and the loud, guns blazing approaches that you needed to mix to survive in the original. All there is now is constant shooting, and both the levels and new mechanics help encourage this lack of gameplay diversity and fun.
I really liked the first game, and it really hurts to have to say this. But you should not get Hotline Miami 2. I will change this review when the level editor comes out, if I feel that it is powerful enough to allow people to get to recreating the amazing style of levels from the first.

I wish I could give this game a nutral rating or something.
To be more precise, I loved the first game a hell of a lot, like, to death.  Nearly got every achievement and played it quite a lot, so as you can imagine I was excited as hell to get my hands on this game.
The good stuff:

The details:
After playing it a hell of a lot, I'd say it's pretty good, but nowhere near as good or as polished as number one.  The main reason being  the gunplay.  You didn't need to use guns that much in the first game because there was not a particular need, which was good because the guns weren't particularly useful in the first game.  They were pretty flawed, and not terribly reliable.  On the enemy end of things, you could out run and manuvere them easily. Areas were closed in, and you could use rooms to put distance between you and the enemy.  In this game, you're forced into wide open areas with lots of off screen enemies who can snipe yo with thier weapons pretty well, so if you're not good with the flawed gunplay, you're gonna have a bad time. It feels more like they designed the game around the twins but didn't realize the majority of the characters didn't play like them.
I really want to play this game to the end, but I have no idea if I'll have the mental stamina to be able to do it despite being two levels from it, I'd much rather play the original or the bugged to hell resident evil revelations 2 than this. I'm close to the end but I can't bring myself to choke down any more of this, let alone play it on a harder difficulty to get more of the story, although I hear it's easier the seond time around due to loadout choice, and having memorized a bit of the layout and enemy behaviour.
I wanted to love this game, but I just can't.  It's not as fun as the first to play, it forces you into a certain playstyle, and goes completely against the idea of versitility the first game instilled in us.  I've already seen the ending online, and it's interesting, but I doubt I'll play it as much as the first one.  All in all a let down, if only due to the poor level design choices, and bad gunplay mechanics.  Newcomers might like this installment more, but I'd still say to stick with the first.

One word to describe HM2: Frustrating.
Frustrating Levels.
Frustrating Gameplay.
Frustrating Story.
Frustrating AI.
Frustrating Design.
Frustrating Camera.
Frustrating Sprites.
Even more frustrating is that I like the original alot. The levels were small and tightly made to accentuate the fast paced action that was the staple to the game. Melee and guns were equally useful. The story was easy to ride along with and started straight forward enough which made the hallucinations more impressive when they started showing up, plus it had a rather decent closure.
Hotline Miami 2 ditches these things for the worse. It's hard to pick which is the most annoying flaw this game makes over it's predecessor, as everything morphs together to create an enormous mass of Frustrating. The big levels, for example, seems like the logical step up from the small apartments of the first, but the small amount of view the camera provides ensures that enemies will see you long before you see them (the gameplay pictures above are NOT what the camera is like, the game version covers about half that, seriously why don't we have THAT camera, Dennaton). That doesn't seem too bad, until you realize that Hotline Miami 2 decided that Gunplay was the step up from Melee, and since a single bullet means death, you will get blindsided and killed about 20 times per level. Oh, and since the Levels are bigger, the restarting because you failed to notice the final guy who blends in very well to the enviroment after spending a few minutes becomes even more exasperating after the 15th f*cking time.
If this were to happen in the first game, you would become angry and charge through the level in a bloodlust and realize that being a madman gets you better results. Then you would mentally pat the game on the head for being a cheeky thing and continue on your way. Not in Hotline Miami 2. Nope, you HAVE to play smart in this one, utilizing chokepoints, luring enemies, remembering window and guard locations, ACCURATELY PLACING SHOTS (the epitome of caution). Then the game has the gall to give you a low rating for being slow and methodical.
Of course, Hotline Miami 2 isn't above giving you bullsh*t in it's levels either. Random weapons spawn are practically non-existant now so if you use too many bullets, which is easy, you have no choice but to be killed by a fat ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who HAS to be shot to be killed. The funny bit is that bullets running out is the least of it. Many levels give me the impression as the creator giving me the middle finger. Like the first room being an open hallway with a thug with a bat, a patrolling enemy with an assault rifle and a previously mentioned fat ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ right behind the guy with the assault rifle. Or a level where there is practically no cover and there are twelve guys with an assault rifles. Or the time the game says, look you can have two machine guns and have them shoot in opposite directions, go matrix on them, but enemies shoot ahead of where your moving so do the math.
The last, final, worst nail in the coffin is the ending. It's as if the writer was asked to tie up the everything, said "F*ck You", and picked an ending completely unrelated to the actions of all the characters. In fact I'm pretty sure that's what happened. My only way this ending makes sense is if there is a secret, less terrible ending.
In closing, avoid this game, even, perhaps especially, if you like the original. It's ambition to become bigger than it's predecessor has ended up crippling itself. At best, the game can only offer a kickass soundtrack and a few enjoyable moments that only register because of the massive amounts of frustration between said moments.
And at worst, you wasted 15 bucks to give yourself a migrane and gray hair.

It feels like Catusquid broke the cardinal rule of game design: Don't put story before mechanics.
+The Writer was fun
+In depth look at events from the first game
+Interesting topics touched in the story
+Decent soundtrack
-Levels aren't as well designed
-Buggy and often inconsistent
-Little reason to enage the story or replay levels

What was so amazing about the first game was the amount of detail in each stage being a functional level. It was inviting to the maniacal and the methotical.
In this installment, the levels are too open and often unforgiving. The change of characters is too frequent for the player to develop a consistent playstyle like 'Jacket' of the first hotline miami, and there's no real engagement for the player to feel involved with any of the storylines.
The dialogue of this Hotline is also about agency, but it feels disconected. Although I am controlling characters for parts of dialogue, I'm not as attached as I was with Jacket. The game touches on some interesting things like gender roles, violence in media, and nature vs nurture, but I felt little concern about what characters were discussing. The reasons why I should complete some levels wasn't presented as well as doing them for no reason as Jacket and having the psychological element.
Often I felt bored or frustrated instead of challenged. I would consistently be killed from offscreen or I would be killed through a wall with melee, and this would shatter my experience. The most fun I had was as The Writer, who used classic playstyle to a new element. Aside from that, I felt helpless without a gun, and comboing wasn't as viable with the larger maps.
With little reward from either gameplay or story, I feel this game just didn't have the love as its precursor did. This game didn't make me question as much about my potential taste for hurting other people. I would've prefered the story of this game just be contained within the digital comics, and a Hotline Miami 2 that flowed as smoothly as the first one. This game tries to do too much at once.

Is this game terrible? No. Is this game worth buying? Definitely not.
Unfortunately this game is one of the most frustrating titles I own and for all the wrong reasons. At heart, this game is a very aesthetically pleasing 2D Puzzle Platformer. It could have been one of the best on the market if it wasn't for one thing. The jumping. Why have a platformer with jumping as bad as this? It defies all belief. It is a massive shame. He will launch himself forwards when you press jump even if you're standing perfectly still and not touching any directional button. I will give them credit for trying to implement a nice wall jump mechanic but unfortunately it only works when and if it wants to.
I have also had numerous problems with the game not working properly. Pausing the game will take about 60 seconds to load and has even crashed the game before. Objectives sometimes will not show up until I've died and tried it again. I'm not entirely sure why these things happen but it is truly remarkable.
These things disappoint me most because it is actually a promising game. The graphics are incredible and it is something that we've not seen much of in the past. The story is a bit lacking but that's not usually that important in a game like this. The melee combat is dreadful but I actually found myself enjoying the shooting mechanic. It fit the style the game was going for perfectly and I wish there was more of it.
The puzzles in the game are very very basic puzzles and shouldn't tax your brain too hard if you're used to this type of game. However the game does utilise the use of beginners traps which is kind of a shame. They are to platforming and jump scares are to horror games. They just feel cheap and unnecessary.
Overall this game isn't the most horrible thing ever but it's such a shame that it let itself down so badly. Jumping is vital in a platformer and they failed to even get remotely close, especially in tandem with the dodgy running mechanic. This game could be worth picking up cheaply in a sale but it definitely doesn't deserve to be high on your wishlist. If ever they decide to make another game like this though, honestly look out for it. If they get it right then it will be a masterpiece.

Let me start by saying that I am not the biggest fan of Left for Dead style games nor the actual L4D series itself.
That said, I can whole heartedly recommend this game to anybody who likes team oriented hack and slash gameplay.  Why?  Well, keep on reading.
Pros:
Fun, addictive gameplay.  Doubly so if you have friends.
Tough difficulty, rarely holds your hand
Gorey, visceral feeling combat
Great SFX
Good GFX, really portrays the doom and gloom feeling of Warhammer
Loot based system keeps you playing
Randomly spawning enemies keeps things fresh
All 5 characters have unique playstyles
Cons:
Difficulty(yes, both a pro and a con) If you try to bite off more than you chew too often, soon you'll find yourself 3 or 4 games without a victory or any loot
Very little reward for failure
Hit boxes are a bit strange, sometimes you will hit when you don't expect to or miss when you expect to contact
Frustrating pick up groups.  It sucks to jump into hard mode with a guy who is level 3 and will probably die at any moment.
This is a game that you want to get your friends into and play with people you can depend on.  Sticking with randoms can work too but it can also be very frustrating. It borrows many elements from the L4D series and if you are even slightly familiar with those games you will instantly recognize them, but this turns out to flow well in it's own way, succeeding to differentiate itself nicely from the L4D style.
Overall, buy this game if you enjoy simple, gorey team-oriented action with a dash of RP elements.
Or if you hate rats.  A lot.

God, it physically pains me to write this, but...
I just cannot recommend Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number.
I love the original Hotline Miami, I think it is one of the best games I have ever played. Incredibly invigorating through its amazing visual design, soundtrack, and fast-paced, strategic in the "think on your feet" kind of way. The second game has the first two made even better, but destroyed the gameplay, sadly.
How did it do that? Through the god-awful level design and shift of focus from fast-paced combat with a mix of ranged and melee attacks to the slow-paced, repetitive gameplay that is a mixture of unfair and punishing.
The levels in the new Hotline Miami game are all extremely large, and are generally so big that enemies will shoot you from outside of your maximum vision range while holding shift. In addition to this, there are way more windows than before, so you get murdered by enemies that you had no clue even existed. The first game was difficult, sure, but in a fair way. Theoretically, someone who was really good at the game could play through the whole thing the first time and never die. It doesn't happen, of course, because nearly no one could be that good on their first try, but it's possible. That is not the case here. In HM2, you will die. A lot. You need to die, a lot, so you can memorize the location of all the enemies in the map. Its slow, repetitive, and frustrating. If you ♥♥♥♥ up your plan even a little bit, you will not be able to do like in the first and improvise your way out of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ situation. You'll get shot from across the map or killed by a dog when there are no melee weapons around.
Speaking of "when there are no melee weapons around": There are never any goddamn melee weapons around. HM2 is now almost entirely focused on gunplay. The first game had incredibly powerful guns that could completely screw you over by firing just a single shot, with attracting tons of enemies to kill you. Of course, in that game, you could improvise and kill all of the approaching enemies. No longer is this something that happens in HM2. Guns are everywhere in the new game, and melee weapons are almost entirely forgotten. And guns aren't fun anymore. Guns are still loud, but the enemy AI only hears the gunfire half the time, and there is no more improvisation and clever, emergent gameplay that comes from shooting a gun. Now, you either shoot all the other enemies, or you die.  There is no juxtaposition between the quiet, knife throwing and stabby fast gameplay and the loud, guns blazing approaches that you needed to mix to survive in the original. All there is now is constant shooting, and both the levels and new mechanics help encourage this lack of gameplay diversity and fun.
I really liked the first game, and it really hurts to have to say this. But you should not get Hotline Miami 2. I will change this review when the level editor comes out, if I feel that it is powerful enough to allow people to get to recreating the amazing style of levels from the first.

I wish I could give this game a nutral rating or something.
To be more precise, I loved the first game a hell of a lot, like, to death.  Nearly got every achievement and played it quite a lot, so as you can imagine I was excited as hell to get my hands on this game.
The good stuff:

Here's the bad stuff:

-mostly weak player characters
-bugs from the previous game are still present and more frequent
-gamebreaking file corrupting bug
The details:
After playing it a hell of a lot, I'd say it's pretty good, but nowhere near as good or as polished as number one.  The main reason being  the gunplay.  You didn't need to use guns that much in the first game because there was not a particular need, which was good because the guns weren't particularly useful in the first game.  They were pretty flawed, and not terribly reliable.  On the enemy end of things, you could out run and manuvere them easily. Areas were closed in, and you could use rooms to put distance between you and the enemy.  In this game, you're forced into wide open areas with lots of off screen enemies who can snipe yo with thier weapons pretty well, so if you're not good with the flawed gunplay, you're gonna have a bad time. It feels more like they designed the game around the twins but didn't realize the majority of the characters didn't play like them.
I really want to play this game to the end, but I have no idea if I'll have the mental stamina to be able to do it despite being two levels from it, I'd much rather play the original or the bugged to hell resident evil revelations 2 than this. I'm close to the end but I can't bring myself to choke down any more of this, let alone play it on a harder difficulty to get more of the story, although I hear it's easier the seond time around due to loadout choice, and having memorized a bit of the layout and enemy behaviour.
I wanted to love this game, but I just can't.  It's not as fun as the first to play, it forces you into a certain playstyle, and goes completely against the idea of versitility the first game instilled in us.  I've already seen the ending online, and it's interesting, but I doubt I'll play it as much as the first one.  All in all a let down, if only due to the poor level design choices, and bad gunplay mechanics.  Newcomers might like this installment more, but I'd still say to stick with the first.

One word to describe HM2: Frustrating.
Frustrating Levels.
Frustrating Gameplay.
Frustrating Story.
Frustrating AI.
Frustrating Design.
Frustrating Camera.
Frustrating Sprites.
Even more frustrating is that I like the original alot. The levels were small and tightly made to accentuate the fast paced action that was the staple to the game. Melee and guns were equally useful. The story was easy to ride along with and started straight forward enough which made the hallucinations more impressive when they started showing up, plus it had a rather decent closure.
Hotline Miami 2 ditches these things for the worse. It's hard to pick which is the most annoying flaw this game makes over it's predecessor, as everything morphs together to create an enormous mass of Frustrating. The big levels, for example, seems like the logical step up from the small apartments of the first, but the small amount of view the camera provides ensures that enemies will see you long before you see them (the gameplay pictures above are NOT what the camera is like, the game version covers about half that, seriously why don't we have THAT camera, Dennaton). That doesn't seem too bad, until you realize that Hotline Miami 2 decided that Gunplay was the step up from Melee, and since a single bullet means death, you will get blindsided and killed about 20 times per level. Oh, and since the Levels are bigger, the restarting because you failed to notice the final guy who blends in very well to the enviroment after spending a few minutes becomes even more exasperating after the 15th f*cking time.
If this were to happen in the first game, you would become angry and charge through the level in a bloodlust and realize that being a madman gets you better results. Then you would mentally pat the game on the head for being a cheeky thing and continue on your way. Not in Hotline Miami 2. Nope, you HAVE to play smart in this one, utilizing chokepoints, luring enemies, remembering window and guard locations, ACCURATELY PLACING SHOTS (the epitome of caution). Then the game has the gall to give you a low rating for being slow and methodical.
Of course, Hotline Miami 2 isn't above giving you bullsh*t in it's levels either. Random weapons spawn are practically non-existant now so if you use too many bullets, which is easy, you have no choice but to be killed by a fat ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who HAS to be shot to be killed. The funny bit is that bullets running out is the least of it. Many levels give me the impression as the creator giving me the middle finger. Like the first room being an open hallway with a thug with a bat, a patrolling enemy with an assault rifle and a previously mentioned fat ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ right behind the guy with the assault rifle. Or a level where there is practically no cover and there are twelve guys with an assault rifles. Or the time the game says, look you can have two machine guns and have them shoot in opposite directions, go matrix on them, but enemies shoot ahead of where your moving so do the math.
The last, final, worst nail in the coffin is the ending. It's as if the writer was asked to tie up the everything, said "F*ck You", and picked an ending completely unrelated to the actions of all the characters. In fact I'm pretty sure that's what happened. My only way this ending makes sense is if there is a secret, less terrible ending.
In closing, avoid this game, even, perhaps especially, if you like the original. It's ambition to become bigger than it's predecessor has ended up crippling itself. At best, the game can only offer a kickass soundtrack and a few enjoyable moments that only register because of the massive amounts of frustration between said moments.
And at worst, you wasted 15 bucks to give yourself a migrane and gray hair.

What was so amazing about the first game was the amount of detail in each stage being a functional level. It was inviting to the maniacal and the methotical.
In this installment, the levels are too open and often unforgiving. The change of characters is too frequent for the player to develop a consistent playstyle like 'Jacket' of the first hotline miami, and there's no real engagement for the player to feel involved with any of the storylines.
The dialogue of this Hotline is also about agency, but it feels disconected. Although I am controlling characters for parts of dialogue, I'm not as attached as I was with Jacket. The game touches on some interesting things like gender roles, violence in media, and nature vs nurture, but I felt little concern about what characters were discussing. The reasons why I should complete some levels wasn't presented as well as doing them for no reason as Jacket and having the psychological element.
Often I felt bored or frustrated instead of challenged. I would consistently be killed from offscreen or I would be killed through a wall with melee, and this would shatter my experience. The most fun I had was as The Writer, who used classic playstyle to a new element. Aside from that, I felt helpless without a gun, and comboing wasn't as viable with the larger maps.
With little reward from either gameplay or story, I feel this game just didn't have the love as its precursor did. This game didn't make me question as much about my potential taste for hurting other people. I would've prefered the story of this game just be contained within the digital comics, and a Hotline Miami 2 that flowed as smoothly as the first one. This game tries to do too much at once.

Deadlight is a 2.5D (zombie) sidescroller with great visuals, good atmosphere and problematic control issues as well as bugs.
Recommended if you can overlook these flaws.
Set in the post-apolyptic Seattle you control a survivor named Randall Wayne looking for his family.
The story gives the game a little background, but aside from the expected minimum, there's not much to say about it: it's there so you have something to keep you interested enough, but there's no depth in the story to make you care about the characters. The plot-twist in the end was also kind of predictable and clichéd.

Gameplay-wise Deadlight is a typical platformer with limited gunplay element and a very few puzzles.
For most of the time these game elements are solid and deliver a couple of hours of fun, since Deadlight is painfully short.
However for some segments the controls don't work the way they intended: your character will do all sort of things you don't want him to, and there are some bugs that will cause problems that can be fixed with a reload only.
Overall Deadlight is a fairly entertaining game,
you can forgive some annoying bugs and problematic control issues.
If you can't and you're also worried about your blood pressure then stay away from this game, as it's almost certain it will cause some serious frustrations.
- Great 2.5D graphics.
- Good atmosphere. Especially if you're a fan of the zombie genre.
- Some parts are repetitive and boring.
- Dull and clichéd story.
- Too short: if you don't go for the Nightmare achievement, which is basicly the '1 life' run version of the story, then the game can be finished with all other achievements in 5-6 hours.
- Keyboard controls don't function at certain part of the game as intended. The "crouch" key is also highly recommended to be remapped.
- Occational bugs preventing game progression, leading to a reload to last checkpoint. These issues are a huge turn-down for those attempting to do "Nightmare" mode.
Chill game if you don't know what to play :)

I expected WAY too much from this game.
As of now, I am on the 17th level, in act 5. And, I have to say that I don't know what to think of Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number. On the plus side, you get a bigger picture in terms of plot, as the game takes place before, during, and after the events of the first game. You get to play as a group of vigilantes known as "The Fans", who are murdering gang members, addicts, all so that they can get the same phonecalls that Jacket got. You also get to play as a detective, trying to solve a number of homicides left by an unknown killer (as of where I am). Thirdly, you get to play as the detective's friend, who is trying to write a book about the "masked maniac" who killed off most of the Russian Mafia. Speaking of Russians, you can also play as a unhealthy redneck who has a snake fetish, and a hatred for Russians. Finally, you get to play as a soldier, fighting Russians in Hawaii. Those are only a few of the characters you can play as, not including special mission characters.
As for gameplay, they could have done such a better job. It's the same concept as the first game, but now you die from two bullets.  Now, I don't mind murdering people to the sound of M.O.O.N with a bloody bullet hole in my arm, but my biggest irk with the game is that the levels are designed with melee in mind, but most levels are only playable with heavy gunplay. Most of the thugs have guns, and the reflexes of a junkie on cocaine, meaning THEY WILL GET YOU BEFORE YOU GET THEM. This is okay if it was HM1, where the levels are nice and short (2-3 areas), but in HM2, most of the levels stretch on to 3-5 areas. Speaking of poor level design, for lack of a better word, it's horrid. in Hotline Miami 1, the designed the levels so that the player would always be in the center of the screen, in HM2, I find myself hugging the right side of the map on most levels, which takes away from the gunplay you need to pass the level. Hell, in some areas, I spawn off frame, which is a huge annoyance.
The masks are sometimes good, sometimes bad. if you even play as a masked character. The writer, Soldier, and Detective are pretty much Richard, and they take up most of the game so far. I've played 5 levels as The Fans, and 2 levels as Jake the Snake lover. The thing they could've done better with The Fans' masks, is make sure they aren't awkward to control. Corey the Zebra has a dodge roll that can avoid bullets and sometimes, melee attacks, but is useless for getting close enough for a kill, because when you stand back up, you're dead. Alex and Ash are two characters, Ash has a gun, Alex has a chainsaw, Ash follows Alex, but Ash is only useful for long range, since he is usually stuck behind a doorway at close range, so then he is only good for luring. Mark the Bear spawns with two machine guns, which can rotate 90° to shoot at the sides, which I haven't used once, sadly, you can only use other guns when the machine guns run out of ammo, making you drop them, you can't  even throw them. Finally, Good Ol' Tony The Tiger: I was extremely disappointed, Tony has been Nerfed to♥♥♥♥♥♥ He still has killing punches, but he plays a custom animation for killing dogs, which is terrible because they now attract enemies when attacking you, meaning you won't survive if you punch the dog, and his finishers now require two clicks to kill, lastly, he can't use ANY weapons, making him almost impossible for most levels, since almost all of them require heavy gunplay.
Although, the worst character has to be The Soldier, you get to choose one gun, and you get a tiny hunting knife, you can't pick up ANY weapons,  you only have a small amount of ammo, which can be refilled, but you only get a fraction of the ammo you start with. The Soldier is my least favorite character because his levels aren't just challenging, they are unfair. Oh, you're out of ammo, and there are still ten enemies left, half of which have rifles? HAVE FUN.  Spoiler about The Soldier
.
I've been bashing this game for the last four paragraphs, so let's focus on the positives. The soundtrack is amazing, they could not have done a better job. So many groovy murder tunes. Secondly, The story, if you've played HM1, fills in the blanks very well, I won't spoil it. Thirdly, the blood is so much more satisfying, it is a lot more like a fluid in the way that you can see it squirt out of your victim. Finally, if you bought the Digital Deluxe Edition, the PAYDAY 2 content you recieve is great, Jacket's masks are awesome, the weapon you get can two hit Heavy FBI units if fully charged, the submaachine gun comes with a custom paint job, the perk deck, when upgraded regenerates armor when an enemy is killed, and regenerates health when an enemy is melee killed. Finally, the way Jacket uses a tape recorder to communicate really shows that he is a ♥♥♥♥ing psychopath. I love it.
So, should you get Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number? Despite all the♥♥♥♥♥♥I've been giving the game, I think you should, if you can get past the poor level design, and awkward character movements, it really does a good job of concluding the Hotline Miami story.

I have finished one playthrough of "Deadlight". Just like I expected, a survival 2D zombie game, that includes puzzling challenges and stunts to survive. Gameplay, I would say decent. Deadlight does not have that action type gameplay. For example, simply enough you can not be "TriggerHappy" or "Run N Gun". This game was developed for the gamer to critically use their mind to solve puzzling traps that were made to kill the dead and the living, for the gamer to take their time before they proceed through the post-apocalyptic set in Seattle, and for the gamer to get frustrated with the controls. ( I jumped off a   window cause of that, I fell of a ledge cause of that, I restarted my last checkpoint several times because of that...yes the controls are not so smooth) and because of that, I realized that what made the game challenging yet frustrating. Deadlight kept me playing because of the storyline, I was curious if Randall Wayne, the main character will find this lovely wife and daughter. Deadlight is a good 2D zombie survival game. For the storyline and puzzling challenges, I enjoyed playing Deadlight to the end. A good ending, which I did not expect. I would only recommend this game to those who are into zombie survival, taking on puzzling challenges, and players who like 2D gaming.

This game is set in Seattle, in 1986. And hey, look, there's the Space Needle! That's cool! There's also a level set in cavernous sewer systems, complete with subway tunnels. Then the game sends you to "The Stadium." Hey, it's Seattle, and it's the 80s! Is it the venerable Kingdome, you ask? No, it's a giant hockey rink. Seriously, this rink is the size of a football field.
Because if there's three things Seattle is known for, it's its extensive, multi-level sewers, its subway system, and its pro hockey team.
It gets worse from there. The voice acting. Oh god, the voice acting. I had a bug while playing that caused the sound to cut out completely during some of the cutscenes, and I was GRATEFUL for it. There's not a single grown woman in this game whose delivery is on any setting other than "hysterical shrieking." I have a few issues with not one, but two separate women in this game begging the protagonist to shoot them in the face.
To say one good thing about it, the combat does a good job of presenting the "shadows," (zombies,) as a legitimate threat. One is easy to handle, but without a gun it's easy to get overwhelmed by just two or three of them at a time. See five of them running at you? It's time to get the hell out of Dodge.
Some of the platforming puzzles are interesting enough, but I completely stopped taking the game seriously when the game gave me a kid's slingshot to shoot pebbles at tin pans to lower elevators.
But then there's the whole, let's-hide-tons-of-hidden-collectibles-in-a-completely-linear-platformer thing. Guys. Not every game HAS to have collectibles. Though I'll give you some credit for making all of the civilian IDs you find have the same last names as famous serial killers. That's sort of interesting in a nonsensical way.
This game is terrible, guys.
I wanted it just to end, like a bad movie. Everyone else is right here: clunky controls, boring story. Pretty cool for a few hours, but I didn't think I'd make it through the last few hours.

I have a hard time recommending this game at full price.  I picked it up for $2.99 during the summer sale and it is worth that.  My main complaint is the sluggish and unresponsive controls.  It's infuriating at times.  Certain time sensitive areas becoming nearly impossible, not because of clever level design, but because of terrible controls.  Instead of getting that feeling when you finally break through like man that was an awesome challenge, it's more like thank god that's over with I hope I never have to deal with that again.  On the plus side the aesthetic is nice, good graphics, backgrounds, etc.  Story is meh but I've seen worse.  Again it's a good pickup while on sale but please do yourself a favor and don't waste $10 on this game.  2/5

While it looks nice, the controls in this game are terrible. What could have been a tense exacting post-apocalyptic nightmare is reduced to a real time event farce which is in turn redused to a frustrating joke. For Melee Combat read Assured Death, as your character completely against your will launches himself into a throng of zombies, then repeteadly misses with a series of laggy haymaking swipes witth his melee weapon before succumbing to the utterly frustrating stamina drain (seeminlgy designed to add insult to injury), before being clawed to pieces followed by you having to endure the red screen of death and indefencible load times again and again. Ballistics weapons are not much better with Zombies appearing from the background, and having to amble towards the screen before being available as targets on the same sice scrolling plane as the protagonist. He is, by the way, a rugged park ranger from the Toronto backwoods who can't swim - any water hazard deeper than his height spells instant death. Die and die again as you tentatively work out a step-perfect route through each screen.  The regaularity with which your character dies removes any tension from the event - fine in Dead Souls, not fine here. A complete missed opportunity poorly executed.

Overall I enjoyed this game, it is similar to Limbo and has a nice arcade feel to it and has some nice graphics. I would recommend this game but only if it is in the sale.
Cons - Controls can be a little confusing at times and it is a little short, Completed in under 5 hours.

The summary for my review of Bad Rats 2 HD Director's Cut GOTY Edition is that it's good.  Real good.
The somewhat longer version goes like this; the game stays very true to the Left 4 Dead formula in which it's based on.  You stay with your team or you die horribly.  Melee combat is visceral and enjoyable and the ranged options range from functional to downright explosive.  Gear allows some variation in play-style, though at the end of the day it's still "kill mouseman, move on to the next."  And that's not a bad thing; Skaven are a lot more enjoyable to kill than brainless zombies.
What truly sets this game apart is the 'love' that was put into it; this is not just Games Workshop getting some money for use of their IP, this is a game  that was obviously created by people who know and enjoy the Warhammer Fantasy universe.  The Skaven are appropriately ratty, and the player characters are brilliantly vocalized, delivering lines exactly as a diehard Warhammer fan would expect to hear.
Update, Post Vermintide 2 Reveal:
When I wrote my initial review, I was an old hat at the game.  Now I'm an old dusty hat with a worn brim in which several Skaven have taken residence within.  I still find the game very enjoyable, more so than many others that have come out recently.  In brief, time has done little to diminish my enjoyment, even after some 700 hours invested.  If anything, the only thing that has soured my view on the game is the anticipation for the sequel.

An enjoyable game marred by cheap deaths.
I put 8 hours into it, and it's fun to play. The platformer style works well and the emphasis on conserving ammunition adds the to the tension. The music is fantastic, especially in the Big Bird chapter, and I'd definitely recommend it to someone looking for some casual gameplay.
The storyline follows a straightforward formula, but it's well told so that doesn't go against it.
However, rather than the plot, music, or mechanics, the one thing I'll remember the most about this game is the cheap deaths. I put 8 hours into playing this game (according to the in-game timer), and I'd estimate that about 2 of those hours were spent repeating levels where the NPCs kill you before you can react, or when the environment decides it's going to kill you when you think you're past the danger zone. For example, in one chapter, you run through a collapsing tunnel and get onto a ladder at the end of it. The music calms, the screen stops shaking, you jump to another ladder and part of the ceiling falls off to kill you. Or another scene where you're running from armed NPCs behind you when two suddenly appear in front of you to kill you before you can shoot them.
In summary, it's a great game but it requires a lot of patience, which is not something I had expected from a 4-6 hour game.

This is an excelent game, a progession of the minecraft genre combined with the RPG MMO genre.
THe graphics, sound and music are well done, and there is plenty of attention to detail, plus as it is still in development, you can add your pennies worth both in the direction it should take and 'bug hunting'.
There are 3 main ellements to this game. The explore, mine and craft mode. Build mode, and Create mode.
The storyline game is reletivly complete and highly playable, though some of the character behaviour and object template distribution still needs work.
You start near your crashed spaceship in a beautiful alien landscape with strange plants. A nearby character gives you a few basic object templates (called scripts in game) which allow you to craft some basic kit (the usual, shovel, axe, sword etc) and a quest.
You are free to roam, cut down trees, dig holes and fight creatures for resource gathering. No special table is required for crafting, if you have the script and the raw mats required then you can make the item.
As with all these games it is wise to remain relativly close to your starting point and to make some useful kit before ranging too far, and at the same time there is the pull of following the story line, meeting new characters and aquireing that pickaxe upgrade or new laser weapon.
In build mode raw materials you have gathered can be used to build with blocks. THere are several shapes (blocks, ramps etc) and free view allowing you to make large and complex architectural structures.
In crafting mode you are presented with a separate interface for what is an easy to use 3D object creator. It takes a little playing with to get but is by no means difficult. Here you create items, vehicles and weapons. For some things, like vehicles and weapons there are pre-designed parts (stocks, engines, seats, wheels etc) and already a host of vids and help blogs on the net with ideas and tips for making items.
A highly enjoable game with a considerable amount of playability and heeps of potential for budding architects and item crafters, if the developers continue in the current direction, polishing and honing their product this stands to be in the ranks of a classic in due time.
If it suffers from one flaw it is that its ambition is immense. Non the less a hightly absorbing enviromnent, playable story line, imaginative and exciting.
Highly recommened.

Edit/Update: Let me update the bit about the bots. They aren't just hit or miss, they're horrendous. Consider this game to be borderline unplayable without friends, because the bots are that bad right now. :\ They will not use healing items, on themselves nor on you, except seemingly at random. They cannot pick up optional bonus items (tomes/etc.), and, worst of all.. On the first map you'll hit a few spots with armored rats.. which will destroy all three of your bots without difficulty every time. You have to utterly babysit that part or be ruined.. and unless you finish a level you can't get loot, soo... The bots need serious work.
The "yes" or "no" ness of this game is gonna depend on your preference.
The game hinges, quite heavily, on the multiplayer appeal. On your own I imagine it could still be fun, but you'll be at the mercy of hit-or-miss bots. Sometimes they pop over just in time to save you, other times they're playing leap frog over  barrel as you die. Not too unusual for bots!
The game itself, unfortunately, may be a lot more 'shallow' than one would expect. Given the Warhammer Universe and all that there is to draw from I presumed, wrongly, that each character would have a bit more 'depth' to them. This may or may not be a deal breaker for you. The only difference in characters is the weapons they can use, and some are pretty similar. There's no progression in terms of skills, passives, or other abilities in any way, shape, or form. I was expecting at least something Borderlands-esque if not more, again just from how varied and broad the Warhammer universe is! There's plenty of items, passives, racial/army traits, and other lore that could be drawn from to give some neat flavor to the characters, rather than just "this guy uses two swords/daggers/one sword, that guy uses a sword and shield, bigger sword, big mace" and that's really it. I was honestly very disheartened at first by that aspect and felt they had so much room to do so much more with this aspect of the characters.
Also, you only get one of each character in each map, so if you like X character and your friend likes X character.. too bad.
That said, you do start to get items with various passives, though it's entirely pure luck and optional challenge-type mission-based goals to get it, so you may just kinda get the short-end on that. Loot is tough to come by and you may just kinda be stuck "farming" the first level or so with frustratingly awful bots. It's up to you if items with passives are interesting enough to warrant serious playtime.
With that said, the levels also seem to be static - this is maybe my second biggest complaint. I had thought maybe the goals would move around, but they do not seem to, at least not on the first few levels. This means that veteran players will have a distinct advantage and, unfortunately, any new player is going to be a weight on the team. The longer you stand aroudn the more rats come your way, they seem to spawn endlessly, so exploring or being lost is punished quite a bit.
I also have to complain a tad about the lighting - it's WAY too contrast heavy! You can go from seeing brightly illuminated clouds in the sky in front of a moon that looks like a sun, then turn and not be able to make out the textures on a barrel because it's slightly in the shadow of a building. There's not nearly enough ambiant light and the lighting feels super stark as a result.
BUT with all that said, the combat is fairly satisfying. It's a bit confusing at times - some creatures you'll drop 20 arrows in and they won't flinch, other times you'll do 5 and they'll drop without seemingly any headshots, so it's a bit hard to really read what is going on.
The melee is what really shines, though that does have a bit of quirkiness. The graphics are solid, save the lighting nuance that bugs me, and that may just be a personal thing to be fair.
I wish the levels were a bit less linear so that it required some 'figuring out' each time, but you'll get down an ideal path pretty quick, know exactly where all the bonuses are, and that sorta farts on the replayability in terms of being interesting. But, again, the combat itself is fairly satisfying.
So, if you think $30 is a good price for some reasonably satisfying first person smashing, and aren't too sour at being stuck in YET ANOTHER Warhammer game as playing nothing but the lame races, and you can deal with the relative lack of super interesting progression, then it probably is the game for you. If you have a few friends who are in the same boat, it makes it a lot better as with any sort of game of this nature. The multiplayer makes it plenty more interesting as usual.
Another note, though, you CANNOT trade. If you get a super cool item your friend would love to have.. too bad. :( Also, keep in mind this game is SERVER BASED. There appears to be NO Offline mode whatsoever. No LAN. So if the servers go up in flames or the company bails out in a year or two, you're stuck with yet another abandoned unplayable game that has no support. So.. that may be a buyer beware for some people. It's becoming more a trend in recent years and it's frightful how easy we can all be left holding the bag.

As of now, I am on the 17th level, in act 5. And, I have to say that I don't know what to think of Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number. On the plus side, you get a bigger picture in terms of plot, as the game takes place before, during, and after the events of the first game. You get to play as a group of vigilantes known as "The Fans", who are murdering gang members, addicts, all so that they can get the same phonecalls that Jacket got. You also get to play as a detective, trying to solve a number of homicides left by an unknown killer (as of where I am). Thirdly, you get to play as the detective's friend, who is trying to write a book about the "masked maniac" who killed off most of the Russian Mafia. Speaking of Russians, you can also play as a unhealthy redneck who has a snake fetish, and a hatred for Russians. Finally, you get to play as a soldier, fighting Russians in Hawaii. Those are only a few of the characters you can play as, not including special mission characters.
As for gameplay, they could have done such a better job. It's the same concept as the first game, but now you die from two bullets.  Now, I don't mind murdering people to the sound of M.O.O.N with a bloody bullet hole in my arm, but my biggest irk with the game is that the levels are designed with melee in mind, but most levels are only playable with heavy gunplay. Most of the thugs have guns, and the reflexes of a junkie on cocaine, meaning THEY WILL GET YOU BEFORE YOU GET THEM. This is okay if it was HM1, where the levels are nice and short (2-3 areas), but in HM2, most of the levels stretch on to 3-5 areas. Speaking of poor level design, for lack of a better word, it's horrid. in Hotline Miami 1, the designed the levels so that the player would always be in the center of the screen, in HM2, I find myself hugging the right side of the map on most levels, which takes away from the gunplay you need to pass the level. Hell, in some areas, I spawn off frame, which is a huge annoyance.
The masks are sometimes good, sometimes bad. if you even play as a masked character. The writer, Soldier, and Detective are pretty much Richard, and they take up most of the game so far. I've played 5 levels as The Fans, and 2 levels as Jake the Snake lover. The thing they could've done better with The Fans' masks, is make sure they aren't awkward to control. Corey the Zebra has a dodge roll that can avoid bullets and sometimes, melee attacks, but is useless for getting close enough for a kill, because when you stand back up, you're dead. Alex and Ash are two characters, Ash has a gun, Alex has a chainsaw, Ash follows Alex, but Ash is only useful for long range, since he is usually stuck behind a doorway at close range, so then he is only good for luring. Mark the Bear spawns with two machine guns, which can rotate 90° to shoot at the sides, which I haven't used once, sadly, you can only use other guns when the machine guns run out of ammo, making you drop them, you can't  even throw them. Finally, Good Ol' Tony The Tiger: I was extremely disappointed, Tony has been Nerfed to♥♥♥♥♥♥ He still has killing punches, but he plays a custom animation for killing dogs, which is terrible because they now attract enemies when attacking you, meaning you won't survive if you punch the dog, and his finishers now require two clicks to kill, lastly, he can't use ANY weapons, making him almost impossible for most levels, since almost all of them require heavy gunplay.
Although, the worst character has to be The Soldier, you get to choose one gun, and you get a tiny hunting knife, you can't pick up ANY weapons,  you only have a small amount of ammo, which can be refilled, but you only get a fraction of the ammo you start with. The Soldier is my least favorite character because his levels aren't just challenging, they are unfair. Oh, you're out of ammo, and there are still ten enemies left, half of which have rifles? HAVE FUN.  Spoiler about The Soldier
.
I've been bashing this game for the last four paragraphs, so let's focus on the positives. The soundtrack is amazing, they could not have done a better job. So many groovy murder tunes. Secondly, The story, if you've played HM1, fills in the blanks very well, I won't spoil it. Thirdly, the blood is so much more satisfying, it is a lot more like a fluid in the way that you can see it squirt out of your victim. Finally, if you bought the Digital Deluxe Edition, the PAYDAY 2 content you recieve is great, Jacket's masks are awesome, the weapon you get can two hit Heavy FBI units if fully charged, the submaachine gun comes with a custom paint job, the perk deck, when upgraded regenerates armor when an enemy is killed, and regenerates health when an enemy is melee killed. Finally, the way Jacket uses a tape recorder to communicate really shows that he is a ♥♥♥♥ing psychopath. I love it.
So, should you get Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number? Despite all the♥♥♥♥♥♥I've been giving the game, I think you should, if you can get past the poor level design, and awkward character movements, it really does a good job of concluding the Hotline Miami story.

You can just tell when something isn't well thought out. For instance when a guy on a motorcycle can kill a few enemies by running them over before being taken down.
There's nothing wrong about microtransactions. Afterall, making games and running servers isn't free. But making it so that your leveling up seems almost impossibly slow when not paying isn't exactly a solution. Take World of Tanks for example. Higher tiers are definitely more interesting, but credit multiplier is highest for middle tier tanks so people still keep them and play them from time to time. In this game, higher level means better equipments, better buffs (absolute advantage over lower level counterparts), and hundreds, if not thousands, of hours played; no catch, no weaknesses.
There's even bigger problem, more fundamental one. Is this game fun to play? Apparently many people are still playing this thing so I guess for them, it is. Well, I'd have to say no, personally. A soldier survives three gunshots to the chest, so one of the viable strategies that people have employed is to ride on a motorcycle and simply run down enemies driving super fast. Graphics are horrid, and buildings look worse than that of 10-something years old games such as counterstrike(could be that my PC isn't good enough but compared to other games I play on the same machine, I stand by this statement). Snipers roam around the edge of huge, mostly empty map looking for some easy kills(teamplay?). Some nutjobs TK their team's snipers to grab free sniper rifles. So it's like GTA WW2, with ♥♥♥♥♥ier graphics than San Andreas, and definitely a p2w. Comparing to other modern FPS, this game has severe shortcomings. See it for yourself. It's free to play.

2017 UPDATED REVIEW:
Unless you enjoy bug-ridden, unfinished games, do not buy.
Unless you are really looking for a sandbox game - which you can play indefinitely in Planet Explorers - I wouldn't touch it.
If you have an AMD card - do not touch it, unless you enjoy below 20 FPS and lag spikes. On a RX490 that runs any game @60 FPS.
Planet Explorers was a VERY ambitious game, but the devs clearly bumped into crazy amount of bumps in the road and obstacles - I'm pretty sure they decided to simply release it and move on.
Although the story is super interesting, and everything feels full of potential..Game ends on a terrible cliffhanger and we can probably expect no new content for the game, as the devs are now working on a completely different project.
Past the first few hours, you'll bump into bugs that make you feel you're playing an Early Access games. Especially as I found bugs now that I'm pretty sure have reported 3 years ago.
Some bugs might kill 30+ hour playthroughs. Some might delete items you spent a good amount of time getting the resources to craft.
I cheered a lot for PE during ~3+ years following its development
Half of my playtime was during the Early Access, half was getting disappointed yet pushing forward on the full release, version 1.1.
In conclusion: only play it if you REALLY enjoy sandbox games and don't care for bugs.
There's much to be praised on the features Planet Explorers has, but overall..the end result overshadows the good points, now that I've seen the 'ending'. Heartbreaking experience.
Original 2014 Review below, if interested. Thanks for reading!
===
The new sandbox experience.
Please note: It seems that the 0.75 version (the first version uploaded to steam) has more features than I know of - I only played 0.72 (pre-steam) to the full extent of it.
It's an alpha, so please do play the Demo before buying (and check the demo version since those could be outdated)!
Be aware of the minimum system requirements! Also, saves can be incompatible between updates - if you don't like "wipes", you should probably wait!
A beautiful, fun and full of potential game that features a very interesting Story Mode, great weapon/item/vehicle editor and easy-to-use build mode with free camera.
There's also an Adventure mode (think Minecraft's Survival Mode - infinite randomly generated map), Build mode (Creative Mode) and also Multiplayer.
Since the game is in early alpha, the storyline isn't complete yet, nor the editor or many other features, but you can already see the game shaping up very nicely and there's a decent amount of stuff to do already.
Fun items like jetpacks, gliders and hooks are already in the game and only need a bit more polishing.
The player-made vehicles (cars and helicopters, currently) and items (swords and guns) add a lot of nice content to play with.
You'll also be able to make objects like tables and paintings, and put decals and effects on your creations.
The (current) cons of the game comes from the fact that it's an early alpha.
The movement/camera scheme can be a bit annoying at times, the optimization must be worked on, and a few other bugs regarding monster movement and AI, terrain loading and collision detection.
But the developers are aware of all those issues, and are working on them (things that slightly annoyed me on 0.72 seem to have been fixed/improved on recent versions).
The plotline is very interesting and engaging - I can't wait until they write more and put more quests & story in the game!
The remaining features you can easily read & watch videos on, or discover for yourself on the demo.
The game is worth it and I hope it succeeds and the development goes on smoothly.
Along with Starbound, it's one of the most worthy sandbox games to watch currently.
Have fun! :D

Planet Explorers is setting out to be a game that really brings the word "sandbox" to life.  That said, we've got to keep in mind that this game is still heavily embedded in Alpha.  This review will be based on the Alpha experience I've had, and may not be accurate as time passes.
Starting out the game I realized very quickly that I was going to need help.  There was no sign of a tutorial anywhere.  I quickly figured out that if I wanted to get something out of this game I'd have to go do some research.  YouTube to the rescue!  After watching several really good tutorial videos on "getting started", I was quickly able to start moving forward in the world.  That said, I later figured out that the "Campaign" mode has a somewhat vague tutorial built into it.  Meaning, while it did guide me, there were still some things I had to figure out on my own.
I'm going to start my actual review with the item editor, since that's a huge plus for this game.  Not watching any tutorials on this, I was able to make a rather nice looking stone sword and shield, but couldn't figure out where they were located in the crafting interface so I could actually craft them in-game.  This was done in "Campaign" mode, so I assume I needed to first learn how to make a "stone hilt" before the weapon would be available to me.  I have to say the item creator is very easy to use and I absolutely love the "mirror" modes while designing.  I also tried to design a stone & wood bike, but I had a few errors in the build (like having no drivable wheel) and couldn't figure out how to fix the problem.
I found food to be a very big problem.  The easiest food I found to make required 1 torch to cook each meat.  To make a torch you needed wood (not a problem) and 1 animal fat per torch.  As most animals can easily kick my♥♥♥♥♥ the animal fat was hard to acquire.  Due to this, I kept running out of stamina and my character became rather sluggish.  Even sleeping 12 hours didn't fix my stamina level, although it brought it up a very minor amount.  It left me a little annoied.  I also couldn't figure out how to farm the seeds I had collected from several plants (used for medical supplies).  Perhaps watching more YouTube videos is in order...
The worlds, I've got to say, are impressive.  For the most part.  There was a lot of flora and fauna in the world I started out in, but I quickly realized that most of it involved flat props, and not actual 3D plants.  It's kinda like how the creatures were in the original Duke 3D.  Flat, but seemed to always attempt to face your direction so they didn't look flat.  I'm hoping this will be changed as Alpha continues, because it almost ruins the beauty of the landscapes when up-close.  Then again, with the lack of instructions, I could have an option set that makes the flora appear in that manor instead of how it should look.
Mining and digging is somewhat similar to other voxel games, like "7 Days to Die" and "Space Engineers", where the ground smoothly deforms instead of cubed removal like how they do in "Minecraft".  Object harvesting is very similar as well.  Trees, for example, must be fully cut down before you actually get resources from them.  That said, at present Trees simply vanish when cut down.  I'd personally like to see some kind of "falling" animation, and the tree vanishing instead as it lands on the ground.
Creatures in the game were somewhat interesting.  I'm not exactly sure how creatures come into being, whether it's simply random generation or there is a massive database of them, but I found the ones I ran into to be somewhat strange in appearance.  One looked like the body of a brontosaurus, with the neck of a giraffe, the face of a clown (no word of a lie), and 6 legs.  I turned away from the creature because I deemed it too ugly to kill.  Another seemed to be a very low to the ground creature, hard to see in the flora.  It had 8 legs, a head kinda like an iguana, and a tail like a rat.  I tried to kill it, but my little dagger did virtually nothing.
That brings me to combat!  I found it to be a bit unnerving, to say the least.  I couldn’t really tell what was damaging me when a creature attacked.  I couldn’t tell if I was getting clawed, if they were biting me, or if I was taking some kind of area damage.  I couldn’t even tell how much damage I was taking, without staring at my health bar.  There was no visual indicator of damage (No numbers/points appeared), which sometimes left me wondering if I was even hitting the creature.  As their health bars are so compact, unless you do serious (or a lot of) damage it’s hard to tell if the creature’s health is even dropping.
Overall I have to say that I’d give the current state of this game a 7/10.  I can’t go any higher because I don’t know if the things that are missing (Tutorial/etc.) will eventually be added.  Right now it seems like a very user unfriendly game.  That said, it’s still early Alpha so I can’t give it too much negativity.  I purchased the game myself, and I’m not regretting that purchase.  We’ll see if that changes as Alpha moves to Beta, and Beta moves to final release…
As it stands, if you want to take the risk, then I’d say this game is definitely recommended.  I find the price-point of $24.99 a little high for an Alpha-Version game, but if you consider most finished games sell for something like $60-80 it doesn’t seem too unreasonable.  This game has the formula to be a serious contender in the "sandbox" genre, assuming the dev team stays true to the promises they're making.

The Good:
It trys to take a more realistic approach to what an actual zombie apacolypse would be like... which means even with good teamwork, you will die... a lot. The way contagion does this is by adding the ability to become infected, and by making ammo and first aid scarce. What that means is that one scratch, and/or one too many wasted bullets can spell your entire team's doom.  (This works well in keeping you on the edge of your seat) You'll usually be very nervous once one of your teammates turn, because they will be able to play as a zombie, and can kill you faster than the A.I.
The Bad:
The game may be finished, but it still seems like it's in early access. There are still many bugs that need to be fixed, but nothing too game breaking. My biggest issue with the game is the zed's hitboxes. One shot that should have been a kill can cost you your life when the game decides to say you missed. In short, this game is probably not going to see any more fixes due to it being, "finished," so if you're not easily♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥when your game decides to derp, give it a try.... but don't expect to have fun past 5 hours in.
The Ugly:
The community... and the lack of it. Almost every server is empty, and if you're lucky enough to find a server with people, they're usually selfish, bad team members that will either leave you to die alone, or call you a great mix of derogatory/ethnic slurs. It's a shame that the community isn't a problem the devs can fix, but you should take it into consideration before you buy.
Conclusion: If you like left 4 dead, but want something that'll be more, "realistic," then get this game on sale. It has too many cons to be bought at its current price.

Overall, an enjoyable game.
The combat is unique, but entertaining. Only headshots do anything, so aiming precisely is absolutely necessary. Ammo is scarce and varied, meaning if you're lucky enough to find a cache, it may only contain ammo for guns you don't have. The weapon loadout is nicely varied too, with plenty of pistols, rifles, shotguns, and even grenades. Plenty of melee weapons, too. If you want to, you can even beat a zombie to death with your cell phone. I wouldn't recommend it, though.
Escape is my favorite mode, since you can solo it and restrict player zombies as desired. Being a zombie is kind of fun, but it's much too easy to just zigzag towards survivors and grab them. Since only headshots do anything and most of the weapons are semi-automatic, zigzagging is very overpowered for player zombies.
As for the other modes, I've gotten some enjoyment out of them, but they're difficult to learn on the fly and the community isn't especially receptive to newcomers. Furthermore, the other modes either can't be soloed or are very, very difficult to solo, so practice isn't an option.
Finally, the workshop add a few nice, community-created touches to the game. I'm a fan of the batsignal flashlight myself.
All in all, pretty fun, especially if you've got some friends to join you.

Some people say, "Sequels are never good.” even though there are some games that prove this statement incorrect.
Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is not one of those games.
Story: 2/10
-Story was constructed poorly compared to HM1. Remember how you could tell Jacket and the Hooker were growing closer by seeing Jacket’s apartment? (The place got cleaned up, she first slept on the couch, then in a bed that was next to Jacket’s bed, and finally the two beds were pushed together) ♥♥♥♥ that. Everything is now in your face. For example, hallucinations. In HM1 they were an interesting look into the psyche of Jacket. In HM2 the tone you get from them is now "oOooOOoo you’re going to die ooOOoOoo spooky!”, they’re flat out a supernatural ghost vision of the future that everybody gets.
-Almost every single character was bland and uninteresting. And those who are get dropped right out of the story as soon as they appear! (e.g. Fans, Martin) And the way it just abruptly ends makes you feel like you've been cheated.
I mean, sure, Hotline Miami doesn't really focus on the story, but the subtle way it was told in HM1 just blows HM2 out of the water.
What's that you say? You play Hotline Miami for the gameplay, not the story? That’s sure to be good right?
Gameplay: 4/10
-You liked the fast paced action of HM1? I’ve got bad news for you. HM2 actually makes you slow down.
-Level design has taken a major nosedive in quality. Just like the story, ha ha
-Because every level is ♥♥♥♥ing huge and open, your strategy for 90% of the time in HM2 is to find cover, bait enemy to come to you -> kill -> repeat. No more massacring everybody in seconds or variations on how to clear a room. In later levels you are practically forced to do this strategy.
-Get ready for unseen enemies to shoot and kill you even when you use shift to look ahead.
-An overabundance of windows and long corridors make for bad and unfun times.
-Every single Hawaii level after the first will give you a headache. What do you mean I can’t pick up guns? You ran out of ammo and there isn't an ammo box? Tough luck, that fat guy is gonna rip your heart out.
-I can honestly say I only had fun playing the Fans and Richter’s levels, they really captured the feel from HM1 in those (except for the prison, which was just a mess)
-Gameplay doesn’t match up with the fast paced music most of the time, because of the baiting strategy
Tldr; don’t buy it unless you’re a fan of Hotline Miami 1 and willing to overlook the massive drop in quality from 1.
