It's zombie apocalypse again - this time as a 2D Platformer. If you're expecting some good natured zombie slashing, stay away. There is some combat, but about 95% of the game is about dodging them and jumping past various obstacles.
The story isn't really anything special, but I never expected anything else from a zombie game: You are Randall Wayne and for the next 3-4 hours divided in 3 acts you're looking for your family/friends. There's a twist in the end, but that's about it. You get to know a little more about your character from his diary entries, monologues and dreams, but the people you're looking for might as well be shadows already (that's what they call the zombies). I never cared about any of them, because the game didn't make an effort to make me like them.
The strongest point of the game is its fantastic art style that really fits well to the grim and depressing atmosphere. Don't get tricked by it being a 2D game though - zombies can and will come at you from the background. Although that's pretty cool, it creates the minor problem that in some cases you don't know if a zombie is on your level and bump into him - and get eaten. Same goes with other objects you can't really tell whether they are part of the background or not. Dying isn't a problem though because the checkpoints are fair. You'll find one after pretty much every other obstacle.
There are some areas in which it isn't immediately obvious what you have to do and some where only trial&error will get you to the next, but all in all it's a pretty easy game. The only platformer I played was Trine, so if I can breeze through it, so can you :)
The voice acting is ok. Some are pretty great, others are unconvincing in their acting. The soundtrack is awesome, although rather sad and depressing.
I've read in other reviews that people had trouble with the controls and a frustrating helicopter scene, but it worked perfectly fine for me with keyboard & mouse and I only got shot once by the helicopter, even though platformers aren't really my thing, so maybe they fixed these issues in some patch that was automatically installed for me.
As for bugs, I found only 2: Once I fell through the world after climbing a ladder in the last act, and right before the end I kind of locked myself out of the game by rolling through the wall back outside a building that was now blocked - Couldn't get back inside and had to reload.
To wrap things up, Deadlight is a pretty average game but I recommend giving it a try nonetheless because I still had a reasonable amount of fun with it.

I've been following this game for some time, and I'm very excited it's made it to Early Access on Steam.  For a small indie game, the ambition this team has is immense.  The sheer scope of what they are creating is really amazing.  What's more, they are actually delivering.
Pros:  Huge world which is fully changeable by digging, shaping and building.  Amazingly-detailed item builder so you can build your own custom swords, shields, even vehicles!  The designs can be exported to .iso files so they can be shared too!  I hope this shows up in the workshop on Steam.
The graphics and sound are nice and character animations are believable.  Gameplay is wide-open with a lot of different ways to enjoy the game.  Single player story mode, Co-Op and competitive multiplayer are all options.  Time will tell if they all pan out.
There is a character designer with lots of options.  Hopefully more will surface as the game comes closer to release.
I think this game will be an amazing journey with lots of things to do.  I look forward to the finished product.
Cons:
Some of these items are due to the game not being finished yet, so they are subject to change.  The voice acting is very amateurish.  Not a big issue overall but there it is.  Combat needs some serious polish.  I feel like I'm switing a weapon, but no feedback when I hit doesn't make it feel like I'm hitting anything or being hit.  There are virtually no combat sounds either.  Combat is probably going to be a decent part of this game, so some polish to make it more satisfying would be nice.

Contagion is the closest thing to being the game equivalent of traditional “George A. Romero” Zombie apocalypse…or max brooks zombie survival guide setting…or the walking dead…you get the picture. Slow, hard to kill…zombies. My review will touch on aspects I feel focus on the strengths and weaknesses of the game. There are plenty of both trust me.
GRAPHICS AND ATMOSPHERE
-the good-
The visuals serve well on initial playthroughs. I honestly felt helpless and weary what could be around the next corner. The stark contrast in environmental lighting made good use of my flashlight. All of it  makes a trigger finger really twitchy. Weather changes with rain in some maps adds nice ambience too.
-the bad-
My only complaint that the exterior parts of some maps lack of variety, changes in lighting in procedural sort of way could remedy this. Much like the ever changing maps on each walkthrough can stir up silent dread awhile longer. After my first 10 hours or so even on solo play-throughs, the fear diminishes pretty quickly.
PVP GAMEPLAY
-the good-
By far the strongest aspect of the game, players will be served PVP modes on ALL game types. Died as a survivor during escape or extraction mission? No worries, you’ll always have a guaranteed turn as the member of the undead. Cut loose and wreak havoc and fear on your friends and enemies.
The game mode Hunted, is specifically catered to this. You can start a game with a group of survivors or a player controlled zombie. Gunning, mauling, and devouring each other till the last man standing wins. Of course, even if you’re killed it’s only the beginning.  Zombie gamplay is present in this mode as well.
Even though I fall in the lets say…..%10 of the gamer population that does not enjoy pvp, I’ve actually had fun…given that the company wasn’t too obnoxious or a bunch of hate mongering trolls. Mind you this pleasant experience only occurred once in my 24 hours of total game play. But hey…if you enjoy trash talkin and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥some one off over the mic or text.…this game definitely for you.
-the bad-
Now for the downsides…. If you’re not big on player versus player….you’ll hate this game. A gratifying experience is slim. The best way to try to enjoy this of this is to wrangle up a group of friends and some how make a private server.  Even that’s not STRAIGHT FORWARD OR FREE, AS IT SHOULD BE.
CO-OP GAMEPLAY
-the good-
When surviving with friends (and at very rare times random players) that have a good sense of teamwork, CO-OP in contagion is tense, gory, and suspenseful  fun!  It requires a lot more thought and planning. Running in with guns blazing has its place but doing it all the time will doom yourself and your fellow survivors….which in most circumstances you DO NOT want…trust me. I admire this pacing cause it’s more of a thinking man’s game.
When player synergy is possible reaching extraction points and claiming victory is quite gratifying in a “high five” sort of way.
-The bad-
9 times out of 10, your co-op mission will fail when joining public games.  Too many things can go wrong such as….
-Having to deal with being lost for long periods of time if joining mid game
-Players that join mid-game as zombies can quickly spoil your chances of survival
- Uncoordinated player survivors will slow progress to a crawl.
-Confusing or vague clues for reaching the next objective
The pvp aspect has too much of a presence in co-op gameplay, even if you create or join a server that disables the “infection” or “player zombie” feature. Once you’re dead…you’re out. There should be a optional “left 4 dead” feature that appeals to PVE players, such as being incapacitated into a “bleedout” status.
Other players could be allowed a window of chance to aid comrades to their feet when health is depleted, at least for a limited amount of times before death. This would give a nice set of balanced options for PVE and PVP, more appealing across the board. At the moment this game unfairly leans to the latter.
SOLO GAMEPLAY
-the good-
If you wish to truly experience terror and what it means to be prey, initial walkthroughs of extraction and ESPECIALLY escape mode on your own will certainly deliver…. Most likely only skilled players will be able to accomplish this, and victory is so very sweet when you’re able to run screaming toward your escape. I’ve only been able to pull it off twice in each game mode, but man it was thrilling.
-The bad-
Replay value on your own is basically zero… Even with procedural map generation, throwing yourself at the similar set of objectives the second time around is quite boring and a tedious chore. If a chain is only as strong as its weakest link, this is it… contagion highly depends on group game play to be anywhere near fun or even approachable the second….third….time around. Most likely there’d be never be a forth….
If you really want this game to have staying power in your library, bring friends....and some how your own server.... >:(
MULTIPLAYER OPTIONS
-The good-
Contagion is well suited for those looking for PVP for public lobbies. Pick a game mode, join a pub server and you’ll shooting or munching on other players in no time. Nuff said.
-The bad-
Okay so….
-No “friend only” lobby option
-No direct private server options
-Servers for RENT are available on contagion….
-Free private servers can only be created via 3rd party programs
With aspect like these, contagion still feels like a mod and not a developer’s fully released game. Lacking intuitive or direct access to people not accustomed to modding or pc gaming.
-FINAL THOUGTS-
If you’re looking for a great combination of zombie survival and PVP gameplay, definitely grab a copy.
For players that have a strong affinity for co-op fun and thrills..... should think twice though….if you have a dependable group of friends and a means for creating your own servers, then it’s worth a buy.
If not….stick to l4d2.

As brutal and more expansive than its predecessor, Hotline Miami 2 will keep you pushing through its difficult levels by using its fantastic soundtrack and unique story to make you hit "R" one more time. The maps are much larger than those experienced in the first title. This increases the difficulty, but also results in many cheap deaths from an armed enemy way out of your vision's range. Don't expect to go melee crazy on these maps, either. Not only are ranged opponents plentiful, but the large range of sight and constant glass windows mean that you can be taken out from almost anywhere. Expect more methodical gameplay from this one.
As for the story, very few games on the market approach what one could call "Kafkaesque" in narrative, most likely because no AAA game in its right mind would choose to go a route so different to most audiences); however, Hotline Miami 2 certainly isn't shy in shattering expectations. The game does everything that an indie title should do: go where AAA titles won't. By this, I don't mean Hotline Miami 2's ridiculous levels of violence, but the narrative flow of the game is extremely scattered, challenging the player to piece it together instead of simply handing over its plot like a made-for-TV movie. It also forces the player to work through a variety of characters, often taking actions that make us feel uncomfortable. For the most part, Evan is the only palate cleanser throughout the game's brutality and moral trauma.
Anyway, if you're wondering if I recommend the game, I do, though I also suggest you prepare yourself for a difficult experience. Whether it be plot or gameplay, nothing is handed to you easily in Hotline Miami 2, but that's also part of its charm.

A modern twist on a cinematic sidescroller platformer, with some puzzle solving elements. Graphically, it's very impressive. The animation of the 3D world around the 2D levels is clever, and the textures are very nicely rendered. A great deal of time and love was put into the design of the environments, and that shows. Sometimes the game is too fast paced to truly appreciate the artwork that went into it, which makes it feel somewhat wasted.
Gameplay features a mixture of running, jumping, combo-moves (bouncing off walls, jumping into a tuck roll, etc.) some combat, and some simple puzzle solving. Some stages feel more like they were an afterthought, while others cleverly mesh with the overall package. A recurring theme throughout the game, is precision trials, where the player is forced to achieve passage through an area in a specific sequence in order to avoid death.
Storyline wise, the game follows Randall Wayne, as he searches for his family and friends, while dodging the hordes of the undead, and an unexplained militant group known as the New Law. Though the storyline sets up quite well, the ending is as disappointing as the rest of it. A lot of the more intriguing tidbits are left unexplained. The ending also comes a little too quickly.
Unfortunately, the controls are also quite frustrating and counterintuitive at times, the game feels slightly glitchy, and ragequits will send you right back to the beginning of an act, even if death only sends you back to the nearest "checkpoint". Quite why this is I do not know, there is never any real way to tell whether or not it's safe to quit the game. All of this drags the game down pretty significantly, which is a real shame as it has such a lot of potential.
In the end, there is a decent amount of entertainment to be had out of this game. The good bits are very good, and even if the story ends up being unsatisfyingly bleak, and the controls are frustrating as hell, you won't regret having played it. It's worth it for the graphics alone.

I've long been waiting for 2 things to come out the last couple of years. A new Left 4 Dead game and a new solid Warhammer game. Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide solves that itch.
Pros:
- Art-style reminds me of Warhammer Online
- Classes are unique enough that it's enjoyable playing each one
- Maps are well thought out with enough choke points but also open areas for the ogre, also allows some exploration for chests. Risking cutting away from your group to check on a chest only to be hopped on by a special.
- The dice system and loot system keeps you addicted and playing for better loot.
- The game is challenging and doesn't hold your hand.
- Great to see the game supports 21:9 resolution. Looks amazing on my 34 inch monitor. (Valve still hasn't done this right).
- Loving the squabble between the characters. People have complained about Kerillian talking too much and being mean towards the other character. I think it's great, I imagine an elf would have issues being teamed up with the rest of them and would not be happy about it.
Cons:
- Loot system can be expanded, allow the ability to turn white shards into green and green into blue maybe. That way I don't have to go back to normal mode in order to work on upgrades for my gear.
- Give us more hard numbers, how much health does each class have, there's some items that just give a description instead of numbers, you did a good job with item upgrades giving hard numbers but it seems to be lacking in other areas.
- Host migration is needed for a game with no check points. Currently if the host drops then you have to go back to the lobby screen. This should be fixed
- Optimization, this game is in beta so it's understandable that there are some performance issues. Hoping the release build has better optimization,
- Some things seem too random, Special skaven either spawn too much or not enough at all. Looking at Left4Dead you almost constantly had to be ready for a special zombie. Would be good to see things tweaked so these were a threat.
Summary: All around i'm enjoying this game, from a long fan of Warhammer and a die hard Left 4 Dead fan Fat Shark has done an amazing job with this game. Hopefully they will follow up the success with some new maps, more great classes, and some more challenging Skaven to defeat. Who knows maybe we'll get a Warhammer: End Times-Chaostide.

Playing as Alex and Ash, Ash sometimes tends to be stuck (But even with that being said they were my favourite characters).

Some personal expectancies in the story weren't quite met, then again either I've missed something...Or the end isn't the end.

Unique graphical style.
Improved difficulty. Frustratingly fun.

Hotline Miami 2 is indeed a brutal conclusion, and the execution was great...

I'm the kind of Call of Duty player that pops open the game case, gathers up my buddies, and jumps right into the fantastic, addictive multiplayer with less than a glance at the single-player and co-op modes. And that's how I suggest you approach the latest entry in the Call of Duty series. Call of Duty: Ghosts hits all of the Call of Duty bulletpoints: precise controls, refined multiplayer gameplay, and a ton of content to keep you coming back again and again. But it doesn't take any chances or bring anything significant to the table, especially in the single-player and co-op modes. Never before has a game in the series felt so stagnant. While the shooter is a solid FPS experience all around, it's missing the creative passion that made its predecessors shine.

I love the single player story line of the game, it has several scenes that have become almost iconic to the Call of Duty series, and the multi-player functionality is different but still similar to the previous games.

The game is actually great, not very innovative, but what it does it does very well.
Did you like Left4dead2? Then you'll most likely like this game. This game borrows a lot from L4D2, so i will be comparing the two. It's the same basic formula, 4 people cooperatively advance through a semi-open map trying to achieve an objective, encountering enemies along the way. Some enemies appear randomly at random times, so you don't always know what to expect. There are several different enemy types to spice things up.
What is does different from L4D2 is classes and melee, melee is the focus of the game. All classes have ranged and melee attacks, although your ranged attacks are limited by ammo or energy, which you can resupply by exploring the enviroment to find supplies. The melee feels heavy and responsive, it's also diversive and most importantly, fun.
Classes could be more specialized and diverse in my opinion, but they still all offer enough to make them unique. They are customizable as well, so you can actually attempt to specialize them to your liking.
The loot system is a hit and miss, depending on who you ask. It's random, and the only thing you can semi-control is how good your odds are. I'm not the biggest fan of that, but i can't argue with the gambling feeling of rolling the dice. You also get no loot if you fail the level, so you can spend 20-30 minutes only to loose in the final fight and get nothing but XP, or as in my case, the game crashing or losing connections, or the host leaving, which is a poor design, let someone else take over the host. So, it's subjective, i guess, you be the judge.
However, it's buggy, very buggy. I have a 50/50 chance of the game crashing when i play. I seem to encounter the same bug over and over, that is the game crashing when i fire a weapon. There are also other less severe yet still annoying bugs. The game runs decent, but not nearly good enough to be acceptable.
Mind you, the game is to release in 4 days, and i honestly don't see how they can fix all the issues before that. So i'd advice you to wait and see after release.
All in all, huge potential, great core features, fun gameplay and well crafted from the ground up. But yet again, unstable at the moment.
I give it a thumbs up despite the problems solely because it's still in Beta, problems like this at launch (or soon after) are unacceptable and i will change the review to a thumbs down if they're not properly handled.
Edit: Since this is getting some views which didn't expect, i cleaned up the grammar a bit and clarified a few points for easier reading. I did not change anything significant that could affect the conclusion of the review.
If you enjoyed Left for Dead, you'll enjoy this game. I highly recommend giving it a shot.

Deadlight is honestly a sub-par platformer in an outstanding post apocalyptic world. The games mechanics and story seem rushed and incomplete. This game will have you running back and forth in a clunky moment system wondering whether or not you are messing up a puzzle, or the games level design is preventing you from proceeding smoothly. Its a shame that the actual platformer aspect of this game is its biggest flaw. Where this game does succeed, lies within its atmosphere and overall look. The post apocalyptic Seattle scene of Deadlight is an amazing world of death and desolation that any zombie enthusiast would appreciate. I honestly spent more time and enjoyment watching the background imagery over trying to navigate the puzzles. If you are a fan of the zombie world, than I would suggest you check this game out next time it is on sale. The story is rushed, the characters are unnatural and sound highly scripted in dialogue, and the movement system is in desperate need of reworking, but if you can get it at a good price, the world and atmosphere of Deadlight are worth your time and coin.

Impressions from the early access:
It is clear that devs know and love WHFB universe, for it shows in the thousand little details throught this L4D-esque game. It's not a fanatsy carbon copy of the L4D games. It very much has its own character, and boy, does it ooze with character. Game is already robust, and has longevity with the loot system therein. Easy to pick up, tricky to master, with many things that need to be learned before you come into your own as a good Vermintide player. Considering this is just a small portion of the final game, this portents good things for this game. If you know and love the WHFB like I do, take a moment and look around you carefully - there is so many things that would put a smile on your face here. This is a labour of love, which is frankly rare for GW games.
TLDR: L4D with melee focus, loot, leveling, creative scenarios. Rich with detail and smothered in Warhammer goodness(not a cheap GW turd). If you love WHFB, you'll dig this, I am sure.

I played this for a few days as I got completely lost in the awesomely designed world. If you like exploration and get a nice vibe from hard-sci-fi-ish stuff, then this is for you. I like that it has a story and characters and that it's not all procedurally generated.
However, there are problems. Why, in a sci-fi game, do we still have to craft wooden pickaxes, axes, shovels, etc, like in Minecraft? The main problems with this game are the hold-overs from the Minecraft formula. They don't find whatsoever in this game. Just give me a laser cutter or something like that. It's just silly crafting wooden, bronze, iron, etc tools. The feeling of mystery was also a bit ruined for me when, while exploring, I ran into a huge fortress with hostile aliens, but upon my return to the camp where the other colonists none of them acknowledged the discovery - immersion breaking.
There are some great ideas here and the technical implementation is great. It looks amazing and the voxel engine works very well. I'm pretty sure I could do without the mining and things, however, and there should be some careful constraints on the pacing for the game if there is to be a cohesive story. Overally I recommend it because I had fun playing it, but obviously it still needs a lot of work as it's still in Alpha.

Alright, by the time I'm writing this recommandation, I did not completed the game yet, but can't help but do it already! Call of duty Ghosts was released in late 2013.
Whats the game about?
This game takes place in a time where the middle east has been destroyed in a nuclear war and countries from south america has created a federation to make an influence on the economical crisis and grow power to quickly invade the central parts of america. The story begins when the Federation hijacks a satilite called (ODIN) that posseses a powerfull weapon and use it to destroy most parts of central america and then begin their campaign to invade it and kill all resistance.
You play as a guy named Logan and with you you have your brother David and your dog Riley.
Together you shoot your way through missions and become a part of a group called Ghosts.
Multiplayer?
The multiplayer of this game is just like any other call of duty games i have played over the years, with gamemodes such as Domination, Team Deathmatch and Search And Destroy. The game provides you with alot of ranks and weapons as you unlock when you level up. Call of duty Ghosts also has a new feuture that makes it possible to customize your character and there are many different outfits to unlock and try out.
Is it worth it?
After i have ben playing for over 60 hours and had my rage moments i cant really say its worth it. The game is horrible with poor performance. and even if you have a powerfull computer you will still experience FPS drops, poor sound quality and laggy servers. The singleplayer is good and is the reason to why i got it in the first place. Overall spending full price on this game today is not worth it and im glad i got it for free.

As most people have said, you either love it or you hate it.  The graphics and effects are pretty impressive for a game like this. And there's definitely a creepy ambience. But what good I have to say about this game ends there. Oh, and I guess the old school cut scenes were neat at first, but definitely got old for me.

Most other reviews hit it on the head when they mentioned the clumsy controls, bad physics, and poor layering.  This game will leave you feeling frustrated more often than not.  Some of the level design was pretty interesting but there were times where getting caught on a fence and shot by the helicopter, jumping when told to and magically hitting an invisible wall leading to either, again being shot by the helicopter or, more often, falling to my death, randomly crouching instead of rolling, or jumping off of hanging obstacles onto platforms and sliding right off to either die or have to repeat just got infuriating and painful.

Deadlight is a beautiful game, but the graphics just aren't enough to salvage it.
The core gameplay is fun enough, but the controls make it more frustrating than it needs to be.
It's challenge level is fairly accessible, but the last chapter is a straight-up rage game, brutally difficult only because of the surprises it throws at you the first time through.
The backgrounds are incredibly detailed, but they'll have you wondering why your character doesn't just take the clearly visible stairs instead of forcing himself through jumping puzzles.
The main character is reasonably well voice acted, but he's surrounded by a cast reading a laughable script in bad American accents.
The story is nothing new, with an ending you'll see coming from the first cutscene.  Although, if you play through the game on Nightmare mode, I guarantee you you'll be surprised -- the secret ending may make no sense at all, but at least it is unexpected.
Two final notes: there's no in-game reward for gathering all the collectibles, so it is safe to skip doing that, and this game has absolutely no Metroidvania aspects at all -- it is a perfectly linear platformer from start to finish.
All in all I can't recommend Deadlight but if it is on sale for cheap it might be worth it for a few hours of themed jumping puzzles.

Gameplay wise the game consists of platforming and fighting zombies or "shadows" as they're called in the game. This is a game I have been waiting for. If you have ever played Starwars Galaxies this game has almost the same feeling along with many other elements. You are free to explore an open world filled with interesting creatures and terrain. You are also free to create what you want. Along with a block based building system similar to Minecraft the world uses voxel terrain where you can mold the land around you into any shape. You can even create caves with smooth walls rather than the blocky nature we find now in many other sandbox survival games.
Besides the normal building system, you can create your own weapons, items, and vehicles. The crafting system is not a simple customization screen, you actally have to build your items from scratch. Although the creation system is tricky at first once you get the hang of it, it is quite simple. There is also a rich story line which I only scratched the surface of since I tend to lean towards the multiplayer side of the game. The only downside is the game is still incomplete, but that is to be expected since the game is still in development.
I Highly recommend this game if you want the freedom to do what you want then this is the game for you. I give this game a 10/10 due to its great potential and player freedom.

I'll start by saying i'm a large fan of hotline miami to begin with, and was pretty eager upon seeing a sequel coming out. While the game remains as the same game I loved, the story revolves around a number of characters, all different in playstyle, ranging from the vigilantes, who are the closest to the original gameplay, to a writer, who is incapable of killing people and must use a bat for the majority of missions.
And as much as I love this game...I can't help but notice numerous faults starting to show... For starters, as anyone who plays this can probably agree on, the door system...is kinda buggy; sometimes enemies will run at you then start spasming out in the door frame, leaving you unable to hit them until a sudden point where they break out and kill you without warning.
Next on the list of problems ranges from weapons connecting with their targets, to being shot by someone outside your view (yes, I know you can look further by pressing shift but on many occasions they still see me before I can see them). While the game requires some skill, i've noticed that the majority of it is this routine: Hide around a corner, either shoot a gun or peak to let the guy around the corner know you're there, then bash/shoot his head in when he comes...and thats straightforward, although the game is starting to feel more like a "see how long you can carry out this routine until a glitch screws it up for you".
All in all, yes, I love this game, I just can't help but feel it doesn't live up to the standards that its prequel had, with numerous obvious glitches, my favourite example being Alex and Ash, the pair make up a single character that has a man with a chainsaw being followed by the other with a pistol...first time I tried him out, the gunsman got stuck in a doorway, and I managed to chainsaw a large man through a wall, before teleporting in afterwards...
To put it all simply...good game, but feels like a rushed product, which none of the glitches being too big to ruin the gameplay, yet are common enough to be an annoyance.

If you're alright with a grueling challenge, interesting (and often confusing) plot, and loads of blood and gore, this might just be the game for you. I personally loved the different characters (can the swans get some love?) and the soundtrack is mind-blowingly good if you happen to like electronic music. I had a blast playing it and couldnt turn away until i beat it! Very addictive.

I recommend to buy this game - preferably discounted. The reason? The positive sides far outweight the negative ones.
Pros:
- wonderful atmosphere, something like The Walking Dead. Serious, depressing.
- cool artwork. Stylish, comic-like environments and backgrounds, with matching music and mostly shadows in the foreground.
- decent gameplay. If you are not a hardcore platforming fan, you'll get a nice challenge, and the game will still be enjoyable. Played on PC, with keyboard.
- relatively long for its price. Took me about 4 hours to finish, which is quite a good deal for 3 EUR. I hope there will be DLCs or something.
Cons:
- sometimes frustrating. There were a couple of places, especially towards the end of the game, where I just quit for a few mins, after 10-15 failed tries at the same place. After a break, I always managed though, so it is doable, the difficulty just spikes on some scenes.
- predictable story. If you read the protagonist's diary, and if you have watched zombie flicks lately, you will probably guess at what is gonna happen next, as well as the underlying theme. It could have been done much better, but it is nicley pushed somewhat into the background by the gameplay.
- probably not very replayable. For 3 EUR I don't expect miracles, but quite honestly, I do not feel that I wanna go back for all those missed secrets at all. Also, no multiplayer of any sort. On the other hand, platforming and zombie fans might disagree on this point.
All in all, Deadlight was a refreshing experience for its price, and quite a decent, well-made game, also an interesting mix of generes and a new approach to the zombie theme.

Get the bad out of the way: the hitboxes are a bit off, and it has crashing for some people.  I expect the crashing to be fixed, since the previous closed beta had more stability and the current beta's stability has also improved in just 2-3 days.  (I no longer crash at all)
Now the good: the atmosphere is top notch.  Party banter is grimdark but hilarious at the same time.  Someone literally says "Your hope will betray you, only faith and hatred sustain"  And he's one of the "good" guys.  The world is bleak and atmospheric, overcast weather, giant green moon looming in the sky, half devoured corpses all over the deserted city, etc.
Gameplay is fun and somewhat random.  Different locations will have different drops and enemy spawns each time you play, the game is *highly* teamwork based, lone players will be mauled to death by hordes of carnivorous rat men, so stick together.  Resources are scarce.  That scarcity leads to some really frantic battles and tactics which seem almost suicidal but end up being bad@$$.  The gameplay is very action based, so expect to time your dodges and blocks and counter attacks.  At the end of each climactic mission, you roll ye olde dice to see what loot you got; the number of dice you get to roll (and thus your chance of getting something awesome) is determined by how many ancient tomes and grimoires you pick up during the level.  It's a risk/reward system, because each tome takes a slot you need for health items, and each grimoire cuts your max health.  If you get them all, your party needs be be highly skilled, because you're made of glass once you do.
Im having a lot of fun right now trying to get all the tomes and grimoires on hard difficulty. . . difficulty goes up to "cataclysm,"  and the core gameplay is very satisfying, it doesn't feel floaty or cheap.  It's awesome when you chop the head off of an elite Stormvermin right as he's about to murder your frenemies  :P  (There's great banter between the party members, and it's clear you all kinda hate each other, but also have a really weird sort of comaraderie)

I'd like to preface this review with a warning to anyone who hasn't played the first Hotline Miami: play that one first. Hotline Miami 2's story and difficulty assumes you've done so. There are other, more critical reasons as well, but I'll touch on that later. This review will be written with those who have played it in mind, but there will be no spoilers for either game.
Holy heck, it's finally here! After two long years and much angst, Hotline Miami 2 is finally on Steam, with new characters, levels, and more groovy tunes than you can shake a bloodied bat at. There's also a semblance of story this time, which is both exciting and slightly worrying: after all, wasn't part of the fun of the first game putting the soggy cardboard puzzle peices together? After about 10 hours marathoning through it all, I'm ready to give the verdict on whether or not Hotline Miami 2 is a worthy successor to the original cult classic.
"Author, you Naughty Dog, why are you focusing on story first, rather than gameplay?" The answer is pretty simple: the inclusion of an actual story this time means that the gameplay scenarios are more tailored and guided than before. That being said, that doesn't mean the story is any good. The variety of characters and subplots is impressive in its own right, but only two of the many characters get an actual conclusion, while the other's stories just seem to... evaporate. The game ended so suddenly my jaw dropped - not because of any plot twists, but because the ending was so frying-pan-to-the-face abrupt. I'll give credit to Dennaton for creating some very interesting characters to follow, but again, little is done with most of them.
Even with the actual story being mediocre, the thematic elements are interesting when dissected. Much like the first game, HM2's story benefits from discussion, as there are plenty of details that can be missed and multiple interpretations to follow. Without giving away much, the plot feels very much like a yin to the first game's yang, and can even be sobering at times. While it certainly isn't portrayed the most spectacularly, it's clear that plenty of effort was put into the story's themes, and that can certainly be appreciated.
Suprise suprise, the nitty gritty of the gameplay isn't that different from its predicessor. What is different is how abilities are handled: instead of playing as one character with a vast swarth of masks to choose from, HM2 switches from character to character depending on the level, due in part to the aformentioned narrative.  The variety and swapping between narratives is fun from a purely gameplay standpoint, as each character has their own interesting twists on how they play, and the screentime between characters never feels too condensed or drawn out.
Unlocks are also changed. Instead of simply unlocking masks, beating levels unlocks specific items for the character, or in the case of the Fans, characters. There are no replay-oriented objectives to do to acquire these items; by the time the game ends, all the items will be unlocked.
Yes, this is getting its own subsection, simply because of how utterly broken the levels become. Besides the fact that there is very little of a difficulty curve (it's more akin to a very steep line), many of the levels are simply too big, rely on scummy techniques to complete, and force very specific, counterintuitive playstyles. Because some levels are so open, moving cautiously and usage of the SHIFT zoom are outright required, lest an enemy shoots at you offscreen. Most of the levels REQUIRE you to use a gun because of how spread out and well-armed the enemies are. Very often there is little choice but to  use the "peekaboo" tactic, baiting enemies out of their locations to have them run into your preferred melee weapon. Often times, completing levels feels more like a chore than an accomplishment. It's so bad, I can't bring myself to start the game again - this is coming from a guy who HAD to find out the full story in the first game.
These wouldn't be so terrible if the first Hotline Miami didn't do level design and player agency within it's level so well. As it stands, these are baffling designs that Dennaton should have perfected by now.
A great compilation of familiar and new artists. Even if some of the levels haphazardly enforce a slower pace, the music selection works well, for the most part. It's not purely bombastic music during gameplay this time around (not that there's anything wrong with bombastic music); depending on the character, his motifs, and the overall setting of the scene, the soundtrack can be very versatile - its not pure adrenaline all the time, like Jacket from the first game. My only complaint is that due to the new variety of songs, the soundtrack seems less focused than before; I guess going from 22 tracks from the first game to a whopping 49 tracks will inevitably cause some trail-off.
I think it's important to treat Hotline Miami 2 as less of a sequel and more of a stand-alone expansion. After all, most if not all of the ideas for this game stemmed from DLC ideas from the first. There's a certain charm in playing with ideas that developers once had on their "MAYBIE?" section of their office whiteboard. The story is structured as a companion to the first game rather than a continuation. Overall, Hotline Miami 2 is a glass of wine that goes well with a bourbon steak; a wonderful compliment to the flavor of the main course, but not really something to be enjoyed purely on it's own.

Get the bad out of the way: the hitboxes are a bit off, and it has crashing for some people.  I expect the crashing to be fixed, since the previous closed beta had more stability and the current beta's stability has also improved in just 2-3 days.  (I no longer crash at all)
Now the good: the atmosphere is top notch.  Party banter is grimdark but hilarious at the same time.  Someone literally says "Your hope will betray you, only faith and hatred sustain"  And he's one of the "good" guys.  The world is bleak and atmospheric, overcast weather, giant green moon looming in the sky, half devoured corpses all over the deserted city, etc.
Gameplay is fun and somewhat random.  Different locations will have different drops and enemy spawns each time you play, the game is *highly* teamwork based, lone players will be mauled to death by hordes of carnivorous rat men, so stick together.  Resources are scarce.  That scarcity leads to some really frantic battles and tactics which seem almost suicidal but end up being bad@$$.  The gameplay is very action based, so expect to time your dodges and blocks and counter attacks.  At the end of each climactic mission, you roll ye olde dice to see what loot you got; the number of dice you get to roll (and thus your chance of getting something awesome) is determined by how many ancient tomes and grimoires you pick up during the level.  It's a risk/reward system, because each tome takes a slot you need for health items, and each grimoire cuts your max health.  If you get them all, your party needs be be highly skilled, because you're made of glass once you do.
Im having a lot of fun right now trying to get all the tomes and grimoires on hard difficulty. . . difficulty goes up to "cataclysm,"  and the core gameplay is very satisfying, it doesn't feel floaty or cheap.  It's awesome when you chop the head off of an elite Stormvermin right as he's about to murder your frenemies  :P  (There's great banter between the party members, and it's clear you all kinda hate each other, but also have a really weird sort of comaraderie)

Would that I could give this a review somewhere between "good" and "bad." I'll be nice and give it "good."
But in reality, it's a very mixed bag. The visuals are really nicely-done, and I love the sound design. Up until the final reveal, I like the plot as well.
The gameplay is good, but at times it can definitely get frustrating. Sometimes you fail because you didn't get the solution to a puzzle or you genuinely made a mistake. But often you fail because the controls didn't respond quickly enough or your character didn't grab the ledge he was supposed to. Basically, the gameplay is... patchy at times. It only gets really frustrating later when it starts demanding that you execute sequences of actions, timed perfectly.
And as I said, the plot is good up until the final reveal. Okay, I won't spoil it. Just be warned that you're going to get the worst sort of unreliable-narrator plot twist you could imagine. It adds little to the story and generally is just a hackneyed way to end the game.
But the game, overall, is something I'm glad I played. If the trailer catches your fancy, you'll probably feel at least somewhat similar.

Below you'll find a written and video impression on the game
Before I start I want to mention that I've never played the first Hotline Miami, so this impression will be from some one who's new to the series, and have judged it under the game's own merit.
Hotline Miami 2 is a top-down perspective action game. If you've played the classic GTAs, you'll be quite familiar with this. Unlike GTA, the game isn't so much open world as it is mission to mission. You'll be brutally gunning down or beating up your enemies. But it's not quite as simple as holding down a trigger and win. The game is challenging where all it takes is one shot to end your game.
Hotline Miami's visual is of some of the best I've seen in pixel art. It's similar to what you might of seen from the 16 bit era, but refined to great detail. The game is brutal, violent, and gory, and it takes a lot of skill to represent that degree of grotesque in 16 bits, as the resolution doesn't leave the artist much room for error. The visuals are vibrant and all cohesively themed in an 80s retro style. It's gorgeous! The audio is of an equal quality with one of the best OST in recent memory.
Though a game like this, that feel quite arcady, can often get away with little to no story. Hotline Miami 2 takes the high road and offers an engrossing narrative that goes much deeper than a simple crime drama. With out spoilers, it goes into the delusional, and I'd compare it to the psychological thriller genre. But do be aware, it also explores some extremely dark and adult themes. This is not a game for children or those who are easily offended.
There's much to love about Hotline Miami 2, but it doesn't get away with out flaws that's worth pointing out. The game does have some bugs, not many, but some and when they appear, they're noticeable. Also the enemy AI, though passable, could be improved on, as they're not always reacting realistically.
Overall, Hotline Miami 2 is a great game that's worth every penny it's asking for. It's challenging, looks and sounds amazing, and brutally honest in it's story telling. I can not recommend this any more!

Let's face it, this is Warhammer: Left 4 Dead and that's a good thing. The most noticable difference is the shift of focus to melee combat which it does fairly well. Ranged weapons are still an option, but for the most part reloading in between shots is long so it turns into a shoot once then switch to melee as you engage kind of affair.
Each weapon feels different and the different classes promote varied playstyles. The loot system is decent as you get more loot die to roll the better you perform each run, and you get to salvage or fuse trash/old/duplicate items into something better. It's a lot of RNG, but nothing you aren't already used to. It's Warhammer after all, you already know what kind of random dice BS you're getting into.
Pros:
- If you like horde-style/coop games, this is a must buy.
- Warhammer Fantasy theme is well implemented.
- Melee combat feels varied and satisfying.
- Various class / weapon combinations will play differently.
- Loot system will always reward you with something. Either get lucky with the dice rolls, or farm it out and fuse loot into better stuff.
Cons:
- No competitive modes.
- Server browser should display ping instead of country.
- More maps and characters would be great.
- No menu-based communications, rarely do people use VoIP or chat.
- Host migration when the hosting player leaves dumps you into loading screens, especially when people leave the party in succession.

I'm impressed. This indie game has accomplished far more and to a much better degree than alot of AAA titles I've played. I suggest picking it up and here's why:
The AI pathfinding is wonderful. A follower only got stuck once and that's because I was trying to build the bridge as we were walking over it and I accidently built ontop of him. So chalk that up to my fault.
Speaking of building I must say this is one of the nicest system I've seen. My only complaint is that I can't make slopes at any angle that I want, but I haven't fully examined the builder so I could've just missed it.
The voxel system creates one of the best mining systems that smoothly change the terrain as you dig and mine for minerals.
The item/vehicle creation is very nice and adds your own touch to the game.
HOWEVER there are some negative point, but these might be solved as time goes on:
The ranged weapons feel inaccurate. Yes you point and shoot and it hits the target, but the pistols feel like the rifles and it all seems the same.
Some claim that the melee combat is like Monster Hunter, but I disagree. You can't specifically mess up a monster's leg or wings. On top of that I haven't found a way to dodge yet so it's been a contest of who can hit harder.
There's no way to sort through the crafting menu. it's alphabetical, but if you forget that what you want is the "portible medkit" and not the "small medkit"(which I don't think there is one) then you can make the mistake of thinking you can't craft any small healing items
Despite these complaints I like this game as is and the proposed additions can hopefully only make it better.
EDIT: Upon review in the upper center of the replicator menu there is a way to sort out scripts. I found that it isn't a user friendly as other sorting systems, butit does exist and makes things simpler to a degree. Thank you to Thariorn for pointing this out to me.

I'll keep it short as it's a game in Early Access, with lots of stuff that has to be done yet.
The game shows *a lot* of potential, with MMORPG-like feeling mixed together with third-person shooter and crafting game mechanics. I haven't personally looked much at the building section of the game, which looks absolutely intriguing and fascinating.
If you want to compare it to other sandbox games like Minecraft, Terraria or Starbound, the biggest changes are that this set in a huge life-like breathing world rendered in "real" 3D (no more pixel graphics!) that you can modify and make yours to the same degree that the aformentioned titles allow you to.
Another big bonus is the fact that there is a single player story mode, something that very few games of this genre offer; however, it definitely feels like a game that is meant to be played cooperatively, so bear this in mind if you want to play in single player only.
Trying to wrap it up: if you like crafting/sandboxing games, and if you like exploring vast, fantastic territories... give this game a shot, you'll probably like it.

I had several problems with the command prompts, it's really finicky about looting bodies and chests at times, target the head? No, Chest? No, Legs? No, Arms? There we go. It didn't help that the exact same command was used for picking up guns, so you have two things at the same small area that need the same key to interact with. The Takedowns were fun when I could get them to show up, there were no small number of times I snuck up behind a guy and spent so much time trying to have it stop flickering on and off that he noticed I was there.
Overall, it's fun at some points, sure, but don't expect a ton from it.

I tried this game many months ago and it had a ways to go.   This weekend I revisited it with three other family members.   It has come a long way and is actually quite the fun game.
Premise: Zombie outbreak
Game Modes we tried:  Escape, Extraction, Hunted, and Panic
Escape: Is much like L4D and L4D2 in the sense you're trying to get away.
Extraction:  You are using your cell phone to find NPC survivors and lead them to safety
Hunted:  PvP last man standing
Panic:  Team Deathmatch (almost) where some players are Zombies.   It had no NPCs when we played which was the biggest thing missing, I don't know if there is an option to fix this or not.   It was okay but not that great with just 4 players due to lack of NPCs.
COOL FACTOR: If you are bitten you might be infected and not realize it.   You can be walking a long and then suddenly double over and turn into a zombie.   You get 4 commands.   Vision which gives you a special vision that shows foot prints for awhile of living non-zombie people.   Roar which lets you attract other NPC zombies that will walk with you and follow you.  Blend which relinquishes control of yourself so you'll move more like the other zombies and not be obviously player controlled, you press blend again to retain control.   It also has a command (as in issue command) power which I suspect lets you tell the other NPC zombies you've attracted to do something.   NEGATIVE: In Panic mode the lone zombie player it created had no NPC zombies to order around which put him at a very distinct disadvantage.
It is already a fun game, if they keep going the direction they are it becomes easier and easier to recommend the game.
CONS: The cell phone, and the numeric keys were not mapped by default so for a long time I didn't know what I was supposed to be doing (no cell phone), and I couldn't toggle my weapons I'd picked up.   Once I mapped the keys this was resolved.

Melee weapons are a bit wonky. Keep distance while using and only use right click, left click appears to be useless as it takes about 10 hits for a kill, while right click takes 1 or 2.
In short, great concept and look, but needs some work. I think they may have released it a bit early, but they are still working on it. Only buy if it's your cup of tea. Please note the date of this review as things may change in the future.

If you enjoyed the original, but were looking for more of a challenge, then Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is just the game for you.  Gameplay has been expanded on considerably with the different story arcs the game follows, from the gun-free writer, to the melee-to-gun quickswapping of the soldiers, back to a more high-octane version of classic masked vigilante combat.
As hinted at, difficulty has also seen a healthy change in HM2.  In the first mission the game tasks you with dispatching as many NPCs as it's predecessor did in it's last, and it only gets crazier from there.  In fact, about 2/3 the way through the story I had earned the 1000 deaths achievo... something I am still a considerable distance from in HM1, despite two playthroughs and a good deal of mission replays.

Below you'll find a written and video impression on the game
Before I start I want to mention that I've never played the first Hotline Miami, so this impression will be from some one who's new to the series, and have judged it under the game's own merit.
Hotline Miami 2 is a top-down perspective action game. If you've played the classic GTAs, you'll be quite familiar with this. Unlike GTA, the game isn't so much open world as it is mission to mission. You'll be brutally gunning down or beating up your enemies. But it's not quite as simple as holding down a trigger and win. The game is challenging where all it takes is one shot to end your game.
Hotline Miami's visual is of some of the best I've seen in pixel art. It's similar to what you might of seen from the 16 bit era, but refined to great detail. The game is brutal, violent, and gory, and it takes a lot of skill to represent that degree of grotesque in 16 bits, as the resolution doesn't leave the artist much room for error. The visuals are vibrant and all cohesively themed in an 80s retro style. It's gorgeous! The audio is of an equal quality with one of the best OST in recent memory.
Though a game like this, that feel quite arcady, can often get away with little to no story. Hotline Miami 2 takes the high road and offers an engrossing narrative that goes much deeper than a simple crime drama. With out spoilers, it goes into the delusional, and I'd compare it to the psychological thriller genre. But do be aware, it also explores some extremely dark and adult themes. This is not a game for children or those who are easily offended.
There's much to love about Hotline Miami 2, but it doesn't get away with out flaws that's worth pointing out. The game does have some bugs, not many, but some and when they appear, they're noticeable. Also the enemy AI, though passable, could be improved on, as they're not always reacting realistically.
Overall, Hotline Miami 2 is a great game that's worth every penny it's asking for. It's challenging, looks and sounds amazing, and brutally honest in it's story telling. I can not recommend this any more!

Let's face it, this is Warhammer: Left 4 Dead and that's a good thing. The most noticable difference is the shift of focus to melee combat which it does fairly well. Ranged weapons are still an option, but for the most part reloading in between shots is long so it turns into a shoot once then switch to melee as you engage kind of affair.

The loot system is decent as you get more loot die to roll the better you perform each run, and you get to salvage or fuse trash/old/duplicate items into something better. It's a lot of RNG, but nothing you aren't already used to. It's Warhammer after all, you already know what kind of random dice BS you're getting into.
Pros:
- If you like horde-style/coop games, this is a must buy.
- Warhammer Fantasy theme is well implemented.
- Melee combat feels varied and satisfying.
- Various class / weapon combinations will play differently.
- Loot system will always reward you with something. Either get lucky with the dice rolls, or farm it out and fuse loot into better stuff.
Cons:
- No competitive modes.
- Server browser should display ping instead of country.
- More maps and characters would be great.
- No menu-based communications, rarely do people use VoIP or chat.
- Host migration when the hosting player leaves dumps you into loading screens, especially when people leave the party in succession.

Definitely a good game.  It has held my attention for the most part.  As it stands right now there's obvious issues as it's an alpha.  The current issues I've ran into so far are as follows:
The AI has some pretty bad pathfinding.  They can get stuck on something as small as a mound of dirt.  Which makes you have to keep an eye on them during escort missions where you've ran for 10-15 mins only to realize when you get to your destination that the person you're escorting got stuck half way back.  You're able to have two companions where if they get too far behind they'll teleport next to you.  This needs to happen to escorted NPCs as well.
There's many different ways to travel, however I've only made a car.  While fun and all, they damage very easily.  This may be because it's a starting car I made but the damage accumulated way too fast.  I was only able to drive for 2 mins tops in the forest area before the car blew up.  Every small mound I went over made the car take damage.  Also I found that the cars handling needs a fair amount of tweaking.
I've only just got past the kill the layerback (whetever they're called) mission.  That's where I hit my first roadblock as the quest was either unintentionally unfair or bugged as you're supposed to escort 2 survivors  to kill the layerbacks.  The one guard NPC always rushes in to melee them only to die and fail the mission.  I must have tried the mission literally 30 times, before I just built a wall around him out of harms way and only then could I finish the mission.  They need to certainly fix that as it's more than just a minor annoyance.
All in all this game has certain potential to be really good.  If you can deal with it's quirks as alpha goes along, there's definitely a lot of fun to be had.  Also the fact that you can build you're own cars, vtols and weapons with pre made parts then add voxels to add your own touch to it is really cool.
While I don't think in it's alpha state the price is justified, it will be worth it at full release.

Okay, this game is GORGEOUS. The backgrounds are more detailed than 90% of big budget AAA titles. Zombies shuffle around in numbers rivaling a Dead Rising game. Hands down the best looking platformer ever made.
That said...the gameplay and story bite.
The writing is atrocious, and they cram tons of it down your throat with cutscenes and diary entries galore. Do yourself a big favor and don't waste time on reading the diary.
The gameplay seems at first to be a tense affair as you parkour to avoid hordes of zombies. The game is at its best when you're trying to stay one step ahead of pursuing zombie packs as you vault from roof to roof. Sadly, this doesn't last long. While the game is gorgeous, it does a poor job of highlighting what you can interact with. The majority of your deaths are going to come not from challenges, but from trying to jump to a ledge, only to find that it was part of the background and not something you could grab on to.
I could stil forgive that if the game was all tense zombie chases, but the entire middle third of the game shifts to an awful sewer level that serves as a literal obstacle course. Some hermit wants to see how agile you are, so he has you run through courses with wooden targets and zero zombies. You carry around a slingshot going PLINK PLINK PLINK against wooden targets that release ramps. This section lasts a good hour or more. WHO IN THE WORLD THOUGHT THIS WAS MORE FUN THAN THE ZOMBIE HORDE LEVELS? The sewers have the same amount of insane background detail as the rest of the game, so it's not even like they rushed it to lengthen the game; the same amount of effort went into creating that snoozefest portion of the game.
So, that's two-thirds of the game with tense zombie chases dragged down  by falling through illusionary platforms, and one-third of the game an unredeemable boring obstacle course. The whole time you get carpal tunnel from hammerin gthe mouse button to skip the diary and story scenes. It's a darn shame because words cannot describe how gorgeous this game is. Even though Mark of the Ninja's gameplay is infinitely better, I had trouble enjoying it after this because now I expect every platformer to be this visually breathtaking.

Far Cry 3 tells the story of Jason Brody, a Californian who is on vacation with his brothers, friends and girlfriend, knowing exotic places in the South Pacific.
Far Cry 3 is first-person shooter with open world features that let's you get the illusion of freedom within a island dominated by a local guerrilla.
Like Alice in Wonderland, which is quoted at the beginning of each chapter, Jason follows the white rabbit, falls into a hole, and finds himself in a surreal place, losing the sense of who he is. His allies are eccentric, he is as lost as a junkie.
The game symbol is the mirror image of a gun. The game tries to reflect the image of the player back to him, showing the absurdity of expecting to be a hero killing countless people.
The game is also about colonization. Vestiges of the Japanese presence on the island tell about the legacy of the atomic bomb, and an agent of the CIA demonstrates an exaggerated patriotism that it's comical. The game criticizes the American ethnocentrism, but his main criticism is about the ease with which the players accepts the violence around them.
One of the highlights is when Vaas talks about the definition of insanity: doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results. There are a lot of metaphors about that. The writing is so good it reminds me of Bioshock.
I recommend this game for people who like to discuss violence in games. It features anthropological problems, insanity, lots of references, and dark humor. In this game you follow the white rabbit, fall into a hole and get crazy. It’s a game that really deceives and traps you. You end up asking questions about yourself.
Positive points
+ One of the best writing you will find a first-person shooter.
+ The game can keep you hooked on it's non-stop action.
Negative points
- You are encouraged to kill innocent animals for no good reason.
- It tries to criticize violence while exposing you to a lot of violence.

Personally I would say this game is a great game, however, I feel there are a few details to know before buying this game. This game was made quite a good number of years ago and therefore the graphics are also a bit outdated so if that is something you can't get over I would not suggest buying this game. Also this game does have a bit steep of a learning curve but once you learn how to play it is definetly worth it.
Now as to why I think this game is so good:
Well first of all there is no story line which some would see as a bad idea but the way Warband uses it, it actually works. It allows for almost any possible course of action to achieve your own personal goals wether it be becoming rich, becoming King, or even marrying a noble lady.
Secondly, the modding community is huge which is constantly adding mods that can increase your experience in the game or even add even more to said experience such as a mod called the Freelance mod which makes it so you are now able to play as a regular soldier in a Lords army.
Thirdly, the multiplayer can have up to 200 players! How many "next generation" games do you hear of being able to have 200 players fighting eachother the the death in brutal and bloody combat.
Fourthly, there is a DLC for this game which I have taken a particular interest in. This mod is the Napoleonic Wars DLC which allows you to play in multiplayer games as a soldier from the time period of Napoleon conquering Europe. This DLC while not having single player (although there is a mod that is coming out eventually that will have singleplayer) seems to draw you in with its organized communities. While the initial prospect of running around in a line and having to listen to orders may seem daunting especially considering that there is generally no space between each person in a line, I assure you it is actually a lot more fun then it sounds. Imagine being able to play as a artillery unit that is able to shoot at unit such as that or playing as cavalry and gloriously charging your enemy and cutting down any that get in your way. Or getting a reputation as a deadly sniper as a part of a skirmisher or line infantry regiment. With 200 players able to play in one server at once all these units can all be in the same server working together. So imagine marching towards enemy positions with artillery flying overhead and the cavalry charging past you while the skirmishers snipe important enemy personel.

If you haven't played the original Hotline Miami, then go play that first. If you have played the original and just wish that there was a few more levels then I can only sort of recommend the sequel; and here's why:
First of all the soundtrack is amazing, it features more tracks and like the original it does so much to spice up the game. Furthermore, the graphics seem to have been slightly updated giving it a better pixel look that is still very much Hotline Miami. Rounding out the good are the masks, while the sequel has less masks (and a few that repeat from character to character) they feel vastly different making it much more interesting to experiment with the different options.
As far as the bad goes, oh boy, where to begin? Starting with the story I have to say that I am not impressed... while I doubt anybody ever played Hotline Miami for the story the second game tries really hard to get you interested by introducing a (huge) new cast of characters that all just kind of exist to be violent sociopaths, some of them have goals sure, but nothing is resolved by the end of the game, which to be fair was the same case with the original but that shouldn't be the case of the sequel. However, I can forgive a lackluster story, but what I absolutely cannot forgive is horrible level design. Whoever did this graphic totally gets just how mishandled the design of the levels were.
Basically it comes down to this, there are more windows in every level meaning that the increased number of enemies will be taking you down with potshots constantly. Furtheremore, some levels have huge open spaces with little to no cover making it impossible for you to see enemies that will kill you with gunfire, it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and it goes against the fantastic pacing of the original where you could charge into a single room and murder everything with a melee weapon, but with numerous new special enemies that require guns to be killed that ♥♥♥♥s that up too. Not to mention the one horrible boss fight that seems to be a stable of the original has now wormed its way into the sequel as well. And while we're at it the game has several bugs where enemies spin around in circles, get stuck in doorways where they are impossible to hit or worst of all when enemies jump through walls and kill you.
Hopefully the level editor and some bug fixes will rectify some of these issues, but as it stands it's just a really, really disappointing experience.

Oh boy, Hotline Miami 2 finally hit the shelves, now's the question, is it worth your money?

BUT

There are 13 characters total, each having at least 3 variants (except The Fans). All around, it does change their playstyle quite well. It falls short however, as all levels use the old ''bait and execute'' design.
The game is much, MUCH shorter. I finished my 1st playthrough in 1,5 - 2 hours.
There's also hard mode, but it should be named ''tedious mode'', as it changes most enemies into those who can only be hurt by gunfire.
Does this game deserve the 14,99 and all the hype around it? Honestly, no.

This is a story worth telling: Yours.
This game is in Alpha but shows more promise to be a huge hit than most others I've seen. It is the future and you are on a ship heading to a distant planet to colonize it. As you begin landing preperations you hit something in orbit and the ship crashes to the surface.
You wake on a grass- grass on this planet anyway- grass covered valley. Your escape craft smashed half burried in the new planet's soil, a crew member is injured sitting nearby and you are her only hope to survive. You must hike over a hill in the distance to bring a doctor to help her. Luck has it, he survived as well.
You learn that other escape ships have landed around the planet and you need to find them. To do this you must EXPLORE.
Okay. That is roughly the first ten minutes of the game.
The rest is literally up to you.
You must gather resources from the planet to survive. You have a handy replicator in your pocket and as rewards the people you help give you some "scripts" that you add to it, then when you have the needed supplies it can create what you need. It is slightly difficult for example to make a working weapon you may need two or three componants. Raw metal or wood and some maybe refined items. The refined items would have to be made ahead of time from the needed resources they call for. Once you ave all the needed building blocks you choose how many to make and press the button. Easypeasy.
You start with wood tools and weapon and as you find other resources you can build better stuff.
I hate to disapoint but their ar no zombies in this game.
The main currency is meat. You get meat from... Thats it boys and girls! Animals. This planet has alot too. The creatures they have made to inhabit the planet are... interesting. The seem to mostly be six limb based and multi-eyed. Very cool all give a feel of alien and I found myself running to the next hill thinking "Wow, what the heck is that?"
You interact with left and right clicks after equiping the correct tool. To fight you left click with weapon. To gather you right click. You have a portable scanner you can use to scan the area around you to look for resources so you know where to dig. Probably alot more I didn't try but what I did manage to check out looked good.
The planet has a day/night cycle and when it gets dark mean buglike creatures that are very aggressive come out to feed. On you. Thats very bad. They emerge from the vast underground caverns that are everywhere under your feet and if you tunnel a mineshaft into one of these caverns you better have some good weapons. And a light source. Because it is dark and dangerous.
All this is played in the single player mode from your computer. An online peer hosted multi-player option is available with play modes of: Adventure, Versus and Build. I tryed Adventure and found them to be alittle buggy and some lagged alot. you have the option to host your own but you must do some port forwarding and I had no luck with that.
If the devs of Planet Explorers keep up the pace, this will be a fine addition to your library if you enjoy adventure.
I believe it is made with the Unity Engine so the games graphics are fair and the models are slightly cartoony, with some animation flaws and simplistic actions. The maps are gianormous!! With many types of biomes.
I have read some of the ideas they have for the future and am impressed and waiting to see it implemented. Entire player created worlds you can visit. All kinds of ecosystems. Fully player DESIGHNED weapons, armor, vehicles, housing and more. In fact an in game building tool allows you to add texture and colors as well as the look of alot of things already. Not to be confused with the standard building in the game anyway...did I mention it is a voxel based game- You can alter the ground's look and build structures via the "minecraft" like build system.
This promises to give adventure, exploreing, building, gathering fun for many, many hours with endless possability for replay.
Dang forgot the natives- big, armored, flame throwing owners of the new planet you dropped onto... And boss fights with giant robots and flying things and....Oh nevermind. You will find them... Of course they could find you too...

Can't in good conscience recommend this game; it's just too early to say whether it'll be good, but for now it's best left alone.
My entire experience in this game comes from the Story mode, so keep that in mind. My experience so far has been of sticky controls, tentative sound effects, and pretty much no combat system to speak of.
In the game you can design your own weapons and vehicles (the vehicle creation is reminescent of Spore's, or any number of similar games). The system for building weapons is great, it allows for incredible aesthetic maneuverability; it falls a little bit flat when you import your gun/sword into the game and try it out. The ways the game determines what makes a sword have high damage are difficult to determine. The highest damage I've ever managed to reach came from a sword that was a literal block of metal, as big as the game would let me make it. Personally, I prefer SHARP swords, though this may be a stylistic disagreement.
Likewise, my long-barrelled rifle seemed awesome and had great damage, but its accuracy was somewhere between "none" and "none at all". This would contradict the little bit I know about real-life guns, which tells me that a longer barrel = greater accuracy.
I have about 19 hours of playtime in the game, and about 12 of those hours I have estimated to be travel time. It's amazing how long it takes you to get from one place to another, then back again when the quests tell you to go back. There are enough monsters on the way to keep a player docile during this transit, and the crafting can eat up a lot of time, too, since it's so detailed.
What SHOULD be taking up some time is the scanning for (and mining of) resources, but I've found that to be a very arduous process. The map is huge, so when the main quest demands you make something with, say, petroleum in its schematic, you're pretty much screwed when the NPCs tell you to head west to look for oil (and the oil is southwest). I guess that's what forums are for.
Then your scanner tells you the targetted resource is deep underground, and it's a pretty peaceful, Zen-like experience to use the game's terrain shaping to tunnel down into the earth. You get a palpable sense of accomplishment when you look at the big cave that used to not exist before you needed something from under it. Getting back out again is a Stygian nightmare. You will hop, you will slide, you will accidentally click and swing your pickaxe and be unable to make actions until your character is done with his animation. Eventually you will use the game's building mechanics to try to pillar-hop, like in Minecraft, except you will clip into your pillar and slide all the way down it.
Then you will write an angry review for a not-nearly-finished game.

It's Left 4 Dead with swords.
Seriously though, this game has a very strong influence of the L4D series, but instead of being a lesser copy, it brings the mechanics of L4D from the now-tired zombie apocalypse into a new, fresh setting of gothic Warhammer fantasy. The focus on melee combat makes for a much more satisfying experience than the slap-slap-slap feel of L4D2's melee weapons. It feels natural and satisfying.
In addition to the somewhat altered Special enemies and level structure, you also get loot! Weapons and equipables come in many forms and tiers, ranging from mundane Whites and Greens, to rare Blues and Golds. This adds a ton of replayability since you're always searching for a bigger, better item for nailing that harder mission or harder difficulty.

Let me start off by saying I've never played Warhammer or Left 4 Dead. Matchmaking FPS's are not my thing and I do not like them.
With that being said, I absolutely love this game. I have stuck with my dwarf sword/board so far and even though right now in beta there are only 3 maps. The game has great replayability.
I will admit sometimes the hitboxes are weird with my ranged weapon and a few little glitches here and there, but nothing game breaking. The AI for the bots is very good, if you get stuck with them. It doesn't feel like you're escorting them.
The game has gear slots that you obtain through running these maps. Higher difficulty = Better chance at loot.
Slots include head, weapon, ranged, and 3 trinkets.
I really hope in the future we get a little more to customize our character, even if it's just cosmetic.
The combat feels like a fast paced and more responsive version of Skyrims combat.
The maps do a very good job at moving along, without feeling like that linear arcade style story.
Very happy with my purchase. I wasn't so sure at whether or not this would be something I would enjoy, but took a shot in the dark and it paid off. I hope the development team continues to make content/DLC/expansions for this game.
