This game is HUGE. Massive. The first game to really drop me on an untammed planet and just tell me "Hey, heres some crap you can do, now go do crap." I feel incredibly unrestricted. This game has already more than impressed me, and I havent even managed to do ANYTHING noteworthy. Feels like the beginning of minecraft all over again; So impressed with my dirt box mudhut that I forget how awful I am and truly just enjoy the exploration.
Surviving isnt exactly hard. The enemies dont exactly come searching you out, and running from most the land monsters is fairly easy... Until you♥♥♥♥♥♥off something bigger than you. But you learn to only make that mistake once or twice. You learn very quickly how you SHOULD act to survive. Taking damage is always very serious, and ranged weapons become your new best friend, despite how much fun I would have running around and cutting things to bits with a sick sword, the game gives me a good realistic slap in the face to remind me that these creatures are fundementally stronger than me, and will kill me in a simple swordfight through outright hurting more. Guns and bows give you the good range to distance yourself enough to have a fighting chance, and you can switch to a melee weapon to do more damage when they get there. (Though usually I panic and just jump around like an idiot still trying to shoot them)
Building a camp isnt entirely manditory during the early parts of the game. Most of your time is spent running around and exploring. I love that. The game doesnt try to chain you down to a spot, and really enforces the idea of going and exploring. They give you scanners, and maps to help you find your way back, so getting lost isnt a huge worry either, the map has landmarks you can fast travel to and find your footing from there. And the scanner helps you find veins of ore to dig to, so you dont have to search forever to find ore, and then huddle around it thinking its the only one you'll ever find. Even still you can mark locations on your map to remind you where it is. Now you dont HAVE to explore, and it is definitely possible to hide in a small radius, but the game gives you plenty of incentive, and doesnt punish you at all for doing so. Its really all about how you want to play the game.
The building system is really cool. It is flawed in places for now, I do feel a bit restricted as I havent found a way to make rigid edges and square corners (However I could have missed that part in the tutorial, which is screens of text with pictures, kind of a scary sight for gamers these days as it has been established that reading is the bane of our existence). That said, it is a sort of lego system, but you can build weapons, shields, guns, vehicles, etc. Though Ive noticed building something cool, like a Katana for example, is somewhat punished because I could never make it as strong as any premade weapon. Same with shields. I did for a while favor the weaker weapon due to the bond I had with it, crying at enemies asking them to die faster because it looked cool (It didnt work :'<  ). In addition, I wish there were some premade vehicles that I could just use until I get the hang of creating my own, while it does make sense for my first vehicle to be a piece of crap that looks like it has less thought put into it than a dune buggy (Basically just a frame since I kept dying in game while using the build menu). All in all the building is a cool idea, and could be better with just a few tweaks here and there. Importing models made from others online would also be INCREDIBLY cool. For example, someone could make themselves some halo vehicles, or a ferarri and share it with friends online.

It is a very fun game...but there are a LOT of major issues that need to be addressed! The ability of the enemy to camp on your spawn, from WITHIN your spawn. Once you have tanks, that seems to dominate the game...which means if nobody on your team has tanks and the other team does....they will camp your spawn with tanks.
The physics engine leaves a bit to be desired--or at least needs some serious tweaking. Going prone and trying to aim down your sights at the enemy is an EXTREMELY difficult task when even on a flat boulder, hill or other large flat object, you are unable to look down your sights most of the time.
With a few tweaks the game could be pretty awesome...at this time, I neither recommend or NOT recommend the game. It has a long way to go to be even close to balanced.
Another point that adds to the frustration in the game is the inability to change gear. Once you have selected your loadout...you are stuck with it til the end of the battle, or until you pick up a different weapon--rifle, pistol, smg from a fallen comrade or opponent. One of the best Early Access games I've played to date. There is a lot of content here.
Offline the single player has a storyline where you take quests and learn the ins and outs of crafting. There is also an Adventure Mode where the world is procedurally generated and you have to explore and survive with only a handful of NPC villagers.
Online works as well. You can play on a server for adventure, versus or just building with unlimited resources.
You can also create your own buildings in build mode as well as create custom vehicles and weaponry with their in game creation system. It's quite robust, albeit a bit clunky at first.
The game still has a way to go, with some UI and camera issues to iron out as well as more character customization options. Like I said, it's one of the best Early Access games you can play now and with content and updates coming regularly it's must have for anyone who enjoys adventure with mixed with crafting.

Where do you even start with this...
This game could have been amazing. I say could because the major issues cannot simply be fixed with patches, the whole engine needs to be redone.
I wanted to start with the qualities of this game but I feel dissapointed, this game could have been so much more. You're given an open world, the ability to shape the world, an in-depth crafting system and a lot of stuff to do.
Let's start off with the biggest flaws of the game - the controls and combat.
Controls are clunky and work against you, the floaty jump seems to serve no purpose and is mostly a waste of time to use because of how combat works. When you engage in combat with any melee enemy they will automaticly lock on to you and keep charging into you. You'll get trapped inside of the bigger enemies and jumping out of the way doesn't seem to do much. Weapons feel bland and uninspired. You get a comicbook style effect when your arrows land and the only visual representation of dealing damage to a target is by looking at the incredibly small healthbar at the top of your HUD.
AI is equally terrible. Usually this wouldn't mean much for a game like this. However, for some reason the story mode is filled with escort missions. You have to carry these worthless drones around, usually just to look at something only to be told to meet back at camp. If friendly NPCs weren't immortal gods with fists of steel dealing 10 times the damage you can ever hope to achieve I'd say they serve no purpose. They get stuck constantly, they're slow and if you dare think you can use that fancy glider while you're escorting someone you're most likely going to have to walk all the way back to pick up your lazy slob friend as the AI refuses to find a way to you. They also tend to stay out of fights until you've been beaten up a bit just out of spite.
If escort missions weren't a part of this game the AI would be just about acceptable, no more than that.
The sound effects are bad and the voice acting is awful, possibly the worst I have ever heard. It becomes rather obvious that the so called voice actors are just the devs doing silly voices. Good audio plays such a major role in video games and putting a bit of effort into improving the audio would go a long way.
The visuals aren't great. The textures are dated and animations look stiff. The wildlife is filled with different animals but sadly a lot of them seem to be reskins and many of them share the same animations. There is however another issue with these "animals". A very important part of coming up with new creatures is to make them somewhat resemble something we already know. Many of these creatures look absurd and I am not sure if they really belong in this world. There's a creature that walks around on four legs, has two arms and for some reason it's wearing a mask. Why? I don't know, it doesn't make sense.
The one thing this game has going for it as far as I can tell is the building mode. If you are the creative type and you set aside some time to understand the building mode you could create some incredible vehicles and weapons. This is a game however and a lot of people aren't interested in spending hours creating 3d models.
I never set foot into the multiplayer of this game as I couldn't bring myself to recommending this game to any of my friends so I can't judge that aspect.
It feels as if the devs know that the game can never be what they wanted it to be and turned to the cash cow that is early access. I would not recommend this game for anyone other than people interested in 3d modeling.

So far so good with this game, and I am loving every second of it that I have played so far.
EDIT: EXCEPT for the Soldier missions. Holy hell they are bad. And it's not exactly the level design (although that could be a lot better) it's more the character's limitation. After every other character with the exception of the Swans being able to pick up any weapon at some point, the Soldier just can't do that for some reason. Instead, you have to pick a gun that you will run out of ammo with and switch between that and a knife. No picking up enemy weapons, and almost every enemy on those levels has a gun, so they can shoot at you before you see them, and on some of the levels the crosshair and bullets blend into the background, making it really really hard to see and dodge appropriately. I almost lost my♥♥♥♥♥♥on Scene 14, and that's not even the worst one. If we were not limited on the weapons, I would like them a lot more. As it stands, this is the weakest aspect of the game because it doesn't allow you to be creative with what the game gives you, and that is the game's strongest aspect. Why limit what makes your game great? If I could skip those missions I would be one happy person.
ANYWAYS
In my opinion, it retains the same gameplay and the same difficulty, but it forces you to adapt your playstyle in a good way. It switches characters for different missions, going from the fans, to the movie to a reporter, soldier, etc. There's a LOT of new characters, and each character has a different playstyle, going from our traditional HL1 to some new playstyles with the new masks.
The first game looked great, and this one looks almost identical, but the gore is amped up a little more this time, and it feels more brutal and bloody. Blood will splatter and spread before it finally settles, and each hit has a pause and a slight wind up with a satisfying crunch for each execution. The game does not fail at all in this aspect, and it will leave you in a horrified pride at the end of each leve, forcing you to look at your handiwork, just like in the first one. No changes here and I love the new executions and brutality that comes with it.
As for the story, this early in (2.3 hours at time of writing) it's hard to say what's going on, and what I can say stuff about would be spoliers, so no news here. Just know that it would be a good idea to have gotten the secret ending in HL1 before playing this game, or at least know about it.
All in all, this is a good sequel, and it is one I am definitely going to be playing to the end. It makes slight improvements upon what was not-too-great before and it adds enough different things and challenges to keep the veteran player on their toes.
I still recommend this game if you liked the first one, but be aware that the character limitations can be a bit frustrating after being used to the freedom in the first game. Hopefully the level editor will solve that issue, but we won't see till that hits sometime soon.

This would be a really enjoyable game if it actually worked properly. There are also a LOT of glitches, audio, graphical, and wall-clipping alike. The story and voice acting were painfully bad at times. But the combat was the thing that annoyed me the most. Despite the many, MANY things that annoyed me, I did enjoy parts of this game a lot. The beginning is especially good. All-in-all, a game that could have been great, but is instead frustrating, buggy, and not at all worth the asking price. Get it on sale if you must, but don't expect much.

+Themes, aesthetics, and environments are all faithful to the lore.
+While it's a greatly executed L4D homage, it distinguishes itself with its RPG elements. With multiple primary weapons, ranged weapons, trinkets, and secondary effects PER class—of which there are five—means that you can really carve out a nice niche and find a playstyle that suits you.
+On that note, classes are fantastic, voice actors are spot on, and each bring something special to the party.
+Loot system is really rewarding. With tomes that players have the option of carrying (at the expense of not having a health item in reserve) and loot die that modify your post game roll to grant you unique items, I not only understood the system right away but felt that it was fair and motivated me to push on.
+The little things, like replacing a main menu with an interactive Inn, makes this game really unique. Reminds me of Dungeon Defenders in that sense.
+Fatsharks did a great job at making hosting/joining easy and straightforward. Rather than being stuck watching a loading bar while you search for a game, you stay within the inn and can continue upgrading and moving around. It's a little thing, but really great.
+Another way they distinguish themselves from Steam's game is through their level design. While it's ultimately linear, there are enough paths, rooms, hidden areas, and alternate routes that make you feel like you take a slightly different way every play session.
Cons
-------------------------
-Melee combat felt sluggish at first. While I did get used to it eventually, I felt like both the player's range and the enemy's were exaggerated.
-Some specials, such as the packmaster, are indistinguishable from the common mob. Considering he loops his noose around your neck and drags you away without providing any window to counter, they could maybe work on his model. Other specials have armor, neon green accesories, and tend to indicate their presence in some way. Suffice it to say, the Predator-esque sneakyness of the Packmaster is rage inducing and I've seen one pull 3 seperate members of my party off to get pummeled. I realize this is as much learning curve as anything else, but I feel like the devs were inconsistent with that one special. Give him some kind of bone effigy strapped to his back or something that towers over him so we could at least see him.
-As some have mentioned, the host system makes for a potentially frustrating game session given that the map resets when the host leaves. While I've learned to host my own games to avoid dropped sessions, this system leaves much to be desired. Especially on higher difficulties, maps can take a good amount of time to complete and, without checkpoints of any kind, a reset could be rage inducing. This is something that they need to seriously consider changing.
-A few bugs here and there. I figured I'd try using my gamepad after a couple of hours (Xbox one remote) and the "X" command to interact and pick up items didn't work. Also, the VOIP didn't seem to function. I'd appreciate seeing an in game mic prompt to show that the channel is at least open, followed by a green coloration if your voice gets through.
-------------------------
Overall, a very pleasant find. This was an impulse buy after having gotten into the Horus Heresy book series for 40k and needing to scratch a Warhammer itch. This in no way disappoints. I could see it potentially getting repetitive after a while, but given that they're releasing a ton of maps at launch and that there's a loot and upgrade system, I feel like there's some depth and replyability to be enjoyed. Given that a simple game like L4D which, when well executed, provides thousands of hours of fun, I can see Vermintide doing the same thing.

What is there to say about Hotline Miami 2? Well, first and foremost, it is a direct follow up story-wise to Hotline Miami 1. As a big fan of the first game, I simply love that idea. If you've played HM1, you are probably familiar with how the story for about two thirds of the game is a bit garbled, with small newspaper clippings or a clickable object here or there to fill in a little bit more, but past that, it's pretty much up to the player's interpretation of the events that unfold. Now, for those that haven't played the first one, I won't spoil anything, but I will disclose that the endings, and there are multiple, EVEN THEN don't 100% explain to players what the heck is going on. This, until HM2 (and the filling in of info with the awesome free digital comic), left folks wondering what all happened, and most importantly, why? Well, ladies and gents, the continuation, at least in terms of story, is fantastic. The continuing plot, which is played out over multiple chapters through the perspectives of different groups of psycho killers slowly begins to piece together a muuuuch larger picture, and this I simply adore. That, along with the booming  90's synth and vomit-inducing color scheme that has carried over well and true from the first game pretty much seal the deal for me....
Hm...I feel like something is missing...
Oh yeah! The gameplay!
Well, to first timers to the Hotline Miami series, this game will most likely come off as having a pretty steep, and I mean STEEP learning and difficulty curve. Alas, this is most likely an intentional part of the game put in by the developers to feel more comfortable and less patronizing to returning Miami fans. But, if you manage to hone your murdering skills, you can get the jist of the game in a relatively brief time. After having played the first Hotline Miami, however, I can say as a returning player that the feel of this game seems almost completely different from the first one. Now, that may have sounded like it had a negative connotation added to it, but I tend to like change. The layout of the levels are a wee bit tighter, the action is certainly faster, and I notice myself getting frustrated on a couple of occasions, but what does that amount to play-wise? Well, suffice to say, I really REALLY like how the game feels and plays. Again, I site the possible thoughts the developers had when making this game for returning Miami players. With each new group of characters you play, they add on a bit of extra challenge, as instead of having access to a veritable "arsenal" of rejected Halloween masks to choose from in the first game, now you must grapple with the unique dispositions of each of the multiple characters and their limitations. For example, and a fair warning for minor spoilers here, one of the primary groups you play as are a couple of vigilantes who are "fans" of the original mask wearin' murder maestro. Now, instead of playing as the leader of the group, or something like that, players have access to each character as their own individual mask. The "Tony's Revenge" mask limits players to the fists only, but those fists act like explosive punchers, insta-killing anything rather than simply knocking an enemy out like with other characters, while the "Mark" mask lets you play with a starter weapon of DUAL SMGS! Excuse me, but that's frickin' sweet. So, getting back on track, these characters limit the player with specific play styles depending on the character, and yet, it doesn't FEEL limiting. Now, i'm not gonna' nitpick this game, but I love this limitation...as stupid as that sounds. I like the challenge of having to play certain levels differently depending on the different limitations the masks give me, despite still being able to choose the mask at the beginning of most of the levels you play with this merry band of murdalizers. I just feel like i'm actually living these characters and their masks rather than simply putting on a mask, even though that was pretty awesome in the first game as well.  So, in short, with HM2, think "limiting, but refreshing".
SO! As a recap to folks interested in or planning to buy this game, know this:
-The game will challenge you if you are new, so take your time, get hyped up over the twitchy gameplay, and lose yourself in the psychedelic synth, and you'll get the hang of it in no time.
-Remember that you are playing the masks and the characters, not just the characters. The limitations on the levels are meant to embody the individuals you are playing. Whether you play as a Russian mobster who starts with a silenced pistol, or a crazy agile girl with a zebra mask that can roll-dodge, play the way you want to challenge yourself, and try to strategize your play style around the way the character acts and feels to you.
-Really get immersed in the crazy story! Since this IS truly a story continuation that has a lot more narrative than the first game, I would highly suggest playing the first one before running through this, but if you are simply looking for an awesome plot and a bunch of characters with complex and interesting backgrounds, this game will certainly fulfill that need as well.
Well, looks like my time is up...so, I hope I at least got you interested in the Hotline Miami series and story, 'cause lemme' tell ya', it's certainly a good series to get into! Try the first game out if you want the complete feel and plot of the game, but even if you are just looking for a solid arcade twitch top-down 90's-themed over-the-top murder simulator with a kickin' soundtrack, this game is certainly for you!

A distinctly short offering -- clocking in at maybe two hours -- Deadlight has aspirations to fuse puzzle-platformers like the classic Flashback or the more recent fellow XBLA port Limbo (from which it draws no small visual inspiration) with the zombie-apocalypse survival setting of titles such as The Last of Us and Day Z. However, it ends up being more like Canabalt with delusions of grandeur, being in large part concerned with running to the right.
The game lacks direction and can't seem to settle on whether it wants you to have weapons or not, taking them away and returning them capriciously. The setting is similarly inconsistent; although largely urban, a fair chunk of the game takes an inexplicable detour underground to what to all intents and purposes is a puzzle dungeon, a series of trial-and-error traps and jumping puzzles that drags on far longer than it needs to.
While trial-and-error gameplay is not particularly egregious in and of itself, Deadlight's poorly designed approach often means that you can suffer instant death from something you had no chance to anticipate; rather than finding the best solution for a challenge, it's more a case of rote memorisation. This is certainly not helped by finickity controls and a number of bugs; one particularly aggravating example was near the end of the game, where I'd repeatedly have to restart a checkpoint only to find my character spinning on the spot, unable to do otherwise.
In terms of story and characters, Deadlight leaves no cliché unturned, with the characters being barely more than stereotypical ciphers and the story, such as it is, loosely stitching together every zombie trope in the book. There is some genuinely atrocious dialogue in the game -- some of the worst writing I've come across in a long time -- delivered with at best forgettable voice acting.
Although clearly tolerable once through, despite its many flaws, it's impossible to recommend due to its brief duration and frustrating gameplay. Crucially, there's nothing here that hasn't been done better elsewhere; it adds nothing to either the puzzle-platformer or zombie apocalypse genres, and even its two-hour length feels like a waste of time.

I wanted to really like this game, I did.
I was a huge fan of the first and how it played out, and while I was expecting some changes to come along in the process, I didn't expect them to be this bad.
The game isn't horrible by any means, but it's not what I want from a Hotline Miami Game. Somehow the game turned from a quick adrenaline pumping sprint through well constructed levels that offered their own challenges to a nauseating slog through a field of wasted potential. The level designs are interesting in their concept, with a certain mix of characters bringing their approach to how to complete the level,  but they don't work in the least with how the game was designed. Everything is a series of open shooting galleries that happen to be packed full of goons with guns- -of course. You probably won't even see them until they shoot you or you have your shift key taped down. The only effective way to get through the game is to lure enemies around corners until you can smack or shoot them, and rinse and repeat until it is safe to move forward. This also highlights how poor the AI (and not to mention Buggy)is, and whereas in the first game the ignorance to the violence and destruction the enemies have was mostly masked by how quickly one had to move through the level, in this game expect to witness guards do endless rounds over broken glass and their bloodied buddies until you decide to poke your head out and lure them back to your murder corner. Some enemies later on won't even realize they've been shot, or pay no mind to a shotgun blast ripping their friend off their feet.
Going back to the story and characters. Once again, I feel a lot of potential was wasted here too. When I saw the trailers and first started playing, I was getting excited to take a peek into some of the heads of these individuals, and while at first I was mostly satisfied with the progress I was seeing, the story quickly loses all cohesion and starts to play out seemingly at random, throwing one scene after the next at you with little to no explination or closure. Normally this would have been alright, but it simply fails to ever follow up or connect anything, and just leaves so much hanging or cuts it off completely before anything really interesting can come of it. I won't even get into how abrupt and unsatisfying the ending felt to me.
Overall, the game isn't bad, and if you can deal with some frustrating flaws, you might be able to find some fun in the game. All the same, I can safely say that I don't desire giving it another play through, and can see where quite a few wouldn't even bother to finish one.
So much wasted potential.

Heyyo,
The first Hotline Miami was easily one of the BEST indie games I've ever played. So far? Looks like Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number continues that trend. The adrenaline rush of perfect combat execution, the AMAZING soundtrack that challenges the entire game as the best part of the Hotline Miami series rings true yet again and the beautiful 16bit 2D visuals... Dennation Games have done it again.
Ok, before I write three sentenses about the soundtrack (SOOO GOOOOODDD!!! LOL!) I better chat about the game. The controls will take some getting used to. It's top-down view and the movement buttons move your character in the relative direction of the screen. Next? The camera focuses on where you're aiming which can cause you to tunnel-vision on distant enemies or enemies off to the side, so you want to both try and plan your attacks whilst executing the biggest combos you can which will get REALLY tricky and usually leads to many restarts. :P
Using the SHIFT key will cause your view distance to push even farther away from your character which gives you better insight into the level. I love how you can walk around the building and scope out the floor plan of at least the primary floor of the building which will come in handy for figuring out how you want to rack up your combo.
So yeah, the controls take a bit to get used to.. but once you do? It makes you wonder why in the hell did DMA Design Ltd (now known as Rockstar North) used the terrible tank controls in GTA 1, GTA London 1969 and GTA 2  instead of this FANTASTIC control scheme. GTA 1 btw came out in 1997, so every PC had a mouse lol, so it wasn't a question of availability. I remember getting so damn frustrated with those games when trying to aim using a keyboard with rotate left or rotate right controls... ugh. lol. Anywho? Zero problems with the controls on Hotline Miami 2. They work great once you wrap your mind around it. :)
As for the storyline? Well, you'll have to play the game to understand it. It revolves around several gangs and their violent actions. I know on the first Hotline Miami there was a secret ending... maybe this game will have one too. I'll have to keep my eyes open for secret pickups.
Even if you're not interested in buying the game? You NEED to buy the soundtrack. It's got so much drive behind it that it even rivals the great music of Unreal Tournament 99... dare I say, it could potentially work just as good if not better in that game? ;)
If you're not familiar with Hotline Miami? That's ok, the first game is dirt cheap to buy and the combo pack of 1 & 2 for $22? That's amazing. Only a couple extra bucks nets you two of the best indie games out there.
As fantastic as the soundtrack is? Hotline Miami 1's soon of "M|O|O|N - Hydrogen" is still my favorite. The build up and the chorus comes together to make the perfect song to have pounding in your brain.

Very Fun game, if I could describe it my worlds would probably be 'difficult but fair'.  Warhammer Vermintide is an action co-op game in which you and a couple of your friends get together and battle hordes of giant rats called Skaven while trying to complete objectives and gather loot before you eventually escape at the end point.
And don't worry, even if you're not a fan or know anything about the Warhammer Universe (like me) you can still very much have fun with this game. Prior knowledge about lore is not required. Just think of it as a fantasy styled Left 4 Dead
- Melee combat is some of the best feeling in a game that I've played in a while. Blows feel 'meaty' and weapons frequently stop when they hit something that makes it feel really realistic almost like you're hitting something with a real weapon.
- Ranged Combat feels great also with a wide array of crossbows/rifles/pistols/shotguns for you to choose from. I've always been a fan of games where guns can co-exist with bows and arrows and this game fills that perfectly. Blowing apart a horde of Skaven with a shotgun feels powerful, while covering a teammate transporting an explosive barrel with a bow and arrow feels rewarding.
- The sound direction for this game is surprisingly well done. Some of the soundtrack when a Skaven horde is about to show up sounds down right terrifying at some points, and I was actually surprised at how well everything fit together.
- Do you like magic? There's a class for that. Do you like ranged combat? There's a class for that. Do you want to have a good mix of both melee and ranged combat? There's a class for that. You can really choose how you want to play and I really liked that. Also, there can only be one of each class in a game, which I liked as a small little touch to encourage diversity in every game.
- The loot system adds a lot of replayability to an already replayable heavy game. Completing a game and then rolling for your loot only to get a rare rifle or hammer is sure to surge anyone’s gambling addiction.
- Some optimization issues, but at the time of this review the game is currently in beta so the devs will probably iron these issues out
- Some issues with bugs (I've had 3 games now where someone has gotten stuck on something)
- Difficult (may or may not be a con, but you will need teamwork to survive)

Finally, a Warhammer franchise game done right.
Vermintide is a four player co-op action game, done in the style of Left 4 Dead. Vermintide borrows quite shamelessly from Valve's shooter, but make no mistake, it's not a low quality rip-off.
Vermintide focuses on melee combat. It's brutal, visceral and immensely satisfying. While I personally wish for slightly more depth to it, the amount of different weapons you can get makes up for the problem. Fans of Dark Messiah of Might and Magic will feel right at home with the melee combat here. If you like hitting ratmen with a giant warhammer and seeing their screaming bodies go flying, you will feel at home too.
The special Skaven are very powerful and can make the game brutally hard - while Left 4 Dead often did not throw multiple special infected at you, in Vermintide teamwork is so much more important, especially when multiple Packmasters (Jockey+Smoker) spawn at the same time as a Rat Ogre (Tank). Gutter Runner (Hunter) AI is actually fantastic as well. Those sneaky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s can hound you for the entire level, choosing only to pounce when your team is split up or distracted. You really have to work together or you won't be getting past Normal difficulty.
In terms of lore and aesthetics, the developers Fatshark have very diligently brought the Old World to life. I love the twisted streets of Ubersreik. The banter between the characters are top-notch and the high quality voice acting really brings out the off-kilter mismatch of heroes they are.
The biggest problem, however, is with the polish of the game. Sometimes the Skaven move erratically, or get stuck on lamp posts. Sometimes the Rat Ogre will hit you and you'll go flying through walls. Sometimes, you'll clip onto the edge of a rock or low wall and need to jump to get out. It's the little things like that which hamper the Vermintide experience - if the developers are diligent and support the game with patches and updates and DLC post-release, then they won't be an issue. Fatshark, however, has a bit of a reputation for not doing that. Hopefully, with Vermintide shaping up to be a big success, they will shed their past habits.
If you want a high optimized and polished gem, Vermintide might not be the game for you. It has it's rough edges, but make no mistake, the game is fantastically fun if you don't mind the occasional FPS spike, or clipping error. I would recommend it to most people unless you are extremely short on cash - then put it on your wishlist and definitely pick it up with a sale.

Keeping in mind that this is in alpha, and it is nowhere near done, I'd say that most of these problems can be fixed, and I am sure they will be even better than I could imagine in time. This game is kinda like minecraft in space, so that's pretty awesome. I also love that there is character interaction, and that the interaction will only get better. Overall, I would reccommend this game strongly. It isn't great yet, but I know it will be.

The story line is a little unique to the zombie apocalypse genre, but after a full playthrough it feels acceptable.  No surprise for a port from 360 version to be expected; clunky controls even with a 360 controller, cut scenes with missing audio (from what I've read online there is a potential fix).
2D platformers aren't my main genre of game that I play, but the puzzles still weren't very challenging.  The difficulty progression seemed to scale alright as the game continued, but again, this won't necessarily require you to have a guide / walkthrough at the ready.
The level design was alright, if anything was great, it would be the atmospheric feel of the levels.  There's a sense that while the game is 2D and you're set to go in only one direction, the environment had me wanting to explore beyond the linear concept of 2D platformers.
The combat isn't too bad, although using the axe while watching the stamina bar can get repetitive when you're only able to effectively kill them by decapitation (or rarely by chopping an limb off).  The firearm mechanics seem to be okay, at best, there might even be a little too much ammo to find and use for how long the zombie apocalypse has been going on in the story.
The 2 things I disliked the most is the rushed scenes at the end with the falling debris; often times debris would fall before you reached the point below it and would one hit kill automatically even from full health. Also while climbing / descending from walls, the clunky controls didn't help either.
tl;dr   6.5/10
+    unique story
+    atmospheric world
+/- challenging difficulty
+/- about 3 hours gameplay, mainly due to replaying certain areas over
- -  expected low quality port (audio not fully functional [cutscenes only], clunky controls)

I have played a lot of zombie FPS (They Hunger, Zombie Master, Zombie Panic, NMRIH, L4D...ect), however I have longed for a game that captured the essence of a George A Romero zombie flick. At last we have a game where the zombies can only be dispatched by shooting them in the head! I am suprised this has not been done before, as it not only says true to the greatest zombie triology of all time, but more importantly, it rewards player accuracy.
The game offers a fantastic atmosphere, good gun mechanics and some interesting maps. What stands out from this game is the fantastic 'hunted' mode, which is essentially a last man standing PVP deathmatch with NPC zombies. However, it has a slight twist, in that when a player dies, they come back playing as a zombie. I loved the PVP element of 'Day Z', so this game mode was perfect for me. At present, I would even go as far as saying that the battles on this game are better, because the game mechanics are so fluid and the zombies are actually a threat.
Contagion is by no means perfect though, for starters, the objective game modes are hit and miss. Although the player is told what to do by a mobile phone, it is often not clear what the objective actually is, or where the player should go. The game is crying out for more maps, which I am sure will come when/if it gets workshop support. Also, I am hoping that the developers adapt the current barracading system, so that players can actually move objects (at present you can only place wooden boards).
Overall, this is a decent addition to the genre. Perhaps the amount of content does not justify the full price tag, but it is definitely worth picking up in the sale for the 'hunted' gameplay mode. Hopefully it will develop and maintain a healthy player count.

Vermintide is a four player co-op action game, done in the style of Left 4 Dead. Vermintide borrows quite shamelessly from Valve's shooter, but make no mistake, it's not a low quality rip-off.
Vermintide focuses on melee combat. It's brutal, visceral and immensely satisfying. While I personally wish for slightly more depth to it, the amount of different weapons you can get makes up for the problem. Fans of Dark Messiah of Might and Magic will feel right at home with the melee combat here. If you like hitting ratmen with a giant warhammer and seeing their screaming bodies go flying, you will feel at home too.
The special Skaven are very powerful and can make the game brutally hard - while Left 4 Dead often did not throw multiple special infected at you, in Vermintide teamwork is so much more important, especially when multiple Packmasters (Jockey+Smoker) spawn at the same time as a Rat Ogre (Tank). Gutter Runner (Hunter) AI is actually fantastic as well. Those sneaky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s can hound you for the entire level, choosing only to pounce when your team is split up or distracted. You really have to work together or you won't be getting past Normal difficulty.
In terms of lore and aesthetics, the developers Fatshark have very diligently brought the Old World to life. I love the twisted streets of Ubersreik. The banter between the characters are top-notch and the high quality voice acting really brings out the off-kilter mismatch of heroes they are.
The biggest problem, however, is with the polish of the game. Sometimes the Skaven move erratically, or get stuck on lamp posts. Sometimes the Rat Ogre will hit you and you'll go flying through walls. Sometimes, you'll clip onto the edge of a rock or low wall and need to jump to get out. It's the little things like that which hamper the Vermintide experience - if the developers are diligent and support the game with patches and updates and DLC post-release, then they won't be an issue. Fatshark, however, has a bit of a reputation for not doing that. Hopefully, with Vermintide shaping up to be a big success, they will shed their past habits.
If you want a high optimized and polished gem, Vermintide might not be the game for you. It has it's rough edges, but make no mistake, the game is fantastically fun if you don't mind the occasional FPS spike, or clipping error. I would recommend it to most people unless you are extremely short on cash - then put it on your wishlist and definitely pick it up with a sale.

Set in the Warhammer Fantasy Lore/Universe, you get to play 5 difference Class.
The Witch Hunter named Victor Saltzpyre that specialize pistols, rapiers crossbow and 2Handed Sword.

The Dwarf Ranger named Bardin Goreksson that specialize on crossbow, axe, hammer and shield.
The Bright Wizard named Sienna Fuegonasus that specialize on single sword, a baton mace and wands with different magic.
The Empire Soldier named Markus Kruber that specialize on Sword and shield, 2Handed Hammer and a Blunderbuss Gun.
The game is simple like L4D but with a catch. The Skav Rats are more smarter, deals a LOT of damage that you never expected and more responsive to you actions so "Teamwork" is "Far More Important". If you do not cooperate with your team you will die and lose horribly. Its no joke because the Skav will horde you down in many ways. Regular Rats which are very simple to kill and have funny reactions but are smart. The Armored Rats which either comes alone, in 2 or a Patrol which YOU MUST AVOID AT ALL COST. You have the Gas Rat that can make you lose your standing defensive ground and will mess you up. You have the Gunner rat which will target one of your team and will deal massive damage. The Taskmaster Rat which will drag you away then hang you. Finally the Rat Ogre which will literally pin you down.
Easy mode is like playing normal mode. Quite easy.
Normal mode is hard mode. Because you can actually lose on the Prologue.
Hard mode is challenging because you will not have any healing potions equip at the beginning.
Nightmare is where Friendly fire is activated and the enemies seems to be more smarter. Also you can practically die instantly without going down for revive so be warn about your health and medkits.
Cataclysm....May the Gods be with you.
Now some mission maps has these Tomes and Grimoire that can be collected to boost your experience and reward but be warn about the risk. Either your health will be reduced to a mere 25% from 100%, you will take more damage or when picking up a tome/Grimoire you will instantly get down. Now if you successfully completed a mission, you will roll dies to gain random weapons so its pretty much RNG. Each weapons give different stats that will help you on your gameplay so they really make a difference on how you want to proceed.
Atm there are some minor bug issues but the Developers has been fixing and working on the issues since Closed Beta so its nice to see they are doing something and making improvement of optimization to the game.
Also, this game is not recommended for any easy going gameplay. This was intentional to be hard because you are playing a Warhammer Game. You have been warned.

Far Cry 3 establishes a bleak and mature tone out of the gate. Jason, our protagonist, should fear the pirates running the tropical retreat of Rook Island. In his eyes, killing is not cool. Not yet. The emotional weight only gets heavier as he tries to save his missing friends from slave-trading psychopaths. In turn, Jason’s gradual transformation from coward to killer unfolds in a natural, believable way, which compensates for the narrow revenge premise. As its unpredictable, often uncomfortable story comes unhinged, Far Cry 3 challenges players’ principles: How far would you go to protect the people you love, and what kind of person would you become to get them back?
Jason begins his evolution after escaping the clutches of Vaas, the mentally unstable leader of a pirate gang and the man who’s kidnapped his friends and family. Before having you hunt down Vaas, Far Cry 3 focuses nearly an hour on teaching you survival skills. Jason scavenges supplies, harvests plants, and crafts useful items from animal skins before ever firing a gun at a man. Choose not to take advantage of the wildlife at large and you’re missing out on important upgrades; bigger wallets hold more cash to buy better weapons, weapon holsters house additional firearms, and larger rucksacks store more goods. Motivation drives exploration because there’s a purpose for everything on Rook Island.

text: I have been playing this game from back in version 0.4 and was very impressed with it back then and still am today. I am a very big fan of voxel games and sandbox building games and when you add in the 'distant planet in the future' factor, that was a huge hook for me. Gathering and creating is very well implemented and feels nice. The ability to custom build your weapons and vehicles is so well done that it can take hours (If you want to spend that log that is) to make something. This game still is in early access so the only complaints I have are moot because they will be addressed. First, the control of your character is blocking and weird at time, not smooth at all. Secondly, the difficulty is too high when you first start out and then you turn into god as soon as you get any decent weapon. And lastly, and I know I am being nit picky, when it rains it will show up inside your home even if it is closed up. All things said, if you are a fan of sandbox games or voxel games, get this game!

If you've got a creative bone in your body, you'll love this game. If you loved building amazing things in Minecraft out of materials that you patiently (and often painfully) harvested yourself, you'll probably love this game. It contains a lot of the things people have come to love from creative adventure/survival games and then throws nice visuals and a pretty rad story mode on it like its no big deal.
The game is no way polished and pretty just yet (its early access), but by playing it, you'll realize just how much amazing potential this game has. I've been following this game and playing it pretty casually for the past year and it found it really interesting how connected the developers were with their community - often seeing developers pick up on suggestions from the forums. When the game updates, the updates are usually worth checking out.
My complaints for the game are minimal and will very likely be worked out by release - things like not-so-great voice acting for NPCs in the Story Mode, the incomplete character creation section, the limited/poor sounds and music, having to hold AI companions hands a lot, and generally strange monster AI behavior.
If you're feeling iffy about the purchase, just wait for final release, It'll likely be a different animal worth way more than its current price tag.

Although if you liked Hotline Miami 1 you will probably like 2. It's longer and I think it's still worth the $15 price tag.

Although this game has a few issues it is still one of the better online fps games, imho.
Technically it is solid.  Very few bugs, no noticable lag issues, weapon balance is okay and the pay to win aspect is not overwhelming.  The default weapons are good enough, and it doesn't take too many hours to grind enough cash to upgrade.  Plus, you can pick up weapons in the field and use them any time.  Graphics, sound, matchmaking and the fps mechanics are all very acceptable as well.
It tends to be a very quiet game.  There is no voice chat, and you can only text chat with your own team, so the smack-talking factor is very low.  I suppose that could be a good thing, but it would be nice to have the option to communicate effectively with your teammates.
That leads me to the single biggest problem with the game, your teammates.  It seems that at least 2/3 of the people who play the game only want to hide in the bushes and shoot at the enemy from the farthest range of their rifle.  Every round, people stand by and watch the enemy capture points and do nothing but take pot shots from too far away to do any good.  It gets incredibly frustrating being one of only 2 or 3 people on the team who are willing to get in close and do the dirty work.  Heaven forbid you do something that might get you killed or scratch the paint on your virtual tank.  Hmm, maybe its a good thing there is no voice chat after all.
Anyway, I have to recommend the game because when you find yourself in a match with people who understand that winning is more important than a good kill:death ratio (which actually happens fairly often), it is a very good game.
I'm going to stick around for a while and I'll keep bugging the devs about adding voice chat until they finally get off their a**es and do it.
See you on the battlefield (and I better not find you hiding behind a tree).

The game itself isn't much upon first glance, but delving deeper, there is a progression level that is more than captivating.
Even if you're a casual gamer such as I, the game offers some quick and easy skirmishes, I have yet to reach the point of being a general, so I can't write about that though.
It's most captivating element is also somewhat of a "grind", making for an alluring paradox, where you might not be willing to gather the necessary resources for unlocking new equipment.
To specify, I've found the accessibility of the german bolt action kar98k a bit harsh, costing about 75k, where I've found that a well-turned-out round of gameplay awards you with approximately 10k. And that is rare for me, seeing how I'm currently stuck with a very powerfully modded MP34, which is insanely efficient at close to medium range, whereas the basic semi-auto g43 (which would be suited for the rather frequent larger maps) requires about 3 shots on the upper body, obviously some serious issues in the damage department, not to mention some trouble with it's accuracy. So, all in all, I'd love to have a more easy to access long range weapon in my character's arsenal, looking at the average map size.
But it's all a subjective opinion based on my point of view, overall the game supplies my need for my long lost love, WWII tactical FPS's, especially CoD1.
There's but one issue that remained with me throughout these low-level skirmishes, and that's the abundance of armored vehicles, and the fact that as an infantry you have no way of dealing with them other than picking up quite rare panzerfausts, which are found in some points of interests on the maps. The only other working solution is to buy your own and deploy with it, but it's a quantity based weapon, meaning you have a fix number of shots after buying it, not to mention it's deploy weight might restrain you from bringing your desired weapons to the field.
I'd recommend if you are willing to look over the initial first impression the game might have, and have the patience to play it through.

I cannot say this game is the best I've played in a while, but it is worth trying out at least. There is at present a limited number of options for maps at the moment (a situation I expect to change in the near future), but from what I can tell the map quantity does not need to be high. It offers a dynamic gameplay so that each playthrough is unique. The maps lock certain ways and unlike others each time, which is unique unto itself. The fact that players who die come back as zombies makes the game that much more fun. It is somewhat limited in scope, however. The physics are not as polished as some other zombie games, and there are only two kinds of zombie to face - regular and armored. The player zombies act as 'leaders' for the horde only in that they can command them; they do not have enhanced hp or special abilities. However, the games modes included do make up for the seeming lack of variety or polish. Hunted is effectively a deathmatch with zombies thrown in for flavor, escape is the classic left for dead style run through, escort is the typical escort-style mission with zombies, and panic is a simple pc v pc human v zombie deathmatch mode. Another plus is the survival-style limited resources provided. Every game mode, no matter the type, forces the player to constantly scavenge for ammunition and equipment, which is how one would imagine a zombie apocalypse to play out. Over all this is a decent game, though if you dislike the survival horror genre stay away. Ammo conservation is paramount to survival here.

Just finished it in hard mode, for my first time to complete it. I started it over a year ago. It's my typical play 15 games at the same time kind of thing, switching back and forth. I really enjoyed this game. It's very different. The objective of the game is not to kill, but to survive, get out alive. There is a nice mix of puzzles as you go thru the levels, figuring out what you have and how you can use it to finagle urself past or by or around or under or thru or etc. The dev's have done a nice job of getting ur heart pumping at the right times, mixing in mood and feeling with the graphics to set the tone, and the music is perfect. A couple of technical points. I read a lot of people complaining about having control problems. Specifically, don't try to play this game with a keyboard and mouse, it's hopeless. I can't imagine how insanely hard it would be. I played it with an xbox controller, and it works nicely. Secondly, sometime late 2013, the audio in the cutscenes quit working. That audio is so crucial to the enjoyment and character and mood, it's truly necessary. I am not sure what is going on, if there was a corrupted binkw.dll that was downloaded in a patch or what. But I read where some guys in the forums were copying the binkw.dll from other games. I copied the one from Mark of the Ninja, which was showing to be the same size and version, etc. and it worked perfectly. Once I did this, the cutscenes were as intended, very well done and perfect. Randall's voice is so necessary in those scenes. I'll say, this isn't the greatest game in the history of earth, but it is a very good one. I give it a B+. I also think that the story-line, feeling, mood, etc. of the game will really stick with you. I like that in a game.

So let's talk about things besides the soundtrack.
This game is hard.
So many levels harder than the original. The techniques you learned in the first will be put to the absolute test in every stage. New enemy types are merciless and require better timing, more accurate throws, perfect item selection and every dirty trick you have to survive. Some levels it feels like Wedin and Soderstrom were making them just to laugh at our tears, but the level of satisfaction you get from killing four men with a fist, a switchblade to the forehead, a single shotgun shell and two kicked in heads? Unbelievable.
The story continues and jogs between before the original and years after it, touching on several characters from the first, exploring completely different people in different ways, and generally causing great mental and emotional distress in so many wonderful ways. You thought it felt good tearing a man's head off with your bare hands? There are points that make you question it. There are points that make you question everything the last level just showed you.
There are still a few bugs, enemies getting caught around corners and becoming invulnerable, certain enemies ignoring walls and doors and jogging though, and the weapon pickups need a bit of a tweak, but still minor issues at best.
If you haven't played the first, you'll be missing a ton of story importance, you'll have a way harder time getting through, and you'll generally be out of the loop the whole game. Do yourself a favour and play the first if you haven't, and if you have, buy this. It's even more masochistic but the soundtrack, (most) of the new characters and the expanded levels are a thing to behold.
Everything you could have expected.
Simply doesn't live up to the original. The level-breaking bugs and poor level design don't help it much, either.

If you love games that envolve team work, sticking together, gathering supplies, and running from hordes of scary and actually threatening zombies while trying to NOT ♥♥♥♥ your pants. Then you should get this game! It's great!
The sound design for the game is great, the music that plays really does keep you on your toes and immerses you further into the game, plus the sound of the zombies that are literally everywhere are so well done that they will literally scare you. You feel helpless in the game when you're alone, you have to make your shots count, melee weapons in this game aren't like they are in Left 4 Dead 2, you have to charge up the attack to deal enough damage to one hit kill a zombie, and for some maybe 2-3 hits. The zombies only die when you destroy the brain, so always aim for the head. Also the gun play in the game is phenomenal! They behave like a real life weapon would, they sound real, and you have to reload the gun yourself. It isn't like other FPS games where they do the reloading for you. Also NEVER and I mean NEVER have a low clip in a gun. That could without a doubt ♥♥♥♥ you over. Plus this game has Steam Workshop for player skins, backgrounds for your phones, ringtones for your phone, and custom maps.
Oh and I will say this, this is without a doubt the best looking game made on the Source engine ever! The graphics are like damn near realistic (better than BF4 on high settings) but it's actually optimized perfectly to run like any other source game would.
Oh I also feel like mentioning that there are plenty of modes, both PvE and PvP. Hunted, a PvP mode, is without a doubt the most fun mode ever. You fight against 7 other human players that are out to get kill you (Free For All like) but getting ammo and weapons is a lot easier, plus there's plenty of zombies that you have to survive from. Once you die then you become a zombie and you have to gather a massive horde to take down the other remaining players. I highly suggest that if you do get the game then you should give it a go.
Now the downsides...yes as amazing as this game is there are a few downsides, there aren't a lot of maps in the core game. You will be let down by the number of maps in the game, but on the bright side the maps play differently each round making it feel new and fresh.
Overall I give this game a 9.7/10 . Just add some more maps to the game and maybe 1 or 2 more weapons and it's perfect!

I want to start by saying that, me not recommending this game, has nothing to do with the game itself per se. It’s the pc port that it’s just awful and makes it unbearable to play (for me at least) as it stands at the moment.
I’ve had constant slowdowns, hiccups, freezes, crashes, you name it.
If the bugs and issues get solved with patching I’ll get right back to it, but until then it’s a big no no for me.
For the game itself I really was enjoying the ambience and story up to the point that I’m at.
The game mechanics (combat/plaforming) rely on stamina management which make you feel really vulnerable adding up to the immersion. You’re not going to rambo your way out of tight situations, you need to think and act fast, that’s the motto.
Although the game is only sidescrolling, it never felt linear nor boring even there being no choice of path to take. It presents you with such a variety of situations that it makes the lack of choice secondary since you get so immersed in it.
Just to end it, I really wish they fix performance issues because I want to play the full experience, not the bugged one :(
Not all hope is lost, since we’ve seen this before with pc ports of XBLA games like this one.
Magicka for instance suffered from lots of issues when it came out on pc, now runs smooth as butter.

Have you played any games with zombies lately? If you have been playing any games at all in the last two years, there's a very good chance you have set your foot in a post-apocalyptic, zombie-infested world at least once. Because zombies are pretty much everywhere these days. Not literally speaking, of course, but they are in a lot of computer games and it has proven to be a successful recipe for developers: The (very unfinished) stand alone version of has been on the number one spot on Steam's top seller list for weeks now. People must really love their zombies. Personally, I'm not much of a zombie person. The main reason is that I don't enjoy horror, or any horror sub genre. I can take my zombies mixed in with humor, is a great movie, but there's no way I'll never manage to sit through . I think we can safely conclude that I'm a coward. But, in spite of my healthy skepticism towards zombies, the game Deadlight, by Spanish developer (there's a pun in here somewhere, I know it), somehow pique my interest. The screen shots looked amazing, the sound track was incredible, and the zombies were so tiny and slow, they could easily be outrunned. Right? So when Deadlight appeared on a Steam sale last year, I finally decided to pick it up. With a real risk of sleepless nights ahead of me - not because I would be playing all night, rather because I would sit in the far corner of our bedroom with a baseball bat, waiting for zombies to bust down the door - I installed the game. And what an install it was. Deadlight weights in at over 4 gigabytes, pretty massive for something that is basically a sidescroller. But there's a reason for this, and a pretty good one, too. Deadlight uses the Unreal engine, and a lot of really great textures to create an amazing looking post-apocalyptic world. It simply looks stunning, and I've found myself stopping from time to time just to have a look at the creator's vision of 1986 Seattle after the apocalypse. What probably adds to the size of the game, and without doubt the complexity of the design and game play mechanics, is that even though Deadlight is a sidescroller, it's not actually 2D: You, playing as Canadian Randall Wayne, can only move in two dimensions: Up and down or left and right, just like in most other sidescrollers. The zombies, or Shadows, as they are called in the game, can sometimes move in and out (or along the Z-axis, if you like) as well, which means that even when everything seems calm a Shadow or five might suddenly come running towards you down a hall you cannot run down yourself. This 2.5D concept is an interesting one, but it sometimes puts you in some particular situations. Your passage might be blocked by a car wreck that you can get over by jumping it, but the Shadows are mostly unable to climb anything, meaning that they can't follow you beyond the car wreck. They could, however, have managed that, had they only moved around the car, something they probably should have been able to, since they just came running up that hallway. But I'm nitpicking. The learning curve in Deadlight is perfectly balanced. As you move through the devastated remains of Seattle, you have to solve the occasional puzzle. They are mostly based around using the environment, moving boxes and hitting specific targets, with a little bit of timing mixed in just to spice everything up. The puzzles are generally pretty easy, and made even easier with the hint messages and environmental highlighting, but both can be turned off if you want to up the ante a little. Wayne's stamina will decrease if you put him through any physical endeavors, like running, hanging from a ledge, swinging the fire axe to decapitate Shadows or any other physical activity. This means that you can't just run around wildly waving your axe: When your stamina runs out, you will get bitten. And when you get bitten, you die. There is no option to save in Deadlight, and saving is done automatically at given checkpoints. Thankfully, the checkpoints are very forgiving and you'll never respawn far from where you died. So, yes, Deadlight is a great game, but it also has a few drawbacks. For some reason, there's no difficulty settings, meaning that if you have beaten the game once, there's no way to beef up the difficulty and make a second play through more challenging. Also, there's no resolution or quality settings and the game will simply max out everything for you. On my laptop, this results in rather sluggish gameplay, but on my desktop it's all right. The most annoying thing about Deadlight, though, is the bugs. I've experienced the odd hangs, especially when going from the game into the game menu, but also during checkpoint loading. The only solution has been to kill the game and restart it. The audio also sometimes disappears during the cut scenes, which was very annoying the first time it happened since I'd turned off the subtitles. It's hard to follow the story told by the cut scenes without the audio and no subtitles. These bugs are the main reason the review score I gave the game is as low as it is, without the bugs, Deadlight would have been absolutely amazing. But if you can live with these shortcoming and bugs and you like puzzle games with zombies, set in a post-apocalyptic world, or any of the genres, you should buy Deadlight. After about 5 hours of gameplay, I'm at 60% completion, and even though I'm not a fast player, the game is good value for money at the current price (€11,99, USD 14.99). If that's a bit pricey for you, though, Deadlight tends to pop up on sale occasionally, so if you're the patient type you can get the next time it's on sale. This review is also available on .

-Let's get the review started hm?-
So, this game is a F2P FPS game, where you either are a german or an american, you fight in the times of WW2, around where the nazis started gassing jews (remember, I don't think they started gassing them straight away).
But anyway, as a nazi, which is the only thing I've played, you get some nice weapons, including the gewehr to start with, this weapon is quite powerful, takes a few quick shots to kill someone and you can have some fun with it.
You also get a hand grenade to start with, that one with the cylinder at the end of a pole, but whatever, you can injure teammates with it, so be careful.
You then (After some time of levelling) Get a melee weapon. I got the shovel because why not? It's an amazing weapon, I just love it.
Okay, so off of that topic, until level 4 (I think it is, correct me if I'm wrong please :) ) You do a game mode where you hold objective points, the more people at the point, the less time it takes to capture that point, at these points, it tells you how many enemies are capping the point, and how many teammates are, just so you know how many US people there are to kill left in the area until you can get a faster cap, the game does work like a real one, where if there are 2 US and 4 germans, the germans will still be capturing the point like there are 2 germans only at the point, if there is 1 german and 1 US, the point will stay at the capture point it is currently at until one leaves the capture zone or dies.
Mkay, so next up, vehicles.
You have 3 vehicles at the start, one is a civillian truck, for germans this is like, a pick up truck with hay in the back, not sure for americans, think it's the same, there is also the real truck, loaded with a gun and I think 5 people can get on, two people sit on the back, 2 in the seats and 1 at the gun, then, there is the best vehicle ever. THE BICYCLE!, this is like, the best thing ever, 2 seated, you can ring your bell by left clicking and you've got like, easy access, harshly seeable towards the other vehicles and there are a lot of them that spawn.

So if you could not tell, it's minecraft on crack, addicting, fun, a small learning curve, took me only 10 minutes to get a full understanding of controls and the build system, be warned though, it is still very much in alpha, and may be there for quite a while, as the AI, enemys, turrents, and even digging are very bad. I seriously doubt this won't be changes in the future, because it is so bad an ally will walk into the wall for an endless amount the time, same with enemys, turrents will shot into the ground if the enemy entired sight than walked into a lower point then is visable to the turrent.
One of my biggest problems is the lack of challange of "explore" mode, all crafting items(weapons, armor, so on) is giving to you off the bat, and you simply have to go out and find the mats. The enemys are randomly spawned, so sometimes a huge monster will spawn right outside the base, and the NPCs seem to kill it without taking any damage, OH and when you first spawn in you fall to your death and respawn on the spot I believe they intend for you to spawn, everytime, dont know if that is just me.
For myself, I never played this type of game, and minecraft did not interest me past day 1. But I have to say, this game looks pretty good, but I also see it getting boring after story mode ends, hopefully explore mode gets a little harder. In the end I recommend it for all the things they are throwing at you for $25 and what this game will be once it is completed.
Edit 1: You can build a wall(you can build these anytime, anywhere BTW) around a monster and then  delete a single stone and shoot it from a safeISH distance away, I would like to see that fixed but I don't really know how that can be with the free build system, I don't know I suppose it is your game and you can play it how you choose. :/
Edit 2: Multiplayer and more on explore mode. So I guess they have a "shop" in the right hand corner in both co-op multiplayer and explore where oh most all the items in the game are for sale. In explore mode you start right by a gold mine site every single time, I learnt this well playing legit over and over, and once I found the shop, if you clear that mine of gold out, you can buy yourself anything from the shop. Same with online co-op so it kinda just feels like easy mode. Also there is a quick travel if you did not realize. Open map and left click on a house icon.
In the end this game seems kid/noob friendly. There is no difficult part besides walking from point A to point B until you can quick travel there in story, and unless you force yourself to play the hard way you will never die/ lose a fight after the first hour or so. I still recommend it as I am hopeing for a more challenging mode/option to come out, as it stands you can play the game anyway you choice, thus making it difficult, but if you are playing on co-op I doubt anyone else will be doing the same.

Well I gave it a good shot and played for 18 hours.
Damage:
You probably don't remember the days when Soldier of Fortune came out and you could literally blow the bad guys arms and legs off. Well I'm not looking for that, as there are kiddies present, but what I am looking for is some damage effect. Since when can a person get wounded by three or four bullets and still run, move and aim like a champion?
HUD:
So you've stealthfully walked, run, swam and crawled your way across half the map to capture a point and when you do a big circle appears over your head and tells every player on the map where you are. Almost as incoherent are the 'enemy spotted' tags which appear over your head if you ever dare fire your weapon. No matter how cleverly hidden you are, every enemy soldier on the map will see a nice red arrow pointing at you if you do. The only solution is to emulate the snipers who camp on top of a hill at the back of the action if you want to rack up the kills.
Tanks:
The tanks are seriously over powered which ruins it for anyone in the infantry. This could so easily be balanced with early access to anti-tank grenades.
Linear Warfare:
The main disappointment for me is the linear battles where you must take point A before point B before point C etc. This makes it far too easy for the enemy to park a tank at point B or just pound it endlessly with shells knowing that if we fail to take that one undefendable barn then the whole battle is over.
Conclusion:
What could well have been a great open world game is now a counter strike clone with tanks that take no damage from rocket launchers. Spawn, get sniped, spawn, get tanked, spawn and get shot by the guy hiding in the loft where you spawned. I almost gave in and was going to spend some money to buy a shovel but thought better of it. Play it for a while until the battle fatigue and shell shock sets in, even throw the devs a dollar or two, then go do something constructive.

Planet Explorers is the makings of a great game.
In its current state, it is clear that it is an alpha. This isn't to say it is intolerable. As a matter of fact, it is remarkbly put together for an alpha. As advertised, there is a campaign mode. It is a surprisingly interesting story about tensions between Martians and Earthlings (both human), as well as a believeable "first contact" scenario. The writing isn't ground-breaking, but it is definitely better than many cookie-cutter stories released nowadays. Regretably with much of the important dialog missing voice overs, it can be difficult to follow. Granted, some people adore Morrowind style dialog, but much of the important voice overs are missing throughout the game. For example, it is very common to be ambushed in the story and forced to run. The problem is that there is no audio that plays signifying a retreat. This can be mildly frustrating, especially when you are killed thinking your teammates are backing you up.
Many of the games descriptions can leave you lost or downright confused. Two examples: when you are picking something up, the button you click is "Get". Not "Take" or "Pickup", but the awkward verb "Get". In addition, quest descriptions can confuse you. Such as receiving a quest with in the first hour to start a colony, only to find out that you need to complete a quest 5 hours in to fulfil that quest. But I digress...
The art direction is rather impressive. Jungles feel thick and plains are reminiscent of rolling wheat farms while still having still having an alient quality to them. It is clear that some of the creatures that inhabit Maria are inspired by apes, cats, and dogs, but the artists did a wonderful job distancing from many obvious qualities. Be it multiple armed, hairless, ape-like creatures, or pseudo-tiki faced giraffe creatures, the game will always take what you expect and tweak it so that only base features are recongizable. It is a shame that the game doesn't have a strong backing, because it is clear that the artists are talented in making the familiar seem alien.
Graphically, it is passable. It has its moments of beauty, such as watching the sunrise shine through a mass of tree branches.
The biggest gripe I have is the combat in the game. Melee is a wonderful way to ensure you die repeatedly, which is fair when you're fighting creatures that are usually 2x larger than you. The main problem is the lack of a basic notification for when you deal/take damage to/from a creature. It leaves most of the combat to be spamming attack, holding shield, then spamming, all while staring at your health bar. With the vehicles, I can see damage notifiers in the form of numbers, which almost feels taunting.
Another problem with the combat is the random difficulty spikes. For instance, while in the mountain/desert regions, I moved from quest point to quest point willy-nilly, but once I reached a random point, I got killed in one laser blow. Repeatadly. The only warning was "Take these turrets! It is our only hope!" And before you ask, the turrets didn't seem to help me.
This is forgiveable however. As it is an alpha, the primary focus isn't on balance but in addition of promised features. And thankfully, there is plenty to do as you gain stronger resources.
Finally, the most important component: the weapon/vehicle editor. It is clear that it is a robust system, if a little difficult to learn. I am not the most creative person, so I have difficulty putting my plans to editor. Thankfully, it is simple to download ISO files (the files that are used as "saves" for the different created objects) and install. While you are forced to download from the game's forums, this game has a pretty strong case for Steam Workshop integration.
All things together, the game is currently in a very accessable alpha. A creativity akin to Spore & Minecraft's community filters through every facet in gameplay, be it through developer or player. If you are a fan of exploration games and creative building, you won't be disappointed by this game. Even if you don't buy today, I really recommend keeping an eye on this game cause I only see it getting better and better.

Not just pay to win, its pay to compete.
Lets cover the freemium aspect of this game first.  Each character you have (think of WOW or MMO games where you can have multiple characters under one account) levels independantly and has his own XP points but your money is global in this sense. Each character has his own guns he has access to and his own path to go down in upgrades (tankers stop going infantry grunts etc). You cannot share upgrades or guns across characters that are even on their own factions.
To upgrade you must play and get money. The amount of funds to buy anything is very very high and requires alot of grinding.  This wouldn't sound so bad to most free2play game players until I point out you will be figting tanks while all you have is a M1 Garand, some M2 Frags and thats it. You can find panzerfausts around the game world, but good luck hitting them when they are way in excess of the range of rockets. You need a bigger tank or an AT gun (dont know if they are in this) to take it out at the ranges tanks like to camp at. That means you need to upgrade an infantryman to a tanker. Which is a very expensive process in itself. Once upgrade you are given the stupidest tank in the world. It can barely be called a tank. Two 50 cal turrets that get in the way of eachother and no anti armor capabilities what so ever.  So to get even a Stuart tank you have to grind grind grind more, but now you are missing an infantryman so you need a new one now on top of that so you can actually play the game since playing as your tanker is just the stupidest ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t ever at this time. It sounds like pay to skip the unfun, but its really pay to win as infantry and most players who didn't get to be a tanker or choose one in the start of the match are boned. Also, why the ♥♥♥♥ can't I switch guns in the middle of a match? Even COD 2 had this down, or is there some secret button that does that? This is in some ways another game thats like that. Some stuff really isn't as out in the open and forefront in terms of UI and design as it should be and often its janky enough to make you confused as to if things were supposed to happen in the ways they do on your screen.
Graphics are messed up, there dousn't seem to be settings to mess with either. Buildings seem to go Playstation 1 when they are far away (but not that far away so it looks terrible and hard to tell whats going on in front of you in terms of enemies due to the polygon mess) Textures seem lower res than they should be and AA dousn't seem like its enough, lighting is simple.
