Sound is messed up. "Why am I dying? Whats going on? *Falls Over Dead* Oh kay..." this happens alot. If people are so far away and shooting at you you cannot hear them and there dousn't seem to be any audio pointing out your getting shot, or shot at.  Maybe your screen will turn red and your HP will go down, but this isn't enough information to accurately react to. Again, even COD 2 had this down.
3D audio is also messed up. Telling where gunshots and footsteps are coming from can either be difficult or completely impossible. CS has had this down and probably COD 2 aswell.
Design is very arcadey. Machine guns are extremely innacurate and burst firing seems to have no gains. Bolt action guns are extremely damaging. So let's talk about things besides the soundtrack.
This game is hard.
So many levels harder than the original. The techniques you learned in the first will be put to the absolute test in every stage. New enemy types are merciless and require better timing, more accurate throws, perfect item selection and every dirty trick you have to survive. Some levels it feels like Wedin and Soderstrom were making them just to laugh at our tears, but the level of satisfaction you get from killing four men with a fist, a switchblade to the forehead, a single shotgun shell and two kicked in heads? Unbelievable.
The story continues and jogs between before the original and years after it, touching on several characters from the first, exploring completely different people in different ways, and generally causing great mental and emotional distress in so many wonderful ways. You thought it felt good tearing a man's head off with your bare hands? There are points that make you question it. There are points that make you question everything the last level just showed you.
There are still a few bugs, enemies getting caught around corners and becoming invulnerable, certain enemies ignoring walls and doors and jogging though, and the weapon pickups need a bit of a tweak, but still minor issues at best.
If you haven't played the first, you'll be missing a ton of story importance, you'll have a way harder time getting through, and you'll generally be out of the loop the whole game. Do yourself a favour and play the first if you haven't, and if you have, buy this. It's even more masochistic but the soundtrack, (most) of the new characters and the expanded levels are a thing to behold.

It really, really pains me to dislike this game so much. I was so excited, Hotline Miami 1 was one of my favourite games to come out on PC in recent years. It was a non-stop adrenaline rush. Unfortunately HM2 is nothing at all like that.
Before I begin, I'd just like to clarify what made the first game so great. It was difficult, but doable, and you could adapt to it on the fly if you had the skills for it. In HM1, you started the level, surveyed the floor, and then you just went. You charged in, executed the first step of your plan, then quickly reacted to what happened, because nothing ever went according to plan.
You can do none of this in 2. For whatever reason, the levels in Hotline Miami 2 are massive and filled with tons of enemies. This puts a big emphasis on scouting the level and firearms, as there are many times when you are running down a hall and someone will snipe you from across the map. This focus on long ranges and firearms basically slows the game down to a crawl. Instead of running in and reacting to what happens like some wired up coke fiend, you have to carefully plot your movements and go at a snail's pace, because if you don't some guy with a shotgun will instantly kill you. With the massive amount of enemies with firearms, huge levels, and large amounts of fat enemies, (which can only be killed with guns), HM2 encourages you to play cautiously and slowly, which just ends up being tedious and frustrating. It devolved from an adrenaline rush into a trial and error puzzle game.
Besides the horrible pacing due to terrible level design, there are numerous problems with the rest of the game. With their awful AI, followers are useless, turning one of the most interesting characters (a brother-sister combo, one with a gun one with a chainsaw) into a chore to play as. Bad AI also extends to the enemies, and you will frequently see enemies get stuck on doorways. The plot becomes very convoluted quickly, as there are multiple parallel plotlines, going along with the alternate history plotline. The game jumps back and forth between perspectives, settings, and times, which would be okay, if they were all interesting. Half of the characters aren't much better than filler.
HM2 is a sequel that forgot exactly what made the first one so great. The awful focus on sniping, baiting enemies, and guns makes the game simply not fun to play, and the lack of choice with playstyles (each level has at most 4 different options of masks/characters, and most only have 1) really limits replayability. I'm hoping that the level editor will allow the Steam Community to make some good levels, but for now, I simply can't recommend this game. It takes 1 step forward, and far too many steps back.

Upon further delving into the mess that is Hotline Miami 2 I can only say "Stay Away". The rampant, exubernat fun of the first game is to be found only in fleeting glimpses that last all too short a time to be worth the asking price of this trainwreck. A decent soundtrack can't save this ship.
In the original game you were mostly given choices; levels were compact and fast with no true path to be spoken of in many instances. You had a large selection of masks to select from that were varied enough to allow experimentation and not too unbalancing in most instances. Gone are those halcyon days.
Hotline Miami 2 is COD meets Hotline. You are playing the devs game through and through, don't be fooled by what some people say. Choices for the player have been cut back to a bare minimum, theoretically in the pursuit of storytelling. That would be fine if the story didn't feel so forced.
The masks that are in the game are only available in certain levels, in the other instances you are either playing as a vanilla character such as a writer that attempts to avoid killing and focuses on unloading firearms and won't pick up bladed weapons (sadly, this character is the most fun to play) or you're playing as a commando with the ability to run out of ammo and ignore weapons on the ground. Seriously. You're a solider that won't pick up guns.
Most levels are far too large and favor firearm combat, the less interesting option in almost every case in the first game. Sight lines are huge and you will frequently be most of the way through one of these oversized maps only to be gunned down in a hail of bullets from an enemy two screens away. The smaller levels seem to be mostly configured to encourage you to huddle behind corners and swat at patrolling enemies.
The enemy selection in this game favors dogs, thugs (the fat guys that can't be meleed), and guns. Did you love the first Hotline for it's intentse firefights? No, you did not. Well HM2 provides plenty of twitch-shooting which gets the job done but feels cheap and boring. It's also worth mentioning that due to this change combos are pretty well a matter of chance. Most maps force you into timidity in order to finish them and this means that the ability to speed through a level racking up combos is shot.
If you can sit through the first four to five hours of the game you'll be treated to a blatant rehash of the biker fight from the first game. Yep, including the whole 'circle-strafe to avoid being sprint killed until you're allowed to fight back bit'. Sound like something you want to relive? Nope? Too bad, because this game is all about forcing the mediocre on you and paying out zilch.
Seriously, I realize I'm being harsh on HM2 but while the body of Hotline is still here the soul is gone. This game is a mess from the very start and what little redeeming there is to find is hampered by glitches and terrible level design. Wait for a sale or just avoid altogether and remember the good days of Hotline Miami before it's drunken cousin came pounding on the door.

Hotline Miami 2 may look like its predecessor, but it’s a completely different beast. The original was a drug; a pulsating, hypnotic thing. Hotline Miami 2 consciously makes it slightly harder to get lost in that flow, but trades that trance for a story that I’m still rapturously unpacking. It gives you the tools and freedom you need to execute unbelievable killing combos, and then gives you ample time to consider the consequences. That might be what has made Hotline Miami 2 such an unforgettable experience for me: Between those two halves — the killing and the consequence — I still do not know which is more brutal. The original Hotline Miami asks a question in one of its early scenes: "Do you like hurting other people?" Hotline Miami 2 expects an answer.

I've played through all of it (I like to finish my games whenever I can, especially if they are short like this one) and I must say I'm very displeased. This game is not worth the money. Maybe if it's on sale for a couple of bucks but that's about it.
So, where do I start... with positives I guess? Good gaphics and environmental sounds. That's about it. Now for the rest:
The plot is weak, predictable and full of holes and inconsistencies. Not to mention 90% of it is fillers that add absolutely nothing to the story. There is an idea there, but not much else. The characters are flat like an ice skating arena. The only character that is, sort of, developing is the protagonist. I say "sort of" because he only does it in the very last cut-scene. Not to mention he's as relatable as crack addict charging you with a broken bottle in his hand. The writer(s) should be somehow punished for all the cringeworthy dialogue too.
The mechanics would be solid if not for all the bugs and the controls which will make you scrach your head so hard you'll be picking pieces of your brain from beneath your finger nails. I mean, who came up with the idea for some vaulting/climbing actions to use up arrow, some to use space bar, and yet others to use left/right arrows? And then, just to confuse you, sometimes you can press two or three different buttons to perform the same action. But only in some cases. So you end up vaulting over the windows back and forth like a mad man, praying for it to stop.
The combat system? If it wasn't for the bugs... Just kidding. It's bad. Looks effective, but it's terrible. And the bugs only make it worse. So, you need to destroy the brain to kill zombies. But somehow when you swing an axe you miss the head. Every. Single. Time. And they stand firm like nothing happened. Like they're impersonating the Black Knight from Monty Python's The Holy Grail: "Tis but a scratch!". But if you manage to push (or rather shoosh) them away and they fall over (under the power of your overwhelming manliness presumably) you can then hit them in their toe as they lay there helpless and they die instantly. I can't even... aaargh...
The voiceovers and the choice of voice actors couldn't be worse, even if they cast Tommy Wiseau A.K.A. "You're tearing me apart, Lisa!"-guy as the mother-in-law who always follows the protagonist reminding him to fix the roof tiles when he comes back to Canada. The protagonist himself sounds like he did movie trailers in the 80's, the Rat sounds like a bored Harvard professor and everyone else is just borderline annoying. I can't even count how many times I tried to hit every "friendly" character with that tennis-ball-looking-thing fired from my slingshot. I even tried that thing where you close one eye and stick your tongue out just before taking a shot hoping it would help the immersion, sadly, to no great effect.
Puzzles were easy and repetitive for the most part, and buggy the rest of the times. The linearity of level progression not only stares you right in the face - it b****hslaps you and shouts "NO!" every time you try to do things even a little bit differently. I think someone in the level design department had serious control issues. I especially "loved" the "secrets" that were "hidden" throughout the game. They basically laid on the ground right in front of you along the main progression path, and not only did they glow blue, but also displayed an interaction icon when you stood nearby. Much secret, such find, very hidden! Wow!
What else... Don't bother, unless you really have nothing else to play, and are not prone to frustration and/or depression. Play  The Swapper instead - the graphics can leave you with mixed feelings, but the puzzles are difficult and satisfactory, the story is amazing and the whole thing just stands head and shoulders over this waste of good graphics engine they call Deadlight.
That is all.

Quick Review as of 0.75 Alpha. If it's a game being sold, it's a game i'm going to review.
--Pros:
Large Open World
Sandbox game
Crafting
Alien Animals
Nice water
--Cons / needs to be improved:
Clunky Controls.
No first person view *** CORECTION** THERE IS FIRST PERSON.
World has no atmosphere, as in no life, nothing happening.
Poor textures.
Poor graphics. (Too much bloom, strange grass that constantly waves, no FOV slider)
Poor animations
Poor combat
Poor UI, especially when building ISOs. Feels like I need a degree in graphic design to use it.
No collision on certain objects, able to walk through them.
No tutorial, or help guide
Poor character customisation.
Poor AI
Limited Dialogue
Starting from the top this game features an open world larger than 7 days to die if I judge at a glance. It has grass lands, deserts and forests. Crafting is also included in the game which uses a similar system to starbound if i recall correctly, similar UI as well, nothing much to say apart from it appears to work as expected if you have played starbound or terraria.
The controls are poor in my opinion. As you first start the game it requires you to hold the right mouse button and drag to move the camera. Or you can press F2 and have it follow your character as you would expect from a game post year 2005. The problem with this is the UI becomes difficult and you can't interact with anything unless you press and hold tab. So for you to talk to a character I have to hold tab, then right click on the character. If I let go of tab I can't click the dialog options.
As you are walking around the world, apart from alien animals wandering around aimlessly the world is empty. It's hard to explain however minecraft also suffered the same problem. No birds or atmospheric sound effects. Nothing really happening in the atmosphere.
The textures are poor. They look like they have just stepped out of 2006. There is too much bloom, the grass is horrible and I know they are trying to go for an alien look but it really grinds against my gears. All of the grass waves in front of you for no apparent reason, there is no logic. Apart from the textures at least the colours are good!
The animations are fairly bad. You jump 3 metres high, and there is no life in your character it's like moving a robot. This is especially apparent when in combat. I think the character only makes 2-3 animations in the whole combat. You also get a shield which I couldn't work out how to use as it's stuck inside his arm and is smaller than a compact disc.
The UI is poor. The ISO designer which lets you build weapons or design vehicles appears at first view like you need a degree in graphic design software. After about 20 mins you start to get the hang of it but personally I gave up because I'm playing a game to have fun, not to make me feel like a designer at work. The UI on 1920x1080 appears very small. I had to put on my reading glasses to see anything. Also The whole layout feels clunky, when talking to people I don't like how you click on the words and how they are 3pt small.
The character customisation needs work. Nothing to choose from and the pre-set faces are terrible. You need to add the option to design your own face like sims, as the pre-set faces are the most ugliest I’ve seen to date.
The AI is Poor. They walk around turning on their back heel like Michael Jackson, or staring at walls. I was attacked in the starting camp and everyone let me get my♥♥♥♥♥kicked, thanks AI  !
At this stage it's absolutely not worth £18.99. For some reason I see people talking it up like it's the best thing since slice bread and WHY?! I am not going to try and pretend it's good so I feel like I got my money’s worth. It's not very good unless you are new to gaming.
It's worth £5 on a steam sale.
It's an avoid from me. First game I switched off and deleted after an hour.

It really, really pains me to dislike this game so much. I was so excited, Hotline Miami 1 was one of my favourite games to come out on PC in recent years. It was a non-stop adrenaline rush. Unfortunately HM2 is nothing at all like that.
Before I begin, I'd just like to clarify what made the first game so great. It was difficult, but doable, and you could adapt to it on the fly if you had the skills for it. In HM1, you started the level, surveyed the floor, and then you just went. You charged in, executed the first step of your plan, then quickly reacted to what happened, because nothing ever went according to plan.
You can do none of this in 2. For whatever reason, the levels in Hotline Miami 2 are massive and filled with tons of enemies. This puts a big emphasis on scouting the level and firearms, as there are many times when you are running down a hall and someone will snipe you from across the map. This focus on long ranges and firearms basically slows the game down to a crawl. Instead of running in and reacting to what happens like some wired up coke fiend, you have to carefully plot your movements and go at a snail's pace, because if you don't some guy with a shotgun will instantly kill you. With the massive amount of enemies with firearms, huge levels, and large amounts of fat enemies, (which can only be killed with guns), HM2 encourages you to play cautiously and slowly, which just ends up being tedious and frustrating. It devolved from an adrenaline rush into a trial and error puzzle game.
Besides the horrible pacing due to terrible level design, there are numerous problems with the rest of the game. With their awful AI, followers are useless, turning one of the most interesting characters (a brother-sister combo, one with a gun one with a chainsaw) into a chore to play as. Bad AI also extends to the enemies, and you will frequently see enemies get stuck on doorways. The plot becomes very convoluted quickly, as there are multiple parallel plotlines, going along with the alternate history plotline. The game jumps back and forth between perspectives, settings, and times, which would be okay, if they were all interesting. Half of the characters aren't much better than filler.
HM2 is a sequel that forgot exactly what made the first one so great. The awful focus on sniping, baiting enemies, and guns makes the game simply not fun to play, and the lack of choice with playstyles (each level has at most 4 different options of masks/characters, and most only have 1) really limits replayability. I'm hoping that the level editor will allow the Steam Community to make some good levels, but for now, I simply can't recommend this game. It takes 1 step forward, and far too many steps back.

Upon further delving into the mess that is Hotline Miami 2 I can only say "Stay Away". The rampant, exubernat fun of the first game is to be found only in fleeting glimpses that last all too short a time to be worth the asking price of this trainwreck. A decent soundtrack can't save this ship.
In the original game you were mostly given choices; levels were compact and fast with no true path to be spoken of in many instances. You had a large selection of masks to select from that were varied enough to allow experimentation and not too unbalancing in most instances. Gone are those halcyon days.
Hotline Miami 2 is COD meets Hotline. You are playing the devs game through and through, don't be fooled by what some people say. Choices for the player have been cut back to a bare minimum, theoretically in the pursuit of storytelling. That would be fine if the story didn't feel so forced.
The masks that are in the game are only available in certain levels, in the other instances you are either playing as a vanilla character such as a writer that attempts to avoid killing and focuses on unloading firearms and won't pick up bladed weapons (sadly, this character is the most fun to play) or you're playing as a commando with the ability to run out of ammo and ignore weapons on the ground. Seriously. You're a solider that won't pick up guns.
Most levels are far too large and favor firearm combat, the less interesting option in almost every case in the first game. Sight lines are huge and you will frequently be most of the way through one of these oversized maps only to be gunned down in a hail of bullets from an enemy two screens away. The smaller levels seem to be mostly configured to encourage you to huddle behind corners and swat at patrolling enemies.
The enemy selection in this game favors dogs, thugs (the fat guys that can't be meleed), and guns. Did you love the first Hotline for it's intentse firefights? No, you did not. Well HM2 provides plenty of twitch-shooting which gets the job done but feels cheap and boring. It's also worth mentioning that due to this change combos are pretty well a matter of chance. Most maps force you into timidity in order to finish them and this means that the ability to speed through a level racking up combos is shot.
If you can sit through the first four to five hours of the game you'll be treated to a blatant rehash of the biker fight from the first game. Yep, including the whole 'circle-strafe to avoid being sprint killed until you're allowed to fight back bit'. Sound like something you want to relive? Nope? Too bad, because this game is all about forcing the mediocre on you and paying out zilch.
Seriously, I realize I'm being harsh on HM2 but while the body of Hotline is still here the soul is gone. This game is a mess from the very start and what little redeeming there is to find is hampered by glitches and terrible level design. Wait for a sale or just avoid altogether and remember the good days of Hotline Miami before it's drunken cousin came pounding on the door.

Hotline Miami 2 may look like its predecessor, but it’s a completely different beast. The original was a drug; a pulsating, hypnotic thing. Hotline Miami 2 consciously makes it slightly harder to get lost in that flow, but trades that trance for a story that I’m still rapturously unpacking. It gives you the tools and freedom you need to execute unbelievable killing combos, and then gives you ample time to consider the consequences. That might be what has made Hotline Miami 2 such an unforgettable experience for me: Between those two halves — the killing and the consequence — I still do not know which is more brutal. The original Hotline Miami asks a question in one of its early scenes: "Do you like hurting other people?" Hotline Miami 2 expects an answer.
It is the purest Far Cry sequel. The story and gameplay very united.

I really do enjoy this game a lot. Although it has some problems. To start off, I want to say that one of the biggest reasons that was a big let down for me is that I checked the server browser and NOTHING popped up. I removed EVERY single filter and NOTHING popped up. Note that I just bought this game today and I'm playing it at a pretty decent time in the day (i.e. it's not early in the morning or very late at night). Set aside that, it's basically a singleplayer game unless someone decides to host a server. I would also like to point out that the load times are extremely slow, they are scraping L4D2's load times. They are THAT bad. Anyways, when I started the map, I noticed very quickly how dynamic the map looked. What I didn't expect was to see a very diverse map with loads of time built into it. After looking around and trying to scavenge some weapons, I found and shot my very first zombie. What I was unhappy to hear was that there is no such dismemberment that can occur with a pistol OR an assault rifle (I haven't found the shotgun yet). Dismemberment to me is a key factor of a zombie game as it really makes you feel like you just shot that zombie's head off or you just shot that zombie's arm off. No, that feeling did not come with this game, sadly. Reguardless of the dismemberment, the models looked very nice and I liked the mostly interactive environment. Being made in the source engine, like half-life or Left 4 Dead, it took after most of the menu screens, blood effects, and the overall world looked similar to something you'd see in L4D or HL which is kinda repetitive to me considering I play most to all of Valve's games which are made in the Source engine. Set aside the how the textures and the models look, I want to talk about the gameplay. What I really liked about this game was how they stuck to their words by saying this was a game that was supposed to be like if a zombie appocolypse actually happened. I can honestly feel like this is how it would feel like. What makes this game a lot different from any other zombie shooting game is that you really have to consider your approach to complete your mission/goal. You mostly have 2 options, go guns out, shooting every single zombie you see and trying to get done with your mission as quick as you can. Or you can do the most recommended method; stick with the shadows, conserve your ammunition, take out enimies that absolutely HAVE to be taken out, and get done with your mission reguardless of the time. I personally chose option A the first time I played this game because I was still trying to figure out the map and find my way around the places, which it did work untill I got trapped in a store with zombies surrounding me from the outside and on the inside. Nonetheless I absolutely loved this game and enjoyed this game quite a bit because it really does make me feel like I'm in a zombie appocolypse. 8/10

If your looking for something different in the action/adventure/survival genre, different game options, and a great story then you need to check this game out.   I have put many hours into this game (prior to Steam version) and I'm still loving every minute of it.
So the good-
*Story-  Yes there is a story!!  This is not just mindless survival there actually is a story that sets the stage for your adventures and definitely adds to the sense of mystery, adventure, and discoveries.  If you like science fiction novels or are looking for a break from zombies/horror then check this out.   I found it a refreshing change from games like DayZ or/and Rust.   If your a parent this is a game your younger kids could play.
*Ambience/Setting-  Although it's on the Unity engine the game looks fantastic (especially if you can max it out) coupled with the most relaxing music (yet not boring) I have experienced in a game.   Normally I turn down or off the in game music but this is the first game I not only leave it on I turn it up!   The map/area to roam is HUGE and definitely has a science fiction feel to it and reminds me a lot of Avatar.   Add in a day/night cycle and random weather patterns and you really feel like your in a strange and new world.
*Game Options-  This game comes with quite the package of options that work quite well for it being in early access phase.   There is a story/campaign mode, build mode (get all resources for building similar to Minecraft), adventure mode, coop, and versus mode.   The building interface of the game works quite well in both "build mode" and "story/campaign" mode.  I actually found myself in story mode taking a break from NPC quests and just building a huge fortress over a mine I dug...was a ton of fun!   There is a creation editor where you can actually build customized items (to include vehicles, weapons, etc.) and then introduce them into your game however there is a bit of learning curve to use this feature (at least for me).   It is a totally open sandbox experience so you can choose your own destiny.
Needs Work-
*NPC Quests Story Mode-  The NPC quests are still a little glitchy and will need more polish.  They work however you sometimes can get hung up on a quest due to strange behaviors by the NPC's.   For example they may get stuck running into a wall and you may need to get creative to free them up (i.e. dig away the wall).
*Combat-  Combat works okay but definitely could use some polish.   Sometimes when you engage an enemy/creature up close there are clipping/blocking issues and you will end up inside the enemy/creature & hit detection could be improved.   Camera angles also could be improved when in combat especially if you are fighting a creature that is above you & your looking up.
*Sound- While I LOVE the music it does sometimes cut in/out at strange times.  For example when you get into a combat scenario the sound will change to a more suspense theme but in the middle of the combat just turn off or switch to the flute/guitar music.   Also the NPC voices could be louder when interacting with them.   I also think animal sounds could be polished a little more as I think they could even add more to the ambience of this world.
Overall I think this is a fantastic game and will improve over time as they work the bugs out and add new features.  It's a refreshing change from what we have been seeing and all of it comes together quite well.   I am sure we will be seeing some very creative builds coming out of the community (similar to Minecraft) in the very near future.
Okay heading back to my mine....never new digging could be so much fun!!
Cheers!

Jason Brody cries out in horror the first time he watches his brother murder a man. When the sibling kills again, there’s a vulnerable tremble to Jason’s whimpering whisper. “I can’t do this, Grant.”
Shortly afterward, in a moment of panicked self-defense, Jason rams a machete through an attacker’s throat.
Far Cry 3 establishes a bleak and mature tone out of the gate. Jason, our protagonist, should fear the pirates running the tropical retreat of Rook Island. In his eyes, killing is not cool. Not yet. The emotional weight only gets heavier as he tries to save his missing friends from slave-trading psychopaths. In turn, Jason’s gradual transformation from coward to killer unfolds in a natural, believable way, which compensates for the narrow revenge premise. As its unpredictable, often uncomfortable story comes unhinged, Far Cry 3 challenges players’ principles: How far would you go to protect the people you love, and what kind of person would you become to get them back?
Jason begins his evolution after escaping the clutches of Vaas, the mentally unstable leader of a pirate gang and the man who’s kidnapped his friends and family. Before having you hunt down Vaas, Far Cry 3 focuses nearly an hour on teaching you survival skills. Jason scavenges supplies, harvests plants, and crafts useful items from animal skins before ever firing a gun at a man. Choose not to take advantage of the wildlife at large and you’re missing out on important upgrades; bigger wallets hold more cash to buy better weapons, weapon holsters house additional firearms, and larger rucksacks store more goods. Motivation drives exploration because there’s a purpose for everything on Rook Island.
Far Cry 3 is important for the same reason as Far Cry 2. It’s a shooter that considers shooters thoughtfully, both in the way they’re designed and the way we play them, and then asks us to do the same.

Short answer: Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥I pulled someone's spine from their body, 10/10 would RIP AND TEAR again.
Long answer: If you've never played Hotline Miami, I suggest you don't play this game. The reason for this is simple enough; apart from a quick reminder of the controls (WASD to move, right mouse to pick up stuff, left mouse to puch/shoot/stab/swing/killpeopleinasmanyhorriblewaysaspossible, etc.), Wrong Number really throws you into the deep end.
You rember how the first game started you out against a handful of enemies armed with baseball bats and metal pipes before steadily increasing the mayhem? The first mission in this one has you against multiple enemies with both melee weapons and firearms. By the time you get the fourth level, you'll be taking on dozens of armed enemies at an intensity similar to about midway through HM1. It doesn't get any easier from there.
This isn't a bad thing, though. It's actually quite nice to have a sequel that assumes you've played the previous game, instead of dragging you though several levels teaching you what you already know. After all, if you needed practice before playing this game, you could always replay the first one.
You'll also have needed to have played the first game to make any sense of the story. It's hard enough working out what the hell is going on without not knowing why half the people are even in it. I feel sorry for anyone without knowledge of Hotline Miami's storyline playing this game, as they'll likely be spending half the time wondering why this fat bald dude with the snake mask (Jake) is even in this game or why there's a rooster headed guy (Richard) constantly popping up to talk♥♥♥♥♥♥at all the different characters.
Anyway, about the story. For the most part it picks off shortly after Jacket's murderous spree comes to an end, whilst occasionally jumping back in time to explain some more of the back story of characters in the first game. Truth be told, there isn't much to say here without spoiling stuff, so I'll just say that everything's still pretty confusing like in the first game. It does all kind of come together in the end, but not in a way you were expecting.
As you probably already know, the game's time is split between multiple characters, each with their own agendas and playstyles. While most of them are new (Detective Pardo, Evan, the Fans, etc.), Wrong Number does see the backstories of both Jake and Beard (the guy who kept giving you freebies after every mission in the first game) fleshed out, as well as the return of Richard to talk creepy nonsense to the playable characters. There's also another character's backstory which gets covered, but spoilers so I won't say anything on that.
In terms of gameplay, it's a lot tighter and tidier than previously. Like I mentioned before, the difficutly is amped up much earlier on. Several new features and revisions have also been implemented to make the game more challenging. For example, you're no longer invulnerable from gunfire while performing ground executions like you were in the first for some reason. Weapons are also no longer left convieniently floating on the ground like before, if you want a weapon you're either going to have to bring your own or take someone else's. There does seem to be an issue where sometimes enemies get caught on scenery and shake/spin like crazy. It's nothing serious, but it does look a bit stupid.
I almost forgot to mention, some of the levels do sort of drag on a bit. While HM1 was all about quick blasting through floors, some of these levels can span 4-5 sections, each with tons of enemies. The worst of this was probably the one where you're forced to play as all of the fans one after the other. That one took me a while, partly because I hated playing as Tony. That isn't to say there aren't levels you can complete in less than 3 minutes, but there are some looooooong drawn out ones on large maps with tons of enemies that seem to go on forever. Not so fun.
Of course, it's mostly the variety of playstyles presented by each of the characters that keeps things fresh. While a few of these are little to no difference to Jacket's Richard mask (Detective Padro, the Henchman, Pig Butcher), most have some very odd quirks. Jake retains his lethal throwing skills, while Beard's levels let you choose one gun to carry through the whole level and can only be rearmed at specific ammo dumps when you run out of ammo. There's also Ash and Alex, who move as a pair with a chainsaw and firearm. left mouse controls Ash's chainsaw attacks, while right mouse makes Alex shoot. When Alex is out of bullets, he'll pick up the next gun he walks over. In truth, Ash and Alex do have some pathing issues as Alex can get stuck outside when you first enter a building, which is pretty annoying.
I'd also like to quickly mention the most interesting character, Evan. When you start his levels, he tries his hardest to only incapacitate instead of outright kill his enemies. Any guns picked up are stripped of magazines or have their shells pumped out and he outright refuses to use any bladed weapons. Get a little too eager while "executing" downed enemies, however, and Even soon enters a rage mode which makes him play more like Jacket, only you get less points this way. As for the other characters, I'll let you see for yourself.
Unlike the first game, where you could choose any mask you'd unlocked for any level, specific characters are locked for specific levels. This means that apart from the Fans, Jake, Beard and the Son, there's no choosing a mask or weapon to influence your playstyle. You either play it how the game wants you to, or you have a problem. In some ways this is pretty nice, it keeps you on your toes and means you can't just pick Peter and easily gun your way through all the levels, but at the same time it means you might have to play a few levels in a way you find rather unfun. It also means that you might only get to play your favourite character a handful of times. For me, the two characters with the most interesting playstyles were Evan and Jake, but both of them only got three levels each.
Game lengthwise, you're looking at around 6 hours for the first run. Maybe less, I got kind of stuck on a couple of points. I'm not ashamed to admit it, this is a hard game. Hell, I got the Karma achievement (1000 deaths) on the first run. You can also cut some time off by not bothering with cutscenes, as these can now be skipped by holding right mouse down for a few seconds. There is replay value just like with the first game and this time there's even a new hard mode to make it even more difficult. You like dying right?
Graphics, nothing to really report here. Still the same look, the only difference being the locations and the types of enemies. No longer just Russians and Cops, now you get to kill Columbians and Junkies too!
Last of all, the music. I don't really need to say much here, it's an even better selection than the first game. The whole synthwave vibe really works and tracks from old favourites like M.O.O.N. and Scattle are joined by new artists such as Magic Sword and IAMTHEKIDYOUKNOWWHATIMEAN. Seriously, it's amazing. If you loved the first game's soundtrack, you'll love this one too.
Wow, that's a lot of words that most people probably won't read. TL;DR: I certainly feel like this game was worth £10. I've thoroughly enjoyed what I've played so far and I've only played it through once. There's still the Hard mode to punish myself with over the next few days. Yum.
If you've played the first game and enjoyed it, GET THIS GAME. If you've played the first and didn't like it, you're not going to like this one. If you haven't played the first game, try that one and then refer to the previous sentence.
P.S. There's going to be a level editor added at some point, I guess I'll update the review when that comes out. More words ahoy.

Contagion is a 2011 medical thriller directed by Steven Soderbergh. The film features an ensemble cast that includes Marion Cotillard, Bryan Cranston, Matt Damon, Laurence Fishburne, Jude Law, Gwyneth Paltrow, Kate Winslet, and Jennifer Ehle. Contagion's plot documents the spread of a virus transmitted by fomites, attempts by medical researchers and public health officials to identify and contain the disease, the loss of social order in a pandemic, and finally the introduction of a vaccine to halt its spread. To follow several interacting plot lines, the film makes use of the multi-narrative "hyperlink cinema" style, popularized in several of Soderbergh's films.
Soderbergh and screenwriter Scott Z. Burns had collaborated on The Informant! (2009). Following that film's release, both considered creating a biopic covering Leni Riefenstahl's life, before Burns brought up the idea of producing a medical thriller film depicting the rapid spread of a virus, which was inspired by various pandemics such as the 2003 SARS epidemic and the 2009 flu pandemic. To devise an accurate perception of a pandemic event, Burns consulted with representatives of the World Health Organization as well as noted medical experts such as W. Ian Lipkin and Lawrence "Larry" Brilliant. Principal photography started in Hong Kong in September 2010, and continued in Chicago, Atlanta, London, Geneva, and San Francisco until February 2011.
Contagion premiered at the 68th Venice Film Festival in Venice, Italy on September 3, 2011, and went on general release on September 9. The film was well received by critics, who praised the narratives and the performances of various actors and actresses. It was also well received by scientists, who praised its accuracy. Commercially, the film was a moderate box office success. Budgeted at USD $60 million, Contagion attained $135 million in box office revenue during its theatrical run.

Deadlight is an interesting game. It is interesting in the fact that it is a... zombie game, yep guys, another zombie game. It handles like an older sidescroller from the older generation of games. It has plenty of fun moments, but it has a pretty fair share of bugs.
The bugs range from zombies clipping through doors, odd collision detection, and a fairly frustrating grip on physics.
The controls are my biggest gripe, perhaps they handle better with a controller, as this is a direct 360 port. Very frequently however you will draw your weapon to aim, and face the wrong way. Climb a fence? Prepare to climb it backwards.
The story leaves much to be desired, but maybe that's what the developers wanted?
On the plus side, when you beat it, you unlock "NIGHTMARE MODE" which doesn't save your data, requiring you to beat the game in one sitting, but... BUT... You do it wearing a hat.
I forced myself to play it, as I had bought it, otherwise the first hour shows the depth of character development, and will probably get you killed a couple of times with the wonky controls. If I would have gotten this for free, I wouldn't have gone past the beginning.

Has a lot of potential and plays very smoothly for an alpha build. Quests and item collection work well, although melee combat is wonky (due to lack of damage animation for monsters, you have to watch the health bar). Building and terrain shifting with various tools is surprisingly functional; I didn't focus on building at first, but it's pretty easy to dig yourself a cave to hide out in, or build some platforms to get around plateaus. Vehicles and item building is also easy; the built-in creator is both powerful and simple to learn and use.
Disclaimer: I wanted to play this game mainly as a wilderness survival game at first, but a couple of things I noticed in singleplayer (story mode) made me reconsider. I wouldn't call these problems since they're mainly design choices, but they're worth noting.
1. "Surviving" in the sense of keeping your character fed/healthy is trivial; you can carry something like hundreds of thousands of items on your person (including a couple of vehicles).
2. The main difficulty in the game comes from combat, which feels frustrating; you can upgrade your armor, but it seems to do little to prevent most large creatures from taking out >1/4 of your health each blow, and there's no simple way to dodge if you're stuck in melee (say, against a flying enemy with an AOE ground attack and who's faster than you).
3. Due to infinite NPC shop storage and basically-infinite inventory, the story mode game sometimes feels like "kill x monsters for meat (currency)", buy next tier of supplies from vendors, do quests to get to new vendors, repeat". To be fair, it's pretty much the entry point for new players, so the parceling out of goods is understandable; it lacks the urgency a survival-oriented game might have, though.
This game shows fantastic promise - it's already stable and playable and with a ton of content even while still in alpha. It's already worth it even in its current state.

This game is very intense, fun, and interesting, especially when playing with people you can talk to obviously, however, be warned, I have encountered a glitch in the time I have been playing this game, and I can promise you there will be more. (Namely, someone got dragged through a normally openable door that was boarded up by a random event on the map loading by a pack leader.)
A second drawback is the fact that treating this like any other FPS will get you slaughtered, your weapons are something you will need to learn several sets of good Rhythms for various circumstances to use properly, as the charge-attack system has a serious degree of depth. As such, mindlessly and repeatedly tapping left mouse in the general direction of the enemy is going to get you killed (Even if you are using a weapon which has a good light attack, as they are not intended to be your exclusive mode of combat.)
As such, the next bit of this review will be explaining how to strategize how to play based on your weapons attributes, to ease the early game hell.
In a weapons basics: Weapons have two modes of attack, light (Standard, good for quickly staggering a single enemy,) and Charged (Seems to be gradual, thus, I will reffer to barely charged attacks as medium, and almost fully charged attacks as heavy.)
Now, the attributes for how hitting something works are very invovled and in depth, each hand to hand weapon can hit a certain number of Skaven before its blade will get stopped, it will do a certain amount of damage, and it will be able to stagger enemies of a certain severity. This tells you what targets the weapon is good at.
See the Templar Zwiehander you start with in your inventory chest as the Witch hunter, it has a dissapointing light attack, but its charged hits have a great number of targets it will hit for medium damage. It is a glorious weapon to throw well timed medium attacks with. Its stagger is bad, meaning you should neve try to fight stormvermin with it, while the hammer the empire soldier has access to has great stagger scores, and is great at dealing with stormvermin.
As such, you can start forming up into strategic roles, but until you understand how to do this, and how to get good with your chosen weapons, this game is rough, and brutally hard. It is not your run of your mill FPS.

This review is specifically for Napoleonic Wars, the DLC for Mount and Blade: Warband since it can't be posted on the DLC page.
Refreshing and unique.
Napoleonic Wars is the kind of game which snares you completely and it will simultaneously make it's way into your heart. The intensity of it's gameplay will make you sweat, curse, laugh and cry. And when I say intensity, I do not mean emptying clips of ammo in a blind rage of hate, it is about making every shot and stab count. Reload times are about 10ish seconds (in which you have to stand/sit still) which makes the way you approach a battle or even a single soldier more like chess sometimes than a shootout. You can also take a gamble on the horrible accuracy of the rifles from that era to charge while getting shot at, only to plant your bajonet in their chests. All the while gleaning over your shoulders praying not to get beheaded by cavalry roaming the field, or being desintegrated by cannonfire.
Napoleonic Wars depends highly on skill, tactics and teamwork. A single soldier with excellent melee capabilities can wipe a defensive strongpoint from the map in any battle. Sieges and battles can be won by a few squads with great tactics, communication and a plan. Artillery pieces that work together can utterly destroy not only the walls of a fort, but the integrety of the enemy morale and their battleplans.
The community is excellent, especially the people who've been with this game for a longer time allready. First game I joined, saw an invitation to a teamspeak server, joined, and eventually there were 5 of us playing battles for 3-4 hours. Very enjoyable.
Also, classical music will accompany you on the battlefield, which is a breath of fresh air and fits the game perfectly.
Pros:
- Gameplay
- Variety of classes and the way they can work together
- Community
- Music
Cons: Not really any big ones in my opinion. If you're critical you could argue that;
- The graphics could be better, but for 200 player battles it can be taxing.
- And perhaps that some actions performed with objects such as boats or traversing obstacles can be a bit glitchy.
Definetly not gamebreaking as far as I'm concerned, and in some cases part of the mechanics. The developers however are still updating this from time to time so who knows what'll happen.
For those in need of quantification: 9.5/10

*MAJOR STORY SPOILERS*
I want this game to be perfect. I really do. But, there are many flaws to this game. But, I like to be positive, so let's start with those.
THE GOOD
The atmosphere, music and story of this game are wonderful. I heard the ending was lackluster, but in my oppinion, so was the first. Some levels are really fun to play. The Fan's first level is a very good start to the game. I'd say what this game does good, it does it to the best degree in gaming. Some how, the music is even better than the first games.
But, after my fanboy hype cleared, I realized something- this is not as fun as the first. Now, being more fun than the first is difficult, but Dennaton could do it. I know they could. We will know address the bad.
THE BAD
I feel Hotline Miami lost some of it's identity, with this installment. Instead of guns being high risk, high reward like the first, you are forced to use them to beat most levels. Speaking about levels, if you played the first game- do you remember the Levels Hot and Heavy and Assault? Remember them being frustrating? Almost every level is like that. The only levels not like that are SOME Fans levels and so far ONE Jake level. All the other levels are huge playgrounds and honestly you could fit 5 Hotline Miami 1 levels into 1 floor of this game. Know, for most games, bigger levels are good, right? Not this one. In the first, dying meant nothing. Yo could get to the same spot in a few seconds. In this one, dying is frustrating. Remember the tip from the first "Don't be afraid of death" Well, in this game, BE AFRAID! One of the most fun sets of characters, The Fans, are killed of fairly early. They were some of the mose advertised characters and then they're killed off with only 4-5 (IF THAT) missions under their belt. Oh, and if you prefered melee (like me) this game will be dissapointing. Melee is so useless in this game (except with Beard, where you are pretty forced to use melee, even with fat guys  on the level) Also, the game limits playstyles. Evan is a prime example of this game limiting playstyles. Evan forces you to play nonlethal, unless you choose no to, but with this added option, animations are longer and clunkier as you try to figure out if you have hopped off while 2 guys with knives rush you. All in all, the Cons aren't subtle in the slightest.
FINAL THOUGHTS
My final thoughts on this game are as follows- If you loved, the first game and haven't bought this game, try it out. After all, you are the best judge of what you want. I only recommend this game because, I love it. Even though it has shining flaws; it's still the Hotline Miami I know and love. This game will only become better with the Level Editor and bug fixes and patches. If you can't get past this games flaws, don't buy. But, if you love the first, give this game a try.
In my oppinion this game is an 8.5/10. And note, this can only be higher as time passes.
TL;DR Buy this game if you liked the first one, as it's more of the same, but still differentiates itself enough to feel fresh. If you don't like what you've seen; don't buy. 8.5/10
P.S. Dennaton- Add Jacket and all of his maks to the Level Editor. Everyone will thank you.

I'll get the bad stuff out first: The level design for this one gets worse and worse as the game goes on. There are significantly more enemies in every level, and the overall difficulty is greatly increased form the first one. It's also way to reliant on guns instead of melee weapons. Gun fights is certainly not Hotline: Miami's strong suit. After playing most of the story, and reading about the ending elsewhere, I wouldn't recommend it if you dislike sad or overly abrupt endings.
Now that that's out of the way, I'm free to talk about what's good with Hotline Miami 2. First of all, the soundtrack. Every beat and bump of the music becomes one with your every action, and the music itself has kept me playing hours after I got bored with the gameplay. The gameplay isn't all bad though. It adds many new characters, and each on has their own unique gimmick. Wanna start off with dual-wielding machine guns? Choose Mark the Bear! Want to control two characters, one wielding a chainsaw, the other a pistol? Choose the goose mask! Each character is certainly more fleshed out than the original protagonist from the first game.
All in all, I'd recommend the game, though it's pretty close to being not recommended. If you loved the first one, and thought it wasn't hard enough/ loved the challenge, then this game is for you. If the first game was a bit eh, or you had trouble completing all the stages, then this game is likely not for you.
I myself would give it a 7.5/10 and worth the 15 bucks to purchase it.

I played Zombie Panic Source back in the day a little bit and had some fond memories of it. Along with that, I've got a bit of a soft spot for mod-teams turned dev and like to give them support where I can. As a result of these things, I picked up Contagion during it's early access period.
My first impressions? It was rough as guts, but had a certain charm. Graphically, not amazing but solid. It is Source engine after all, it's old but it's capable. It was a little bit limited in terms of maps and modes at the time but, being early access, I couldn't expect it to be fully featured. The melee was atrocious, and was so hard to use that it wasn't worth using. Animations etc were a bit clunky and sometimes awkward, but forgivable coming from a (until recently) mod team. The gore was humorous, seeing heads pop open was always fun to see. One thing that really irked me though was the teleporting...sometimes the zombies, either AI or player controlled, would teleport a metre or so at a time which made it impossible to shoot them in the head. It's fair to say that I liked the game but that I had a few gripes.
I went away from it for a while, distracted by other games (it happens to me very regularly) and came back to it a little more recently, probably just after it had officially launched. By this time, Barlowe Square had been launched and the bugs ironed out, melee was FAR more usable and a lot of the teleporting was gone. It was nice to see things progressing.
What do I think now? To be honest, it still feels like it's in beta a lot of the time, but end stages of beta. There are still problems. Player controlled zombies seem to be able to hit me from 2 metres away. There is still a shortage of maps. The animations are still mostly awkward. On the other hand, things are improving steadily. More maps are on their way out soon, along with more weapons. Steam Workshop has been integrated. The melee system is being revamped, animations and textures are getting work done. Just recently, split screen mode was added (AWESOME FUN!) It still has a few issues, but they don't get in the way of me enjoying myself.
I now play regularly with a number of mates, running our comms through GameVox. With only two of us, we can have a great time playing Escape or Extraction. With any more than that, we can quite happily play Hunted mode. In my opinion, this game is best played with friends. Playing against unknown wombles is still fun, but having a laugh with your mates while you play is where it's at. Contagion will never be perfect, but it's faults are forgivable due to the insane amount of giggles that we get out of it. That, and it scratches that zombie game itch like no other games I've played.
I'd give it a 7.5 out of 10 currently, but with what's on the road map I could see that easily going to an 8 or 8.5. Contagion has some rough edges but it also has a strange appeal, and I certainly don't regret buying it. If anything, I actually feel a bit guilty that I paid so little for it (weird, I know).

I have only played the singleplayer story mode so far so I'm basing my experience on that bit.
The game also includes a build mode, and even online co-op play among others which I will definitely be trying out later.
The game offers a day-night cycle which is faster than real life, but still long enough to have an impact on your plans and adventures. The nighttime is pretty dark and you will have to use torches, headlights, flashlights or other sources of lighting to find your way around the landscape.
This game is in a really good state for an early access game! I would recommend this game to anyone who likes survival, exploration, crafting, and building games.
If you like survival, exploration, crafting and building this is totally the game for you!
You can craft anything from tools to guns, building modules, sentry guns, you name it. There's a lot of different crafting materials you can gather such as wood, stone, iron, copper, tin, different types of plants and more.
The game plays very well and runs smoothly (> 60 fps) on highest settings on my quad core i7 920 (3.2 Ghz OC) with 6 GB RAM and a GTX 770 GPU.
The terrain deformation is absolutely the best I've ever seen. You can literally mine out a cave or structure the way you want it.
It's a voxel based game which means the terrain deforms a lot more natural than a block game would. I can see why this is one of the strongest selling points for this game. This opencl (cuda?) technique the devs are talking about does really seem to do a lot for this game!
The textures are not "next-gen" at the moment, but very much acceptable for such a complex game. I guess this could be improved once they near a final release. It's definitely not game breaking though.
The combat is very acceptable. It's pretty straight forward, click to smash (a la minecraft) but that's totally fine with me to be honest. You are also rooted into place when performing actions which is awesome and makes combat somewhat harder.
Now, this is an early access game, but the only negative things I've been able to find after an hour or so of gameplay is that the world feels a bit empty. It doesn't feel static, since there's a lot to see like different types of animals and foliage/trees/mountains. It could feel a little more vibrant.
The music is fantastic, although there is only one song which loops. It doesn't get annoying because it's a really calm and smooth composition. It runs for a while too so it doesn't get repetitive at all.
Sometimes the combat music can get a little annoying when you're entering and leaving combat in fast intervals.
There is voice acting for most if not all conversations so far. Some of the voice acting is great and some not so great, but also by far not the worst I've experienced. Could use a little more work in some areas though.
There are some basic quests to help you figure out how crafting and gathering works which is great. The game really does a good job of easing you into the game so far. But it doesn't hold your hand too much either, which is a great thing.
I haven't touched the real storyline so far, so I'll have to see how well the story is played out. But I have high hopes!
This game is definitely worth the money and I would certainly recommend this game in it's current state!

This game is very intense, fun, and interesting, especially when playing with people you can talk to obviously, however, be warned, I have encountered a glitch in the time I have been playing this game, and I can promise you there will be more. (Namely, someone got dragged through a normally openable door that was boarded up by a random event on the map loading by a pack leader.)
A second drawback is the fact that treating this like any other FPS will get you slaughtered, your weapons are something you will need to learn several sets of good Rhythms for various circumstances to use properly, as the charge-attack system has a serious degree of depth. As such, mindlessly and repeatedly tapping left mouse in the general direction of the enemy is going to get you killed (Even if you are using a weapon which has a good light attack, as they are not intended to be your exclusive mode of combat.)
As such, the next bit of this review will be explaining how to strategize how to play based on your weapons attributes, to ease the early game hell.
In a weapons basics: Weapons have two modes of attack, light (Standard, good for quickly staggering a single enemy,) and Charged (Seems to be gradual, thus, I will reffer to barely charged attacks as medium, and almost fully charged attacks as heavy.)
Now, the attributes for how hitting something works are very invovled and in depth, each hand to hand weapon can hit a certain number of Skaven before its blade will get stopped, it will do a certain amount of damage, and it will be able to stagger enemies of a certain severity. This tells you what targets the weapon is good at.
See the Templar Zwiehander you start with in your inventory chest as the Witch hunter, it has a dissapointing light attack, but its charged hits have a great number of targets it will hit for medium damage. It is a glorious weapon to throw well timed medium attacks with. Its stagger is bad, meaning you should neve try to fight stormvermin with it, while the hammer the empire soldier has access to has great stagger scores, and is great at dealing with stormvermin.
As such, you can start forming up into strategic roles, but until you understand how to do this, and how to get good with your chosen weapons, this game is rough, and brutally hard. It is not your run of your mill FPS.

If you're crashing on Windows 10 after ~15min playing try this out, this is the only thing that fixed it for me
> Click on Windows Start button
> Type "Services"; it'll automatically begin doing a search as you type
> Click on the thing that comes up and says, "Services"
> Scroll aaaall the way until you get to "Touch Input and Handwriting Panel Service"
> Right click, click "Stop"
> Enjoy the game!
If in game, it takes forever to "Log in" to Ubisoft's Fary Cry 3 servers, then fails, and then it does this every time you go to the menu while in game, try either or both of the following:
1. Windows Firewall
> Click on Windows Start button
> Type in "Firewall"
> Click on Windows Firewall with Advanced Security
> On the left column/window, click on "Inbound Rules"
> Scroll on down to the area with a bunch of stuff that says "Far Cry 3", Far Cry D3D11, etc
> Enable all dat jazz
2. Change compatibility of farcry3.exe
> Go to whatever hard drive location you store all your Steam games (Folder is called SteamLibrary)
> Once in SteamLibrary go to SteamApps,
> then common,
> then Far Cry 3,
> then bin
> For example on my computer the final path looks like this "E:\SteamLibrary\SteamApps\common\Far Cry 3\bin"
> Right click on "farcry3.exe"
> MAKE SURE its farcry3.exe, not farcry3_d3d11.exe, game will crash on startup if you mess with it
> Click "properties"
> A window should pop up with a bunch of tabs on top; click on the "Compatibility" tab
> about 1/4 way down the window it says "Compatibility Mode" with a little checkbox that says "Run this program in compatibility mod for:"
> Check the checkbox
> Select "Windows 8" from the dropdown menu
> Click OK at the bottom of the window
> Finally enjoy your god damn game
> Oh no wait you have to go through like 10 hoops with Uplay's Google Authentication bullsh!t, where you have to download an app ON YOUR PHONE. You can only have fun after that.

While I would love to recommend this game, I simply cannot.
Believe me, I wanted to like this game, it seemed to have everything going for it on the surface.
The beautiful artwork and design are what drew me into purchasing this game. I still believe that the artists who worked on this game did an amazing job and should be congratulated by moving their talents to an actual game company that also cares about gameplay and player enjoyment and not pain and regret of purchase.
But I digress…
The idea of a side-scroller platformer based on zombies pursuing me drew me even closer.
But then I played it and looked under the hood.
Before I get into the specifics of the actual gameplay issues, I would like to address the fact that the programmers could not even figure out how to develop a game that allowed one to in-game pause successfully without a loooooooooong pause before the popping up the menu or even better, freezing the entire game and forcing you to cntrl-alt-del to see it's not responding and end task the game.  Correct me if I'm wrong but I do not think that is how games are supposed to work.  Don't believe, feel free to peruse the forums, you'll see what I'm talkng about.
Now the main complaint:
The controls are horrendous and I do mean horrendous.
If you do foolishly purchase it, like I did, you will probably find yourself rage quitting more times than actually playing it.
There are certain levels that are plagued with absolutely poor game mechanics and I shall name but a few that I encountered, feel free to search the forum that contains oodles and oodles of more examples of why this title should go the way of vaporware.
There is a level where a helicopter chases you throughout the level, what a cool concept! But because of obvious gameplay issues it turned out to be anything but cool, more like maddening as your character, Randall, dies, dies, dies, and dies some more.  The reason?  Zombies?!  Nope.  It is all due to a wall that seems for some strange reason to slow your progress at the exact moment when you should be sprinting quickly away.  A wall, you say? Yes, a wall but not just any wall…a hellish nightmare borne out of the mind of a sadistic programmer’s deepest dark soul.  You see, this wall I refer to, for some reason contains a serious code issue that makes the character lag to the point and does not just slow them down but slows the game down!  Yes, you heard that correctly, slows the character’s animation and the game controls and results many times in death.
Go ahead search the forum, I’ll wait.
Okay, now that you have returned to read on…
Another level I found completely irksome and irritating to the point I wanted to smash my X-box controller into tiny indecipherable pieces was when your character must sprint through a door and then quickly make it through a collapsing building.  Again, this sounds great on paper but very, very poor in execution. You see, the building collapsing in question was not the issue, it was the fact that more often than not your character either mysteriously dies by invisible but deadly debris or even better, smacks face first into the wall or runs up the wall but then slides back down instead of what was supposed to happen- jump in the other direction to ascend to the other side.  This may sound rather comical but believe me after the millionth time of hearing the same canned dialogue over and over when restarting the checkpoint, it is anything BUT funny!
Oh if you do happen to make it over that demonic part I swear was spawned from a programmer’s sick and twisted fantasy of fun, don’t worry, you still have to make two more perfect precise timed movements- one involving crouching while simultaneously jumping through a hole in the wall.
Now I am all for a good challenge and have played many, many demanding games in my forty-some years, but because the game’s controls are so ungodly awful, the challenge here is more based upon persistence until the controller decides to awaken from its sluggish slumber and the code-gods in the program somehow miraculously and inexplicably bless one to progress through this level after performing the same exact actions again and again.
The next level I would like to address is a hellish level so seemingly benign appearing that it may not appear as agonizingly painful at first.  It is ironically located in the “safe zone”, yet it is anything but safe on my sanity.
It begins after Randall crashes through the door and appears on the second floor above a group of ravenous shadowy creatures.  There is a large window located to the opposite side of the room and a boarded up window that he must obviously smash through.  What to do here is apparent, well at first.
As I attempted initially to extinguish all the zombies below me and to run across to the room, it seems that the programmers their grotesque minds said in unison, “nah, too easy, let’s make this area an infinite spawn point to force the player to run across the room while attempting to smash a boarded up window, and yeah, let’s also make another infinite spawn point on the other side of that window so that the player is truly trapped and yet must somehow shoot supports to a large window on the outside wall high above. Oh and let’s then force them to make their way back through the window through an ever increasing horde before climbing up a set of stairs to leap victoriously to safety…yeah that’d be great! They’ll have loads of fun doing that!”
Basically the player is swarmed the entire time. Again, this would be fine but the asinine broken gameplay rears its ugly head again since reloading a pistol for some reason often causes Randall to face the opposite direction of the oncoming swarm of infinite spawning zombies, fun fun, isn’t it?! And for some reason reloading a pistol takes a click for each bullet to enter the chamber.  So basically while trying to fend off a horde of zombies, your character faces away from them as you click, click away and become overrun with zombies. Oh I forgot to mention that yes, there are bullets to pick up on the other side of window but I dare you to try to find time grabbing them before getting annihilated by the infinite mob.
But aside from all of these mysterious decisions to take a potentially fun game and decide to turn it in a pile of putrid trash that zombies would not even ingest, this is not what ultimately prompted me to write my tale of warning to all potential buyers out there.
What mainly prompted me was that after locating the developer’s webpage, I found something even more curious, no support.  Nada, zip, zilch, zero, zed. It seems as though they just do not care whatsoever and these same individuals have also mysteriously vanished from the forums.  They put out a patch about a year ago and were never heard from since.  If you don’t believe me, go to their webpage at
and you will see what I mean, no community forums, no support, no fixes in the works, no future patches coming, nothing but an announcement that they have moved on to join the next-gen console competition.
Search the forums on Steam and you will find tons of threads about more gamebreaking issues and poor programming that I somehow did not encounter but others have!  One hopeful player even went to the exhaustive length to list all the bugs and glitches in hopes to catch the attention of the uncaring programmers’ eyes.
So, I warn not to get fooled by the pretty pictures and the flash sales for a lot less, there are much better games out there with much better gameplay and more supportive developers.

If you like the first game, I reccomend trying this out. If you haven't played the first game, first of all, this isn't for you.
For fans of the first game, I'm warning you : It's simply not as good.
The levels are too open, and too large and long, think Hot and Heavy. It's bascially 25 versions of Hot and Heavy, with a heavy focus on gunplay.
Character swapping is a great idea on paper, but in practice it leaves you feeling frenetic, never really finding a comfort zone or a being able to get used to any one character. It doesn't help that some of them are plain gimmicky and not fun to use (The Writer as a pacifist, in particular.)
The difficulty curve has been ramped significantly, and at times can be hair pullingly frustrating, but with perserverance nothings impossible. Sometimes you will feel like it's luck though.
For what it's worth though when the game comes together it's still the same, fun, violent Hotline it always is. The game works best when you're playing as one of the "Default" characters with no powers and allows you to play it to the same freedom you would the first. The story is not as strong, and the sense of insanity isn't quite there but there are some twist and turns and enough good ideas I'd play it still.
All in all, if you liked the first game, do try it, but don't be too hurt when it's not as great as the first one.

First off, let me say that while I have 100 hours recorded playing this game, there probably isnt near that much content.  I experienced the notorious "invisible walls" glitch, whereby my character would inexplicably stop and be unable to proceed forward, as though there was a wall in front of him, although nothing actually appeared on the screen.  It took quite a bit of manipulating the movement keys, alternately crouching or standing up, backing off and running forward, and other such tricks to find the window to allow me to proceed.  As such, climbing radio towers required quite an investment of time, hence the hours I racked up playing.
However, from the online search I did it seems that only a small minority of players experience this glitch, and even with it this game was immensely enjoyable.  The designers did an exceptional job in not forcing you to play the game a certain way.  You can achieve most of the objectives any way you like.  So, if your prefernce is to stand off at a distance and dispatch opponents with silenced sniper rifles and bow shots you can do that.  Alternately, you can sneak in and take opponents by stealth at close quarters.  Or you could charge in guns blazing and blow everything up.  Any of those methods will work.
The main story line is well done and proceeds at the right pace, without making you feel like its dictating yoru actions.  There is lots to do on the island outside the main plot.  You can search for relics, lost letters from Japanese servicemen stationed on the island during WWII, engage in races with all sorts of vehicles from boats to dune buggys to ATVs.  Take a hangglider ride.  Play some poker.  Like I said lots to do.
My machine is pretty slow so I played the game on the lowets graphics settings and it still looked good to me, but Ive never put much emphasis on graphics so your opinion may be different.
All in all, and excellent FPS with a good stroy and excellent game design.  Well worth adding to your games library, especially when it is on sale for less than $5.

The game overall was straight forward and not overly difficult but yet it still wasn't a cake walk. I did feel at times when you failed a certain point and it made you redo an entire segment that required precise jumps and actions; was frustrating. I felt like at the times the overall story lacked some definition and forced you to read diary pages in order to fill in the blanks; I don't want to sit and read through pages of story.  The ending will be somewhat expected and not overly shocking, but you will enjoy it on some level. Overall the gameplay which consisted of tough jumps and some shooting was enjoyable yet not groundbreaking.
If you appreciate great artwork, zombies, great gameplay and decent audio then Deadlight is the game for you.

Sadly, I'm going to have to agree with most reviews on here that Deadlight has too many problems to overcome. The biggest problem, as most note, is the horrendously stiff controls. What kept me going, though, was the superb animation, lighting, and level building. The sense of decay in a crushed out Seattle was beautiful in a eerie sort of way. So after about 4 hours I've had to move on from Deadlight.

It's not a particularly lengthy adventure, but it's worth the price.

The difficulty curve has been ramped significantly, and at times can be hair pullingly frustrating, but with perserverance nothings impossible. Sometimes you will feel like it's luck though.
For what it's worth though when the game comes together it's still the same, fun, violent Hotline it always is. The story is not as strong, and the sense of insanity isn't quite there but there are some twist and turns and enough good ideas I'd play it still.
All in all, if you liked the first game, do try it, but don't be too hurt when it's not as great as the first one.

Hotline Miami 2 is a GOOD game, but not a GOOD sequel for Hotline Miami games. The ideas that made HM1 so satisfying are contradicted in HM2.
HM1 is a fast paced, beat-em up from enemy to enemy, where YOU change your plan if it does not work from level to level. I fell in love with this playstyle and still play HM1 to this day.
HM2 just went against all that HM1 built on, which is a real bummer.
1. The game and character design doesn't let YOU change your plan to beat a level, THE GAME CHANGES YOUR PLAN FOR YOU. The new characters are cool additions because each one carries a backstory, but in-game each one forces you to change and the "A-Ha" moment you get when you find a nice route through a level is ruined becaause you didn't find it, the game forced you to find it.
2. The game feels generally slower and I felt less like a badass. With all the increased enemies in each level, I felt like I was played a cover shooter more than a "run through a house and be a walking death machine". Not to mention that when you knock over an enemy the ground pounding takes FOREVER. It is signifigantly slower than that of HM1 and it led me to so many deaths. This is especially true in the Hawaii levels because when you run out of ammo, you feel so weak.
3. There are no secrets or collectables. I personally, but not for all, was really into finding all the secret letters and secret masks. There are none in this game.
4. This game is feeling more like an angrier Super Meat Boy. The steep difficulty curve in this game, and especially with some levels.  I felt like I was playing Super Meat Boy, just running in and suiciding because of all the enemy sightlines. I would try to adapt but, like the the first point, I couldn't because the game stops me from trying different varieties.
Hotline Miami is fun game to play, but it doesn't feel like Hotline Miami. the music and atmosphere is still there, but I felt so weak and slow. I would recommend this game for someone who wants a top-down beat-em up, but not for someone who wants the genuine Hotline Miami experience.
