Hotline Miami 2, a game that I had the highest hopes for, and those hopes were exceeded by this piece of video game excellency.
Take Hotline Miami, add more characters, more levels, and a tighter-focused plot, and that's what you get here.
I can't say anything about the story without spoiling it, but the plot goes down a very Pulp Fiction-esque route, with many characters slowly coming together, while jumping from various time periods and locations.
The sole problem I have with Hotline Miami 2 lies with the level design, and this could be a make it, break it deal for most people. The levels, for the most part, are more shooting oriented, and are bigger and open ended. There's also a ton of windows, this game becomes less adrenaline-fueled killing, and becomes check around the corner and make sure no room has windows. Yes, it does get frustrating on some levels, getting killed by something you can't see because the maps are so large, but it's still an overall fun experience, just a different one.

Deadlight is a survival horror side scroller. Odd combo you might think, but much like games like Trine it takes it's 2D plane and packs in an AMAZING amount of detail all over that really set the scene of post apocalyptic Seattle. You play Randall, a man who has survived becoming a "Shadow" and is trying to find his family and reach a safe haven.
This is a first impressions review:
To start off like I said the detail is amazing, growing up in the Pacific Northwest seeing the detail they put into the areas really made me happy and gave a me a nearly home feeling (despite the fact it was destroyed). The game has a nice flow to it and controls pretty smoothly. The character so far is believable and has a reasonable enough agenda. And he looks exactly like a rough guy from Seattle would.
The fact that you rather avoid zombies than kill them due to stamina and lack of ammo really brings in the survival horror feel for me, and the planning in obstacles really polishes the side scrolling bit. My pet peeves arise from two things however, one some of the obstacles are a bit tedious, seeing as they might require a still jump but naturally it's hard to place yourself under it and you end up jumping all over and wasting time. The second is a stricly mouse and keyboard issue, the aiming of the gun being just a bit too stiff to really gun down a zombie about to bite me.
Overall this game is definitely worth getting from what I've seen in just my first hour of playing.

I don't have time to right a full review, but Occam's Chainsaw had it right. THIS is the zomie atmosphere I have wanted for so long. I've only been playing around with last man standing, and it's great. You truly get a sense for being alone in a zombie apocolypse.
When you see a flashlight, you feel a mutual need to stick together and watch each other's back. As you find other and move about looking for resources, you'll wonder if these are the last people left. Then, in the distance, you'll hear a sole pistol go off. Then maybe followed by the distant echo of a clip being emptied... did they survive? Will you meet later and join forces?
I can see why people might not like the game as much. But what some have complained about, I see as features. The maps are pretty big, but this isn't COD. It's an experience that is slow, but always building tension. The zombies can't see you through walls, but they do get some help. The humans are generally more OP against the zombie players, but this is great. As you wear down their ammo and pick off straglers.
The game can be slow, the maps big, and sometimes the time between action, long. But this is why I love the game. I'll go back to L4D when I want to mow down a hoard. But till then, I'm loving this! Great work. Hope to see more in the future

And when I looked at other reviews, I saw a lot of people were dissappointed about this game for some of the following reasons: bad level design, bad AI, doesn't encourage recklessness, bad story, or is a cover shooter.  A lot of these can be agreed with at certain times (mostly in hard mode, cause seriously it is balls hard), but a lot of them can also be argued against.  For instance when people say the level design is bad because the maps are really big and you think you just beat this level you have been struggling on for an hour, but suprise fat guy or shotgun guy comes out of the blue and kills you (Dead Ahead looking at you).  Now is this unfair at times, yes definatley, but this is a trial and error based game.  Your suppose to die multiple times until you get the formula right, and if that fat guy or shotgun guy comes around again you will know that they are there (especially if you calling it bad level desgin).  Bad AI can also be agreed with, can't tell you how many times a dog has spun in circles then killed me through a wall, but a lot of the times it's kinda funny to see mobsters and dogs freak out.  Also what did you expect a perfect game without the full game even being out yet (level creator)?  There will definatley be patches to help fix the bugs in the future.  Doesn't encourage recklessness on hard mode can definatley be agreed with and most of the Hawaii levels(you only get 1 gun, you gotta be careful with that♥♥♥♥♥♥.  However on normal mode a lot of the missions can be played very recklessley, especially in the Richter chapter (you have to play recklessley to beat that♥♥♥♥♥♥.  The bad story I honestly can't make too much of an arguement on because the story either rubbed you the right way or the wrong way as far as I see it.  And finally this game is a cover shooter.  Honestly on normal you can almost play anyway you want (except Hawaii levels) , but when you start playing hard mode, there is no way for you to rush in. In short a lot of the problems with this game are completely understandable and completely agrreeable, but in my opinion I found the game to be a lot of fun with great gameplay, and a lot of replay value. Crysis + Just Cause 2 = Far Cry 3... but better
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Take the FPS gun-play of Crysis, but with more relaxed enemy AI (depending on difficulty). Now mix in the sandbox play of Just Cause 2, but with a smaller, more manageable island size that makes hiking across it much more reasonable. You pretty much get Far Cry 3. It still has some annoyances of "open world / 50+ hours of gameplay!" games, but it's far more entertaining. It's a "summer popcorn movie" video game. Turn your brain off, and you'll have a blast.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
PROS:
+ Smaller world size + less dense off-road areas makes getting about (even on foot) much more manageable and enjoyable. (ie: they don't need a cheaty-feeling gimmick like Just Cause 2's grappling hook and parachute to get about, because simply hiking around gets you where you're going pretty fast.) This is one of the few open-world games where I feel they got the world size just right.
+ Unlike Far Cry 2's or Just Cause 2's "everything looks the same" worlds, FC3's areas are different-looking enough to be distinct and interesting to get around. Yes, it's a lot of green, but they mix up areas of vegetation (bamboo forests, trees, fields) and elevation (mountains, hills, plains, pits, etc), then mix in cave networks (!) to add enough variety to keep it interesting hiking and exploring. Because the world is small enough to cross on foot reasonably, I find myself driving along and seeing something interesting. So, I get out of my vehicle to go explore and site-see. I don't really do that in other open-world games, because usually everything looks the same and there's nothing interesting. FC3 does it right.
+ Yes, like almost all open-world games, there's item "scavenger hunts" that act as gameplay filler. But, the landscape is so varied, and they hid some stuff in cave systems, so it makes exploring and finding stuff actually pretty entertaining! Plus, they give you the option to buy maps that show all loot & special item locations. This way you can choose to either explore randomly, or highlight all locations and purposefully go get them. Even when you get to the location of some loot, you may be surprised to find it's 20M below you. So, you then have to go find the cave opening that takes you down to it. Some loot is located in ship-wrecks in shark-infested waters. So, you head out on a jet ski, look around... looks like the coast is clear... dive in... SHARK! I usually find scavenger hunt BS to be the bane of existence in open-world games, but I've been loving the heck out of it in FC3.
+ The concept of hunting animals to upgrade gear seems a bit gimicky, but I found it enjoyable. I spent most of my early hours in the game just tracking and hunting animals... with an AK-47 and sniper rifle!
+ When games started delving into better graphics, they went overboard with Bloom, HDR, post, etc. I turn all that off, because the game ends up looking like a smudgy, blurry mess and I can't tell what's going on. In Far Cry 3, they seem to have hit some kind of perfect balance. I have the graphics cranked up to max, even post, and I can see things vividly, bloom isn't over-done, everything looks great. I think my one small beef with the graphics is that the sky in the game engine seems unnaturally dark, even mid-day. The clouds and blue in the sky just seems like it's not bright enough to seem realistic. It's like there's a perpetual smog haze in the sky.
NEUTRALS:
* they padded the game with the usual open-world tropes ... racing events, mini-games, oddball missions (some about hunting, some about killing a random pirate, etc). You don't have to do them, but the hunting ones tend to be a must-do, since they hand out the best animal skins needed to craft the best gear.
* you have to install and create a UPlay account. I know folks find that annoying, but from a business perspective it's clever. They can cut the price of games like FC3 way down to use as loss-leaders to get folks to install UPlay. Once UPlay is installed, chances are good that folks will browse what it is and what's in the UPlay store. It's a way to get folks to check out your online store. But, I do find it annoying. There's just too many online game "services/stores" these days to keep up with it all, and UPlay only has a small library of games. It's annoying when companies make you install an entire game service/store when there's hardly much in it. Everyone wants to be the next Steam.
CONS:
- Respawn rates are still annoying, seemingly ripped from FC 2. If you're in hostile territory, enemy vehicles magically show up to a fight every 30 seconds. Some areas only clear out after story missions, and they will keep spawning enemies while you're standing there. Seems a bit awkward.
- Ammo is dropped by enemies based on the guns they use (makes sense). Since most early-game enemies are only using assault rifles or shotguns, you get tons of that ammo and hardly any other. So, you find yourself hunting animals with an assault rifle. You buy a sniper rifle, then hardly use it since you don't find enough ammo and have to buy more. It's annoying.
- There's gun shops. The way they work is that you buy a gun to unlock it, then you can always come back and swap to it if you want to change your load-out. I like that, but I think they could have done away with the gun shop and just made guns part of the scavenger hunt. You can find some of the guns on enemies, so if you grab it you can bring it back to the shop to unlock it for free. They should have kept that method and just had you find all the guns, and simply have a storage locker at bases. The gun shop gets abusive pretty fast, because, if you're a completionist, you'll have cash coming out your wazoo and have all the best guns unlocked early on without much to look forward to.
- There's an rpg-lite xp and skill system. It seems contrived and annoying at times. Instead of just letting you naturally get better as you do things, you get xp to "build your character as you like". But, most skills are locked away until you do more missions. So, if you're a completionist that loves to explore and finish areas before moving on, you'll be sitting on lots of unspent skill points waiting for skills to unlock. It's just super annoying. Unlock them all from the start. Stop punishming me for taking my time to play the game.
- Your character is super-whiney. If you muted his voice, you'd think you were a bad-a** in the game with everything you do. But, he makes a whiney little remark when you slaughter an animal for the umpteenth time. Cut scenes have him whining about stuff, or making really dumb decisions that you wouldn't make in the open-world game play. He's a bro-ster d-bag supposedly coming of age, but he never seems to grow up.
- The open-world gameplay lets you tailor how you engage enemies and bases. Then the story missions throw all of that out the window by forcing contrived handicaps on you (eg: must sneak, must stealth kill, must run-n-gun, must ride in a vehicle and man the mounted gun like a rail shooter). And your idiot character decides to walk right into traps over and over. Don't let me be a bad-*** in open-world game play just to make me feel like an idiot in cut scenes. It's insulting.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Overall, FC3 gets the open-world part right, but drops the ball on the story line. However, FC3 gets so much right, and has been a royal blast to play, it's easy to overlook the cons. I'm getting older, and a game has to really impress me to keep my attention. I've been playing FC3 pretty much nonstop since I installed it, and that's saying something. Problem is, the open-world part has kept me coming back, but the trudging through the story has kept pushing me away. I finally finished it, and once the sotry is done, the open-world part and collecting stuff seems pointless. But, it's an interesting sandbox to explore.

Vermintide wears its inspirations on its sleeve: mechanically it is extremely similar to Left 4 Dead. But it inovates in two big ways:
First, it adds a Warhammer theme with some of the coolest looking environments, weapons, and characters I've ever seen in a first person shooter (or slasher, as the case may be), and of course an enemy far more interesting that the played-out zombie apocolypse, the skaven.
Second, it shifts the focus away from ranged combat, and instead focuses primarily on first person melee combat like that in Chivalry or Vermintide's creator's previous title War of the Roses. There are still all manner of nifty guns, bows, and staves to use, but it's flip-flopped from a game like L4D2; melee is your primary and ranged is your secondary.
First person melee combat is harder to get right than your average FPS, but fortunately, Vermintide nails it. Swings feel appropriately weighty, combat is brutal and frantic, and the whole thing ends up being much more challenging and skillful than I expected from this sort of game.
Vermintide also sports a rather impressive loot and progression system, with tons of amazing looking weapons with a very diverse set of combat styles to chose from. Fortunately, though there are some straight upgrades to be found, the game seems to keep things balanced so that a new player could still play with higher level friends without being completely helpless. Most of all, it provides rewards for continuing to play, which is something that was lacking from a game like L4D, and helps keep the game feeling fresh even as you play levels multiple times.
Big recommendations to Warhammer fans, obviously, as well as co-op horde game fans, and (the category I fall into) people desperate for well-done unique first person combat, melee and otherwise. I would discourage people who are looking for a single player experience (there are bots, but they do a pretty poor job compared to even the least skilled player), and people who really didn't like Left 4 Dead's way of doing things. For me, this has become one of my favorite games of the year extremely quickly.

I have played 30 hours of Heroes and Generals at the time of this review, I have not paid for anything in H&G, and I have a love-hate relationship with this game. I feel like I like this game, but when I actually play it, it annoys the absolute bejesus out of me (can't swear due to Guidelines, choose what fits for you). Maybe not too unusual amongst players who understand this feeling, but I'll explain in this review.
The maps: I like how the open maps would generally reflect how large an actual WW2 mission is, but it's how slow you feel when you try to flank the enemy on foot for those who have just started. When you see couple snipers hiding on a building 100 metres away and shooting you, you'd want to do something about that. But you'll waste 10 mins of your life trying to take the long route around just so you don't get shot by a sniper and have enough health to kill anyone oblivious of your position.
The guns: a simple variety of guns doesn't confuse any new players too much in "what's what, that's that". But it's how long you have to grind with all your terrible starting weapons just to work up to that sniper rifle you so dearly want after picking it up from someone that's *cough cough* actually paid for it. If you get sidetracked and pay to be a tank crewman and found out it's not that fun, you have wasted so much time playing beforehand to save those credits.
The ribbons: how you unlock everything (all through leveling up certain ribbons) is fine and dandy. But it's how long it takes you to get the next level that feels very irritating. You get all the good stuff WAY TOO (insert your f-word of choice) FAR away from where you began. And this will tie in with the actual gameplay part later.
The vehicles: tanks, planes, cars and bikes. All fitting very well in the theme of WW2. But as soon as you get to level 4 there will be tanks EVERYWHERE, and there's nothing you can do to either stop it or avoid it once you pass level 4. If you're in an Assault map, have fun shooting those planes if you can actually find them.
The gameplay: now I have nothing good to say about this part. If you just wanted a different game to play and don't want it to cost you a cent, this isn't it. Because there is nothing fun about have the two worst possible guns against anything else to earn any of the better guns. If you're free-to-play like myself, there's nothing more annoying than being owned by all the better guns that you only dream to have.
But the worst aspect about this game by a full trip between the Poles is gold. I am in no position yet to critise that you can pay for stuff in games, it's how the devs want to earn money. But actually paying for this gold is so expensive, the cheapest option (1400 gold) is $7.95 cents instead of the conventional $5, $10, $20, etc. I live in Australia so if I have $7.95 US dollars that's ~$10.40. That's really expensive for the cheapest option available, and even then that won't get you the sniper rifle. And the maximum amount of gold given: 26000 gold for $114.40. WTSF? Who the hell is actually paying for that, is there nothing else for you to spend ~$130.00AUS on instead of, idk, a better game?
I seriously don't like this game when I'm on my own and getting dominated so hard in an Assault match because of the predominance of tanks, planes and sniper rifles on the enemy team. But all I can hope is oen thing: have the people that paid for the game match with people who paid for the game.

An interesting but fun concept. Take the combat/gameplay from old school games like "Out of this World" and "Flashback", but remove the puzzles... replacing them with environment obstacles. Which means you do a lot of ledge jumping and running in a 2D level layout but with 3D level backgrounds going on.
It took me about 3-4 hours to finish this game, but it had moments when the gameplay suffered as controls were not precise. An example is jumping over a walk and shooting someone... sounds easy but sometimes there was a delay to pull the gun out and other times there was not.
The story is alright but the internal dialog of your main character can be a bit cliché. Most of the games you use an axe to protect yourself, but you do get a hand gun/shot gun which makes a couple of areas fun to kill zombies.
I could have used more secrets/areas to find as when I did find secrets... it was actually satisfying even if there was no major reward.
Not a bad 2D zombie game with an old school gameplay throwback, but I couldn't say it is for everyone. If you enjoyed games like Blackthorne or Flashback, but want it to be more casual and less looking for keycards; then this is for you!

All the changes from the first seem to be for the worse.
The biggest change is to the level design. The levels are overly large and full of long corridors. That wouldn't be a problem on its own, but the increased amount of guns leads to so many instances of getting shot from someone you couldn't possibly see, even using the (really messed up for some reason) shift camera feature. This is combined with an overuse of windows to make it even more common to get shot at.
This leads to most levels being best handled by baiting guards out with quick movements in and out of rooms to then handle them one by one. It's just boring compared to the fast pace of the first, where going from room to room with a melee weapon was very feasible, and even encouraged. There's less room for improvisation with combat; no more kick a door into a guy then throw this then grab his weapon then stab this guy, and that was the best part of the first!
The switch to having characters with perks instead of multiple masks to choose from reduces the creativity you can have in the levels. You've basically got one or two ways of handling each situation, and it's often dictated that no, you have to play this way, this character only, no options. Many of the interesting characters are also seriously underused; some characters get two levels and then you never play them / with their mechanics again.
On the bright side, it looks fantastic and vibrant, and the soundtrack is second-to-none. Highly recommended!
It's a shame because there's still some great gameplay buried in here, but the rigid design and terrible maps mean I can't see myself replaying this over and over like I did the first.

This game really feels unpolished to the point that the gameplay is a little baffling.  Note that I'm just playing the co-op mode, and the perspective is based on that:
-Objectives are written in a first-person perspective, relying on character knowledge the player doesn't have.
-Equipment is scarce to the point of being bizarre.  Sure, you don't expect there to be ammo lying all over the place, but things like melee weapons are just as scarce, despite every location being littered with items you could use as a melee weapon.
-Characters often comment on using itmes on doors that aren't supposed to open, leading you to frustratingly use keys on each and every door you come across to find the one that will finally open.
-There's next to no feedback on the weapons and the type of ammo they should be using.  Sure, you'd expect  a bunch of strangers to not necessarily know everything about weapons they find, but it really doesn't feel like the intention of the game, considering you get the names of all the guns.  You don't have any feedback on the ammo you pick up either - how much of the shotgun shells do you have when you don't have a shotgun?  Your guess is as good as mine.
-Melee doesn't have the kind of impact you would expect - especially with something like a Sledgehammer.  There's no real feeling of force when you attack someone with a large weapon - leaving the whole experience rather unsatisfying.
It's not unplayable or anything.  It's just really bizarre.  While I appreciate the slower, careful pace compared to a game like Left4Dead, the lack of polish really gets in the way of a really good time.
Shame too.  There's potential here.  This game really should still be in early access.

This game is extremely fun and addictive, the gameplay is interesting, balanced and engaging, and the addition of the crafting and drop system is a great way to add longevity to the game. It takes some of the best parts of L4D and Payday 2 and mixes it with the fantastic Warhammer universe.
It is a game where you can play missions on an extremely brutal difficulty, where your entire team of 4 has to coordinate extremely well and spend a large amount of time to get through a max difficulty mission.
All that time and energy and focus spent can be wiped away in a second. If your host crashes, disconnects, has to leave because his mom called for dinner or any other reason, you're completely hosed. The game will migrate to a new host, and in the process RESTARTS THE ENTIRE LEVEL.  All that time and energy fighting through difficult circumstances, gathering the tomes and grimoires throughout the mission that increase reward and difficulty, all to completely disappear right at the end. I've had this happen in beta literally right as we were about to enter the getaway cart.
It's almost rage-inducing in frustration, and makes you feel like you just wasted a large amount of your time and energy for nothing.
Disconnects and crashes aren't frequent, but even having it happen once every couple days, when that mission can easily take 30-60+ minutes of intense focus, is completely unacceptable. I really think there is a gem of a game here, but feeling like my time and energy is completely negated by a system that is half-implemented is just something that I can't bear.
EDIT: After playing it quite a bit with an organized team, and otherwise hosting my own games, I've had way too much fun with this game to not recommend it. Hopefully they add in dedicated servers, and until then I will just play with people I trust not to disconnect or host myself.

Contagion is a great drop-in game for first-person shooter gamers looking for an atmospheric experience in the zombie-driven survival-horror genre.
This game highlights mortality and vulnerability to the zombie plague. Bites and scratches have a high chance of spreading an infection to you, unlike other games where your character is virtually immune to the zombie epidemic.
Going the other way, zombies are relatively unfazed from damage by weapons, unless you manage to hit the good ol' sweet spot in classic zombie games: hit 'em in the head.
The maps are fun to replay in the Escape Modes, as the objectives and path navigation changes from game to game. It stays fresh by also randomizing the weapons and ammo available during each playthrough, as well as switching up the locations where they can be found. Popular item spots may suddenly be empty in the next play-through.
This game does have a few flaws though, such as zombies dodging to the right as you attempt to snipe them from afar, the lack of an unarmed grapple/shove to keep a zombie from biting you in the dark, and melee attacks which get weaker the longer you ready or charge an attack.
With those few flaws in mind, it's a great game for anyone to just jump right in and play.
Already there is talk in the forums about character customization options, more maps and game modes, and improvements for gameplay and additional game mechanics like weather and hunger. This game has a lot of potential, and if you see this game on sale it's definitely worth picking it up!

I would NOT recommend Deadlight for its regular price. On a sale though - you can try.
What puts me off is that quite big part of this game (let's say ~50%) is basically a well concealed QTE. You are to navigate thorugh environment to avoid lots and lots of insta-death hazards and the fact that controls are somewhat clunky and not always responsive is definitely not helping in this case. And if you don't do those "QTE" sequences in a way predicted by creators, gg. There is very little room for mistakes.
To make things even worse, some checkpoints are made in such a way that after a failed sequence you are forced to watch the same cutscene or hear out the same dialogue / monologue. Or both. And this can sometimes happen over and over and over as you figure out what you are actually supposed to do and in what order.
What also may be a problem is that some locations are not so good at telling you where to go or what to do. Since the game is made in 2,5D, sometimes it's hard to see it you can actually go past some wall, because there's a hole in it, or maybe you should try and jump over. May be the cause of your death on occasions.
For those who like collectibles - game is littered with them, sometimes in the most bizzare locations. And for fans of platforming and "move a box in a proper place" puzzles - don't worry, there's a also quite a lot of those in here.
As far as I know you cannot rebind controls, which are just shown on I guess Xbox controller as a picture and that's about it. What's provided on keyboard is not bad at all, but those few people using arrow keys might be put off, since everything is based on WASD and keys around it.
Other than that game provides some "tactical" combat with zombies (or Shadows, as they are called iirc), which goes down to either shooting them (easy way) or chopping them with a fire axe (more complicated). The latter is tied to your stamina reserves, which can make battles quite a nice challange. On occasions.
Also maybe that's just me (and I was too lazy to search any info about it), but I had my sound being cut off in cutscenes (aka loading screens) between maps, which left me with just subtitles. Sound did come back when the game resumed though.
Steam tells me that I spent around 5 hours on this game in order to finish it. If I didn't have to repeat so many insta-kill sections so many times, it would probably be cut a little - to 4h, maybe even 3,5h.
That's about all.

Deadlight is a game where we take on the role of a survivor, Randall Wayne, as he searches for his family in an apocalyptic Seattle.
The sound and audio in Deadlight are phenomenal. Deadlight features a wonderful sountrack that fits each level perfectly. The voice acting in Deadlight is quite well done as well, though at times the narrative can be a little emotionless. There are no cutting or static issues with the audio in Deadlight. Deadlight delivers a wonderful experience through sound. 4.5/5
Visually Deadlight is stunning. Brilliant aesthetics and effects really bring this game to life. Deadlight is by far the most beautiful sidescroller game I have ever played. The textures are crisp, clean, and high quality. No texture clipping or inconsistencies were experienced. 5/5
Deadlight's story is well written. The story in Deadlight is both narrated through Randall's thoughts and read through his diary. The added depth to the story that comes from the reading of Randall's diary really gives the player insight into Randall's world. The story is full of tense moments and unexpected twists.  5/5
Mechanically Deadlight are well done, but not perfect. Deadlight features some environment interaction, though this is mostly limited to opening doors and solving puzzles. The movement in Deadlight is quite fun- being able to blast through levels as fast as possible, or taking it slow. The game has some issues with regards to keyboard controls, as it is difficult to make some jumps, though this is not really an issue. The gameplay can be a little "iffy" at times, such as events not firing or forcing the player out of areas. No crashes were experienced.  3/5
Deadlight is a game that takes place in a beautiful world, with amazing sounds and voice acting. The story in Deadlight is fantastically executed and deep. The game has very basic mechanics, despite this, the game is worth every penny.
Final numerical score 17.5/20 or 87%

The main reason why I think this game is disagreeable is due to the sometimes-irrational pay-to-win system and the absurdity of the weapon prices.
It is very difficult to advance through the experience levels and buy/upgrade weapons, forcing people to use real currency to buy in-game content. Also, there are some mechanics in the game which are very redundant and serve basically no purpose:
- Knives have the almost exact same statistics as the shovels, yet they cost twice as much.
- The TM-35 mine does the exact same damage as the M1A1 mine, yet costs twice as much.
The price system is also quite unrealistic and focused on a pay-to-win style:
- The cost of purchasing and mounting a scope on a rifle (M1903) costs almost twice as much as the rifle itself, the total cost of the scoped rifle being more than a heavy tank (M26 Pershing).
- A pair of binoculars are as expensive as a Bazooka or a light tank (M2A2).
- A pistol (M1911) is 2.5 times as expensive as a motorcycle (42WLA).
However, even with these faults, I still think that this game shows promise in the future if these issues are corrected. Its weapons are historically accurate and the game concept is unique compared to other FPS games like Half-Life 2.

A game that has a series of unfortunate problems, many of them originating from the L4D franchise from which this game has been designed from. Not to say that the core experience makes it a bad game by any means, the melee and gore is very satisfying when It works but there's just too many glaring problems for me to personally enjoy it for more than a few hours at a time and following an incredibly bug-filled release that yet remains to be fixed, the developers have also gone out of their way to mislead the community by announcing how they have such "BIG PLANS" for the game just to utterly STRUGGLE to release the world's weakest DLC including 3 maps, 3 achievments and 2 new weapons (one which is for an already horrendously overplayed character, they've done zero effort to try and balance the 5 that currently exist) that cost 10€ whilst leaving the old maps that are bugged to all hell in the dust with even weaker updates inbetween fixing nothing but crashes that should have been solved at release.
As for the actual game design / mechanical problems, I'm gonna list these now:
------------------
1. Melee range of Skaven. These little buggers can be armed with tiny rotten planks barely poking out of their hands and still whack you from over 5 bodylengths away. Mix this with the fact that they can effortlessly hit you through massive chunks of walls (even floors/ceilings) and you got a recipe for frustration. HP is precious like all hell and having huge amounts of it be lost to quite frankly bull sh*t scenarios is a big no-no and these frustrations are only reinforced by the constant clumsy slow-downs all character suffer from before, during and after weapon swings that cannot be alleviated in the slightest even with a potion of speed which breaks the melee combat pacing. To put it in numbers, Skaven are as of right now hitting about 20-60% further away than they should be (depending on the Skaven). Now mix this with some very buggy skaven animations including warping, pushing/stun immunity when climbing, clipping into walls & objects and you're goinna have a bad time.
This is an issue that has been openly admitted by the developers themselves. One of the leading causes for this is the FOV which makes no attempt whatsoever to adapt melee ranges you perceive above 65 FOV which has for whatever reason been made the standard, an incredibly dumb decision for a melee oriented messy fighting game.
----
2. Hitboxes. Contributing to point 1, the enemy hitboxes in this game are excruciatingly random. They can either be non-existant, allowing you to merge your body with theirs (and have their body physically fade out of existance as they repeatedly hit you) or have 2-3 of the weakest grunts be able to flawlessly box you in at giant open areas. Both scenarios are much unwelcome things to be had in a melee fighter so collission as of right now remains to be a serious problem of not only consistency and flow often breaking up in fights but also managing to nick the weapon balance in the game. If you collide with a teammate, they will get pushed around. If skaven collide with themselves, they will just clip into each-other and form grotesquely durable glitchy meatshields that even I, a main dwarf player struggle to take down with dozens of full power cleaves using a 2h battle-axe. Have just a few common skaven glitch inside of a rat ogre and.. Well.. You're gonna have a bad time.
----
3. Battle Clutter. There are literally hundreds of enemies swarming you from all directions at any given time while you are cramped up together with 3 other friendly melee fighters.. And there is absolutely no indication or outliners whatsoever to help you see amidst the sea of corpses and blood that if the thing you are hitting is a friendly or a non-dead Skaven as all characters currently in the game suffer from "Skaven Lookalike Syndrome" with perhaps only the Empire Soldier being an exception due to his height & shiny plate and decapitated Skaven splurting significant amounts of blood to form an improvised lamp post. When you combine the hitbox clutter from point 2, however, It also becomes increasingly difficult to differentiate between dead, injured and alive Skaven from even moderate attack groups as they all die in dramatic'esque animations & poses before ragdolling onto the ground. This wouldn't be a problem if you could actually have an effect on these animations by say, pushing them away/cancelling them by swinging your weapon into said ragdolls but instead, they all individually have to stand up and have their incredibly frustrating "vision obscuration" sequence before GTFO'ing. There's also an ongoing series of glitches that make Skaven ragdolls stand upright, even when dead which makes this all much more frustrating. But even then, bodies obscure way too much of the screen which forces you (in even moderate fights) to adapt a spam-swinging strategy instead of trying to get a grasp of a situation.
----
4. Loot & Inventory system leaves much to be desired. After my very first run with my friend playing the Soldier, I had the absurd luck to have a blue rare two-handed sword for said Empire Soldier to drop for me as I was playing as a Wizard while my friend got a staff. Could we trade the two things? NNNNNNNNNNnnnnope. Salvage that crap and better luck rolling the loot dice next time. To put it bluntly, It's a zero flexibility 100% RNG loot system that makes no attempt whatsoever to give you loot related to the hero you were playing that run and It's just a giant questionmark for me as to why they would ever consider this to be good design for a co-op RPG released late 2015. It is particularly crippling because there is literally no other customization to be had to for example, make your character stronger or enable him/her to carry more ammo etc.
----
5. Level design. The first map is beautiful with far-reaching scenery and big atmospheric battle-grounds when you're not crunching through blood-soaked urban quarters. After that, however, you're thrown into a series of horribly generic sewer sections that all look identical save for the 2~ gate opening sections. Following the smelly sewers, you're shot right back up into a ginormously downsized version of map 1 that is nothing but the same cramped urban areas where the only even remotely open area at ALL in the entire map is at the end where you have to go and pick up 5 bags of grain, slowly carrying them one by one to a wagon before getting in yourself and finishing all the early access content. This boring trend has continued with the release maps and they all also follow the consensus of being INCREDIBLY buggy, both having you fall down the map on a dozen locations, be dragged outside of it by packmasters and have drastic FPS drops happen consistently.
----
6. The AI. It is either insanely dumb or insanely cheaty & unfair. For the dumb scenarios I've met, I had all the rats at the end of map 1 try to run up the stairs, targeting only my furthest-back teammate and completely ignoring me as I was slaughtering them en-masse by charging up cleave attacks over and over again. They even repeatedly collided with me and didn't give a damn, allowing us to roll through what would've been a challenging fight. I've also had it blatantly SPAM spawn enemy Skavens right infront of our faces nearby an elevator close to a corner, popping them in by the hundreds and causing them to glitch around in eachother and up against the walls which we took advantage of and slaughtered hundreds of them over and over again with ease before It abruptly stopped. This may not be a big deal on a case-by-case basis but It definitely is a cause of worry as the rest of the released game remains to be grossly untested.

Far Cry 3 is a jewel, regardless of what critics may say. The antagonist is original and ruthless. The combat is intuitive and engaging. The environment is beautiful, lush, and open. There is something for everybody in this vast tropical getaway that turns quickly into a deadly environment of piracy and death.
Do you like stealth? Do you like shooting? Do you like killing moves? Do you like vehicles? Or do you just want to do everything the game has to offer? You play the way you want when you want. It's pretty accurate to say Far Cry 3 is "Skyrim with guns," because it has a lot of those RPG elements and the open world feel.
Some folks hate on the story for being racist, but I see that as unintentional and certainly not the point of the game. The same critics will make the same arguments against Tarzan and other similar types of stories. The whole premise is to be an unassuming young adult who is thrusted into a deadly environment where you must become a predator.
By the end of the game, your transformation is complete and I believe Ubisoft Montreal did a great job ending the game. My only criticism is that the multiplayer was lackluster with a cookie cutter death match and poorly conceived coop that the next game rectifies. This game is worth playing and I'd highly recommend it for how all-encompassing the experience really is.

Deadlight has all the tools to make it a great game, beautiful graphics, fast paced platforming and exploration elements and the tension of a zombie outbreak that seems to constantly be on your tail. Unfortunately, the clunky control scheme will have you failing simple jumps, dying over simple mistakes and being ripped apart by zombies quite regularly. For a story based platformer, I didn't find myself rooting for the hero or even care about his companions, especially when each of them seems to have a shorter life expectancy than a femal black stoner in a horror film. When you finally do keep a companion alive what results is one of the most frustrating escort quests in any game, where a fast paced "chase sequence" is jarringly broken over and over again while you stop to open doors or help your otherwise useless companion up ledges.
That's one of the fundamental problems with this game - it's poor pacing and direction. Sections where you would surely be making a quick escape are full of jarring climbing sections that you seem to take at a rather sedate pace, utterly destroying any tension. There are a few headscratching puzzles that are genuinely fun to solve, and larger open areas that are basically big obstacle courses, but they're so few and far between that the constant running from room to room will eventually become dull. As well as that the pretty graphics, this game's saving grace, quite often clutter the screen making it difficult to determine where you're meant to go.
To sum up, Deadlight is a good idea, it just isn't fun due mainly to poor pacing and slack controls, something that's unforgiveable for a platformer, and proves that good graphics do not make a good game. It's not the worst zombie based game I've ever played (that accolade goes to Trapped Dead), but I wouldn't rate it much higher.

Dennaton Games have been under the influence of Overkill studio, it seems, seeing that they now share the same nasty habbit for over-hyped launch of unfinished and unoptimised sequels.
First of all, if you played the first game in the series - do not buy this game solely out of your experience with first game.
As do you, I expected adrenaline pumping in my veins as I rush through challenging mazes crawling with thugs while listening to fast paced awesome soundtrack.
That is not the case here, developers decided that game needs more open space, guns and bugs. This simple decision managed to transform the run-n-gun/slasher into top-down shootout simulation.
But let's review the issues with the game in a bit more organised order, shall we?
Let me start with bugs - game literally crawls with those:
1) In one of the first levels you may encounter immortal SWAT officer with two pistols. You can't kill him. At all. If you shoot him - he will fall down on his back, rest for a while and pop right back up. If you shoot him while he is standing next to wall - he will fall backwards as intended, but if you do so a few more times - forcing him with each fall advance a little bit backwards - he will eventually glitch out of level boundries.
2) You are able to kill enemies through walls with mellee weapons.
3) Enemies are sometimes feeling like spinning around on same spot. Dogs are most commonly known to do it.
4) Enemies are sometimes feeling like VERY rapidly spinning in fatal funnels, which also makes them VERY hard to hit.
5) Second (gun wielding) swan really likes to stuck anywhere it is may only be possible. Especially he loves to do it on spawn, but as soon as swan #1 leaves the spawn - it becomes locked, therefore trapping swan #2 without any chance of saving him from there
6) You are able to teleport through walls or doors if you decide to finish off the enemy wich just happens to be behind wall or door
7) This one is more like game design flaw, but still - enemies are always clipping through one another if they feel like they need it. Which often results in, for example, two dogs using the same route to approach the enemy. But player visually is able to see only single dog, since the second dog is running "inside" the visible dog, therefore granting the player a false sense of advantage.
8) Game simply fails to bloody launch for quite a lot of people
9) Somehow developers managed to oversee the very popular issue with non-latin symbols in user name even though the game has russian localisation.
10) Basicly any bug from Hotline Miami Enhanced Edition applies here with few expectations.
11) In most cutscened featuring the stairs you are able to descend/ascend the stairs, changing the scenery but staying behind the transaction point. Moving anywhere will cause the game to change the scenery to previous floor, since the game detected that you are behind the transaction zone, but it will lead in player appearing behind the transaction zone of previous floor, where he attempts to move and game detects that player is behind the transation zone and changes the scenery to... you got the idea.
12) Doors and cutscenes. If doors are to have feelings - the first feeling they would have is a love. Love to move. There is nothing more pleasant for door but to open-close itself very rapidly during cutscenes.
The gameplay:
1) I especially love the swans (two characters working in pair with one another.). While the idea is very appealing and had a great tactical potentional behind it - there are quite a few issues with that
1-a) First of all, as mentioned before, second swan REALLY likes to get stuck.
1-b) Also, the same second swan often feels like not keeping up or hiding behind the corner, basicly making the whole idea of covering fire obsolete, since most often he is not able to hit enemies from his position and therefore endangers his partner.
1-c) Second swan is practically invisible to enemies and never takes any damage, like that stupid girl from Last of us.
At this point, I simply refused to pick swan duet until forced by the game since it is simply unplayable in it's current state.
Continuing with gameplay issues:
2) Level design changed from comforting maze of industrial or residential buildings to... unsultingly wide open boxes of industrial or residentual building.
Why is it bad?
2-a) It greatly cripples the value of mellee weapons, forcing player to pick firearms over the sharp steel, because player will often find himself in situation where he needs to cover A LOT of empty ground in order to reach gun-wielding enemy.
2-b) If firearm is not available or circumstances are simply not favorable for player, he often finds himself simply camping an waiting... and waiting...until those cinrcumstances are finally changed to his favor. Alternative is dying and starting over, but then:
2-c) Levels are frikkin' enormous sometimes and it takes at least twice more time to cover a floor as if compared to the first game. Some of you may say that this is a good thing since it adds the challenge, but I tend not to agree with those of you simply because it breakes the pace of what was supposed to be a fast-paced action.
2-d) Most players will eventually find themself walking with SHIFT (looking far away in direction) almost constantly, since most of the rooms/hallways for some unknown reason manage to cover two screens. Sometimes even three. Add it up to nauseating effect that SHIFT-walking induces in player - and you got yourself a bad mood after 15 minutes of a gameplay.
3) The camera. While the camera acts more or less adequately while simply walking around, you will be, as I mentioned before, find yourself SHIFT-walking to simply be able to observe the situation within the limits of single room. However, the behavior of camera while holding SHIFT, walking and trying to aim at something distant is... not pleasant.
4) AI. AI is even more stupid than in first game.
4-a) It is able to pinpoint the source of the gunshot, but fails to give a single ♥♥♥♥ about anything else.
4-b) AI is able to detect the sound of gunshot at a set range, but level design was not accounted for. If you see the enemy behind the wall, approach the wall and shoot the gun - he will run through the whole map, but will eventually come to the exact location where shot was fired. While his comrades in room next to you will not give a damn.
4-c) Some enemies will simply ignore gunshots even if you shoot at point-blank range, those are most commonly smoking or otherwise occupied enemies.
4-d) As in previous game, enemies will completely ignore the havoc around them, blood, gore, breaking glass around them, flying by them bullets unless they see or hear the reason of those festives - the player. As well as they completely ignore gunshots of other hostile (to player) entities. They will completely ignore the fact that the guy standing next to them suddenly drops dead. Some specific kinds of enemies even ignore the fact that they were shot and now bleeding to death, proceeding with patrolling as usual.
4-e) Gunshot noise was SEVERELY reduced if you compare it to previous game. Which allows players to easily exploit it by simply standing next to a doorway and shooting a single bullet to attract attention of few enemies, dispatch them as they approach a fatal funnel and repeat process if necessary. As for now, this is most efficient way to play through the game.
5) Levels featuring the conflict in Hawai are easily completed by simply camping next to ammo boxes. There are plenty of enemies that are impossible to dispatch without a gun and since you are getting only a single gun - you are chained to this damn box of bullets.

I bought this game a while back during a SteamSale for ~3 bucks. I have not regretted it.
Gametime: With a "first time through"-time of ~3 hours this game definitly is on the shorter side of games but for a price like that I was not disappointed. When you know what you are doing and try to rush things, you can even finish this game under an hour.
Gameplay: This is your typical 2D Jump & Shoot game. Not much new here but what it does it does well enough to be played. There are also a lot of collectibles to be found throughout the world.
Graphics: The game plays on a 2D-plane, but still looks very pretty IMO. One has to admit, though, that a lot of fog is used on the background, but given the type of game this is, it makes sense and is still well executed!
Sound: Backgroundmusic is not really scary at "scary" party and not really actionlike on actionparts. That is actually good, because it does not distract from the gameplay that much. (I won't buy the soundtrack of the game, either, though!)
The Voiceacting is kind of bad at points but overall average!
Story: Yeah, as you might have guessed, this is a generic zombie-apocolypse-story. There is a twist at the end and another twist at the bonus ending but even those are not really out of the ordinary!

I know that this review is gonna get me a lot of flame, but I believe that this game, aside from the bad optimization and low fov, actually has some value to it.
Let me put it simply. The singleplayer is not bad, although I ran into the game crashing on one mission and I wasn't able to progress past that point. That's a big problem and isn't acceptable for a next gen game. But what I want to focus on is the multiplayer.
The multilayer has 3 aspects: normal PvP, Squads, and Extinction. As you can see from my hours spent, I have quite the amount of time spent in it, and all of it thanks to what I think the saving grace of this game is: Squads.
What is Squads exactly? Squads mode is bassically a multiplayer mode that allows ou to level a virtual squad that can be used in the regular multiplayer. This comes in three flavors: Safeguard, Squad Assult and my personal favorite: Wargame. What this allows you to do is to play the normal multiplayer BUT against bots.
Now, A lot of people might think of it to be vitriolic to play with bots, but for people with a slow internet connection and who live nowhere near where games are being played it's the only option. The bots are smart, fairely competent and are quite fun to play with due to the fact that they dont flash bm or yell at you for stupid reseaons. For people like me who don't have the ping to play compeititvely online, this was a saviour as it gave me the Call of Duty experiance that I wanted without having to suffer from terrible lag.
Yes, there is optimization problems, yes, the fov is bad, but for me, as a person who loves playing by himself the squads mode was enough to fill my 100+ hours of multiplayer experiance. And I'm still not done with it.
The other mdes, such as Extinction and Safeguard are really good to solo, where Safeguard actually gives you an extra AI squad member to play with so it's not insanely imbalanced.
So if you are like me and love playing with bots (I know your out there), then this game isn't a bad choice. Mechanically, it sound and the graphics, although dated, is not exactly hideous. But I recommend buying it with caution, esspecially if you have fov problems.
So not a hearty recommendation, but if you just want to play by yourself and don't mind 30 fps and the fov, then it's a safe buy.
EDIT: I realize that my review doesn't show how many multiplayer hours I spent, but as of today, I have spent 155 hours in the multiplayer. Quite amaing for a crappy game, no?

In the trailers, they NEVER mentioned that we are gonna get small confined maps full of zombies that can spawn just from anywhere, and only a handful of 'survivors'.

just a 'go here, find this, go there'-like objectives. Firearms are limited and zombies come at you in endless numbers. It's the same ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t every round.

You run around, fight zombies by unrewarding and boring fighting mechanisms, and you get to the end 'somehow'.
Perhaps they wanted to make a zombie sandbox game. I thought that's what this could be. I was wrong.

In a deathmatch game, those with best camping skills are rewarded.

I can see what they wanted to make. In their imaginations, this was the best realistic zombie simulator.

This game is great. In some ways, it's better than the first, and in others, it's worse.
First things first, this game
. The lore is pretty deep, and it goes into some characters you see in the first game (Beard and Jake) and explains why they are there, and were there in the first place.
Jacket, although canoncially still there, is replaced by a new gang of 4 "masked murderers." They all have their own abilities, and actually are pretty fun to play. It just comes down to what levels they are the most useful on. The other new characters aren't anything special, but they are all connected in the game in some way, for example
Coming down to story and how it's explained, it's a great story, and I wanted to keep going. The way it's presented is weird, though. The game constantly shifts from person-to-person, and you'll go from 1991 to 1989 to 1985, and then back to 1991. It's honestly hard to follow. You get caught up in what happens with one person, then you just shift back to another and get thrown right into their story again. The dialogue is also pretty shallow at points, and there is plenty of dialogue in this game. It's a change for the good, though, because you get the right idea of who these people are and why they're here.
Gameplay-wise, it's all the same. You have your group of characters that function the same as Jacket, but you also have more unique characters. Beard, however, is the hardest out of them all. You pick a weapon before you start, and you have to balance your use of knife and gun. It adds an extra challenge, and is actually pretty fun.
Music is absolutey amazing, just like the first. Difference is, there are 50 tracks in this game, and all of the music sounds more professionally done and better than the first, but doesn't hold the power the first had.
Artwork, again, is really the same, except there is far more detail in the scenery and in the animations.
Enemy AI is also pretty much the same, except it's been improved on a little bit in this game, and the enemies themselves fuction fairly well. I expect bug fixes, though, becuase I'm sock of enemies 5 feet away not seeing me through doors and then getting stuck in them, invincible, and dogs spinning around endlessy in some corners.
Level design is fair, with some levels having good and complex designs for each area, and some just being too open and having too many enemies. It's more frustrating when you keep dying in this game than it was before because there are more ridiculous things that can happen.
If you're going to buy either of these two games, start with the first. Hotline 2 is more focused on explaining why things were in the first game, and going on about what happens after all of the previous events cool over. The first one is more fun to play, and this one is more of a linear, story-based game.
+ A story that allows you to follow the perspectives of each character
+ Improved pixel artwork and animation quality
+ Killer soundtrack with over double the amount of songs from the first game
+ A (Mostly) functioning level editor is now available and fun to play with (With a new character, too)
+ A hard mode that's unlockable after completing the game, giving you mroe challenge and playtime
- Level design is way too big and has the possibility of you dying to cheap off-screen kills
- You constantly switch between characters and their perspectives during the game, and it breaks up the story immensely
- Melee combat is not as effective as before due to throw range being literally 5 feet in front of you and oversized levels, RIP
- Alex and Ash function like toddlers (But still fun to play as)
- You can't skip the Dennaton Games intro anymore.
The game is great but it comes with its flaws, and overall I find it a worthy sequel to the first but completely different from the first in every way. If you loved the fast-paced gameplay from HM1 and preferred the idea of quick thinking, then wait until this goes on sale.

One of the best Zombie games available. From the modding team that brought you Zombie Panic Source comes Contagion, a standalone game which involves co-op and PvP elements across several game modes.
I would play this game with friends, but complete strangers can often work well in a team too. Contagion has various game modes, "Escape" which involves a group of survivors escaping an area, such as a Police Station and City area. "Hunted" which pits human players against one-another in a world populated with zombies that just want a good meal. Finally there is "Extraction" which has a group of survivors looking for NPC's in a remote area and defend them against the zombies in the worldspace, and then lead them to safety. Each of these game modes has several difficulty levels.
Mechanics are relatively standard for an FPS, with the ability to drop ammo and switch ammo types to give to your teammates, the melee system is also well made and works well for those not looking to draw attention to their kills, I would give them an 8/10 as there can sometimes be annoying glitches or inaccurate shots. Remember, these Zombies actually pack a punch so don't get trapped and always aim for the head, a headshot is easily worth 20 chest shots.
Sounds easily gets a 10/10, each weapon sounds unique as well as the game worlds and Zombies.
Graphics are again amazing, a 9/10 for these. There is optional gibbing, which allows the player to blow chunks out of a zombie, blow their legs out from underneath them or just make a head go boom. numerous graphics settings also let you customise your game, and seem to be well optimised as well.
Overall I would give this game a 9/10 and recommend it as a must-buy to anyone who enjoys the zombie genre.

Deadlight is a sidescrolling survival horror/puzzle game with nice presentation value, mostly solid controls, and a tendency to take itself just a bit too seriously in the story department.
Let me clarify: for its price, this isn't a bad title by any means. The above strengths make up for the shortcomings well enough. It's just that when you have a game with a setup this relatively simple, you'd expect it to surprise you in at least a few ways. Portal did this with a pitch-black sense of humor that blended seamlessly with a frighteningly sterile, claustrophobic atmosphere. Unfortunately, while the atmosphere is certainly there, there are a few things that really hamper the experience its trying to create.
The Abe's Odysee style sidescrolling makes for some great visuals, as the interplay of the background and foreground does a lot to enhance the otherwise banal sight of zombies wandering around the broken urban landscape. Sadly this leads to a bit of frustration when you can't tell if a zombie is within axing range or just outside, and you'll burn up your  stamina or bullets really fast swinging or shooting frantically at the so-called "Shadow" only to find that he'll still get ahold of you. Furthermore, there is some highlighting of climbable surfaces, but its not terribly consistent, so often of times you'll die in the same space over and over only to find there was a wire or pipe you could have latched onto. It gets even worse when the game reflex-tests you by sliding down a hill or chasing you through the busy streets, all the while tripping over piles of cardboard boxes you had no idea were in your way to begin with and wondering why you couldn't just take the staircase instead of hopping from handrail to handrail like an Assassin's Creed character. A few times I walked by a zombie trapped in a car and was a little disapointed that he couldnt reach me from where he was, a missed opportunity for a trap mechanic for all those times you're in a hurry to take cover. Use of the sort-of 2D is excellent visually, but from a game mechanic standpoint I wish it had been developed more.
Melee combat is appropriately messy and hectic, though sometimes a bit too much as occasionally you'll whiff completely on a finishing blow you know should have connected. The stamina bar that depletes with everything from climbing and swinging to running and simply holding onto a ledge also gives you good cause to mind your limits, as running out makes your swings pitifully ineffective and slow. Ammo however should not have been so plentiful at times, and headshots get far too easy when you realize all the zombies are roughly the same height and typically come at you from the same angle, though some will duck a bit lower to charge. It gets the most intense when you start to see zombies pour in from the background and you know it just isnt worth the risk to clear all of them, forcing you to find a way to get out of reach double-quick. I especially like how hard they are to get past when they group up, and how fast you die if you just try to shove past them, which has the nice effect of making you pay attention to all the angles so you can avoid or go around them. The puzzles are bit basic and usually involved shooting a target to clear the way, moving a block to climb up, or in a few circumstances--I wish there were more-- baiting a zombie into a trap. They work fine as a way of breaking up the game's more frantic moments, but they could stand to be a bit more challenging.
I won't go too far into the soundtrack, except to say that it sets the tone wonderfully. The sound as a whole in this game presents itself adequately: the zombies sound like zombies, the guns sound like guns.
And then Randall opens his mouth.
This game's writing has what I like to call "Hideo Kojima syndrome": the story isn't exactly bad, but the writing is horrendous to the point where the voice acting is hard to judge because you can't tell if they're phoning it in or speaking at the grade level they assume the audience to be. Every line from Randall or any of the characters sounds like something you'd hear in a middle school creative writing class: obvious, redundant, and surprising only in its capacity to convey only the vaguest impression of an emotion.  And while this game's story goes through the motions of practically every zombie-themed game or movie--main character looking for his family which may or may not be dead, predatory military scavengers leeching off of survivors, one lone supporting character survivor at the end, etc--it could have easily been redeemed with some  greatly improved writing to go with the honestly pretty damn good atmosphere this game already has. The concept-art cutscenes range from boring to unintentionally hilarious, especially at the end when the main character has a terrifying revelation that (insert the most obvious twist ever here) and his eyes go so wide I wanted to take a screenshot and use it as my steam icon, preferably with humorous text at the bottom.
"YER DEAD!"
--stereotypical southern military dude, who was at least nice enough to let me turn around, draw, and kill him in spite of having me in his sights the whole time.
Wait a second, this game takes place in Canada! What are stereotypical southern military dudes doing in...nevermind.
So why am I recomending this game? Because I'm a sucker for it's spiritual predecessor, Abe's Odysee. BecauseI love the visuals that the 2D plane grants and the jumping, running, and climbing feel really good. Because I don't always feel in control of the combat. Because its a game that dares to do something new with a motif that's been done to death in other genres. and that alone makes it very hard for me to dislike this game. So go ahead, take a chance. At worst, you'll be giving a developer with considerable potential a shot at making a better game later.

Like Left 4 Dead? Wish it had progression and variety? Well this is the game for you.
Seriously, it's about time someone took the L4D formula and improved upon it. This game is pretty much exactly what you would want from a L4D-inspired game. The basic formula is the same but there's so many improvements that make it more refreshing to play. Also the difficulty is much higher. It's much harder to protect yourself against all incoming threats, the chances of you not taking damage are very unlikely.
Satisfying melee combat, effective but limited range capabilities. That's more so the kind of game this is in comparison to Left 4 Dead. There's much more emphasis on melee combat, and you'll really want to save your ranged ammo for special enemies. Funnily enough, this game has its own version of the Smoker/Jockey, the Hunter, the Spitter, and the Tank,
The Smoker-like enemy grabs you from a range much like a Smoker, but he drags you away from your team much like a Jockey. The Hunter-like enemy pounces you, but is capable of teleportation in order to escape. The Spitter-like enemy is much more threatening than a Spitter, as he throws acid jars that cover huge distances and is capable of throwing more than 1. The Tank-like enemy is pretty much the exact same as its L4D counterpart, big huge brute that takes A LOT of damage, while punching and knocking people away from it. The difference though is that in this game, you can block his punches with melee weapons, which while still deals damage to you, it prevents knockback.
Each character you can play as has specific weapon types they can use, and you can change between any of them at any time. You can mix, salvage, and upgrade weapons respectively. You get weapon drops from completing levels via dice rolls. You can improve your chances of good dice rolls by picking up Tomes in the level, which take up your medkit slot. So you have to do some risk and reward stuff. Get better rewards by going without a medkit, or play it save and bring a medkit with you.
Overall, there's a lot more to this game, and I really hope they continue to support it with more content in the future. There's so much they can do with it, and I hope they don't waste their opportunities like Valve did with Left 4 Dead.

Pros:
-Great melee system - every weapon feels responsive and is different to use.
-Loot based system that adds replayablity.
-Really nice graphics that set the mood and atmosphere of a fantasy world on the eve of the end of the world.

-Very challenging game - at least right now on normal.   You will need to have good teamwork and gear to go past Normal.

-13 levels at release - the three levels they have in the pre-order beta are enough fun for a few hours though, and each level will have a lot of replaybility thanks to the tomes and grimories, which are optional objectives that will give you better loot if you get to the end with them.
Cons:
-Some odd bugs here and there still with Skaven appearing out of thin air, or through walls.   Nothing majorly breaking with the exception of the now and again crash.
-Some performance/optimization issues need to be ironed out a bit but I have faith that the devs will get that taken care of.
Bottom line is that if you like co-op games, you like L4D or Warhammer Fantasy in general ,you need to buy this game.  At 30$ the game is very reasonably priced.

Jason Brody cries out in horror the first time he watches his brother murder a man. When the sibling kills again, there’s a vulnerable tremble to Jason’s whimpering whisper. “I can’t do this, Grant.”
Shortly afterward, in a moment of panicked self-defense, Jason rams a machete through an attacker’s throat.
Far Cry 3 establishes a bleak and mature tone out of the gate. Jason, our protagonist, should fear the pirates running the tropical retreat of Rook Island. In his eyes, killing is not cool. Not yet. The emotional weight only gets heavier as he tries to save his missing friends from slave-trading psychopaths. In turn, Jason’s gradual transformation from coward to killer unfolds in a natural, believable way, which compensates for the narrow revenge premise. As its unpredictable, often uncomfortable story comes unhinged, Far Cry 3 challenges players’ principles: How far would you go to protect the people you love, and what kind of person would you become to get them back?
Jason’s allies and enemies don’t feel like video game characters – they feel like people.
Jason begins his evolution after escaping the clutches of Vaas, the mentally unstable leader of a pirate gang and the man who’s kidnapped his friends and family. Before having you hunt down Vaas, Far Cry 3 focuses nearly an hour on teaching you survival skills. Jason scavenges supplies, harvests plants, and crafts useful items from animal skins before ever firing a gun at a man. Choose not to take advantage of the wildlife at large and you’re missing out on important upgrades; bigger wallets hold more cash to buy better weapons, weapon holsters house additional firearms, and larger rucksacks store more goods. Motivation drives exploration because there’s a purpose for everything on Rook Island.
The many secrets hidden in its gigantic, open world aren’t arbitrary video game collectibles. Lost letters from World War II detail past struggles on Rook Island. Stray memory cards detail the depravity of its drug operations. Disregard the first-person shooter veneer – yes, this is a violent action game, but that’s a small slice of a grand adventure. There’s a history to Rook Island that bolsters the astonishing sense of place established by the captivating culture and scenery. You’ll explore ancient underground ruins, walk among the locals, and buddy up with the leaders of the native Rakyat tribe. It’s this allegiance that puts Brody on his dark path.The Rakyat can give Jason the power he needs to save his friends, brother, and girlfriend.
This is where Far Cry 3’s character progression comes in. The more brutally and often he kills, the more experience Brody earns to become a better murderer. Before long, the man who couldn’t handle the sight of blood learns to chain vicious machete executions, fire pistols from ziplines, and throw knives into eyeballs from 20 meters out. Fear disappears. Jason starts enjoying the slaughter.
Loss of control is an important theme throughout Far Cry 3. Jason and the majority of the main cast have a hard time keeping it together, either because they’re coming unglued or have already lost it. Jason’s allies and enemies don’t feel like video game characters – they feel like people, largely because the fantastic performances are among the best acting in video games. Vaas’ manic outbursts make you fear his volatility; his madness is amusing until he snaps. His boss Hoyt is frightening because he’s as intelligent as he is irrational. As a wise old butler once said, some men just want to watch the world burn – Hoyt wants to profit on scorching the earth. Meanwhile, Vaas’ rivalry with the Rakyat gives him a reason to put Jason down.
Jason, while not necessarily likable, is a great lead because of his relatable flaws. He and his friends lived a posh, pre-paid life in Santa Monica, but immaturity strained his relationships and ambition. Murder is the first thing he’s been good at and he starts living for it. “It feels like winning,” he tells a freaked-out friend.
And it does. The allure of Far Cry has always been the open-ended tactical choices available during each encounter, and the variety of ways you could take down targets. With dynamic variables like aggressive wildlife and roaming pirates, your stealth and aggro options open up more than ever. I loved letting bears and tigers out of their cages in pirate outposts – the animals took care of the dirty work for me and I’d claim the enemy’s checkpoint as my own.
Causing panic is great, too. Like Far Cry 2, Molotovs or explosive barrels cause chaotic fires that trap and burn enemies. You can combine these last couple things if you’re a real sicko – flaming bears are a frightening sight. You could snipe thugs from a mountaintop, drive into a camp with Rakyat warriors (or C4 charges) in the back seat, or use a knife and bow to kill quietly. If you’re really bold, why not stab a couple guys after dropping from your hang-glider?
The satisfaction of claiming an enemy stronghold as your own is the same regardless of how you get it done. These bases become hubs for selling loot found in chests, buying better weapons, and attaching scopes and silencers. Better yet, they’re fast-travel spots, allowing you to navigate Rook Island’s breadth efficiently. Outposts are a great convenience, but they also represent something larger. Where Far Cry 2 positioned you in the middle of a civil war to play both sides, Far Cry 3 gives you a one-sided goal: Take over the island and spread the Rakyat tribe’s influence. This is the imprint Jason leaves on the world, and the reason he’s destined for Rook Island.
The cooperative mode shares the predictable progression system, but compensates with a character-driven side-story campaign focusing on entertaining moments rather than depth. Those characters are as uneven as the co-op design, though. Mikhail the Russian and Callum the Scot are funny dudes whose one-liners make them feel like unlikely action heroes. Their partners, on the other hand, are obnoxious, annoying clichés who feel like they just learned about profanity.
Co-op leaves the open world behind in favor of linear levels with branching paths – with three or four players, taking advantage of high ground and flanking positions gives your team an incredible sense of empowerment. With just two, it becomes a frustrating grind. Enemies don’t scale, and the missions are specifically designed for four people. You’ll need a full crew to protect bomb-carriers while blowing up bridges or guarding vehicles from enemy waves. At times, it feels like a mindless shooter with senseless direction, but there are brief bursts of friendly fun in blowing up walls, driving quads, and wiping out hundreds of enemies.
Both online modes feel superfluous and out of place, but neither is bad. Both serve a purpose for a certain crowd, but the kind of person who connects with Jason Brody’s story likely won’t fall for simple co-op and a forced-but-functional competitive side.
It’s easy to see why someone would want to visit Rook Island – it’s a stunning tropical location with plenty of fun activities, scenic views, and history worth discovering. Far Cry 3 disrupts that paradise to challenge your feelings about enjoying violence. Because of lunatics like Hoyt and Vaas, you’ll see beautiful things you never would have. You’ll do terrible things that make you uncomfortable and meet fascinating, disgusting people. You’ll sympathize with Jason Brody’s difficult choices as he turns from vapid young man into a monster.
Far Cry 3 is important for the same reason as Far Cry 2. It’s a shooter that considers shooters thoughtfully, both in the way they’re designed and the way we play them, and then asks us to do the same. Should massacring hundreds be a great way to entertain ourselves? Maybe not. But it is.
